US imposes sanctions on International Criminal Court, hours after former judge wins Nobel
Oct 9 - US President Donald Trump's administration imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court on Friday, hours after one of its former judges won the Nobel Peace Prize, putting Washington on a diplomatic collision course with European allies.
The Trump administration has long been hostile to the court and has previously imposed sanctions on its prosecutors and judges. Friday's move would go far further, by potentially punishing companies that provide services to the court itself.
"President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement reviewed by Reuters ahead of the official announcement.
"That is why, today, the United States is sanctioning the International Criminal Court. We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate."
Washington has long been angry over ICC arrest warrants issued for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and over a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan which the ICC has since closed.
The court, founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide, counts 125 countries as member states, including all EU countries and all members of the NATO alliance apart from the United States and Turkey.
It has received strong public backing in the past from member countries including major US allies, and is based in the Netherlands, an EU and NATO member.
Navi Pillay, the South African jurist who won the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday for her work in international criminal justice, served as a judge on the ICC's Appeals Chamber from 2003-2008. In its citation, the prize committee said it had sought to "issue a reminder" at a time when "judges and institutions of international law are under political attack".
"An international legal system in which war criminals are held to account and the victims of abuse see justice served is a precondition for a peaceful world," the committee said.
Rubio said the sanctions had been structured to give the court and its member states an opportunity to address US concerns.
He did not provide further details, but a senior State Department official said the US Treasury would issue a set of licenses "to protect American interests", an apparent reference to temporary exemptions to some sanctions.
US EXPECTS ALLIES TO 'REIN IN THE COURT'
US sanctions typically bar all US-based companies from any work with a sanctioned organization, forcing banks to shut accounts, insurers to end coverage and software companies to halt cooperation.
The Trump administration previously imposed targeted sanctions on court officials during his first term, which were rescinded under President Joe Biden. Washington announced new sanctions just days after Trump returned to office in January 2025.
Court officials have been preparing for months for the prospect of sanctions on the court itself, shifting office computers from Microsoft software to open source equivalents and making new arrangements for banking and health insurance.
The court's registrar Osvaldo Zavala Giler called earlier this week for the EU to be prepared to use a so-called "blocking mechanism" that lets it shield European countries from the extra-territorial effects of sanctions.
In his statement, Rubio said the United States had delayed its sanctions hoping that the ICC and the countries party to its founding Rome Statute would address US concerns, but they had failed to do so.
"Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC. We expect our allies, many of whom are part of the ICC and that rely on American servicemembers for their defense, to rein in the court," Rubio said.
"We have structured this action to provide an opportunity for States Parties to negotiate and present a solution to address our concerns. If these efforts do not bear fruit, we will continue to adjust accordingly," Rubio said. REUTERS

EU aviation body widens Saudi airspace warning after Houthi strikes
Oct 9 - Europe's EASA aviation safety body said on Friday it had expanded the area of Saudi Arabian airspace where it recommended airlines not to operate, after Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis attacked Riyadh airport.
In an update to a conflict zone information bulletin first issued on September 30, the EU regulator said recent attacks demonstrated the Houthis' ability and intent to strike targets deeper inside Saudi territory, including the capital. EASA added an area in northwestern Saudi Arabia to the advisory.
Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said earlier on Friday that three Saudi nationals were killed and several people were injured in two attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Thursday.
The Houthis have renewed threats against airlines flying to Saudi Arabia and said on Thursday they had struck the capital's airport with two cruise missiles.
"These recurrent missile and drone attacks, together with the activation of air-defence systems, create an increased risk of misidentification of civil aircraft, as well as risks associated with missile and drone overflights, interception activity and falling debris," EASA said.
OPSGROUP, a membership-based organisation with almost 10,000 aviation professionals that shares flight risk information, sent a "do not fly" warning for Saudi Arabia to its members on Friday, citing risks of sustained missile attacks and "misjudgment" in defensive responses.
"We now recommend avoiding operations in Saudi Arabia entirely, including the use of Saudi airports as en route alternates," it said in the memo shared with Reuters.
LUFTHANSA, INDIAN AIRLINES SUSPEND FLIGHTS
Following Thursday's attacks, Lufthansa Group and three Indian airlines said they would suspend flights to Riyadh expected in the coming days.
King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh is Saudi Arabia's second-busiest airport after Jeddah. It handled 296,800 flights in 2025, equivalent to about 813 a day, according to Saudi Arabia's General Authority for Statistics.
Global flight tracker FlightRadar24 showed 131 flights to and from Riyadh had been cancelled by 1305 GMT on Friday after hundreds of cancellations the previous day. REUTERS

Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of ‘all-out invasion’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of ‘all-out invasion’
Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of sending troops deep into its territory and warned that it must defend itself against an “all-out invasion,” escalating a confrontation between the former allies.
Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos alleged that Eritrean forces, including mechanized units, had advanced up to 60 km into Tigray. His October 8 letter was addressed to French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot and circulated to other UN Security Council members, Reuters reported Friday. The letter described the incursion as a “blatant act of aggression” and sought international support for Ethiopia’s right to self-defense.
Ethiopia’s Foreign Ministry said on Thursday that Gedion briefed UN Deputy Secretary-General Amina J. Mohammed on what it called Eritrea’s “continued aggression,” demanded the immediate withdrawal of Eritrean forces and urged a “clear and principled UN response.”
In separate talks with senior UN officials, Ethiopian State Minister Berhanu Tsegaye alleged direct Eritrean military involvement “across different fronts along the border” and called for the UN to unequivocally condemn the “flagrant violations of sovereignty.”
Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel rejected Ethiopia’s accusations on Friday, calling them “audacity and duplicity in their most extreme forms.” He accused Addis Ababa of pursuing a war of aggression for more than three years, citing statements by Ethiopian leaders about acquiring sovereign access to the Red Sea and taking control of the port of Assab.
There are fears that renewed clashes between federal forces and Tigrayan fighters could plunge northern Ethiopia back into war. The Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which formed an alliance with six other armed groups seeking to overthrow Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government, declared a “defensive war” last month. Its forces seized airports in Mekelle, Tigray’s regional capital, and the cities of Axum and Shire, prompting Ethiopian Airlines to suspend flights to the region.
On Sunday, the government-allied Tigray Peace Force announced it had retaken Mekelle following the TPLF’s withdrawal. The TPLF said it had decided to “temporarily leave” and operate from another location while continuing military operations.
Conflict monitor ACLED reported suspected Ethiopian drone strikes against Eritrean forces near the border town of Adigrat on Wednesday and Thursday. A resident told Reuters that explosions continued overnight into Friday.
Ethiopia has accused Eritrea, Egypt, and Sudan of supporting the rebel alliance. The three countries have rejected the allegations. Last week, Addis Ababa expelled ten Eritrean diplomats and closed its embassy in Asmara, prompting Eritrea to sever diplomatic ties. Eritrean troops previously backed Ethiopia’s federal army during the 2020-2022 Tigray war, which ended with the Pretoria peace agreement.
Relations with Eritrea have deteriorated over Ethiopia’s pursuit of sovereign access to the Red Sea. Ethiopia became landlocked when Eritrea gained independence in 1993, and Asmara views Addis Ababa’s ambitions as a threat to its sovereignty.
The African Union has urged restraint, while UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has called for dialogue to resolve the disputes between the Horn of Africa states and prevent further escalation.

Who is Navi Pillay, winner of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:02:58 UTC
23:02:58 KST

Who is Navi Pillay, winner of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize?
The 85-year-old South African judge has spent decades fighting apartheid and genocide.
South African judge Navanethem “Navi” Pillay has been awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize, becoming the fifth South African to win it.
Making the announcement on Friday, the Norwegian Nobel Committee praised Pillay for her decades-long efforts to prosecute genocide and war crimes, which have been marked by “judicial rigour, personal integrity and considerable courage”.
From defending activists in apartheid-era South Africa, to more recently overseeing a United Nations inquiry which declared Israel responsible for genocide in Gaza, the 85-year-old, who is also a judge at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), has specialised in international law for decades.
Here’s what we know about her life and why she has been awarded the world’s top peace prize:
Who is Pillay?
Navanethem Pillay, known as Navi Pillay, was born in the racially segregated city of Durban in South Africa’s Natal province in 1940 to parents of Tamil descent.
After earning a law degree from the University of Natal, she became the first woman in Natal province to start her own law firm. Early in her career, she helped defend numerous anti-apartheid activists in the country.
She later became the first woman of colour to sit on the High Court of South Africa. She went on to preside over the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR), which prosecuted those charged with humanitarian crimes during the 1994 Rwandan genocide.
Pillay was the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) from 2008 to 2014. More recently she chaired the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory which determined last year that Israel is responsible for carrying out genocide in Gaza.
Currently, Pillay is a judge on the International Court of Justice, acting in a case in which Myanmar is accused of genocide against its mostly Muslim Rohingya minority.
What work is she best known for?
Pillay has spent much of her life advocating for human rights in her home South Africa and abroad. While studying, she took part in boycotts and marches against apartheid. She later joined the legal defence of some of the country’s most prominent anti-apartheid figures, such as Phyllis Naidoo and Strini Moodley.
In 1973, Pillay took on a case that helped secure basic rights, including legal access, for political prisoners on Robben Island, where Nelson Mandela was jailed.
In a 2016 interview with the Diplomatic Courier, Pillay said her early human rights work was “shaped by what (she) had experienced under apartheid”.
“I used many of the challenges to my advantage, I had to learn international humanitarian law so as to defend cases of racial discrimination,” she said.
Pillay oversaw a UN commission of inquiry which concluded in 2025 that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.
In a statement on the report, Pillay urged UN member states to do everything they can to establish a ceasefire in Gaza and to “ensure justice and accountability for all victims”.
What has she been awarded the Nobel Prize for?
The Nobel committee said Pillay was being honoured for her “efforts to promote peace and international law”.
It called her one of “the great defenders of international legal principles in our time”, having helped hold states and national leaders to account and bring “hope to victims of violence and conflict”.
The committee stressed the role Pillay played in the Rwandan genocide tribunal, saying her influence helped establish “that rape and sexual violence could constitute a crime against humanity – as well as genocide”.
“In the same case, Ms Pillay was instrumental in a separate legal breakthrough: for the first time, a defendant faced charges of incitement to commit genocide purely on the basis of spreading propaganda,” said the committee.
Why is her win so significant?
The committee said honouring Pillay is especially important at a time when international law “is under tremendous pressure and its institutions are under attack”.
That message was echoed by rights advocates and international officials.
The UN’s rights chief, Volker Turk, said her award was “a recognition, a reaffirmation that human rights, the rule of law and justice and accountability are fundamental to everything, to peace, to security and prosperity”.
International Criminal Court (ICC) President Tomoko Akane said the award carried special significance “at a time of profound challenges to the international legal order and the rule of law”.
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa praised the award as a tribute to Pillay’s “courage, integrity and lifelong commitment to justice”.
Haakon Gjerlow, acting director of the Peace Research Institute Oslo, said it “sends a clear message that peace depends not only on political leadership, but on strong, credible international institutions and the courageous people who dedicate their lives to defending them .”
Ashok Swain, a professor of peace and conflict research at Uppsala University, told Al Jazeera that the selection of Pillay was a “pleasant surprise” and the “best possible choice”.
He said the Nobel committee likely took into consideration Pillay’s lifelong record fighting genocide and apartheid. He added that the award to the South African jurist could also be read as a message to United States President Donald Trump, who has long argued that he is deserving of the peace prize and whose administration has clashed with South Africa over debunked claims that white Afrikaners are facing “genocide”.
Furthermore, last year, the Trump administration issued sanctions against members of the ICC in what many critics saw as an attack on the system of international law.
The ICC had previously issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity.
The ICC responded by describing the US sanctions as a “flagrant attack against the independence of an impartial judicial institution” and the victims of war crimes around the world. It said it would continue its work “without regard to any restriction, pressure or threat”.
How has Pillay responded?
Pillay appeared to learn of the award as media reports circulated, telling a group of supporters applauding her: “I don’t know about this. So my question is: Is it true?”
She also jokingly referenced Trump, saying, “If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump.”
Once the news was confirmed, Pillay said she would dedicate the award to “all of the survivors of international crimes”.
“This award strengthens my conviction that we must stand together in defence of the rule of law, in defence of independent courts and an international legal order based on principle.”
Earlier, the Nobel committee said it had struggled to get in touch with Pillay to notify her. “If you see a Norwegian number calling, please pick up,” said committee chair, Jorgen Watne Frydnes.

A rare double waterspout struck the coast near Marsala, in western Sicily, on Friday, 9 October, before moving inland and causing damage to buildings, vehicles and farmland.
The two swirling columns formed over the sea near Marsala's port before reaching land and moving towards the surrounding Trapani area.
The Alcide De Gasperi school in the Terrenove district was also severely damaged.
In nearby Petrosino, a car was hit by the tornado and thrown into a ravine. The two people inside were injured and taken to hospital.
Footage filmed from the Biscione seafront in Petrosino, near Sibiliana, shows the tornado approaching the mainland from the sea.
The extreme weather left a trail of damage across the coastal area, with emergency services responding to the aftermath.

Ukraine Strikes Russian Missile Launch Institute and Intercontinental Ballistic Missile Disposal Facility
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:02:40 UTC
23:02:40 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Strikes Russian Missile Launch Institute and Intercontinental Ballistic Missile Disposal Facility
Ukrainian forces struck two Russian missile-related facilities in the Nizhny Novgorod region overnight on October 9, targeting infrastructure involved in missile launch systems and the disposal of intercontinental ballistic missiles.
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine confirmed the strikes, identifying the targets as a branch of the Barmin Research Institute of Launch Complexes and a facility responsible for dismantling intercontinental ballistic missiles.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the General Staff, Ukrainian forces hit a facility belonging to the Barmin Research Institute of Launch Complexes, a branch of the Center for Operation of Ground-Based Space Infrastructure, near the settlement of Dalneye Konstantinovo-5.
The institute specializes in the development, maintenance, and operation of missile launch positions, fueling equipment, and missile control systems, making it part of Russia's missile infrastructure.
In a separate operation, Ukrainian forces targeted the Center for the Disposal of Intercontinental Ballistic Missiles near the settlement of Surovatikha, also in the Nizhny Novgorod region.
The General Staff said the strike was intended to weaken Russia's military-industrial capacity to produce explosives and components used in rocket propellants.
In addition to the two facilities in the Nizhny Novgorod region, Ukraine's General Staff confirmed a strike on the Redkino Experimental Plant in Russia's Tver region.
The Redkino Experimental Plant is a major chemical production facility in Russia’s Tver region, specializing in small-batch manufacturing of specialty chemicals. The enterprise produces more than 40 types of chemical products supplied to Russia’s aviation, aerospace, and other industrial sectors.
Its product range includes ferrocene-based compounds used as combustion catalysts in solid-propellant rocket engines, alongside specialized materials, protective coatings, and fuel additives. These substances serve both civilian industrial purposes and military production needs.
Ukrainian forces also targeted the Lukoil-Ukhtaneftepererabotka oil refinery in Ukhta, Russia's Komi Republic, approximately 1,700 kilometers from the Ukrainian border, as Kyiv continues strikes against Russian energy facilities in response to Moscow's attacks on Ukrainian territory.

Fjord Details a Family’s Sudden Nightmare in Norway
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:02:05 UTC
23:02:05 KST

Romanian filmmaker Cristian Mungiu makes thoughtful movies about social issues that cross international borders: In 4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days, a young Romanian woman risks her life for an illegal abortion. R.M.N. explores xeno-phobia in a small Transylvanian village, dissecting the complexity of spontaneous human impulses in the process. Mungiu’s films can spur us to think anew about issues we’d rather keep in the background, and they can at times be deeply moving. They can also feel dreary and instructive, in an eat-your-vegetables way.
Mungiu’s Fjord, which won the Palme d’Or at Cannes earlier in the year, offers a healthy dose of very nutritious vegetables, and in places the story almost—almost—stretches the bounds of believability. But its actors, including Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve, as well as two young newcomers, make you believe in one family’s sudden nightmare. Do the authorities entrusted to protect our children always know what’s best for them? Fjord suggests, provocatively, that the answer may not always be yes.
Mihai Gheorghiu (Stan), who is Romanian, and his Norwegian wife Lisbet (Reinsve) have just relocated with their five children from Romania to Norway, to be closer to Lisbet’s parents. Mihai and Lisbet are also deeply religious, and appear to be raising their children in a sometimes strict but undeniably loving home. One day, at the children’s new school, an instructor charged with protecting the students’ welfare notices a bruise on the shoulder of the eldest Gheorghiu daughter, Elia (Vanessa Ceban). The administrator takes swift action, and before Mihai and Lisbet can fully grasp what’s happening, their children—including their infant, who’s still breastfeeding—are whisked into foster homes. Their struggle to reunite their family involves risky twists and a great deal of frustrating bureaucracy.
Unless you know Norway’s judicial system, you might be tempted to wonder: Could one family really be broken up that fast, with so little evidence? Mungiu’s premise seems somewhat far-fetched, intensified for dramatic reasons, though it’s worth noting that his script is based on a real-life case in Norway. And recently, in the U.S., Child Protective Services interviewed the children of former Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg, separating the children from their fathers for 24 hours, after receiving a tip alleging that they were at risk. The report was proved false, but the incident shows how easily a system designed to protect kids might be manipulated.
Regardless, the plausibility of Fjord’s premise is academic in the context of the performances given by Stan and Reinsve. Reinsve (so terrific in 2025’s Sentimental Value) is resolutely unglamorous here, a dutiful wife and mother decked out in dowdy clothes. But her distress over the loss of her children crosses the planes of her face like a muted shadow; you sense some anger beneath that meek veneer. And Stan, who is Romanian American, gives layers of complexity to Mihai as a father figure. He clearly loves his kids, but he also has a temper. Stan doesn’t make Mihai easy to read, just as the movie around him doesn’t offer any easy conclusions.
Yet amid all the child-custody drama Fjord lays before us, a subplot involving the deepening friendship between Elia and a neighbor couple’s daughter, Noora (Henrikke Lund-Olsen), ends up being the film’s most powerful and moving element. These two young teenagers aren’t just navigating a new friendship; they’re exploring feelings that may or may not be the roots of romantic love. Sometimes kids tell us what we need to know about life, even if it’s not always the lesson we expect or want. And sometimes they steal a movie away from the grownups. Fjord, perhaps unbeknownst even to the man who made it, really belongs to them.

Palantir’s Thiel slams Pope Leo’s AI warnings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Palantir’s Thiel slams Pope Leo’s AI warnings
Pope Leo XIV is tapping into public fears of artificial intelligence (AI) to distract people from the Catholic Church’s latent child sex abuse scandals, Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel has claimed. The gay US tech billionaire also accused former President Barack Obama of exploiting opposition to AI for political gain.
The remarks come as AI developers themselves warn that the technology could soon spiral beyond human control. OpenAI chief Sam Altman and xAI owner Elon Musk have backed calls to slow the development of increasingly powerful AI models after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned that rogue systems could seize control of vast swathes of the internet within months, causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage.
The warnings have fueled demand for the tougher oversight of AI, with rival tech giants calling for safeguards against a technology they fear could evade human control.
During a series of closed-door lectures in Nashville, Thiel singled out both leaders while stepping up his warnings about the Antichrist, a prophesied figure traditionally associated with deception and opposition to the teachings of Jesus. Thiel has argued that such a figure could exploit fears of AI and other catastrophic threats to halt technological progress and impose a heavily regulated “one world government.” His remarks, delivered on September 28 and October 5, were revealed by Politico on Thursday.
“Many people know that AI is politically unpopular and want to leverage that to boost their own popularity,” Thiel said. “Both Obama and the pope fall into this category. Obama knows the Democrats have no ideas, but they can at least oppose AI.”
Obama recently urged Democrats to develop a more comprehensive strategy on artificial intelligence.
The openly gay Republican surveillance company billionaire went on to accuse Leo XIV of using the debate over AI to shift attention away from decades of sexual abuse scandals within the Catholic Church.
“He needed something politically popular to distract from the church’s child sex abuse scandals, and he found it in AI,” Thiel said, referring to the pope’s first encyclical, published in May.
Leo XIV has made AI a major focus of his papacy, warning about the dangers of unchecked development and its impact on human dignity, individual freedoms and the concentration of power.
Earlier this week, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told Politico that the world should accept some “bad things” from AI, including hacks, scams and misuse, in exchange for its benefits. However, he drew the line at “the really catastrophic risks,” including “a serious loss of control to AI.”
Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates has also called for government regulation, warning that AI in the hands of malicious actors could trigger events causing “a billion deaths.” Nobel Prize-winning computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton has similarly warned that increasingly powerful systems could eventually escape human control, with catastrophic consequences for humanity.

Arrested German spy chief lashed out at his old agency over allegations he spied for Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:01:23 UTC
23:01:23 KST

BERLIN — Former German intelligence chief August Hanning angrily challenged his successor after learning that the agency he once headed, the BND, had passed allegations that he was a Russian spy to investigators.
In a three-page letter sent on Aug. 17, less than three months before his arrest this week, Hanning demanded answers to 11 questions from BND President Martin Jäger.
In the letter, obtained by WELT — which, like POLITICO, is part of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network — Hanning complained that the BND had passed allegations by a former intelligence agent that he was a Russian spy to investigators without consulting him.
Advertisement
Jäger did not respond to the letter at the time, according to Hanning, who spoke to WELT before his arrest.
Hanning’s subsequent arrest, including on suspicion of attempted treason, has caused considerable concern abroad. Grzegorz Malecki, the former head of Poland’s foreign intelligence service, told WELT that the case was “extremely concerning” and could deepen allies’ distrust of the BND. He warned this had the potential to undermine intelligence-sharing with Germany.
The BND has also raised eyebrows within Germany’s intelligence community over allegations that it allowed Hanning’s former chief of staff, who is also in custody, to work for Hanning outside his official duties.
While civil servants are generally permitted to take on outside employment, any approval allowing a member of the BND to work for Hanning would have had to be decided at the senior management level, said Günter Heiss, a former intelligence coordinator under former Chancellor Angela Merkel. “Without knowing the details, I would never have approved anything like this had I been in a position of responsibility at the BND.”
Bernd Schmidbauer, a former minister of state and intelligence coordinator under Chancellor Helmut Kohl, told WELT that Hanning had made major contributions to Germany’s national security. The affair was therefore “not only a tragedy for the German intelligence services, but also for the former senior official himself,” Schmidbauer said.
Hanning was among Schmidbauer’s closest aides during the 1990s and went on to lead the BND from 1998 to 2005.
Dirk Banse is an investigative reporter at WELT. Philipp Fritz is WELT’s Eastern Europe correspondent. Uwe Müller is a freelance reporter based in Berlin.

Saudi coalition vows 'firm' response after airport attack
October 9, 2026
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen launched strikes that destroyed targets used by the Houthis, a coalition spokesperson said Friday.
Major General Turki al-Maliki said three rocket launch platforms were destroyed, adding that Houthi attacks on civilians would be met with a "firm response."
The Saudi-Houthi conflict has intensified in recent weeks, with Saudi Arabian authorities having said Friday that Houthi attacks on Riyadh's main international airport on Thursday killed three Saudi citizens and injured several people of "different nationalities."
The King Khalid International Airport was targeted twice on Thursday, the kingdom's civil aviation authority said.The first attack aimed at airport facilities and the second targeted an aircraft that belonged to the Saudia airline.
Houthi attacks on Riyadh raise the stakes of reignited conflict
Hundreds of flights were canceled because of Thursday's attacks, according to flight-tracking site FlightAware.
The Indian Embassy later said Air India had suspended operations through to Saturday, while the Lufthansa Group said its airlines would suspend flights to Riyadh through to October 16.
The European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) on Friday recommended airlines not to operate in additional portions of Saudi Airspace in an updated bulletin.
The EASA said recent attacks had demonstrated the ability and the intent of the Houthis to strike targets deeper inside Saudi territory, including the capital.
On Thursday, the Iran-backed Houthis warned employees at Saudi oil facilities that oil installations remain a target.
The Saudi-Houthi conflict: What to know
The Houthis have fought a Saudi-led coalition since 2015, when the kingdom entered Yemen's civil war to reinstate the internationally backed government in Sanaa. Houthi rebels took control of the capital in 2014.
But ever since, the Saudi-led coalition has found it hard to turn the tide of the war that quieted under a UN-brokered ceasefire in 2022.
In the last weeks, the Houthis stormed down Yemen's coast, capturing a wide swath of territory that has given them greater control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
A Saudi-led coalition has pressed a counteroffensive against the Houthis fighters and recaptured several areas along the strait, Yemeni officials have said. But the fighting appears to be far from over.

Mother, 2 children killed after hippopotamus attack in DR Congo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:00:52 UTC
23:00:52 KST

James Tasamba
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
A mother and her two children were killed when a hippopotamus sank a boat they were sailing in in the northwestern Democratic Republic of Congo, a human rights non-governmental organization said Friday.
The incident took place Thursday night in Bikoro territory in Equateur province, according to Christophe Yoka, coordinator of the Framework for Development and Well-being organization.
Yoka told reporters in Bikoro that the victims were traveling on Lake Tumba at night when a hippopotamus appeared and violently crashed into the canoe they were sailing in.
He said there were four members of the same family on the boat and that only one had survived.
The woman’s body reportedly bore serious injuries attributed to the animal's attack.
The presence of hippos on the lake represents a real danger for the inhabitants who use wooden boats daily to move around and transport their goods, Yoka said, adding that the incident is part of a series of encounters between communities and wildlife.

Latvian citizen handed six years in prison for financing Russian military with €43 donation through Belarus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:00:28 UTC
23:00:28 KST

A Riga city court sentenced Latvian citizen and pro-Russian activist Polina Kamlyova to six years in prison for financing the Russian military. On Oct. 7, the court found that Kamlyova had transferred approximately 43 euros toward the purchase of a device designed to jam drones. She was also sentenced to three years of probation supervision.
Prosecutors said Kamlyova did not transfer the money directly. In December 2024, an acquaintance in Russia linked to the Kaskad military-patriotic special training center asked her to help raise money for the “Kupolny Pokrov REB FPV-4,” an electronic countermeasure system intended to disrupt or jam FPV drones. Due to sanctions, it was not possible to transfer money from a Latvian bank directly to Russia, and so Kamlyova asked an acquaintance in Belarus to make the payment on her behalf without telling him its true purpose. He transferred 157 Belarusian rubles, about 43 euros, from his account to the Russian bank account of Kamlyova’s acquaintance, the Latvian prosecutor’s office said
Kamlyova denied any wrongdoing. In her final statement, published by Baltija.eu, she said she did not know the transfer was intended for military use:
“The prosecution says the messages on my phone concerned a request from the Russian army. But that was not said in the correspondence. I was communicating with a private individual. I did not transfer anything myself; I had no funds. There was no intention to finance the war. There was no intent!”
Kamlyova said the correspondence was found when her phone was checked at the Latvian border after she returned from Russia. She said a State Security Service officer looked through her photographs with her permission but then began reading and photographing her messages on his own phone without her consent. Latvian law enforcement agencies have not officially disclosed how they obtained information about the transfer.
As was reported by the independent exiled publication Mediazona, Kamlyova worked at a garment factory and was a member of the Latvian Russian Union, a political party that appeals to Latvia’s Russian-speaking minority. She ran for a seat on the Rēzekne city council on the party’s ticket in 2017.

The invisible chore that may matter more for women’s relationship happiness than housework
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:00:23 UTC
23:00:23 KST

A new two-part study suggests that women in heterosexual relationships tend to report greater relationship and sexual satisfaction when their male partners share more of the mental and emotional effort required to run a household and relationship. The research, published in Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, also indicates that this behind-the-scenes burden predicts women’s contentment more strongly than the division of physical chores like cleaning or cooking. Men, however, tended to report greater relationship satisfaction when their female partners carried more of this unseen labor.
Research on the division of domestic labor often focuses on routine physical tasks like washing dishes and taking out the trash. Running a home, however, also involves what researchers call the mental load. This concept refers to the nonphysical management of family life, combining cognitive labor, such as anticipating household needs, scheduling appointments, and organizing routines, with emotional labor, such as offering reassurance, calming family tensions, and monitoring a partner’s feelings.
As a 2021 theoretical paper argued, the mental load is often invisible, has no clear boundaries, and is never truly finished. Physical chores have an obvious end point, but remembering to restock groceries, managing a child’s school calendar, or sensing that a partner is distressed can happen at any hour of the day or night.
In a 2019 qualitative study, researchers observed that women disproportionately handle the planning and monitoring tasks in family life, which frequently creates unacknowledged relationship tension. This dynamic fits into broader patterns of relationship balance, such as a study of young adults covered by PsyPost in 2017, which showed that having less power in a romantic partnership tends to harm women far more than men.
The research team, led by Verena Klein of the University of Southampton, wanted to test whether the mental load predicts romantic and sexual satisfaction separately from physical housework. The authors noted that prior work often treated domestic work only as physical actions, leaving out the constant mental organizing that many women carry. They designed two studies to explore how this cognitive and emotional division relates to both partners’ everyday well-being, preregistering the first study’s design and planned analyses.
In the first study, the researchers recruited 452 heterosexual women from the United Kingdom who lived with a male partner. The participants had an average age of about 42 years, their relationship durations ranged from 1 to 44 years, and roughly 55% had at least one child. The participants completed questionnaires assessing how they and their partners divided mental load, who completed routine physical chores, and how strongly they endorsed traditional gender roles. Relationship and sexual satisfaction were each measured using single questions rated on numerical scales.
To capture the mental load, the researchers created a 17-item scale covering five distinct areas: family management, household management, emotional labor related to children, emotional labor focused on the partner, and relationship nurturing. Because no validated measure of mental load existed when the data were collected, the scale was developed for this study. These areas were grouped into two broad measures: relationship mental load, which covers household organization and couple-focused emotional care, and parental mental load, which covers child-focused organizing and reassurance. Participants rated who completed each task on a 5-point scale ranging from “more me” to “more my partner.”
The results of Study 1 indicated that women reported greater relationship and sexual satisfaction when their male partners were more involved in the mental load of the relationship. These associations were modest in size: correlations of 0.24 for relationship satisfaction and 0.15 for sexual satisfaction, on a scale where 0 means no association and 1 means a perfect one.
When looking at specific facets, emotional labor, such as sensing when a partner is upset and planning romantic events, was linked to higher sexual satisfaction, whereas purely administrative cognitive tasks were not. Parental mental load was tied to higher relationship satisfaction for mothers, but its direct association with sexual satisfaction was not statistically significant.
In regression analyses that included physical housework, gender ideology, and relationship mental load at the same time, mental load was the only factor that predicted women’s relationship and sexual satisfaction. However, its link with sexual satisfaction disappeared once the researchers accounted for women’s overall relationship satisfaction, and parental mental load did not predict sexual satisfaction. Physical housework distribution and traditional gender attitudes did not predict satisfaction once mental load was considered.
Women’s mental load was also largely independent of whether they held traditional or egalitarian views on gender roles. This suggested that even women who actively reject conventional domestic roles can still end up carrying this invisible management burden.
“What surprised me most was the role, or rather, the lack of a role, of women’s gender-role attitudes,” Klein told PsyPost. “We expected traditional attitudes to be associated with a more unequal division of housework, and they were. But mental load was different: gender ideology basically didn’t explain who carried it. Even women who explicitly held egalitarian views could still be carrying a disproportionate share.”
“That’s what made this result stick with me: this isn’t simply a belief problem,” she added. “You don’t have to believe that you should be responsible for these things to end up being responsible for them. That doesn’t mean egalitarian attitudes don’t matter. But our findings suggest that they don’t automatically translate into equality in everyday practice.”
While the first study provided important insights from women, it could not capture how both partners within the same couple perceive their division of labor. To address this, the researchers conducted a second study, which was not preregistered, using a dyadic design that surveys both partners together so scientists can examine how each person’s experiences relate to the other. They recruited 156 heterosexual, cohabiting couples from the United Kingdom and the United States through an online platform, with an average age of about 38 years and an average relationship duration of 13 years.
Both partners completed the same questionnaires used in the first study, evaluating their own division of labor alongside single-item satisfaction measures. The researchers used the Actor-Partner Interdependence Model, a statistical technique designed for couples that tests how a person’s own reports and their partner’s reports predict satisfaction outcomes at the same time.
Both men and women agreed that women performed a greater share of household chores and handled substantially more of the mental load. On the scale, a score of 3 meant an equal split, lower scores meant the respondent did more, and higher scores meant their partner did more. Women’s average relationship mental load score was 2.31, indicating that they saw themselves doing more, while men’s was 3.36, indicating that they saw their partners doing more. The gap was even wider for parental mental load (1.71 for women versus 3.53 for men) and smaller for physical chores (2.57 versus 3.18).
“What’s striking is how clear this inequality was,” Klein noted. “In our couples data, both women and men reported that women were carrying more of it, this wasn’t just women perceiving an inequality that men didn’t see. Both partners’ reports pointed the same direction.”
When examining how this division related to satisfaction, the authors discovered a gender difference. For women, relationship and sexual satisfaction were highest when relationship mental load was shared equally between partners. In contrast, men reported greater relationship satisfaction when their female partners handled a larger share of the mental load. For sexual satisfaction, men were also most content when their female partners reported that the mental load was divided equally.
“I don’t think that means men are consciously thinking ‘I want my partner to do everything,'” Klein said regarding the differing relationship satisfaction patterns. “I’d be careful about reading it as a conscious preference. But it does show that the same unequal arrangement can have very different consequences for each partner, and it raises the question of whether some traditional arrangements remain comfortable for men even as social norms around equality are shifting.”
For parental mental load, the patterns looked different. Both mothers and fathers reported higher relationship satisfaction when they felt their partner took on more of the child-related mental load, and when their partner perceived them as doing more. However, parental mental load did not show a link to sexual satisfaction for either men or women, echoing the findings from Study 1.
Geoff MacDonald, a professor of psychology at the University of Toronto who was not involved in the study, told PsyPost that the most central takeaway is how both partners recognized the domestic gap.
“For me, it’s that both men and women agree that women take on more of the mental load around household tasks, and this can have consequences for women’s well-being in a relationship,” he said. “Our lab thinks a lot about why women are happier being single than men, and why men desire partnership more than women, and we often discuss this division of household labor. These results are very consistent with the idea that women are right to be concerned about what they’re signing up for.”
MacDonald added that while the finding aligns with general expectations in the field, it expands the empirical picture. “It is consistent with thinking in this area, but provides new data on the mental load part that I haven’t seen before,” he noted.
To help partners address these imbalances in daily life, Klein emphasized translating abstract ideas of fairness into practical habits. She pointed out that real progress requires moving beyond simple chore distribution to recognize the ongoing mental effort behind running a home.
“The first step is simply making mental load visible,” Klein said. “It happens in someone’s head, has no clear starting or finishing point, and partners often genuinely don’t realize how much of it one person is carrying.”
“So couples shouldn’t only ask, ‘Who does the laundry?’ but also, ‘Who notices that the laundry needs doing, remembers it, knows which clothes need washing and how they should be washed (which clothes can go together, what temperature to use etc.), and makes sure it happens?'” she suggested. “Asking ‘Who noticed the immunization appointment was due?’ or ‘Who remembered what groceries we needed?’ is much more useful than simply saying, ‘We should share things more equally.’ And I think there’s an important difference between dividing tasks and dividing responsibility. If one partner has to remind the other what needs to be done, they’re still carrying part of the mental load.”
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these results. Because both studies relied on cross-sectional surveys, the data show associations between labor divisions and relationship happiness rather than proving that one directly causes the other. It remains possible that couples who are already happier and feel more connected communicate better, which might naturally lead to a fairer division of daily responsibilities.
The study also had limited variation at the extremes: no woman reported that her partner handled all of the mental load, and no man in the couples study reported handling all of it himself. That restricted range may have made some patterns harder to detect. In addition, the participants were drawn entirely from the United States and the United Kingdom, and the authors did not track weekly hours spent at paid jobs, which could influence how much free time each partner has to manage home affairs.
MacDonald raised additional questions regarding what the mental load measure actually captures. “I think the main concern is the validity of the mental load scale, which the authors flag themselves,” he told PsyPost. “There’s a potential argument, for example, that perceptions of a partner’s household contributions are reflecting a broader variable like perceived partner responsiveness, such that this may be reflecting a larger issue than just household contributions. That is, maybe household mental load is just one of many domains in which it is a problem to have a thoughtless partner.”
“I’d also say that a partner’s contribution to mental load may be a reflection of personality traits like conscientiousness, which also has effects across multiple domains,” MacDonald added. “For example, men’s conscientiousness has been previously shown to contribute to women’s sexual function in heterosexual relationships. So it would be helpful if there was more data on the validity of the measure, particularly discriminant validity that accounts for cross-domain effects.”
Perceived partner responsiveness refers to how much people feel their partner understands and cares for them, while conscientiousness is a personality trait marked by being organized and dependable. Discriminant validity refers to evidence that a scale measures something distinct from closely related qualities.
“The authors make the valid point that the kinds of relationship and family contributions that are more typically ascribed to men, like managing finances or doing household repairs, are things that can typically be put off if need be (e.g., the grass can be cut any time but the diapers need to be changed right away),” MacDonald observed. “But, since this is about mental load, in theory worrying about the financial situation or planning out renovations can also create a constant mental load. So, it would be interesting to factor in other domains outside of household labor to get a fuller picture of mental load and its effects on relationship well-being.”
He also suggested examining how these imbalances influence individuals before they enter relationships. “It would be very interesting to see single people’s assessments of these mental load dynamics, and investigate directly if they relate to people’s desire to be in a partnership,” MacDonald said. “Maybe these dynamics are having effects long before people partner, even leading partnership not happening at all.”
Klein noted that much remains to be understood about how mental load operates across different populations and evolving cultural standards. She added that while public conversations around domestic labor are changing, long-term empirical evidence on cognitive burdens remains scarce.
“What we know robustly, across other studies too, is that women carry the larger share of mental load, especially around childcare and parenting decisions, and that this comes with costs: higher stress, lower life and relationship satisfaction, and potentially negative effects on their careers,” Klein explained.
“I think there are reasons to believe that gender norms are changing, but our study cannot tell us whether mental-load inequality itself is changing over time,” she continued. “We have decades of research, including cohort studies, tracking how heterosexual couples divide physical housework and how that division has shifted across generations. We simply don’t yet have enough longitudinal evidence on mental load to say, ‘This generation is different from the previous generation.’ That evidence is still missing.”
Future studies could track couples over longer periods to see whether changes in how couples divide this work are followed by changes in satisfaction. Exploring how mental load relates to specific sexual experiences, such as personal desire or intimacy, could also help clarify how daily domestic teamwork shapes life behind closed doors.
“We have become much better at asking who cooks, who cleans and who does the childcare. But we also need to ask who remembers, anticipates, plans, organizes and worries about all of those things,” Klein concluded. “That work is much less visible, but our findings suggest that it matters for women’s relationship satisfaction. And the fact that women can carry a disproportionate share of this work even when they hold egalitarian gender-role beliefs speaks to how deeply internalized these gendered expectations can be.”
The study, “Unequal Burdens, Unequal Benefits: Housework, Mental Load, and Gendered Satisfaction in Heterosexual Relationships,” was authored by Verena Klein, Esra Ascigil, Tanja Oschatz, and Rotem Kahalon.

Lithuanian prosecutor’s office grills LRT, former judge sees ‘censorship’ risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

The Prosecutor General’s Office has sent LRT a list of questions about the way its journalists conduct investigations by secretly recording actions or conversations, with some experts saying the move resembled signs of censorship.
“I cannot understand such a request because it certainly does not comply with the principles of freedom of expression or, more broadly, those of the media in a democratic state,” said Toma Birmontienė, a professor at Mykolas Romeris University and a former Constitutional Court judge.
In September, the Prosecutor General’s Office sent a detailed list of 15 questions to LRT, asking how covert recordings are regulated internally
The office said it opened an investigation on its own initiative to protect the public interest. The decision followed an ongoing criminal investigation into a recording pen allegedly left by an LRT journalist at a social democrat meeting.
“Frankly, I see this situation as censorship – an attempt to censor, an attempt to control, to find some other mechanism. The other mechanisms for exerting control have failed, so the impression is that this is the second act in a long-running play,’ Birmontienė said in reference to the months-long protests over the independence of the public broadcaster.
The European Broadcasting Union (EBU) on Wednesday also said it was worried about the investigation, saying it posed a risk to investigative journalism.
‘Strange curiosity’
Deimantas Jastramskis, a professor at Vilnius University’s Faculty of Communication and a member of the supervisory LRT Council, pointed out that the prosecution does not specify the context or purpose of its investigation in the letter.
‘It seems even stranger when we consider the context in which LRT and the media have been operating for the past year or longer, and the fact that politicians have been directing all kinds of requests to LRT through various agencies.
LRT’s Editorial Policy allows journalists to gather information covertly when there is evidence that the conduct they seek to document would demonstrate unlawful or dishonest actions by individuals, where there is a clear public interest in exposing them and informing the public. Journalists must also obtain prior approval from the editor responsible.
“If the letter were linked to a specific case or complaint, everything would be clear, and its purpose would be easier to understand,’ Jastramskis told LRT.lt.
The professor said the letter could be interpreted as an indirect reproach to journalists who seek to defend the public interest through their work.
“I would describe this as a completely ill-considered move by the Prosecutor General’s Office,’ he said.
Journalists should not be afraid to make covert recordings when necessary, according to Jastramskis.
‘The letter from the prosecution is relevant not only to LRT but to the entire media sector engaged in serious journalism. It suggests that journalists should have to justify themselves, explain their actions and answer even absurd questions simply because they are trying to serve the public interest,’ he said.
An abstract request
Džina Donauskaitė, head of the Lithuanian Centre for Journalism and an expert at Vilnius University’s Faculty of Communication, said the prosecutor’s request raised questions about why the inquiry was launched.
“Did the prosecutor simply read LRT’s editorial policy guidelines and decide to check whether they were contrary to the public interest? Or is the Prosecutor General’s Office trying to find out how the media operate?
“Why is it trying to find out how the media work – out of curiosity or for other reasons? The prosecution’s request is very vague, and it is unclear why it was made or in what context. It looks like pressure on the media,’ Donauskaitė told LRT.lt.
LRT has faced considerable pressure from various institutions in recent years, which raised further suspicions, she added.
According to Donauskaitė, the letter amounts to interference in the organisation’s internal procedures and journalistic methods.
“Since when has the prosecution been checking organisations’ internal procedures?” she added.
Common practice
Freedom to conduct investigative journalism is particularly important, Donauskairtė said, adding that journalists’ ability to do their work without it would be restricted.
“This is not in the interests of the prosecution itself or law enforcement agencies more broadly, because recent journalistic investigations, including those conducted with international partners, have shown that such investigations prompt law enforcement agencies to initiate numerous legal proceedings against institutions or organisations where corruption or violations of the public interest have occurred.
“If journalists cannot work freely, their investigations will fail to resonate with audiences. This is a way of preventing questions from being asked and obstructing journalists’ work in an attempt to put pressure on them,” Donauskaitė said.
Jastramskis, the Vilnius University professor, also said that journalists in all democratic countries use covert recordings in their investigations.
“This is necessary when the public interest requires a certain degree of intrusion into privacy,” Jastramskis said.
The public interest
Journalists have used covert recording in numerous investigations. For example, journalists from Info TV used the technique in an investigation into then MP Kęstutis Pūkas, who sexually harassed women applying to become parliamentary assistants.
In considering the use of covert recording equipment to obtain some of the information, the Constitutional Court ruled that the Constitution guarantees and protects the public interest in being informed.
It also stated that the public has more than sufficient grounds to want to know more about people involved in public or political life than about others.
The Constitutional Court also noted that the media may inform the public about a public figure without their consent to the extent that the person’s personal characteristics, behaviour or other circumstances of their private life may have implications for public affairs, making the information published a matter of public interest.
In its ruling, the Constitutional Court also referred to judgments by the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR), which has found that unjustified restrictions would prevent the media from fulfilling their role as a “public watchdog”.
Professor Jastramskis also points out that various newsrooms have their own editorial standards, which they have clearly set out. He says the existing rules governing covert recording are sufficient.
“You can always regulate many things in greater detail, but more detailed regulation carries risks. If we regulate everything, we will become quite constrained. [...] We have the Lukashenko regime next door, where everything is certainly regulated.”
“The current rules stipulate that such activity must be approved by an editor. Would it make any difference if they additionally required everything to be sent by email or a form to be completed? What would that change in practice? Nothing,” Jastramskis said.
Protecting public interest – prosecutors
Last week, Elena Martinonienė, head of the Communications Division at the Prosecutor General’s Office, told LRT.lt that the investigation had been launched on a prosecutor’s initiative.
The aim is to assess whether the provisions of LRT’s Editorial Policy allowing covert information gathering safeguard the constitutional right to respect for private life and comply with the relevant legislation governing the media and covert information gathering.
Martinonienė said the prosecution disagreed that the investigation posed a threat to journalists’ freedom.
“In the prosecution’s view, journalists’ freedom and the public interest are safeguarded precisely when the editorial rules governing journalists’ work raise no doubts about their compliance with the Lithuanian Constitution and the law,” she said.
“Only after all the information necessary for the assessment has been received will a decision be made on whether there are grounds in this case to apply the measures provided for by law to protect the public interest,” Martinonienė added.

Polish prosecutors seek to drop case against South Asian men who slaughtered goat in kebab bar

Polish prosecutors have asked a court to discontinue a case against three South Asian men who were caught illegally slaughtering a goat at the back of a kebab bar.
They say that the men did not realise they were breaking the law, that such practices are normal in their home countries, and that that the meat was for their own consumption. Prosecutors therefore believe the crime was of low social harm and not worth the court’s time.

The case involves two Bangladeshi nationals and one Indian, all legal residents in Poland. The incident came to light in December 2025, after witnesses reported seeing the trio leading a goat through the centre of the city of Wałbrzych, before taking it to the back of a kebab bar.
After killing the animal, the men began butchering it for meat, which they were still portioning out when the police arrived. They told officers that the meat was intended for their own consumption. The kebab bar was closed for renovations at the time.
The men also said that such slaughter was customary in their home countries and they were unaware that, with limited exceptions, animals in Poland may generally be slaughtered only at authorised slaughterhouses, reports broadcaster RMF
A spokesman for prosecutors, Mariusz Pindera, told the Wirtualna Polska news website that the men’s unfamiliarity with Polish law did not “absolve them of the obligation to comply with the regulations”.
However, “the harmfulness of the act is relatively low, although I know that what these people did shocks many people”, he continued. “We must be realistic about the fact that the court proceedings will take some time, thus blocking the docket for other cases. A trial also entails costs for the state.”
Prosecutors have therefore asked the court for a so-called conditional discontinuation of the case, a very common procedure under Polish law. Almost 25,000 such motions were submitted last year by prosecutors, citing the low social harm of the offences involved, reports Wirtualna Polska.
The court must now decide whether to accept or reject the prosecution’s motion. In the latter case, prosecutors would be required to proceed with an indictment against the suspects and seek a conviction. No hearing date on the motion has yet been set.

Not all cases involving illegal animal slaughter have been treated as causing low social harm. Last month, a court in the town of Limanowa convicted three men for carrying out illegal halal ritual slaughter and selling unapproved meat.
The main suspect, a Polish man, was found guilty of overseeing the operation, while two Azerbaijani nationals were convicted of helping distribute the illegal meat. The verdicts can still be appealed.

However, the country has itself been experiencing growing levels of migration in recent years. Most of the new arrivals are from neighbouring Ukraine and Belarus, but there are also growing numbers from outside Europe, too.
Indians are now Poland’s third-largest immigrant group, numbering around 25,500, according to recent data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS). Among first residence permits issued by Poland last year, Indians (9,230) and Turks (7,533) were the fourth and fifth largest recipients.
Poland’s current government has blamed some immigrant groups for a rise in crime and has stepped up deportations of those found to have broken the law. However, data show that, overall, immigrants are less likely to commit crimes than Poles themselves.

MEPs linked to Russia oppose European Parliament resolution declaring Russia’s new State Duma illegitimate

The European Parliament has adopted a resolution refusing to recognize Russia’s State Duma as a legitimate representative and legislative body. The measure passed on Oct. 8 with 482 votes in favor, 41 against, and 39 abstentions. “The ‘fake’ ballot was held in a climate of fear and against the backdrop of Moscow’s continued illegal war against Ukraine,” read a press release put out by the European Parliament on Oct. 9.
“[The European] Parliament notes that during the recent fake ballot, there were no genuine alternative candidates, no free media, no credible observers, and no political freedoms, with critics of the regime having been either imprisoned, murdered, or forced into exile. MEPs also condemn the fact that so-called “elections” were conducted in parts of the Russian-occupied Donetsk, Kherson, Luhansk, and Zaporizhzhia regions of Ukraine, as well as in Moldova’s Transnistrian region and in the Georgian regions of Abkhazia and Tskhinvali/South Ossetia,” it added.
According to the Parliament’s roll-call voting record, lawmakers who opposed parts of the resolution included German MEP Petr Bystron, who had been suspected of receiving money from an influence network linked to Viktor Medvedchuk; Slovak politician Luboš Blaha, who has met with Russian Foreign Intelligence Service chief Sergei Naryshkin; and Czech MEP Ondřej Dostál, who traveled to Moscow at the invitation of a Russian foundation linked to the GRU military intelligence agency.
Among those voting against the resolution were 23 members of the far-right Europe of Sovereign Nations (ESN) group, including Alternative for Germany (AfD) lawmakers Petr Bystron and Christine Anderson, Slovak MEPs Luboš Blaha and Milan Mazurek, Czech lawmakers Kateřina Konečná and Ondřej Dostál, and Luxembourg politician Fernand Kartheiser.
Also opposing the measure in the final vote were Polish far-right politician Grzegorz Braun and German MEPs Michael von der Schulenburg and Ruth Firmenich, who were elected on the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) ticket. Braun had previously been stripped of parliamentary immunity in connection with a Polish investigation into his alleged denial of Nazi crimes at Auschwitz (in July 2025, Braun publicly denied the existence of gas chambers at the Auschwitz-Birkenau concentration and extermination camp).
The Insider compared the roll-call vote with published information about lawmakers’ contacts with Russian representatives. It found that four of the politicians listed above — Blaha, Dostál, von der Schulenburg, and Firmenich — traveled together to Moscow in May 2025. The trip was timed to coincide with the 80th anniversary of the end of World War II. While in the Russian capital, the MEPs met with Russian politicians and public figures.
In an official declaration published by the European Parliament, Dostál listed the Russian Peace Foundation as a third party that covered part of the trip’s expenses. Dostál said he paid for his flight, accommodation, and meals himself, while the foundation provided bus transportation from the airport.
The Insider previously reported that the Russian Peace Foundation has links to Russian military intelligence. According to internal GRU correspondence, the organization has been involved in passing information about foreign visitors to the intelligence service for assessment and possible recruitment.
In the same investigation, The Insider reported that Luboš Blaha traveled to Moscow with David Lindtner, an adviser to Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico. During that trip, Blaha met with Sergei Naryshkin, director of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR). According to statements published by Blaha, they discussed the May 2024 assassination attempt against Fico, along with the activities of political opponents of the Slovak government.
Petr Bystron, another lawmaker on the list, had previously appeared in an investigation into the pro-Kremlin media platform Voice of Europe, which European intelligence services say was financed by a network linked to the aforementioned Medvedchuk. As The Insider previously reported, citing Der Spiegel and Deník N, Bystron and fellow party member Maximilian Krah were suspected of receiving money in exchange for cooperation with the platform. In 2025, the European Parliament lifted Bystron’s immunity in order to allow an investigation in a separate case to proceed.
A Transparency International database also contains records of meetings between some of the lawmakers and Russian representatives. According to the data, in May 2025 von der Schulenburg met in Moscow with Russian diplomats and State Duma representatives, and in July of that year with a representative of Russia’s mission to the European Union in Brussels. Energy Ministry explains regional differences in power outages
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:57:27 EEST
22:57:27 KST

Eastern, southern and central Ukraine currently face electricity deficits due to Russian attacks and the resulting damage, while most of the country's power generation capacity is concentrated in the west, where nuclear power plants are located and electricity imports from Europe enter the country, the Energy Ministry has said.
The western region could potentially generate more electricity than it consumes, the ministry said in a Telegram post on Friday.
Transmitting electricity from western Ukraine to Kyiv or Kharkiv requires high-voltage transmission lines and autotransformers, which Russia is deliberately targeting, the ministry said.
Energy infrastructure has become the main target of Russian strikes ahead of winter. Attacks on transformers and high-voltage networks carrying electricity between regions have temporarily reduced the power system's ability to transmit electricity to consumers, it said.
“As a result, damage to the transmission ‘highways’ leaves electricity ‘trapped’ in the regions where it is generated or imported,” the ministry said.
Consequently, power restrictions may be unnecessary in western Ukraine, while shortages are more acute in central, southern and eastern regions. The transmission networks lack sufficient capacity to carry such large volumes of electricity and were not designed for this level of load, the ministry said.
The situation is compounded by mass attacks, localized strikes in frontline areas and equipment failures caused by system overload. Equipment breaks down daily and energy workers repair it, the ministry said.
Differences in the duration of power outages are therefore the result of physical limitations, rather than arbitrary decisions, the ministry said.

Estonia pays family caregivers just €60 a month, with no national scheme
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:57:00 UTC
22:57:00 KST

Estonia pays family caregivers just €60 a month, with no national scheme
Thousands of people in Estonia care for loved ones at home, but caregiver benefits vary widely by municipality and average just €60 a month.
As of December 2025, 8,111 people in Estonia received caregiver benefits averaging €61.47 a month, with benefits for those caring for adults averaging €59.59.
In all, 10,180 people provided care at home last year, though the Social Affairs Ministry does not track how many were relatives of those they cared for.
Tasked with overseeing social assistance, local governments consider care needs and the burden on caregivers when determining eligibility, but set their own benefit amounts, resulting in wide variations in support across the country.
Minister of Social Affairs Karmen Joller (Reform) doesn't agree that should be the case.
"Support shouldn't essentially depend solely on where someone lives or their formal status, but on their assessed needs," Joller said, responding to an MP query.
Monthly caregiver benefits can range from €25–150 for adult care and from €30–210 for caring for a disabled child. The minister explained that eligibility may depend on the extent of care needed, the severity of the disability, whether the caregiver otherwise works or is in school, where both people live as well as what other services the person under care receives.
By comparison, round-the-clock general care in an Estonian care home costs an average of €50.37 a day last year, with public funding covering an average of €23.51 a day — or less than half of the total cost — for the nearly 16,800 people receiving such care.
Minister: At-home care needs aren't typically as high
Joller highlighted that public funding has increased since the nationwide care reform, with care recipients and their loved ones previously left to pay for about 80 percent of care home costs. In 2025, their share of the bill had fallen to an average of 53 percent.
The ministry has not calculated how the public cost of caring for someone at home compares with care home services for someone with similar needs.
The minister, however, said care home residents generally require round-the-clock help and supervision, while those being cared for at home typically don't need the same level of support, making the comparison difficult.
Joller said the state hasn't considered a nationwide benefit system that would automatically pay relatives a set share of care home costs when they care for an older or disabled family member at home, nor does the Ministry of Social Affairs intend to take over caregiver appointments and benefit payments.
Local governments appoint caregivers and may pay them benefits at their own set terms and rates, she noted, while also having the flexibility to arrange support through home care or other services that support people continuing to live at home.
Care reform review due by year-end
Joller said Estonia's care reform has increased municipal funding, with nearly €70 million in additional funding expected this year. The money is intended to help cover both care home costs and support services for people living at home.
Asked whether the ministry believes the current support system for family members and caregivers is sufficient, Joller said work to improve it is ongoing, with an analysis of the care reform's impact and a repeat study on the population's caregiving burden both due by year-end.
"Based on those findings, we will assess which problems require additional solutions and whether any changes are needed in service provision, funding or legislation," she said.
At the ministry's request, the Estonian Chamber of Disabled People (EPIKoda) has also developed an online platform for family caregivers, and also offers counseling and support groups.
"It's crucial to support family caregivers' own well-being, health and ability to work and ensure that the burden of care doesn't fall on relatives alone," Joller said.
The goal, she added, is to ensure that caring for a loved one doesn't force people to quit their jobs, undermine their financial security or come at the expense of their own health.
