Yair Golan calls Khamenei killing a mistake, says Iran war left Israel worse off
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:55:54 UTC
22:55:54 KST

Yair Golan, leader of Israel's opposition Democrats party, said Friday that the assassination of Iran's supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, at the start of the latest war was a "mistake" that ultimately harmed Israel's strategic interests.
Speaking in an interview with journalist Yossi Yehoshua at a cultural event in Rishon LeZion, Golan said he firmly believed eliminating the Iranian leader had been the wrong decision. "I unequivocally believe that killing the elder Khamenei was a mistake," he said. "Not because he didn't deserve to die, but because it doesn't serve the interests of the State of Israel. There is always a certain advantage to having an elderly, long-serving leader. And he was already 86."
Golan also argued that Operation Roaring Lion, Israel's latest military campaign against Iran, had weakened the country's long-term strategic position. "My impression is that Khamenei's son, if he is functioning at all, is controlled by the most extreme elements of the Iranian leadership," he said. "After we eliminated the top layer of leadership, we were left with people who are more extreme and more violent."
"Israel was at the height of its achievements against Iran at the end of Operation Rising Lion. From a long-term strategic perspective, Operation Roaring Lion worsened our position because Netanyahu himself set an unrealistic objective that was never achieved: overthrowing the Iranian regime."
During the same interview, Golan also described Israel's ultra-Orthodox population as "parasitic," saying the goal should be to transform it into a productive, educated population with professional skills.
‘Netanyahu squandered an extraordinary strategic opportunity’
In a post on X following the interview, Golan expanded on his criticism of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, arguing that the failure was not the military operation itself but the absence of a diplomatic strategy to capitalize on it. "This is the failure I'm talking about, and it rests entirely with Netanyahu," he wrote. "The killing of the elder Khamenei could have been a historic turning point. But Netanyahu, through his arrogance and considerations of political survival, squandered an extraordinary strategic opportunity."
"Instead of leading a regional diplomatic initiative that would guarantee Israel's security, he sold the Americans illusions about overthrowing the Iranian regime, without a diplomatic strategy to secure what would come the day after," Golan wrote.
He argued that removing Iran's veteran leadership had strengthened more radical figures within the country's security establishment. "Under Netanyahu, Operation Roaring Lion worsened our strategic position instead of improving it," he wrote. "Responsibility for setting the objectives, managing the campaign and its results lies with Netanyahu. This is how a historic military achievement is turned into a severe strategic failure. Netanyahu must be held accountable for the decisions he made and the outcome he left behind."
From praising Khamenei's killing to calling it a mistake
Golan's latest remarks stand in contrast to his initial response to Khamenei's assassination in late February, when he publicly welcomed the operation and praised the Israeli and American forces involved. At the time, he described the killing as "a dramatic and significant step," saying the two countries had demonstrated "intelligence superiority and impressive operational capabilities."
"Ali Khamenei was the architect of regional terrorism, the man who made Israel's destruction a goal, financed and armed terrorist proxies and deepened instability across the Middle East," he wrote on X. He also addressed the Iranian people, saying: "You have been freed from a cruel tyrant who oppressed you for decades, and a real opportunity for freedom and a better future has opened."
By early April, however, about a month and a half later, Golan had begun questioning the decision. "It is possible that the assassination was a mistake and harmed Israel's security," he said at the time. His latest comments Friday went further, portraying the assassination and broader military campaign as a missed strategic opportunity for which he holds Netanyahu directly responsible.

EU and China clinch deal over cars after heated trade talks as Brussels pushes to rebalance trade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:51:44 UTC
22:51:44 KST

EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič described the deal as marking the end of the “first phase” of negotiations. Brussels is pushing for a fundamental rebalancing in trade relations with Beijing.
EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič announced a deal with China on Friday to curb imports of Chinese hybrid vehicles into the EU and facilitate access to rare earths.
While the understanding signals a preference for a diplomatic resolution to the growing trade imbalance, European leaders are pushing for stronger measures to level the playing field. They are expected to review the details at a summit in Brussels next week.
The EU has also floated retaliatory measures if the outcome falls short of expectations.
Šefčovič travelled to Beijing on Wednesday for two days of intensive talks with his Chinese counterpart, Wang Wentao, in a bid to rebalance EU-China trade relations.
The EU is facing a record trade deficit with China of €1 billion a day, as a surge in low-cost Chinese imports threatens entire sectors of European industry.
“We have reached a shared understanding to moderate China's export of hybrids and plug-in hybrids to the European Union,” Šefčovič said. “This opens up the prospect of cutting China's exports by more than half.”
The commissioner said the deal would also improve access to the Chinese market for a range of EU products, from “car parts to olive oil and footwear”, representing almost €4 billion in current export value. It should generate at least €225 million in duty savings, he added.
Market access has been at the heart of EU-China discussions since negotiations began last June. Beijing has been reluctant to relinquish access to the EU's 450-million-consumer market, which provides an outlet for its excess production.
Meanwhile, Brussels has proposed several legislative measures aimed at restricting Chinese companies' access to the European market, while pressing Beijing to open up its own market to EU businesses.
Šefčovič also said China had agreed to facilitate exports of rare earths, which are essential to Europe's green technology, defence and automotive industries.
“We have reached a shared understanding to further facilitate China's export licensing for rare earths and permanent magnets,” he said.
The EU has accused China of “weaponising” its dependence on Chinese rare earths after Beijing restricted exports in 2025 amid a trade war with the US.
Šefčovič described the agreement as the conclusion of a “first phase of negotiations”.
The deal comes ahead of a meeting of EU leaders in Brussels next week, with expectations running high for concrete results from negotiations led by the European Commission on their behalf since last June.
A consensus on China has been emerging across the EU this week.
All EU countries now run trade deficits with China. On Monday, Germany and France urged the European Commission to take strong action against unfair Chinese trade practices that cause severe market distortions.
In a joint document, Paris and Berlin called for measures that could include “an immediate cut-off from the internal market if needed”.
On Wednesday, MEPs overwhelmingly adopted a resolution calling for resolute measures against Beijing.
Meanwhile, 44 EU industries, including chemicals, machinery, metals, solar, glass and cement, issued a joint statement on Friday warning that “Europe cannot maintain and grow its industrial base, quality jobs, and attract investment without the ability to respond effectively to unfair trade practices and distortions”.

Yandex said specialists are still assessing the scale of the damage in Kaluga. The attack has caused interruptions across some of the company’s digital services; however, the specific systems that were affected and whether the disabled modules can be restored have not been announced. Preliminary reports do not mention any human casualties.
Construction of the Kaluga data center began in 2022 on the territory of the Grabtsevo industrial park. Yandex’s original project was designed to house more than 3,800 server racks, with a total design capacity of 63 MW — one and a half times that of the company’s most powerful data center at the time of announcement. The site is intended both for Yandex’s own services and for customers of the Yandex Cloud platform.
According to official documents of the Kaluga city administration, the first phase of the facility was commissioned in December 2023. In October 2024, the System Operator of the Unified Energy System reported the connection of Yandex’s largest data center to the power grid with a maximum power consumption of 49 MW, though the company has not disclosed the amount of server equipment at the site at the time of the attack.
The day before, drones knocked out a data center in the Ryazan Region
Overnight into Oct. 8, Ukrainian drones attacked Yandex’s data center in the city of Sasovo in the Ryazan Region, located on the grounds of the Sasta machine-tool plant. The strike caused a fire at the facility, forcing the management to suspend operations. As of the evening of Oct. 8, the company could not confirm whether the damaged equipment could be restored.
The data center in Sasovo opened in 2014 and is designed to house tens of thousands of servers. It is currently home to two of Yandex’s three supercomputers, which the company uses to develop and train artificial intelligence models, including YandexGPT. The extent of damage to these assets remains unknown.
On Oct. 8, large-scale disruptions occurred in the operation of Russian internet services. As The Insider reported, users ran into problems opening the websites of Russian media outlets, Russian Railways, the real estate platform Cian, the classifieds portal Avito, and other platforms. Cian confirmed that the disruptions were linked to an incident at a facility of its infrastructure partner. Problems were also recorded in the operation of Yandex’s own services.
On the Yandex Cloud status page, the company reported that the ru-central1-b zone, associated with the data center in Sasovo, was completely unavailable. Customers were advised to move their workloads to other availability zones. At the same time, the outage imposed restrictions on creating new virtual machines, Kubernetes clusters, and databases.
On Oct. 8, the independent outlet Verstka also found that Yandex had concealed satellite images of its four cloud data centers, including the facilities in Sasovo and Kaluga. On Yandex Maps, the sites are blurred, and when searched by address, the service does not indicate that data centers are located there. When and why the company hid the images remains unknown.

In addition to Yakovenko, at least eight other political prisoners have died in Russian custody since the start of 2026:
- Roman Sidorkin died on Jan. 9 in the Saratov Region. The former employee of a defense company in the Kursk Region had been convicted of treason after investigators accused him and his former wife of passing technical documentation and samples of military products to Ukrainian intelligence. Sidorkin developed bronchitis-like symptoms in December 2025, and later pneumonia. He was hospitalized only four days before his death.
- Oleg Tyryshkin, a former miner and trade union activist from Kemerovo Region, died on Feb. 4 at age 64. He had been sentenced to two years in a penal colony over a comment posted on the social network VK about the 2004 death of Akhmat Kadyrov, the first president of Chechnya and the father of its current leader, Ramzan Kadyrov. Activists who corresponded with prisoners said heart problems were the cause of his death. Tyryshkin had previously complained about his health, including about a brain cyst.
- Alexander Dotsenko died on Feb. 19 after a massive heart attack. The jewelry artist had been sentenced to three years in a penal colony in a case involving anti-war postcards left in a Lenta supermarket in St. Petersburg. His wife, Anastasia Dyudyayeva, received a 3½-year sentence in the same case. After Dotsenko’s heart attack, prison officials failed to inform his relatives and lawyer about his condition for several days.
- Vladimir Osipov died in March at a pretrial detention center in Ukhta, where he had been transferred from the Moscow Region. The 56-year-old had been sentenced to 6½ years in a penal colony over posts made on Odnoklassniki about the Russian military and Vladimir Putin. Ambulances were called for Osipov several times during his trial, and at one hearing the judge refused to postpone his final statement despite complaints of high blood pressure.
- Andrei Akuzin, a 53-year-old artist from Komsomolsk-on-Amur, died by suicide on April 8 at a local pretrial detention center — six days after he was arrested. His friend said the criminal case stemmed from an online comment. Russia’s financial monitoring agency, Rosfinmonitoring, added Akuzin to its registry of “terrorists and extremists” only after his death.
- Vegan Khristolyub Bozhiy, formerly named Dmitry Kuznetsov, died on April 17 at Penal Colony No. 2 in Voronezh. The 43-year-old preacher and YouTube blogger, whose name can be loosely translated as “Vegan Christ-Lover of God,” had been sentenced to three years in prison over videos criticizing the invasion of Ukraine, the Soviet army, and Islam. It later emerged that he had been found hanged in a punishment cell and that, according to media reports, a negligence case was opened against the prison’s employees. His relatives did not believe the official account of suicide.
- Vladimir Yarotsky was found dead on the morning of May 7 at Penal Colony No. 9 in Khadyzhensk in Russia’s Krasnodar Region. The artist had been sentenced to five and a half years in prison on charges of spreading “false information” about the Russian armed forces and “desecrating symbols of military glory” over posts that included a caricature of Putin featuring a penis and a St. George ribbon. Authorities said Yarotsky died by suicide. Another prisoner said the artist had complained of pressure from the prison administration.
- Ibragim Kudzhanov, a 52-year-old resident of Ukraine’s Luhansk Region, died at Penal Colony No. 8 in the Omsk Region. His death became known in July. Kudzhanov had been sentenced to 5½ years in prison for serving as a driver in Ukraine’s Aidar Battalion in 2018 and 2019. His daughter said he had been tortured with electric shocks after his detention and that he died from a second heart attack accompanied by an aneurysm and kidney failure. His son, Artyom, is also imprisoned in Russia after being sentenced to 12 years in a penal colony on espionage charges in 2025.

New horizons open for Iran-Afghanistan economic co-op during Iran’s trade delegation’s trip to Kabul
TEHRAN- During the trip of a trade delegation from the Iran Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines and Agriculture (ICCIMA), led by Ghadir Qiyafeh, Vice President of the Chamber, to Kabul, the capacities for Iran-Afghanistan cooperation in mining and mineral industries, agriculture and conversion industries, technology transfer, and the creation of production and processing chains were examined.
Meetings with Nooruddin Azizi, Afghanistan’s Minister of Industry and Commerce, and Haji Akhtar Mohammad Mohammadi, First Deputy of Afghanistan’s Chamber of Agricultural and Livestock Production, along with participation in the Fifth Abu Hanifa International Exhibition and B2B negotiations between Iranian and Afghan traders, formed the main axes of this trip.
Iran-Afghanistan cooperation in mining, mineral industries emphasized
Ghadir Qiyafeh, Vice President of the Iran Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines and Agriculture, during the trip to Kabul at the head of a trade delegation, in a meeting with Nooruddin Azizi, Afghanistan’s Minister of Industry and Commerce, referred to Afghanistan’s mineral capacities and emphasized the development of Iran-Afghanistan cooperation in mining and mineral industries.
Azizi, referring to the issue of mining machinery, welcomed the expansion of relations and economic cooperation with Iran.
In this meeting, attended by Hamed Asgari, Deputy for International Affairs of the Iran Chamber; Mahmoud Omati, Vice President of the Mashhad Chamber; Hossein Beykzadeh, Vice President of the Karaj Chamber; Arash Alavi, member of the Board of Representatives of the Iran and Kerman Chamber; and Mohsen Amini, member of the Food Industry Committee and member of the Board of Representatives of the Iran Chamber, the capacities for economic cooperation between the two countries were examined.
Ghadir Qiyafeh, Vice President of the Iran Chamber, considering Afghanistan’s mineral capacities, emphasized the necessity of strengthening interactions and developing cooperation between the economic actors of the two countries in mining and mineral industries, and considered the existing capacities in this sector as a basis for expanding Iran-Afghanistan economic cooperation.
Then Nooruddin Azizi, Afghanistan’s Minister of Industry and Commerce, referring to the issue of mining machinery, emphasized the importance of cooperation in this area and welcomed the development of relations and expansion of economic cooperation between Afghanistan and Iran.
In this meeting, emphasis was also placed on using existing capacities to deepen economic relations and develop private sector cooperation between the two countries, especially in mining and mineral industries.
At the meeting of the Vice President of the Iran Chamber with the First Deputy of Afghanistan’s Agriculture Chamber, it was raised:
Ghadir Qiyafeh, Vice President of the Iran Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines and Agriculture, met with Haji Akhtar Mohammad Mohammadi, First Deputy of Afghanistan’s Chamber of Agricultural and Livestock Production, and discussed the capacities for developing economic and agricultural cooperation between the two countries.
In this meeting, Mahmoud Siyadat, President of the Iran-Afghanistan Joint Chamber; Kamaluddin Tawhid, President of the Afghanistan-Iran Joint Chamber of Commerce; Mohsen Amini, member of the Food Industry Committee of the Iran Chamber; and Ali Asghar Beigi, Vice President of the Yazd Chamber; a number of representatives of Iran’s parliament; and members of Afghanistan’s Chamber of Agricultural and Livestock Production were present.
Ghadir Qiyafeh, Vice President of the Iran Chamber, referring to existing capacities in Afghanistan’s agriculture and livestock sector and the country’s need for technology and production inputs, emphasized the readiness of Iran’s private sector to develop cooperation, transfer technology, and use joint capacities.
The head of Afghanistan’s Chamber of Agricultural and Livestock Production also emphasized the development of economic and trade relations with Iran and focused on expanding cooperation between the two chambers and using the private sector capacities of both countries.
Later in this meeting, Mahmoud Siyadat, President of the Iran-Afghanistan Joint Chamber, referring to Afghanistan’s high capacity in agriculture and livestock, proposed the development of technical cooperation, technology transfer, and the creation of production and processing chains.
He also emphasized increasing imports from Afghanistan and said: “These imports can be developed with a focus on goods needed by Iran, including oilseeds, animal feed, and legumes.”
The President of the Iran-Afghanistan Joint Chamber, referring to measures taken in agriculture and pest control, including sending specialized teams to Afghanistan, considered cooperation capacity broad in sectors such as industrial livestock farming, poultry farming, production and processing of agricultural products, and related industries, and emphasized the need for greater support and organization to activate these capacities.
Focus on Afghanistan’s capacities in agricultural processing and conversion industries required
Ghadir Qiyafeh, Vice President of the Iran Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines and Agriculture, on the sidelines of the Fifth Abu Hanifa International Exhibition of Afghanistan and at the B2B negotiations ceremony of traders and economic actors of Iran and Afghanistan, emphasizing the extensive economic capacities of the two countries, said: “Iran’s view of Afghanistan should not be merely as a market for supplying Iranian goods; rather, it should move toward joint investments.”
At this ceremony, Ghadir Qiyafeh, Vice President of the Iran Chamber, referring to the extensive presence of Iranian companies and firms in this year’s exhibition, stated: “Last year, when I came to Afghanistan to attend the Abu Hanifa Exhibition, I did not witness such a crowd and welcome from the economic actors of the two countries, but this year, with the efforts of the Iranian chambers and the Afghanistan Chamber of Commerce and Investment, the presence of Iranian companies and firms has increased, and the level of the exhibition has significantly differed from last year.”
He thanked the Afghan side for hosting and planning, and added: “Alongside the historical, civilizational, and cultural ties between Iran and Afghanistan, there are serious fields for activity, joint investment, and trade exchanges between the two countries.”
The Vice President of the Iran Chamber continued: “In recent years, Iranian industrial goods in various fields, including electricity, energy, oil, petrochemical materials, and conversion industries, have been used in Afghanistan, and this shows that Iranian goods, industry, and firms are present in Afghanistan’s economy.”
Qiyafeh considered one of the important obstacles to developing economic relations between the two countries to be the issue of financial, monetary, and banking exchanges and said: “Part of the obstacles exists on the Iranian side and part on the Afghan side, and one of the serious obstacles is the issue of financial and banking exchanges.”
The Vice President of the Iran Chamber expressed hope that with follow-up by friends in the Afghanistan Chamber of Commerce and Investment and given the promises made by Afghan authorities, in the future we will witness the establishment of a branch or representation of one of the Iranian banks in Afghanistan’s capital and, in return, the establishment of a branch of an Afghan bank in Iran, so that monetary and financial exchanges between the two countries are facilitated.
The Vice President of the Iran Chamber, emphasizing the need to change the view toward economic relations between the two countries, said: “We should not see Afghanistan only as a susceptible market for Iranian goods; our view should be toward joint investments, because joint investment can also guarantee the future of exports.”
He considered Afghanistan’s capacities in processing and conversion industries, especially agricultural conversion industries, significant and added: “A significant part of Afghanistan’s economy depends on agriculture, and this sector can be a suitable ground for developing joint cooperation.”
Qiyafeh also referred to the development of Afghanistan’s steel industry and said: “Today, steel production and melting factories have been established in Afghanistan and supply part of the country’s needs, but there is still a broad field for technical and industrial cooperation between the two countries.”
The Vice President of the Iran Chamber called mining and mineral industries one of the attractive areas of cooperation between Iran and Afghanistan and said: “Afghanistan enjoys very extensive mineral capacities, and in a correct expression, many elements of the periodic table exist in this country.”
He continued: “Iranian companies, with the experience and technical knowledge gained over several decades, can be present in this sector in Afghanistan. This cooperation can begin with exploration and continue through extraction, processing, and production of the final product.”
Qiyafeh, emphasizing that the development of mining and mineral industries requires the provision of necessary infrastructure, added: “If mining and mineral industries in Afghanistan are to develop with investment from other countries, especially Iran, the construction of new roads, development of railway lines, and establishment of power plant units are necessary.”
He said: “Solar, hydro, wind, and thermal power plants can help supply the energy infrastructure needed by this sector.”
Emphasis Qiyafeh, referring to the public ownership of mineral resources in Afghanistan, said: “Just as in Iran mines are recognized as public property and belong to all the Iranian nation, Afghanistan’s mineral resources also belong to the people of Afghanistan.”
He proposed: “Part of the minerals should first undergo primary processing inside Afghanistan, and from the revenue and profit obtained, processing capacities and industrial units should be developed.”
The Vice President of the Iran Chamber emphasized: “With the method adopted today, one cannot expect a serious transformation in Afghanistan’s mining sector in the near future, and it is necessary to plan for developing the value chain and processing of minerals inside the country.”
Readiness of Iranian companies for investment
Qiyafeh, referring to the presence of Iranian companies at the Fifth Abu Hanifa International Exhibition of Afghanistan, said: “Among the Iranian companies present at this exhibition, more than 10 groups are interested and ready to invest in Afghanistan, and some of them have announced their readiness to invest in conversion industries.”
Mahmoud Siyadat, President of the Iran-Afghanistan Joint Chamber of Commerce, emphasizing the existing capacities for developing economic cooperation between the two countries, said: “Afghanistan’s current conditions, especially continued security and industrial and production growth, have provided a suitable ground for entering a new phase of economic partnerships between Iran and Afghanistan.”
Making the remarks at the gathering held jointly by the joint chambers of commerce of Iran and Afghanistan, he focused on the sustainability of security and the continuation of Afghanistan’s industrial and production growth and spoke of readiness to enter a new phase of trade and investment cooperation between the two countries.
Mahmoud Siyadat, President of the Iran-Afghanistan Joint Chamber, referring to the presence of representatives of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Parliament at this event, emphasized: “The presence of individuals who are influential in policymaking and policies related to Afghanistan and see the country’s conditions closely is valuable at this ceremony, and we hope their perceptions and views are considered in future policies and decisions.”
He continued: “I hope we enter a new phase of partnerships. The Iran Chamber made great efforts so that part of Iran’s capable economic forces attend this round of the Abu Hanifa Exhibition, so that Afghan economic actors become closely acquainted with these capacities and the path for more cooperation is paved.”
Siyadat also, referring to the presence of Afghan exhibitors at the exhibition, said: “For offering goods and services, this opportunity may be a unique opportunity, and I recommend they have a more active presence during the exhibition days.”
He added: “We have considered places for holding meetings and sessions, and we are ready to cooperate in legal and contractual areas.”
The President of the Iran-Afghanistan Joint Chamber, referring to the capacity of joint chambers and economic organizations of Afghanistan, said: “The Iran-Afghanistan Joint Chamber, the Afghanistan-Iran Joint Chamber, and Afghan economic organizations are three chambers at the head of which is the Afghanistan Chamber of Commerce and Investment, and these collections are ready to cooperate as wings of flight.”
Siyadat noted: “Fortunately, the will of the rulers of both countries is also on developing relations, and we hope this exhibition is the beginning of a new season for deeper, broader, and more lasting cooperation between the two countries.”
Referring to the ties between the Iranian and Afghan peoples, he said: “I don’t think we can find in the world two peoples and two countries with this level of closeness, affinity, and common roots that exist between Iran and Afghanistan.”
Alireza Beykdeli, Ambassador of Iran in Kabul, while attending the gathering of the joint chambers of commerce of Iran and Afghanistan, said: “Traders of the two countries, while trading and earning profit, bring closer the brotherly peoples of Iran and Afghanistan, who are truly one nation in two countries, and this approach will bless the wealth of all economic actors.”
Iran’s Ambassador in Kabul, referring to the transformation in economic cooperation between the two countries over the past two years, said: “During the two years I have been here, I have witnessed a transformation in the concept of economic cooperation. The day I came, most questions were about how to obtain a visa and how to see facilitation in this area, how to pass a container through the border, and how to access a company; but today conditions have changed greatly and we are witnessing a rise in the level of exchanges.”
He continued: “Today, trade elders talk about a pipeline for transferring crude oil to Afghanistan, a refinery, the Herat-Mazar-e-Sharif road, and the construction of a factory and kiln. Grand ideas are proposed; ideas worthy of two nations.”
Beykdeli, stating that good days await Iran-Afghanistan relations, said: “I thank all those who join hands in this path with good intentions, and I hope we witness an ever greater increase in the level of relations between the two countries.”
Turning neighborliness into economic partnership in Iran-Afghanistan relations needed
Following the dispatch of the Iran Chamber’s trade delegation headed by Ghadir Qiyafeh, Vice President of the Iran Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines and Agriculture, to Kabul, delegation members attended the opening ceremony of the Fifth Abu Hanifa International Exhibition.
Qiyafeh at this ceremony, emphasizing the capacities for economic cooperation between Iran and Afghanistan, considered the presence of economic actors at this event beyond an exhibition presence and said: “The presence of economic actors at this exhibition shows Afghanistan can be more than before at the center of regional economic cooperation and play a role as part of the region’s production, trade, transit, and investment network.”
Referring to the importance and position of the Abu Hanifa International Exhibition in the region, he stated: “The importance of this exhibition lies precisely in the point that joint investments can be formed here. An exhibition is not only a place for offering and introducing products; sometimes it can be a place where a new economic geography takes shape.”
The Vice President of the Iran Chamber continued: “The political geography of countries is known and fixed for all, but economic geography can be built; together and with our Afghan kin, we can define and rebuild this geography.”
Qiyafeh, stating that borders can become trade routes, said: “Borders can be turned from stopping points into trade routes, and neighborliness can be turned into partnership.”
Referring to the economic capacities of countries around Afghanistan, he added: “Countries around Afghanistan each possess part of an economic system. Some of these countries have different resources and capacities, and each has advantages. The important issue is that we can put all these advantages together.”
Qiyafeh, referring to the capacities for cooperation between the economic actors of Iran and Afghanistan, stated: “Today, Afghan and Iranian investors can together create an economic event. Iran has very good and successful experiences and knowledge in developing mines and also in agriculture.”
The Vice President of the Iran Chamber concluded: “As your Iranian brothers, we once again extend our hand for cooperation, and we hope next year when we attend this exhibition, we will witness investments coming to fruition and future horizons opening.”
Based on what was raised in these meetings and gatherings, the development of Iran-Afghanistan relations is no longer limited to the exchange of goods; rather, both sides emphasize joint investment, technology transfer, the creation of production and processing chains, the removal of financial and banking obstacles, and turning neighborliness into economic partnership. If this approach is realized, the Abu Hanifa Exhibition can become a starting point for shaping a new economic geography and more lasting cooperation between the private sectors of the two countries.

Invalid signatures halt Swiss vote to ease solar power plant rules
A Swiss popular initiative aimed at loosening planning rules on solar power plants has failed due to a high number of invalid signatures. The 18-month deadline for collecting 100,000 valid signatures has now passed.
The construction of solar power installations in Switzerland is often blocked by heritage conservation bodies or townscape committees.
+ Alpine nimbyism freezes Swiss green energy dreams
The federal popular initiative “For solar installations exempt from planning permission” had not been submitted with the required number of signatures by October 8, 2026, the Federal Chancellery announced on Friday in the Federal Gazette. The deadline for collecting signatures had therefore expired.
More
Swiss Alpine solar farms struggle to deliver on their promise
The initiative committee did not include any nationally recognised figures. The Federal Gazette lists seven private individuals from an interest group. The committee is based in Basel-Country.
The association’s website states that 117,500 people are said to have signed the petition. During the verification process in July and August, it emerged that almost 20,000 signatures were invalid, said Roland Weiss, one of the initiators of the initiative, in response to an enquiry from the Keystone-SDA news agency.
More

“Our lawyer is currently investigating the circumstances.” It is currently being clarified how such a high number of invalid signatures could have arisen despite the involvement of signature-collection firms.
The initiative, which has now failed, called for a new constitutional article to be enshrined for solar installations on buildings and structures.
For such installations, no planning permission would have been required either within or outside protected townscapes and landscapes.
Exceptions would have been possible for installations on cultural monuments of national or cantonal significance, as well as on historic sites. In such cases, a planning permission could have been granted subject to certain conditions.

Nobel Peace Prize winner Navi Pillay dedicates award to survivors of international crimes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:49:11 UTC
22:49:11 KST

South African jurist Navi Pillay, the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize winner, has dedicated her award to survivors of international crimes and called on world leaders to uphold international law and protect human rights.
“Let me dedicate this award to all of the survivors of international crimes,” Pillay told a news conference on Friday in the historic courtroom in Nuremberg, Germany, where Nazi leaders were prosecuted after World War II.
The 85-year-old said the setting held particular significance as she received news of the award.
“Perhaps it was meant to be that I was in this historic courtroom ... when the announcement was made and I was informed of the award,” she said.
Pillay, who has spent decades working in international justice, warned that legal institutions and human rights protections were facing growing political pressure.
Pillay warns against attacks on international courts
“We are living through an era when international law and human rights are under significant political attack,” she said, pointing in particular to criticism of the International Criminal Court (ICC).
“This worsening reality is particularly visible with the attacks on the International Criminal Court,” she added.
US President Donald Trump last month urged countries that are members of the ICC to withdraw, denouncing the court as a “rogue institution.”
Pillay called on political leaders to respect their legal responsibilities and avoid actions that undermine international protections.
“My message to leaders, political leaders, is that ... you have a legal obligation to protect human rights and refrain from war,” she said.
A career shaped by international justice
Pillay has held several prominent roles in international law. She headed the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, which prosecuted those responsible for the 1994 genocide, and currently serves as a judge at the International Court of Justice (ICJ).
She is also serving in a case in which Myanmar faces allegations of genocide against the Rohingya minority.
Pillay previously presided over a United Nations commission that concluded last year that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.
Her award comes amid continuing international debate over the enforcement of international law, the accountability of states and the independence of judicial institutions.
Pillay used her Nobel recognition to reiterate that protecting survivors and upholding human rights must remain central responsibilities for governments worldwide.

ULAN BATOR, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- The credit rating agency Standard & Poor's (S&P) has affirmed Mongolia's long-term sovereign credit rating at BB- and its short-term rating at B, maintaining a stable outlook, the government's press office announced on Friday, citing the agency's statement.
The stable outlook reflects S&P's expectation that Mongolia will sustain robust, mining-led economic growth while keeping the accumulation of net general government debt at a relatively low level over the next 12 months. However, the agency noted that rising social spending and large-scale infrastructure projects could put pressure on public finances.
S&P said it expects Mongolia's economic growth to remain strong, with real gross domestic product (GDP) projected to expand by an average of approximately 5.6 percent annually through 2029. The mining sector is expected to remain the main driver of economic growth, although the composition of the country's export basket has been undergoing structural changes.
The latest assessment follows credit rating updates by the other two major international rating agencies. In August, Fitch Ratings affirmed Mongolia's long-term issuer default rating at B+ with a stable outlook. In October, Moody's Ratings affirmed the country's long-term sovereign credit rating at B1, also with a stable outlook.
Mongolian officials view the assessments by the three major international credit rating agencies as an important indication of international confidence in the country at a time of heightened global uncertainty. They also see the ratings as a positive signal to international investors that could help attract greater investment into Mongolia. ■

Loneliness linked to greatest quality-of-life decline among young Australians: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
21:48:40 CST
22:48:40 KST

MELBOURNE, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- Loneliness hits young Australians aged 15 to 24 harder than any other age group when it comes to their overall physical and mental wellbeing, a study has found.
Young people experience greater quality-of-life losses from loneliness than older adults, despite receiving less attention, according to a statement released Friday by Australia's Monash University.
The study, published in Value in Health, analyzed more than 53,000 observations from almost 22,000 Australians aged 15 and over across four rounds of a national survey.
Researchers examined how changes in loneliness and social isolation were associated with changes in their health-related quality of life over time, accounting for factors including employment, income, physical and mental health conditions and major life events.
Loneliness was reported by 18 percent of people aged 15 to 24, compared with 12 percent of those aged 65 and over. In contrast, social isolation alone was more common among older Australians, the study showed.
The study measured health-related quality of life on a standardized scale ranging from 0 (death) to 1 (full health). Among young people aged 15 to 24, loneliness was associated with a 0.079-point reduction in health utility, the largest decline associated with loneliness across the age groups studied.
Across all age groups, health utility was 0.061 points lower among people experiencing loneliness alone, compared with those experiencing neither loneliness nor social isolation. The reduction was 0.020 points for social isolation alone and 0.102 points for people experiencing both.
Lead researcher Fikru Rizal from Monash University said the findings reinforced the importance of recognizing loneliness across the lifespan and distinguishing it from social isolation, which refers to objectively having fewer relationships and less frequent social contact. ■

The government has also approved 1 billion Mongolian tugriks (about 277,000 U.S. dollars) in funding to expedite the import of bear tranquilizer guns, sedatives, chemical agents and other necessary equipment.
Relevant officials have also been instructed to use advanced technologies to collect and compile data on the bear population in the country.
According to the Ministry of Environment and Climate Change, more than 750 bear sightings have been reported in residential areas across Mongolia since the spring of this year.
Experts say encounters between bears and livestock, as well as bear sightings in residential areas, have increased in recent years. They attribute the trend to several factors, including climate change, food shortages in bears' natural habitats and the overexploitation of natural resources. ■

Helsinki moves to restrict high-emission travel ads to meet climate goals
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
21:48:34 CST
22:48:34 KST

HELSINKI, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- Finland's capital Helsinki has decided to ban outdoor advertisements promoting airline flights, cruises and fossil-fuel-powered cars on city-controlled advertising spaces as part of efforts to meet its climate goals, Finnish media reported Friday.
According to Finnish daily Helsingin Sanomat, the Helsinki City Council approved the move on Wednesday. The restrictions would cover commercial billboards in public spaces, including advertising displays at public transport stops.
The ban, however, will not take immediate effect. According to city documents, Helsinki's existing outdoor advertising contracts run until March 31, 2035, and cannot be unilaterally amended. The restrictions are expected to be incorporated into future contracts, with their precise scope and implementation details yet to be determined.
The move comes as Helsinki steps up efforts to meet its climate targets. The city aims to cut direct greenhouse gas emissions by 85 percent from 1990 levels by 2030 and achieve net-zero emissions by 2040, according to the city government.
Commenting on the decision, Mia Eloranta, communications manager at Finnish national carrier Finnair, told Finnish newspaper Hufvudstadsbladet that much of today's advertising takes place on digital platforms, including mobile phones, adding that the airline would comply with the rules.
The proposed ban has also raised concerns in the tourism industry. Noora Lofstrom, CEO of Visit Aland, told Finnish broadcaster Alands Radio that restrictions on airline and ferry advertising could make it harder for visitors to learn about travel options to the Aland Islands, an autonomous region of Finland. She expressed hope that regular passenger ferry services would be exempted from the ban.
Marika Nojd, communications director at ferry operator Tallink Silja, said that the company welcomed Helsinki's efforts to promote sustainability but stressed that any advertising restrictions should be applied consistently. She added that the company was developing new biofuels that could become available by 2035.
The move follows similar initiatives elsewhere in Europe.
In neighboring Sweden, Stockholm proposed a new advertising policy in September that would restrict promotions for fossil fuels and high-emission transport, including hybrid vehicles, on city-controlled advertising spaces. The proposal is currently undergoing public consultation.
Helsinki's initiative also draws on approaches adopted in Amsterdam and The Hague, where local authorities have moved to restrict advertising linked to fossil fuel consumption. ■

China becomes S. Africa's largest trading partner in manufactured goods: SARB
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
21:48:19 CST
22:48:19 KST

JOHANNESBURG, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- China has overtaken the euro area to become South Africa's largest trading partner in manufactured goods, the South African Reserve Bank (SARB) said on Thursday in its September 2026 Quarterly Bulletin.
The SARB said it periodically revises its effective exchange rate (EER) indices to accurately reflect changing trade patterns and developments in the domestic economy, and the EER measures the rand against a weighted basket of currencies of South Africa's major trading partners, with each partner assigned a weight based on its trade relationship with South Africa.
"China has been South Africa's fastest-growing trading partner since 2003, moving from sixth position in the 2003 EER revision to second position in the 2014 and 2020 revisions, and to first position in the 2026 revision. China's trade weight increased from 24.5 percent in 2020 to 28.6 percent in 2026," the SARB said.
Over a longer period, China's weight rose from just 3.1 percent in 1999 to 28.6 percent in 2026, it added. At the same time, the euro area's trade weight declined from 35.7 percent in 1999 to 26.01 percent in 2026, moving it into second place.
South Africa is China's largest trading partner in Africa, while China has remained South Africa's largest trading partner for 17 consecutive years, with bilateral trade reaching 53.58 billion U.S. dollars in 2025. ■

NEW DELHI, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- India's federal health ministry Friday said it has proposed stricter restrictions on the advertising of prescription medicines, seeking to extend existing regulatory requirements to drug retailers, wholesalers and distributors in a move aimed at curbing unauthorised promotion and strengthening patient safety.
The proposed amendment to the Drugs Rules, 1945, seeks to make prior approval of the federal government mandatory for advertisements relating to medicines listed under Schedule H, H1 and X.
The draft amendment has been notified through a Gazette notification dated Sept. 28, 2026, following consultations with the Drugs Technical Advisory Board.
The measure is expected to reinforce safeguards relating to medicines that require appropriate medical supervision, including certain antibiotics, psychotropic medicines and other prescription-only drugs, the ministry said.
According to the ministry, the move is aimed at curbing unauthorised promotion of prescription medicines and strengthening safeguards for public health.
In India, Schedule H, H1 and X drugs can be sold only under specific conditions, usually with a doctor's prescription. These rules help regulate medicines that may have serious side effects or carry a risk of dependence or misuse.
The ministry has invited objections and suggestions from stakeholders and members of the public within 30 days from the date on which copies of the Gazette containing the draft rules are made available to the public. ■

Africa CDC urges heightened regional preparedness as Ebola cases reach 8,750
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
21:48:09 CST
22:48:09 KST

ADDIS ABABA, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) has called for strict regional preparedness to avert further spread of the ongoing Ebola outbreak, as the number of confirmed cases has reached 8,750 alongside a mounting death toll.
Addressing an online press briefing on Thursday evening, Wessam Mankoula, an Africa CDC official, lauded Kenya's preparedness and ongoing response efforts, as the country became the latest country to record a Bundibugyo Ebola case.
Calling for enhanced regional preparedness and solidarity, he highlighted that the East African country's prior investments in preparedness have enabled it to respond quickly to the imported case and strengthen contact tracing.
"Ebola is crossing another border. However, at the Africa CDC, we are calling for vigilance, not banning," said Mankoula.
Kenyan authorities are currently tracing contacts linked to its first imported case and have enhanced disease surveillance to avoid the potential spread of the virus, after a 40-year-old patient, a Kenyan citizen who had lived in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) for seven years, died from the disease in a Nairobi hospital on Monday.
Africa CDC officials stressed that the imported case has triggered concern over the disease's spread. The patient moved across the DRC, Uganda, and Kenya before testing positive, highlighting how quickly the virus can cross borders and threaten regional health security.
Mankoula said the current crisis, regarded as the fastest-growing and second-largest Ebola outbreak on record, at week 21, has recorded 4.1 times more cases and 3.7 times more deaths than the next-highest comparator, the 2014-2016 West Africa Ebola outbreak.
The latest data from the African Union's specialized continental public health agency showed that confirmed cases in the ongoing Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak have reached 8,750, with more than 4,208 deaths and a case fatality rate of 48.1 percent. Some 2,288 patients have recovered from the deadly disease, while 1,066 patients are currently in isolation.
Beyond the DRC, Uganda, and Kenya, 10 other countries across the continent have been previously designated as high-risk: South Sudan, Rwanda, Zambia, the Central African Republic, Tanzania, Ethiopia, Angola, the Republic of the Congo, Burundi, and Somalia.
The Africa CDC declared the ongoing Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak a public health emergency of continental security on May 18, one day after the World Health Organization declared the situation a public health emergency of international concern.
Ebola is highly contagious and can cause fever, vomiting, diarrhea, generalized pain or malaise, and, in severe cases, internal and external bleeding. ■

"We are opening traffic using temporary infrastructure so that people can use the crossing right away. This is the first phase of the project. Next, we plan to build a full-scale complex for processing trucks and buses. Once construction is completed, it will be able to additionally process up to 360 trucks and 50 buses per day," Kalashnyk concluded.

French police have recovered two paintings by French artist Auguste Renoir that were stolen from a museum in the southern French town of Cagnes-sur-Mer last month, French broadcaster BFMTV reported Friday.
The paintings, Madame Colonna Romano (Mrs. Colonna Romano) and Jeune femme au puits (Young Woman at the Well), were recovered Thursday, Oct. 8.
The two works were estimated to be worth between €8 million ($9 million) and €10 million ($11.2 million).
The theft took place on Sept. 8, when two burglars entered the Renoir Museum, the artist’s former residence, through a hole cut in the garden fence.
The suspects stole four artworks but abandoned two as they fled when police arrived.
The four targeted paintings were the museum’s most valuable works, according to the prosecutor’s office.
Six people were arrested Wednesday in the southern Alpes-Maritimes department, the Herault department in southern France and the Jura department in eastern France.
Two of the suspects are believed to have carried out the burglary.
Cagnes-sur-Mer Mayor Bryan Masson described the suspects as “real professionals” after the theft, saying they had worn helmets, gloves and masks and appeared to have detailed knowledge of the museum.
Following the recovery, Masson congratulated the Marseille Interregional Specialized Court and the law enforcement agencies involved in the investigation, including units specializing in judicial investigations and the trafficking of cultural property.
“These two paintings are not simply works of art. They belong to the history of our town, our heritage and the legacy left by Auguste Renoir in Cagnes-sur-Mer,” Masson said.
He described their recovery as a “great relief” for local residents and those attached to the museum.
The investigation into suspected organized theft and criminal conspiracy is ongoing.

Eggs cost nearly 20 times US prices in occupied Oleshky, where Ukraine’s ombudsman says people die of hunger every day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:45:10 UTC
22:45:10 KST

People in Russian-occupied Oleshky, a town in southern Ukraine, are running out of food and medicine and have no way out, a local resident told RBC-Ukraine. Ukraine's human rights ombudsman told the outlet that civilians there are dying of hunger every day.
The part of Kherson Oblast across the Dnipro River has been under Russian occupation since 2022, with civilians facing food and medicine shortages and restrictions on leaving. The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine has documented deteriorating conditions in Oleshky and neighboring Hola Prystan. There has been no practical breakthrough toward an organized evacuation, though 358 people who need help to leave Oleshky and nearby settlements have been verified. About 2,000 people remain in Oleshky, Kherson Oblast head Oleksandr Prokudin estimated.
The resident, who spoke anonymously, said food is extremely scarce, and residents are waiting for a humanitarian corridor to leave. The local market offers mostly vegetables and fruit, such as tomatoes, cucumbers, zucchini, pears, and apples. Russia made its ruble the only legal currency in occupied Kherson Oblast from 1 January 2023, pushing out the Ukrainian hryvnia. Prices at the market start at 500 rubles (about $6), and "if you're lucky, 10 eggs can be bought for 3,000 rubles" (about $36), the resident said. That is about $3.60 an egg, nearly 20 times the US average of about $0.19, or $2.27 a dozen in August, US government data show.
Russian troops enter homes and threaten starving Oleshky residents for food and alcohol, officials say
Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, told RBC-Ukraine that civilians in the occupied area were dying every day.
"There is a humanitarian catastrophe there. Ukrainian civilians die there every day because they lack even basic food and water. There have been no medicines there for a long time. According to our information, there is simply hunger there," he said.
Practically no medicines
The resident said there were practically no medicines available. Expired drugs were being sold at about 100 rubles (about $1.20) a pill. His father has Parkinson's syndrome and has been concussed twice. The resident said he was forced to reduce his father's dose by 25% so the supply would last at least until the new year.
Thousands are starving in occupied Oleshky. People have no food, no way out, and Russian forces bomb incoming aid
The resident's apartment had burned down, and his house remained damaged. His family had made the house livable and was living there, he said. His wife had lost more than 40 kilograms while the family relied on vegetables and fruit.
Beyond Oleshky: villages with no transport or aid
Four villages in the Hola Prystan community—Kokhany, Kardashynka, Velyka Kardashynka, and Mala Kardashynka—are effectively blocked, according to the Skhid-SOS fund. The fund told RBC-Ukraine that no transport reaches the villages and no humanitarian aid has been delivered for a prolonged period, although it is difficult to get more information from the villages. Residents are forced to walk or cycle to other settlements to find food, despite the risks of mines and drone strikes.
Civilians used as a buffer
Lubinets also said Russian troops were using civilians as a buffer and as protection against the Ukrainian military, RBC-Ukraine reported. Because Ukrainian citizens remain in Oleshky, Ukraine cannot conduct active combat operations there, he said—which, in his view, allows Russia to hold civilians effectively as hostages on the front line.
Food arrives by drone, but how much reaches residents is unclear
Ukraine has delivered food to Oleshky by drone since March, Prokudin said. Nearly 400 parcels weighing almost 4 tons reached their drop-off points on the night of 4 October, Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi said. How much of the food stays with residents is unclear. Prokudin has said Russian forces shoot down supply drones, confiscate or resell the packages, and detain and beat residents who receive them.
After a previous delivery, Tetiana Hasanenko, head of the Oleshky City Military Administration, said that Russian troops take drone-dropped food and accuse those who receive it of cooperating with Ukraine, and that some residents got several packages while others got none.

2026-10-09
16:43:41 EEST
22:43:41 KST

Ukraine has recovered EUR 700,000 from abroad in a corruption case involving the state-owned Polygraph Combine Ukraina, the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) has reported.
One of the defendants admitted guilt and agreed to compensate for the damage, NABU said on Telegram on Friday.
The funds had been frozen in the defendant's accounts in France. Following approval of a plea agreement by Ukraine's High Anti-Corruption Court and with the consent of France's National Financial Prosecutor's Office, the freeze was lifted and the money transferred to the state-owned enterprise's account, NABU said.
The recovery resulted from the work of a joint investigation team comprising NABU detectives, Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) prosecutors, and law enforcement officers from France and Estonia. The team also received expert and coordination support from the StAR Initiative, Eurojust, and the OECD GLEN and GFAR Action Series platforms, NABU said.
This is the third recovery of assets from abroad in the case. In October 2025, French company SURYS transferred EUR 3.37 million to the Ukrainian state, followed by another EUR 450,000 in June 2026. The total amount recovered in the case has now reached EUR 4.5 million, NABU said.
In August 2026, Ukrainian anti-corruption authorities sent to court a case concerning an alleged international corruption scheme involving passport production, with estimated losses of around UAH 500 million.
The former head of the Polygraph Combine is accused of misappropriating the enterprise's funds, receiving an undue benefit in the form of copyright to security-feature designs used in foreign passports and ID cards, and laundering proceeds from their use. Another defendant is a former department head at the enterprise.
According to NABU, in 2013 the then-head of the combine acquired an Estonian company through nominees and made its involvement a condition of cooperation with foreign partners. The intermediary purchased holograms directly from a French manufacturer and resold them to the state-owned enterprise at prices four to six times higher, investigators allege.
Four participants in the scheme have been convicted by the High Anti-Corruption Court under plea agreements. Almost UAH 180 million has been returned to the state, nearly UAH 6 million allocated to support Ukraine's Defense Forces, and more than UAH 20 million reimbursed to the state-owned enterprise, NABU said.

Bulgarian teacher in Sydney turns 100, receives greetings from King Charles III
Friday 9 October 2026 15:52
Friday, 9 October 2026, 15:52
PHOTO Facebook/RodinaSydney
Font size
Bulgarian-born Gina Kozhuharova, who taught generations of students at the English Language High School in Plovdiv, has celebrated her 100th birthday in Sydney, Australia. To mark the occasion, she received an official congratulatory letter from King Charles III, Australia's head of state. The news was shared by the Rodina Bulgarian Cultural and Social Association in Sydney.
Decades after leaving the classroom, Gina Kozhuharova is still fondly remembered by her former students in Bulgaria.
“She taught us not only the finer points of English pronunciation, but also good manners and, above all, love and compassion,” one of them wrote in a comment on the association's post.
Gina Kozhuharova has strong ties to the Bulgarian community in Australia. Her brother, Stefan Kozhuharov, founded the Rodina Bulgarian Cultural and Social Association in Sydney and was awarded the Order of Australia for his contribution to society and the Bulgarian community.
For the association, her centenary is also a tribute to the generations of Bulgarians who have kept their identity and traditions alive far from home.
Rodina wished her good health, peace and many more happy moments with her loved ones. And the messages from her former pupils in Bulgaria are a touching reminder that, even after all these years and thousands of miles, a much-loved teacher is never forgotten.

Yair Golan: Killing Khamenei was a mistake, 'not because he didn't deserve to die,' but because it did not serve Israel's interests

13:41:46 UTC

Killing Khamenei was a 'mistake,' Yair Golan says
Golan says Iran’s surviving leaders are more extreme and violent, accuses Netanyahu of setting an unrealistic goal of regime change
Democrats leader Yair Golan said killing Iran’s supreme leader Ali Khamenei did not serve Israel’s interests, arguing that the operation left more extreme figures in power.
“I think that, without a doubt, eliminating Khamenei senior was a mistake. Not because he didn’t deserve to die, but because it did not serve Israel’s interests,” he said at a Friday Culture event in Rishon LeZion.
“There is a certain advantage to having an elderly, long-standing leader like Khamenei. He was 86, after all,” Golan said. Of Khamenei’s son and successor, he added: “If he is even functioning at all, I get the impression that he is controlled by Iran’s ultra-extremist security leadership.”
“After we wiped out the top tier of leadership across so many key areas, we were left with individuals who are more extreme and more violent,” he said, arguing that Israel’s achievements against Iran peaked with Operation Rising Lion in June 2025.
Golan said the subsequent Operation Roaring Lion “did not improve our position,” accusing Netanyahu of setting “an unrealistic war objective — overthrowing the Iranian regime — which ultimately failed and was never achieved.”
Khamenei was killed in an Israeli airstrike on his Tehran compound on February 28, in the opening wave of the joint U.S.-Israeli offensive against Iran.
Golan, a former IDF deputy chief of staff, heads the left-wing party formed by the merger of Labor and Meretz. His remarks came ahead of Israel’s October 27 election, with his party among the opposition factions seeking to oust Netanyahu.

Bulgarian filmmaker Ina Sotirova receives five Caribbean Film Awards nominations
The winners will be announced on 10 October
Friday 9 October 2026 15:37
Friday, 9 October 2026, 15:37
Ina Sotirova
PHOTO imdb.com
Font size
Filmmaker Ina Sotirova is driven by a desire to help change the world around her through her work. In pursuing this goal, she strives to keep her finger on the pulse of everyday life, exploring the concerns and experiences that matter to people, even those they keep hidden or consider too personal to share. Her ability to tell stories with honesty, through the eyes of the people who live them, has earned her the admiration of audiences and recognition for her work.
Her fourth film, Stinky Mango, received several nominations at the Diversity in Cannes event, winning the award for Best Ensemble Cast in Cannes. It subsequently received an award for innovative storytelling at the Films That Move festival in Jamaica.
PHOTO Mango Magic Movie
A year later, we have another reason to catch up with Ina Sotirova. Stinky Mango has received three nominations at the Caribbean Film Awards – for Best Short Film, Best Actor for Sheldon Shepherd, and the Caribbean Cultural Heritage Award. Sotirova herself is nominated for Best Emerging Director. Whether she takes home any of the awards will become clear on 10 October, at the inaugural edition of the awards ceremony in Wilmington, United States.
Her latest film, The Sisters and the Storm, has also been nominated for Best Documentary. The project was funded through a UNICEF programme:
“Last year, on 28 October, Hurricane Melissa struck the south-western part of Jamaica. It was extremely powerful and caused widespread devastation. Even today, people are still struggling to recover,” Ina Sotirova tells us.
PHOTO Mango Magic Movie
“Earlier this year, UNICEF and the Jamaica Film and Television Association (JAFTA) launched an initiative to fund three short documentaries exploring the impact of the hurricane on women and children. I submitted my project, The Sisters of the Storm, and was awarded one of the three grants.
“The film tells the story of three girls who either have no families or have been removed from their homes because of domestic violence or other problems. They live in what are known as children's villages. The hurricane destroyed one of these villages, forcing them to move to a similar facility in Jamaica's capital, Kingston, where they don't feel at home.”
Filming presented an unusual and emotionally demanding challenge because of the circumstances of its young protagonists:
PHOTO Mango Magic Movie
“They are children, some of whom have no parents. We had to protect their identities. This isn't a typical documentary where you see interviews with the people involved. We made it more like an audio diary.
“Because we weren't allowed to show the children on screen or reveal where they were living, we had to be very creative in how we approached that part of the filmmaking process. As a result, the film became a much more poetic and intimate portrait of these children at a particular moment in their lives.”
Filming took just five days, although editing continued for another two months:
“I think this is the fastest film I've ever made. It's only eight minutes long, but I should point out that making an eight-minute film is harder than making a fifteen-minute one, because it takes much more skill to decide what really matters.”
PHOTO Mango Magic Movie
Is there a story from everyday life in Bulgaria that our compatriot feels strongly enough about to turn into a film that could capture the interest of audiences in Jamaica or elsewhere in the world?
“Of course. Wherever you look, there are stories,” Ina says emphatically. “There are things I feel I should learn more about myself. I simply haven't yet had the time or opportunity to immerse myself in those stories.
“I'm particularly interested in communism and how its legacy continues to shape contemporary culture. So, at some point, I'll explore those stories too.”

Bogazici Film Festival unveils 2026 poster as global culture calendar gathers pace

09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
The 14th Bogazici Film Festival will be held in Istanbul from Nov. 8-15, as cities worldwide prepare for a busy week of film screenings, exhibitions, concerts, literary gatherings and stage performances. 
Organized by the Bogazici Culture and Arts Foundation with support from Türkiye’s Ministry of Culture and Tourism General Directorate of Cinema, the festival will bring together productions from Türkiye and abroad alongside talks, masterclasses and industry events. 
Anadolu serves as the festival’s Global Communication Partner. 
This year’s poster, designed by Fatma Betul Okuyucu, combines imagery associated with Istanbul and cinema through a layered collage. 
Different textures, handwritten elements, colors and illustrations are arranged in a composition that expands outward from its center. The design seeks to reflect Istanbul’s movement, energy and inclusive character while conveying the atmosphere of a film festival. 
Turkcell and Turkish Airlines are the main sponsors, while public broadcaster TRT is the institutional partner. Festival announcements and programming information will be published on its website and social media accounts.
Film festivals in London and New York 
In Britain, the 70th BFI London Film Festival will begin Wednesday and continue through Oct. 18, presenting new films, television productions and immersive works in London and cinemas across the UK. 
The festival will open with the European premiere of Simon Stone’s Elsinore. Ten productions will compete for its Best Film award, with the winner scheduled to be announced on Oct. 18. 
Across the Atlantic, the 64th New York Film Festival will continue through Oct. 12. Its main selection comprises 34 films, while screenings are also being staged across New York City’s five boroughs through Friday. 
The festival, organized by Film at Lincoln Center, opened on Sept. 25 with James Gray’s Paper Tiger and will close with Ava DuVernay’s 14th. 
Frankfurt becomes center of the publishing world 
Authors, publishers, literary agents and readers will gather in Germany for the 78th Frankfurt Book Fair held from Wednesday through Sunday. 
Czechia is the 2026 Guest of Honour at the international publishing event, which will also explore links between literature, film, audio production and gaming. 
The program includes Pulitzer Prize-winning historian and author Jill Lepore, International Booker Prize winner Yang Shuang-zi, German writer Shida Bazyar and children’s author Cornelia Funke. The fair will initially focus on industry professionals before opening more widely to the public from Friday.  
Exhibitions, ballet and classical music 
New York’s Museum of Modern Art is presenting The Surrealist Book: Tomorrow Lives in Mirrors, an exhibition exploring the role of books and printed works in the Surrealist movement. It opened Sunday and will remain on view through Jan. 23. 
The Metropolitan Museum of Art has also opened Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous, examining the artistic relationship and continuing influence of Lee Krasner and Jackson Pollock. The exhibition runs through Jan. 31. 
In Paris, the Paris Opera Ballet will open its dance season Saturday with a gala at the Palais Garnier. The program will bring together the company’s dancers, Junior Ballet and Ballet School, followed by works from choreographers Juliano Nunes, Jean-Christophe Maillot and Aszure Barton. 
New York’s Carnegie Hall, meanwhile, will welcome the Berlin Philharmonic on Friday and Saturday as part of its new season. Conducted by Kirill Petrenko, the orchestra’s program includes Italian opera selections featuring tenor Jonas Kaufmann and works by Ottorino Respighi. 
At the Sydney Opera House, conductor Donald Runnicles will lead performances devoted to Brahms from Thursday through Saturday. The venue’s family-focused Wild Things festival will also continue until Sunday with theater, workshops and outdoor performances.

Protesters clash with police in Brussels as unions and students march

Protesters clash with police in Brussels as unions and students march
BRUSSELS – A small group of protesters clashed with police in Brussels on Oct 9 as union members, joined by hundreds of students, marched as part of a national strike against planned government budget cuts.
A few dozen masked protesters dressed in black threw rocks and other objects at police, as anti-police slogans echoed through the streets and anti-police graffiti covered nearby walls. Firefighters extinguished several fires, including on buses, while police responded with tear gas, according to Reuters witnesses.
The clashes occurred as thousands of protesters took to the streets of the Belgian capital, including students inspired in part by demonstrations in neighbouring France. The strike disrupted public transport and air travel, while many schools and childcare facilities were also affected.
Among the demonstrators, some carried placards reading “I skipped class to defend class” and “Education is a right, not a privilege”.
The Belgian walkout is part of a wave of protests sweeping Europe, with students in France and Italy, among other countries, taking to the streets over education funding, while tens of thousands have rallied in Spain over a housing crisis.
Police said while the march itself, joined by around 30,000 people, passed off peacefully, clashes erupted near Brussels Central Station and in central Brussels where groups threw bottles, bricks, stones and fireworks at police, set fires and damaged public property.
Police said officers used water cannon and tear gas to disperse the groups and that 21 people had been detained or arrested, including 13 minors.
The strike was called by Belgium’s two largest unions, the socialist FGTB/ABVV and Christian CSC/ACV, which oppose government budget measures they say would make workers, pensioners and low-income households bear the burden of efforts to reduce the country’s deficit.
Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever said on Oct 8 that painful budget measures were needed now to avert a looming debt and interest-cost spiral that would otherwise leave future generations with a heavy bill.
Student groups, whose protests began earlier in October in Liege and spread to Brussels on Oct 9, say they are also protesting rising education costs, overcrowded classrooms and reforms they fear will make higher education less accessible.
“We’re not taken into account at all, and no one seems to realise that it’s hard for us too, both for workers and for students,” said Emilie L’Honneux, a 23-year-old student from Liege.
“We’re struggling too, and we are the future of this country,” she added. REUTERS

Russia has equipped the "Shaheds" it uses to attack Kyiv with new 32-element antennas — what challenges this creates for Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
New "Shaheds" have been found to contain 32-element CRPA antennas designed to counter Ukrainian electronic warfare systems. This makes suppressing GPS navigation twice as difficult.
The Shaheds attacking Kyiv now have new protected satellite navigation antennas of a new type with 32 elements. Presidential adviser and radio technology specialist Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov explained what this means and what difficulties it creates, reports UNN.
We continue to detect new protected satellite navigation antennas of a new type with 32 elements in the Shaheds attacking Kyiv. Previously, the enemy used antennas with 16 elements. What does this mean? A Shahed can find its target either in operator-controlled radio mode (via a MESH modem) or by using satellite navigation signals (GPS and others)
According to him, to counter GPS guidance of the Shaheds, Ukraine creates interference on satellite navigation frequencies using electronic warfare systems. In turn, the enemy installs special CRPA antennas on the Shahed that can neutralize signals from our electronic warfare systems. The more elements there are, the more sources of electronic warfare signals the antenna can suppress.
Previously, we conventionally had to ensure that there were always 16 electronic warfare sources around the Shahed, whereas now, conventionally, there need to be twice as many. This race is difficult for us because it is easier for the enemy to increase the number of elements on an antenna than for us to add electronic warfare points
