Central China's Hubei unveils investigation report on major fireworks accident
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
20:55:49 CST
21:55:49 KST

WUHAN, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- The emergency management department of central China's Hubei Province on Friday released an investigation report regarding a fatal fireworks accident that occurred in the city of Yicheng in the province on Feb. 18.
The accident took place at approximately 2:22 p.m. at a store located in Jinpu Village in this city, which caused 12 deaths and direct economic losses of 12.79 million yuan (about 1.9 million U.S. dollars).
According to the investigation, the direct cause was that a customer surnamed Xie illegally test-fired a firework in front of the store, which ignited a large quantity of fireworks displayed outside the store, triggering a chain of explosions and fires both outside and inside the premises.
People outside fled into the store, but the front door was blocked by the burning fireworks and the rear rolling shutter door was closed, preventing timely escape and resulting in heavy casualties.
The investigation pointed to a number of problems exposed by the accident, including illegal and irregular operations at fireworks and firecracker retail stores, lax government oversight of permit approval, ineffective performance of duties by local Party committees, governments and departments, and inadequate supervision of the flow of oversized or over-dosage products into the market.
The report noted that Xie has been arrested by public security authorities on suspicion of negligently endangering public safety by dangerous means. As the store's actual operator, surnamed Lin, had died in the accident, no criminal responsibility is recommended.
Yang, a co-operator of the store, is recommended to receive administrative penalties, with suspected criminal conduct transferred to public security authorities. ■

China's finance ministry pledges vigorous, effective implementation of more proactive fiscal policy
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
20:55:45 CST
21:55:45 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- China's Ministry of Finance said on Friday it would vigorously and effectively implement a more proactive fiscal policy, step up counter-cyclical adjustments, and introduce additional measures in a timely manner in response to macroeconomic developments.
In a report on the implementation of China's fiscal policy in the first half of 2026, the ministry said it would make full use of existing policy measures while planning and rolling out practical and effective new measures as needed, with a focus on expanding domestic demand, improving supply and safeguarding people's livelihoods.
The ministry said it would accelerate the allocation and use of fiscal funds, optimize the structure of government expenditure, and improve spending efficiency. It also pledged to expedite the issuance and use of government bonds to support project implementation.
Special treasury bonds will be issued to inject capital into eight central financial institutions, strengthening their resilience to risks and ability to serve the real economy, according to the report.
China has pledged to continue implementing a more proactive fiscal policy in 2026, with the deficit-to-GDP ratio set at around 4 percent and the total government deficit at 5.89 trillion yuan (about 875 billion U.S. dollars), this year's government work report noted. Expenditure in the general public budget is, notably, projected to reach 30 trillion yuan for the first time.
China's gross domestic product, meanwhile, grew 4.7 percent year on year in the first half of 2026, the National Bureau of Statistics has revealed.
During this same period, China's general public budget expenditure rose 1.5 percent year on year to 14.33 trillion yuan, with spending on healthcare and on social security and employment increasing by 10.8 percent and 7.6 percent, respectively, official data showed.
By the end of June, the central government had allocated 9.4 trillion yuan in transfer payments to local governments, accounting for 90.3 percent of the annual budget. Authorities also allocated 125 billion yuan in subsidies for consumer goods trade-in programs, helping generate roughly 1.1 trillion yuan in sales.
Fiscal policy support has also been reinforced via closer coordination with financial measures to stimulate investment and consumption.
This year, the central government earmarked 100 billion yuan for a package of six coordinated fiscal and financial policy tools aimed at boosting domestic demand. In the first seven months, these measures supported more than 20 trillion yuan in newly extended credit to relevant sectors, up 4.5 percent year on year, finance ministry data revealed.
Four investment-focused measures supported approximately 1.51 trillion yuan in private investment, while two consumption-focused measures supported around 1.88 trillion yuan in household consumption during the same period.
Authorities have also expanded interest subsidies for personal consumption loans and loans to micro, small and medium-sized enterprises and service-sector businesses, while introducing a new mortgage interest subsidy policy for eligible first-time homebuyers.
The mortgage policy, which took effect on Oct. 1 with a tentative implementation period of one year, provides an annualized interest subsidy of 1 percentage point on eligible commercial mortgage loans for first homes, with the subsidy period extending up to five years. This measure is intended to reduce borrowing costs for eligible homebuyers and support housing demand.
Looking ahead, the ministry said it would also support efforts to expand domestic demand on all fronts, promote technological and industrial innovation, safeguard and improve people's well-being, prevent and defuse risks in key areas, and deepen fiscal management reforms. ■

China records 826 mln domestic tourist trips during 2026 National Day holiday amid diverse offerings
China
Unknown Publisher

Tourists view a giant floral basket installation at Tian'anmen Square in Beijing, capital of China, Oct. 1, 2026. China recorded 826 million domestic tourist trips during the seven-day National Day holiday, with tourism spending totaling 738.38 billion yuan (about 109.67 billion U.S. dollars), the Ministry of Culture and Tourism said Friday. On a daily average basis, the number of domestic trips rose 6.3 percent from the eight-day National Day and Mid-Autumn Festival holiday in 2025, while tourism spending increased 4.3 percent, according to the ministry. (Xinhua/Ju Huanzong)
BEIJING, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- China saw 826 million domestic tourist trips during the recent seven-day National Day holiday, with tourism spending totaling 738.38 billion yuan (about 109.67 billion U.S. dollars), the Ministry of Culture and Tourism said on Friday.
On a daily average basis, the number of domestic trips rose 6.3 percent from the eight-day National Day and Mid-Autumn Festival holiday in 2025, while tourism spending increased 4.3 percent, according to the ministry.
The holiday witnessed a vibrant cultural scene, with 180 large-scale performances held nationwide, including 125 concerts and 55 music festivals.
Beyond cultural performances, the integration of tourism with culture, commerce and sports continued to deepen. Mass-participation sports events and digital innovations offered visitors new experiences and helped drive tourism-related consumption.
Meanwhile, around 40 percent of tourists visited revolutionary sites or took part in activities such as flag-raising ceremonies and patriotic performances.
This trend takes on added significance this year, which marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March (1934-1936). The arduous journey helped lay the foundation for the eventual victory of the Chinese revolution.
Dai Bin, president of the China Tourism Academy, said the flow of visitors to revolutionary landmarks reflects people's emotional identification with revolutionary traditions.
When they travel, they don't just want to see history. They also want to draw deeper inspiration from the revolutionary legacy for their lives today, Dai noted.
Measures to boost tourism consumption have also helped expand holiday options for visitors and enhance their travel experiences.
Under a nationwide cultural and tourism consumption campaign running from late September through October, local authorities have organized a variety of activities and distributed more than 310 million yuan in consumption subsidies. ■

BEIJING, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- Ding Yexian, former deputy head of the standing committee of the People's Congress of the Xizang Autonomous Region in southwest China, has been expelled from the Communist Party of China (CPC), China's top anti-graft agency announced on Friday.

Ding violated the political, organizational and integrity discipline of the CPC, committed serious duty-related crimes and is suspected of bribery, the statement said.
In line with Party regulations and laws, a decision has been made to expel him from the Party, revoke his entitlements, terminate his capacity as a delegate to the 10th Party congress of the Xizang Autonomous Region, confiscate his illicit gains, and hand over his case for judicial proceedings. ■

South Africa withdraws asylum directive after violent anti-migrant protests
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
20:55:28 CST
21:55:28 KST

JOHANNESBURG, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- South Africa's Department of Home Affairs on Friday withdrew a directive instructing its Refugee Reception Offices to process asylum applications following a Constitutional Court ruling, amid violent anti-migrant protests in Johannesburg and Durban on Thursday.
In a statement, the department said Director-General Livhuwani Tommy Makhode had withdrawn the directive issued on Sept. 28 concerning the intake of asylum seeker applications following the Constitutional Court's July 7 judgment in the Scalabrini of Cape Town case.
The department said that implementing the ruling had "immediately led to serious consequences" that the court order could not have foreseen, adding that within days, refugee offices were overwhelmed, officials were placed at risk, and serious threats to public safety and order emerged.
It stressed that the directive was "a purely operational attempt to support the implementation of the Court's order" without the knowledge of the Home Affairs Minister or any other political office-bearer, rejecting claims that the decision was politically motivated.
The department said it would start a fresh process to find an appropriate and sustainable way to comply with the court's order. It also reaffirmed its respect for the judiciary and the rule of law.
The withdrawal came after violent protests on Thursday in Johannesburg's Soweto township and Durban, where demonstrators opposed the processing of asylum applications and demanded tougher action against irregular migration.
South African police said 10 vehicles were torched in Soweto and another 14 in Durban during the unrest. Foreign-owned shops were also looted, while three foreign nationals were arrested in Durban, according to police. ■

BEIJING, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- Liu Zengyuan, a railway engineer, watched familiar fields slip past the train window. This time, he was not heading to a construction site, but going home for the National Day holiday on the high-speed line he had helped build, just days after it opened.
This line, which officially entered service on Sept. 28, links Xiong'an in north China's Hebei Province with Shangqiu in Henan Province in central China. For Liu, it has cut the trip from Renqiu, his workplace in Hebei, to his hometown of Heze in east China's Shandong Province, from four or five hours to only two.
On the same day, China opened three other high-speed rail sections, connecting Xi'an with Ankang in Shaanxi Province in northwest China, Yichang with Xingshan in central China's Hubei Province, and Harbin with Yichun in Heilongjiang Province in the country's northeast. During the National Day holiday, from Oct. 1 to Oct. 7, these new lines made it easier for people to visit relatives, and brought new vitality to tourism along the routes.
During the holiday, a Beijing resident surnamed Wang took his family by high-speed rail to Hengshui Lake, a national nature reserve in Hebei Province. He was pleasantly surprised to find the journey so convenient, as the trip took less than two hours, and a shuttle bus at the station took them straight to the scenic area.
This new line ended the history of Hengshui having no high-speed trains directly running to Beijing. Thanks in part to the new rail line and local promotions, 32 A-level scenic spots across Hengshui received 715,000 visitors during the holiday, soaring 202.84 percent year on year.
"Cities are much closer now, not just on the map but in everyday life," said Qu Xiaoyuan, an Ankang cultural and tourism official. His brother, who works in Xi'an, called him the day the Xi'an-Ankang high-speed railway opened, joking that he could dash to Ankang for a nice meal at home and still be back in Xi'an that night.
The line has cut travel time between the two cities from three hours to as short as 45 minutes. Ankang, a mountainous city in southern Shaanxi, is rich in ecological resources, and the new railway has taken a growing number of holiday travelers to its forests and rivers.
Ankang West Station, a new station built for the high-speed line, handled 50,800 outgoing passengers during the holiday, which was more than expected. The city also launched shuttle services linking the station with major scenic spots, where visits rose over 40 percent year on year.
As these new lines draw passengers from a wider area, weekend and short-holiday tourists may increase significantly, driving demand for multi-purpose and experience-oriented tourism products, Qu said.
Further east, the Yichang-Xingshan line brings destinations like southwest China's Chongqing and central China's Wuhan and Zhengzhou within two hours of Xingshan, weaving the Three Gorges, dense forests and cloud-shrouded peaks scattered along the route into easy, spontaneous trips.
Xingshan Station handled 14,216 outgoing passengers during the seven-day holiday, up 54.61 percent year on year. Local businesses in the city used high-speed rail tickets to link hotel discounts and reduce or scrap scenic spot admission fees.
Meanwhile, the northernmost high-speed railway in China connects Harbin, a major ice-and-snow tourism destination, with Yichun, a popular summer retreat and forest tourism spot. It cuts railway travel time between these two cities from about seven hours to roughly two hours, making it easier for more tourists to include Yichun in their holiday plans.
"Yichun used to be a 'maybe' destination because getting there was a hassle, but thanks to the new high-speed rail, it's now a 'must-go'," said a Shanghai visitor surnamed Zheng, adding that the new line has made the stay of his family in Heilongjiang more colorful.
Wang Wei, director of the Yichun Municipal Bureau of Culture, Radio, Television and Tourism, said the new railway will bring Yichun into Harbin's "two-hour economic circle," creating new opportunities for its winter tourism, forest study tours and forest wellness tourism.
Ma Botao, of the China Railway Economic Planning and Research Institute, said for cities newly connected to the railway network, seizing the opportunity depends on how well they position themselves.
"Generally, large cities focus on research and development, finance and headquarters economy, while small cities should leverage their local agriculture, ecology, tourism and distinctive industrial strengths to undertake supporting manufacturing, agricultural product processing, and wellness and cultural tourism, serving as both industrial supporting bases and leisure backyards for central cities," Ma explained.
Behind these expectations lies a network that keeps growing. By the end of 2025, the country's total operating railway mileage had reached 165,000 km, including more than 50,000 km of high-speed rail.
Under national plans, China's high-speed rail network is projected to hit 70,000 km by 2035, featuring eight north-south vertical lines and eight east-west horizontal lines. Once complete, the network will connect major cities, city clusters and key economic zones across the country. ■

Berlin rejects claim it dropped Franco-German tank project
BERLIN, Oct 9 - Germany on Friday dismissed remarks by the head of the French armed forces who said Berlin had decided to quit a troubled Franco-German tank project.
The dispute is the latest sign of strain in Franco-German defence cooperation after the two countries scrapped a joint next-generation fighter jet project in June.
The project involves tank maker KNDS, a holding company created between France's Nexter and Germany's Krauss-Maffei-Wegmann (KMW). Germany's Rheinmetall and France's Thales are also involved.
Berlin and Paris agreed in 2017 to work on the Franco-German Main Ground Combat System (MGCS) tank to succeed the German Leopard 2 and the French Leclerc, but the project has been marred by delays and infighting between the countries.
"Germany and France announced several months ago that they would adjust their joint Main Ground Combat System (MGCS) cooperation program, thereby incorporating the lessons learned from Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine," a spokesperson for the German Defence Ministry said.
"This does not mean the MGCS project has failed. On the contrary: We remain committed to equal partnership in the MGCS and are focusing on future technologies for armored combat."
The head of the French armed forces, Fabien Mandon, had described the result of the joint programme as "not good" at a parliamentary committee hearing on Thursday.
"We have noted that the Germans have decided to drop out of the project," he said.
Later, the French Defence Ministry issued a statement on behalf of Mandon, stressing the work on the joint tank had not been in vain.
It said the programme was continuing and retained "major importance, with a renewed focus on enhanced connectivity, collaborative combat, automation and robotics".
In June, Germany and France scrapped a major project to develop and build a new-generation fighter jet, bowing to industrial rivalries over Europe's most ambitious defence programme.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron had concluded that there was no prospect of breaking months of deadlock between arms firms involved in the plan, German officials said at the time. REUTERS

Greens' Polanski loses key London by-election, Wali-Abdi becomes first Somali-born UK MP
UK Green Party leader Zack Polanski failed to secure seat in parliament on Thursday after losing the Holborn and St Pancras by-election to the Labour Party's candidate.
Sagal Abdi-Wali, the leader of the local council, won the central London constituency's seat with 12,292 votes, compared to Polanski's 8,928.
The defeat follows a media storm over the party's decision to pass the 'Zionism is Racism' motion at its annual conference—a vote which Polanski abstained from.
The 43-year-old former actor and hypnotherapist has moved the party leftwards, criticising Israel's genocide in Gaza and calling on the government de-proscribe direct action group Palestine Action.
While critics suggest Polanski’s defeat will put his leadership under question, the Green leader told Britain's Sky News he would stay on in his role, describing the result as part of "Andy Burnham's honeymoon".
Former leader Caroline Lucas who struggled to contain her anger over what she said was his lack of leadership over the motion on Zionism at last week's conference.
Under former prime minister Keir Starmer, Labour ceded ground to the Green Party, which made record gains in London in May's local elections as its appeal widened among younger, left-leaning voters in the capital and other urban areas.
The Greens have fallen back in opinion polls since Burnham made policy pitches that boosted Labour's standing among left-leaning voters, including a tougher line on Israel and a more ambitious approach to relations with the European Union.
The Greens have positioned themselves as an alternative to Labour for left-liberal voters and gained momentum after beating the governing party in a by-election last year in one of its northern England strongholds.
Thursday's by-election came after Starmer, stood down as a lawmaker in September after being ousted as leader in July.
Who is Sagal Abdi-Wali?
Abdi-Wali, who came to Britain as a child refugee from Somalia after escaping the Somali Civil War, said she was honoured to represent an area that had given her opportunities in life.
"I hope this moment also says something about who gets to belong," said Abdi-Wali. "For people who look like me, I hope they see themselves reflected in this place and know that their path too belongs here."
The MP made history in May, becoming Camden's first black female leader in the local elections, after being first elected as a local councillor in 2022.
She also served as the Cabinet Member for Better Homes, managing the borough's housing and neighbourhood development.
Critics have accused Abdi-Wali of being silent on Israel's genocidal war on Gaza since October 2023, as well as dodging questions on the subject during her campaign.
The former councillor did not sign the Palestine Solidarity Campaign pledge that called on the local candidates to work to end complicity in genocide.
Abdi-Wali also skipped a local elections hustings organised by the Camden Muslim Network, which Polanski and Liberal Democrat candidate Patrick Stillman attended, and later attended a similar event hosted by the Board of Deputies of British Jews.
Agencies contributed to this report.

Malaysia shuts schools as haze from Indonesian fires chokes Southeast Asia
Kuala Lumpur’s Air Pollutant Index says air quality at unhealthy levels amid smog from forest fires.
Malaysia has closed schools in its capital and several states as smoke from Indonesian forest fires pushes air pollution to unhealthy levels.
Schools were ordered to close on Friday across Kuala Lumpur, the administrative capital Putrajaya and in the states of Johor, Malacca, Negeri Sembilan, Pahang and Selangor.
The move, which affected roughly two million students, came as Kuala Lumpur recorded an Air Pollutant Index (API) reading of about 170. The API is a government-run measure of air quality.
Singapore, at the southern end of the Malay Peninsula, saw its air quality fall into the “very unhealthy” range, according to IQAir.
“The haze issue is indeed at a worrying level,” said Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim. He added that he had spoken to Indonesia’s President Prabowo Subianto, who had agreed to take “the necessary steps”. However, he offered no details on what that might entail.
Anwar said he had asked Malaysia’s minister of foreign affairs to push for an urgent meeting of ASEAN environment ministers. Kuala Lumpur is stepping up cloud seeding to trigger rain, he added.
“Appropriate measures must be taken by the relevant ministries and agencies to protect schoolchildren and students, including senior citizens and patients with respiratory illnesses,” King Sultan Ibrahim said. He declared that schools should close when API readings hit 150 or higher.
Under Malaysian guidelines, API readings above 100 are classified as unhealthy, above 200 as very unhealthy, above 300 as hazardous, while readings beyond 500 constitute the threshold for declaring a local emergency.
Education Minister Fadhlina Sidek promised parents more advance notice of closures in future.
In August, Indonesia’s coordinating minister for political and security affairs said that El Nino conditions were threatening more fires during the dry season.
A month later, smoke started to blanket the region as the country experienced its worst fire season in over a decade.
Fires have burned across six provinces, with at least 200,000 hectares scorched, Al Jazeera’s Jessica Washington reported.
Indonesia’s Ministry of Health has recorded more than 170,000 respiratory infections, but the actual figure is likely higher as it only covers those who sought out healthcare, she noted.
The haze has also worried organisers of Singapore’s Formula One weekend, which is set to start on Friday and end on Sunday.
Organisers have insisted that they will race regardless and will have masks and extra medics, adding that it is “not a threat”.

Unknown Publisher

15:52:56 EEST
21:52:56 KST

Consumer prices in Ukraine rose by 2.1% in September 2026, following increases of 0.1% in August and 0.3% in July, the State Statistics Service reported Friday.
The statistics agency recalled that prices had risen by just 0.3% in September 2025. As a result, year-over-year inflation reached 10.0% in September 2026, up from 8.1% at the end of August, 7.7% at the end of July and 7.2% at the end of June.
Core inflation also rose to 2.0% in September 2026, compared with 0.5% in August and 0.3% in July. Given that core inflation stood at 1.3% in September 2025, the year-over-year rate increased to 8.8%, up from 8.1% at the end of August.
According to the State Statistics Service, food and nonalcoholic beverage prices on the consumer market rose by 1.9% in September compared with August of this year. Eggs saw the largest increase, surging by 43.6%. Prices for sugar, rice, grain products, lard, milk, nonalcoholic beverages, fish and fish products, sunflower oil, meat and meat products increased by between 1.7% and 8.3%. Meanwhile, fruit and vegetable prices fell by 5.7% and 2.3%, respectively.
Clothing and footwear prices increased by 8.5%, including a 9.4% rise in clothing prices and a 7.6% increase in footwear prices. Prices (tariffs) for housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels rose by 0.8%, mainly due to increases of 5.6% in water supply tariffs and 5.5% in sewerage tariffs.
Healthcare prices rose by 1.7%, primarily due to a 2.6% increase in pharmaceutical product prices. Education services became 17.4% more expensive, including increases of 23.3% for higher education and 14.3% for secondary education.
Fuel and lubricant prices increased by 5.2%, while fares for road passenger transportation rose by 2.5%.
As reported, the National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) lowered its inflation forecast for 2026 to 10.0% from 9.4% in its previous forecast issued in April, while revising its forecast for 2027 to 6.9% from 6.5% in late July.
However, NBU Deputy Governor Volodymyr Lepushynsky subsequently noted in a column for Interfax-Ukraine that the July forecast update did not take into account new attacks on and the destruction of logistics infrastructure, which have led to additional increases in consumer prices that the central bank estimates at 0.4-0.6 percentage points (pp).
Later, the NBU estimated that a further increase in fuel prices would add 0.3 pp to inflation.

Private firms driving lunar development, but competition for resources poses risks: Space executive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:52:31 UTC
21:52:31 KST

Tugba Altun and Emir Yildirim
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
Private aerospace companies are playing an increasingly important role in developing infrastructure for future operations on the Moon, but competition for limited resources and suitable locations could create international disputes without clear regulations, a space industry executive told Anadolu.
Stirling Forbes, CEO of Forbes-Space, said the growing involvement of commercial companies marked the beginning of a "second space age," distinct from the government-led competition of the Cold War era.
Speaking on the sidelines of the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC) in Antalya, Forbes said private companies were increasingly building infrastructure for both government and commercial use.
"These commercial companies are contributing to the construction of a shared, sustainable infrastructure that will generate returns for Earth," he said.
Forbes pointed to companies developing launch vehicles, lunar rovers, power systems, communications infrastructure and landing facilities.
"These missions range from, of course, the rockets from SpaceX or Blue Origin, down to the rovers of Astrobotic or Lunar Outpost, even to the infrastructure of power systems, communications, even landing pads," he said.
The growing range of commercial projects, he added, was laying the groundwork for a more diversified lunar economy.
Moon could become refueling hub for deeper space missions
Forbes said advances in artificial intelligence and robotics would be essential for future lunar operations, particularly in environments where machines must function autonomously without constant human intervention.
Such technologies could reduce risks to astronauts during early exploration and generate innovations with applications in industries on Earth, he said.
One potential business model involves using the Moon as a refueling station for spacecraft traveling farther into the solar system.
"I think, with the construction of more of this infrastructure on the Moon, one of the main business models is for the Moon to essentially be used as a fuel station," Forbes said.
He envisioned spacecraft stopping at lunar facilities to refuel before continuing toward Mars, the asteroid belt and other destinations.
Forbes also welcomed the growing participation of countries beyond the traditional space powers, citing Türkiye's planned lunar mission as an example.
"We live in a very exciting time of this commercialization, but also democratization of space," he said.
He described Türkiye's lunar program as "a fantastic example of new nation-states getting involved in this race for the Moon," while emphasizing the potential economic and technological benefits of space exploration.
Competition for lunar resources raises concerns
Despite the opportunities, Forbes warned that the concentration of valuable resources and suitable terrain in limited areas of the Moon could lead to disputes over access.
He estimated that only about 6% of the lunar surface offered favorable conditions for future infrastructure, based on factors such as access to water ice, solar energy and relatively flat terrain.
That concentration, he argued, could encourage powerful countries to seek control over strategically valuable locations, potentially excluding smaller nations and private companies.
Forbes called for transparent international regulations to ensure sustainable and nondiscriminatory access to lunar resources and infrastructure.
"We have to be very vigilant that this does not happen, and we have to build the regulations and structure to help the Moon go in a commercially sustainable direction rather than increasing militarization," he said.
He warned that allowing powerful countries to dominate lunar development could prevent emerging space nations and companies from benefiting from future opportunities.
Forbes said commercial companies should play an active role in shaping the rules governing lunar activities rather than leaving decisions exclusively to national governments.

More than 100 humanitarian and human rights organisations have said that the Gaza ceasefire “exists only on paper,” citing continued Israeli attacks, restrictions on humanitarian aid and obstacles to reconstruction a year after the agreement.
In a joint statement on Friday, the organisations said Israeli attacks, shootings and military aggression had killed more than 1,400 Palestinians over the past year, including at least 324 children.
“A ceasefire is meaningless if children continue to be killed and families remain unable to rebuild their lives,” said Inger Ashing, chief executive of Save the Children. “Since the ceasefire was announced, nearly one child has been killed every day.”
The groups called on governments to halt the killings, ensure unimpeded humanitarian access and support Gaza’s reconstruction and accountability for violations.
Displacement and destruction deepen winter fears
The statement said Israeli forces had pushed the so-called Yellow Line deeper into Gaza, beyond the withdrawal line established under the agreement, leaving Palestinians confined to an increasingly crowded area.
Nearly 2 million people still need shelter, while more than 80 percent of Gaza’s structures have been damaged, according to the organisations.
With winter approaching, displaced families face the prospect of living in unsafe buildings or tents vulnerable to cold, strong winds and flooding.
A damaged building collapsed in Gaza City in September, killing 21 people, including 12 children, the organisations said.
Norwegian Refugee Council Secretary General Jan Egeland warned that Israeli restrictions on equipment and construction materials were continuing to obstruct recovery and prevent families from rebuilding their homes.
Hospitals struggle as hunger and medical needs mount
Gaza’s health system remains under severe pressure, with none of the territory’s 36 hospitals operating at full capacity, the statement said. Critical shortages of medicines, medical equipment and fuel continue to limit treatment.
More than 18,500 patients, including at least 4,000 children, need medical evacuation, according to the organisations, which said more than 1,000 patients had died while waiting.
Meanwhile, 1.4 million people face crisis-level hunger or worse through the end of the year, the statement said, underscoring the scale of the humanitarian emergency despite the ceasefire.
The organisations urged governments to press for unrestricted aid deliveries, enable reconstruction and ensure accountability for violations.
“Accountability cannot be buried under the rubble,” said Agnes Callamard, Secretary General of Amnesty International.

Yesterday, the Italian Embassy in the Netherlands hosted the seminar “Towards Responsible and Safe Innovation in the European Space: Security and Governance.” The event, organized in collaboration with the University of Florence and the CybeRights Centre, brought together representatives from European and national institutions, the private sector, and researchers to discuss the main challenges and opportunities related to European technological security and resilience, with a particular focus on semiconductors, artificial intelligence, digital infrastructure, and cybersecurity.
                                    
The seminar was attended by Michiel Boots, Director General of the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Climate Policy of the Kingdom of the Netherlands; Roberto Viola, Director General of the European Commission’s DG Connect; Andrea Simoncini, Professor of Constitutional Law at the University of Florence; Andrea Simoncini, and Giuseppe Garcea, Co-founder and Director of the startup AxeleraAI, as well as other representatives from institutions, academia, and the business world.
                                    
The first panel, “Advancing European Technological Sovereignty: Bridging Institutional, Academic, and Industry Perspectives,” explored the role of collaboration between institutions, research, and industry in strengthening European technological sovereignty, emphasizing the primary role of innovation, investment, security by design, and skills development. The second panel, “Interdisciplinary Approaches to Technology and Security Governance,” presented the research activities of the CybeRights Center at the University of Florence, fostering academic discussion on cybersecurity and responsible innovation. The dialogue highlighted opportunities for collaboration between Italy and the Netherlands—two countries that offer complementary technological ecosystems and play significant roles in the semiconductor, research, and innovation sectors. It also provided a European perspective on the competition between the U.S. and China for leadership in AI and new technologies. Industry and academia jointly emphasized that our task is not to choose between innovation and security, but to create the conditions that will enable Europe to innovate responsibly, compete successfully, and remain resilient and secure.
                                    
The initiative is part of the bilateral dialogue between Italy and the Netherlands dedicated to Van Wittel–Vanvitelli, which will soon include a meeting between the two countries’ foreign ministers.

Kidnappings and Home Invasions Soar as French Syndicates Extort Crypto
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:51:00 UTC
21:51:00 KST

Reported by
A father beaten and forced into a car trunk. A magistrate and her mother held hostage for 30 hours. A family terrorized overnight in northern France for digital cash. Over the past two years, a violent wave of kidnappings and home invasions has swept across France targeting cryptocurrency executives, influencers, and their loved ones, as criminal networks increasingly turn to physical torture to extort digital fortunes.
Organized criminal networks increasingly turn to home invasions, physical torture, and abductions to extort digital fortunes. Authorities have recorded 77 such incidents so far this year, up from 67 in 2025 and roughly 20 in 2024, according to data from France’s National Prosecutor’s Office for Organized Crime, known as PNACO.
While the early wave of violence primarily targeted high-profile industry executives and wealthy influencers, law enforcement officials warn that criminal syndicates are increasingly hunting ordinary citizens suspected of holding digital wallets. Just weeks ago, four armed intruders held a family captive overnight in the northern town of Vendin-le-Vieil, forcing the father to hand over about 40,000 euros, or $47,000, in cryptocurrency.
"This phenomenon, initially characterized by high-profile attacks on prominent figures in the sector, such as influencers, entrepreneurs, or platform executives, now appears to be spreading to a wider audience," PNACO said in a statement to OCCRP. "Perpetrators may indeed target individuals who are little known or entirely unknown to the general public, provided they identify them, rightly or wrongly, as holders of crypto-assets."
The home invasion in Vendin-le-Vieil is part of a chilling sequence of physical extortion cases across the country. In December 2024, the father of a Dubai-based French crypto influencer was kidnapped, beaten, and forced into the trunk of a car. In May 2025, the daughter of a cryptocurrency exchange founder narrowly escaped a broad-daylight abduction attempt in Paris when her partner and bystanders intervened. In February, a French magistrate and her mother were held hostage for 30 hours to exert leverage over the magistrate’s partner, the head of a cryptocurrency firm.
French law enforcement currently has 13 active judicial proceedings underway, with 95 suspects—including 13 minors—placed under formal investigation for offenses that include organized kidnapping, false imprisonment, aggravated violence, and money laundering.
Investigators say the spates of violence are rarely the work of lone actors. Instead, inquiries have revealed compartmentalized networks managed by shadowy masterminds who use social media to hire young operatives, often with prior criminal records, through digital intermediaries.
"The different participants do not necessarily know each other, and the perpetrators may be recruited only for a one-off operation," PNACO noted. "This multi-level organization complicates the identification of sponsors and the reconstruction of the entire criminal chain."
The international reach of these networks has already prompted cross-border crackdowns. Following intelligence supplied by French authorities, a key suspect arrested in Morocco was sentenced to 25 years in prison.
Prosecutors point to data leaks, public social media disclosures, and targeted phishing scams as the primary avenues through which criminals identify potential victims. Once a target is secured, the unique properties of digital currency make it an uniquely attractive target for violent coercion.
"Unlike a suitcase of notes, a transaction can be carried out very quickly," PNACO said, emphasizing that the speed of blockchain transfers allows perpetrators to drain millions within minutes before law enforcement can intervene.

CJP protest on October 10: SC's order on Delhi restrictions explained in 10 points
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09

21:50:16 KST

The Supreme Court on Friday pushed back against sweeping transport restrictions in Delhi ahead of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP)’s October 10 protest, observing that security measures should not bring the city’s public transport network to a standstill.The bench cautioned that an entire city cannot be shut down in the name of managing a protest, warning that blanket curbs on metro and train services could cause severe hardship to ordinary citizens.A bench led by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, with Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, was hearing petitions challenging the proposed closure of 57 metro stations and the cancellation of long-distance trains to the capital.Here are 10 key takeaways from the proceedings and the court’s directions:
1. No complete shutdown of metro services
The court made clear that metro trains cannot be completely stopped. “There shall be no complete prohibition on the movement of metro trains,” it said in its order.
2. Authorities must reconsider restrictions
Solicitor general Tushar Mehta told the bench he would urge the authorities to allow metro and other railway services to operate in a suitably regulated manner.
3. Public convenience must be protected
The bench highlighted the impact on students, employees, senior citizens and other commuters who rely on public transport to reach Delhi from neighbouring areas.
"Exercise caution. Exercise an abundance of caution. There is nothing wrong with that. You are responsible for maintaining law and order. But that responsibility is not merely about protecting State property", it said.
4. Security measures must be proportionate
Chief Justice Surya Kant said authorities could restrict unruly movement but should not deprive ordinary citizens of transport facilities.
5. Court invokes proportionality
"One very important principle that we follow for every citizen is the principle of proportionality. You have to prevent certain things. Take measures only to the extent necessary to prevent them. But that does not mean you should use a hammer to kill a fly. That principle must be kept in mind," the CJI said.
6. Train cancellations raised in court
Senior advocate Kapil Sibal flagged the cancellation of long-distance trains, arguing that passengers scheduled to arrive during the notified period would be unable to reach Delhi.
The bench said authorities should examine which areas required regulation and which did not, stressing that “there should be a free flow of traffic”.
8. Traffic advisory ordered
The court directed Delhi authorities to issue a traffic advisory for people travelling within the city by road.
9. Revised decisions must be publicised
Authorities were directed to give wide publicity to decisions on regulated metro and railway operations to minimise further inconvenience to commuters.
10. Centre asked to consider an alternative protest venue
The court asked the Union government to consider identifying a suitable location with adequate facilities for peaceful and lawful protests.The CJP protest is scheduled for October 10 at Jantar Mantar, with organisers demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged electoral roll irregularities.

Poland: Lifeline for Ukrainian refugees confronts donor fatigue and online abuse as anti-Ukrainian sentiment grows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:50:00 UTC
21:50:00 KST

Poland: Refugee lifeline faces funding drop and online abuse
October 9, 2026
Hours after Vladimir Putin announced his "special military operation" in Ukraine on February 24, 2022, Russian troops began attacking Kyiv's Antonov Airport close to the home of Nastya Podorozhnya's family.
Nastya was 24 at the time and living in Krakow in neighboring Poland, having recently graduated from the city's Jagiellonian University.
Alarmed by the reports coming out of Ukraine and fearful of what was to come, Nastya rushed back to Ukraine two days before the invasion to be with her family and help her sister and her three children cross the border to safety in Poland.
Helping compatriots fleeing Ukraine
Nastya realized she could use her experience of living in Poland — how to get a doctor's appointment or simply buy a tram ticket — to help the many women and children arriving in the country from Ukraine.
Poles were offering help and food at the border, but some people sought to take advantage of the vulnerable arrivals.
"I spoke to activists engaged in anti-human trafficking and they said what was happening at the border in the first weeks after the invasion was like Christmas, Easter and birthdays rolled into one for traffickers because people were so easily trusting the volunteers," Nastya told DW in a two-bedroom apartment in central Krakow her organization uses to provide shelter to vulnerable women refugees escaping domestic abuse or trafficking.
Hotline still fields 100 calls a months
Named Martynka, after Nastya's youngest niece, the organization also runs a hotline. It has received more than 5,000 requests for help since March 2022 and now gets about a hundred every month.
Her small team provides psychological and moral support in four languages as well as legal assistance and counselling.
"One of the very young women who lived with us for a long time was drugged by her boyfriend who she met as a teenager when she escaped the full-scale invasion and after years of relationship she found out that he has been drugging her and selling sex with her to other people" she said.
Nastya said she was motivated to help partly because of a traumatic experience of her own. While studying in Krakow, a Ukrainian man tried to rape her outside of her dormitory.
After a long and difficult legal process, during which police detained the suspect before releasing him, he was eventually found guilty of violating Nastya's bodily autonomy and given a restraining order.
"This terrible, traumatic experience not only gave me horrible PTSD, which later on sort of helped me be empathetic and understand survivors with PTSD, but also it put me through the system of justice and how survivors are being treated," she added.
Aid cuts and donor fatigue
Since 2022, around 100 women and children have found shelter in the apartment. Her team's work relies largely on donations from international organizations.
But cuts to USAID have led to increased competition for grants, while donor fatigue has forced the team to cut its one-to-one therapy sessions.
"Ukraine is not in the headlines anymore," says Nastya. "The international attention has moved elsewhere. For all of summer 2026 we have been running a very challenging fundraising campaign. It is so hard to convince people to donate to a Ukrainian organization right now. There is something called exhaustion, donor exhaustion, fundraising exhaustion."
The UNHCR's acting representative for Poland, Czechia and Slovakia, Jun Shirato, confirmed the difficult situation in the aid sector.
Speaking to DW in Warsaw, she said that funding cuts last year have forced UNHCR to scale back its staff in Poland by two thirds, from 120 at its peak in the months after the invasion to 40 now. The UNHCR has now closed three of its regional offices opened in Krakow, Lublin and Rzeszow after Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Its sole remaining office in Poland is in Warsaw.
Changing attitudes to Ukrainians
Nastya's fundraising efforts increasingly meet with online abuse, too.
Attitudes toward Ukrainians in Poland have changed. In the months after the invasion, many Poles opened their homes to refugees, including Nastya's sister and her daughters.
The situation is now very different. Earlier this year, new rules restricting access to child benefits and free healthcare for refugees who don't work were introduced.
In the first half of this year, reports of hate crimes committed against Ukrainians in Poland rose by a third according to Polish police statistics.
Historical disputes fuel tension
At the same time, historical disputes between Poland and Ukraine, have resurfaced, fueling further hostility toward the Ukrainian community, which accounts for more than three quarters of all foreigners living in Poland.
In May, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's decision to name a military unit after the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which took part in the murder of tens of thousands of Poles during the World War II, triggered outrage in Poland.
Polish President Karol Nawrocki stripped Zelenskyy of Poland's highest state honor, the Order of the White Eagle.
While Poles focus on the UPA's massacre of Polish citizens, many Ukrainians view the UPA and nationalist leaders like Stepan Bandera as heroes because they fought against the Soviet occupation after the war.
"This week we are supporting a family of Ukrainians whose car was completely destroyed. No windows left in the car and with spray paint someone wrote 'Bandera people go back where you came from,'" said Nastya, adding, "I think it is so devastating and I've recorded a video about it. We have hundreds of comments there, of people wishing me death, wishing me to go back where I came from. It is very tough emotionally."
Animosity stoked by Russian bots
Nastya said the hostility is also driven by Russia using online bots to stoke tensions between Poles and Ukrainians.
"They do not want us to be together, or to remember who our common enemy is. They don't want Ukrainian refugees to integrate or feel welcome," she said.
Despite the strain, Nastya remains optimistic that she and her team can continue their work.
"For some reason I am — and this is the weirdest thing. I love my job so much. I want to do this beautiful thing. I would easily send my mother, my sister, my best friend to Martynka for support. I know there are few organizations that could provide such wonderful help."

No, the French army did not deploy tanks against protesting students
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:49:32 UTC
21:49:32 KST

No, the French army did not deploy tanks against protesting students
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on: Modified:
France's student protests have sparked a wave of misleading content online. A viral TikTok falsely claimed the French army had deployed an armoured vehicle against protesters, when it was actually returning to a nearby military base. Other posts recycle 2023 footage of retirement protests as current events, while an AI-generated image was falsely presented as showing a police officer being attacked. Vedika Bahl examines how old, out-of-context and AI-generated content is fuelling misinformation.
France's student protests continued on Thursday, blockading schools and marching through cities across the country against underfunding, poor school conditions and a lack of teachers. The demonstrations have been violent in places, with hundreds of students, law enforcement officers and teachers injured. The violence has triggered discourse surrounding some protesters' use of violence, as well as accusations of heavy-handed riot police, as rights groups accuse them of using excessive force against children.
But alongside the protests, a wave of misleading content has been circulating online, including claims that the French army has deployed armoured vehicles against students.
One TikTok video, viewed more than 2 million times, appears to show an armoured vehicle driving past a group of protesting high school students. Captioned: "They brought back the tank", the video prompted outrage among internet users who believed the army was being deployed to suppress the demonstrations.
Whilst the video is genuine, its context is misleading.
The FRANCE 24 Observers geolocated the footage to a car park opposite Bernard Palissy High School in Gien, central France. The location matches details visible in the video, including the school building, a dividing wall and a nearby house with several chimneys.
But if it's not linked to the student protests, why was a French army vehicle passing directly outside the school?
Around 500 metres from the school's campus are the barracks of the 12th Equipment Support Base, a military unit responsible for maintaining armoured vehicles for the French army. The vehicle in the video was travelling back to the nearby barracks. There is no evidence that it was deployed against the students or that its presence was connected to the demonstrations.
The French Ministry of the Armed Forces confirmed this to FRANCE 24, describing the journey as a "routine journey with no connection to current events at the school".
The misleading video is part of a broader wave of content circulating around the protests, including old footage, images taken out of context and AI-generated material.
One viral post, for example, claims to show protesters "seizing" the Paris Stock Exchange, describing the footage as the beginning of a "global revolution".
But the video predates the current student protests. It has been online since 2023 and shows protesters entering the offices of Euronext, the company that operates financial markets including the Paris Stock Exchange.
The footage was filmed during protests against the French government's decision to raise the retirement age and predates the current student demonstrations by several years.
AI-generated imagery has also been presented as authentic footage from the protests.
One Facebook post claimed to show a policewoman being chased and beaten during a high school blockade. The image attracted thousands of comments and likes.
However, the image was generated using OpenAI tools, with its digital watermark indicating that it was AI-generated.

Annual inflation in Ukraine rises to 10%
Consumer prices in Ukraine rose by 2.1% in September compared with August and by 10% year on year.
Source: a new express report by the State Statistics Service of Ukraine
Details: Core inflation stood at 2% compared with August 2026 and 8.8% compared with September 2025.
Prices for food and non-alcoholic beverages rose by 1.9%. Eggs saw the sharpest increase, rising by 43.6%.
Prices for sugar, rice, grain products, milk, non-alcoholic beverages, fish and fish products, sunflower oil, meat and meat products rose by between 1.7% and 8.3%.
Meanwhile, fruit and vegetable prices fell by 5.7% and 2.3% respectively.
Clothing and footwear prices rose by 8.5%, with clothing up by 9.4% and footwear by 7.6%.
Prices for housing, water, electricity, gas and other household fuels rose by 0.8%, mainly due to increases in water supply tariffs (5.6%) and sewerage tariffs (5.5%).
Healthcare prices rose by 1.7%, primarily due to a 2.6% increase in medicine prices.
In addition, fuel and lubricant prices rose by 5.2% in September, while fares for road passenger transport increased by 2.5%.
Finally, education services became 17.4% more expensive, with prices for higher education rising by 23.3% and secondary education by 14.3%.
Background: In September, the National Bank of Ukraine decided to raise its key policy rate to 16% amid mounting inflationary pressures.

A prosecutor from the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO), based on an investigation by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU), has sent an indictment to court in a case involving the alleged embezzlement of UAH 129 million allocated for the restoration of critical infrastructure in Kamianske district, Dnipropetrovsk region.
Seven people have been charged, including a local businessman alleged to have organized the scheme, the head of the municipal enterprise that commissioned the reconstruction, the director and deputy director of the company that won the tender, the head of an intermediary company used for procurement, a deputy head of the design organization and an employee of a company controlled by the alleged organizer, SAPO said in a Telegram post on Friday.

Under the contract, the winning company was required to purchase pipes. Investigators found that the pipes were bought from the manufacturer at market prices and then resold to the municipal enterprise at prices more than three times higher, SAPO said.
The alleged scheme caused losses of more than UAH 129 million to the municipal enterprise. The suspects allegedly took control of the funds and disposed of them at their own discretion, the anti-corruption prosecutor’s office said.
The alleged organizer and people under his control subsequently laundered the funds by transferring them to accounts of other related companies, SAPO said.
The beneficial owner of the company that won the tender was a prominent local businessman who was wanted by the US Federal Bureau of Investigation for property crimes, SAPO added.

Russia has a plan for Ukraine this winter, Ukraine says: intercepted document reportedly outlines up to 1,000 missiles, drones, and bombs targeting 60 critical infrastructure sites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:46:56 UTC
21:46:56 KST

Russia is planning a winter strike campaign involving up to 1,000 missiles, drones, and bombs targeting, among other facilities, electrical substations, hydroelectric and thermal power plants, and boiler houses. The information is contained in a document that, according to sources cited by The New York Times, Ukraine's Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal presented as an intercepted Russian plan to destroy energy infrastructure systematically. The newspaper reported on 2 October.
Russia has been striking critical infrastructure across Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion. Such attacks have become particularly frequent ahead of and during winter. Ukraine's recent battlefield gains may have prompted Putin to reconsider his strategy and attempt to force Ukraine to surrender through winter strikes, analysts at the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) suggest. Russia's reported plans to attack Ukraine's energy, water supply, and sewage systems could threaten the basic living conditions of millions of people. Such strikes could increase pressure on civilians and the Ukrainian economy while forcing the state to divert more resources to emergency infrastructure repairs instead of defense needs.
The New York Times was unable to verify the document's authenticity independently, but noted that it was written in Russian and dated August.
Warehouses, a home-improvement store, a farm: Russia’s strikes aimed past the grid at Ukraine’s civilian economy
A representative of Ukraine's defense-industrial sector who has reviewed the document believes it is more of a calculation than a finalized Russian military operations plan, according to Schemes, an investigative journalism project by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL), in a report published on 8 October.
60 targets: how Russia could attack Ukraine's critical infrastructure
The document outlines how many missiles, drones, and bombs Russia would need to deprive Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Odesa of electricity, heating, water, and sewage services, Radio Liberty reported on 9 October. The document's full list of priority cities also includes Dnipro, Zaporizhzhia, Mykolaiv, Kherson, Poltava, Chernihiv, Kryvyi Rih, Cherkasy, Kropyvnytskyi, Lviv, Vinnytsia, and Ivano-Frankivsk.
According to the document, Russia plans to begin by attacking substations near Ukraine's western border, through which the country receives electricity from Europe. Hydroelectric power plants could be targeted next, followed by facilities intended to shut down Ukraine's three operational nuclear power plants, Radio Liberty reports. The document lists a total of 60 key targets.
According to Schemes, the document states that Russia would need up to 770 Molniya and Geran drones, Dan-T/Banderol missile-drones, 170 FAB guided aerial bombs, and 75 Kinzhal and Iskander-M ballistic missiles to carry out the attacks.
Sewage systems could become Russia's next target
The document devotes particular attention to water supply and wastewater systems. These include pumping stations, treatment facilities, and other infrastructure essential for cities to provide residents with water and dispose of wastewater.
Russia has not previously attacked such facilities on a similar scale, The New York Times notes.
Preparing for possible attacks on water supply and sewage systems is significantly more difficult than protecting energy infrastructure, Oleh Popenko, head of the Ukrainian Union of Utility Services Consumers, told Current Time, RFE/RL's Russian-language network.
“Sewage is a very complex system. There are specific challenges: where to discharge wastewater, how to organize treatment facilities, and so on. Some work is also underway in this sector, but it will be much more difficult here than with district heating utilities,” Popenko says.
Creating alternative routes in case sewage pumping stations are destroyed is an expensive and technically challenging task, he adds. Such construction could cost billions of hryvnias.
14 dead in Pryluky, two each in Kyiv, Kremenchuk, and Oleksandriia: Russia’s night of 70 missiles
The priority is to equip water utilities with backup power sources so they can continue operating during power outages. However, if Russian strikes damage the sewage system itself, resolving the problem quickly will be much more difficult, Popenko believes. Specific solutions, including wastewater disposal and the operation of treatment facilities, will have to be determined according to the extent of the damage.
Sewage pumping stations play a particularly important role. They pump wastewater onward for disposal and treatment. If such a station is put out of operation by a strike, the city needs an alternative way to divert wastewater while the damaged facility is being repaired, Popenko says. Bypass pipes or channels could be installed for this purpose, but setting up such a system during wartime is far from easy.
Air defenses remain crucial to Ukraine's winter preparations
Preparations for winter are underway, but protection for energy infrastructure remains inadequate, Popenko believes. The main concern is large substations that transmit electricity from nuclear power plants and distribute electricity imported from Europe.
At the same time, some protective measures are already proving effective. Despite drone attacks over two days, one of Kyiv's substations withstood the strikes, and the city did not lose power, although scheduled outages were in effect, the expert says.
Popenko considers a repeat of last winter's scenario, when parts of Kyiv went without heating for weeks, entirely possible. Russian forces continue to attack energy facilities, and in his assessment, strengthening air defenses in Kyiv is the only way to protect its combined heat and power (CHP) plants from large-scale attacks.
“There are no other ways — for example, building some sarcophagi around CHPs or constructing shelters — because Russia can destroy these facilities again through massive strikes. And then the city risks being left 50–60% without heat,” Popenko believes.
Residents are also preparing for winter, but their options vary, he says. Some homeowners' associations participate in government programs to insulate apartment buildings and purchase backup power supplies for elevators and pumping stations. Owners of private houses are buying generators, among other measures. However, such equipment and preparations require substantial funds, meaning not everyone can afford them, he notes.
Ukraine has already experienced prolonged power outages during previous winters, particularly in 2022 and 2023. At the time, some regions went without electricity for 18–20 hours a day, the expert says. This experience may help people prepare for possible disruptions, but it does not eliminate the risk of further attacks and infrastructure damage.

University president reveals clash with Kisch amid Oct. 7 mourning, warns of academic brain drain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:46:51 UTC
21:46:51 KST

It has been a tumultuous term as chairman of the Association of University Heads Prof. Daniel Chamovitz. Now, as he prepares to step down, Chamovitz reveals what took place between him and Education Minister Yoav Kisch, discusses the brain drain from Israeli academia and questions why tens of millions of shekels promised to help students serving in the military reserves have yet to arrive.
"I was convinced he was calling to ask how he could help," Chamovitz recalled of a phone call from the education minister about two weeks after the October 7 massacre. "By then, it was already clear that we had lost so many people and that students had been kidnapped, and he asked me why I had signed a letter opposing his decision. I was in the middle of a shiva mourning visit for one of our students.
"I said, 'What? Yoav, I thought you were calling to see how the university was doing.' He said, 'No. Why did you sign it?' I said, 'Yoav, do you understand what happened here?' He replied that things had happened throughout the education system. What happened next was not my most presidential moment."
The letter in question was written by the Association of University Heads, known by its Hebrew acronym VERA, and signed by university presidents ranging from those of Bar-Ilan and Ariel universities to the Weizmann Institute of Science and the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.
The letter opposed Kisch's attempt to require universities to expel students who expressed support for terrorism, arguing that the universities were already taking action against such students on their own.
"While we are burying our dead, visiting the families of those we have lost and dealing with a very small number of cases involving expressions of support for murderous terrorist organizations, you are advancing such a decision? We have lost confidence in you," the university presidents wrote.
Clashes from the start
Chamovitz said his first conversation with Kisch focused on appointments to the Council for Higher Education.
"He told me, 'The only thing I have is appointments.' I tried to explain to him that there are public appointments and scientific appointments to the Council for Higher Education, and that the public appointments are his to make. He replied, 'I want them to be my appointments.'
"What do you mean, yours? Do you know who is a good biologist and who isn't? How can an education minister know which scientist is suitable to serve on the Council for Higher Education?
"When you start making appointments based on loyalty, you begin putting the system at risk. There were people whose appointments we ultimately agreed to because we thought they were qualified. But it makes no sense for a politician to say, 'I want Professor A or Professor B on the Council for Higher Education.' That's never how it worked."
Chamovitz then turned to the main challenges facing Israeli academia.
"Israel has fallen in the OECD rankings for funding per student since 2000, and that's why we're beginning to see a significant brain drain. No university wants to talk about the numbers because they're troubling.
"I'm talking about researchers who already held professorships here, with grants and laboratories, who decide to go on sabbatical and never come back. Over the past three years, Israelis leaving academia in Israel for positions abroad has become more than just an isolated curiosity. It's a worrying phenomenon."
Do you have data on this?
"It's more than just a feeling. You can see it happening. Let's call it social science rather than exact science."
Isn't it natural for an outstanding researcher to receive offers?
"It's happening more than it used to. The Finance Ministry's Budget Department sees higher education funding as an engine of growth for the country. They're doing everything they can not only to protect the higher education budget but even to increase it. But it's not among the government's political priorities."
According to Chamovitz, there is also a threat from elements within the government seeking to restrict academic freedom.
"There's absolutely no doubt that some members of the outgoing government are uncomfortable with universities having the freedom to ask questions. There have been legislative proposals aimed at restricting universities, such as the one introduced by Knesset member Avichai Boaron, which Minister Kisch supported. Academia and research thrive when universities have the freedom to operate and conduct research."
He added: "People confuse freedom with loyalty. Around the world, we see forces demanding that universities be loyal, whether in Turkey, Russia, China or certain U.S. states.
"And loyal to whom? Loyal to the ruler. Every time that happens, academia collapses. Look at what happened in Hungary, Turkey, Russia and Germany 100 years ago.
"Academia and research thrive when universities have the freedom to operate and conduct research without thinking about what the ruler wants. When we came under attack, it was because people interpreted statements or positions as disloyalty. Universities are not partisan."
"All the politicians who attack us in the media have no problem calling and saying, 'Hi Danny, this is Knesset member so-and-so. My daughter is amazing. She wants to get into medical school. She's just 50 points short.'"
Ben-Gurion University has seen its share of controversies. One example involved Knesset member Almog Cohen, who barged into a humanities and computer science class taught by Dr. Sebastian Ben Daniel, a lecturer who had made statements against IDF soldiers.
Chamovitz, however, appears unfazed.
"It's very convenient for politicians to attack academia. But there's something really, really funny about it: All the politicians who attack us in the media have absolutely no problem calling me and saying, 'Hi Danny, this is Knesset member so-and-so. Listen, my daughter is amazing. She wants to get into medical school. She's just 50 points short,'" he said.
The missing millions
Three years of war have taken a toll on universities, and especially on students, with military reservists bearing the brunt of the burden.
"As chairman of the Association of University Heads, I was involved in the various assistance programs. The government was supposed to transfer a relatively small sum of 10 million shekels to the universities to help reservists for the 2020-21 academic year, and we never received it. There's also a signed agreement with the chief reserve officer for 80 million shekels, and none of that money has arrived."
According to Chamovitz, although some reservists are frustrated by the situation, most have not dropped out of school. Universities have made accommodations and provided them with benefits.
"They actually performed better academically than the average student," he noted.
Education Minister Yoav Kisch responded: "He's quick to point out others' faults while ignoring his own. Since taking office, I have led significant decisions at the Council for Higher Education to benefit combat soldiers and students serving in the reserves, and advanced a historic legislative change giving them priority in admission to higher education. I strengthened academia, particularly in Israel's peripheral regions, worked to expand medical education in Israel and opened four new medical schools within two years.
"Professor Daniel Chamovitz and some of his fellow university presidents opposed every attempt at change for political rather than substantive reasons. They fought against opening additional medical programs, even at the cost of having fewer doctors in Israel.
"When faced with incitement and expressions of support for terrorism on campuses, they took a weak and cowardly approach. At the same time, they fought to keep control of the Council for Higher Education in their own hands.
"They had grown accustomed to education ministers who simply rubber-stamped their decisions.” That era ended when I took office."
"It's amusing that Chamovitz, of all people, gave an interview to Yedioth Ahronoth on Thursday and lectured me about the politicization of academia. There is no limit to the hypocrisy."
The Defense Ministry also responded regarding funding for students serving in the reserves:
The ministry allocated 10 million shekels for the 2025-26 academic year to assist undergraduate students studying STEM subjects — science, technology, engineering and mathematics — who serve in the military reserves and qualify for the A+ classification.
"The ministry instructed universities to submit the necessary approvals and documentation for the financial assistance they have already provided to students. Once the required documentation is received, the transfer of funds can be completed in accordance with the government decision."

There is a thread linking Marrakech and Tangier, and on Thursday evening it passed through the halls of the Yves Saint Laurent Museum in Marrakech. A thread of light, of images, of shared memory. As part of the 6th edition of the “Les Rencontres de la Photographie de Marrakech” initiative—dedicated this year to the Bicentennial of Photography, 1826–2026: Two Centuries of Light—the preview of the art book dedicated to the Palace of Italian Institutions in Tangier, featuring the unique perspective of Massimo Listri, took place. A collaborative evening, organized in partnership with the Italian Embassy, the European Institute of Sardinian Studies, the Italian Cultural Institute in Rabat, and the YSL Museum in Marrakech, to celebrate what photography does best: bringing together heritage and the present, on opposite shores of the same Mediterranean. Then it will return home: it will be officially presented in December in Tangier, right inside the palace it depicts.” A thought for the absent maestro, Massimo Listri, who was unable to attend the event: “We would have been happy to share this moment with him.” And thanks to Serena Cinquegrana, director of the Italian Cultural Institute in Rabat, who guided the audience on a visual journey through the palace’s rooms, vistas, and light. “The Palace of Italian Institutions is much more than a historic building,” Salzano noted. “It is the former palace of Sultan Moulay Abdelaziz, which has served as the seat of the Italian State in Morocco since 1926. It is a place where histories, cultures, and generations have intersected. A living heritage that continues to speak when we look at it, share it, and pass it on.”
