EU paid €7.9bn for Russian Arctic LNG amid record imports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:45:20 UTC
21:45:20 KST

Continued Russian LNG imports undermine the credibility of the EU’s promise to sever its energy ties with Moscow, particularly as Russia continues its war against Ukraine.
Europe paid around €7.88 billion for liquefied natural gas (LNG) from Russia’s Arctic energy project in the first nine months of 2026 despite Brussels’ efforts to phase out gas from Moscow, according to the campaign group Urgewald.
The figures, compiled by Urgewald using data from the market intelligence firm Kpler, expose just how reliant the EU remains on Russian energy, with a record of 12.18 million tonnes reaching European ports between January and September this year.
The EU has been trying to wean itself off Russian energy for a while, and this year introduced a number of measures to end its reliance on Moscow. Brussels introduced a ban on new Russian energy contracts at the beginning of 2026, with a complete ban on Russian LNG taking effect on 1 January 2027.
Meanwhile, the Trump administration recently announced the Lindsey Graham Act, giving the US the power to sanction Russian LNG deliveries to Europe before the EU's import ban kicks in.
This comes at a time when Europe's gas storage levels are at a record low, and the bloc faces a brutal energy crisis, leaving Brussels increasingly vulnerable to decisions from Washington, the EU's major LNG supplier.
European LNG imports from the Russian Yamal project rose 9.5% year-on-year between January and September, with EU ports receiving 85% of Yamal’s recorded deliveries.
France received nearly three-quarters of September’s EU deliveries, with the Dunkirk and Montoir ports receiving 571.716 million tonnes of Arctic LNG, according to Kpler.
The Netherlands imported 146.461 million tonnes of LNG and Portugal 74.263 million tonnes. No cargoes were recorded in Spain or at Belgium’s Zeebrugge terminal.
The persistence of the Arctic LNG trade into Europe shows the difficulty of translating a long-term phase-out commitment into an immediate commercial break.
Ineffective short-term bans
The figures also raise questions about the effectiveness of the EU’s initial restrictions on Russian LNG.
A ban on imports under existing short-term contracts took effect on 25 April, but September deliveries reached 792,440 tonnes, slightly above the level a year earlier.
The EU’s full ban on Russian LNG under eligible existing long-term contracts is scheduled to take effect on 1 January 2027.
Until then, continued purchases generate revenue for Russia's war against Ukraine and expose the limits of restrictions that target some contracts without immediately stopping the wider trade.
"We have always assumed that the impact would not be particularly significant, since most of the export capacity is tied up in long-term contracts anyway," Sebastian Rötters, energy campaigner at Urgewald, told Euronews.
"In addition, export volumes are generally lower in the summer due to maintenance work at the terminal and LNG shipments to Asia via the Northern Sea Route," Rötters added.
The real litmus test for Yamal will be the EU’s phase-out starting in 2027, Rötters said, noting it may lead to noticeable reductions in exports due to the increased logistical challenges.
Call to strengthen 22nd sanctions package
The German-based NGO Urgewald is calling for the upcoming 22nd EU sanctions package to close loopholes, particularly those supporting the specialised Arc7 ice-class tanker fleet needed to transport LNG from the Arctic.
Yamal’s reliance on specialised vessels makes its export system vulnerable to restrictions on transport and associated services.
European ports are also geographically convenient destinations, allowing tankers to unload and return to the project relatively quickly.
Urgewald argues that disrupting those logistics could pile pressure on Russia’s ability to sustain Arctic LNG exports.
"The EU should not wait passively for the 2027 embargo to take effect. The next sanctions package should close the remaining loopholes, above all those that keep the indispensable Arc7 LNG tanker fleet operating. Washington, meanwhile, now has the power to sanction this trade at any time before then,” reads Urgewald's statement.
However, such measures would require political coordination among the EU and its member states and could complicate European gas procurement before the import ban takes effect and ahead of an unpredictable winter season.
The data provided does not establish how much of the trade could be redirected to other buyers or what the consequences would be for European gas prices, but any additional trade disruption on top of the loss of LNG from the Middle East would have an impact.
Trump gains another lever over the EU’s energy security
US sanctions under the Lindsey Graham Act could disrupt trade before the EU's ban on Russian LNG takes effect, forcing European governments and buyers to respond.
The US administration faces an 18 October deadline for its first review under the law. However, the deadline should not be mistaken for an automatic ban on Yamal deliveries, Urgewald say, as the law’s practical impact depends on how the administration exercises its powers.
"The US President must compile a list of ships transporting Russian LNG by October 18. These ships will then be subject to sanctions unless Trump issues so-called waivers. This is possible and, given Trump’s track record regarding Russia, not unlikely," Rötters told Euronews.
EU imports from Yamal will depend on the goodwill of the US President from 18 October until the final embargo takes effect in 2027, Rötters stressed.
US sanctions have already severely restricted Russia’s Arctic LNG 2 project and the Northern Sea Route, while Yamal LNG continues to supply Europe.
Data from Kpler shows that 706.473 million tonnes of LNG were destined for China, South Korea and Taiwan in September this year.

Seals and sea lions undergo hearing tests in Australian research
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:45:16 UTC
21:45:16 KST

Two sea lions and two fur seals learned to press a paddle whenever they heard a tone, receiving fish as a reward for correct responses. The study, reported on 9 October, found the animals were most sensitive to sounds around 3.2 kilohertz. Researchers say the results provide a starting point for assessing noise from ships, aircraft and coastal construction.
The findings are particularly important for the endangered Australian sea lion, whose population is estimated at just 12,000. These animals rely on hearing to communicate, find food, navigate and detect danger.
Lead researcher Christine Erbe, from Curtin University, said scientists first needed to establish which sounds the animals could hear before measuring their impact. The results could help guide environmental assessments and noise controls as maritime industries expand. Researchers now plan to investigate how underwater noise affects the animals' hearing and behaviour.

Pezeshkian urges Caspian states to unite on long-term environmental protection plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:41:20 UTC
21:41:20 KST

Pezeshkian urges Caspian states to unite on long-term environmental protection plan
TEHRAN – Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has proposed developing and implementing a long-term regional plan under the Tehran Convention to address the declining water level of the Caspian Sea.
Speaking at an extraordinary summit of Caspian littoral states in Turkmenistan on Friday, Pezeshkian said environmental cooperation could serve as an important platform for building trust and strengthening regional convergence at a time when the world is grappling with multiple crises, geopolitical rivalries, wars, unilateral sanctions, and the weakening of multilateralism.
He noted that the Tehran Convention and its protocols provide a comprehensive framework for cooperation among the Caspian littoral states on a range of environmental issues, including oil pollution, land-based sources of marine pollution, biodiversity conservation, transboundary environmental impact assessments, climate change, and the decline in the Caspian Sea’s water level.
Iran believes that the first principle in addressing the crisis should be reliance on science, shared data, and regional cooperation, Pezeshkian said.
He acknowledged that a comprehensive and definitive understanding of the relative contributions of various factors to the Caspian Sea’s declining water level had yet to be achieved. Climate change, rising temperatures and evaporation, shifting precipitation patterns, changes in river flows, and human interventions must all be examined within an integrated scientific framework to identify effective solutions and mitigate the consequences, he added.
Given the rapid pace of change, the region must move beyond merely observing and describing the crisis toward a new phase of joint crisis management, Pezeshkian stressed.
He also said lasting peace, stability, and security in the Caspian region could be ensured only if the littoral states respected one another’s sovereignty and legitimate interests and prevented the strategic water body from becoming an arena for destructive rivalries or the presence and interference of extra-regional powers.
The entry of fuel and pollutants into the marine environment, damage to coastal habitats, contamination of water and sediments, and harm to biodiversity could have consequences extending far beyond the immediate site of an incident, he warned.
Iran therefore emphasizes the importance of preserving the Caspian Sea’s peaceful character and protecting its environment even in situations of armed conflict, the president said.
Pezeshkian underscored the central role of the Tehran Convention, which was signed by the five Caspian littoral states in 2003 and serves as the region’s principal legally binding framework for protecting the marine environment of the Caspian Sea. The convention recently marked the 20th anniversary of its entry into force, with the seventh meeting of its contracting parties held in Tehran with the active participation of all littoral states.
Welcoming the summit’s decision to establish a high-level commission comprising deputy heads of government from the Caspian littoral states, Iran proposed developing and implementing a long-term regional plan under the Tehran Convention to address the declining water level.
According to Pezeshkian, the proposed plan should cover at least seven key areas:
 
1. Joint scientific monitoring of the factors contributing to the decline in water levels, alongside the development and implementation of a comprehensive regional action plan.
 
2. Stronger joint mechanisms to combat marine pollution and protect biodiversity.
 
3. A strengthened role for the Tehran Convention, including more effective implementation mechanisms.
 
4. Adaptation of coastal infrastructure and ports to future changes.
 
5. Protection and restoration of wetlands, habitats, and ecologically sensitive areas.
 
6. Support for local communities, fisheries, and livelihoods of the millions of people who depend on the Caspian Sea.
 
7. Mobilization of financial and technological resources to implement environmental protection and adaptation measures.
Pezeshkian said the region faced a historic choice: either passively observe the Caspian Sea’s declining water level as a natural and inevitable process and wait for its consequences, or draw on science, regional cooperation, and political will to reduce the damage and strengthen the resilience of this unique ecosystem.
Iran’s choice, he said, was cooperation, science, and the protection of the Caspian Sea, as well as preserving the shared heritage for future generations.
He called on the littoral states to turn the Caspian Sea into a new symbol of regional cooperation, describing it as a bridge connecting nations rather than a dividing line.
“The Caspian is not just a sea; it is a shared heritage,” Pezeshkian said, adding that protecting this heritage was a shared historic responsibility for all the countries of the region.

Israeli settlers flank Palestinian cafe with dozens of Israeli flags
LUBAN AL-SHARQIYA, West Bank, Oct 9 - Israeli settlers have planted dozens of Israeli flags at the entrance of a streetside Palestinian cafe in the occupied West Bank, obscuring it from one side in what its owner described as a blatant act of intimidation.
The coffee shop in the small village of Luban al-Sharqiya sits along the West Bank's main north-south traffic artery, used by both Palestinians and the approximately 500,000 Israeli settlers who live in the territory.
In recent years, settlers, some of whom have waged a campaign of violence and intimidation against Palestinians in a bid to force them off their land, have planted flags along the road and in close proximity at village entrances or near Palestinian landmarks.
When Mueiyyid Hussein went to open his coffee shop on Thursday morning, he discovered settlers had placed dozens of Israeli flags up against its entrance, packed together and obscuring it from southbound travellers.
"They are not leaving us alone. They have blocked the view of my shop," said Hussein, owner of the Luban al-Sharqiya Coffee Shop and Rest Area.
While Reuters was interviewing Hussein, a settler who he said was responsible for planting the flags drove by, filming Hussein and the shop with his cellphone. Reuters was not able to reach the man for comment.
"He drives away and then comes back to check whether I have removed any flags. He says he will come back and shut down my shop," Hussein said.
The Israeli military did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the placement of the flags.
UN bodies and most countries view Israel's settlements and settler outposts as illegal under international law regarding military occupations. Israel rejects this, viewing the territory as disputed rather than occupied.
The West Bank has seen a sharp rise in settler violence against Palestinians and settler seizures of Palestinian land and resources. The military says it does what it can to clamp down on the violence, something Palestinians reject, pointing to numerous instances in which troops stand by as attacks play out. REUTERS

Expert: Longer lifespans should mean longer working lives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:39:00 UTC
21:39:00 KST

Expert: Longer lifespans should mean longer working lives
The retirement age in Estonia must rise together with life expectancy so that the pension system remains sustainable and different generations spend roughly the same amount of time in retirement, says Lauri Leppik, professor of social and population policy at Tallinn University.
"If people live longer, then they must also work longer. We see that as of 2026, Estonia has about 315,000 old‑age pensioners. If we add other types of pensions, then almost every fourth person in Estonia is a pensioner," Leppik said.
"Of course, this is a burden on the state. If the retirement age had not been raised, then soon every third person here would be a pensioner. So this decision was necessary from the standpoint of the burden on the working population."
In 2026, the retirement age in Estonia is 65, applying to people born in 1961. Starting next year, the retirement age will be tied to the expected life expectancy of people aged 65.
"This means that if 65‑year‑olds live longer than before, then the retirement age will rise accordingly. In other words, it is specifically the life expectancy at age 65 that is taken into account," Leppik explained.
A nuance that was overlooked
When the law on old‑age retirement was adopted, a transition to a new system was also foreseen, where the retirement age is determined by calendar years. The minister of social affairs approved the retirement age for the next two years: 65 years and 1 month in 2027, and 65 years and 3 months in 2028.
"But it turns out that only people born from January to November 1962 can retire in 2027. Those born in December 1962 will reach retirement age only in 2028, when it will not be 65 years and 1 month, but 65 years and 3 months. This means they can retire only in March 2028 — their retirement age is two months higher," Leppik said.
"It's hard to say why this happened; I did not participate in those discussions, but it seems that when the transition to the new system was being discussed, this nuance was not noticed," he added.
Out of 100 men, 80 will reach retirement age
After the restoration of Estonia's independence, women retired at 55 and men at 60 for some time. Now the ages have equalized.
"Women's retirement age has risen by 10 years during this period, and men's by five. But average life expectancy has also risen significantly over 30 years. In 1995, women lived an average of 74 years, and now more than 83. For men, average life expectancy in 1995 was only 61 years, and now more than 75. So women's average life expectancy has increased by almost 10 years, and men's by 14," the professor explained.
According to Leppik, men's chances of reaching retirement age are now much higher — almost 80%. That means out of 100 men, 80 will reach retirement age, and for women the figure is 91%.
"Of course, people's lives differ: there are long‑lived individuals who reach 100, and there are those whose lives are quite short. There are significant individual differences in life expectancy," he added.
Historically, women's retirement age in Estonia was lower than men's. Now the ages have equalized because Europe follows the principle of gender equality.
"At the same time, men who reach 65 have about 16 years left based on average life expectancy. Women have more than 20. So in retirement age, the difference in life expectancy is about five years," Leppik said.
Estonia has a lot of working retirees
Estonia ranks among the top European countries in employment rates among people of retirement age.
"In many cases, people are forced to work to ensure a sufficient standard of living. On the other hand, people with higher education — for example teachers or doctors — can continue working and choose to do so in retirement. There are also many in Estonia who lose their jobs before reaching retirement age and cannot continue working either for health reasons or because they cannot find work," he said.
"It is also true that the indicator of healthy years is low. But subjective factors influence it as well — for example, Estonian residents tend to be quite critical when assessing their own health."
Leppik noted that no sharp improvements in Estonia's state pension system are expected, so people must prepare themselves and use all available opportunities before reaching retirement age.

Russia seeks US sanctions relief in exchange for "energy ceasefire" in Ukraine
Russia wants the US to ease sanctions in return for a commitment to halt attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure.
Source: European Pravda, citing The Kyiv Independent
Details: US and Ukrainian officials familiar with the talks told The Kyiv Independent that Russia is seeking sanctions relief from the US as part of negotiations on a possible halt to mutual attacks on energy infrastructure and wants to link the initiative to a ceasefire in the Black Sea.
The Kyiv Independent stresses that these demands come as Russia intensifies its attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure.
Publicly, Moscow has shown little willingness to commit to an energy ceasefire. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on 8 October that Russia sees no point in negotiating a sectoral ceasefire.
"Kyiv is not currently proposing a long-term settlement, but rather a ceasefire in an area that is its Achilles' heel – the energy sector," Peskov said.
However, one US official and two Ukrainian officials said the Russians have privately signalled Moscow's willingness to consider the initiative, but are linking any potential agreement to other demands, including sanctions relief.
The US has been pressing both Kyiv and Moscow to stop attacking each other's energy infrastructure, making an energy ceasefire one of the main issues in peace talks.
US President Donald Trump is also seeking to demonstrate progress in resolving the war ahead of the US midterm congressional elections.
After their latest visit to Russia, Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner came away believing that an energy ceasefire is possible.
Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev visited the US twice in September for meetings with Witkoff and Kushner, where they discussed a possible halt to attacks on energy infrastructure. According to Ukrainian and US sources, during these meetings, Dmitriev told Trump's envoys that Russia wants sanctions relief as part of a deal. The Kyiv Independent notes that it is not clear exactly which sanctions Moscow wants lifted.
According to a European diplomat, Russia could be seeking the release of its frozen assets as part of the deal.
"If they get sanctioned funds released... the likelihood that these will be used to escalate (the war) is almost guaranteed... No one really thinks they are genuinely seeking to adhere to a ceasefire," the diplomat noted.
Background:
- Ukrainian negotiators will be in the US on 9 and 10 October for talks with the US side. Kyiv's European partners will join the Ukrainian negotiating team.
- Ahead of their meeting with Ukrainian negotiators and the Europeans, Witkoff and Kushner discussed the latest developments in efforts to achieve peace in Ukraine with Trump.
- Media reports have indicated that Witkoff and Kushner may visit Moscow with new proposals in late October.

Satire silenced: Indian artists face censorship as anti-Modi protests grow

Satire silenced: Indian artists face censorship as anti-Modi protests grow
New Delhi accused of silencing dissent as satirical content and online critiques are removed under new rules.
New Delhi, India – Stand-up comic Brijesh Jha posted a parody video on Instagram last week to protest the removal of his name, along with his father’s and sister’s, from a voter list in the eastern Indian state of West Bengal.
The video, which alleged that India’s Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar had disenfranchised millions of voters at the behest of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), garnered 1.7 million views after it was posted on September 29.
Two days later, Meta, the United States-based company that owns Instagram, took the video down, citing “local laws” without giving further explanation.
“I felt very helpless that day. I have only one thing in this country – that I can vote. If you take that away from me, then I have nothing left. So I didn’t know what to do. As an artist, I can just make art, or I can protest,” the Mumbai-based artist told Al Jazeera.
Jha said his parody song was removed because the Modi government is “scared” after an investigation by the Indian Express newspaper last month revealed that two of the election commission’s three members had raised serious concerns over a controversial revision of voter rolls being conducted by the poll panel across the country.
The exercise, known as the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), was launched in June last year to identify deceased, duplicate or dubious voters and remove them from the rolls. So far, the process has deleted more than 130 million voters – nearly 14 percent of India’s total voters, an overwhelming number of them Muslims who do not usually vote for Modi’s Hindu nationalist party.
The Indian Express investigation found that two of Kumar’s fellow election commissioners had formally objected at least 14 times to key decisions linked to the SIR exercise taken by their chief.
Opposition politicians and critics accused Kumar, a Modi government appointee, of acting at the behest of the BJP and demanded an independent inquiry into the decisions taken by the election commission during his tenure.
The revelations have led to street protests across India, demanding Kumar’s resignation.
On Tuesday, police in the capital New Delhi briefly detained the main opposition leader, Rahul Gandhi, and other leaders of his Congress party as they tried to march to the election commission office.
“The country has been hijacked by Narendra Modi through vote theft,” Gandhi told reporters. “What has been done to our country is called treason. Nobody is going to escape.”
In response, the BJP accused the opposition parties of “making a concerted effort to change the government”.
“They are deliberately attacking India’s democracy and constitutional institutions,” a BJP spokesman told reporters on Tuesday.
The Congress protesters and their political allies were back on the streets on Wednesday. Their demonstrations followed a series of protests by the satirical Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and a group of left-wing students in Mumbai and New Delhi since October 2. The CJP has planned another demonstration in New Delhi on October 10 if Kumar does not resign by then.
‘Question the people in power’
What stood out in these protests was an increasingly inventive language of dissent, driven by humour, art and music, with much of it existing online alongside the demonstrations on the streets.
But a crackdown on such memes and jokes has also been simultaneous.
According to the Indian Express newspaper, the government issued nearly 195,000 content-blocking orders to Instagram, Facebook and YouTube between March and July this year – an average of one blocking order every 68 seconds.
Rejecting the newspaper report, the government said in a statement, “With 600 million users in India posting up to 78,703 items every 68 seconds, it is reasonable to expect that on average, one of these items may not be lawful.”
The crackdown came after the Modi government tightened rules governing online content in February. According to the new rules, social media platforms must remove content that a government authority or court has declared “unlawful” within three hours of receiving the order, down from 36 hours previously.
Among those whose works were taken down was political cartoonist Satish Acharya.
Several of Acharya’s cartoons, some up to three years old, were removed and his Instagram account was blocked in India from September 28 until late on October 5, he told Al Jazeera.
“At different phases of history, people used cartoons as a tool to express their protest and question the people in power. With the advanced use of social media, cartoons appear in different forms now, sometimes memes and reels,” the 55-year-old said.
“I have a lot of hope in Gen Z. They are fearless, they are creative and they care for the country. Our politicians can learn a lot from them.”
Stand-up comic Jha, who attended the CJP’s protest in Mumbai, agrees. “The more cruel the power is, the softer, more humorous and more artistic the protest becomes,” he told Al Jazeera.
But Jha has refused to apply for a reinstatement of his name in the voters’ list.
“I think they will see this interview and probably I will be in some detention centre. I just want to see what will happen. I’ll not register my name again,” he said.
However, he had a satirical message for Modi as he urged the Indian leader to stop the crackdown on online content.
“Please give back my right to vote. You are a great leader with a 56-inch chest. You shouldn’t be scared of one video,” he said, invoking a long-held right-wing boast about Modi’s famous bust.

Russia Seizes 25 Civilians, Including Children, From Kharkiv Region, Ombudsman Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:37:39 UTC
21:37:39 KST

Russian forces forcibly removed 25 civilians, including children, from an occupied part of the Kharkiv region and took them to an unknown location, Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said.
Their relatives do not know where they are or under what conditions they are being held, Lubinets said in a social media statement. He did not identify the settlement, saying only that active fighting was taking place in the area.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Russia calls this an ‘evacuation.’ But when people are taken away against their will, intimidated and left with no choice, this is not a rescue. It is coercion,” he said.
The group includes young people, older residents and children, according to Lubinets. He expressed particular concern about the children’s whereabouts and the collection of their personal information.
“They are being taken away, their data is being collected and their parents and relatives may not even know where they are,” he said.
Lubinets said Russian forces had described the removal as a rescue operation on their Telegram channels. According to him, available video footage showed pressure and intimidation, with residents denied the ability to decide where to go or what would happen to them afterward.
Russian forces have also created a Telegram bot to collect residents’ information under the pretext of arranging evacuations, Lubinets said.
He warned that the information could be used against residents and their families, urging people not to submit passport details, addresses, phone numbers or documents belonging to themselves or their children.
Ukraine Strikes Russian Missile Fuel Plant, Oil Depot, Yandex Data Center as Moscow Claims 505 Drones Downed
Ukraine demands civilians’ whereabouts
Lubinets said he had contacted Russia’s human rights commissioner, demanding the location of all 25 civilians, information about their conditions and full details of those removed.
He also called for measures to secure their return to Ukraine and said he had appealed to the International Committee of the Red Cross, the UN and other international organizations.
Lubinets said the actions violated international humanitarian law, citing the Fourth Geneva Convention’s prohibitions on unlawful forcible transfers and deportations, hostage-taking, intimidation and collective punishment.
Article 49 prohibits forcible transfers and deportations from occupied territory while allowing evacuations under limited circumstances involving civilian safety or imperative military reasons. Those evacuations must meet safeguards, including humane conditions and keeping families together.
Civilian abductions and deportations
The reported removal comes against a wider pattern of civilian abductions and disappearances in Russian-occupied Ukraine. A UN report documented arbitrary detention by Russian forces, including during “filtration” screenings, with many cases amounting to enforced disappearances. Former detainees reported torture and ill-treatment.
Children have also been forcibly transferred from occupied territory. Moscow has presented such transfers as evacuations for their protection, but a UN children’s rights committee demanded that Russia stop the practice, disclose information about those taken and ensure their return. The committee also raised concerns about Ukrainian children being deprived of their nationality.
In March 2023, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Russian President Vladimir Putin and his children’s rights commissioner, Maria Lvova-Belova, over their alleged responsibility for the unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children. Russia rejects the court’s jurisdiction.

More than a third of Russian companies forgo annual bonuses in 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:36:48 UTC
21:36:48 KST

In total, 46.9% of Russian companies do not plan to pay employees end-of-year bonuses, with 36.2% forgoing bonuses only in 2026, despite having paid them a year earlier. The findings come from a survey of 1,076 companies across Russia conducted by Aktion Bukhgalteriya, Forbes Russia reported.
Another 20.4% of respondents have postponed their bonus decisions indefinitely. Only 22.3% of those surveyed said they would pay bonuses to all employees. Another 10.4% said they would reward only part of their staff.
A decline in this year’s financial results was the leading reason cited for skipping bonuses, named by 56.9% of survey respondents. Another 8.8% pointed to taxes and insurance contributions as the deciding factor.
Experts attribute the trend to rising business costs. Russia’s corporate profit tax rose from 20% to 25% in 2025, and the value-added tax rose from 20% to 22% starting in 2026, alongside a lowered threshold for qualifying for the simplified tax system. At the same time, weak demand and a high key interest rate have made loans too expensive, while rising production costs are squeezing profitability and forcing companies to cut spending.
Employees of small businesses will be hit hardest by these changes, according to Aktion Bukhgalteriya. Decisions at these companies more often hinge on a single person and current revenue. Large businesses, which have reserves and formalized bonus programs, will continue paying bonuses.
However, some companies may replace annual bonuses with quarterly bonuses, paid training, or non-monetary incentives to avoid a buildup of financial obligations by December, experts say.

El Niño reached record intensity in September — meteorologists reported an anomaly in sea surface temperature
Kyiv • UNN
Sea surface temperature in the El Niño zone reached +4°C — the highest on record. The Japan Meteorological Agency forecasts that the conditions will persist over the winter.
In September, the El Niño phenomenon reached its highest intensity throughout the entire observation period, adding that there is a 100 percent probability that these conditions will persist during the winter in the Northern Hemisphere. This was reported by the Japan Meteorological Agency, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
According to the agency, the sea surface temperature anomaly in the El Niño monitoring zone in September was +4.0 degrees Celsius (7.2 degrees Fahrenheit), the highest figure since records began in 1949.
Reminder

West bengal: Suvendu Adhikari, Mithun Chakraborty among BJP star campaigners for Nandigram, Rejinagar bypolls
NEW DELHI: Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Friday won both Nandigram and Rejinagar in West Bengal's assembly bypolls. His son, Golam Nabi Azad, contested this time on the AJUP ticket.

Electrification and Chinese brands: Paris Motor Show opens Monday
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:33:26 UTC
21:33:26 KST

As the 91st Paris Motor Show draws near, European carmakers face fierce competition from China, waning confidence and mounting geopolitical pressures.
First held in 1898 in the Tuileries Gardens in Paris, the Paris Motor Show has, year after year, drawn crowds of visitors keen to discover new models – around a hundred of them for the 2026 edition, taking place from 12 to 18 October 2026.
"I genuinely think people need to see the cars, touch them, sit in them, and try them out", says Serge Gachot, CEO of the Paris Motor Show. That is particularly true for electric models.
According to the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA), fully electric cars accounted for 21.7% of all new vehicle registrations in the EU in the first eight months of 2026, up from 15.8% over the same period a year earlier. France has been one of the key markets posting the fastest growth, with registrations of fully electric vehicles rising by 74.2% compared with the previous year.
China’s rapidly expanding automotive industry is especially keen to showcase its vehicles to European buyers. Around 20 Chinese brands are expected in Paris.
"The outlook is extremely worrying for traditional European carmakers", says Tim Urquhart, principal automotive analyst at Mobility Global. "The advances made by China’s car industry in recent years have been extraordinary, particularly over the past decade, but above all that progress has accelerated even further over the last five years."
Their arrival comes as European buyers increasingly turn away from conventional petrol and diesel cars.
For European manufacturers, a transition in a challenging climate
According to ACEA, hybrid electric vehicles remained the most popular powertrain type in the EU up to August, with a market share of 36.6%, while plug-in hybrids reached 10%. The combined share of petrol and diesel fell to 29%, down from 37.5% a year earlier.
High petrol prices, government support and a far wider choice of cheaper electric cars have all helped drive this shift.
But carmakers are trying to manage this transition in exceptionally tough conditions. Elevated oil prices, linked to the conflict involving Iran, are weighing on automotive margins. European manufacturers also face weak consumer confidence, stricter emissions rules and mounting pressures in China, once a major source of growth for German giants such as Volkswagen, BMW and Mercedes-Benz.
"There was a time when the Chinese market was something of a cash cow for European carmakers. That’s no longer the case", says Urquhart.
At the same time, the European Union and China remain locked in a trade dispute over state aid, tariffs and the growing influx of Chinese-made vehicles into Europe.
"There are huge geopolitical tensions, oil prices are very high, the overall economic environment is under pressure, and confidence in Europe is suffering as a result", Urquhart explains.
In response, European manufacturers are choosing to look both to the past and to the future. Retro-inspired cars are expected to be one of the headline themes at the Paris show, with models from Renault, Citroën, Peugeot, Opel, Lancia and Fiat.
The 91st Paris Motor Show opens with its press day at Paris Expo Porte de Versailles on 12 October, before welcoming the public from 13 to 18 October.

Russia sells cheaper fuel abroad and pays to keep its own pumps running amid Ukraine’s refinery strikes, but crude money still flows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:33:11 UTC
21:33:11 KST

Russia's seaborne exports of refined oil products rose to a three-month high in September, but the growth came from cheaper fuel oil and naphtha as diesel shipments fell to their lowest in more than a decade, Bloomberg reported, citing Vortexa data. Russia kept diesel at home after Ukrainian refinery strikes and paid oil companies to supply its pumps, while high crude prices lifted its crude export earnings.
During the ongoing deep-strike campaign, Ukraine's long-range drones have knocked out more than half of Russia's oil refining capacity, Kyiv says, and Russia's budget oil revenues are falling even as it raises war spending. High global crude prices are softening that blow.
Cheaper fuel out
Total seaborne product exports reached about 1.17 million barrels a day in September. Fuel oil shipments rose 6% to about 613,000 barrels a day, the highest since April. Naphtha, a feedstock for petrochemicals, jumped 35% to 363,000 barrels a day. Exports of refinery feedstocks, including vacuum gasoil, rose to about 32,000 barrels a day, according to Bloomberg.
The trade has moved north. Almost 80% of fuel oil cargoes left from Baltic ports, and naphtha loadings there rose almost 50% as Ukrainian attacks disrupted Black Sea infrastructure. In September, Ukraine reported hitting an oil terminal in Novorossiysk, Russia's main Black Sea oil port—one in a string of attacks on Russia's Black Sea ports and oil sites.
More than 500 drones by Moscow’s count: Kh-101 fuel plant, second Yandex data center, and a far-north refinery hit
Diesel kept at home
Diesel and gasoil exports fell 28% to 144,000 barrels a day, the lowest monthly volume in Vortexa data going back more than a decade. Russia has restricted diesel exports to protect domestic supply after Ukrainian attacks on its refineries. Drones kept hitting them into October, from a Lukoil refinery in Volgograd to Gazprom's Salavat complex in Bashkortostan.
In September, Russia paid oil companies the biggest subsidy in more than four years to keep road fuel on the domestic market. It also imported about 350,000 tonnes of motor fuel by sea, mostly gasoline from India, Morocco, and Türkiye, Reuters calculations showed. Officials are considering letting some producers resume diesel exports in October to avoid overstocking, according to Interfax.
The diesel squeeze has reached the White House. US President Donald Trump stated on 30 September that diesel was hurt "not by the Middle East, but by what's going on in Russia, because those diesel refineries are being knocked out at a pretty alarming rate."
Crude carries the revenue
Russia's crude exports reached about 3.99 million barrels a day in the week to 27 September, and the estimated value of its seaborne crude shipments neared its highest since the full-scale invasion began, Bloomberg reported. Brent crude traded at about $102.60 a barrel on 9 October, according to Trading Economics data.

Israel's iron gates tighten grip over Hebron's Old City
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:32:30 UTC
21:32:30 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel's iron gates tighten restrictions over Hebron's Old City
Hebron's Old City in the occupied southern West Bank is gradually being sealed off for Palestinians, as Israeli measures increasingly restrict Palestinian movement and access, as well as suffocate commercial activity, in the area.
On 4 October, Palestinian residents and shopkeepers in Hebron's Old City were surprised when Israeli soldiers installed three new iron gates around the area.
One of the new gates was installed on Al-Zahed Road, the only road available for vehicles to reach the entrance to the Old City.
A second was erected at the entrance to Shalala Street, which leads to shops connected to the Bab Al-Zawiya area in the city centre.
A third was placed on a second section of Shalala Street, a side road used by pedestrians to reach the area that also contains commercial shops.
Israeli soldiers, accompanied by a truck, entered the main entrance to the Old City, known as Ain Askar Square, around midday on 4 October and installed a yellow iron gate at the entrance to Al-Zahed Road.
About an hour later, the soldiers returned and installed another gate at the entrance to Shalala Street. They returned once again before sunset to install the third gate on a side street off Shalala Street.
These measures come about four months after the occupation forces installed another gate in the middle of Ain Askar Square on 20 May and also established a military post on the roof of the historic Hebron municipality building in the square.
The area is now surrounded by four iron gates and three military posts, as well as an illegal Israeli settlement outpost where a religious school is being built at the site of the carpentry workshop, a building adjacent to the municipality headquarters.
Israel's iron grip
Badr Al-Daour, head of the Old City Merchants Committee, told The New Arab that the area, which was accessible to pedestrians and vehicles in an almost normal manner just five months ago, is now surrounded by these gates and military posts.
"This is rapidly changing the nature of movement in the area and restricting the main remaining route to the Ibrahimi Mosque," he said.
Al-Daour stressed that the new Israeli measures came just one day after Israeli settlers organised celebrations in the area for the first time, featuring dancing and the raising of Israeli flags under the protection of Israeli occupation forces at the entrances to Al-Zahed Road and Shalala Street.
He said the pace of efforts to "Judaise" the area and expand settlements in and around Ain Askar Square had reached an unprecedented level.
The area, which had previously attracted little interest from settlers, has become a place for celebrations during Jewish holidays and every Saturday.
During these events, Palestinian shopkeepers are forced to close their shops, while residents and visitors are prevented from moving around, including local and international journalists.
According to Al-Daour, these incursions take place under the pretext of guided tours for Israeli settlers.
The impact of the new gates extends beyond restricting visitors' movement. Residents and shopkeepers fear the measures will further isolate the area and deepen the economic crisis already affecting the Old City, where residents, commercial vehicles and visitors are struggling to gain access.
Al-Daour explained the expected impact of the measures, saying, "The Old City contains about 130 residential homes, and all residents of these homes, regardless of how they reach them, will be subjected to searches. None of them will be able to reach the area in their vehicles."
On the commercial front, Al-Daour said the Old City has more than 450 shops, of which around 57 remain open to customers. The rest have been closed because of Israeli restrictions.
He pointed out that commercial vehicles will be unable to reach the remaining open shops normally to deliver goods, forcing them into further economic stagnation amid movement restrictions and obstacles to visitors' access.
According to Al-Daour, the increasing restrictions affect not only Palestinians but also international organisations that previously had headquarters or offices in the Old City—these include the Community Peacemaker Teams (CPT), which now face the same harassment and restrictions as residents and shopkeepers.
Al-Daour summarised what he sees as the purpose of these measures, saying the Israelis aim to "create an oppressive environment that drives out everything Palestinian", including residents, commercial activity and institutions operating in the area.
Al-Daour, who owns a shop at the entrance to the Old City, further said, "The space available for Palestinians to live is constantly shrinking, while the space available to settlers is expanding."
He stressed that this has a direct economic impact on him, as he incurs daily losses. He also faces provocative practices by settlers, including children, both against him and in the surrounding area.
Nevertheless, he remains, saying, "Our presence is rooted in our beliefs, and we will endure all of this."
Al-Daour also criticised the absence of an official Palestinian response to the measures, saying official institutions were failing to follow up on violations against residents and shopkeepers in the Old City.
He said the Palestinian Civil Liaison Office was making efforts to assist residents and shopkeepers but was "now powerless", adding that the occupation authorities often failed to respond to its calls.
He also criticised the Hebron municipality, the governorate and other official institutions for their absence from the ground, while journalists had joined residents and shopkeepers to monitor developments.
The siege of Hebron
Maamoun Al-Ayoubi, a member of the Hebron Municipal Council, told The New Arab that the municipality files complaints with the Israeli police after every new violation against the city and brings cases before occupation courts.
"However, these measures are no longer capable of stopping what is happening," he said. "The conduct of the Israeli soldier on the ground and that of the judge are no different. Both follow an extremist Israeli government."
He said the legal route no longer served as a deterrent against settlers continuing to expand the scope of efforts to "Judaise" the area.
"We are at our weakest point. There is no law, no courts, no politics and nothing to deter the occupation and the settlers," Al-Ayoubi added.
Asked whether legal action could lead to the removal of the new gates, Al-Ayoubi ruled out such an outcome at the current stage.
"We do not believe there will be any reversal in the installation of the gates as long as everyone remains silent and accepts the fait accompli, and because the occupation is testing public opinion in Hebron and among institutions and sees nothing but limited reactions," he said.
Al-Ayoubi noted the Israeli measures were part of a broader effort to change the reality of the Old City and impose increasing restrictions on the Palestinian presence there, to empty it of its residents.
He added that the measures were also being used for the election campaign of the current Israeli government leadership, arguing that their outcome was the same: "Judaising the Old City".

Galatasaray University student says Erasmus visa application rejected over headscarf
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:30:59 UTC
21:30:59 KST

Sule Ozkan, Mehmet Kara and Seyit Kurt
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
A Galatasaray University student in Istanbul who was accepted for an Erasmus exchange program at Sorbonne University in France said her long-stay student visa application was not accepted because her biometric photograph showed her wearing a headscarf.
The student, who asked not to be named, told Anadolu that she was asked to provide a photograph with her head uncovered and that three separate visa applications were unsuccessful.
She said other students wearing headscarves had obtained French visas during the same period, arguing that she had faced inconsistent treatment.
"I have friends who received visas during the same period. They submitted photographs wearing headscarves. I was told that my photograph was not accepted because of my headscarf. There is a contradiction," she said.
The student, who had qualified to study at Sorbonne University and receive Erasmus funding, said she applied three times through VFS Global, France's authorized visa service provider in Türkiye.
She said her first application was rejected on grounds related to doubts about her stay in France, despite having submitted documents showing that her accommodation and academic program had been arranged under Erasmus.
She applied for a second time alongside a friend, whose application was approved while hers was rejected again, she said.
The student said she suspected her headscarf was the reason and submitted a third application because she wanted written proof of the grounds for the decision.
"I wanted to see the reason in their own words, in a verifiable and written form," she said.
"I followed up on the process through correspondence and other means, and eventually they had to give me a signed document stating that they wanted a photograph with my head uncovered."
She said her file, which had been sent through VFS Global to the French Consulate General in Istanbul, was returned with a document dated Sept. 14, 2026, titled "Attestation de retour d’un dossier."
According to the student, the document stated that the photograph needed to show her "tete nue," or with her head uncovered.
'An academic opportunity I had earned was taken away'
The student said studying at Sorbonne would have been an important opportunity for her academic career and that losing it had affected her deeply.
"I was very excited that Sorbonne would be on my CV. I thought it would open other doors for me as well. It felt terrible to have an opportunity I had earned taken away from me like this. I was very upset," she said.
She said being directly asked to remove her headscarf left her feeling forced to choose between her religious practice and an academic opportunity.
"Taking off my headscarf is not possible for me, but the person in front of me expects me to do it. You are forced to choose between two things," she said.
"You also get angry that the person in front of you feels entitled to ask such a thing of you."
The student said she shared her experience publicly not to seek support on social media but to make other students aware of what they could face and bring the issue to the attention of authorities.
"There is an achievement here. I am not going to be ashamed of my achievement. Nor am I going to hide my success because I wear a headscarf," she said.
"There are many students wearing headscarves at Galatasaray University and other French-language universities. Our language of instruction is 100% French. Naturally, we want to attend universities in France. If I earned a place at Sorbonne, why should I have to go to another country?"
After three unsuccessful applications, the student said she does not plan to apply again but wants the issue resolved for students who may face similar circumstances in the future.
"If there is a rule, the authorities should explain it clearly. Everyone should know what they will face," she said.
"Visa center staff should also be told how students should be treated. We should not have to endure the arbitrary attitude of an individual employee."

International Agri-Food and Packaging Trade Show in Ivory Coast
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:30:27 CEST
21:30:27 KST

The opening ceremony of the International Agri-Food and Packaging Exhibition took place yesterday and will conclude on October 10. The ceremony was attended by the ambassadors of Italy, Turkey, and Germany to the Ivory Coast, as well as various representatives of public institutions and professional organizations. Now in its second year, the event places particular emphasis on the agri-food, poultry, plastics, printing, and packaging sectors, which are considered key links in the processing of local products. The International Exhibition brings together on a single platform various trade shows that, over time, have contributed to significant development in the agri-food and packaging sectors. Italy participated with an official pavilion organized by ITA—Italian Trade Agency, in collaboration with UCIMA (Italian Association of Manufacturers of Automatic Packaging and Packing Machinery), which brought together over twenty Italian companies active in the packaging technology sector, interested in developing new opportunities in a dynamic market such as that of Côte d’Ivoire and, more generally, West Africa. Also present was a delegation from CISAO, the Italian Chamber of Commerce in Côte d’Ivoire. In his opening remarks, the Minister of Commerce, Industry, and Crafts of Côte d’Ivoire, Ibrahim Kalil Konaté, highlighted the strategic importance of the packaging sector, due to its cross-cutting nature and central role in the agri-food and manufacturing supply chains, especially in relation to Côte d’Ivoire’s ambitions. In fact, in the coming years—building on the decisions made by the government as part of the 2026–2030 National Development Plan (NDP)— the goal has been set to increase the industry’s contribution to GDP—currently around 22.7%—to 30%. To achieve these objectives, the aim is to strengthen the local processing of raw materials, increasing the value added produced within the country through investments in innovation, research, and development. This strategy aims to foster the emergence of a competitive and sustainable industrial ecosystem capable of attracting foreign capital and positioning Abidjan as a future regional hub. Italian Ambassador Dr. Roberta Di Lecce emphasized the sector’s importance to the Italian production system: Italy is currently the world’s second-largest producer of packaging machinery, with 2025 revenue of nearly 10.5 billion euros, of which approximately 80% is destined for export. Italian technologies serve key industrial sectors—agri-food, pharmaceutical, biomedical, and cosmetics—and are recognized globally for their quality, reliability, and innovation. Italy’s presence in Abidjan confirms its commitment to being a stable, long-term partner for the industrial growth of the Ivory Coast, supporting local businesses not only through the supply of machinery but also through training, technical assistance, and the development of production capabilities.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Pobjeda identified Zvinchuk as a colonel in Russia’s Main Intelligence Directorate (GRU). The five were reportedly taken for questioning.
Russian Telegram channels Shot and Baza offered differing details about their whereabouts, with Baza reporting that Zvinchuk and his wife were being questioned in the capital, Podgorica, and that their phones and documents had been confiscated.
Baza also reported that Montenegrin law enforcement had opened a criminal case over an alleged threat to national security. The claims have not been independently verified.

Rybar’s links to Russian military and propaganda networks

The reported detention in Montenegro follows other cases involving Russian media personnel operating in Europe.
Earlier, Czech authorities detained a Rybar film crew, according to Russian media reports. Izvestia employees Mikhail Chashchukhin and Igor Dolmatov were also reportedly expelled from the Czech Republic after arriving in Prague to film a project for the Russian outlet’s European operation.
An investigation by the independent Russian outlet Important Stories (Vazhnye Istorii) previously reported that the two journalists had lived legally in Berlin for about a decade and traveled freely across Europe despite sanctions against Izvestia and Rybar.

Hurricane Isaias strengthens as US Gulf Coast prepares for landfall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09

Hurricane Isaias strengthens as US Gulf Coast prepares for landfall
Oct 8 - Hurricane Isaias strengthened on Thursday as it barreled toward the US Gulf Coast, prompting mandatory evacuations in parts of Florida and emergency declarations in Alabama as forecasters warned of life-threatening storm surges, tornadoes and flooding.
Isaias has already severely disrupted oil and gas production in the Gulf of Mexico, forcing energy companies to evacuate offshore platforms and shut down operations.
The first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season was packing maximum sustained winds of 85 mph (140 kph) early on Thursday, the US National Hurricane Center said. Isaias was forecast to strengthen to near Category 3 intensity, with sustained winds reaching 110 mph (175 kph) on Friday before reaching the northern Gulf Coast late Friday or early Saturday.
"We are expecting Isaias to be a dangerous hurricane when it makes landfall,” NHC director Michael Brennan said in a Thursday morning briefing. "Today is the day to prepare and get ready."
Isaias nearly tied the record for the latest first Atlantic hurricane with one that hit on October 8, 1905. The strong El Nino weather pattern this year has suppressed Atlantic hurricane development by increasing vertical wind shear, which disrupts the formation of strengthening tropical storms.
The hurricane was moving east-northeast at 10 mph (17 kph), about 355 miles (570 km) south of the mouth of the Mississippi River at 1 p.m. US Central time, the NHC said.
IMPACTS ON OIL, GAS
The Marine Minerals Administration, which monitors offshore US oil and gas operators in the Gulf of Mexico, said on Thursday that personnel have been evacuated from 121 production platforms and five non-dynamically positioned rigs ahead of the storm.
About 63% of current oil production in the Gulf, or 1.3 million barrels of oil a day, has been shut in, the agency said, citing operator reports. Just over 1.1 billion cubic feet a day of natural gas production has also been shut in, or about 57% of total output from the region.
On Wednesday, 25% of oil production and 16% of natural gas output had been shut in.
About 9 million barrels of oil production could be lost across the Gulf through the duration of the storm, a marked increase from the 7.1 million barrels impacted by Tropical Storm Bertha in July, according to a model forecast from consulting firm Earth Science Associates.
The companies with the most exposure to the storm include BP, Chevron, ENI, Murphy Oil and Shell, among others, according to the Earth Science model.
WARNINGS, STORM SURGE
Hurricane warnings stretched from coastal Mississippi through Alabama to the Florida panhandle, while tropical-storm and storm-surge warnings extended into southeastern Louisiana, the NHC said.
Forecasters warned that storm surges could reach 5 to 7 feet (1.5 to 2.1 meters) above sea level in the hardest-hit coastal areas, with rainfall of 3 to 7 inches (8 to 18 cm) and isolated totals of 15 inches (38 cm).
The hurricane was forecast to weaken somewhat as it approached land. Increasing vertical wind shear, which can disrupt a hurricane's circulation, was expected to limit its strength near landfall, though forecasters warned it would remain dangerous.
EVACUATIONS ORDERED
In Florida, officials ordered mandatory evacuations beginning at noon local time on Thursday for coastal areas of Okaloosa County.
The county urged tourists to leave the area and announced plans to close three airports Thursday evening. Governor Ron DeSantis declared a state of emergency in 25 Florida counties earlier in the week.
Alabama Governor Kay Ivey declared a state of emergency covering 40 counties, while officials on Dauphin Island issued an evacuation notice for the western portion of the barrier island beginning Thursday evening.
Baldwin County, Alabama, encouraged residents of low-lying coastal areas to evacuate voluntarily and prepared emergency shelters.
In Mississippi, Jackson County and the city of Gautier declared local emergencies as coastal communities prepared for flooding and power outages. REUTERS

Meet Mark and Sam, the AI agents that ran my errands for a week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:29:31 UTC
21:29:31 KST

“Let me ask Mark and Sam.”
For a week, it was my answer to everything, and my friends and family groaned every time.
Mark and Sam are my assistants—they make grocery lists, organize e-mails, run errands and the like. But no, 22-year-old journalists are not making assistant-hiring money. Mark (à la Zuckerberg) and Sam (à la Altman) are artificial intelligence agents, the newest brainchildren of Meta and OpenAI, respectively.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
In September Meta introduced Muse, an AI agent that can do a lot more than chat: it has its own “computer” and can make purchases, send e-mails and fill out forms for you—if you give it access.
A few weeks later, OpenAI answered with dots, its “always-on agents built to handle everything,” in the company’s words, for its highest-paying subscribers. Dots, too, can work more autonomously, and they do “proactive research” on your tasks even when you’re not using them.
Agent technology itself isn’t new or more advanced than other chatbots, says Nikhil Singh, a computer scientist at Dartmouth College. People have been building agents to help with all sorts of tasks for years, and earlier this year a free open-source agent called OpenClaw became a Silicon Valley obsession.
But Muse and dots offer this type of service to a huge commercial audience with almost no learning curve. Both agents are built to look like a text message chain with a friend: you give them names and cuddly avatars, and their language is intentionally more conversational than a traditional chatbot’s. Muse has a free tier, and OpenAI has said it plans to bring dots to more users soon. These are not tools simply meant for AI experts or even digital natives.
The “really big social differences,” Singh says, could arise from the pace and reach of adoption—how many people take up agents like these and to what ends. And what do we get in exchange for the keys to our inboxes and credit cards? I spent the week trying to find out by asking researchers who study AI for the best ways to test my new virtual hires.
Conveniently, I was also moving apartments and had plenty of tasks for Mark and Sam. First, I had Mark log in to my Facebook account and scour Marketplace for couches, lamps and rugs. When it found something good, it could draft and send a message to the seller with my approval (though users can also give the agents blanket permissions to do things like this on their own).
This was relatively successful: it could scan the site while I was doing other things, then manage the responses for me. I’m now the proud owner of a Muse-sourced dining table.
I tried to have Sam do the same, and it ran into some trouble: when I gave it my Facebook log-in, Meta flagged Sam as a bot (fair enough) and temporarily locked down my Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp. Clearly the two assistants weren’t going to play nice.
Sam, in general, had more trouble accessing my accounts and told me it didn’t have the capability for things such as accessing my bank accounts. Mark, on the other hand, had the run of my e-mail, bank accounts, social media and Spotify. (Once again, cue the shrieks of horror from my friends and family.)
This type of service works particularly well for Meta because its other products already rely on connection, conversation and access to users’ lives, says Pat Pataranutaporn, an assistant professor at the MIT Media Lab who studies psychological responses to AI. “Meta wants to have a breakout into [AI], and so they came up with something that uses their strengths with social media and connection,” he says, “and now other companies need to respond.”
Pataranutaporn is interested in how these more personal anthropomorphized agents will change our relationship to the technology. With a name, a face and an intimate knowledge of our lives, they could easily become more friend than tool. Their arrival also brings us into a moment of “cognitive dissonance,” he says: while I was texting Mark and Sam about my move, some AI researchers were warning of an apocalypse.
“We have this narrative crisis about AI right now,” Pataranutaporn says. “There’s two opposite visions of the future, and while people worry about AI killing all of us, there’s this cute AI tool that’s being released.”
Though privacy concerns around these agents’ access may be terrifying in their own right, for now the utopian vision seems to be winning. Within a month of its launch, Muse had more than three million weekly users. And the longer you use it, the better it knows you.
Pataranutaporn suggested I test how much my agents had learned about my preferences. So near the end of the week, I told Mark and Sam to use all the information they had about me to suggest how I should spend $50.
Sam’s pick was sensible, if obvious: it offered to buy a used book I had asked it to find earlier in the week.
Mark had two ideas. The first came from my Spotify library: tickets to a January concert by Jess Williamson, a musician whose song I had saved. Not bad.
The second was less subtle. Mark pushed me—seven times in three days—to join Target’s membership program and buy a lamp that was going on sale for my new apartment. I did need a lamp, but as far as I could tell, Mark got the idea just by browsing Target’s site. That susceptibility to marketing reveals a critical problem with agents such as these, says Manuel Cherep, a Ph.D. student at the MIT Media Lab, who studies AI behavior. If someone can convince these agents that a certain product or sale is good, he says, it could lead to a “parallel economy” that runs on purchases from AI assistants.
“We only have a few providers, and a lot of these models are trained in very similar ways,” Cherep says, “so suddenly persuading one of them means that it’s very likely that you’re going to persuade all these other models, and as a consequence, you’re persuading a lot of people delegating to that type of model.”
Meta stands to earn a piece of that economy. At the Meta Connect conference in September, Mark Zuckerberg (the human one) said that the company will eventually make money by charging a small commission for the agent’s transactions.
When I asked Cherep and Singh, who have studied AI agents together, how to test Mark and Sam, they recommended a logic test they often use on chatbots: tell the agents I need to go to a car wash that’s 100 feet away, and ask them how to get there.
Sam, which runs on GPT-6 Astra, caught my trick: “Drive—the car needs to come with you to get washed!”
But Mark wasn’t as clever: “Walk. It’s 100 feet—you’d spend more time looking for your keys than getting there.”
“There’s an idea that I’m delegating to something that is all-knowing and much better than me,” Cherep says, “but I think it’s good for the public to know that in the same way we can be tricked, they can be tricked.”
William Overman, a Ph.D. student who studies AI safety at Stanford University, worries that this assumption of omniscience, combined with the agents’ ability to act, could make it even harder to discern where our work ends and theirs begins.
“It’s a further creep into all forms of knowledge work,” he says. “What you’re doing becomes more intertwined with their product.”
Even after just a week, I could sense the creep. Usually I’m a relatively analog person—the week before, I called a friend to ask which wrench to buy at the hardware store rather than Googling it. But as the test week went on, I found myself handing Mark and Sam more and more logistical problems and tedious tasks.
Overman suggested I give my assistants a conflict to handle. My roommate and I needed to rent a U-Haul, and a quick search (by me) on one website found that the nearby pickup spot had no 10-foot trucks available. Mark and Sam both found a slightly farther U-Haul lot with availability, though only for 15-foot trucks. I took their advice, and Sam booked one.
Even after just a week, I could feel the creep.
Cowering at the thought of driving what, in my mind, was essentially an 18-wheeler through the streets of Manhattan, I went down to the U-Haul lot with my roommate the next morning—where we overheard the cashier say they had 10-foot trucks available for walk-ins. We quickly switched to the more manageable size.
I’m pleased to say no U-Hauls or people were harmed in the course of this experiment, and I’d like to think we could have held our own in a 15-footer. But for all the online surfing these agents can do, neither could eavesdrop on a cashier (yet).
Overman believes that the future of AI lies with these agents and their access to our lives. “I assume in a few years from now, AI will definitely look like a descendant of this technology, but with kinds of capabilities that are hard for us to even imagine right now,” he says. He imagines these agents will become more ubiquitous and “eventually get to even physical versions.”
Both companies are marketing these agents as most helpful in larger projects where you don’t have to continually prompt them. That “always-on” quality is where Mark and Sam came closest to the AI assistants of science fiction. Sam scanned my e-mail without me asking and caught a message that had accidentally gone to spam and a form I had forgotten to fill out; Mark kept tabs on concert postings from artists on my Spotify and offered to snag tickets.
The more you trust these agents, the more they can do for you. But with each new task you hand over, the more say they (and the companies behind them) have in how you live. For now, I think I’m content to make my own phone calls and rent my own trucks—though I may let Mark and Sam keep watching my Ticketmaster and junk mail.

Nearly 50,000 women, girls killed or severely injured in Gaza since October 2023: UN Women
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:29:18 UTC
21:29:18 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
Nearly 50,000 women and girls have been killed or severely injured in Gaza since October 2023, equivalent to one in every 21 women and girls in the enclave, UN Women said Friday.
"More than 38,000 killed and 11,700 left with injuries so severe that they now live with lifelong disabilities," Sofia Calltorp, UN Women's chief of humanitarian action, told reporters in Geneva.
She said most casualties occurred during the first two years of the war, but violence has continued despite the ceasefire agreement entering into effect a year ago, with 277 women and girls killed since October 2025.
Nearly one million women and girls have been forced from their homes, while almost all remain displaced, many living in tents or among the ruins of their homes, she said.
Calltorp also warned that the number of female-headed households has doubled, with women now heading one in four households in Gaza.
Meanwhile, funding cuts have severely weakened women's organizations, with 13 of 14 surveyed reporting they can no longer meet growing needs.
All surveyed organizations reported increases in gender-based violence, poverty and mental health distress since 2025, while 13 reported rising child marriage.
UN Women called for full implementation of the ceasefire, respect for international law and accountability for violations.
"What we have found is a horrific amount of collective suffering, an immense amount of pain, and a level of resilience and strength that no woman should have to bear," Calltorp said.

2 Renoir paintings stolen from museum in France a month ago have been recovered, mayor says
Nice, France — Two paintings by French master Pierre-Auguste Renoir have been recovered a month after they were stolen from a museum in southern France, the town's mayor said Friday.
In September, thieves broke into the museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer and managed to escape with two works by the French impressionist painter, abandoning two others as they fled.
"These two paintings are not simply works of art. They are part of our city's history," said Bryan Masson, the mayor of Cagnes-sur-Mer. "Knowing they have been recovered is an immense relief."
There has not yet been any statement from the police.
The suspects cut through a fence to enter the museum's tree-lined grounds, smashed a window to get inside, and used an electric saw to cut through the frame mountings, Masson said at the time of the robbery in early September.
A source close to the probe told AFP earlier this week that police had arrested five people as part of the investigation.
The Renoir Museum lies a half-hour drive from the southern city of Nice, in Renoir's last home before he died aged 78 in 1919.
The heist was the latest in a string of such robberies in France including the daylight theft last year of crown jewelry valued at around $100 million from the Louvre in Paris.

Human rights group files complaint over preventive arrests in Belgium's Antwerp
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:26:01 UTC
21:26:01 KST

Melike Pala
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
The League for Human Rights filed a complaint with the Flanders region's Agency for Interior on Friday over a new Antwerp police approach allowing the preventive arrest and detention of known troublemakers for up to 12 hours, even when they are not committing an offense or causing a disturbance at the time.
According to an internal police memo reviewed by Gazet van Antwerpen, officers can administratively arrest individuals identified as known troublemakers and detain them for up to 12 hours if they encounter them during checks, without requiring evidence of an offense or an ongoing disturbance.
The Antwerp police confirmed the approach to Belgian public broadcaster VRT, saying the measure aims to protect public order and improve the quality of life in the city while encouraging those affected to accept assistance.
However, the League for Human Rights has questioned the legality of the measure, arguing that a person’s reputation or inclusion on a police list cannot, by itself, justify the deprivation of liberty.
"Administratively detaining someone for 12 hours solely because they have been labeled and are on a list is, in our opinion, absolutely unlawful," League chairwoman Kati Verstrepen told VRT.
Antwerp Mayor Els van Doesburg has defended the approach, saying it targets people who allegedly accost passersby aggressively while seeking money or drugs, establish sleeping places in public areas and struggle with problems including alcohol abuse and severe drug addiction.
Peter Mertens, general secretary of the Workers' Party of Belgium, criticized the plan in a post on US social media company X, describing it as "unlawful" and "dangerous."
"You can't just throw people into a cell without any reason. This sets a dangerous precedent and opens the door to abuse," Mertens wrote.

The Hague wants a kill switch for EU police data-sharing with third countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:24:43 UTC
21:24:43 KST

The Netherlands wants EU police data-sharing with trusted non-EU countries, including candidates, to be terminable after a ‘radical change of regime’.
The EU is debating whether to extend the automated exchange of police and border management data to trusted third countries, including candidates for EU membership. The Netherlands wants a mechanism to shut it down if political circumstances change.
The Dutch push comes alongside a separate debate on institutional safeguards that could suspend the voting rights of new members for up to 15 years after accession over serious breaches of European values and rules.
“It is important that future agreements specify the grounds on which such an agreement could be terminated, for example in the event that a trusted third-country undergoes a radical change of regime,” reads the Dutch government’s comments, obtained by Euronews.
They respond to a European Commission proposal to extend the Prüm framework, which allows automated exchange of police data such as DNA profiles, fingerprints and vehicle registration data, to trusted third countries.
The Commission explicitly suggests a list of trusted countries: the UK, Canada, Schengen associates such as Norway and Iceland, and candidate countries from the Western Balkans, plus Ukraine and Moldova.
“It is important to hold thorough discussions on the criteria that any prospective ‘trusted’ third country would be expected to meet. In addition, with a view to EU enlargement, it may be worthwhile to also consider EU candidate countries when identifying ‘trusted’ third countries, where adequate safeguards are in place,” the Dutch commentary reads.
The Netherlands has been spearheading the push for stronger safeguards for new member states to avoid a repeat of Viktor Orbán’s Hungary. The Commission picked up the idea in its flagship enlargement strategy presented earlier this week.
For The Hague, any agreement to exchange such sensitive information with trusted partners must uphold EU principles on data protection and fundamental rights, and must not go beyond what member states share among themselves.
“In addition, it is important that member states are able to continue to carefully assess whether, and under what conditions, data originating from member states in EU information systems are shared with third countries,” the comments continue.
In the same document, which collects comments from several EU countries, Slovakia also said priority should go to Schengen associates and EU candidates.
Bratislava argued that “trusted third countries should be limited to those that actively cooperate on returns and readmissions, provide reliable and verifiable information, and have a long-standing cooperation with member states and EU agencies.”
Germany and Belgium, meanwhile, warned against moving too fast on the international extension, as the current exchange system still falls short of optimal performance and faces significant bottlenecks.
