21:07:04 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of Economic Affairs said Friday that it had approved additional subsidies to accelerate drone development, CNA reported.
The economics ministry approved 27 projects totaling approximately NT$780 million (US$24.42 million). Taichung-based Aerospace Industrial Development Corporation (AIDC) received the largest subsidy, NT$100 million, to develop heavy-duty drones with advanced networking capabilities.
The ministry’s Department of Industrial Technology said the program supports the development of complete drone systems and key flight-control, payload, communications, and power technologies. It will also promote cooperation between drone manufacturers and component suppliers, using field testing to improve product maturity and strengthen Taiwan’s supply-chain autonomy.
The department said it approved 27 of 49 applications for 2026, totaling approximately NT$780 million. This marked a significant increase from 2025, when it received 19 applications and approved seven projects totaling NT$326 million.
The department said the projects fell into two categories. Six complete-system projects received approximately NT$282 million and cover long-endurance vertical-takeoff drones, heavy-load logistics, smart agriculture, and hydrological monitoring. Another 21 projects involving critical technologies received approximately NT$497 million.
The department said AIDC plans to improve the drones’ resilience to signal interference through optical-image matching, 3D positioning, dynamic data-link switching, AI recognition, and multimodal sensing. The drones are intended for emergency deliveries to outlying islands, maritime rescue, and deliveries to remote communities.

Head Of Russian Pro-War Blog Detained In Montenegro
Unknown

2026-10-09

21:07:02 KST

The head of a leading Russian pro-war blog linked to the country's Defense Ministry has been detained in Montenegro, along with several other people who work for the publication.
Montenegrin Prime Minister Milojko Spajic on October 9 confirmed media reports that Mikhail Zvinchuk, the director of Rybar, and other Russian citizens had been arrested. The blog itself also confirmed the arrests.
Zvinchuk is under British and European Union sanctions, with the EU stating he was in a working group set up by Russian President Vladimir Putin to mobilize support for the war in Ukraine.
The US State Department has offered a $10 million reward for information on him and other Rybar figures for seeking to interfere in the 2024 US elections.
'Hybrid Action'
"We have been warning that attempts at hybrid action and destabilization relentlessly follow our European path," wrote Spajic on social media following the arrests.
Montenegro applied for membership in the bloc in December 2008, received candidate status in December 2010, and officially opened accession negotiations in June 2012.
"The message following today's successful action in which the head of the Rybar information network was apprehended is clear: Institutions are doing their job, Montenegro is protecting its interests, and no one will jeopardize our European future," he added.
Montenegrin media outlets reported that five arrests were made in Risan, a small town of some 2,000 inhabitants in the Bay of Kotor -- which has a sizeable Russian expatriate community -- on the country's Adriatic coastline. The group were filming a documentary criticizing Montenegro's push for EU membership, they said.
A statement on Rybar's Telegram channel, which has some 1.5 million subscribers in Russian and 80,000 in English, said the detained people "were on the country's territory legally and officially."
It said they were planning to film at Cetinje Monastery, an important Serbian Orthodox site that's about a 90-minute drive from Risan. The statement said Rybar was in touch with Russia's Foreign Ministry to resolve the situation and "expected all detainees to be released."
Former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev, now deputy head of the national-security council, suggested in a social media post arresting Western citizens in Russia to exchange for "our people."
There was no immediate response from Montenegrin security and judicial authorities to RFE/RL's request for additional details. Some local media are reporting that Zvinchuk's wife, Valeria, is among those detained.
Rybar has become one of the most influential pro-Russian military channels on Telegram since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. In recent years, it has also expanded its activities into the western Balkans, including Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina.
Montenegro has long had fraught relations with Moscow. In 2016, authorities there accused Russia of plotting with a group of Serbian ultranationalists to stage a coup, a charge the Kremlin denied.
Ties soured further when the small Adriatic republic joined NATO in 2017.

Passport-free travel, AI agents and longevity: Key takeaways from the WTTC Global Summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:06:54 UTC
21:06:54 KST

The 26th edition of the World Travel & Tourism Council Global Summit just concluded in Malta – here’s what you may have missed from the ‘Davos of travel’.
Hundreds of the world’s biggest names in travel gathered in Malta this week for the 26th edition of the World Travel & Tourism Council (WTTC) Global Summit to discuss the challenges and opportunities the industry is facing.
Covering everything from luxury travel and longevity to the future airport experience and how destinations can grow sustainably, the panels gave an insight into what governments and businesses will be focusing on in the coming years.
Euronews Travel was reporting on the ground – here’s what you may have missed.
Justin Trudeau: Tourism is the best counter to an increasingly insular world
Canada’s former Prime Minister Justin Trudeau was this year’s main speaker, joining WTTC President and CEO Gloria Guevara on stage to chat about “how to shape the opportunity ahead”.
Directly addressing the “Trump Slump”, Trudeau said in recent years “the US hasn’t been very good at making travellers feel welcome”.
He said: “There’s a tendency right now in countries around the world, and we’re seeing it to a greater or lesser extent in certain countries or governments, that are encouraging people to look inward, turn inward, to go a little more insular and be mistrustful or in opposition to the rest of the world. That’s not necessarily a productive path for the world, and the best counter to that is tourism.
“It’s getting to know people who are different. It’s wanting to travel, being curious about the world, being empathetic. These are the instincts that people need to be developing, and this is something that makes your industry so great.”
When pressed on which single destination Trudeau would recommend to visit in Canada, he suggested Montréal, his home city.
“Montrealers, we love good restaurants, we love good art. We fill our summers with festivals, in winter, it’s worth coming to see the snow,” he added.
You won’t need to use your passport to travel within the next five years
In a panel discussing the implementation of digital identity and changing the border experience, Dubai Airports CEO Paul Griffiths said that passports will no longer be a necessity for travel within the next five years.
The barrier isn’t the technology, but a lack of coordination between the different systems that must be connected to make this happen, he added.
Panellists envisioned a future where travellers won’t need to use their passport when passing through borders, when collecting hire cars, or even checking in to hotels.
AI is already being used to plan holidays – the next stage is letting agents book your trip
Tourists across the globe are becoming “super-empowered travellers” by using AI to plan out their trips, according to Christie Travers-Smith, a director for EMEA Strategic Partnerships at Google Inc.
The next big step for AI? Building enough trust for customers to hand over their credit card information and allow AI agents to book for them.
While the luxury sector is leading the way, ‘longevity as standard’ is what all hotels should be aiming for
Bryan Johnson’s antics have brought longevity out of the fringe and into the mainstream in recent years, and luxury hotel groups have been paying attention, introducing things like hyperbaric oxygen therapy and infrared saunas.
But Tim Gray, the founder of Health Optimisation, argues that “longevity as standard” is what all hotel groups should be aiming for.
What that means is allowing travellers to stick to the basic principles of recovery – eating well, sleeping well, staying hydrated and staying active – even while away from home, and that starts from small things like adding black-out blinds and removing blinking lights, to ensuring that mini bars are stocked with healthier options.
All of the fancy tools are just meant to help “turbo charge” the basics. Having tried out HPO.TECH’s hyperbaric oxygen therapy for ourselves at the WTTC summit, we can certainly see how jet-lagged travellers could benefit.
Measuring success by value, rather than volume
For many years, the travel industry’s main measure for success was the number of tourists flowing into a destination.
Today, the indicators people are paying attention to are changing – governments are now shifting from “volume to value”, according to Michelle Fridman, Secretary of Tourism of Jalisco, Mexico.
“We are looking for those tourists that are better tourists, that stay for a longer period, that spend a bigger amount of money, that consume local products,” Fridman said during a panel on destination stewardship.
“More importantly, we are looking for those that respect and are interested in our identity.”
She added that Jalisco is “the most Mexican destination, and we want to keep it that way”.
It was a sentiment shared across the panellists, with Miguel Sanz, Director-General at Turespaña, saying that his role was now more of a “tourism curator”, with efforts being made to attract a different kind of traveller to Spain.
The idea was further explored on the “impact-oriented traveller” panel, with Mark Weingard, CEO & founder of Iniala, noting that it’s important for the industry to not become too focused on bringing in high-value travellers “because then we are almost being elitist” and “saying only the wealthy can travel”.
“At the same time, I think it's very important that we position travel that it benefits the cities that it's in, that it doesn't destroy the culture, it doesn't destroy the neighbourhoods and that we are making sure that the work that we are doing in hospitality actually gives back to the community,” he added.

What happened to OpenAI’s $20bn? Revenue scare rattles AI trade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:06:26 UTC
21:06:26 KST

US tech futures rebounded on Friday, a day after a report that OpenAI’s annualised revenue was $20 billion (€17.8bn) below earlier estimates helped send the Nasdaq down 1.25% and hit chipmakers and cloud giants.
Wall Street looks set to recover some ground on Friday morning after confusion over how much money OpenAI, the ChatGPT maker, is actually bringing in shook investor faith in the artificial intelligence boom.
Nasdaq 100 futures were around 0.8% higher, and S&P 500 futures were up 0.4% in early trading on Friday.
On Thursday, the Financial Times reported that OpenAI’s annualised revenue, which projects recent sales over a full year, was "approaching $50 billion (€44.6bn)" at the end of September, according to figures shared with investors.
That is about $20 billion (€17.8bn) less than the company projected last month.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell 1.25% to around 27,193, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, which tracks major US chip stocks, sank 3.4%. A jump in oil prices added to the pressure.
Where did the $20 billion go?
In short, nowhere.
The gap does not mean OpenAI missed a target or lost sales: the roughly $70 billion (€62.5bn) figure was an estimate, not a company forecast, built on a different way of counting revenue.
According to the FT, the higher number came from OpenAI’s backers recalculating its sales to match the method of rival Anthropic, which counts what customers spend on its AI models through cloud platforms such as Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud as revenue, while OpenAI excludes such sales.
Taken at face value, OpenAI’s figure trails the $65 billion (€58bn) Anthropic reportedly hit at the end of July, although the different accounting methods make a direct comparison difficult. At the time of writing, OpenAI has not publicly reacted to the reports.
The figures matter as OpenAI, valued at $852 billion (€760bn) in March, is reportedly seeking at least $30 billion (€26.7bn) in fresh funding at a $1.4 trillion (€1.25tn) valuation.
Shares in firms that have bet big on OpenAI’s growth were among the hardest hit after the news broke on Thursday.
Oracle, which has agreed to supply OpenAI with vast computing power, slid 5.5%, while CoreWeave, an AI cloud specialist with multibillion-dollar contracts with the firm, lost nearly 8%.
Microsoft, a major OpenAI shareholder, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta all fell by more than 1%. Like Oracle, all four are hyperscalers that are pouring money into AI data centres.
Chipmakers slid too, with Nvidia down almost 3%, AMD down around 4% and Broadcom, which is building a custom chip with OpenAI, down 4.35%.
In Tokyo on Friday, shares in SoftBank Group, which owns about 13% of OpenAI, fell as much as 7.3% before paring losses.
Chip demand still strong
Despite the negative news, other signals this week suggest demand for AI hardware remains robust.
South Korea’s Samsung estimated on Thursday that its third-quarter operating profit hit a record 107.4 trillion won, or $80.2 billion (€71.5bn).
The figure, if confirmed, would be the biggest quarterly operating profit ever reported by a technology company, beating the $63.7 billion (€56.8bn) in operating income that US chip designer Nvidia booked in its latest quarter.
Taiwan’s TSMC, the world’s biggest contract chipmaker, said the same day that September sales rose 54.6% year-on-year, taking third-quarter revenue to a record NT$1.49 trillion, or $46.8 billion (€41.8bn).
Investors will get a clearer read next week, when Dutch chip equipment maker ASML reports on 14 October and TSMC on 15 October.
Potential listings by Anthropic, as soon as November, and OpenAI next year could bring their audited accounts into the open.

Kenya wants five of its citizens captured fighting for Russia in Ukraine to be treated as victims of human trafficking rather than prisoners of war, Foreign Affairs Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi told Kenyan lawmakers on 8 October, Bloomberg reported. Botswana is also seeking a citizen's return.
In 2025, Ukrainian ambassador Ivan Kholostenko called Russia's role in Africa neocolonialism. As Africa Corps troops prop up friendly regimes, the Kremlin is carrying out "a typical colonial practice of resource extraction," taking gold, diamonds, bauxite, and uranium, according to Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence. Russia also uses the continent as a recruiting ground for its war: nearly 500 Africans have died fighting for Russia, Ukraine says.
Five Kenyans in a Ukrainian camp
Kenya is negotiating to bring the five men home, and President William Ruto has raised the matter with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Mudavadi told the Senate. One has been held since November 2025, the others since March and April. The youngest is 23, Bloomberg reported. Kenya's honorary consul found them held in humane conditions at the Zakhid-1 camp, with access to medical care, the government said. Ukraine also holds the remains of four Kenyans.
Victims or fighters for hire
African governments say some of their citizens went to Russia for promised work as drivers, security guards, or cooks and were then forced into military service. The Kenyans "report having been recruited under false promises of employment," Mudavadi said.
"The circumstances of their recruitment and conscription are consistent with trafficking in persons," he said.
Ukraine's POW authority sees most foreign recruits differently. "The main motive for most of these mercenaries is financial gain," Dmytro Usov, secretary of Ukraine's Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War, said in November 2025, while stressing that many had ended up in Russia's army through fraud or coercion.
Ghana negotiates Ukrainian drone deals as 1,780 Africans fight—and die—in Russia’s ranks
Ukraine holds that prisoners of war go home through exchanges, but Russia has never asked to trade for any foreign fighter except North Koreans, the headquarters said in May, adding it may consider other solutions if diplomats and lawyers find one.
Thousands of foreigners in Russia's ranks
Russia has recruited more than 28,000 foreigners from 135 countries, and more than 5,000 have been killed, a Ukrainian government website cited by Bloomberg says. Ukraine holds at least 213 foreign prisoners of war, not counting Russians and North Koreans, 37 of them African, according to documents Bloomberg saw. Russian dictator Vladimir Putin claimed on 3 September that people are "coming forward voluntarily and signing contracts."
Kenya's government counts 354 citizens linked to the war: 84 killed or missing, 34 hospitalized in Russia, and 62 repatriated. Petitioners told senators that 841 Kenyans remain unaccounted for. Mudavadi said his March visit to Moscow put Kenya on a Russian recruitment "stop list," with no new Kenyans enlisted since.
Some African governments take steps
In August, Botswana stopped eight citizens from joining the Russian military at airports in Botswana, South Africa, and Ethiopia, Bloomberg reported.
Ghana accused Russia of luring its citizens into the war the same month, after Kenya and South Africa. The European Parliament said in March that Russia strips African recruits of their documents. Ukraine, meanwhile, is drafting its first Africa strategy.

Iranian students win BRICS Smart City 2030 Award
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:06:13 UTC
21:06:13 KST

Iranian students win BRICS Smart City 2030 Award
TEHRAN – A team of three students from Sharif University of Technology has won first place in the third International Student and Young Scientist Project Competition, “SMART CITY 2030,” held in Moscow on October 5–6.
The competition brought together more than 3,000 students from leading universities across BRICS countries to develop innovative solutions for sustainable urban development.
The event is part of the international platform Sustainable Urban Development Management in BRICS Countries, which provides opportunities for students, postgraduate students, and young researchers under the age of 35 to present projects and exchange ideas.
The Iranian team’s winning project, titled Minab App, was developed in memory of 168 students who were killed in a US attack on a school in Minab, Hormozgan Province, on the first day of the recent war imposed on the country.
The project proposed initiatives focused on smart-city technologies, creating safer urban environments, and improving energy and transportation systems. It also emphasized the importance of educating children from an early age and raising awareness about environmental protection as key elements of sustainable urban development, IRIB reported.
This year, young scholars from BRICS member states proposed 600 projects in seven main categories.
According to Lyudmila Sergeyevna, director of the center for Business and Management Studies at Russia’s Higher School of Economics, the project of the Iranian students is one of the best ideas, saying that the proposal is highly commendable, as it emphasizes the institutionalization of environmental protection skills among children.
Plan to develop environmental education curriculum
The Department of Environment (DOE) and the Education Ministry have discussed the possibility of developing a national education curriculum to promote environmental responsibility and awareness among children.
Referring to the inefficiency of short-term and incoherent teaching, Mohammad Medadi, an official with the DOE, said that achieving sustainable development and boosting the country’s resilience are not possible without institutionalizing an environmentally friendly attitude and lifestyle in society. So, educational approaches need to be reviewed, he added.
Environmental protection education should be taught from preschool to high school. In addition to scientific training, it should focus on ethical aspects based on cultural, religious, and social teachings.
The initiative also aims to train and empower parents and teachers, the official further noted.
Promoting environmental protection among children
In October 2025, the DOE and the Institute for Intellectual Development of Children and Young Adults (IIDCYA) signed a memorandum of understanding to promote environmental protection among children and young adults.
The MOU was inked by Hadi Kiadaliri, the deputy head of the DOE for education and public participation affairs, and Hamed Alamati, the IIDCYA director, at the place of IIDCYA headquarters in Tehran.
The signing ceremony was concurrent with the second day of National Children’s Week, which was observed nationwide from October 7 to 13, with the theme ‘children, joy of life’.
Since education plays a key role in boosting environmental protection, the DOE is implementing a national project that aims to train eco-friendly students, dubbed ‘environmental helpers’, in 20 percent of elementary schools across the country.
According to Mohammad Medadi, an official with the DOE, the project was launched in cooperation with healthcare providers on September 23, 2025, the start of the past academic year.
It aims to identify students who are interested in environmental issues and encourage them to participate in a working group focusing on environmental-related subjects, IRNA quoted Medadi as saying.
These students will later train other students to raise their environmental awareness. The project is assumed to cover all schools in five years, the official added.
Moreover, informal education in the form of extracurricular activities is planned to be carried out. Consequently, the development of a national environment subject is placed on the agenda. It will contribute to creating a roadmap for formal environmental education according to which relevant content would be included in the curriculum, he further noted.
To instil eco-friendly behaviors, environmental education has to be introduced at an early age, when children are in elementary school or even preschool. However, there will be some challenges.
Education is an ongoing process; temporary or short-term courses would not induce long-standing behavioral changes. It requires time to see favorable results, Medadi said.

Two Renoir paintings stolen from French museum are recovered
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:05:12 BST
21:05:12 KST

Two Renoir paintings stolen from French museum are recovered
- Published
Two paintings by Auguste Renoir stolen a month ago from a museum in the south of France have been recovered, the local town hall has said.
The two works were seized on 8 September when thieves cut through a fence and smashed a window at the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer, where the French impressionist had lived during his final years.
The local mayor praised authorities for recovering the paintings and said the news gave immense joy and profound relief.
Six suspects have also been arrested in relation with the heist at Renoir Museum, the town hall confirmed in a statement.
The theft was the latest in a series of high-profile art heists in Europe.
The two missing paintings were the Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (1910) and Jeune fille au puits (1886).
The thieves had used an electric saw to cut through the frame mountings inside the museum and had initially made off with four paintings, but dropped two of them in the museum's garden as they fled
"These two paintings are far more than works of art. They are part of our city's history, our cultural heritage and the legacy Auguste Renoir left to Cagnes-sur-Mer," said Mayor Bryan Masson, who is part of France's National Rally.
The town hall said initially that it would provide further details of the recovery on Friday, but cancelled a planned press conference.
The Renoir Museum is home to 12 of the famous painter's artworks.
Opened in 1960, it houses a variety of objects that once belonged to him, including his easel and wheelchair, as well as photographs and personal letters.
Earlier this year paintings by Renoir, Paul Cézanne and Henri Matisse were stolen from a museum near the Italian city of Parma, in a raid that lasted just three minutes. They were recovered in August.
France saw its biggest art robbery in years last October, when crown jewels were stolen in broad daylight from the Louvre in Paris.
Disguised as construction workers, the thieves broke into the Louvre's first-floor Apollo Gallery during the museum's opening hours.
They used an angle-grinder to open display cases and made off with €88m (£78m) of jewels that once belonged to France's 19th-Century queens and empresses.
The Louvre was subsequently criticised for under-investing in security.

U.S. Air Force wants a new brain for its older F-16s
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:04:49 UTC
21:04:49 KST

- The U.S. Air Force will brief industry on Oct. 20-21 on a new mission computer for F-16 Block 40, 42, 50 and 52 jets.
- All one-on-one slots are booked, and sensitive briefings are limited to companies certified to handle export-controlled data.
Every one-on-one meeting slot at the U.S. Air Force’s upcoming industry day for a new F-16 mission computer is already booked, and the service has now restricted access to the event’s sensitive briefings to companies certified to handle export-controlled military data.
The Air Force Life Cycle Management Center’s F-16 program office will host the event on Oct. 20 and 21 at the Hope Hotel and Conference Center at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Dayton, Ohio. In an Oct. 8 update, the program office said that access to Controlled Unclassified Information, and to any industry day sessions where it may be discussed, is limited to companies with an active Joint Certification Program registration, the DD Form 2345 process that clears U.S. contractors to receive export-controlled technical data. The event itself is unclassified.
Attendance is capped at 80 people, with no more than two per company, and registration closes Oct. 14. The program office said all 24 of the 25-minute one-on-one sessions with the program manager, contracting officers and technical leads were reserved by Sept. 24.
The program, called the Next-Generation Mission Compute, would replace the Modular Mission Computer on U.S. Air Force F-16 Block 40, 42, 50 and 52 jets, the variants that make up the core of the service’s Viper fleet. The mission computer runs the jet’s combat systems, including radar, targeting, weapons and displays, and a more powerful one would let the U.S. Air Force add new capabilities without major changes to the airframe. The new computer is also meant for foreign customers that fly the same F-16 versions.
The program office first asked industry for ideas in a sources-sought notice published May 29. That notice said a primary goal is to physically separate the computer’s safety-critical, real-time functions from its mission software, and it called for the software to follow the Agile Mission Suite government reference architecture, an open framework meant to let new applications be added more easily. The current Modular Mission Computer traces back to the Common Configuration Implementation Program, which brought roughly 650 Block 40, 42, 50 and 52 jets to a common avionics standard between 2000 and 2010.
The U.S. Air Force plans to keep these F-16s flying into the 2040s and in 2022 launched a separate modernization effort, the Post-Block Integration Team program, covering 608 jets at a value approaching $6.3 billion.
On the first day of the industry day, the program office plans to brief its acquisition strategy and schedule, with hardware and software overviews and open questions, before moving to the individual company sessions. A second day is set aside for additional one-on-one meetings if needed.

Iraq rejects Syrian request over suspected ISIL detainees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09

Iraqi security forces lead suspect ISIL militants for questionings, after they were transferred from Syria to Iraq, at Al-Karkh Central Prison in Baghdad, Iraq, on Feb. 12, 2026. (AP File Photo)
Iraq has rejected Syria’s request to repatriate thousands of suspected ISIL members transferred from Syrian detention centers to Iraqi custody earlier this year, a senior Iraqi security official has said.
Iraqi National Security Advisor Qasim al-Aboudi said on Oct. 7 that a meeting had been held recently between Syria, Iraq and the United States to discuss the fate of the prisoners.
Al-Aboudi said Syria had requested that the approximately 4,000 Syrian prisoners be handed over to be tried in Syria, but Iraq refused. Iraq has determined that about 400 Syrian detainees were not ISIL members and can be released, he told The Associated Press. About 50 have already been repatriated. Hundreds of the Syrians still detained in Iraq are believed to be high-ranking members of the extremist group.
“Iraq is conducting investigations, and anyone proved to have committed crimes in Iraq will be tried under Iraqi law,” he said.
Some prisoners could later be transferred to their home countries to complete their sentences, he said.
Syria did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
More than 5,700 prisoners with alleged ISIL ties — including some 4,000 Syrians — were transferred from northeast Syria to Iraq after fighting broke out in January between Syrian government forces and the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), which had long guarded the detention centers where they were held.
Some ISIL-linked prisoners managed to flee during the chaos of the clashes, and there were fears that a larger-scale escape would take place. While the group lost control of the territory it once seized in Iraq and Syria years ago, its cells still periodically carry out attacks in both countries.
The discussions come as the United States has ended a 12-year mission to fight ISIL in Iraq, with the last U.S. troops withdrawing from the country last month.

Sofia exhibition explores the ‘Contours of the Soul’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:02:57 UTC
21:02:57 KST

Author
Elizabeth Radkova
News
Sofia exhibition explores the ‘Contours of the Soul’
Paintings by patients of the Prof. Nikola Shipkovenski Mental Health Centre mark World Mental Health Day
Friday 9 October 2026 14:27
Friday, 9 October 2026, 14:27
Изложба в София търси контурите на душата
PHOTO Daniela Popova
Font size
“Art is a wound turned into light.”
Georges Braque
According to Bulgaria’s National Mental Health Strategy, around 5% of the population suffer from severe mental disorders, including schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and severe psychoses. Nearly 20% of Bulgarians experience anxiety and depression, with the country ranking 17th worldwide for the prevalence of these conditions, according to the Global Mental Health Report.
World Mental Health Day, observed on 10 October, is an opportunity to reflect on these issues and raise public awareness. This is precisely what the doctors at the Prof. Nikola Shipkovenski Mental Health Centre in Sofia have set out to do. They have launched an inspiring initiative to mark the occasion through the visual arts – an exhibition entitled Contours of the Soul.
We spoke to one of the driving forces behind the project, Dr Antoana Uzunova, a resident doctor specialising in psychiatry at the Prof. Nikola Shipkovenski Mental Health Centre.
Dr Antoana Uzunova
PHOTO Personal archive
“The idea for this exhibition actually came about two years ago, when I mentioned during a conversation with a graphic designer that many of our patients were creative and that quite a few of them painted,” Dr Uzunova recalls.
“I shared the idea with several patients. They were really excited about it, and their enthusiasm gave me even more energy and inspiration to carry on and make it happen – or rather, for my colleagues, the team and me to make it happen together. It was also made possible thanks to the House of Cinema, which gave us the opportunity to hold the exhibition, and our partnership with Collegium Private Psychiatry.
“The title Contours of the Soul was suggested by a colleague. I think it is a beautiful metaphor because the soul has no boundaries, yet part of our role is to explore and understand it, as far as that is possible. And art is one way of doing so,” Dr Antoana Uzunova explains.
Every patient who wanted to take part was welcome. As it turned out, many possessed enormous creative potential, sometimes without even realising it themselves.
PHOTO Antoana Uzunova
“At the time, we had a patient who was a very creative person. She encouraged the other patients to express themselves through art. Even people whose everyday lives are rather grey, and whom I would never have imagined had such talent, produced works with remarkably deep and varied themes, each touching the viewer in its own way,” Dr Uzunova says.
Why do so many people with mental health conditions turn to art?
“I think it gives them a sense of freedom, a kind of relief, because very often their inner world and the processes taking place within them are far from easy to cope with. Art is one way of releasing some of the inner burden they carry.”
But is it possible to identify a mental disorder from someone's paintings?
“Personally, I'm not an expert in this field, so I can't really say. There are paintings which, when you look at them, would give you absolutely no reason to suspect that the artist has a mental illness. But there are others in which certain characteristics can be discerned.
“You might find an answer to your question in the books by Associate Professor Aleksandar Marinov, who was another source of inspiration for this exhibition. He worked as a psychiatrist in the town of Byala and wrote two books based on the art of his patients. They contain numerous illustrations of paintings, along with a considerable amount of theory about the relationship between art and mental illness.”
How important are hobbies for maintaining good mental health?
“I think they're very important. I often ask the patients I work with about their hobbies, what they enjoy doing, and I try to encourage them to pursue those interests. Because when someone has sunk into a hole, so to speak, they lose motivation and forget about the things they once enjoyed.
“What I've seen among the patients, particularly in the run-up to this exhibition, is just how much it has helped them develop this potential within themselves.”
PHOTO Antoana Uzunova
Prevention, as the saying goes, is the most important part of treatment. What can we do to maintain good mental health?
“Yes, of course. It's always important to talk about prevention and looking after our health. There are all sorts of practices that can help, including physical activity and sport, but above all, talking and communicating, because as human beings we need to connect with one another.
“Perhaps each of us should set aside 10 or 15 minutes every morning just for ourselves – and generally try to make more time for ourselves and for personal reflection. We should make time for the people close to us and for the things we love doing.
“We need to take care of our mental health in the same way that we look after our physical health.”
The exhibition Contours of the Soul opens at the House of Cinema in Sofia at 6 pm on Saturday, 10 October. The paintings will remain on display until the end of the month.
Editor: E. Karkalanova
PHOTO Poster design: Daniela Popova

German corporate insolvencies hit 13-year monthly high in July
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:02:55 UTC
21:02:55 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
Corporate insolvencies in Germany reached their highest monthly level in 13 years in July, with local courts registering 2,373 cases, an 8% increase from a year earlier, official data showed Friday.
The figure was the highest monthly total since July 2013, when 2,459 cases were recorded, according to the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis).
In the first seven months of 2026, corporate insolvencies rose 6.9% year on year to 15,185 cases.
Creditors' claims associated with those insolvencies totaled approximately €21.9 billion ($25.4 billion), down from €31.8 billion in the same period last year.
Destatis attributed the decline in claims despite the higher number of insolvencies to a greater number of economically significant companies having filed for insolvency in January-July 2025.
Transport and storage recorded the highest insolvency rate in the first seven months of this year, with 85.5 cases per 10,000 companies, nearly double the overall rate of 42.8.
Accommodation and food services followed with 70 cases per 10,000 companies, while construction recorded 62.9.
Meanwhile, consumer insolvencies fell 5.9% year on year to 7,111 in July.
However, the total for January-July increased 1% from a year earlier to 46,043 cases.
Destatis noted that insolvency applications are included in the statistics only after a court's initial decision, which in many cases comes approximately three months after the original filing.

Gazans and UNRWA-registered excluded from new UK asylum system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:01:45 UTC
21:01:45 KST

Breadcrumb
Palestinians in Gaza and UNRWA-registered refugees excluded from new UK asylum system
Britain does not intend to apply its new asylum system to Palestinians in the Gaza Strip or those registered with the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees (UNRWA), according to information received by The New Arab.
This is despite the British Home Office saying one of the system's aims is to provide accommodation for vulnerable Palestinians fleeing the horrors in the territory, which has been subjected to an Israeli war of extermination for three years.
Informed British government sources told TNA, "Palestinians who have remained in Gaza do not meet the conditions" of the proposed asylum routes.
The sources added that "asylum applications will only be considered for Palestinians who have left Gaza and obtained recognition of their refugee status," justified by saying Palestinians should be outside their country of origin "to qualify for refugee status under international frameworks."
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood announced at the governing Labour Party's annual conference last week a comprehensive package of reforms to the UK's asylum system, including reopening a resettlement route to the UK in partnership with the United Nations.
She vowed that Britain would receive "vulnerable refugees from around the world" and "give them a chance for a new and better life here [in Britain]," expecting the first group of these refugees to arrive before the end of this year.
Shabana noted that "about a quarter of them will be Afghan women and girls fleeing persecution under Taliban rule and Palestinians who have fled the horrors of Gaza."
According to the sources, who asked not to be identified, Palestinians "who have left Gaza and obtained recognition of their refugee status may be referred to the UK through procedures approved by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees."
Asked about Palestinian refugees in Jordan, Syria and Lebanon, the sources said the new system would not apply to them either.
They explained that these refugees "fall under the mandate of the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees (UNRWA), rather than the UN refugee agency," and therefore the UN refugee agency "generally cannot determine asylum applications for individuals covered by UNRWA's mandate."
The New Arab's information acknowledges that the Home Office is working to establish a cooperation arrangement with the International Refugee Assistance Project, known as "IRAP", to "assess eligible [Palestinian] cases and support access to safe and legal routes."
According to sources familiar with the refugee file at the Home Office, the effort aims to "ensure that Palestinian refugees can benefit from the UK's resettlement programme on an equal footing with other refugee groups" and "prevent them from being subjected to any unfairness resulting from the way international refugee protection arrangements operate."
Regarding the criteria under which the British government will accept asylum applications from these Palestinians, the sources said that the most important are "vulnerability and the need for protection."
However, they stressed that the Home Office "retains the authority to make the final decision" on admissions to the UK, indicating that acceptance will not be automatic or easy once asylum applications are received.
The sources explained that all people proposed for asylum "will undergo security and biometric checks, such as facial, eye and voiceprint checks to verify identity, as well as criminal record checks" before potentially travelling to the UK.
UN refugee agency officials or the International Refugee Assistance Project are expected to carry out this task. The checks will also include personal interviews and all procedures required by the British Home Office to verify the eligibility of people proposed for asylum in Britain.
However, the Home Office "will retain the right to exercise an oversight role and intervene if any concerns arise" regarding people proposed for asylum, the sources confirmed.
The reforms announced by Shabana include two other options through which Palestinians and others could be brought to Britain as refugees: "community sponsorship" and "work sponsorship".
Under the first option, charities and non-profit organisations will submit asylum applications while providing guarantees to offer accommodation, help with finding work and integration into the community.
The second option would see companies host refugees and provide them with employment opportunities, in addition to providing the same guarantees.
Both options aim to receive refugees without placing any financial burden on the state budget.
Applications under the two routes are due to open in spring 2027.
A Home Office spokesperson expects the first group of refugees to arrive towards the end of the same year.
However, the spokesperson said to The New Arab that a cap would be set on the number of refugees brought in from different countries.
He noted that Britain would initially receive "hundreds, with the number reaching a few thousand as levels of irregular migration decline."
Separately, the sources also noted that students from the Gaza Strip will benefit from the new reforms, such as allowing British universities to apply to sponsor students under what was described as "a distinct route that operates independently from refugee resettlement programmes."
The sources confirmed that through this route, "the [British] government will continue to support eligible students in Gaza to leave the territory to attend UK universities."
They added that eligible students will enrol at universities from the next academic year (2026-2027).
The sources confirmed that the proposed students will also undergo the checks required of potential refugees through the other routes.
Article translated from Arabic by Afrah Almatwari. To read the original, click here.

‘Deeply offensive’: India hits out at Vance comments
India has accused US Vice President J.D. Vance of making “deeply offensive” comments, after he described foreign workers as “indentured servants” while announcing Washington’s suspension of a key green-card sponsorship process for major technology companies, including several Indian IT firms.
“Resorting to terminology that carries painful historical and colonial legacy connotations is deeply offensive,” India’s Foreign Ministry said in a statement on Friday. 
Vance made the comments at a White House news conference on Thursday, accusing eight tech companies of replacing American employees with lower-paid foreign workers. The suspension covers new and pending applications under the Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) process for Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), Wipro, HCL Technologies, and Capgemini.
PERM is a key step for employers seeking to sponsor foreign workers for permanent residency, or green cards. New Delhi defended Indian professionals as highly educated and skilled contributors to the US economy and innovation sector. It also pointed to generations of immigrants whose labor and enterprise have helped build American prosperity.
Statement on announcement made by the US Department of Labour ⬇️ 🔗 https://t.co/FZawXUTqcl https://t.co/67vMRyJ5EF
— Randhir Jaiswal (@MEAIndia) October 9, 2026
It said skilled-worker mobility benefits both economies by supporting innovation, research, competitiveness, and job creation in the US, adding that Washington’s latest measures “do not advance the shared ambitions of both countries.”
The sharp Indian reaction comes as trade talks between Washington and New Delhi are deadlocked, with Indian Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman saying Monday that it is “very difficult” for both sides to make further concessions.
The Indian market shrugged off the US ban, with shares of all the Indian IT companies involved lifted by the broader market. Indian IT industry body Nasscom said Indian technology companies had significantly reduced their reliance on H-1B visas, with relatively few employees seeking green cards through PERM.
Vance singled out Microsoft, alleging that it had laid off 6,000 American workers last year while benefiting from 6,300 H-1B visas and nearly 3,000 green cards. However, the tech company disputed the comparison, saying about 80% of its roughly 6,000 H-1B applications last fiscal year involved extensions or status changes for existing employees rather than new hires. 
The suspension does not invalidate existing H-1B visas or affect the status of visa holders and their dependents, but could disrupt the green-card process for eligible employees at the affected companies, New Delhi noted.

Nordic public service media companies have agreed to prepare for crises by increasing cooperation.
Among other things, the unified work will aim to prevent cyber threats and the dissemination of disinformation.
Yle published a statement about the agreement on Friday.
At the same time, the broadcasters made a commitment to help their Nordic neighbours if a crisis should strike. For example, if one country loses access to their own news and information sources, residents will be able to get the necessary updates via another Nordic public broadcaster.
Apart from Yle, the Finnish Broadcasting Company, the participating public broadcasters include:
- RÚV (short for Ríkisútvarpið), the public broadcaster of Iceland.
- DR, the Danish Broadcasting Corporation.
- NRK, Norway’s state-owned public service broadcaster.
- SVT, the Swedish national public TV broadcaster
- SR, Sweden's national publicly funded radio broadcaster.
- UR, the Swedish Educational Broadcasting Company.
The media companies emphasised that journalistic independence is a core principle of the agreement. Cooperation therefore doesn't mean one company could decide what another broadcasts.

Cocktail of the week: All Roads’ daiquiri – recipe | The good mixer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:00:28 UTC
21:00:28 KST

Our daiquiri sums up what All Roads is all about: familiar flavours with a little twist. Pineapple, rum and lime are a classic combination, and the addition of scotch bonnet jam brings a subtle warmth that makes this just as good for those first crisp autumn evenings as it is on a sunny day.
All Roads daiquiri
Serves 1
For the pineapple and scotch bonnet jam
75g fresh pineapple, roughly chopped
30g caster sugar
1 small slice scotch bonnet chilli, or more to taste, or 1 pinch chilli flakes
For the drink
10ml overproof white rum – we use Wray & Nephew
45ml white rum – we use Havana Club 3-Year-Old
25ml fresh lime juice
30g pineapple and scotch bonnet jam (see above and method)
First make the jam. Put the pineapple and caster sugar in a saucepan and cook over a low heat until the fruit begins to soften. Blend smooth – we use a stick blender – then add the scotch bonnet to taste and keep cooking gently for 20-25 minutes, stirring regularly, until the jam thickens and turns lightly golden. Take off the heat, leave to cool completely, then lift out and discard the chilli (if using chilli flakes, leave them in). Decant into a small jar or container and keep in the fridge until needed.
To build the drink, put everything in a cocktail shaker filled with ice, shake hard until well chilled, then double strain into a chilled coupe.
- Malika Green and Paschelle Brown, All Roads, London SW9

Which cities dominated 2020 voter fraud talk? A city’s Black population was the best predictor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:00:15 UTC
21:00:15 KST

White Americans who hold racially resentful attitudes are particularly prone to believing claims of election fraud, especially when those allegations target predominantly Black communities. The authors argue that such claims give people who feel threatened by Black political power a way to reject election results they dislike while still professing support for democracy. The findings were published in Political Behavior.
To understand this reaction, social scientists often examine racial resentment. In political research, this concept does not simply refer to overt hatred; instead, it describes a subtle belief system that downplays systemic barriers faced by Black Americans and views minority political or economic gains as unearned. According to the social theories the authors draw on, when members of an advantaged group feel their social standing is slipping, they often look for ways to protect their position.
Following landmark political shifts, scholars began documenting how these racial attitudes influence trust in the voting process. For instance, a 2016 study showed that racial resentment was linked to suspicions of widespread election misconduct following the historic election of Barack Obama. Later work deepened this connection: a 2021 study found that racially resentful White Americans tend to become less satisfied with democracy when their preferred candidate loses an election.
Fraud allegations may also serve a particular purpose for dissatisfied voters. In a 2021 survey experiment, researchers found that exposure to unsubstantiated claims of voter fraud lowered people’s confidence in the integrity of elections without reducing their support for democracy itself. These findings raised a question the new study set out to answer: whether fraud accusations carry a racial charge that makes them especially persuasive to resentful White voters.
To test this dynamic, a research team led by Kevin T. Morris of the Brennan Center for Justice and Ian Shapiro of Tennessee State University conducted three distinct investigations. The authors sought to understand how racial attitudes interact with claims of election malfeasance.
“The motivation for this study was an urge to understand whether and how racial considerations shaped people’s trust in the 2020 general election,” Shapiro told PsyPost. “I suspected that fraud narratives, with their focus on crime, provided a vehicle for some White Americans to perceive specific elections as corrupt while maintaining trust in a system that had traditionally benefited them.”
The authors first examined whether real-world public discussions of election fraud actually focused on Black communities. They analyzed approximately 2.7 million public posts published on Twitter in 2020 containing the phrase “voter fraud.” From that collection, the researchers isolated about 95,000 posts that mentioned American cities with at least 100,000 residents, comparing those mentions against local demographic data and election tallies.
The social media data showed that cities with larger Black populations appeared far more often in voter fraud conversations, a pattern driven by the period after the election; before Election Day, none of the city characteristics the researchers examined predicted how often a city was mentioned.
The 10 cities mentioned most often relative to their size, a list that included Detroit, Philadelphia, and Atlanta, had an average Black population share of about 36 percent, compared with about 16 percent for the large cities in the analysis and under 7 percent for U.S. municipalities overall. In statistical models, a city’s Black population share was the only reliable predictor of these mentions; how strongly a city voted for Joe Biden was not related to how often it came up.
“I think what surprised me most was how clearly racial composition mattered in predicting which places became targets of social media fraud narratives,” Shapiro said. “Partisanship and racial politics are closely linked, but the only predictor of how frequently a city was mentioned on social media was the Black share of the population. Not even Biden’s vote share was associated with fraud narratives, other things equal.”
“Prior to election night, narratives about fraud were all over the place. They were prevalent but lacked shape,” Shapiro explained. “On election night in 2020 and in the weeks after, attention narrowed to specific places that became focal points for fraud accusations. Those places were not random.”
Next, the researchers evaluated how these public narratives corresponded to shifts in individual attitudes over time. They examined data from roughly 4,300 White participants in the 2020 Cooperative Election Study who answered questions about election confidence both before and after Election Day. The authors tracked changes in confidence while controlling for conservative ideology, support for Donald Trump, age, gender, education, income, and Fox News viewership.
Confidence in the election dropped sharply among White Trump supporters after Election Day, as is typical for voters whose candidate loses. But even after accounting for this pattern, along with ideology and the other factors, higher racial resentment was associated with an additional decline in confidence. This link held among Trump supporters, whereas resentment was not related to changes in election confidence among White supporters of Biden.
“Trump voters generally trusted the election less after it looked like he had lost. That’s normal,” Shapiro observed. “But confidence fell off a cliff among Trump supporters who scored higher in racial resentment, following the election and the accompanying focus on Black cities.”
To test whether racial cues directly cause people to believe fraud claims, the researchers conducted an online survey experiment in July 2024 with 1,500 White American adults. Participants read a mock news report describing either an apolitical story about a local restaurant, allegations of voter fraud in a fictional suburban city portrayed as largely White, or identical allegations in an “inner-city” described as predominantly Black. The stories included matching photographs of either White or Black election workers, voters, and local election administrators. After completing the questions, participants were debriefed and informed that the city was fictional and that election fraud is rare.
Across the entire sample, reading about fraud increased suspicion compared to reading about the restaurant, but participants overall did not view the Black city as more fraudulent than the White city. Important differences emerged, however, when examining specific subgroups. White Republicans who read about the predominantly Black city scored an average of 0.65 on a scale measuring belief in fraud, compared with 0.58 for Republicans who read about the White city, a gap of 0.07 points, or about 12 percent. This partisan comparison was not part of the authors’ preregistered analysis plan.
Personal levels of racial resentment also shaped how participants responded. Participants with higher resentment showed elevated suspicion of fraud even when assigned to read about the restaurant, and the fraud stories moved their beliefs considerably more than those of less resentful participants. Resentful participants also tended to find accusations more believable when they targeted the Black city, though this pattern was statistically reliable for only one of the resentment measures, and the authors describe the evidence as somewhat mixed. Fraud beliefs lined up more closely with resentment toward Black Americans than with White consciousness, a measure of attachment to one’s own racial group.
“The survey experiment confirms prior findings that just talking about fraud can substantially affect how much of it people think is happening,” Shapiro noted. “Despite fraud being so rare, words have power. And when those words are tied to tangible places for a political purpose, the effects can be substantial.”
These findings align with a study covered by PsyPost in 2024, which found that White Americans who felt their racial group faced widespread mistreatment were consistently more skeptical of election fairness from 2012 to 2020. That earlier research measured perceived discrimination against White Americans rather than resentment toward Black Americans. It also found that strong White identity without a sense of grievance went along with greater faith in elections, which is broadly consistent with the new study’s finding that White consciousness tracked fraud beliefs less closely than resentment.
The results also support research covered by PsyPost in 2025, which indicated that higher levels of racial resentment are tied to broader anti-democratic views among White Americans. Morris and Shapiro argue that skepticism about ballot integrity often intersects with underlying anxieties regarding multiracial governance.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The social media analysis relied on public posts from Twitter, which may not capture the complete range of political discussion experienced by ordinary citizens offline. In addition, the researchers could not distinguish between posts promoting fraud claims and those seeking to debunk them, and some messages could have been amplified by automated accounts or foreign entities rather than regular voters.
Shapiro also emphasized that the investigation centered on how narratives are received rather than how political leaders strategize behind closed doors. “The data we use can’t really tell us about the motivations behind elite-driven narratives,” he told PsyPost. “The paper didn’t directly show people Trump’s social media posts or anything like that.”
“However, it’s not a stretch to suspect that the narratives we see spreading on social media took some structure and encouragement from elites,” Shapiro added. “A lot of agenda setting and attitude formation happens from the top down. This study is more about where and among whom these racial narratives find, excuse me for this, fertile ground.”
Shapiro is now examining how these rhetoric-driven policies affect the electorate. “I’m looking into how restrictive laws passed in response to these narratives turn people off from voting,” he explained. “I’m interested in what psychological mechanisms drive that process for different people.”
Reflecting on the democratic stakes, Shapiro stressed the broader danger these narratives pose to public trust. “This study is important because we’re in an era when people are cynical about all sorts of institutions, including elections,” he remarked. “But things like losers’ consent—accepting election results even when your side loses—and the belief that elections are a viable way to hold leaders accountable are at the heart of democratic functioning. Politically convenient narratives about crime and race threaten these pillars of democratic life.”
The study, “On Fertile Ground: How Racial Resentment Primes White Americans To Believe Fraud Accusations,” was authored by Kevin T. Morris and Ian Shapiro.

Rosalind Eleazar Gives One of the Year's Best Performances in the Acerbic and Tender Misty Green
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:00:05 UTC
21:00:05 KST

It was probably around 100 years ago that stalwart Hollywood star Marie Dressler said, “You’re only as good as your last picture.” Today, that hard-nosed observation not only holds; in a culture measured out in here-today-gone-tomorrow limited series and independent films that fail to find their audience, it’s more apt, and more potentially heartbreaking, than ever.
Misty Green, the title character and the heartbeat of Chris Rock’s fourth feature film as a director, is living out Dressler’s maxim. Misty, played by Rosalind Eleazar, is a gifted singer and actor who desperately needs a break. But there are good reasons she’s not going to get it. Even though she has an Emmy from her role in a hit series, she’s on her way to being forgotten. She has no patience for Hollywood BS and refuses to play the usual games. But she’s also prickly and unpleasant—she has alienated most of the people who might be able to help her—and a self-destructive streak hinders her further: She’d rather go out for a night of clubbing and coke than stay in and learn her lines for the next day’s important audition.
So now she’s in desperate straits. Essentially homeless, she’s been camping out in the apartment of a rich—and dead—ex-lover, but the guy’s angry widow has just given her seven days to pack up and vacate. During all this, her fragile brother, Jay (Daniel Kaluuya), who has been diagnosed with bipolar disorder and whom she loves deeply, shows up at the flat that’s not even her own, needing more from her than she can provide.
We’ve seen the story of the wannabe comeback kid before. And Misty Green isn’t always a thoroughly graceful film. One of the weaker links may be the character played by Rock himself, Jordan, a director who wants to help Misty but harbors amorous feelings that don’t feel wholly believable; Misty could use some help, but she may not need that kind of savior. But overall, Rock’s writing is sharp and perceptive, and he’s attuned not just to the horrors of trying to make it in Hollywood, but also to Misty’s specific plight—and to the reality that she’s at times almost repugnantly dislikable.
Eleazar, best known for her role in Slow Horses, knows just how to shape this character without ever softening her. Misty is gifted, arrogant, impossible; at times, you begin to wonder if she even deserves a break. But Eleazar, giving one of the best performances of the year, tears our expectations to shreds: Who are we to decide what she deserves? At one point, during an audition, one of the men in charge of potentially hiring her blurts out, “Are you mixed?” and her eyes, moments ago dancing with fire, become glacier cold.
Misty has made her way along a path paved with irrelevant, if not outright racist and sexist, questions and assumptions—it’s little wonder she can barely take any more. But even stronger than her resentment is her belief that she still has something to give. It may be a stereotype to characterize actors as needy people, but Eleazar captures an almost existential longing that goes beyond garden-variety neediness. And at her lowest moment, Misty’s desperation becomes nearly unbearable to watch. Eleazar brings us right to the knifepoint of her degradation, and it pierces us too.
But Rock wouldn’t leave Misty in despair; he gives her the empathetic yet unsentimental ending she deserves. It’s almost impossible to like Misty, and yet, in a film that’s both acerbic and tender, Eleazar makes us love her, almost against our will. Hollywood, a place of dreams, can be inhumane to those who dream the biggest. Misty Green opens a safe space for them—without the false promise of a happy ending.

Why South Korea and Ukraine Are Fighting Over Two Prisoners of War
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

On Sept. 23, President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine spoke at the UN General Assembly about the military support Russia was getting from North Korea and the deaths of North Korean soldiers on the Ukrainian front. “Recently, we sent two North Korean prisoners of war to the Republic of Korea,” he revealed. He seemed to be trying to highlight the global reach of Russia’s war and also hoping that the revelation would increase popular and political support in Seoul for providing weapons and aid to Ukraine.
Zelensky ended up igniting a diplomatic dispute between Ukraine and South Korea. Seoul claimed that Ukraine had agreed to keep the transfer confidential; Kyiv denied that such an agreement existed and downplayed the episode as a misunderstanding. Now South Korea is recalling its ambassador to Ukraine.
The quarrel over diplomatic protocol highlights the human cost paid by two soldiers caught in a geopolitical conflict linking European and Northeast Asian security. Their story captures the complicated geopolitics of the two Koreas now playing out on a European battlefield. It also underscores South Korea’s push for inter-Korean peace, even as North Korea tests Seoul’s patience by launching hypersonic missiles and planting landmines.
The men from North Korea
The two soldiers at the center of the dispute were captured while fighting in the Kursk region of Russia in January 2025. They were part of a 10,000-strong North Korean contingent reinforcing Russian troops on the front line. Shortly after their capture, Ukraine’s military released video footage of the two soldiers. The images helped confirm North Korea’s direct involvement in the Russia-Ukraine war. Human Rights Watch raised concerns about Ukraine’s decision to release the video and expose the soldiers, given the potential repercussions for their families in North Korea, including torture, forced labor, imprisonment, or execution.
North Korean soldiers are instructed to take their own lives rather than risk capture. One of the captured soldiers reportedly attempted suicide before a Ukrainian medic stopped him. In North Korea’s eyes, a soldier who survives by surrendering, or worse by defecting to the South, is a traitor. Under the regime’s well-documented system of collective punishment, three generations of a defector’s family can face retribution through guilt by association.
By revealing the prisoner of war transfer to South Korea in New York, Zelensky offered Pyongyang an incentive to make an example of these soldiers’ families to demonstrate the consequences of defection. This stands in stark contrast to the regime’s response to the deaths of North Korean soldiers in Russia. Kim Jong Un, the leader of North Korea, promised their surviving families a “beautiful life” and granted them new luxury apartments.
The North Korean regime may have already tracked down the families of the prisoners of war after Ukraine confirmed their capture in January 2025. But Zelensky’s disclosure at the United Nations renewed the danger facing the two soldiers now resettled in South Korea, a point Seoul highlighted in its protest to Kyiv. A life in South Korea offers these soldiers personal safety, but one could imagine it might come at a crushing cost: abandoning their homes and living with the guilt that their families may suffer in their place.
Mending the rupture between Seoul and Kyiv
If this episode were only about the two North Korean soldiers, their resettlement might have passed unnoticed. The diplomatic kerfuffle between Kyiv and Seoul is rooted in the different geopolitical narratives that each nation seeks to project, or in Seoul’s case, downplay.
For Ukraine, publicizing the presence and resettlement of North Korean prisoners of war provides a valuable opportunity to solicit support from South Korea, a major arms exporter and a vital partner to NATO. Since 2022, Kyiv has been urging Seoul to supply it with lethal weapons, including Patriot interceptors and 155mm artillery shells. In light of Pyongyang’s direct military support for Moscow, Ukraine has intensified pressure on South Korea to move beyond non-lethal military, humanitarian, and economic assistance.
For South Korea, Ukraine’s public disclosure of the resettlement of these soldiers undermines its diplomatic outreach to North Korea. In his address to the UN General Assembly, President Lee Jae Myung of South Korea reiterated his vision of inclusive, peaceful coexistence built on “respect for each other’s systems” and the restoration of cross-border trust with North Korea. Accepting North Korean soldiers while publicly promoting dialogue weakens Lee’s reassurances to Pyongyang that Seoul desires “stable, peaceful coexistence.”
Pyongyang has maintained silence regarding these two soldiers. But North Korea considers South Korea’s reception of defectors as part of an effort to undermine its regime and eventually bring about unification on Seoul’s terms. While North Korea now defines the Koreas as two separate states, article four of South Korea’s constitution commits the nation to “peaceful unification based on the basic free and democratic order.”
As two nations dedicated to promoting freedom and democratic principles, South Korea and Ukraine must look beyond this diplomatic disagreement to protect their partnership. Seoul provided $400 million in aid to Ukraine in 2024 and announced $2.3 billion in long-term reconstruction aid through 2027. In return, Ukraine offers critical, real-world intelligence on North Korean military tactics and the weapons technology Pyongyang receives from Russia.
Given the complex legal situation of North Korean combatants captured by Ukrainian forces, Kyiv and Seoul must establish a protocol for handling North Korean prisoners of war and non-combatant defectors who seek asylum in South Korea. The need for such a policy will only grow. Similar episodes may unfold as the presence of North Korean troops and laborers in Russia grows, increasing the potential for future defections. Zelensky recently warned that another 10,000 troops from North Korea could soon be deployed in Russia.
With Kyiv’s cooperation, Seoul should affirm its commitment to accept future North Korean prisoners who voluntarily request resettlement, subject to standard security screening. That policy must fully comply with South Korean law and uphold international humanitarian principles and the values of a democratic society. To safeguard these individuals, both governments should protect prisoners’ identities, grant confidential access to impartial humanitarian representatives, and ensure that decisions are not made under coercion. Prisoners of war should not be forcibly repatriated, and public announcements of their transfer must be avoided without their explicit consent.
Crucially, not every captured North Korean soldier will want to go to South Korea. Their wishes must be determined through private, independent interviews conducted without pressure from governments, intelligence agencies, advocacy groups, or the media. Both governments may have followed such protocols. It remains unclear whether Ukraine eventually deviated from the agreed approach script or whether there was simply miscommunication.
Yet for the two soldiers already resettled, no policy can erase the personal toll. They must now rebuild their lives in a country they were raised to view as the enemy while carrying the lingering anguish about the fate of the families they left behind.

Developers crowd into Lüganuse as municipality navigates project surge

Developers crowd into Lüganuse as municipality navigates project surge
Lüganuse municipality in Ida‑Viru County has become a favorite location for various developers, which has forced the municipality to hire additional staff to process planning applications.
In Lüganuse, VKG and Kiviõli Keemiatööstus are expanding their oil‑shale mines; the state wants to establish two defense‑industry parks in the municipality; both a nuclear power plant and a VKG limestone‑product factory are being planned for the area.
A large part of the new Haljala–Kukruse section of the Tallinn–Narva highway, which will be publicly presented on Monday, also falls within Lüganuse's borders. In addition, various wind‑farm developers are showing active interest in the municipality, said Lüganuse Municipal Council Chairman Mart Kivistik.
"At the moment we have five detailed plans, four special plans, and one has been established — Evecon Energia's. In reality, this is an enormous burden for our small municipality. Initially more than 160 positions were launched. I think the real number will remain around one hundred, because so many locations will fall away," Kivistik said.
According to Gregor Raudvere, board member of Varja Windfarm, which wants to build wind farms in Lüganuse, the municipality's advantage is its favorable location and the low level of local opposition.
"In Lüganuse, I would say the attitude of residents is certainly one factor that speaks in its favor — this has been mentioned a lot elsewhere too. But Lüganuse also has very good wind conditions, Lüganuse has the Püssi substation, which is one of the largest node substations in Estonia, and there is a lot of free land and people who are willing to allow turbines to be erected on their land," Raudvere said.
For the municipality, the interest of various industries means that additional workforce is needed to make the proceedings run more smoothly, Kivistik noted.
"It is quite a large resource cost to answer all kinds of inquiries and matters that come with all of this. In that sense, we have created additional positions," Kivistik said.
In various proceedings, the municipal council chairman has been bothered by the fact that the experts assessing impacts tend to view the processes more from the developer's perspective than from that of the local resident.
"I would say from my own experience, since I have attended many of these meetings, that experts should explain more substantively and the presentations should be better, more prepared and impartial," Kivistik said.
Lüganuse municipality was formed by the merger of the former Lüganuse, Sonda and Maidla municipalities and the towns of Püssi and Kiviõli. The municipality has almost 8,000 residents, most of whom live in the town of Kiviõli.

BNN IN FOCUS | Political scientist’s view: “Where will we make the cuts?” – Rajevskis warns of the cost of banning grain transit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:59:43 UTC
20:59:43 KST

Latvia is planning to ban the transit of grain from Russia and Belarus, but it remains unclear how thoroughly the consequences of such a decision have been assessed. While the move might provide political satisfaction, what impact would it have on Latvia’s economy? Filips Rajevskis, political scientist and co-founder of Mediju tilts, stresses that the “grain issue” needs to be considered from a broader perspective.
The political scientist points out that grain transported through Latvia in transit is mainly traded by American commodity traders. “Of course, there may always be moral objections, but we must take into account that the grain no longer belongs to Russians and that this is not a Russian business. It is the business of our strategic partners – major American commodity traders who handle these transactions. This means their country’s interests are also involved,” Rajevskis says.
He also stresses the importance of examining how Latvia’s neighbours are acting. “Estonia was very quick to announce that it would not transport any grain. That is logical because Estonia has never been a grain transit country. Therefore, its loud announcements do not really mean much. At the same time, we can see that Estonia quietly secures an exemption from sanctions for a Russian magnesium plant to protect its own economic interests. It is not loud statements but quiet actions that reveal countries’ real economic interests. Latvia must finally understand, both in its foreign policy and its external economic policy, that we have national interests of our own. We should not harm our partners who guarantee our security either.”
When BNN noted that Lithuania had announced plans to propose a complete halt to grain transit at both Baltic and European Union level, Rajevskis responded that attention should be paid not to what Lithuanian officials say, but to what is happening at the Klaipėda terminal, where potash is handled. “That will be potash purchased by American traders, and they will continue handling it without any concerns. Latvia is also a transit country for potash. So we need to approach this issue sensibly and realistically.
