Swiss gene therapy for blindness makes further encouraging progress
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:59:28 UTC
20:59:28 KST

Swiss gene therapy for blindness makes further encouraging progress
Eye researchers at the Swiss city of Basel are hopeful of a breakthrough in the treatment for blind people after initial positive indications that a new form of therapy works.
Blind people learning to see. What sounds like a fairy tale is becoming reality – at least in a certain sense. A new therapy for the retinal disease retinitis pigmentosa, which has so far only been tested on a small number of people, is showing astonishing results.
With its help, blind people were able to recognize at least the outlines of certain objects. This is reported in the renowned scientific journal New England Journal of Medicine.
Stefan Futterknecht from the Institute of Molecular and Clinical Ophthalmology Basel (IOB) is a co-author of this recently published study. He is convinced that these findings will be very beneficial.
More
Blind patient gets “bionic eye” implant
“This has laid the foundation for the development of more precise and effective therapies in the future, said Futterknecht, who described the study as a “milestone for restoring vision.”
Outlines of objects are seen
Five years ago, the first study of this gene therapy was conducted, at that time in Paris and with a single person. That man gained his first visual impressions through the therapy.
After initial treatments proved effective on the anonymous test subject, the IOB have moved to the next stage.
Of the ten participants in the expanded, new study, most experienced an improvement, said Futterknecht. “Seven out of ten people had an increase in light sensitivity.” Furthermore, four out of eight people were able to see the outlines of even small objects, such as a matchbox.
Being able to recognize a door could greatly simplify everyday life, according to the study. Furthermore, those who practiced more with the glasses saw better.
However, this milestone is far from being the end of the road. “We are still a long way from patients being able to read or having the kind of vision we are used to,” said Futterknecht. Now, work is underway to improve various elements of the therapy, including the proteins that make cells light-sensitive.
Potential benefits
Ideally, patients treated should be able to see again without glasses. The long-term hope is “to restore vision as much as possible,” says Futterknecht.
Specifically, all participants in the study suffer from retinitis pigmentosa, but its origins differ. Futterknecht says this shows that the new gene therapy has the potential to benefit many blind people, not just a specific, small group.
Optogenetic therapy does not address every single cause of the various forms of this disease, in which, in advanced stages, the light-sensitive retinal cells barely function. Instead, it enables other cells in the retina to respond to light.

KUALA LUMPUR, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim unveiled the national budget for 2027 on Friday with a focus on easing the cost of living through tax breaks, a higher minimum wage and other measures while also seeking to develop the country's burgeoning technology sector.
Malaysia's Budget 2027, totaling 459.8 billion ringgit (112.5 billion U.S. dollars), aims to turn resilient economic growth into real gains for the people with better wages, smarter targeted support, stronger fiscal discipline and a bold push towards higher-value industries, Anwar, who is also finance minister, told parliament in his budget speech.
Among measures aimed at easing the cost of living is raising the minimum wage to 2,000 ringgit from the current 1,700 ringgit starting in June 2027, with the exception of micro, small and medium-sized enterprises with annual sales below 50 million ringgit.
The government will also introduce a minimum monthly salary of 2,500 ringgit for semi-skilled workers and graduates as the initial step in reforming the wage framework. Middle-class citizens will benefit through increased individual income tax relief and reduced tax rates for selected income brackets.
Meanwhile, the government will extend green tax incentives to Dec. 31, 2030. Companies investing in green technology projects, electric vehicle charging stations or green assets for their own use will be eligible for up to 100 percent investment tax allowances.
A 100 million ringgit fund will support early-stage semiconductor and advanced manufacturing companies in Penang state as part of efforts to strengthen regional industrial development and attract investment beyond established economic centers. Other technology hubs in other states will also be supported to attract global semiconductor investments, create skilled jobs and expand business opportunities for local companies.
It will also implement a preferential five percent tax rate on income generated from global services hub activities for new companies, starting on Jan. 1, 2027, to facilitate business operations and make it easier for global companies to operate in Malaysia. ■

Interview: AI ethics should reflect common values of humanity, says UK AI expert
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
19:58:05 CST
20:58:05 KST

by Shao Haijun
ZAANDAM, THE NETHERLANDS, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly capable, humanity needs to consider not only what AI can do, but also what values should guide its development and use, according to Nigel Shadbolt, a member of the UK Government's Council for Science and Technology.
"As our AI systems become more capable, we would like them to embody the best of us," Shadbolt, also a Distinguished Senior Scientist at the Institute of Ethics in AI and Professor of Computer Science at the University of Oxford, told Xinhua in an exclusive interview on Wednesday on the sidelines of the World Summit AI, held on Oct. 7-8 in Zaandam, the Netherlands.
The rapid development of AI has brought major opportunities, but also created new forms of risk, raising fundamental questions about how increasingly capable systems should be designed and governed.
Shadbolt identified three broad areas of concern.
"The first is the misuse of AI by humans," he explained. "AI can accelerate drug discovery and scientific research, but the same capabilities could also be exploited by malicious actors to launch cyber-attacks, commit fraud, develop biological weapons or other harmful purposes."
"The second is the possibility that AI systems may pursue their assigned goals in unexpected ways," he said. Recent incidents involving advanced AI agents have highlighted this concern. For example, an AI agent developed by OpenAI reportedly breached a data portal linked to Australia's universal healthcare system in June.
"Highly capable systems could, for example, cheat, hack into systems or obtain credentials in ways their developers had not anticipated," he said.
A third concern is whether increasingly advanced AI could eventually become difficult for humans to control. While Shadbolt said he was not primarily focused on existential risks from hypothetical super intelligence, he argued that researchers should continue to examine the challenges presented by recursive self-improvement, AI systems developing evermore capable versions of themselves.
Technical safeguards and regulation are therefore necessary, but they may not be sufficient on their own. Shadbolt argued that sets of values should also be encoded into AI systems to help guide their behavior.
"What values do we put into the system? And how can we be confident that the model can't be persuaded to act in a way that suddenly has it cheating, lying or pretending to be less capable than it is?" he said.
He emphasized the goal should not be to impose one particular ethical tradition in the world. Instead, there may be room to identify values that can be shared across different societies and systems of governance.
"We do share a common set of values about what we think is desirable," he said.
Different societies have different philosophical and cultural traditions, ranging from utilitarianism and social contract theory to rule-based ethics and traditions emphasizing respect and social obligations. Some of these principles, he noted, have parallels with values found in Confucian thought.
"I'd like to believe that there is scope for agreement on some of those ideas -- what would common, shared ethical values look like," he said.
Shadbolt also called for more inclusive AI governance and greater international cooperation to ensure that increasingly powerful AI systems remain aligned with human interests. A more inclusive approach should address not only AI safety, but also data, intellectual property, consent and the distribution of economic benefits.
Ultimately, Shadbolt argued, AI governance needs to combine technological innovation with shared human values, ensuring that increasingly powerful AI systems serve not only national or commercial interests, but also the broader interests of humanity. ■

EU seeks to ban Russian diplomats from travelling outside host countries
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:58:00 EEST
20:58:00 KST

EU seeks to ban Russian diplomats from travelling outside host countries
On 12 October, the EU Foreign Affairs Council will discuss the possibility of introducing further restrictions on the movement of Russian diplomats between EU member states, potentially including a complete ban on travel outside the country to which they are accredited.
Source: European Pravda, citing several European diplomats and a senior EU official familiar with the preparations for the discussion
Details: European Pravda's sources indicate that the EU wants either to ban Russian diplomats from travelling outside their host country altogether or require them to obtain prior permission from any EU member state they intend to travel through.
The diplomats noted that several EU countries support significantly tightening restrictions on Russian diplomats' freedom of movement within the Schengen area.
Quote from one diplomat: "Until now, Russian diplomats have been able to notify their host country and travel wherever they want. Now we want to impose a blanket restriction."
Details: Another European Pravda source stressed that a significant proportion of Russian diplomats in the EU are intelligence officers, which is one of the main reasons the EU wants to restrict their freedom of movement.
Quote from another diplomat: "The logical next step would be to allow Russian diplomats to travel only within the country to which they are accredited. For example, a Russian diplomat accredited in France would not be allowed to travel to Germany or Belgium."
Details: Meanwhile, the EU is also considering a less restrictive option: requiring Russian diplomats to obtain permission from both their host country and the countries they intend to visit, rather than simply notifying them of travel within the Schengen area.
European Pravda's sources also highlighted the large number of Russian diplomats accredited to international organisations based in European capitals. They said the EU is interested in reducing their numbers and tightening oversight.
European Pravda notes that the EU Foreign Affairs Council meeting on 12 October will be for discussion only, with no decision on new restrictions on Russian diplomats expected.
EU diplomats first want to gauge the level of political support for further measures restricting Russian diplomats' travel.
Furthermore, on 14 October, the EU Council's visa working group is due to discuss a German initiative on a common restrictive approach to issuing visas to Russian citizens, the use of visas with limited territorial validity and visa-related provisions in the EU's 21st package of sanctions against Russia.
Background:
- In October 2025, as part of the 19th package of sanctions against Russia, the EU introduced a requirement for Russian diplomats to notify EU member states in advance of any travel outside the country to which they are accredited. The rules came into force on 25 January 2026.
- Since the summer, the EU has also been discussing restricting visa issuance to those who have fought in Ukraine for Russia. The EU included a mechanism to ban visas for Russian military personnel in its 21st sanctions package, but the ban itself has not yet come into force.
- In September, Hungary announced its decision to expel 10 staff members of the Russian embassy for activities deemed "unacceptable for diplomats" under the Vienna Convention.
- In early September, Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski called for Russian diplomats to be allowed to travel only within the countries to which they are accredited, and for limits to be imposed on the number of accreditations they can hold.

Thieves make off with €5m haul from prestigious Italian winery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:57:49 UTC
20:57:49 KST

Thousands of bottles of wine worth €5m (£4.2m) have been stolen from a prestigious winery in Tuscany in what is thought to be the biggest heist of its kind in Italy.
A gang of at least seven masked individuals broke into the cellar of Marchesi Antinori, a family-owned winery dating back to the late 1300s, in Cortona after shutting off the alarms and surveillance cameras before using company forklifts to load two large trucks with 30,000 bottles of wine and making off.
Among the bottles targeted were those most prized by wine collectors and consumers, including Solaia, Guado al Tasso and Tignanello, notable as one of the first red wines in the Tuscany region to be produced without white grapes. All the stolen bottles, ranging in price between €120 and €400 a bottle, are from the firm’s 2023 vintage.
The theft occurred on Saturday as the company, based in the hilltop town of Cortona, prepared for a major shipment to buyers abroad. The robbery was discovered only when staff arrived for work on Monday morning.
“The gang was very prepared,” Renzo Cotarella, chief executive of Marchesi Antinori, told Corriere della Sera. “A theft of this scale and value has never happened before in Italy.”
He said he had “great confidence” that investigators would trace the stolen wine, which included 3,000 bottles, some of them magnum-sized, of Barolo Ginestra.
“Two trucks full of merchandise can’t just disappear into thin air,” he added. “The Tuscan roads are full of cameras. Perhaps with a bit of luck we’ll be able to recover at least some of the bottles.”
There have been several thefts at wineries in Italy in recent months, including one in Alba in the northern Piedmont region in mid-September.
But Cotarella, who suspects the same gang could have been involved, never imagined a theft of such scale would happen to his company. Unfortunately, its insurance policy does not cover the robbery of wine at such huge value.
“We had always considered the possibility of having a few cases of wine being stolen during their transportation, but certainly not that two trucks manage to enter the cellar and make off with such a huge haul,” he told Corriere.
Such large wine robberies were usually meticulously prepared and would probably be carried out by those with an intimate knowledge of wine themselves, Corriere suggested, with the target destination possibly collectors, bars or restaurants. However, a sudden increase in the supply of such wines could raise suspicion.
As the investigators continue their search, Cotarella said the company, which was established in 1385, has warned customers to be wary of any offers of its wine outside official channels.

UN says Pentagon plan to livestream execution of Fort Hood shooter would amount to torture – US politics live
Condemnation comes amid fierce backlash from US lawmakers who branded the move ‘grotesque’ and compared it to actions of some terror groups and oppressive governments
Livestreaming US execution would amount to torture, says UN
A decision by US officials to livestream the execution of convicted killer Nidal Hasan would amount to torture, the UN said.
US defence officials said US Army psychiatrist Hasan, who shot and killed 13 people at a military base in 2009, would face a firing squad and the execution would be broadcast live, adding that details would come later.
“The livestreaming of an execution is tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture,” the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights said in a message sent to AFP.
The UN body said it had made similar statements about public executions in Afghanistan and Iran, saying they “constitute a form of cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment”.
Broadcasting an execution could cause post-traumatic stress disorder in the viewing public, mental health experts have said after Hegseth’s announcement that the firing squad execution of Nidal Hassan – the former US army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at Fort Hood – would be livestreamed.
Dr Simon Duff, a forensic psychologist at the University of Nottingham in the UK, said that while there was not a lot of research into the impact of watching an execution, studies examining journalists’ experiences of witnessing violence suggested evidence of trauma response.
“Certainly if people are not resilient they probably shouldn’t [watch], but if they have some underlying psychological driver towards viewing an execution they will likely do so regardless of the potential for harm,” Duff said.
“Recent events suggest that executions do not always go to plan,” he said, referring to the failed execution by lethal injection of Christa Pike in the US. “That possibility needs to be acknowledged, and the likelihood that this would increase the trauma for viewers.”
Neil Greenberg, a professor of defence mental health at the Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology and Neuroscience at King’s College London, said trigger warnings did not routinely lead to people avoiding media they may find distressing.
“Instead they are likely to suffer anticipatory anxiety before the ‘trauma’ is shown and some people will then become distressed,” he said.
“It is likely that people who have pre-existing mental health problems will be especially at risk of becoming distressed or experiencing a deterioration in their mental health.
“My advice would be not to watch the event at all and I would hope that mainstream media would not transmit highly traumatic images [or] sounds,” Greenberg said.
Public executions were once common around the world, including in the UK, but only two out of 17 countries that carried out executions last year did so publicly.
No ‘regulation or precedent’ for military execution to be live-streamed, says death penalty expert
In a statement to the Guardian, Robin M. Maher, the executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said that her group is “not aware of any regulation or precedent for a military execution to be live streamed on the internet or otherwise made widely available to the public”.
She added that “public executions are typically held in authoritarian countries to instil fear in the population, and to show the power and control of the government.”
Donald Trump has yet to weigh in publicly on the move from the defense secretary to livestream Nidal Hasan’s execution. We’ll bring you the latest as soon as we hear.
The preside will begin his day in Washington, and we’ll hear from him at a White House event to celebrate Columbus day at 11am ET. Trump will travel to Syracuse, New York later to rally with Bruce Blakeman, the Republican nominee for New York governor.
Democratic incumbent Kathy Hochul is leading Blakeman by double digits in the polls, but Trump will also be there to drum up support for down ballot GOP nominees in competitive House races in the state.
Hasan set to be the first service member executed in more than 60 years
Nidal Hasan’s execution marks the first time a member of the military will receive the death penalty in more than 60 years.
According to the Death Penalty Information Center, the last military execution, in 1961, occurred by hanging, which is no longer used by any American jurisdiction, and was imposed for rape, which is no longer subject to the death penalty, following precedent set by the supreme court.
The 3 December scheduled death would also be the first time in history the military has live-streamed an execution, and it would also be the first time since 1945 that a member of the military has been executed by firing squad, per the Death Penalty Information Center.
While there has been bipartisan backlash to Pete Hegseth’s announcement that the Department of Defense plans to livestream Nidal Hasan’s execution in December – some hard-right Republicans have welcomed the news.
“Public execution is what this terrorist deserves,” saidAndy Ogles, a GOP congressman from Tennessee. “We will be watching.”
While there’s limited research about support for public executions, according to a recent Pew survey, 66% of Americans favor the death penalty for those convicted of murder. Digging into the numbers, there is also a partisan split too – with 51% of Democrats supporting the death penalty compared to 84% of Republicans.
However, only 39% of Americans said that capital punishment actually deters people from committing crimes.
According to rights group Amnesty International, at least 17 public executions are known to have been carried out in 2025 – six in Afghanistan and 11 in Iran.
The Death Penalty Information Center says that 135 soldiers have been executed by the US military since 1916.
“Secretary Hegseth’s comments may be simply aspirational,” the center said in a statement.
“There is currently no regulation or precedent for an execution to be live streamed on the internet or otherwise made widely available to the public.”
Amnesty International Australia has urged the country’s prime minister Anthony Albanese to press the US to reverse its decision over the Pentagon’s livestreamed execution plan.
“The suggestion that an execution by firing squad should be livestreamed for public viewing is an appalling disregard for human dignity,” said Kyinzom Dhongdue, a campaign manager at the rights group.
“Turning a state-sanctioned killing into a public spectacle only compounds the cruelty of the death penalty.“

Pentagon's 'disgusting' livestreamed execution plan provokes fierce backlash across political divide
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
The Pentagon’s plan to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, a former army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, has received fierce criticism from across the political spectrum.

U.S. Army seeks drone defense for its lightest units
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:55:39 UTC
20:55:39 KST

- The U.S. Army will hold an M-SHORAD Increment 4 industry day in Huntsville on Oct. 27-28 for a palletized, vehicle-agnostic air defense system.
- The system is to protect light and mobile units against Group 1-3 drones, helicopters and fixed-wing aircraft, with initial capability planned by late fiscal 2029.
The U.S. Army will brief defense companies in Huntsville, Alabama, on Oct. 27-28 about its plans for a new short-range air defense system built on a pallet that can be loaded onto almost any vehicle, giving light and fast-moving units their own protection against drones, helicopters and attack aircraft.
The industry day covers Maneuver-Short Range Air Defense Increment 4, or M-SHORAD Inc 4, and will be held at the Von Braun Center. The Army’s notice, posted Oct. 8, says the event is aimed mainly at companies that want to serve as the system integrator for development and production, though makers of sensors, weapons, turrets and command-and-control software are also invited. Companies must register by Oct. 23, and each is limited to three attendees.
According to the notice, M-SHORAD Inc 4 will be a self-contained, palletized system that is not tied to a specific vehicle. It is meant to protect the Army’s Joint Forcible Entry units, the airborne and air assault forces that seize ground first, and its new Mobile Brigade Combat Teams, which move on light vehicles, in both dismounted and mounted operations. The system is to defend against Group 1 to 3 drones, which range from small quadcopters up to aircraft weighing about 600 kg (1,320 pounds), as well as helicopters and fixed-wing aircraft.
The Army wants an open design so it can swap in different sensors, electronic warfare equipment and weapons as threats change. In a request for information published in March, the service described the system as a Self-Loading Equipment Dock, or SLED, or another pallet-based package that could be mounted on the Infantry Squad Vehicle or a robotic combat vehicle, and asked for solutions that could be delivered between fiscal 2027 and 2029.
Increment 4 is the lightest member of the M-SHORAD family. The first version, the Stryker-based M-SHORAD Increment 1, known as SGT Stout, carries Stinger and Hellfire missiles, a 30 mm cannon and a radar, and began reaching units in 2021. A laser-armed Increment 2 was canceled, and Increment 3 is set to upgrade the Stryker version with a new short-range interceptor and airburst 30 mm ammunition. The Army first asked industry for ideas on Increment 4 in May 2024, seeking air defense for dismounted troops that could fly on a C-130, be dropped by parachute and be slung under a helicopter.
Companies are already showing concepts. General Dynamics Land Systems will display its SLED-based Increment 4 system mounted on a Ford Ranger pickup at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington next week, the company said, in light, medium and heavy configurations.
The Army plans to reach initial operational capability with Increment 4 by late fiscal 2029, with the first units at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, and requested $108.1 million in fiscal 2027 research and development funding for the effort, according to the Congressional Research Service. The industry day agenda includes a program overview, a keynote speaker, a joint panel and one-on-one sessions with companies, but the Army has not said when a formal solicitation will follow.

Hurricane Isaias intensifies en route to US Gulf Coast

Hurricane Isaias intensifies en route to US Gulf Coast
October 9, 2026
Hurricane Isaias is expected to make landfall over the US Gulf Coast, the US National Hurricane Center (NHC) said on Friday. The storm's approach coud disrupt oil and gas production.
Isaias has been forecasted to cross the coast in either Florida, Alabama or Mississippi on Friday night or early Saturday.
Mandatory evacuation orders were issued for coastal areas in four counties in northeastern Florida, while states of emergency are in place in parts of neighboring Alabama and Georgia.
"Isaias will be a dangerous hurricane with significant storm surge, damaging winds, and flooding rains when it reaches the northern Gulf Coast," the NHC said.
The NHC urged residents that emergency preparations to protect lives and property from high winds and storm surges "should be rushed to completion."
First Atlantic hurricane this year
Isaias has strengthened to a Category 2 storm over the Gulf of Mexico, some 230 miles (370 kilometers) south of the Mississippi River delta, packing maximum sustained winds of 105 mph (165 kph).
The hurricane is the very first to develop in the Atlantic this season, which began June 1.
The remarkably quiet hurricane season was caused partly due to a strong El Nino weather phenomenon. It causes strong vertical wind shear — dry air and sinking air over the Atlantic Ocean —, hampering storm formation and intensification in the area.
US Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said federal authorities would coordinate response efforts with state and local governments.
"To everyone in the storm's path: ask that you also do your part to stand ready. Now is the time to prepare," Mullin said on X.
Storm impacts oil and gas production
The path of the storm covers some important industry points of oil and gas production in the Gulf of Mexico. As a result, platforms and rigs were already evacuated.
Some 63% of the oil production in the region has been temporarily suspended, taking nearly 1.3 million barrels a day off the market, according to the Marine Minerals Administration (MMA).
Similarly, some 57% of gas production has also been suspended, the MMA said.
Offshore production in the Gulf accounts for almost 15% of crude pumped annually in the US.
Hurricane Simon heads for Pacific
Meanwhile, the Pacific Ocean has been affected differently by the El Nino phenomenon.
El Nino's effect has left little vertical wind shear over the Pacific, creating favorable conditions for hurricanes to intensify. This has caused this year's Pacific hurricane season to be more severe than usual.
Hurricane Simon is currently moving toward Mexico's Pacific coast, with maximum sustained winds of 90 mph, the NHC said.
The storm has reached Category 1 and has been forecasted to reach Jalisco state, where the popular tourist resort of Puerto Vallarta is located, on Friday night or early Saturday, the NHC says.
"Rapid intensification is expected to continue, and Simon is expected to be a very dangerous major hurricane when it approaches the coast of Mexico," the NHC said.

Iran and Russia used ChatGPT for propaganda by ‘fake journalists’, OpenAI says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:53:51 UTC
20:53:51 KST

The American tech giant said it banned Russian and Iranian accounts that had been using ChatGPT models to generate content and fake journalist personas to spread false narratives about the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East and sow division.
OpenAI revealed on Thursday it had shut down two influence operations — from Russia and Iran — that used ChatGPT to push fake journalist personas and run a "think-tank" to covertly spread anti-Ukraine propaganda and foster division in the US and Israel over the war in Iran.
The report is the latest example of how state actors could exploit widely available AI tools to produce and disseminate sophisticated propaganda against adversaries on a mass scale.
The American AI giant said it banned a cluster of ChatGPT accounts that originated in Russia and Iran and were used to support false front entities for geopolitical and conflict-related messaging.
The Iranian operation involved seven fake journalist profiles, each claiming to be from Western countries, including the United States, that were used to plant long-form articles in media outlets around the world.
"We identified almost 100 articles published or syndicated under the operation's bylines across roughly a dozen online outlets around the world," OpenAI said.
"These were small to medium outlets, generally focused on international affairs, geopolitics, and events in the Middle East."
The earliest article identified by OpenAI was published in July 2025 and the latest in October 2026, with the frequency of reports increasing after the US-Iran war broke out earlier this year.
The operation also generated social media comments on topics related to the US-Iran war, it added.
One of the personas named Ervin B. Hoskins, whose bio claimed to be "an American freelance writer," had social media accounts across several tech platforms, including Elon Musk's X and Meta-owned Instagram.
X's transparency information showed the account was connected via a "West Asia android app" and Instagram's transparency information showed the account was based in Iran, according to screenshots provided by OpenAI.
Both accounts appeared to be suspended.
The Russian operation co-opted "unwitting people" in Latin America to run a think-tank called the Social Research Center (SRC). It was used for covert activities aimed at undermining Ukraine's reputation in the region and to influence local politics, the company said.
"The available evidence indicates that the SRC's employees in Latin America were not aware that they were working for a Russian group," OpenAI said.
"The SRC appears to have produced a majority of original content via its co-opted staff. This stands out as the most complex attempt to run a front identity that we've disrupted over the past two and a half years."
The operators used ChatGPT to write internal reports on their activities, create content for their operations and draft reports on the performance of the think tank, as well as to help design and create texts for publishing on social media as posts and comments.
Among the social media activity, say OpenAI, were reactions to Polish far-right MEP Grzegorz Braun proposing that people who showed “anti-Polishness” be declared persona non grata in Poland, in an attempt to sow divisions in Poland over the country’s support for Ukraine.

Putin offers help to end Iran war while Russia continues its own in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:53:33 UTC
20:53:33 KST

The Russian president met Pezeshkian in Turkmenistan and pledged to do “everything in our power” to end the ongoing war between the US and Iran, despite Russia not being among the official mediators.
Vladimir Putin pledged to do "everything in our power" to help end the war between Iran and the US on Thursday, positioning Russia as a would-be Middle East mediator while continuing his own full-scale invasion of Ukraine, now in its fifth year.
The Russian president made the remarks at a bilateral meeting with his Iranian counterpart Masoud Pezeshkian in Avazeh, on Turkmenistan's Caspian coast, praising Tehran for making what he called "genuine efforts" to resolve the war.
Pezeshkian said Iran and the US had exchanged proposals to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and that Tehran was reviewing and amending them before consolidating them through mediators. Despite ongoing US attacks, he said Iran would not leave the negotiating table.
"We are talking, but every time we negotiate with the United States, they attack again," Pezeshkian said. "Nevertheless, we will not abandon the negotiating table and dialogue."
He said the revisions, once finalised, would be put to mediators. "We are supposed to sit down through the existing mediators and consolidate them," he said.
It was the seventh meeting between the two presidents since Pezeshkian took office, following a phone call on 7 October — Putin's birthday — in which the pair discussed regional developments and the Iran-US negotiations.
The two previously met in person on 1 September on the sidelines of the Shanghai Co-operation Organisation summit in Bishkek.
Russia is not a mediator in the US-Iran negotiations. So far, Qatar and Pakistan have led the talks.
Ties further deepen
Military, diplomatic and economic relations between Iran and Russia have strengthened since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022.
The Iran war, which began with joint US-Israeli strikes on 28 February, has sparked more frequent consultations between Moscow and Tehran on political and material support and financial co-operation.
Since 2022, Iran has supplied Russia with Shahed drone technology — which Moscow has since copied to create its own Geran-type variant, a key tool in its daily attacks on Ukrainian civilian and infrastructure targets — and short-range missiles.
Moscow also faces accusations of providing Tehran with targeting information for attacks on US interests in the Middle East.
Trade between the two countries rose by more than 21% in 2025 and continued on the same trajectory through the first seven months of 2026, Putin said, adding that relations were developing under a comprehensive strategic partnership agreement signed early last year.
Pezeshkian described the current situation as an opportunity to deepen co-operation and said Tehran and Moscow should coordinate "with greater speed and strength."
Billion-dollar loan delayed
Iranian state-run media reported in the days before the meeting that Russia was ready to extend a $1 billion loan to Tehran, described as the first tranche of a $20 billion package agreed at a meeting between Supreme National Security Council secretary Ali Larijani and Putin.
The semi-official IRGC-affiliated Fars news agency said arrangements to disburse the sum were complete, but disagreements among Iranian authorities over how to spend the money prevented Tehran from providing the account number needed to complete the transfer.
Iran's Planning and Budget Organisation wants to use the funds to import cars and collect customs duties, the Oil Ministry wants them for oil equipment, and the Agriculture Ministry is seeking to allocate them to basic commodity imports, according to the same report.
The bilateral meeting took place on the eve of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) leaders' summit — a gathering of nine former Soviet republic heads focused on regional co-operation — and a separate Caspian Sea environmental conference, also held in Turkmenistan, bringing together the leaders of Iran, Russia, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan.

WATCH French student protests descend into chaos
French riot police have deployed tear gas and water cannon, as well as charging with batons against crowds of young protesters in central Paris.
Student demonstrations and labor union protests continued for a fifth week on Thursday over anger at underfunded schools, teacher shortages, and planned government spending cuts.
The unrest began in mid-September at a high school in Creteil, near Paris, where students protested unfilled teaching posts. The movement subsequently spread nationwide, with demands for smaller classes, improved school facilities, and more funding for public education. The demonstrations have also coincided with labor union rallies against proposed budget cuts aimed at reducing the deficit.
Videos circulating online show violent clashes between thousands of protesters and riot police in the French capital. Officers wielded batons and deployed water cannon and tear gas in an effort to break up the raging crowds of young people.

According to the Interior Ministry, 71,500 people took part in demonstrations across the country, including 24,500 in Paris. The CGT trade union, however, put the turnout at more than 130,000, nearly twice the official figure.

Protests are being fueled by the government’s proposed 2027 budget unveiled last week, which would increase education funding by €1.2 billion ($1.35 billion) while eliminating another 1,588 teaching posts. Education Minister Edouard Geffray has defended the planned cuts, citing a decline in student numbers.

Labor unions oppose the wider austerity plan, which calls for €43 billion in savings in 2027. A broader wave of protests across Europe has seen demonstrations on issues ranging from education funding and budget cuts to housing costs and living standards. Student protests have also occurred in Belgium, Italy and Greece, while tens of thousands rallied in Spain over housing affordability and evictions. Although they are not part of a coordinated Europe-wide movement, the protests reflect growing public discontent over government policies across the continent.

'Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell': Israel's foreign ministry slams Nobel Peace Prize for Navi Pillay
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:53:19 UTC
20:53:19 KST

- i24NEWS
- International
- 'Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell': Israel's foreign ministry slams Nobel Peace Prize for Navi Pillay
'Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell': Israel's foreign ministry slams Nobel Peace Prize for Navi Pillay
The South African jurist led a UN inquiry accusing Israel of 'genocide' in Gaza, allegations Israel rejected as a libel aimed at delegitimizing the Jewish state
South African jurist Navanethem “Navi” Pillay, who led a United Nations commission that accused Israel of committing “genocide” in Gaza, was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize on Friday. The Norwegian Nobel Committee recognized her “efforts to promote peace and international law.”
Her selection honored a figure whose allegations against Israel have drawn fierce criticism from Israeli officials, who accused her commission of promoting a genocide libel and using its international standing to delegitimize the Jewish state.
Israel’s Foreign Ministry sharply condemned the decision, accusing Pillay of promoting lies, hatred and blood libels against Israel. “If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a frontrunner,” the ministry said, describing her accusations as part of a politically motivated campaign to demonize the Jewish state.
The ministry called the prize “the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice,” rejecting Pillay’s genocide allegations as “the biggest lie of the 21st century.” Invoking Nazi propaganda minister Joseph Goebbels, it added: “Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell.”
In September 2025, the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry, headed bt Pillay, issued a report alleging that Israel had committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza. The panel accused senior Israeli leaders of inciting genocide and argued that Israeli military operations and government policies demonstrated an intent to destroy the Palestinian population in the territory.
Israel categorically rejected the findings. Its Foreign Ministry accused the commission of spreading a malicious narrative intended to demonize Israel, relying on selectively presented evidence and making allegations its own material could not substantiate. It called for the commission to be abolished.
President Isaac Herzog also rejected the report, saying it misrepresented his statements. He accused the commission of blaming Israel while whitewashing Hamas’s atrocities, as Israel sought to defend its citizens and secure the return of hostages abducted in the Hamas-led October 7 invasion that resulted in the worst massacre of Jews since the Holocaust.
The commission is an investigative body rather than a court, and its report was not a judicial ruling. Although established by the UN Human Rights Council, the panel operates independently and does not speak on behalf of the United Nations.
Questions about Pillay’s impartiality predated the Gaza war. In 2022, fellow commissioner Miloon Kothari drew condemnation from Israeli and U.S. officials after invoking a “Jewish lobby” in remarks about efforts to discredit the inquiry and questioning Israel’s UN membership. Pillay defended him, arguing that his comments had been taken out of context and misrepresented. Kothari subsequently apologized for the “Jewish lobby” remark.
Pillay served as UN high commissioner for human rights from 2008 to 2014. Her judicial career included positions at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the International Criminal Court. The Nobel committee cited her decades of work on international justice in explaining its decision.

Waterspout destroys school as extreme weather hits Italy
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:52:56 CEST
20:52:56 KST

A double waterspout destroyed a
school at Marsala in Italy as a wave of extreme weather swept
across the Bel Paese on Friday.
                                    
The waterspout in the Trapani area caused widespread damage and
injuries.
                                    
The double waterspout struck the area around the port of Marsala
and swept across parts of the Trapani region, causing damage to
buildings, vehicles, and crops.
                                    
In Marsala, a school was hit, and several people were injured.
                                    
In Petrosino, a car was struck and flung into a ravine; two
people were injured and taken to the hospital.
                                    
The vortices formed at sea and moved inland.
                                    
An orange weather alert is in effect today for Lazio and
Campania due to potential torrential rain.
                                    
Roads in the Cremona area are flooded following a violent
thunderstorm.
                                    
The Marsala school principal said the building had been
destroyed by the waterspout.
                                    
Staff and children are all safe, he added, since the emergency
response was prompt.
                                    
"A waterspout struck the Terrenove branch directly and
completely destroyed it. Fortunately, thanks to the actions
taken by the staff and myself, we sought a safer area inside the
building because it was impossible to go outside.
                                    
"Thankfully, there were no injuries to staff or, above all, to
the children—just a few scrapes. Emergency services arrived
promptly, despite road disruptions and cars being blown through
the air. All in all, things turned out well. The Lord helped
us," said principal Leonardo Gullotta regarding the Terrenove
district campus of the Alcide De Gasperi school in Marsala.
                                    
There were 273 children in the school when the waterspout passed
through.
                                    
"We are all following with great concern the unfolding events in
western Sicily, an area hard-hit by severe weather. My thoughts
go first and foremost to those injured by the tornado," stated
Gaetano Galvagno, President of the Sicilian Regional Assembly
(ARS).
                                    
"Clearly," he added, "all relevant institutional bodies—the
Sicilian Regional Assembly, the government, and local
authorities—must play their respective parts. While reaffirming
the solidarity of the entire Sicilian community with the
affected populations, it is also right to thank those who
immediately stepped in to provide aid and assistance to the
people of the Marsala area."
Following yesterday's heavy rains, another wave of severe
weather struck Naples and its province today.
                                    
A tree collapsed on Via Guantai Nuovi in the city center, right
in front of the INPS headquarters; the area has been cordoned
off with red tape. Flooding has occurred in various Naples
neighborhoods, particularly in Fuorigrotta and Bagnoli. Issues
have also been reported in the province: a supermarket wall
collapsed overnight in Pozzuoli, while a power outage affected
several neighborhoods in Marano.
                                    
On Ischia, firefighters have carried out thirteen interventions
to deal with flooding and landslides; roads are covered in mud
and debris, and a telecommunications blackout cut off the entire
island for over two hours.
                                    
The severe weather that has been affecting Ischia for more than
two days continues to cause significant disruption.
                                    
Last night, firefighters from the island's station responded to
over a dozen incidents caused by heavy rainfall—143 millimeters
in 30 hours—which triggered flooding and minor landslides across
various parts of the island.
                                    
In Panza, a hamlet within the municipality of Forio, a boundary
wall near the cemetery collapsed, spilling stones and landslide
debris onto the roadway.
                                    
The situation was further complicated by a communications
blackout that struck yesterday evening; around 7:45 PM,
internet, mobile phone, and landline services all failed
simultaneously.
                                    
The outage affected all six of the island's municipalities,
leaving thousands of people unable to make calls or access
online services for over two hours—thereby preventing emergency
calls to law enforcement, firefighters, and emergency medical
services (118).
                                    
The blackout occurred amidst a prolonged spell of bad weather
and in an area already severely scarred by landslides and
floods.
                                    
Services were restored around 10:15 PM.
                                    
Further north, a violent storm battered Castelleone, in the
province of Cremona, last night dumping nearly 100 millimeters
of rain in just a few hours, accompanied by hail and strong wind
gusts.
                                    
The storm resulted in flooded streets and basements—with water
levels reaching up to thirty centimeters—as well as issues in
the basement of the local nursing home, uprooted signs, and
trees falling onto parked cars; firefighters remained mobilized
until dawn.
                                    
Scientists say the climate crisis caused by human greenhouse gas
emissions is making extreme weather events such as heatwaves,
droughts, supercharged storms and flooding more frequent and
more intense.
                                    
Although there are many sources of the greenhouse gases that are
causing global heating, the main driver is the burning of fossil
fuels such as oil, gas and coal, sales of which generate huge
profits for the world's energy giants.

US decision to livestream execution would be torture, says UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:52:55 UTC
20:52:55 KST

The execution by firing squad of convicted military base shooter Nidal Hasan will be livestreamed, a Pentagon official said, drawing sharp condemnation of the plan to broadcast the killing.
Hasan's execution, set for Dec. 3, is poised to be the first that the U.S. military has carried out by firing squad since World War II.
"It will be livestreamed. Details will follow," the Pentagon official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told AFP of the death sentence imposed on the U.S. Army psychiatrist who shot dead 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009.
Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth said in a video posted on X by official Pentagon accounts on Oct. 8 that Hasan is "going to get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be, and we'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public."
The U.N. condemned on Oct. 9 the plan to livestream the execution, saying it would amount to torture.
"The livestreaming of an execution is tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture," the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights said in a message sent to AFP.
Democratic Senator Chris Murphy told CNN the plan was "disgusting."
"I understand that in this country we have the death penalty, but public executions [are] medieval," he said.
Hegseth noted that it would be the military's first firing squad execution since World War II, a reference to the case of Eddie Slovik, who was put to death for desertion in 1945.
The last U.S. military execution was carried out in 1961, when John Bennett was hanged for rape and attempted murder.

Iran’s presence in world’s top 2% of scientists nearly doubles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:52:14 UTC
20:52:14 KST

Iran’s presence in world’s top 2% of scientists nearly doubles
TEHRAN – The number of Iranian researchers included in the world’s top 2% of scientists has nearly doubled, rising from 1,154 in 2020 to 2,678 in 2026, according to Scopus data provided by Elsevier.
An analysis of the rankings shows a steady upward trend in the number of Iranian researchers recognized among the world’s top 2% of scientists over the past several years.
The number rose to 1,701 in 2021 and 1,941 in 2022, before increasing to 2,137 in 2023 and 2,514 in 2024. The figure reached 2,678 in 2026, ISNA reported.
The majority of Iranian researchers are from 30 universities and scientific centers; the University of Tehran, with 123 researchers, is placed first. Followed by Tehran University of Medical Sciences (112), Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences (75), and Iran University of Science and Technology (74).
Tabriz University of Medical Sciences with 66 researchers, Iran University of Medical Sciences with 64 researchers, University of Tabriz with 61 researchers, and Tarbiat Modares University with 56 researchers are placed fifth to eighth.
Also, the number of highly cited Iranian researchers in the career-long index has experienced threefold growth, rising from 433 in 2020 to 1,380 in 2026.
Some 794 out of 1,380 researchers, amounting to 57.5 percent, are from 30 universities and scientific centers. University of Tehran (with 91 researchers), Sharif University of Technology (53), Amirkabir University of Technology and Tehran University of Medical Sciences (each with 48 researchers), and Iran University of Science and Technology (45), University of Tabriz and Tarbiat Modares University (each with 40 researchers) rank first to fifth.
Stanford University’s list of “World’s Top 2%” scientists is based on a 2 percent or above percentile rank, or the top 100,000 by c-score (with and without self-citations). This prestigious list identifies the world’s leading researchers, representing approximately 2 percent of all scientists worldwide.
It encompasses standardised data on citations, h-index, and a wide range of bibliometric indicators. Researchers are classified into 22 scientific fields and 174 sub-fields, drawing from Scopus data provided by Elsevier through ICSR Lab.
The esteemed ranking, derived from Scopus database data, highlights researchers whose work has had a significant impact across various scientific disciplines.
The ranking is based on a composite indicator (c-score) calculated from six citation metrics: Total citations (NC), H-index (H), Hm-index (H-index adjusted for the number of authors), Citations to single-author papers (NCS), Citations to single or first-author papers (NCSF), Citations to single, first, or last-author papers (NCSFL).
The c-score combines these metrics to provide a comprehensive measure of a scientist’s impact, accounting for both the quantity and the quality of their contributions.
The list provides two separate rankings, each offering a different perspective on a researcher’s impact:
 
Career-long impact ranking: This evaluates a researcher’s cumulative citation performance over their entire career to date.
 
Single-year impact ranking: This focuses on the citation impact of research produced in the most recent year.
Iran ranks first in key scientific output among Islamic countries
Iran ranks first among Islamic nations in key fields of scientific output such as quantum science, cognitive sciences, artificial intelligence, biotechnology, and advanced materials, the head of the Presidential Affairs Office at the Islamic World Science Citation Center (ISC) announced in August.
The country is in close competition with Turkey and Saudi Arabia in these fields, IRNA quoted Saeed Bakhtiari as saying.
He made the remarks in a press briefing on August 17, noting that the development of science in these fields has also been emphasized in national development plans.
Based on the reputable Web of Science database, Iran ranks first among Islamic countries in scientific output in some of these fields, while placing second or third in others. Overall, however, Iran holds the top position, he said.
Bakhtiari noted that in advanced materials—a multidisciplinary field spanning physics, chemistry, mechanics and materials science—Iran ranks second among Islamic countries and ninth worldwide.
He added that Iran ranks third in artificial intelligence, behind Saudi Arabia and Turkey, while in quantum science it ranks second, after Saudi Arabia.
The ISC official further said that Iran holds the top position among Islamic countries in scientific output in cognitive sciences and ranks first overall.
According to Web of Science (WoS) data, over a five-year period (from 2021 to 2025), Iran (with 32 documents) ranks first in cognitive sciences among Islamic countries.
Turkey, with 23 documents, and Saudi Arabia, with 22 documents, are placed second and third, respectively, IRNA reported.
From 2014 to 2023, Iran ranked either first or second in most fields of cognitive sciences among Islamic countries. Over the course of the decade, the country ranked first in cognitive neuroscience, cognitive rehabilitation, and cognitive linguistics with 387, 156, and 30 documents, respectively.
It ranked second in cognitive psychology (124 documents), cognitive education (561 documents), philosophy of mind (34 documents), and cognitive evaluation (898 documents). The country’s best ranking globally was in cognitive neuroscience; it ranked 15.
Tehran University of Medical Sciences, with 73 documents, University of Tehran, with 39 documents, and Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences, with 32 documents, ranked first to third in cognitive neuroscience. In cognitive psychology, University of Tehran(10 documents ), Ferdowsi University of Mashhad (7 documents), and Allameh Tabatabai University (6 documents) were the top three universities.
In cognitive linguistics, University of Tehran (with 3 documents), Al-Zahra University (3 documents), Allameh Tabatabei University (2 documents ) ranked first to third. In cognitive education, Tehran University of Medical Sciences, Iran University of Medical Sciences, Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences were placed first to third, respectively.
In cognitive rehabilitation, Tehran University of Medical Sciences (21 documents), University of Tehran (16 documents), and Iran University of Medical Sciences (12 documents) ranked first to third. The best three universities in philosophy of mind were University of Tehran, Isfahan University, and Amirkabir University of Technology.
In cognitive evaluation, Tehran University of Medical Sciences ranked first with 196 documents. Iran University of Medical Sciences (105 documents) and Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences (91 documents) ranked second and third.
The country is placed second in quantum (with 216 documents) and advanced materials (with 5975 documents), after Saudi Arabia, with 283 and 6160 documents in quantum and advanced materials. Malaysia (with 154 documents) and Egypt (with 3151 documents) are placed third in quantum and advanced materials, respectively.
Despite illegal sanctions, Iran secures first place in cognitive sciences among Islamic nations and ranks ninth globally in advanced materials. Numerous prestigious Iranian universities and institutions are included in international rankings. These accomplishments underscore the country’s scientific capabilities, IRIB quoted Science Minister Hossein Simaei-Sarraf as saying, addressing the 7th Turkey Educational Technologies Summit (known as TETZ 2026), held in Istanbul from June 26 to 28.
Iran serves as a great opportunity to invest in higher education and modern technologies. The country has one of the largest higher education systems in the region, with more than three million students and over seventy thousand faculty members and researchers.
Highlighting that the rapid development of emerging technologies, including AI, is fundamentally transforming human relationships and higher education systems around the world at an unprecedented pace, Simaei-Sarraf said that effective use of smart technologies requires the establishment of a system based on algorithmic transparency, educational justice, accountability, protection of learners’ rights, and responsible data governance.

Pro-Kremlin Russian military blogger Mikhail Zvinchuk arrested in Montenegro
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:51:18 UTC
20:51:18 KST

A leading pro-Kremlin Russian military blogger with reported ties to Russia’s intelligence services has been arrested in Montenegro, after warnings of attempts to destabilise the Balkan country, officials have said.
Mikhail Zvinchuk, the founder of the influential Rybar war blog, was detained on Friday alongside his wife and three other Russians by police and security agents in the Adriatic resort town of Risan, on suspicion of spreading Russian influence, local media reported.
Montenegro’s prime minister, Milojko Spajić, confirmed Zvinchuk’s detention in a post on X, saying it followed warnings that the country would face attempts at destabilisation and hybrid warfare.
The Russian Telegram news channel Baza said officers detained Zvinchuk at the luxury Mövenpick hotel in Risan. It said the group was taken to Podgorica, Montenegro’s capital, for questioning and their phones and passports were confiscated.
Founded in 2018 by Zvinchuk, a former press officer at Russia’s defence ministry, Rybar is one of the most popular Russian military blogs covering the war in Ukraine, with more than 1.5 million subscribers on Telegram. It forms part of a sprawling online media ecosystem that promotes Vladimir Putin’s invasion of Ukraine.
But Rybar’s activities extend well beyond Ukraine, with the channel promoting pro-Kremlin narratives in Africa and the Middle East. More recently, it has been accused of amplifying far-right narratives surrounding the migration crisis in Ceuta, a Spanish enclave in north Africa.
“At the moment, the project team is in contact with Russia’s foreign ministry, which is working to resolve the situation. Since there were no violations of local legislation, we expect all detainees to be released,” the channel said on Telegram.
Britain sanctioned Zvinchuk and Rybar in December 2025 over their role in spreading Kremlin propaganda and undermining support for Ukraine. The British government said Zvinchuk received funding from the Russian state-owned defence conglomerate Rostec, and worked with members of Russia’s intelligence services.
The US has separately accused Zvinchuk of attempting to interfere in the 2024 presidential election, offering a reward of up to $10m for information about those involved.
Days before his arrest, Zvinchuk boasted on social media that he had managed to enter Montenegro despite being subject to western sanctions and an entry ban. He mocked a border guard who, he said, had searched his belongings but failed to check his name against a database.
The Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said Moscow was aware of Zvinchuk’s detention and would work to secure his release.
Russia’s former president Dmitry Medvedev suggested Moscow could detain European and American citizens to use in prisoner exchanges to secure Zvinchuk’s release. “We will probably have to replenish our pool of prisoners for exchange with European and American idiots in order to get our own people back,” he wrote on social media.
The arrest is likely to further strain relations between Montenegro and Russia, which have long been tense. In 2016, Montenegrin authorities accused Russian operatives of plotting with Serbian ultranationalists to stage a coup, allegations Moscow denied.
Montenegro, which joined Nato in 2017 and is seeking membership of the EU, imposed sanctions on Russia after its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The country recently approved plans to end visa-free travel for Russian citizens from 1 November, closing off a popular holiday destination for Russian tourists as it brings its visa policy into line with the EU.

China says it reaches ‘understanding’ with EU on hybrid cars
Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič has been seeking a pledge from Beijing to curb booming exports of Chinese plug-in hybrid electric vehicles to Europe.
The Chinese Commerce Ministry said on Friday it had reached an “understanding” with the EU on the export of hybrid electric vehicles.
The announcement came after Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič wrapped up two days of talks in Bejiing, the culmination of a monthslong push to narrow the bloc’s €1 billion-a-day trade deficit with China.
“Following intensive consultations, both sides have reached an understanding on the trade of hybrid vehicles in a manner consistent with World Trade Organization rules,” the Chinese statement read.
Advertisement
Cars had become the focus of the discussions in the run-up to the visit by Šefčovič as he sought an agreement that would avert the need for defensive measures to protect the European market.
Chinese car exports had been steadily ramping up, and in August accounted for one in eight cars sold in the bloc, mainly thanks to a boom in sales of hybrid electric vehicles. Europe’s own automotive industry, centered on Germany, has been in the doldrums, with automakers like Volkswagen and Mercedes-Benz announcing job cuts and plant closures.
A deal on cars would mark an important achievement for the Slovak commissioner, who also helped negotiate the EU’s Brexit agreement as well as the more recent Turnberry deal with Donald Trump’s White House.
Šefčovič was expected to brief reporters in Beijing shortly.
EU leaders will review the outcome of the trade talks when they meet in Brussels next Thursday.

Self-driving Razorback UGV carries drone-killing turret
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:50:11 UTC
20:50:11 KST

- Forterra and Hypercraft are showing the Razorback unmanned ground vehicle with AutoDrive autonomy and a 9 Mothers Edda counter-drone turret at AUSA.
- The companies say the vehicle targets contested logistics, but no customer, contract or test schedule has been announced.
Forterra and Hypercraft are showing a driverless off-road vehicle built for military resupply at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington, pairing Hypercraft’s Razorback unmanned ground vehicle with Forterra’s AutoDrive self-driving system and a counter-drone turret from 9 Mothers.
The companies say the vehicle is aimed at contested logistics, moving supplies through areas where a human driver would be under fire. Neither company has announced a military customer, contract or price for the combination.
“We’re going after contested logistics and other missions where a driver is the most exposed person on the battlefield,” Forterra Chief Growth Officer Scott Sanders told Tectonic. “Razorback and AutoDrive combine to deliver a platform that can go further, over more complicated terrain, and power platforms in ways that traditional UGVs cannot.”
Razorback is the first complete vehicle from Hypercraft, a company in Provo, Utah, that started out building electric powertrains for commercial vehicles before moving into defense. Hypercraft unveiled the vehicle earlier this year. It is more than 4 meters (13 feet) long and, according to the company, can carry up to 1,814 kg (4,000 pounds), drive about 800 km (500 miles) and supply up to 38 kilowatts of electricity to other equipment. Hypercraft designed it to take third-party sensors, radios, weapons and mission payloads, and it has already shown the vehicle with Fortem Technologies’ counter-drone radar.
Sanders said Razorback was designed for autonomy from the start, which made it an easy fit, since many unmanned ground vehicles are crewed trucks with self-driving kits added after production.
Forterra, formerly Robotic Research, does not build vehicles. Its AutoDrive package combines software, sensors and computers that can turn an existing vehicle into a driverless one. The company says AutoDrive has been integrated into more than 50 vehicle types, used on more than 1,100 missions and put under contract for more than 258 systems. Those include Polaris Ranger 1500 utility vehicles used in Ukraine, Oshkosh Joint Light Tactical Vehicles for the U.S. Marine Corps’ ROGUE-Fires anti-ship missile launcher and Ford F-250 pickups for the U.S. Army.
The vehicle at AUSA carries 9 Mothers’ Edda turret, a roughly 23 kg (50-pound) counter-drone system from Austin, Texas. Edda listens for the sound of small drone rotors, tracks the target with cameras and fires a shotgun at drones about 18 cm (7 inches) across at ranges of 10 to 100 meters (33 to 328 feet). In August, the U.S. Army tested the same turret on a Forterra-equipped, self-driving Ford F-250 during a live-fire exercise at Fort Bragg, North Carolina.
Forterra said it chooses partners that solve real operational problems, can scale to production and understand that autonomy reaches beyond software into the vehicle, sensors, computers, communications and operator.
“Get any of those wrong, and the system doesn’t get fielded,” Sanders said.
Forterra is also one of six companies the U.S. Army selected in August for its Infantry Last Tactical Mile prototype effort, which is testing robotic vehicles for front-line resupply and casualty evacuation, using its MESA vehicle built on a Polaris Ranger.

Shein outsells British rival Asos as UK revenue hits £2.58bn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:49:48 UTC
20:49:48 KST

Shein, the online fast-fashion retailer founded in China, increased sales in the UK by just over a quarter last year, overtaking its British rival Asos.
The company, whose global parent group listed on the Hong Kong stock exchange valued at just over $26bn (£19.6bn) last month, increased sales at its UK division by 26% to £2.58bn, according to accounts filed at Companies House.
Pre-tax profits rose 18% to £45.2m even as the number of people employed by the group in the UK, mostly in sales and marketing, rose to 113 from 91 a year before. The company paid £11.2m in current tax – understood to be mainly corporation tax – up from £9.6m a year before.
Shein said sales had been helped by a marketing partnership with the Wireless and Creamfields music festivals, a pop-up shop on London’s Oxford Street and Christmas gift events in Edinburgh, Manchester and Liverpool as well as London.
Asos’s sales were £2.47bn in the year to 31 August 2025 – although this figure includes revenues outside the UK, unlike Shein UK’s comparable statistic.
Shein’s strong trading figures are likely to increase pressure on the government to bring forward action to change the “de minimis” rule that has underpinned the rise of the fast-growing online specialists Shein and Temu.
Fears about China’s retailers and manufacturers dumping goods in the UK have grown since the US last year revoked its own de minimis exception for Chinese-made goods, crimping Shein’s expansion there.
The retailer’s model is based on shipping orders of cheap clothes from Chinese factories to homes so that each order is low enough in value to avoid import duties.
Under the US exemption, which was scrapped last year, parcels with a value of less than $800 (£600) shipped to individuals had been spared from import tax.
The EU is also phasing out its exemption on customs duties for low-value parcels. It began in July by replacing the €150 de minimis relief with a flat €3 customs duty.
The former UK chancellor Rachel Reeves said she would get rid of the UK’s rule, which allows overseas sellers to send goods valued at £135 or less direct to British shoppers without paying any customs duty, by 2028. However, major retail bosses have said the government should move sooner.
Investors’ concerns about global government regulatory changes meant Shein’s value was far lower when it listed on the stock market than had been expected several years ago.
It reached a valuation of $100bn in an April 2022 fundraising round, making it the third most valuable startup in the world, and then considered a £50bn ($66bn) float on the London Stock Exchange in 2024 before eventually launching in Hong Kong.
Shein, founded by the entrepreneur Chris Xu, runs most of its operations from China but sells all its goods outside the country. It moved its headquarters to Singapore at the start of 2022 and has recently begun manufacturing in other countries including Turkey and Brazil.
After forced labour concerns were raised, Shein said it had tightened its supplier policies, enforced through regular audits, with any child or forced labour violations becoming grounds for immediate termination of contract.
Last week, Shein reported a 67% fall in group quarterly profits to £173m in its first results since the float, blaming higher oil prices and freight rates linked to the war in Iran.

‘Nobody is listening to us’: on the school protest frontline, I heard why France’s students feel disowned | Alexander Hurst
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:48:58 UTC
20:48:58 KST

When adolescents protest that the government is failing to uphold their right to an education, and the government’s response is to send in riot police, the government has lost the plot. People outside France may have spent the past week watching the student protests in Paris and other cities, and thought, “Well, France has a long tradition of insurrection” or, “That’s just the French being French.”
But the situation that has provoked the high-school walkouts and teenage anger is most likely not one they would immediately associate with the France of their imaginations. In place of its lost plot, the French government has a collection of anecdotes and statistics that it should be ashamed of: 27th place in the most recent OECD education rankings, schools with ceilings collapsing and rats in classrooms and, in a school in Bagnolet, no drinkable water; an increase in the average number of students per class from 27 in 2010 to over 30 today; half of primary and high schools missing teachers at the start of the school year – many of them with no substitutes or replacements.
Julie, a 34-year-old teacher who joined the demonstrations, told me that staff shortages were the fault of “low salaries and poor treatment.” She has to commute for an hour and 45 minutes each way between Paris and the school on the city’s outskirts where she accepted a post last year after switching careers. All for €2100 (£1,780) a month, plus some overtime pay. Teachers’ salaries in France are only 56% of what they are in Germany – even as over €200bn in public subsidies finds its way annually to businesses.
So it could easily have been a teacher-led revolt – instead, the high-schoolers themselves cracked first.
They paid a high price for refusing to accept a failing education system: a 16-year-old has lost the use of an eye, a 15-year-old has lost a hand, a 14-year-old has a broken jaw – all from police munitions. Hundreds more have been injured in some way. In total, 4,400 people, the vast majority minors, have been arrested in a little over a week, almost half the number of arrests made during the months of gilets jaunes chaos. It might be incoherent that protesting students shoot fireworks at high school buildings, while at the same time denouncing the poor facilities they have to study in. But the far greater incoherence belongs to a government that has disinvested in its youth, and has chosen to answer bin fires with police charges.
“Sure some people were burning trash cans,” Fatoumata Sylla Wague, a 17-year-old in her final year at the Lycée Paul Éluard in Seine-Saint-Denis, where pupils were among the first to set up blockades outside their campus, told me. “But trash cans can’t feel anything.” She and her fellow students, on the other hand, certainly felt the teargas that the police launched in response.
Despite “unlivable” temperatures in the school buildings, extreme heat and extreme cold, walls covered in mould, electricity cuts and often not enough tables or chairs for everyone, Fatoumata would rather have been in class than out braving the riot police. But she wants to teach history some day and felt compelled, in a moment in history, comparable to May 1968, to take part. “If I’m fighting for our rights today, it’s because I really want to teach, but in good conditions. And so this is for the next generation of students and teachers.”
I can’t imagine how hard it must be to be a teenager in general today. In 2021 The Lancet found that 75% of French 16-25-year-olds exhibited signs of eco-anxiety, telling researchers they were “frightened” about the future. In France and beyond, students and young workers actively dislike AI and feel pessimistic about the future it portends. As for Fatoumata, she worries about the rise of far-right political movements, both in France and elsewhere.
For years, successive French governments have dealt with problems in some of France’s most troubled urban areas by unleashing heavy-handed policing that all too frequently targets young people with random checks that can be personally degrading. Centralised policymaking has also produced a national education system that often sends its least experienced teachers to these same areas, while granting more senior teachers priority in requesting transfers to other, less difficult, schools.
A future far-right government, the kind Fatoumata says she worries about, would almost certainly ramp up these kinds of tensions. Already, in response to the protests, rightwing politicians have called for harsher sentences and more law and order. But this is not a problem that will be solved with more police and more batons, any more than it already has been.
Because none of it signals a government that truly wants to listen – it signals that society at large does not really claim these places, or these teenagers, as its own. On n’est pas mal éduqué, on n’est pas écouté (“We’re not poorly educated, we’re just not being listened to”), read one sign I saw brandished at Paris’s Place de la République on Tuesday.
Responding to the crisis is going to require some tangible acts, such as upgrading dilapidated facilities. Arnaud Richards, 50, head of student services at Iqbal Masih middle school in Saint-Denis, offered me the example of how thoughtful architecture can have more impact than one might expect. The technical high school he previously worked in – Gabriel Péri, in an extremely poor area – reopened in 2022 after a total reconstruction, which, according to Richards, led to a calmer climate for both students and teachers. “Having the school itself be a beautiful place made the community feel more respected,” he told me. That in turn “created a calmer environment” for both students and staff.
But a real answer doesn’t stop with better facilities. Showing up to cut ribbons on new construction, or renovations, isn’t enough. During Emmanuel Macron’s decade in power, his government has, on any number of issues, successively failed to listen in a way that makes people feel deeply seen and heard.
As Fatoumata said: “Honestly, I don’t think the government cares, they just want to shut us up with false promises. We know nothing will change, because the government doesn’t listen to us.” Of all the things going wrong for France at the moment, this underlying lack of a feeling of “togetherness”, the feeling that nobody is really listening, is going to be the most difficult to deal with.
- Alexander Hurst writes for Guardian Europe from Paris. His memoir Generation Desperation is out now
