Best Battery-Powered Leaf Blowers (2026): Tested for Power, Battery Life, and Noise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:10:00 UTC
19:10:00 KST

Leaves are a problem of addition by subtraction: Just a couple of mature trees can drop enough debris that you need to remove, and in the process, consume hours of your weekends. Mowing leaves into mulch is a compelling option, but you’ll still need to wrangle them off driveways, walkways, flower beds, and patios. Gas blowers have long been the standard, but rising noise bans, finicky engines that are hard to start, and battery advances are cutting into their appeal.
If you’re on the fence about a leaf blower, know that owning one of any kind will reduce the amount of raking you do, but rarely eliminate it. For small yards, or if you (or your neighbor) have just one medium-sized deciduous tree, a rake and a tarp may be all you need. On the other hand, if you live in an arboretum, the long runtime of a gas backpack blower may be worth the maintenance headaches—unless you’re willing to invest heavily in multiple batteries.
I’ve tested the newest crop of battery-powered blowers on everything from heavy fabric leaves to gravel, mulch, and even knocking over a concrete paver. Today’s models deliver serious clearing power without the gas-can hassle, though runtime is always the primary trade-off. Here’s everything you need to know about battery-powered blowers.
Featured
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
Best Overall
When factoring in overall performance along with the quality and diversity of Ego’s outdoor tool ecosystem, this blower is the best option for most users. In testing, it delivered gaslike power, easily knocking over a 5-pound brick paver on high speed where lesser machines required turbo mode, and it cleared the test patch of leaves without issue, without relying on turbo. Even with all that power, it was the second-quietest machine on turbo, registering about 89.7 decibels at an arm’s-length distance of 30 inches—though Ego still suggests hearing protection.
A bright, 1.75-inch LCD serves as the tool’s dashboard and is easy to read even in direct sunlight, though some details, like confirmation that a battery is installed, add clutter without much information. The electronic cruise control is intuitive: squeeze the variable-speed trigger to your desired speed, press the speed lock button, then release the trigger. The blower maintains that pace until you press the speed lock button again.
Ergonomically, the blower’s relatively narrow frame keeps the tool comfortable and tight to your body during operation, and the unit naturally pitches the nozzle towards the floor. A plastic grid covering the air intake and battery location helps prevent stray leaves from clogging the vents. The included fan nozzle widens the airflow for clearing hardscapes, though on a lawn, it can scatter leaves rather than help corral them. The tool sits securely on a wide base so it doesn’t tip very easily, and has a stubby, 4.5-inch-long nozzle beneath the blower tube that works for drying a car or a grill.
Ego's was nearly the most expensive blower we tested, and its 56-volt battery powers a capable range of outdoor power equipment, from lawn mowers to string trimmers and chainsaws, making it a good choice for outfitting your garage or shed. The manufacturer has also branched into lifestyle gear, including portable power stations that run on its tool batteries, fans, wet-dry vacuums, and even a fun-looking mini bike. The downside of this leaf blower is runtime, which Ego attempts to offset by packaging the kit with two 4 amp-hour batteries. It had the shortest runtime of the tested models, a direct trade-off for its high performance. The thinking is that you can charge one battery while using the other, which may work for most users since few people blow continuously for 11 minutes.
Best Budget
The Skil checks two important boxes for a battery-powered leaf blower: It was the least expensive model we tested and tied for the longest runtime, at just over 33 minutes on high. Skil, a sister company to Ego, couldn’t match our top pick’s power—it would only knock over the brick on turbo and took a bit longer to push a brick-topped tarp—but it’s capable for most common leaf-blowing jobs. It was also the quietest blower in our test, registering 78.6 decibels on high, though Skil still recommends hearing protection.
The trigger system is as simple as it gets: Pull the variable-speed trigger, or rotate the dial with your thumb to set cruise control for longer sessions. Like most blowers, a separate button engages boost mode. The air intake is covered on all four sides by a black plastic grid that didn’t clog with leaves during testing, though if one gets sucked in it should be easy to pull off. This compact blower measures just under 36 inches long and is one of the few models that can stand upright when the battery is attached, which could help with storage.
Like the Ego, it has a short tube built into the housing, which is handy when you need high-volume airflow in a tight space. The secondary handle, while not very useful for clearing the lawn, makes the tool easier to rotate, position, and hold at awkward angles for jobs like clearing gutters, directing airflow around a vehicle for pushing water or snow, or clearing a workbench.
The Skil’s impressive runtime is partly due to the 6-amp-hour battery it comes with, though the blower is also available with a slightly less capable 4-amp-hour battery for about $20 less. That 40-volt battery can power a range of core lawn and garden tools, including mowers, trimmers, and chainsaws, and the system has earned a solid reputation for performance and runtime. Skil doesn’t yet have much in the lifestyle department—it does have a handy inverter which helps get more use out of the battery between weekends, but doesn’t offer the range of battery amp-hours Ego does.
Best Mix of Power and Runtime
At the intersection of power and endurance, the Husqvarna 350iB feels as capable as the Ego but offers roughly three times the runtime. This well-designed, capable tool costs as much as our winner, but delivers somewhat less value: It comes with only one battery, powers a smaller lineup of tools, and carries a three-year warranty instead of Ego’s five. In testing, it cleared our test patch of leaves with ease and, in turbo mode, knocked over the paver. It’s also relatively quiet at both high and turbo speeds, and recharges quickly in just under an hour and a half.
The 350iB’s high power is plenty strong for all but the most stubborn jobs. The tool is well-balanced, keeping the tube pitched slightly downward when walking. Thoughtful design details include punchy springs that help eject the battery, rubbery feet to protect the surface you set it on, and a second nozzle with a stiff plastic scraper that helps dislodge wet, matted leaves from a patio. The controls rely on graphics rather than words, but the buttons are intuitive to decipher.
If you’re new to outdoor power equipment and expect to build a system out to cover the basics, Husqvarna is a good choice to handle core lawn and garden tasks like lawn mowing, string trimming, and cutting wood with a chainsaw. The system doesn’t offer the variety of lifestyle tools that Ego or Ryobi do, however, and Husqvarna’s tools tend to cost more than comparable models. But for homeowners who prioritize power and runtime, the 350iB makes a strong case for the Husqvarna system. The higher price and shorter warranty are the main trade-offs.
Best System
The Ryobi has an excellent mix of power and balance, plus a rubbery nozzle tip that makes it easy to pry debris off the ground. But price-wise, it sits between better-performing models and our favorite budget pick. The blower’s power and ease of use are hampered by a scant 12-minute runtime, despite having the largest amp-hour battery in the test. That short runtime, combined with the long recharge time, makes it less practical for larger cleanup jobs, unless you have a second battery.
The Ryobi measured under 85 decibels on high. The rear intake is lined with foam that helps tame the noise. There’s no boost or turbo button here, so you pick between two cruise control settings for max power or max runtime, or squeeze the variable speed trigger. It’s a capable blower, but its biggest advantage is the 40-volt system behind it: Ryobi offers one of the widest ranges of tools that use the same battery, making the platform, rather than any single tool’s performance, its strongest selling point.
Like nearly every outdoor power equipment manufacturer, Ryobi uses the same battery across a range of push mowers, string trimmers, and chainsaws. But the company also offers useful niche tools, including a leaf vacuum mulcher, handheld power washer, and log splitter. The same battery can power heavier-duty equipment, too, including a two-stage snow blower, rear-tine tiller, and auger. For someone planning to build out a broad outdoor power equipment collection, that range is a significant advantage.
Others Tested
Greenworks 80V Electric Leaf Blower for $190: This was a powerful blower with about 15 minutes of runtime on high, which was longer than our favorite model. It also stayed well below 90 decibels, even in turbo mode. The blower is very narrow and comfortable to hold, and has a 4-year warranty on the battery, which was the longest in our test. Sometimes the tool is on sale for less than $200 as a kit, which is a good value for the power, and a recharge time of about 40 minutes. On sale, it’s about the same as our budget pick, which felt as powerful and had a longer runtime.
FAQs
What to Look for (and What to Skip) in a Leaf Blower
Here’s what I’d focus on when buying a blower for leaf cleanup:
Volts: In the cordless power-tool arms race, leaf blower batteries range from 18 to 80 volts. Some of that difference is marketing trickery: an advertised 20-volt max battery or tool delivers essentially the same power as an 18-volt model, and the same goes for 36- and 40-volt options. But, unless you’re a minimalist who wants one battery to power everything from a drill/driver to lawn and garden gear, you’ll probably be happier with a leaf blower that uses at least a 36-volt battery. A few capable 18-volt blowers use two batteries—either simultaneously to mimic the power of a 36-volt tool or in succession to increase the runtime—but they tend to cost more and only make sense if you already own the batteries. For smaller jobs, though, a standard, single-battery 18- or 20-volt blower may be all you need to clear a patio, clean out the garage or shed, or dry a car.
Amps: Volts get most of the marketing attention on the box, but a battery’s amp-hour rating tells you more about how long a blower runs. Think of voltage as the car’s engine and amp-hours as the size of the gas tank—you want to know both. Batteries with higher amp-hour ratings cost more than otherwise-similar battery voltages, and they tend to be heavier. For leaf blowers, manufacturers typically pair kits with batteries rated from 4 to 8 amp-hours. You can buy higher-capacity batteries separately, and it pays to know the range of options a manufacturer has. A battery with a higher amp-hour typically takes longer to charge.
Systems: Underestimating the range of tools a battery can power in pursuit of “the best” is, in my opinion, a mistake. Often, the difference between two top-performing tools is negligible, and with cordless power tools, that difference often comes down to runtime, which you can address with a higher-capacity battery. If your garage is already stocked with one brand’s outdoor power equipment (OPE), it makes sense to stay within that platform and buy the blower as a bare tool, leveraging the batteries you already have. Switching brands just to buy “the best” probably isn’t worth it to introduce a whole new battery and charger.
If you’re new to OPE—and a leaf blower is a common first purchase—the breadth of tools that share the battery matters. Some manufacturers stick to the lawn and garden basics, so one battery can power a blower, mower, string trimmer, and hedge trimmer, while others offer a much wider range of tools, from log splitters to snow blowers, and even some handy lifestyle products like portable power stations. Before buying, consider what else you can power with the battery that comes with your leaf blower because, chances are, lording over leaves won’t be your only lawn and garden chore.
Traditional 18-volt power tool manufacturers—the ones who make drill/drivers and circular saws—all offer leaf blowers and the simplicity of a one-battery platform, but they’re not powerful enough to replace a gas unit. Ryobi, for example, uses 18-volt batteries across its traditional power tools, and some outdoor equipment, but its most capable gas alternative options run on 40-volt batteries.
Detent clasp: Blowers have two or more connection points: where the tube meets the housing and where the nozzle attaches to the tube. Look for models with a detent at those junctions—a small, often brightly colored spring-loaded clip that snaps into place with a satisfying click when the parts connect. I find these connections hold more securely and last longer than simple friction-fit attachments.
Stubby nozzle: Recently, blowers aimed at car detailers, with short tubes and sometimes a pistol grip, have become popular. Manufacturers responded by adding a stubby, 3- to 6-inch tube that the main blower attachment slides over. When you remove the longer tube, this short one works to direct the volume of air with an overall shorter tool length that’s easier to use around cars or in tight spots (the blower’s nozzle doesn’t fit on this stubby tube, though, so you lose some velocity).
What I’d Worry Less About:
Weight: Across the board, regardless of voltage, a good battery-powered blower will weigh about 10.5 pounds with the battery attached. If you need a lighter option, look for an 18-volt powered blower. Some have better balance than others, meaning that when you hold them without squeezing the trigger, as you would while walking around, the tool stays mostly level or the nozzle end tips down a bit. These models will cause less fatigue than one that forces you to rotate the nozzle upward. With the former, you only need to make a slight horizontal twisting motion to spread the stream of air. Most modern leaf blowers also draw air in a straight line through the rear of the tool, unlike gas-powered models with intakes mounted to the left or right of the engine. Those offset intakes can create a twisting motion that increases hand fatigue and may even suck in your pant leg.
CFM, MPH, and Newton: This sounds counterintuitive, considering how much marketing goes into boasting about a leaf blower’s cubic feet per minute (CFM) and MPH, but these figures are a guide, not necessarily the only reason to buy a specific model. A blower needs both to be useful: CFM tells you how much air it moves, while MPH tells you how fast that air is moving. But there’s no universally adopted testing method for these specifications when it comes to battery-powered blowers (ANSI/OPEI B175.2, the standard test on the books, applies only to internal combustion engines). That means brands can test their units differently — for example, measuring MPH where the motor meets the tube rather than at the end of the blower tube, which gives you a better sense of the airspeed you’ll actually get in use. Some CFM numbers are also measured with the unit running in its max, boost, or turbo setting, rather than on high speed.
Newtons, a unit of force, is a rating that’s appearing more frequently on the spec sheets of higher-voltage, battery-powered leaf blowers and is the best apples-to-apples comparison of blowing power. However, because there’s no testing code for battery-powered leaf blowers, reporting newtons is optional and, like CFM and MPH, consumers have no way of knowing whether the test is standardized. Generally speaking, a good midrange blower will produce around 20 newtons, while models that produce more are typically higher-performing units. Treat newtons as a guide rather than a definitive specification while buying.
Wide nozzles: Some blowers come with a wide-tip nozzle, which can be useful for clearing paved surfaces like patios and driveways or blowing water off flat surfaces. But in practice, it’s not enough of a game changer to be a deciding factor. The narrower nozzle is typically what you’ll use, and you can twist your hand back and forth to create a wider pattern when needed.
How Noisy Are Battery-Powered Leaf Blowers?
When tested from 30 inches away to approximate the noise you’d hear at arm’s length, the blowers ranged from 78.6 decibels on high to 95.2 decibels on turbo. Most user manuals recommend wearing hearing protection when using these tools, particularly for extended periods. By comparison, a handheld gas blower might produce 100 to 110 decibels. That might not sound like a lot more noise, but generally, a 10-decibel increase is perceived by the ear as roughly twice as loud.
Much of the noise reduction comes from eliminating the idling gas engine. Your neighbors will thank you for going battery-powered, too: In open air, sound typically drops by about 6 decibels each time you double your distance from the source. That means your neighbor across the street might hear your battery-powered blower at roughly the same volume as standing next to a washing machine.
What Else Are Battery-Powered Leaf Blowers Good For?
Besides clearing leaves and grass clippings, these fume-free tools are handy for all sorts of jobs. Use one to dry wet surfaces after rain or washing, including your car, patio furniture, or deck. In winter, a blower can remove a light dusting of snow from your car, making it easier to clear areas like the roof. With a cautious trigger finger, you can also clear dry leaves from gutters—just avoid wet, matted debris, which will only turn into a mess below. When grilling or firing up a pizza oven or outdoor fire pit, a gentle stream of air from a safe distance can help get the flames going. Indoors, a blower can clear dust from baseboard heating assemblies or remove lint from your dryer vent.
How I Tested Battery-Powered Leaf Blowers
I put each blower through a series of tests to gauge power, runtime, noise, and ease of use. I spread about 8,800 3x3-inch polyester crafting leaves—nearly 4 pounds’ worth—over a measured 6-by-6-foot area and used each blower to clear the section, noting which models could do the job on high and which required a boost or turbo mode. To test blowing power, I placed a 5-pound concrete paver a fixed distance from the nozzle and recorded which machines could knock it over on high and which needed turbo.
For runtime, I fully charged each battery, ran the blower at its highest standard speed, excluding any turbo or max settings, and timed how long it lasted. I measured noise with a smartphone decibel-meter app held 30 inches from the air intake while each blower ran on high and at any available turbo or max setting. I also performed practical tests to see how well each model moved gravel and wood chips and cleared water from surfaces such as a grill and patio furniture.

Candidate for Latvia’s State Chancellery director has only sports-related experience in public institutions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:09:46 UTC
19:09:46 KST

Kaspars Gorkšs, who has been nominated for the position of Director of Latvia’s State Chancellery, has previously gained experience in state or municipal institutions only in the field of sports, according to information provided by the State Chancellery to LETA about his professional background.
A second competition for the position of State Chancellery Director was announced on the 7th of August this year. One of the requirements was that candidates have experience working in state and/or municipal institutions.
Gorkšs currently works at the Employers’ Confederation of Latvia (LDDK), where he has served as Director General since the 3rd of April, 2023. At the same time, he has also been Director of the Jūrmala Football School since the 9th of November, 2020.
Previously, from March 2021 to October 2023, he was a board member of the Latvian Sports Federations Council. For three years, from March 2020 to March 2023, he served as Executive Director of the Latvian Association of Team Sports.
From March 2018 to October 2019, Gorkšs was President of the Latvian Football Federation.
According to information provided by the State Chancellery, Gorkšs also has teaching experience, having delivered lectures in the University of Latvia’s Sports Law course from September 2023 to August 2024.
Gorkšs studied at the University of Latvia, where he obtained a bachelor’s degree in law and a master’s degree in political science.
As previously reported, following the final round of the selection process, Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs (United List) will submit the candidacy of LDDK Director General Kaspars Gorkšs for government approval as Director of the State Chancellery.
The government is scheduled to consider his appointment at its meeting on the 13th of October.
Kulbergs explained that he expects the State Chancellery to become a strong, data-driven centre of government that helps decisions be made more quickly and accurately.
“I believe Gorkšs has the appropriate experience to implement the changes I have outlined for the State Chancellery. All three finalists are strong leaders with experience both within and outside public administration, and I thank each of them for participating in the competition,” Kulbergs said.
Of the nine candidates who reached the second round, the evaluation committee selected three for the final stage: former Director General of the State Revenue Service and current sectoral attaché at the Central Finance and Contracting Agency Ieva Jaunzeme, Director of the Latvian School of Public Administration Agita Kalviņa, and Gorkšs.
During the third round, candidates were assessed on their management competencies, including strategic vision, decision-making and willingness to take responsibility,
 results orientation, change management and team leadership.
The selection process for the State Chancellery Director took place in three stages.
After evaluating 18 applications, nine candidates advanced to the second round, while three reached the final stage.
In accordance with the competition procedure, the candidate evaluation committee made a decision on the results of the third round and informed the prime minister.
As previously reported, former State Chancellery Director Raivis Kronbergs was detained in May in the so-called timber industry case.
He was initially suspended from his position, but the parties later agreed that Kronbergs would leave the post.
The State Chancellery serves as the centre of Latvia’s government. Its task is to ensure the functioning of the government and provide the prime minister and Cabinet with information based on data and research.
This includes conducting data analysis, assessing different policy scenarios and involving experts from various fields to support more accurate, evidence-based decision-making.
The State Chancellery is headed by its director, who is the country’s highest-ranking civil servant.
Since September 2015, the State Chancellery has been responsible for the centralised selection of heads of state institutions within Latvia’s direct public administration.

Bipartisan majority of Americans blame Trump policies for rising costs, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:09:41 UTC
19:09:41 KST

Bipartisan majority of Americans blame Trump policies for rising costs, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
WASHINGTON, Oct 9 - Some 78% of Americans blame President Donald Trump's policies for rising prices that are outpacing their earnings, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll that found majorities of Republicans and Democrats citing the cost of living as their top concern ahead of next month's midterm elections.
Fifty-seven percent of Trump's Republicans said that costs have been growing faster than their paychecks, a stark example of how his pursuit of import tariffs, war with Iran and other policies have clashed with a central 2024 campaign promise to kill inflation and lower prices "on day one."
Inflation instead has increased, to the point where the US Federal Reserve has pivoted to rate hikes to quell price increases policymakers have attributed to a variety of factors, including rising global energy costs following the start of the Iran war, and the administration's imposition of aggressive import taxes.
Concerns about the economy and the war have driven Trump's public approval to record lows and have been weighing on support for his party ahead of the November 3 election that will determine control of Congress for the next two years.
About one in four Republicans disapproved of Trump's handling of the economy, a view shared by 63% of independents and 92% of Democrats. Disapproval was even sharper when it came to inflation, with 68% of all respondents and 40% of Republicans dissatisfied.
Jeffrey Talley, 65, a retired bank examiner from Mission Hills, Kansas, is a registered Republican, who said he voted for Trump in 2016 but not in 2020 or 2024 and now plans to vote for Democrat Adam Hamilton in what has become an unexpectedly competitive Senate race in the state.
"I'm pretty much against all the nonsense that's going on in the Middle East with the Iran war, and pushing up the price of gasoline ... that's been very disheartening," said Talley. He views the election as a chance to elect "somebody to put a check and balance on the craziness that's going on in the White House."
The six-day Reuters/Ipsos poll, conducted online and nationwide and completed on Monday, gathered responses from 4,506 US adults. It had a margin of error of 2 percentage points for Americans in general and 3 points for Republicans, Democrats and independents.
'EVERYTHING HAS GONE UP'
The national average price of a gallon of gasoline was $4.36 on Thursday compared with $3.11 a year ago, while diesel fuel prices stood at $6.28 after a record run-up perhaps felt deepest in farm states including Kansas.
Another Kansan, 41-year-old Athena Barrett of Kansas City, said Trump's performance had motivated her to register to vote because "I don't really like what the president is doing."
"Gas prices ... food prices, the cost of living -- everything has gone up; what's going on with Iran, and all the stuff with immigration," said Barrett, who is Hispanic.
Hispanic voters supported Trump in large numbers in 2024, but polls have shown support eroding.
White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said Trump had ended the "inflation crisis" of his predecessor in office, Democrat Joe Biden, by boosting the economy with tax cuts and lowering the costs of prescription drugs. "The president has delivered tangible wins for American families," Rogers said by email.
Inflation spiked to a 40-year high during Biden's term and played an important role in Trump's 2024 election victory.
Its persistence, albeit off the highs of the COVID pandemic, has meant higher daily prices for things like gas, ground beef and airline tickets as well as higher interest rates. The 30-year home mortgage is now at 7.5%, double what homebuyers were used to just six years ago.
Poll respondents cited the cost of living as a top issue in their decisions on how to vote, with 54% of respondents, including 40% of Republicans, saying they felt it had increased a lot in the last year, compared with 30% who said it was up only a little and 10% who said it was unchanged.
Some 78% of the respondents - including 64% of Republicans and 76% of independents - said some blame lies with the White House, with most Americans viewing tariffs as an important cause of higher prices.
LITTLE HIT TO SPENDING
The poll provided only limited indications of people cutting back on spending. Some 63% of respondents said they were eating out at restaurants less often, and 56% said they were spending less on entertainment or streaming services.
Smaller shares said they were driving less or falling behind on bills.
Economic data does show Americans in general still making modest gains in their income, even after accounting for taxes and rising prices. Overall hourly wage gains are growing roughly in line with the consumer price index, meaning much of any growth in pay is eaten up in higher prices, the type of treading water that can sour attitudes about the state of the economy.
Surveys of consumer confidence by both the Conference Board and the New York Federal Reserve have reflected a dim outlook.
Some of Trump's policies still resonate: 45% of respondents said unauthorized immigration was a root cause of higher prices, echoing the argument made by the administration that people in the country illegally create extra demand for things like housing, pushing up costs.
Herman Sims, 67, of Dallas, has voted Republican since 2012, and plans to continue doing so in a close Senate race between Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico even though he works for a trucking company hit hard by high diesel prices.
While he said he disagreed with Trump's decision to go to war with Iran, he would not vote for a Democrat: "What I've seen with the Democratic Party is they care more about themselves and will tell you anything, but they're more about spending." REUTERS

Montenegro Detains Founder of Russian Pro-War Channel Rybar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:05:36 UTC
19:05:36 KST

Authorities in Montenegro have arrested Mikhail Zvinchuk, the founder of the influential pro-war Russian Telegram channel Rybar, in an operation targeting suspected Russian influence activities, officials confirmed Friday.
The U.S. State Department is offering up to $10 million for information leading to the identification or location of Zvinchuk, a former Russian Defense Ministry press officer, and other Rybar staff over their alleged involvement in election interference and malign influence operations.
Montenegro’s police and National Security Agency (ANB) carried out the operation targeting “hybrid activities” by Russian information networks, security sources told the news outlet Vijesti.
Those detained include Zvinchuk’s wife, Rybar creative director Valeria Zvinchuk and with three associates, the outlet reported.
Montenegro’s Prime Minister Milojko Spajić, whose government is seeking to bring Montenegro into the European Union by 2028, confirmed Zvinchuk’s detention.
“Montenegro is protecting its interests and no one will endanger our European future,” Spajić wrote on X.
Intelligence agencies had monitored the group for several days after its arrival in Montenegro to film material about the Balkan country’s alignment with EU visa policies, the Russian news outlet Readovka reported.
Authorities suspected the material was intended to undermine Montenegro’s tourism industry, economy and national interests, according to the report.
Unconfirmed reporting by the Russian Telegram news channel Baza claimed that officers detained Zvinchuk at 7:30 a.m. local time at the Mövenpick Hotel in Risan. It said the group was taken to Podgorica for questioning and their phones and passports were confiscated.
Rybar said its team was in Montenegro legally to film a local monastery and that it expected their prompt release.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said the Russian Embassy in Podgorica was working to establish the circumstances of the detention.
Dmitry Medvedev, the deputy chairman of Russia's Security Council, said that Russia may need to "top up" its prisoner exchange fund with European and U.S. citizens in order to free its own citizens being held in Europe following Zvinchuk’s detention.
"It’s a mistake, of course, for our people to be traveling around European countries. Even if they have good intentions and important goals. Potentially, all (and I emphasize — all) Russians are being hunted down," said Medvedev.
"Now, it is quite likely that we will have to replenish the exchange fund with European and American idiots in order to get our own people out. There’s no other way: when in Rome, do as the Romans do…," said Medvedev.
Rybar has about 1.5 million Telegram subscribers and publishes daily military analysis of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Zvinchuk is subject to Western sanctions.
Reuters contributed reporting.

U.S.-Ukraine meeting in Miami: Media learn what the negotiations will focus on
Kyiv • UNN
Trump's envoys will meet with Ukrainian representatives on October 9 in Miami. Allies, NATO, and the EU will join the negotiations.
The US administration has named the topics of the talks between President Donald Trump's envoys and Ukrainian negotiators in Miami on October 9. RFE/RL reports this, UNN writes.
Details
"The US and Ukraine will hold talks in Miami on October 9 to discuss proposals aimed at ending the war in Ukraine, amid continuous Russian strikes on vital infrastructure facilities in Kyiv and other cities ahead of winter," the publication says.
The White House confirmed that Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will meet with Ukrainian representatives on October 9 "to discuss a new joint proposal covering all aspects of the conflict and aimed at ending the war."
A senior US administration official told RFE/RL that the meeting "will provide an opportunity to identify areas where the parties to the conflict can cooperate, even if their positions remain different."
Previous meetings produced practical results, including a prisoner exchange, the official said.
The first meeting will be followed by a broader session involving representatives of European allies, NATO, and the EU.
Sources familiar with the plans said that "the Miami meeting will focus on proposals that US negotiators began developing with Russian and Ukrainian interlocutors during recent visits to the region."
An expanded meeting involving national security advisers from the United Kingdom, France, and Germany, as well as representatives of NATO, the EU, and the US European Command, is scheduled for 11:30 a.m. local time. The talks are expected to resume later at 1:45 p.m.
Representatives of the White House National Security Council and the US Treasury Department are also expected to participate.
The agenda also "includes a postwar prosperity and reconstruction plan for Ukraine and other aspects of a potential settlement," the sources said.

Ukraine's Diia government services app has added an online service allowing people to terminate their employment in temporarily occupied territories, the Digital Transformation Ministry said.
To use the service, users should open the Services section in Diia, select Obrii.Work and then "Termination of employment in temporarily occupied territories." They must verify their employment details, complete and review an application, and sign it using Diia.Signature, the ministry said in a Telegram post.
Applications will be processed automatically through the Obrii system within one working day. Users will then receive a notification in the app, the ministry said.
Since Russia's full-scale invasion began, 11,700 people have applied to terminate employment in temporarily occupied territories, according to the Economy and Environment Ministry, citing the State Employment Service.
The Digital Transformation Ministry said it plans to expand the range of digital services available through the platform, including grants for training and assistance with retraining.
Obrii is a digital ecosystem for Ukraine's labor market being developed jointly by the Economy and Environment Ministry and the Digital Transformation Ministry. The State Employment Service administers the platform.
In June, the two ministries opened registration for closed beta testing of the first tools in the Obrii ecosystem. Development and integration costs for the current and following years have been estimated at $5 million to $10 million.

‘I would choose it again’: A Turkish bookbinder’s 60-year journey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:04:02 UTC
19:04:02 KST

For nearly 60 years, Mehmet Karsli has dedicated himself to the patient, intricate art hidden beneath a book's cover.
“We only see the cover of a book, but there are many processes underneath it,” says the master bookbinder, who has spent much of his life repairing and restoring books.
The process involves carefully taking a book apart, repairing damaged pages, stitching them back together, applying glue, trimming the edges, and finally crafting a new cover.
Each stage demands attention to detail, and even the smallest mistake can undo hours of painstaking work.
“If you make a mistake in even one letter when lettering the cover, you have to discard it and make a new cover,” he tells TRT World.
Yet despite the craft's demanding nature, Karsli’s passion never faded.
“I have been in this profession for about 60 years, and believe me, I have never been tired of working.”
From apprentice to master
Born in 1951 in Musalikalesi village in the Akdagmadeni district of Yozgat, Karsli moved to Ankara at age nine.
After completing primary school, he began an apprenticeship at a bookbinding workshop in Hacettepe, balancing his early training with his education.
He spent his days learning the craft and attended middle school in the evenings. After graduating, he enrolled in the printing department of an industrial vocational high school.
His interest in books and bookbinding, however, began with something much simpler: the quality of paper.
At the time, Karsli recalls, good-quality paper was difficult to find. Most notebooks were made from second- or third-grade paper, which deteriorated easily when people erased writing.
But one of his friends, whose father worked as a printer, had notebooks made from better-quality paper. Their appearance caught Karsli's attention.
“He would come with beautiful notebooks, and that is how I became interested in this craft,” he says.
That early fascination eventually led him to a bookbinding workshop, where he discovered that learning the profession required far more than an interest in books.
The training followed a gradual process. Apprentices first learned by watching experienced bookbinders before moving on to stitching, repairing, rounding the spine, and cutting the book.
Making covers came much later.
“After learning to round the spine, you would only move on to making the covers after another year to a year and a half,” he tells TRT World.
Karsli likens the craft to a city's infrastructure, where much of the essential work remains hidden beneath the surface.
In traditional bookbinding, pages are stitched together, headbands are woven at the top and bottom of the spine, and the edges are trimmed. A board is then prepared to form the cover's foundation, before leather is thinned, shaped, and applied.
What appears to be a single finished object is, in fact, the result of numerous carefully executed stages.
The work beneath the cover
For Karsli, bookbinding began with the practical need to protect and hold written pages together.
“Bookbinding has existed since the invention of paper,” he says.
As writing on individual sheets became more common, people needed covers to keep the pages together and protect them from damage.
The craft's terminology also reflects its traditional materials. The word cilt, derived from the Arabic word for “skin” or “leather”, came to describe a book's protective covering, reflecting the widespread use of leather in traditional bindings.
Karsli distinguishes between two approaches to the profession: modern bookbinding and the traditional methods associated with Ottoman craftsmanship.
The classical tradition he describes belongs to a broader heritage of book arts that developed over centuries.
Important bookbinding examples emerged in Anatolia during the Seljuk period, and the craft later developed distinctive characteristics under the Ottomans.
In the classical Ottoman period, bookbinding was practised in palace workshops alongside calligraphy, illumination and miniature painting.
Its defining features include the decorative shamsa (a star-shaped, circular, or oval rosette medallion) and the headband, both of which require specialised techniques.
The headband is woven at the top and bottom of the book's spine, while the shamsa is a prominent decorative motif on traditional covers, often featuring vegetal or geometric patterns.
Restoring an old manuscript requires the same meticulous approach: first assess its condition, then carefully remove accumulated dirt.
“When a manuscript comes in, the first thing you do is give it a dry cleaning. After the dry cleaning, if there are any torn areas, you restore them,” he explains.
Once you've repaired the damaged sections, you stitch the pages together and begin work on the cover.
“After stitching it, you make the cover. Then you stamp the shamsa onto the cover. After the shamsa, you decorate it with gold or in a simple style. You weave the headband,” he explains.
“Then you glue the covers together, and a finished work of art emerges.”
What is particularly striking in Karsli’s story is that after decades in the profession, he chose to become a student again.
In 2010, his works were displayed at a group exhibition in Istanbul. Master bookbinder Islam Secen saw Karsli’s pieces there and expressed an interest in meeting him.
“He said, ‘I want to meet this master’.”
When Karsli later visited Istanbul, he sought out Secen not just to meet him, but to ask to become his student.
“I said to him, ‘Master, I sometimes receive questions about classical bookbinding, but I do not know this art. Could you teach me?’”
For the next year and a half, Karsli travelled regularly from Ankara to Istanbul to study classical bookbinding under Secen.
By then, he already had his own workshop and a steady stream of customers. Nevertheless, he made time for the training, closing his workshop every Friday evening and taking an overnight train to Istanbul.
“I went to Istanbul for a year and a half.”
“On Friday evening, I would close the workshop, take the train at night, and arrive in Istanbul in the morning.”
“I would attend the course, return in the evening, and open my workshop on Monday.”
Do it with love
Alongside his training and development as a bookbinder, Karsli built a career working in public institutions.
He began working at Ankara University's Faculty of Agriculture at a young age and secured a permanent position there when he turned 18.
In January 1982, he moved to Parliament, where he continued working until his retirement in 1996.
Retirement, however, did not mean stepping away from the profession. Instead, it gave him the opportunity to devote himself to his own workshop and the craft he had loved since childhood.
His decades of dedication have also brought recognition.
In the 60th year of his career, Karsli received an award from Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, an honour he describes as one of the most meaningful moments of his life.
For a man who has spent much of his life learning, practising and teaching a centuries-old craft, the lesson he hopes to pass on extends well beyond bookbinding.
“Whatever you do, do what you love,” he tells TRT World.
“If you love what you do, you will surely succeed.”

NL’s only legal medicinal cannabis grower goes bust
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:03:36 UTC
19:03:36 KST

NL’s only legal medicinal cannabis grower goes bust
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Patients who use medicinal cannabis face having to switch to imported products after the only licensed grower in the Netherlands was declared bankrupt on Thursday.
A court in Groningen declared Veendam-based Bedrocan bankrupt two weeks after the company had applied for protection from its creditors. The firm, whose main growing site is in Emmeloord, employs around 70 people.
Bedrocan ran into trouble after the health ministry ended its contract at the start of this year. All medicinal cannabis sold in Dutch pharmacies is bought and distributed by the state-run Bureau for Medicinal Cannabis (BMC).
The ministry ended the deal in anticipation of a change in the law that will let growers sell directly to pharmacies. But health minister Sophie Hermans (VVD) told MPs in July that the change is not expected to take effect until July 1, 2028.
That left Bedrocan unable to supply the BMC and not allowed to sell to pharmacies itself, the Volkskrant reported. The state was by far its largest customer.
Limited stockpile
The BMC built up a stockpile of Bedrocan cannabis before the contract ended, but the minister said it was limited and had a finite shelf life. The BMC will switch to imported cannabis during 2027, with products matching current THC and CBD levels as closely as possible.
Around 7,000 people in the Netherlands are prescribed medicinal cannabis, according to the Volkskrant. They include people with multiple sclerosis (MS), severe pain, certain forms of epilepsy, and patients in palliative care.
Patients fear a different variety will not work as well for them. Cannabis contains many compounds that together determine its effect, and the mix depends on the plant and how it is grown.
The MS association has written to Hermans warning that some long-term patients depend on a specific variety.
Bedrocan also supplied patients in other European countries through the BMC. The BMC is due to stop exporting at the end of 2026. In September, Bedrocan told foreign pharmacies and wholesalers to order from it directly.

Ambassador De Felice meets with the Slovak Minister of Tourism
Focus on strengthening collaboration in the tourism and hospitality sectors
ROMA,
09 October 2026, 12:04
ANSA English Desk
Share
Link copiato
- ALL RIGHTS RESERVED
The Italian Ambassador to Bratislava, Gianclemente De Felice, was received by the Minister of Tourism and Sports of the Slovak Republic, Rudolf Huliak. During the cordial meeting, they discussed prospects for strengthening bilateral cooperation, particularly in the tourism and hospitality sectors, including through the signing of a bilateral cooperation protocol. The significant growth in direct flights between Slovakia and Italy has, in fact, led to a steady and substantial increase in visitor numbers. According to data released by the Slovak Ministry, the number of Italian tourists increased by 25% in 2025 compared to the previous year, and in the first six months of 2026, growth was 35% compared to the same period in 2025. Bratislava remains the preferred destination for more than half of all visitors.

Hong Kong outlines new liquidity reforms as US market rally pulls funds away
City is pressing ahead with market reforms as a surging US stock market intensifies competition for capital
2-MIN READ2-MIN

Hong Kong’s securities watchdog is renewing its push to boost market liquidity, setting out further reforms as emerging markets grapple with capital outflow pressure amid a rally in US equities and a strengthening dollar.
Speaking at a conference organised by the Asian Securities & Financial Markets Association (Asifma) on Friday, Julia Leung, CEO of the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), outlined measures ranging from extended trading hours and shorter settlement cycles to cross-market margining and board lot reform aimed at improving market liquidity and efficiency.
“The SFC is working with the HKEX [Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing] to develop margin offsets across its clearing houses,” Leung said, adding that the move would free up capital for “more productive” uses.
Leung also said the HKEX’s clearing house, OTC Clear, would enable same-day settlement for bond deposits and withdrawals later this year, streamlining the process and making non-cash collateral “a more attractive funding pool”.

A national verdict on Trump 2.0 is coming. Nine midterm voters share where they stand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:00:25 UTC
19:00:25 KST

US voters are about to deliver their first national verdict on the second presidency of Donald Trump. On 3 November, millions of Americans will vote in midterm elections to decide control of the House of Representatives and Senate, as well as the governorships in 36 states. The results could have a huge impact on Trump’s final two years in office.
Today, the Guardian launches its 2026 midterm voter panel. Our reporters have interviewed nine voters across the country and the political spectrum about the issues that matter to them, from the cost of living, immigration and healthcare to the war in Iran and whether they trust their political leaders.
The answers – highlights of which are published below – offer insight into the national mood with less than a month to go until election day. The Guardian will return to its voter panel before the final votes are cast.
What’s the most significant issue for you in the midterm election?
Justin Daniels 45; Detroit, Michigan; Democrat/progressive
 So, I’m an economics student, and one of the things I’ve noticed more and more is, we work more, but we seem to be getting further and further behind. Why is it that my grandfather could work an eight-hour union job and have enough to take care of five or six kids, and yet I work the same job and I’m struggling to get by? That makes no sense to me. I don’t understand why so many CEOs are saying companies are making record profits while people have to have two and three jobs.
Yajaira Martinez 43; Pharr, Texas; independent/disaffected Trump voter
 My biggest hit that I’m having right now is labor. I don’t have labor. I don’t have workers that can, you know, finish the houses as fast as we used to. It causes a ripple effect when it comes to supply and demand – houses taking longer, interest rates going higher, so everything is just going up in value.
Scott Akridge 60; Marietta, Georgia; Democrat/liberal
 It would be likely ICE. I feel like that right now is having the largest, most powerful negative impact on people in this country. And it’s very blatant, and I feel like stopping that would be a good touchstone for how we all move forward.
What do you think is the most significant thing Donald Trump has done in his second term?
Caleb Davis 22; Greenville, South Carolina; Republican/conservative
 His recent deal to establish or re-establish American hegemony in Greenland is a really big deal. Making sure that America has access to Greenland, and China does not, is a very important thing that Donald Trump has done. Also, with the Iran war, it is very important what we’re doing there, and I hope for as quick and decisive a success as can possibly be reached.
Sally Rasmussen 62; Medford, Wisconsin; independent/progressive
 I’m going to say the assault upon not only the immigrant community, but every community that he sees as being vulnerable. Giving the American people or a certain sector within the American population permission to be cruel and to exalt in this public display of cruelty – we are going to spend a long time recovering from that.
Morgan Akin 85; Redding, California; Democrat/moderate
 There’s a number of things, but destroying public structures, buildings and so forth in Washington DC, and then building new ones that have no relevance whatsoever to democracy or the people of the country. He is benefiting from his office, increasing his income [by] billions of dollars, while Americans are suffering with high gas prices and food prices and so forth. I just filled my car up, just before you called. I have a Honda CRV, which is not a big car, and it cost me $78 to fill it up.
Does your life feel better or worse than it did two years ago?
Sharon Anderson 70; Etowah, Tennessee; Maga Republican
 My life is better. Myself and my husband, we are both retired. I’m retired from the education field. I was clerical; I was not in a teaching role. My husband was assembly line. He was a blue-collar worker. He worked for General Motors. But I’d say that we’re better off because I feel safer. I feel more hopeful for the future. The economy, of course – things could be better with gas prices, but I think that that’s a temporary problem right now.
Justin Daniels 45; Detroit, Michigan; Democrat/progressive
 Economically, much worse. It’s worse than it was two weeks ago. I have a pickup truck. Filling my gas two weeks ago, two months ago, was $80. Now, it’s $120. I’m expecting it to be $150. And not only that, is my [utilities] bill going to go up. What else is going to go up? Groceries are going to go up just because shipping is going up. I’m not getting a raise yet, again, we’re making record profits. Who are those profits going to? Not you and me, not the people who need the money.
David Ferrari 19; Tallahassee, Florida; Democrat/progressive
 My parents went out of business during Trump 2. My parents started a business, like, 20 years ago in the auto industry. They were very, very lucky because neither of them have college degrees. What sort of started in Trump’s disastrous Covid response, that was one of the first times that my parents had to take out a big loan that they weren’t sure about. In their industry, the tariffs have completely shaken up everything. It has caused them to have a lot less certainty, and eventually that built up, and they couldn’t go on any longer. They’ve got a new business in the works. We’re doing OK, but that was something that did personally affect me.
Patti Fucci 46; Roswell, Georgia; independent/moderate
 I never thought, in 32 years, as a Venezuelan American, that I had to carry my passport with me everywhere I go. I never thought that I will live in fear in the United States, even though I’m an American citizen.
How optimistic are you about America’s future?
Sharon Anderson 70; Etowah, Tennessee; Maga Republican
 I’m very optimistic. This country’s been through worse and she’s always came out on top. I don’t think that there’s a better country in this world. I don’t think there’s a more powerful country in this world. As far as the best in leadership, I think we have it. As far as goals and policies that this country should strive for, I think Donald Trump has those in place.
Scott Akridge 60; Marietta, Georgia; Democrat/liberal
 I’m not very optimistic. Thirty years ago, I would have said yes. We were the shiny new penny that everybody loved after World War II. Now we see the reverse: European countries have gotten their footing and are passing us. China is the worry. Xi is a smart man, a benevolent dictator. If we continue down this path of electing the Trumps of the world who do not embrace science, education or long-term economic stability and infrastructure, this country will continue to decline.
Justin Daniels 45; Detroit, Michigan; Democrat/progressive
 Oh, I think America’s future is behind it. I believe we’re starting to witness the collapse of the American empire, sad to say, but just understanding how economics work and how everything is based on the petrodollar. I understand why Trump wanted to get away from EVs [electric vehicles], because if EVs took over, then less oil would be needed and the US dollar would be needed less and less. But what good is being the richest person on an ash heap? All the water is dehydrating. As the earth gets hotter and hotter, water is not sitting on the planet’s surface anymore, it’s in the air. It’s just going to be more storms, more lakes drying up, and what’s going on right now? Oh, we need all the fresh water for datacenters. What do you need datacenters for if nobody’s going to be here?
Sally Rasmussen 62; Medford, Wisconsin; independent/progressive
 I take great encouragement from some of the voices of the Black community, the immigrant community, people who have been involved in activism for decades – I do have optimism. It’s hard to balance sometimes, because there are certainly times when I feel like, oh, who even cares? And why is our country so special that we wouldn’t fall down the hellscape of authoritarianism? But there is a large movement, there is a large resistance, and it’s growing week by week. And I think we have a long tradition in this country of believing that we do have rights. We have these incandescently beautiful founding documents.
David Ferrari 19; Tallahassee, Florida; Democrat/progressive
 I see movements domestically – obviously, the DSA [Democratic Socialists of America] that has been killing it in the primaries. They’ve already done more damage than the Tea Party or Occupy Wall Street ever did, and it feels like this is just the beginning. So I’m very, very optimistic, and I think the world that we can accomplish, a world where everyone’s needs are met, at least in the wealthiest nation in the history of the planet.
How do you want the Iran war to end?
Yajaira Martinez 43; Pharr, Texas; independent/disaffected Trump voter
 Let’s be realistic: war is created for money to be created. I just feel everything just needs to end. Everybody, every country, needs to focus on themselves, and the United States needs to focus on the United States’ people.
Sharon Anderson 70; Etowah, Tennessee; Maga Republican

Christa Pike’s botched execution is a reminder of the horror of the death penalty | Moira Donegan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:00:24 UTC
19:00:24 KST

Christa Pike had asked to be hanged. In the weeks before her botched execution by lethal injection on 30 September, in which she survived two lethal doses of barbiturate pentobarbital and had to be hospitalized, Pike and her legal team had challenged Tennessee’s execution protocol.
The state’s lethal injection regimen had failed before. In May, Tony Carruthers was also sent to Tennessee’s death chamber, only to leave alive after prison officials struggled to find a vein.
In Pike’s case, her lawyers argued, the lethal injection protocol was likely to fail again.
She also had vein issues, they said; if she was subjected to an ordeal like Carruthers’, in which prison officials punctured their prone prisoner more than a dozen times over the course of an hour in an attempt to administer the drug, Pike’s history of trauma, which is lengthy and acute, would serve to make the experience unconstitutionally torturous.
Pentobarbital, the drug that was set to be used to kill Pike, also risked a needlessly painful death.
“The drug supposedly burns very bad,” Pike said in a taped interview just weeks before her scheduled execution. “And so that sounds scary to me because they used the word Draino in speaking about this drug, and the thought of suffocating and drowning on my own bodily fluid and blood isn’t very appealing to me.”
It was to avoid this ordeal that Pike requested to be hanged by the neck until dead instead. Her request was denied. From the execution chamber during Tennessee’s failed attempt to kill her, witnesses said that they could hear Pike complaining about a burning pain in her arm, which felt, she said, like it was about to burst.
After nearly a week of being unconscious and intubated at a Nashville hospital after her failed execution attempt, Pike is now awake and talking. Her arms are severely injured from her execution attempt and not fully usable, but she’s still shackled to her hospital bed anyway. She still remains “foggy” from the effects of the state-administered overdose, and it’s unclear whether she will recover full cognitive function as doctors assess the state of her brain damage.
But she remembers the moments when Tennessee tried and failed to kill her. She is reportedly very angry.
We should be angry, too. In our name, a woman was tortured.
In many death penalty cases, there are real questions about the factuality of a condemned person’s guilt or the fairness of their trial and appeals process.
That is less true in Pike’s case: there is no factual doubt that in 1995, when she was 18, Pike, now 50, lured her 19-year-old classmate Colleen Slemmer into a wooded area, and with an accomplice, Pike’s 17-year-old boyfriend, tortured her for about half an hour before finally killing her by smashing her skull in with a piece of concrete. Slemmer’s mother has been a particularly vocal advocate for Pike’s execution, and is reportedly furious that her daughter’s killer has survived.
The wishes of victims and their families should be crucial to what our understanding of justice means. No one knows better the meaning and significance of violence than the people who it is inflicted on.
But it is also true that Pike’s criminal trial did not take into account factors in her life that might have explanatory, if not mitigating, power – such as the reality that she committed murder at the end of a childhood that had been marked by horrific, repeated, and severe sexual and physical violence.
And it is true, too, that when we assess what justice looks like, we must ask not only what would be most meaningful and satisfying for victims but also what best reflects our values and meets our obligations as a state. By that metric, the death penalty has always failed. It does not mete out justice so much as lower the collective community to the level of its worst perpetrators.
Lethal injection used to be a way for us to deny this. The protocol was developed in the US and first adopted for executions in the late 1970s. It was meant to replace older methods of state killing, such as gas chambers, electric chairs and firing squads, offering what was positioned as a more dignified and civilized, and supposedly less painful, way of murdering a human being.
What lethal injection did instead was medicalize the death penalty’s brutality, allowing its proponents a kind of polite denial of what the punishment actually is.
Pike shows us what it really is. It is violent, brutal and cruel. It is painful, no matter how much medical science is used to deny or obscure this; it is superfluous and contrary to the needs of justice, and it degrades those who engage in it.
For a long time, I thought of the death penalty as dangerously final, opening up the possibility of innocent people irretrievably lost, of mistakes that can’t be taken back. And it is true that this happens: America has executed innocent people.
But Pike’s experience shows us that this is not the end of execution’s horror. There is something worse.
Tennessee has issued a temporary moratorium on executions, and the governor has called for a review of what went wrong in Pike’s execution. But he should know what went wrong: the problems with the lethal injection protocol, as well as with the death penalty more broadly, were not mysteries even before the state of Tennessee failed to kill Pike.
It is still possible that Pike will have to fight not to be sent back to the execution chamber again. And this is another harm of the death penalty: the repetitiveness of its injustice, the way it keeps us from learning from our mistakes.
Rarely do we get a second chance to do right by someone like Pike. The state of Tennessee should not get a second chance to try to kill her.
- Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist

The genetic signature of assortative mating appears to be growing stronger in the United States
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:00:11 UTC
19:00:11 KST

When people pair up with partners who share their traits, such as educational background or lifestyle habits, they can leave subtle footprints in the human genome that persist across generations. A new study of hundreds of thousands of people in the United Kingdom and the United States finds genetic signatures of this partner matching, known as assortative mating, with the signatures for education and smoking appearing stronger among more recently born Americans. The findings were published in Behavior Genetics.
Assortative mating is the non-random pairing of individuals who have similar characteristics. When people choose a partner, they frequently select someone with similar schooling, body measurements, or daily habits rather than pairing up by chance. Over multiple generations, this non-random pairing can concentrate specific traits within families and alter how inherited traits are distributed across a population.
When partners who share heritable traits have children together, genetic variants related to those traits tend to become linked across the genome in ways that would not occur under random mating. Geneticists refer to this genome-wide connection as gametic phase disequilibrium, which occurs when DNA variants on completely different chromosomes become statistically correlated.
In a 2018 study, researchers developed an approach to detect this pattern by comparing genetic predictors calculated separately from even-numbered and odd-numbered chromosomes within unrelated people. Under random mating, genes on separate chromosomes have no relationship to one another, so any positive correlation between these chromosome halves provides evidence of cumulative partner matching across past generations.
Partner matching matters beyond individual couples, because concentrating similar traits within families may widen social and health differences between households over time. Similarity between partners does not necessarily mean people choose each other for those traits, however. For instance, a study covered by PsyPost in 2025 indicated that educational similarity between partners arises mostly through shared social and family backgrounds rather than direct selection on education itself. Gretchen R. B. Saunders of the University of Minnesota conducted the new study to evaluate whether education, physical traits, and health behaviors show genetic signatures of partner matching, and whether those signatures have changed across twentieth-century birth cohorts.
To explore these dynamics, Saunders analyzed large genetic datasets from two major resources: the UK Biobank in the United Kingdom and the All of Us Research Program in the United States. The analysis included 82,398 likely spouse or long-term cohabiting opposite-sex pairs and 16,273 full sibling pairs from the UK Biobank, along with 333,491 unrelated individuals from the UK Biobank and 228,875 unrelated individuals from the All of Us cohort. Because existing genetic discovery models were developed primarily using participants of European descent, the researcher restricted all samples to individuals of European genetic ancestry to maintain statistical accuracy.
The investigation examined eight traits: educational attainment, height, body mass index, and five smoking and drinking behaviors. The substance use measures included whether an individual ever smoked regularly, their age when starting, the maximum cigarettes smoked per day, whether they quit smoking, and typical drinks consumed per week. For each participant, polygenic scores were constructed, which are numerical scores that sum up thousands of tiny DNA variations across the genome to estimate an individual’s genetic predisposition for a trait.
The author used several analytical strategies to track mating patterns across generations. First, the study measured direct similarities in physical traits and habits between spouses in the UK Biobank, as well as similarities in their polygenic scores. Next, polygenic score correlations among full siblings were examined to see if they exceeded the 0.50 level expected under random mating, which indicates assortative mating in the parents’ generation. Finally, the author calculated correlations between even-numbered and odd-numbered chromosomes in unrelated individuals to detect broad genomic signatures of assortment and tested whether these signatures changed across birth years.
The results indicated positive similarities between spouses for observable traits across all eight measures, evaluated on a correlation scale where 0 represents no resemblance and 1 represents a perfect match. Educational attainment showed the highest spousal correlation at 0.45, closely followed by weekly alcohol consumption at 0.42. Moderate spousal resemblances appeared for smoking cessation at 0.33, body mass index at 0.26, and smoking initiation at 0.23.
These patterns also pointed to two distinct trait clusters among couples. People with higher educational attainment tended to partner with individuals who were taller, had a lower body mass index, and were less likely to smoke. In contrast, individuals who engaged more heavily in smoking or drinking tended to pair with partners who shared similar substance use habits and higher body mass index values.
When examining polygenic scores, spousal genetic resemblances mirrored these observable traits but were smaller in magnitude. The strongest genetic pairing occurred for educational attainment, with a spousal genetic correlation of 0.16, followed by height at 0.08 and smoking initiation at 0.06. Sibling comparisons also supported the conclusion that partner matching occurred in previous generations, as full siblings shared more genetic similarities than the expected 0.50 benchmark for most analyzed traits.
On average, the genetic correlations between partners were about 80 percent smaller than the correlations for the traits themselves. Part of this gap is expected, because polygenic scores capture only a fraction of genetic influences, but it exceeded 90 percent for habits that can change during a relationship, such as drinks per week and cigarettes per day. Saunders interprets this as a sign that partners also come to resemble each other through shared settings and mutual influence, while traits largely set before partners meet, such as height and education, showed the smallest gaps.
In addition, comparisons between spouse pairs and sibling pairs suggested that genetic assortment was either stable or expanding from the parental generation to the offspring generation. Traits such as educational attainment, height, and smoking initiation displayed increases in genetic resemblance between partners compared to the excess similarity observed between siblings.
In the unrelated samples, the even-odd chromosome method provided evidence of persistent genetic assortment across the genome. Both the UK Biobank and All of Us cohorts showed an even-odd chromosome correlation of roughly 0.07 for educational attainment and 0.04 for height and smoking initiation. Under random mating, this correlation would be expected to be zero. Cross-trait analyses also indicated that genetic predispositions toward higher education were negatively correlated with genetic predispositions toward smoking across separate chromosomes, though the author notes such patterns could also partly reflect shared biology or subtle population differences.
Birth-cohort analyses indicated differences in how these patterns shifted over the twentieth century between the two countries. In the UK Biobank, which included people born between 1936 and 1970, the even-odd measure remained largely stable across decades, showing an increase only for smoking cessation. In the American All of Us cohort, which spanned birth years from 1900 to 2005, genetic assortment showed notable increases across generations for smoking initiation, smoking cessation, and educational attainment. Specifically, the genetic signature for educational assortment in the United States rose from approximately 0.04 among those born in the 1930s to 0.09 among those born around 2000.
Saunders notes that the stronger U.S. trends may partly reflect the All of Us sample’s much wider range of birth years, which makes small changes easier to detect. She also points to differences between the two countries, including a faster and more varied expansion of American higher education and declines in U.S. smoking that were more sharply divided along social lines.
“The main takeaway is that patterns of similarity between partners can leave detectable genetic signatures across generations,” said Norbert Meskó, a full professor in the Department of Cognitive and Evolutionary Psychology at the University of Pécs and director of the Evolutionary Psychology Lab, who was not involved in the research. “People resemble their partners in education, smoking, and alcohol consumption, and this study also finds smaller but consistent similarities in genetic scores associated with these characteristics.”
“The finding that deserves particular attention is that some of these genetic signatures were stronger in more recent U.S. birth cohorts, especially for educational attainment and smoking-related traits,” Meskó told PsyPost. “This suggests that the accumulated genetic consequences of assortative mating may differ across generations. However, I would distinguish this finding from direct evidence that people today are choosing more similar partners: the study primarily infers historical mating patterns from genetic data.”
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. The study focused exclusively on participants of European genetic ancestry, which means the results cannot be assumed to apply to other ancestral or cultural backgrounds where social dynamics and mating customs might differ.
“I find the broad evidence for assortative mating more convincing than the evidence that it has become stronger over time,” Meskó explained. “These are comparisons between people born in different periods, rather than direct observations of partner formation across successive generations. Differences in recruitment, participation, survival, and population composition could influence those comparisons. Large samples improve statistical precision, but they do not automatically eliminate systematic bias.”
Additionally, the UK Biobank does not formally record marital status through official registries, meaning spouses were identified using shared addresses and household characteristics. While strict checks were applied, minor misclassifications could have occurred, which would tend to make the estimated partner similarities smaller than they truly are.
“The clearest potential misunderstanding would be to conclude that our genes determine whom we fall in love with, or that people somehow recognize and select partners with similar genetic profiles,” Meskó warned. “Neither conclusion follows from this study. People meet within schools, workplaces, neighborhoods, and social networks that already structure their opportunities to encounter potential partners. Similarity arising through those settings can also produce genetic similarities between partners.”
“Likewise, a polygenic score associated with education is not a measure of someone’s fixed educational potential,” Meskó added. “It is a statistical predictor derived from associations in particular populations and environments. Finally, the implications for inequality should be treated as plausible consequences rather than outcomes directly demonstrated here. The study does not establish how much these mating patterns have increased socioeconomic or health inequalities.”
It is also worth noting that non-random mating cannot be separated entirely from other social processes, such as partners adopting each other’s habits over time or meeting simply because they share the same neighborhood or workplace.
“I would particularly welcome longitudinal research that measures people before they form a relationship and follows both partners over time,” Meskó said regarding next steps. “This would help distinguish three processes: choosing someone who is already similar, meeting someone through a shared social environment, and becoming more similar through life together. Combining that design with genetic data and information across generations would make the historical interpretation stronger.”
“Overall, I see this as a useful contribution to understanding how social patterns of partnering become reflected in genetic data,” Meskó concluded. “Its strongest message is that partner similarity matters for interpreting population genetics; its more tentative message concerns how that similarity has changed over time.”
The study, “Changing Patterns of Assortative Mating for Educational, Substance Use, and Anthropometric Traits,” was authored by Gretchen R. B. Saunders.
