Russia’s Aerospace Forces received their second batch of newly produced Su-34 (NATO: Fullback) fighter-bombers this year on Wednesday, Oct. 7, according to the manufacturer the United Aircraft Corporation (UAC), part of the Rostec state-owned consortium.
“The timely fulfilment of this state defense contract is a key task of the UAC. Our workforce carries out this important job with honor,” UAC CEO Vadim Badekha was quoted as saying.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
He added that the two batches, the earlier delivered in July, would not be the last this year, saying, “These aircraft are the basic strike power of our frontline aviation and demonstrate their efficiency in real combat conditions.”
The numbers of aircraft provided under the latest consignment were not declared by the Russian authorities, but defense analyst Guy Plopsky, posting on X, said it could be as many as four.
Open-source assessments suggest that production of the Su-34, has almost doubled since the start of the 2022 full-scale invasion, with annual output likely to reach around 30 aircraft this year.
Defence Blog said UAC likely delivered 18 Su-34s throughout 2025 to the Russian military, while a Russian aviation outlet noted that the year’s deliveries consisted of seven batches in total.
“Undisputed best seller”
The Su-34 is built at the Chkalov Aviation Plant in Novosibirsk. The latest version, designated Su-34M/NVO, includes uprated avionics, electronic warfare suites, including the Khibiny electronic countermeasures system and sensor pods linked to its increased use of UPMK glide bombs.
Trump May Leave 100,000 Ukrainians in US Immigration Limbo Rather Than Renew Protections
Numerous videos on pro-Kremlin social media show Su-34s launching bombs, including the “ODAB-500,” a 500-kilogram (1,100-pound) steerable glide bomb; the “FAB-3000,” a 3,000-kilogram (6,600-pound) bomb; others fitted with thermobaric warheads; and a range of air-to-surface missiles.
Rostec claims the Su-34, which some experts say was the only post-Soviet aircraft built primarily for Russian forces’ own use rather than export, is the “undisputed best seller in the world of combat aviation.”
“The aircraft is valued and respected by the military for its versatility, powerful armament, and high flight and technical performance,” the company wrote.
In the UAC announcement published to coincide with the latest delivery, Badekha said production is continuing as normal.
“We are maintaining a high pace of production of combat aircraft, fulfilling our obligations to the Russian defense ministry. Our employees at the plants are constantly refining production processes to ensure the necessary volume of aircraft production,” he said.
Potential reliance on foreign components
A July 2025 analysis by the International Partnership for Human Rights (IPHR) suggests the Su-34 relies heavily on foreign components, based on wreckage found in Ukraine.
Based on the wreckage salvaged in Ukraine, researchers identified 221 foreign electronic components from the aircraft, sourced from 59 companies in eight countries, primarily the US, followed by Japan, the EU, Switzerland, Taiwan and South Korea.
It is unclear how many foreign components went into the latest batch delivered to the Russian military.
The West begs to differ
According to the UAC, Russian pilots consider the Su-34 to be “a well-developed aviation system with a good reserve for the future,” with “a wide range of weapons with the ability to employ advanced strike systems,” based on its performance in combat operations in the war in Ukraine.
However, many Western analysts disagree. The Hush-Kit aviation Substack commented in March this year that: “If it quacks like a dead duck and dies like a dead duck, then maybe it is a dead duck.”
The article calls the Su-34 “the Worst Warplane of the 21st Century” and explains in detail why, during the war in Ukraine, it has “a woeful, unparalleled 25% loss rate.”
While the article attributes much of this to technical shortcomings in the aircraft’s design, weapons and sensor suites, it also points to its aircrew, who “often use predictable, high-altitude, straight-in attack profiles, with a lack of, or ineffective use of its technology.”
Kyiv has frequently targeted Russia’s Su-34s since 2022.
A July 2025 operation reportedly took four Su-34s out of action in Volgograd, while another aircraft was lost in a training flight crash. In a separate operation in June, Ukrainian forces also damaged an unspecified number of Su-34s.
In late March 2026, a Su-34 was shot down over the battlefield, according to defense outlet Militarnyi – two months after Ukraine reportedly downed two Su-34s on the same day. On Aug. 20, the Ukrainian military struck the Russian Akhtubinsk military airfield in the Astrakhan region, damaging a Su-34.
During an attack on the Khanskaya airfield on Oct. 4, drones operated by the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) also destroyed two Russian aircraft – a Su-35 and a Su-34.

US judge orders return of migrant deported to Africa
A US federal judge has ordered the administration of President Donald Trump to facilitate the return of an Egyptian man deported to Equatorial Guinea, finding that the transfer violated his constitutional rights.
Arizona District Judge John Hinderaker said in a ruling seen on Thursday that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) had deported Ahmed Soliman, 31, from the US in April without a meaningful opportunity to challenge his destination. Soliman arrived in the US at age four.
Soliman had lost his immigration status following convictions for aggravated assault and possession of a synthetic narcotic but secured protection against deportation to Egypt over fears of persecution because he is gay and members of his family had reportedly been tortured and imprisoned by Egyptian authorities.
His lawyer, Dana Camilleri, said he has been held incommunicado in Equatorial Guinea since September 11 after speaking out about detention conditions there, including threats at gunpoint by police officers. US Congresswoman Adelita Grijalva, a Democrat representing Arizona’s 7th District, subsequently urged Washington to secure his release, citing reports that he had been “hooded, bound, and beaten with guns and shoved down a flight of stairs” in the Central African country.
DHS argued that Equatorial Guinea’s diplomatic assurances against persecution or torture made an individual hearing unnecessary. Judge Hinderaker rejected the argument, saying the approach provided “no notice of the country of removal and no opportunity to be heard,” according to the court order dated October 6. He ordered the Trump administration to report within three days on Soliman’s whereabouts, custody, and physical condition, along with steps taken to secure his return and the anticipated timeline.
The case adds to growing controversy over Trump’s third-country deportation policy, under which immigrants Washington deems ineligible to remain in the US are sent to nations where they often have no ties.
Human Rights Watch’s analysis of US immigration data counted 536 such transfers to Africa between January 20, 2025 and August 5, 2026, including to Ghana, Equatorial Guinea, Eswatini, South Sudan, Rwanda, Uganda, Cameroon, DR Congo, and the Central African Republic.
Rights groups have reported beatings, threats at gunpoint, and inadequate medical care in Equatorial Guinea. In Eswatini, Laotian deportee Phone Chomsavanh was released on October 4 after more than a year in a maximum-security prison, AP reported, citing his lawyer.
The arrangements have also faced legal challenges in Africa over secrecy and alleged rights violations. In April, the Uganda Law Society sought court orders to halt transfers it called a “patent international illegality,” alleging that parliament and other mandated institutions had been bypassed. In June, rights lawyers sued Ghana at West Africa’s top human rights court on behalf of 27 deportees, accusing Accra of returning migrants to countries where they faced harm and demanding disclosure of the agreement’s terms.
Nigerian Foreign Minister Yusuf Tuggar rejected pressure to accept Venezuelan deportees last year, saying the West African country has “enough problems” of its own.

Hitler Mussolini Simeón Flores won by 25 votes in Queropalca, a district of just over 730 people in the Huánuco department, running for the centre-left Ahora Nación party. He is not Peru’s first elected Hitler.
Peruvian man named Hitler Mussolini has been elected mayor of a small Andean district after winning a local election by a narrow margin on a left-wing party ticket.
Hitler Mussolini Simeón Flores, 45, won the mayoral race in Queropalca, a district in the province of Lauricocha in the Huánuco department north of Lima, running for the centre-left Ahora Nación party.
He received 229 votes — 34.5% of the 663 valid ballots in Queropalca — ahead of his closest rival, Gaspar Benilde Osorio Zambrano of the Popular Renewal Peru party, who took 204 votes, or 30.8%.
The district has an estimated population of just over 730, according to 2024 official data.
Simeón Flores also manages the Simeon Sac investment group in Pillco Marca, in the same department.
The vote was part of regional and municipal elections held across Peru following right-wing firebrand Keiko Sofía Fujimori's victory in the country's presidential election.
This is not the first time a Hitler has won over the voters in the South American country.
Centre-right We Are Peru party's Hitler Alba served as mayor of another small Andean town of Yungar between 2011 and 2014.
In 2018, he went up against Lennin Vladimir Rodriguez Valverde, who tried to challenge the validity of his candidacy. Alba won against other candidates, garnering 47.7% of the vote.
Alba, who dubbed himself "the good Hitler," campaigned under the slogans "Hitler returns" and "Hitler with the people".
He said at the time that his father did not know about the Nazi German dictator's legacy when he named him.
Lawmaker and surgeon Hitler Saavedra served in Peru's Congress as a member of We Are Peru from 2021 until his death in 2024 at the age of 46.
It is not uncommon for Peruvians to choose historic or otherwise unusual names for their children regardless of negative or controversial connotations.

Swiss luxury group Richemont sheds jobs at watchmaker Montblanc
Swiss luxury goods group Richemont is restructuring its Locle-based watch brand, Montblanc, in response falling demand.
The luxury group is currently organising the transfer of 17 employees to other companies within the group and has also made six staff members redundant, the tradce union Unia Neuchâtel told AWP.
Of the 45 employees at Montblanc, a brand founded in 1997, “23 have accepted or are currently negotiating a transfer, and six have been made redundant”, said union secretary Solenn Ochsner. She added that the job cuts had been finalised at the end of September.
Richemont “is offering them positions at other group entities, including Cartier. Some – a minority – have agreed to work at the Minerva manufacture in Villeret”, based in the Bernese Jura and acquired by the Geneva-based company in 2006. According to Ochsner, the terms of employment will not be quite the same, and some staff will face longer daily commutes.
The trade union representative explained that Montblanc was suffering from the crisis facing the entire watchmaking industry, which is hitting entry-level and mid-range watches particularly hard.
At Minerva, whose historic workshops dating back to the 19th century have been transformed by Richemont into a centre of excellence, the situation “is going very well”, as the brand specialises in the very high-end market, she emphasised.
When contacted, Richemont was not immediately available for comment.
In the first quarter of its staggered 2026/27 financial year, the luxury group’s overall sales were not dampened by the crisis in the Middle East or the persistent downturn in China, surging by 17% to €6.3 billion (CHF5.9 billion), driven mainly by jewellery.
The watch brands, however, returned to growth after two years of decline, rising by 6% to €873 million.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:44:35 UTC
18:44:35 KST

Russian drones hit Ukraine's power grid, warehouses, a food warehouse, a home-improvement store, and a farm overnight on 9 October, Ukrainian officials and emergency services reported. The strikes triggered emergency power cuts in Kyiv and other regions and killed at least three people across the country.
As Russia continues its daily terror attacks, it has likely begun its winter strike campaign early, aiming to make civilian life in Ukraine unbearable, ISW assessed. Those strikes now reach beyond the grid to the businesses that store and sell goods, adding to damage Ukraine's Economy Ministry expects to reach up to $10 billion this year.
Power cut in Kyiv and other regions
Russia launched 136 drones overnight, 93 of them jet-powered, Ukraine's Air Force said. Air defenses downed or suppressed 114. Drones hit eight locations, and debris fell at seven more.
DTEK, Ukraine's largest private energy company, introduced emergency power cuts on Kyiv's right bank and in the Bucha and Vyshhorod districts on the grid operator's orders. Ukrenergo, the national grid operator, imposed emergency outages in some regions, citing the strain Russian attacks put on the system. Planned schedules were suspended there. Hourly cuts across parts of Ukraine had already been set for the whole day.
The cuts came a day after a Russian strike knocked out several grid elements supplying Kyiv, leaving many consumers without power. Russia has sharply stepped up attacks on Ukraine's energy system in recent weeks, deliberately targeting power lines and transformers, Ukraine's Energy Ministry said.
Ukraine’s war leadership sets new electronic warfare tasks as Russia’s jet-powered drones slip past nearly half of its air defenses
Warehouses and a store
In the Bucha district of Kyiv Oblast, Russia hit warehouses and injured three people, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said. One was hospitalized. Rescuers were searching for a woman who may be under the rubble.
In Odesa, a strike damaged the roof of a warehouse storing food and started a fire, the region's emergency service reported. In the south of the oblast, Russia damaged buildings at holiday resorts and destroyed a café.
Near Chernihiv, Russia hit a site just outside the city after 03:00, the city council said. A Suspilne correspondent at the scene reported that a drone hit the Epicenter store, part of a large Ukrainian home-improvement chain. Russian forces also struck a farm in the Kulykivka community. No one was hurt in Chernihiv Oblast.
Russia has already destroyed more than two-fifths of Ukraine's modern warehouse space.
Three killed overnight
In Zaporizhzhia, Russia struck near an apartment building, killing a man, the Zaporizhzhia Oblast administration said. The number of injured rose to nine, including a 14-year-old girl, regional prosecutors said. One strike landed near an after-school education center.
In Ivano-Frankivsk, falling drone debris started a fire, and a man born in 1959 was killed, Ivano-Frankivsk Oblast head Svitlana Onyshchuk said.
In Shyroka Balka, Kherson Oblast, a Russian drone dropped explosives on a house at about 06:20, killing a 74-year-old woman and injuring a 68-year-old man, regional prosecutors reported.
Russia injured three women in a Kharkiv suburb, Kharkiv Oblast head Oleh Syniehubov said. In the Nikopol district, a 24-year-old woman was injured, Dnipropetrovsk Oblast head Oleksandr Hanzha said.
Poland scrambled military aircraft as Russia struck targets in western Ukraine, its Operational Command said.
The past day's toll
Over the past 24 hours, Russia killed two people and injured 18 in Zaporizhzhia and the Zaporizhzhia district, regional council head Ivan Fedorov said. In Sumy Oblast, one man was killed and 14 people were injured, including two 12-year-old boys, the regional administration reported.
In Kherson Oblast, four people were injured, including a child, Kherson Oblast head Oleksandr Prokudin said. In Mykolaiv Oblast, a Russian drone injured two children aged three months and one year, acting oblast head Heorhii Reshetilov said. Three people were injured in Kharkiv Oblast, Syniehubov reported.
In Donetsk Oblast, Russia killed 35 people and injured 25 on 8 October, Donetsk Oblast head Vadym Filashkin said. Thirty-two of them died in Kramatorsk, most in a Russian bomb strike on two passenger buses.

UN says Gaza shelter supplies cover just 17% of winter needs as nearly 2M require aid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:44:06 UTC
18:44:06 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
- 'The current items that we have outside of Gaza, they have been determined to be potentially dual-use, or detained as a dangerous good,' IOM regional crisis coordinator tells Anadolu regarding stranded sheltering materials at border
Nearly 2 million Palestinians in Gaza urgently need shelter assistance as winter approaches, while Israeli restrictions continue to prevent the entry of critical supplies, the UN migration agency said on Friday.
 
The IOM said in a statement that nearly all of Gaza's population remains in need of shelter assistance one year after a ceasefire was announced, with available stocks and incoming supplies covering only 17% of identified winter needs.
 
"Families who have already endured repeated displacement and devastating loss must be able to face the winter in safety and dignity," IOM Director General Amy Pope said in the statement.
 
More than half of tents and makeshift shelters are in "poor condition," which requires replacement, while many Palestinians are living in war-damaged buildings at risk of collapse.
 
An assessment by an IOM partner identified more than 3,600 buildings requiring demolition, removal or evacuation due to safety risks.
 
Meanwhile, nearly 1.8 million people are living in displacement sites, 56% of which face medium to high flood risks, raising concerns about further displacement as heavy rainfall approaches.
 
The agency said approximately 8,600 emergency shelter kits remain stranded outside Gaza after being turned away by Israeli authorities.
 
The IOM urged immediate and sustained access for tents, emergency shelter kits, temporary housing units and construction materials to strengthen shelters, repair damaged homes and provide safer accommodation, stressing that equipment, fuel and spare parts are also essential for debris removal and early recovery.
 
"The solutions are known, the supplies are ready and humanitarian teams are prepared to deliver," Pope said.
 
Israel blocks Gaza shelter supplies with 'dual-use' claims
 
Israeli authorities have blocked emergency shelter supplies from entering Gaza by classifying them as potentially "dual-use" or "dangerous goods," the IOM regional crisis coordinator told Friday in response to Anadolu's question.
 
Speaking in a UN press briefing in Geneva, Karl Baker warned that continued restrictions could worsen overcrowding and increase the spread of communicable diseases during winter.
 
"The current items that we have outside of Gaza, they have been determined to be potentially dual-use, or detained as a dangerous good," Baker said.
 
He described the classification as "unfortunate," noting that the kits consist of basic materials such as wood and tarps needed to construct emergency shelters.
 
Baker said IOM continues to work with authorities to secure access, but efforts are sometimes unsuccessful when supplies are classified as dual-use items.
 
Asked about the consequences of continued restrictions and the risk of further displacement caused by winter flooding, Baker warned that existing shelter conditions would deteriorate.
 
"Without these sort of shelter solutions entering Gaza, we will just see a deterioration in the quality of the shelter which they currently live in," he said.
 
He warned that colder temperatures, rainfall and potential flooding could force displaced Palestinians into increasingly crowded areas.
 
"The population density will increase, and then we will see once again rises in everything from communicable diseases to, of course, the lack of community cohesion," Baker said.

South Africa’s Navi Pillay Wins Nobel Peace Prize
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:43:26 UTC
18:43:26 KST

The Nobel Peace Prize was awarded Friday to South Africa’s Navi Pillay, the judge who headed the Rwanda genocide tribunal and who last year presided over a UN commission which accused Israel of genocide in Gaza.
Pillay, currently a judge on the International Court of Justice in a case where Myanmar also stands accused of genocide, has been “instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide are prosecuted,” said Jorgen Watne Frydnes, the chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee in Oslo.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Pillay headed the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry (COI), which does not speak on behalf of the world body, and which last year found that genocide was occurring in Gaza.
Pillay told AFP at the time that her team had shared “thousands of pieces of information” with prosecutors at the International Criminal Court.
The UN said the prize for Pillay was testimony to the “value” of rights.
The Nobel jury said it was honouring her at a time when “the system of international law is under tremendous pressure and its institutions are under attack.”
“At a time of existential challenges – including more wars and conflicts than the world has seen in a long time – international law is no longer just a supplement to peace and security. It is an absolute necessity,” Watnes said.
“Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career,” the committee said.
Prizes and Honor
The prize – the ultimate diplomatic and humanitarian accolade – is sure to irk US President Donald Trump, whose administration has repeatedly attacked international justice institutions.
Since returning to the White House in January 2025, Trump has made no secret of his desire to win the prize.
“If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump,” Pillay said to a standing ovation captured by Amnesty International Secretary General Agnes Callamard in Nuremberg and posted on the social network X.
Last year, the prize went to Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, who subsequently gave her Nobel gold medal to Trump.
The prize comes with a gold medal, a diploma and a prize sum of $1.2 million.
The award will be presented at a formal ceremony in Oslo on December 10, the anniversary of the 1896 death of the prizes’ creator, Swedish inventor and philanthropist Alfred Nobel.
The Peace Prize is the only Nobel awarded in Oslo, with the other disciplines announced in Stockholm.
On Thursday, the Nobel Prize in Literature was awarded to Canadian poet Anne Carson for her modern twists on Greek mythology and antiquity that have inspired new forms of writing.
The 2026 Nobel season winds up Monday with the economics prize.

South African jurist Navi Pillay wins 2026 Nobel Peace Prize
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:42:36 UTC
18:42:36 KST

Necva Tastan Sevinc
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
South African jurist Navi Pillay, who previously led a UN commission of inquiry that concluded Israel committed genocide in Gaza, was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize on Friday for her contributions to peace and international law.
The Norwegian Nobel Committee praised Pillay's decades-long efforts to strengthen international justice and hold perpetrators of war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide accountable.
"This year's laureate has significantly enlarged the scope and impact of international law," the committee said, highlighting her work in international courts and as UN high commissioner for human rights.
Born into a family of Indian Tamil origin in Durban, South Africa, under apartheid, Pillay began her legal career challenging racial discrimination and defending opponents of the apartheid system.
She later served as a judge on South Africa's High Court, the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the International Criminal Court, before becoming UN high commissioner for human rights.
The Nobel committee highlighted her contribution to landmark rulings establishing that rape and sexual violence could constitute crimes against humanity and genocide.
Pillay has also served as an ad hoc judge at the International Court of Justice in the case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar over allegations of genocide against the Rohingya minority.
UN investigation into Gaza
Pillay chaired the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory from July 2021 until her departure in 2025.
Presenting the commission's findings to a UN General Assembly committee in October 2025, she said its legal analysis had established Israel's responsibility for genocide in Gaza.
"We concluded that the State of Israel is responsible for the commission of four genocidal acts in Gaza with the specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza, as such," she said.
"The Commission also found that the Israeli President, Prime Minister and former Defence Minister have incited the commission of genocide," she added.
The Nobel committee said Pillay's career demonstrated the importance of international legal institutions in preventing conflict and securing accountability.
"In awarding this year's Nobel Peace Prize, the Norwegian Nobel Committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law -- national and international -- underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently. Peace requires justice," it said.

He also insisted that only top-tier, elite foreign talent that's not available domestically should be brought in.

Resorting to terminology that carries painful historical and colonial legacy connotations is deeply offensive," said the ministry, adding it will continue to follow developments related to the issue.The unusually blunt pushback suggests India's patience is wearing thin after a series of bilateral setbacks, ranging from trade and tariffs, immigration and talent mobility to India's ties with Russia and Washington's Pakistan outreach. "The suspension of PERM applications does not, by itself, affect the validity of existing H-1B visas or the status of H-1B visa holders and their dependents, though there could be some impact on the permanent-residency/Green Card process of eligible employees of the affected companies," said the ministry.While the America First signalling through the announcement seems designed for an electoral boost in the upcoming mid-term polls, it's unlikely to help the already rocky state of India-US ties. The timing is also problematic as it creates poor optics for PM Narendra Modi's visit to the US in December for the G20 summit. It also comes just ahead of Secretary of State Marco Rubio's visit to India this month, during which India will look to raise its concerns related to the issue.
The US announcement is the latest flashpoint in ties after the US Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 (SRIA), a new law that empowers the president to impose up to 100 percent tariffs on countries importing Russian oil. Modi had raised India's anxieties about that issue in a phone call with President Donald Trump late last month.

‘Switzerland has spoken’. Will UBS leave?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:41:17 UTC
18:41:17 KST

‘Switzerland has spoken’. Will UBS leave?
New regulations will leave lender with options ranging from retaining billions of dollars of additional capital to shrinking international operations.
Three-and-a-half years after UBS acquired its stricken rival Credit Suisse in a state-orchestrated rescue, Switzerland’s biggest bank is once again confronting fundamental questions about its future.
Last month, the bank was dealt a crushing blow when the Swiss parliament’s upper house backed a proposal that would force it to hold an extra $16 billion of capital.
The final proposals, designed to prevent a repeat of the 2023 crisis, still have to pass through the legislature’s lower chamber. But UBS executives are resigned to losing the political battle. “Switzerland has spoken,” said one person close to the bank’s leadership.
The defeat has left UBS with few good options, ranging from retaining billions of dollars of additional capital to shrinking its international operations. Or the nuclear choice: leaving the country altogether.
Leave Switzerland
Chair Colm Kelleher acknowledged publicly for the first time last month that UBS could reconsider its Swiss base if the regulatory tightening proved too onerous.
Two of UBS’s largest investors have already urged the bank to shift its headquarters out of Switzerland if the planned reforms are rubber-stamped by the parliament’s more left-leaning lower house.
Artisan Partners, a top-10 shareholder, wrote to the bank’s board last week saying Switzerland was “no longer an attractive or desirable location” for the country’s largest lender — whose balance sheet significantly exceeds the size of the country’s economy. Cevian Capital, which owns about 1.5%, issued a similar warning last year.
Some investors have pointed to the US as a potential destination for relocation because of its less stringent capital framework, while others say a large Eurozone economy closer to UBS’s traditional home, such as Germany, could house the group. The UK is considered less viable because its capital requirements are more similar to those in Switzerland.
Several governments have raised relocation with UBS over the past few years, according to a person familiar with the matter.
But leaving would carry significant costs. Morgan Stanley analysts estimate that the government could impose an exit tax as high as $10 billion on UBS.
Swiss finance minister Karin Keller-Sutter, who has spearheaded the government’s reforms, said last month that if UBS left the country it would be “much more expensive and legally very complex” than if it stomachs the new capital rules.
Do a deal
Rather than relocating on its own, UBS could pursue a deal with a foreign rival, allowing it to escape Switzerland’s capital regime. One person familiar with the bank’s thinking said that UBS would have more options once the integration of Credit Suisse was complete.
By then, the bank will have absorbed most of the costs of integrating its former rival and expects to be generating significantly higher profits, giving it greater financial flexibility to pursue a deal. It could then consider a transaction that “provided regulatory capital relief”, the person said.
One way of achieving this could be through a reverse takeover in which a smaller foreign bank — potentially in the US — acquires UBS in an all-share deal but UBS shareholders emerge with a majority stake in the combined group.
Giulia Aurora Miotto, an analyst at Morgan Stanley, said such a structure could avoid the exit tax, although it would require a smaller bank to merge with UBS and potentially cede control of the combined group.
There is also the possibility of a mega-merger with a Wall Street or European bank as a route out of Switzerland.
Some UBS insiders see Morgan Stanley — where Kelleher spent much of his career — as a potential partner with obvious synergies. “You would be combining the largest US wealth manager with the largest international one,” said a person familiar with the matter. There is no indication that any side is pursuing a transaction currently.
Split in two
Another option would be to split UBS in two, allowing its prized and highly profitable domestic business to remain Swiss while shifting its sprawling international operations outside the country’s regulatory purview.
A senior executive at a rival European bank said this would be their preferred option if they were in UBS’s position.
Under such a structure, a “Swiss UBS” containing the domestic retail and corporate bank could remain headquartered and regulated in Zurich. Meanwhile, its investment bank and overseas wealth businesses could sit under a separate foreign-domiciled parent, potentially in the US, UK or Eurozone.
However, analysts point out that much of UBS’s overseas business — particularly its Asian wealth-management operations — is already booked directly through UBS’s Swiss parent bank via foreign branches rather than subsidiaries, complicating a clean separation and limiting the capital benefit it might provide.
There appears to be little appetite within UBS for such an overhaul. A senior UBS employee told the Financial Times that any alternative to remaining in Switzerland was more likely to “involve a radical move” rather than a restructuring.
Shrink in America
If implemented, the new capital rules would fall particularly heavily on UBS’s US operations, by far its largest foreign subsidiary, with some industry observers saying the bank could consider offloading some or all of the business.
Under the current proposals, the bank would have to cover 90% of the value of its foreign units with common equity tier one capital at the parent bank, up from about 60% currently. At present, UBS is also allowed to use cheaper additional tier one (AT1) debt to cover some of the requirement.
Morgan Stanley analysts pointed to the US unit’s weak profitability in recent years, with margins below those of other parts of the group. “Holding significantly more capital because of [the reforms] could make the case for selling the [US business],” they said.
Johann Scholtz, an analyst at Morningstar, said UBS would probably regard maintaining a meaningful US investment banking presence as “strategically important”, leaving US wealth management as the business with “the clearest economic rationale for separation” or a spin-off.
He added that UBS’s US wealth business was largely a domestic adviser-led franchise that had relatively limited overlap with the group’s international wealth operations, which are built around entrepreneurs, family offices and ultra-high-net-worth clients with global financial needs.
But such a move would run directly against UBS’s global ambitions. Goldman Sachs analysts describe the US, alongside Asia, as a key pillar of UBS’s growth strategy in global wealth management.
Chief executive Sergio Ermotti said this week that the bank needed a presence in the US “to be successful”, suggesting that shrinking substantially in the country was not currently under consideration.
Stay put and pay up
The simplest — if costly — option for UBS would be to accept the higher capital requirements and continue running the group under its current structure from Switzerland.
Although UBS has estimated the additional required capital to be $16 billion, analysts believe the shortfall would be closer to $6 billion-$8 billion once excess capital already held at the parent bank is taken into account.
The senior UBS employee said the bank was most likely to stay in Switzerland and adapt to the new rules, which would be phased in over several years.
Scholtz at Morningstar said his “base case” was that UBS would meet the higher demands by retaining a higher proportion of earnings. “The requirement appears manageable and should not require an equity raise,” he added.
But that could have significant consequences. Morgan Stanley analysts said the 90% requirement would represent “a significant constraint on UBS’s current and future strategy”, potentially limiting its ability to grow internationally.
Kian Abouhossein, an analyst at JPMorgan Chase, estimates the proposal would knock half a percentage point off UBS’s return on tangible equity — a key measure of bank profitability — in 2028, while leaving it operating under “the most stringent regulatory environment globally”.
For now, UBS has said its goal is “to continue operating successfully as a global bank from Switzerland” as it weighs its options.
As it does so, some rivals are allowing themselves a degree of schadenfreude. “If UBS wants to be Swiss, these are the consequences it has to live with,” said the rival executive. “A competitor that has to hold more capital is good for us.”

The Italian parliament approved an electoral reform on Thursday that's dividing the press along political lines. The reform will introduce a prize for the majority-winning alliance, awarding it bonus seats in both houses of parliament if it wins at least 42 percent of the national vote. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni says this will reduce the post-election bargaining that often results in shaky governments. The centre-right paper Il Giornale hails this reform, which it says restores more power to Italian citizens via a preferential voting system and declares Italy's "Third Republic". The conservative daily Il Tempo's editorial attacks the "nervous left". There are two ways to examine electoral law, it says: the first is suited to career politicians and aspiring candidates, and involves "obsessing over technicalities and dissecting every clause." The other way tries to take the long view, giving the system a strong push towards a bipolar structure, which is what the Meloni government has done, it says approvingly.
The Italian left has struggled to build a united alliance ahead of next year's elections, and the left-wing press are furious about the reform. Centre-left daily La Repubblica calls it the "law of power" and in its editorial deplores the "ultimate betrayal." It says through a "political makeover worthy of a magician, Meloni forced her own majority to approve an electoral law that only she and her inner circle wanted". La Stampa says Meloni has changed the rules while Il Fatto Quotidiano says Italian President Sergio Mattarella can veto this "latest piece of garbage" – but wonders if he will do so.

La Croix's correspondent in Saudi Arabia reminds us that Yemen's Houthi rebels have launched several brazen attacks against the kingdom in recent weeks, including strikes on Saudi airports. How is it possible that Saudi Arabia spends billions on military equipment but cannot thwart attacks from a tenacious but underequipped rebel group, the paper asks. According to La Croix, there are several reasons: internal struggles between Saudi's national guard and regular army, both of which are affiliated with different powerful families. The central command is also very hierarchical and paralyses any initiative on the ground.
We turn next to the US where Nidal Malik Hasan, an army psychiatrist found guilty of a mass shooting in Fort Hood, Texas in 2009, will be executed by firing squad. As the Washington Post tells us, if it goes ahead, it would be the first such military execution since April 1961, when an army sergeant was hanged for rape and murder. On Thursday, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said the execution will be public and livestreamed. Hegseth said he wants people to watch the execution, so they understand "there are serious consequences for these types of things". If this goes ahead, the US would be added to a notorious list of countries in the world that hold public executions. Last year, of the 17 public executions, six were in Afghanistan and 11 in Iran.
We end with the biggest shakeup of internet addresses in more than a decade. ICANN is a US non-profit organisation that controls the application approvals for domain names. It has unveiled new trends in IP addresses. Applications for more than 1,600 new addresses have been made. ICANN last expanded web domains in 2012, the Times of London tells us. At the time, new domains like .app, .web, .babysitting and .pizza were approved. This time around, AI is a big drawcard. AI companies are seeking to grab domains like .superintelligence or .chatgpt, while Meta has applied for .wearables. There are many novelty ones too. Among some new domain name applications are ".fart", ".bro", ".maga" and ".trump" and ".god". A Belgian LGBT non-profit wants to own .meow, which it says will be for the community but also cat lovers!

Frozen testicular tissue transplanted in bid to restore fertility after chemotherapy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:39:37 UTC
18:39:37 KST

Protecting fertility is a major challenge for young men undergoing aggressive treatments such as chemotherapy. Freezing their own testicular tissue before such treatments could help.
A young patient in Edinburgh has undergone a pioneering procedure, receiving a transplant of his own testicular tissue, frozen before he began chemotherapy, in a development that could pave the way for male fertility preservation, a first such procedure in the UK and second worldwide.
“This is a big step towards helping boys facing treatments that damage their fertility to have children of their own,” said Rod Mitchell, professor of developmental endocrinology at the University of Edinburgh’s Institute for Regeneration and Repair.
The 19-year-old received a bone marrow transplant in 2023 to treat a serious blood disorder. Before starting treatment, he had testicular tissue removed and frozen because the high-dose chemotherapy could permanently damage the cells needed to produce sperm.
Three years later, tests showed that the patient had no sperm in his semen. In August 2026, doctors implanted some of his previously frozen testicular tissue back into his body in the hope that it would begin to produce sperm, the University of Edinburgh said in a press release.
“Fertility is something I’ve struggled with personally for a long time. I’ve always wanted to have children of my own but at some point, I found myself starting to slowly accept that that might never be possible for me,” the patient said after the transplant. “Having this procedure has given me genuine hope for the future.”
In the next eight months, doctors will remove and examine some of the transplanted tissue to determine whether sperm have been produced.
Why freezing tissue
Protecting fertility is a major challenge for young men undergoing aggressive treatments such as chemotherapy.
Semen freezing is an established option for adolescents and young men. It is not available to prepubertal boys, however, because they do not yet produce semen, leaving them with no means of preserving their fertility.
Storing testicular tissue could offer an alternative. It contains spermatogonial stem cells, which produce sperm from puberty onwards. Doctors hope that tissue frozen before treatment can later be returned to the patient and allow sperm production.
The Edinburgh testicular project was established in 2015 with the support of Children with Cancer UK. Since then, more than 1,200 patients in the United Kingdom and more than 3,100 worldwide have now had testicular tissue stored for potential future clinical use.
“We are beginning to see some of these young men return to explore their fertility options. This study offers real hope for future fertility in boys facing cancer treatment,” Mitchell added.
Experimental phases
The trial procedure in Edinburgh is the first of its kind in the UK and only the second reported worldwide.
The first reported transplant of frozen testicular tissue took place in Belgium in January 2025. In that case, the cryopreserved tissue was reintroduced into an infertile man who had undergone chemotherapy in childhood, after 16 years in storage.
The researchers wrote in the preliminary results of the study that dormant stem cells within the transplanted tissue revived and began producing sperm cells, a process known as spermatogenesis.
When researchers evaluated the tissue a year after surgery, they confirmed that the sperm cells had developed fully.

2026-10-09
09:37:26 UTC
18:37:26 KST

South African judge Navanethem "Navi" Pillay won the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday "for her efforts to promote peace and international law," the Norwegian Nobel Committee said.
In September last year, Pillay oversaw the publishing of a report by the UN Commission of Inquiry that concluded that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza and that top Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, incited these acts — accusations that Israel called scandalous.
Navanethem also served as the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights from 2008 until 2014.
Pillay held states and national leaders accountable and brought hope to victims of violence and conflict, and demonstrated a firm moral compass in her long career, the Norwegian Nobel Committee added.
"A common thread runs from her early work defending Nelson Mandela and others who stood up against apartheid to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time," the committee said.
The peace prize is the fifth Nobel awarded this week, after literature, chemistry, physics and medicine. Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado won in 2025.
The Nobel Peace Prize, worth 12 million Swedish crowns, or about $1.2 million, is due to be presented in Oslo on December 10, the anniversary of the death of Swedish industrialist Alfred Nobel, who founded the awards in his 1895 will.
UN human rights office welcomes Nobel Prize winner Pillay as staunch defender of human rights
The United Nations human rights office on Friday welcomed the news of Navi Pillay's Nobel Peace Prize win, acknowledging her longstanding advocacy for human rights.
"It is amazing news, we need more dedication and commitment to human rights," Shabia Mantoo, spokesperson for the UN human rights office, told reporters in Geneva.
Navi Pillay was the former head of the United Nations Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory and a former International Criminal Court judge.
"We hope it will encourage and continue to encourage and inspire others to speak out in protection and promotion of the human rights of all people around the world," Mantoo said in reaction to Pillay's win.
The UN human rights chief also said on Friday that Navi Pillay's Nobel Prize win was a collective win for human rights and for all those seeking justice and accountability, including through the International Criminal Court.
“The fact that the Nobel Award Commission decided to give this to Navi Pillay is a collective win for human rights, but also for seeking justice and accountability in this world," said Volker Turk of his predecessor Pillay who was High Commissioner from 2008-2014.
"And it's clear that we need international criminal accountability mechanisms, including the International Criminal Court, and it's clear that we have a very strong signal that this is absolutely critical in today's world," he told reporters.
International Criminal Court emphasized importance of international justice
The International Criminal Court said the Nobel Peace Prize awarded to its former judge was important recognition for the role of international justice as a cornerstone of peace.
"This is an important recognition of the vital role that international justice plays as a cornerstone of lasting peace," ICC President Tomoko Akane said. "At a time of profound challenges to the international legal order and the rule of law, this recognition carries particular significance."

UN forecasts global growth to slow to 2.6% in 2026 amid energy shock
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:36:10 UTC
18:36:10 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
Global economic growth is projected to slow to 2.6% in 2026 from 2.9% last year as higher energy prices driven by the Middle East war test economic and financial stability, UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) said Friday.
In its Trade and Development Report 2026, the agency forecast global growth of 2.7% in 2027.
Developing economies are expected to grow 4% this year, down from 4.7% in 2025, while facing new technological and policy barriers.
Global goods and services trade is projected to expand 4%, after reaching a record $35 trillion last year, partly reflecting higher prices.
 
AI supports uneven growth
The US economy is forecast to grow 2.1% this year before slowing to 1.8% in 2027. AI investment and a stable labor market support demand, although persistent inflation erodes real wages.
Western Europe remains constrained by weak investment, trade fragmentation and volatile energy prices, while South Korea and Japan benefit from demand for semiconductors and electronics.
 
Developing economies face barriers
UNCTAD Acting Secretary-General Pedro Manuel Moreno said stronger-than-expected global resilience masked growing divergence.
Outside a few fast-growing Asian economies, the developing world is no longer catching up with advanced economies, he said.
Industrialization, goods trade and integration into global value chains are becoming less reliable routes to higher incomes as governments increasingly pursue strategic and national security objectives.
Advanced economies account for around 70% of new investment in semiconductors, AI and clean technologies, Moreno said, while developing economies lead in critical minerals but struggle to add value.
He also warned of volatile portfolio flows and an expected third consecutive annual decline in official development assistance.

Speaking to the Greek daily Kathimerini, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio noted that the situation surrounding Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine has reached a dangerous strategic stalemate, stating that “right now, there don't seem to be prospects of a negotiated settlement.”
Moscow subsequently agreed with Rubio’s assessment, with Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov confirming that Russia sees no current prospects for a diplomatic settlement, according to TASS.
On September 25, Zelenskyy stated that Washington had proposed a technical-level three-way meeting involving Ukraine, the United States, and Russia.
Speaking to journalists, Zelenskyy noted that the American side suggested preparing the format and holding the talks in the United Arab Emirates, though no specific date had been set yet.
The proposal followed weeks of diplomatic efforts, including a briefing in Kyiv by US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner after their three-hour meeting with Russian leader Vladimir Putin in Moscow.

German logistics group Rhenus plans up to 14 terminals along the Middle Corridor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:35:52 UTC
18:35:52 KST

Global logistics company Rhenus Group plans to build a new multimodal hub in the Kazakh city of Aktau and develop up to 14 terminals along the Middle Corridor. This network will link Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan and Türkiye, and connect the route to the company's infrastructure in Europe.
German logistics giant Rhenus Group is set to roll out a network of up to 14 terminals along the Middle Corridor, also known as the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR), with a new trimodal container terminal in Aktau.
For European businesses, the expansion could provide more capacity and more reliable transport links with Asian suppliers and markets. The European Commission said in September that it aimed to mobilise up to €12 billion in public and private investment in the Middle Corridor, with the goal of tripling trade flows and cutting freight transit times by 2030.
Rhenus is working with Kazakhstan’s national railway operator (KTZ) and the Port of Aktau to develop a new multimodal logistics hub on the Caspian Sea.
"Overall, we want to build 14 terminals along the Middle Corridor, from Uzbekistan through Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan to Türkiye. We then want to connect them to our network in Europe, where we already have 23 container ports and around 70 port facilities," said Tobias Bartz, CEO and Chairman of the Management Board of Rhenus Group.
According to the Kazakh Ministry of Trade and Integration, freight traffic along the Trans-Caspian trade route increased up to 62%, and container traffic rose to 2.7 times, reaching 56,500 TEU between 2025 and 2025.
Container traffic along the Middle Corridor reached 76,900 TEU in 2025, up 36% from 2024, according to the route’s international association.
The planned terminal will connect sea, rail and road transport, span at least 30 hectares and add annual handling capacity of at least 150,000 TEU — almost twice the corridor’s reported container traffic in 2025. The project is moving into the next phase, in which partners will carry out a traffic-flow analysis and a feasibility study.
"Kazakhstan plays a key role in connecting China, Central Asia, the Caspian region and Europe. The next joint steps with our partners are therefore important building blocks in our long-term commitment to the region," Bartz added.
Thus, the project seeks to integrate separate national infrastructure along the Middle Corridor into a unified commercial logistics network.
Rhenus Group expands its network in Central Asia
The Aktau project is not Rhenus’ only investment in the region. In January 2026, the company acquired its first rail terminal in the Almaty region. The facility provides container storage, bonded warehousing and block-train handling.
In Uzbekistan, Rhenus plans to invest around €11 million in modernising a terminal in Andijan with the state railway company.
The terminal is expected to handle around 200,000 TEU a year.

The suspects are believed to include the two alleged burglars, who reportedly broke into the museum at dawn by cutting through a fence.
After a major manhunt, at least five people have been arrested in France in connection with the theft of four artworks from the Renoir Museum on 8 September.
The two suspected burglars are believed to be among those arrested.
French newspaper Nice-Matin, which first reported the arrests, said the suspects could be linked to an organised criminal gang.
The theft took place at dawn on 8 September, when a group of thieves described as "well-equipped" and "well-informed" broke into the museum through its gardens, according to the town’s mayor, Bryan Masson.
They sliced through a fence and entered the museum through the ground floor by smashing a window, and then cut the clips securing the artwork frames with an electric saw, Masson said in remarks carried out by local broadcaster Ici Azur.
According to Masson, the pair were "spotted thanks to the town's video surveillance cameras". Initial reports estimated the stolen haul to be worth up to €9 million euros.
In a written statement obtained by the AP news agency, two of the stolen works were found left in the museum garden as the thieves fled from police who had been alerted by the alarm. But the two others - Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (1910), and Young Woman at the Well (1886) - are still missing.
The Renoir Museum, located between Cannes and Nice, is the Mediterranean coastal town most famous attraction. Open since 1960, it was the painter's last home before his death in 1919 from pulmonary congestion when he was 78-years old.

Intense diplomatic manoeuvring in Athens over first Russian team in European tournament
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:32:32 UTC
18:32:32 KST

The Kazan club was the first Russian club to play an official European club match in Greece, after discreet pressure to keep Russian symbols out of the Serafio pool.
According to information obtained by Euronews, the presence of the Russian club Sintez Kazan in the qualifying group of the Euro Cup in water polo, hosted by Apollon Smyrnis at the Serafeio Swimming Pool of the City of Athens, was accompanied by intense diplomatic manoeuvring behind the scenes.
This tournament marked the official return of Russian teams to European cross-border sports competitions, after their abrupt removal when Russia launched its invasion of Ukraine. The draw carried out by the European confederation meant that this comeback would take place in Greece.
This, however, did not go unnoticed by the Greek government, which at the same time is participating in the EU's collective sanctions against Moscow. Because of those sanctions, the Russian team was unable to find a direct flight to Athens or to any destination in the European Union.
No national anthems played
The issue reached the Greek Ministry of Foreign Affairs, which issued guidance both for heightened but discreet security measures and for keeping Russian flags out of the Serafeio Swimming Pool, as well as any playing of the Russian national anthem. This obstacle was overcome by the decision not to play any national anthem at all, not even the Greek one, but only club anthems such as that of the hosts Apollon Smyrnis.
No mention of the countries of origin of the teams was made on the tournament poster, a deliberate move, although no one hid that "we are talking about Russia's comeback to aquatics".
Inside the pool, behind one of the goals, there was a row of flags (including those of the City of Athens, Apollon Smyrnis and several countries such as Greece, Germany and Israel, but not Russia).
The Greek government confirmed to Euronews that it was assured not only that there would be no Russian symbols in the arena, but also that the Kazan team would compete as a neutral side, as had been the case for Russian teams and athletes in aquatics up until last summer.
However, that regime has changed, and Russia can now be represented in full, according to European Aquatics. That is why on its official website (source in Greek), Kazan is explicitly listed as representing Russia, with the colours of the Russian flag also displayed.
Change of stance towards Russia
Last July, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) itself changed its stance towards Russia and largely relaxed the sporting sanctions against it, while clarifying that the final decision for each sport would be taken by the respective sports federation.
Since then, some federations have proceeded to lift sanctions (for example, judo, wrestling and others), while there are also those, such as athletics, that continue to ban Russian athletes from taking part, prompting Moscow to challenge this ban at the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS).
The World Aquatics federation, in contrast to the athletics body, was one of the first to move towards lifting sanctions on Russians, as early as 13 April (source in Greek), well before the IOC issued its well-known recommendation.
World Aquatics thus became the first major Olympic federation to fully scrap the political exclusion guidelines that had been in place since 2022, following the Russian invasion of Ukraine.
Its board decided to fully restore the membership rights of Russia and Belarus, on the grounds that "sport must stay out of political conflicts". The decision provided for a complete return, even allowing the use of national symbols (jerseys, flags, anthems), provided the national federations comply with the regulations.
The European Aquatics Federation reacted to the immediate application of this new statute and, at the end of April, officially requested from World Aquatics a postponement or delay (source in Greek) in its implementation. It argued that it wanted to protect the European summer events and avoid upending their planning, which is why athletes who competed then did so under neutral and independent status.
It was decided that no Russian athlete or team would return with full national symbols before 1 September 2026. After the extension expired, from 1 September, the new European Aquatics framework came into force, under which at youth level Russian athletes and teams compete without any restrictions, while at senior level Russian clubs are allowed to enter European club competitions but their athletes and staff are required, for the duration of the matches, to retain the status of Approved Neutral Athlete.
Sport federations divided
In this way, on Thursday night, Sintez Kazan became the first club in a team sport to play in an official international competition since the start of the war in Ukraine, openly representing Russia.
It was drawn in the group that Apollon Smyrnis is hosting at the Serafeio, and faced Partizan Belgrade, losing 14-13. Over the weekend, it will play German side Duisburg, Italian club Savona and the hosts Apollon Smyrnis.
European federations in football (UEFA), basketball (FIBA), handball (EHF), volleyball (CEV) and ice hockey have not taken similar steps to lift restrictions.
Only last week, CEV decided to allow Russian national teams back into its competitions in both indoor volleyball and beach volleyball, but it did not take a corresponding decision regarding Russian clubs in European tournaments.
"We had been absent from the European stage for a long time and that added an extra burden, a responsibility, because we knew we were the first Russian team in such a long time to represent Russia. Unfortunately, we lost our opener against Partizan, but I believe we have the ability to win the next matches and qualify for the next phase", Kazan goalkeeper Pyotr Fedotov told Euronews.
From the qualifying group being staged in Athens, three of the five participating teams will advance to the next phase. Hosts Apollon Smyrnis have already laid the foundations to be one of them after their emphatic 16-9 victory over Duisburg in the opening game.

Navanethem ‘Navi’ Pillay wins Nobel peace prize
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:32:14 UTC
18:32:14 KST

The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza.
The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”.
“Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career,” the committee said, mentioning her early work defending Nelson Mandela under South Africa’s apartheid regime, serving on international criminal tribunal, and then as the UN high commissioner for human rights, as well as chairing the UN independent international commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory.
That commission concluded last year that the state of Israel was guilty of genocidal acts in Gaza “with the specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza”, and said the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, its president, Isaac Herzog, and its former defence minister Yoav Gallant had “incited the commission of genocide”.
“It is clear that there is an intent to destroy the Palestinians in Gaza through acts that meet the criteria set forth in the genocide convention,” Pillay said on the publication of the commission’s findings in September last year.
Israel refused to cooperate with the commission, arguing it was biased, and rejected its report as “scandalous”. The Israeli foreign ministry reacted furiously to news of Pillay’s award on Friday.
“If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a frontrunner,” the ministry said on X, adding: “Awarding Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize isn’t a recognition of justice. It’s the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice.
“Now that the Nobel commission has rewarded the biggest lie of the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell.”
In its statement, the Nobel committee said Pillay, 85, had “contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law”.
“Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time,” the committee said.
“In awarding this year’s Nobel peace prize, the Norwegian Nobel committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently,” its statement said.
The committee said it had not been able to locate Pillay before its announcement on Friday morning. She was attending a meeting of human rights lawyers and jurists in Nuremberg, Germany, at the site of postwar war crimes trials of Nazi leaders, and heard the news from colleagues. She responded in disbelief.
“I don’t know about it so much. The question is: is it true? Being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify it,” she said.
“The last thing I did was the report on Gaza naming what’s happening there as genocide,” Pillay added. “One of the main reactions to that report was people [complimented] me for my courage. You can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth. You interpret the law. You look at all the facts, so it’s an impartial decision.”
Pillay is currently overseeing a genocide case against Myanmar at the ICJ.
South Africa’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, said: “Justice Pillay’s crowning as winner of the Nobel Prize allows us to celebrate the progressive contributions she has made to strengthen peace, uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally.”
Edwin Cameron, a retired South African constitutional court justice, said: “The award of the Prize to Navi Pillay re-emphasises that the prize embodies an international aspiration to peace, and to respect and understanding across borders – and that leaders of great stature in our country – [Desmond] Tutu, Mandela, now Pillay – are recognised outside it, on the international stage.
“This may help reset our national debate on South Africa’s position in the region, and in Africa,” he said.
Yasmin Sooka, a human rights lawyer and commissioner on both South Africa and Sierra Leone’s truth and reconciliation commissions, said Pillay “follows in the footsteps of Chief Albert Luthuli and Archbishop Desmond Tutu, carrying forward South Africa’s proud tradition of linking peace with justice and human dignity”.
“From defending apartheid’s most vulnerable to her pioneering role in the Akayesu judgment, she has transformed international justice. That judgment helped establish rape and sexual violence as weapons of war – a historic breakthrough that placed survivors’ experiences at the heart of international justice,” Sooka said.
In 1998, the international criminal tribunal for Rwanda found Jean-Paul Akayesu, a former mayor of Taba, guilty of genocide and crimes against humanity.
“At the ICC, as UN high commissioner for human rights, and leading the inquiry that found Israel responsible for genocide in Gaza, she has brought unwavering integrity and courage to holding power accountable,” Sooka added.
Last year’s award of the peace prize to the Venezuelan opposition leader, María Corina Machado, drew widespread criticism because of her calls for US military intervention in her country. Machado heightened the controversy in January by handing her winner’s medal to Donald Trump. The prize committee insisted that the honour of being a Nobel laureate could not be transferred.
On Monday, Pillay joked that she could do the same: “If you clap a little bit more, I’m going to share this prize with Trump.”

Ministry of Finance can eliminate the ambiguity in the interpretation of aircraft leasing, due to which the BEB is prosecuting airlines — lawyer
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:30:25 EEST
18:30:25 KST

Ministry of Finance can eliminate the ambiguity in the interpretation of aircraft leasing, due to which the BEB is prosecuting airlines — lawyer
Kyiv • UNN
A general tax consultation from the Ministry of Finance could eliminate the ambiguity in the interpretation of aircraft leasing. The ministry should also resolve existing disputes.
The Ministry of Finance of Ukraine has legally established mechanisms for resolving discrepancies concerning the taxation of aircraft leasing from non-residents. A generalized tax consultation would ensure a uniform approach to interpreting such transactions and protect taxpayers from sanctions and criminal prosecution. Sviatoslav Bolinskyi, CEO of the Bolinskyi and Team law firm and an attorney, expressed this view in an exclusive comment to UNN.
The Ministry of Finance may resolve the ambiguity in the interpretation of aircraft leasing
The problem of taxing leasing payments by Ukrainian airlines to non-residents remains unresolved despite complaints from aviation industry representatives about pressure from the Economic Security Bureau. As UNN previously reported, in 2024 the ESB began to interpret payments for the use of leased aircraft as royalties, which served as grounds for initiating criminal proceedings against at least five airlines. Investigators independently changed the interpretation of the transactions without corresponding amendments to tax legislation or international conventions on the avoidance of double taxation.
Representatives of the aviation industry point out that aircraft leasing is a global practice and that no country interprets it as royalties. To resolve the situation, they approached the Ministry of Finance of Ukraine, which, as the regulator, can put an end to differing interpretations of the legislation. The Ministry of Finance agreed to develop a generalized tax consultation to resolve the problem. The Ukrainian Air Transport Association has now established a working group to prepare specific examples of the incorrect interpretation of leasing transactions and develop a draft generalized tax consultation, which it plans to submit to the ministry by October 14.
According to lawyer Sviatoslav Bolinskyi, the Ministry of Finance has the necessary powers to ensure legal certainty on this issue.
"In accordance with the Regulation on the Ministry of Finance of Ukraine, approved by Resolution No. 375 of the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine dated August 20, 2014, the Ministry of Finance is the central executive body responsible, among other things, for formulating and implementing unified state tax and customs policy, as well as state policy in the field of combating offenses in the application of tax and customs legislation," the lawyer noted.
He explained that the legislation provides for a special mechanism to eliminate ambiguities in the application of tax provisions, namely, a generalized tax consultation (GTC).
In particular, pursuant to Ministry of Finance Order No. 811 dated September 27, 2017, grounds for providing such a consultation may include circumstances indicating ambiguity in certain provisions of tax legislation. In the case of aircraft leasing, the ambiguity lies in the fact that, until 2024, tax and law enforcement authorities had raised no claims regarding aircraft leasing and had not attempted to interpret these transactions as royalties.
Thus, the Ministry of Finance has the tools to regulate issues related to the interpretation of aircraft leasing and the relevant payments, as well as their legal nature, through the instrument of a generalized tax consultation, which is approved by an order
This is not about the need to adopt a new law or amend the Tax Code, but about establishing a uniform approach to applying the provisions already in force, including with consideration of international treaties ratified by Ukraine.
A tax consultation can protect airlines from fines
An important aspect of a generalized tax consultation is the guarantees provided by the Tax Code for taxpayers who act in accordance with its provisions.
According to Bolinskyi, after the relevant GTC is approved by an order of the Ministry of Finance, taxpayers who follow it in their activities receive legally defined protection from liability for the respective actions.
If the order has been issued, in such a case the taxpayer (tax agent and/or its official) who acted in accordance with the general tax consultation may not be held liable, including financially (penalties and/or late-payment interest), for acts containing signs of a tax offense, in particular on the grounds that the tax consultation was subsequently amended or revoked
Thus, the adoption of a general tax consultation could become an important safeguard against new claims by tax or law enforcement authorities. Airlines will receive clear tax rules for leasing transactions, while government bodies will have a single guideline for applying the relevant provisions of the law.
At the same time, the consultation itself does not change the provisions of the Tax Code or international treaties, but should explain the procedure for applying them.
According to Sviatoslav Bolinskyi, the key question is whether the detectives of the Economic Security Bureau will pay attention to the Ministry of Finance's clarification.
Therefore, in Bolinskyi's opinion, it is important that, when preparing the general tax consultation, the Ministry of Finance take into account the need to regulate the situation not only for the future, but also with regard to transactions from previous years.
At the same time, it is apparently possible for the Ministry of Finance to issue a general tax consultation and extend its effect to a situation that arose earlier, but whether the Ministry of Finance will provide for this remains to be seen
The consultation may contain clarifications of provisions that were in effect at the time the payments were made; however, this does not mean the automatic termination of criminal proceedings or the reversal of decisions adopted earlier. That is why it is fundamentally important for the aviation industry that, when preparing the general tax consultation, the Ministry of Finance take into account not only future transactions but also existing tax disputes.
