South African jurist who accused Israel of enocide wins Nobel Peace Prize
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:30:01 UTC
18:30:01 KST

The Nobel Peace Prize will be awarded to Navi Pillay, a South African jurist who served as the fifth United Nations high commissioner for human rights, the selection committee announced Friday in Oslo. Pillay also served as president of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and as a judge on the International Criminal Court. She is known for her harsh criticism of Israel, which she has accused, among other things, of war crimes and crimes against humanity.
Following the announcement, Pillay was greeted with cheers and applause. She responded jokingly, "If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump." According to the committee, Pillay was honored for her exceptional courage and integrity in advancing a more comprehensive international legal order. The committee also credited her with helping ensure the prosecution of war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide.
Pillay recently chaired the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the "Occupied Palestinian Territory." In September 2025, the commission issued a report concluding that "Israel is responsible for the commission of genocide in Gaza." The 72-page report said there were "reasonable grounds" to conclude that Israel had committed four of the five acts listed under the Genocide Convention since the start of the Gaza war: killing members of a group, causing serious bodily or mental harm, deliberately imposing conditions intended to bring about the group's destruction and imposing measures intended to prevent births within the group.
The commission also concluded that President Isaac Herzog, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant had "incited the commission of genocide."
Pillay accused senior Israeli officials of seeking to establish permanent military control over Gaza and alter its demographic composition. She warned that the objectives of ethnic cleansing and establishing settlements in Gaza remained in place.
She also condemned Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich's plan to annex 82% of the West Bank and Netanyahu's approval of the E1 settlement expansion, describing the plans as "abhorrent" and saying they "must be condemned widely."
Israel's Foreign Ministry condemned the decision to award Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize.
"If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a frontrunner," the ministry wrote on X. "Her role in the relentless, politically motivated demonization of Israel and promotion of the genoLIE speaks volumes."
"Awarding Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize isn’t a recognition of justice. It’s the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice," the ministry added. "Now that the Nobel commission has rewarded the biggest lie of the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell.
The Nobel Peace Prize has been awarded since 1901 under the terms of the will of Alfred Nobel, the inventor of dynamite. Unlike the other categories of the prestigious Nobel Prizes, whose winners are selected by Swedish committees, the Peace Prize is awarded by a separate committee whose members are appointed by the Norwegian Parliament, as Nobel stipulated in his will.Recipients are selected according to the criteria set out in Nobel's 1895 will, which states that the prize should go to the person who has done "the most or the best work for fraternity between nations, for the abolition or reduction of standing armies and for the holding and promotion of peace congresses." This year's prize is worth 12 million Swedish kronor, approximately $1.2 million.
Thousands of people are eligible to submit nominations for the Nobel Peace Prize, including government officials, lawmakers, current heads of state, university professors in fields such as history, social sciences, law and philosophy and previous Nobel Peace Prize winners. This year, 287 candidates were nominated, but their identities will remain confidential for 50 years.
As in the previous year, President Donald Trump was among the nominees, although this time he did not exert as much pressure in his bid to win the prize as he did last year.
"I don't know what their decision is going to be," he said Wednesday. "They have a reputation for maybe not giving it to people like me."
Last year's prize went to Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado for her struggle to promote democracy in her country. Later, after the United States captured Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, she presented Trump with her Nobel medal. The gesture did not help her, however, as the American president subsequently chose to back Maduro's vice president, Delcy Rodríguez, who now serves as president and is cooperating with his administration. Machado remains unable to return to her country.
Both individuals and organizations are eligible for the Nobel Peace Prize. Recent recipients include a Japanese organization campaigning for global nuclear disarmament, imprisoned Iranian women's rights activist Narges Mohammadi and human rights activists from Belarus, Russia and Ukraine.
The most recent sitting head of government to receive the prize was Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, who won in 2019 for his efforts to reconcile with Eritrea. His country subsequently descended into a bloody internal conflict.
Nobel Prize week began Monday with the announcement of the winners in medicine: Prof. Karl Deisseroth of the United States and professors Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel of Germany, who were honored for their research into the "switch" that turns nerve cells in the brain on and off using flashes of light.
On Tuesday, the Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to American scientist Francis Louis Halzen, who discovered a new way to detect one of the most elusive particles, the neutrino, using a detector built in Antarctica.
On Wednesday, Henri Boris Kagan of France and Kenso Soai of Japan were announced as the winners of the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
On Thursday, Canadian poet and essayist Anne Carson won the Nobel Prize in Literature.
The winner of the Nobel Prize in Economics will be announced Monday.

A New Mexico Community Was a Place to Build a Life. Then a Hypersonic Missile Factory Showed Up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Sally Schultz thought she had struck gold when she purchased land in Rio Rancho Estates, an unincorporated, census-designated community just outside the city of Rio Rancho, New Mexico. A single mother of four, Schultz came there following a divorce to build a homestead of her own and finally gain some stability in her life.
For $3,500, she was able to purchase half an acre for her trailer in a rural area located close to numerous elementary schools and parks. In a relatively short time, she was able to coax crops like corn, squash, and green chile from the ground. This cheap land became Schultz’s haven, giving her a second chance at life.
Then a missile company showed up next door.
“We’ve already been through so much,” she says, “and now we have to leave. It is the unknowing that is scariest.”
Castelion, a startup founded in November 2022 by three former SpaceX executives, is building Project Ranger, which it claims will be America’s “largest dedicated hypersonic manufacturing production facility.” Construction is set to be complete by the end of the year.
The company’s chosen site for its mega-campus is, in some cases, it appears, a little more than 1,000 yards away from roughly 450 properties in Rio Rancho Estates, including Schultz’s. That puts the homes squarely within a danger zone should any explosive chemicals stored onsite catch fire.
A year into Castelion’s relationship with the state of New Mexico, the company—which declined to speak with WIRED for this story—still hasn’t answered basic safety questions, even as an official hazard assessment found buildings would simply be left to burn in the case of fire, releasing hydrochloric acid gas into the air. Emails between the company and Rio Rancho officials reviewed by WIRED also show Castelion was negotiating fire safety standards even after construction was well underway.
“I live next door to where World War III will be manufactured,” says local resident Laura Lundberg.
Big Plans
Castelion has become a bit of a darling among the new wave of defense tech startups. The company has recently hit a valuation of $13 billion—more than four times its Series B valuation of $2.8 billion from last year.
It has received over $500 million in US military contracts in just 18 months, swiftly securing its spot as one of the “Arsenal of Freedom” suppliers.
The firm touts its ability to make hypersonic missiles—a label for any missile flying at five times the speed of sound or higher—at a lower cost than its competitors. The US Army’s Dark Eagle is the most mature domestic hypersonic weapon, and it costs an estimated $41 million per missile, according to a 2023 Congressional Budget Office study. Castelion’s main product, Blackbeard, is a solid-rocket-powered missile that was set to sell for $384,000 per unit.
In reality, the missiles are looking as if they will turn out pricier than initially advertised.
Castelion kicked off the year with a nearly $50 million Navy contract to build full-scale prototypes of its Blackbeard missile. By June, the Navy expanded the effort, adding another $23.4 million to supply the first 50 operational Blackbeard prototypes. Then, in August, the Navy doubled down with another $90 million contract to cover manufacturing services for the same 50 Blackbeards—pushing the total to $163.4 million for 50 missiles, or $3.3 million per unit.
And most recently, in September, the Navy awarded Castelion the company’s largest contract yet—up to $200 million.
Recently, Castelion released the first photo of its Blackbeard hypersonic strike missile, but concrete performance figures for Blackbeard remain hidden. Castelion has not publicly released any test data to verify its weapon’s efficacy.
Project Ranger will become Castelion’s biggest manufacturing and testing hub. The company broke ground on the 1,000-acre facility on January 21, and it’s targeting mass production as early as next year.
The facility wasn’t always supposed to be in New Mexico, though.
Unredacted
In August 2023, the company applied to build a rocket factory in Churchill County, Nevada, under a different name—Pallas Industrials. Chief financial officer Andrew Kreitz signed a special use application, which disclosed the company’s plans to build rocket motors and ground-test them up to eight days a month at the site.
In response to the application, Churchill County officials provided eight pages of staff analysis and required the company to provide testing conditions and safety protocols. Not long afterward, Pallas Industrials pulled out of Nevada under the new name: Castelion. A few months later, the company began testing the soil in western Rio Rancho.
Rio Rancho Estates residents say that by the time they started noticing soil-probing trucks in the spring of 2025, Castelion was already in a conversation with New Mexico officials about using the land for the missile factory.
In June 2025, Sandia National Labs delivered a hazard report as part of the New Mexico Small Business Assistance Program, originally intended to help local small businesses access the expertise of Los Alamos and Sandia National Laboratories at absolutely no cost.
Under the Freedom of Information Act, Sandia later released a heavily redacted version of the report. Instead of scrubbing the underlying data layer of the file, the lab simply put black ink highlight over black text, leaving the full unredacted report accessible via copying and pasting.
The report alleges Castelion’s plans to build and operate the missile factory present significant risks.
It identifies a massive “storage facility fire” as the worst-case scenario. Castelion is set to store colossal stockpiles of propellants on Project Ranger’s site. The company has publicly stated its plans of working with at least one heat-sensitive chemical oxidizer—ammonium perchlorate—and storing up to 250,000 pounds inside covered magazines and bunkers, according to the Sandia report. But outside those bunkers, the report notes, Castelion is allowed to keep up to 81,000 pounds of active explosive material at a time inside the hazardous integration facilities during the assembly process.
A detonation of the facility’s largest allowed stockpile of explosive material would require a buffer from the nearest inhabited building of almost nine football fields in length. Sandia calculated that a worst-case explosion could shatter large windows as far as almost four miles away and have a 3.2 percent chance of causing minor eardrum damage to people 400 yards from the detonation.
Sandia declined to provide comment for WIRED. One of the hazard reports authors, Meg Davidson, has since left Sandia Labs and is now a senior manager of strategic partnerships at Castelion. She did not respond to requests for comment.
The report identifies a fire at the test stand as “the most probable foreseeable hazardous event.” A chemical fire would release a toxic haze containing byproducts like hydrogen chloride and chlorine. In gas form, both are highly corrosive and can cause severe eye, skin, and respiratory tract burns. Even short-term inhalation at high concentrations can cause chemical lung damage and asphyxiation.
Emails obtained through public records requests reveal that the Rio Rancho Fire Department determined 17 of the 26 buildings at the Project Ranger site would be left to burn if a fire ignited, due to the risks a chemical blaze would pose first responders. Firefighters would be barred from even entering the high-risk facilities.
Such events are hardly unheard of. WIRED reported on a June incident at Anduril’s Mississippi facility where a test run of an ammonium perchlorate–based rocket motor ended in an explosion. The blast—which didn’t cause any casualties—underscored the technical risks of scaling solid propellant production.
In May, a storage tank holding approximately 7,000 gallons of methyl methacrylate, a flammable liquid used to manufacture acrylic plastics and resins for military and commercial aircraft, began to overheat at a GKN Aerospace plant in Garden Grove, California, leading local authorities to evacuate more than 40,000 residents.
Despite these warnings, internal emails obtained through public records requests reveal that Castelion was still negotiating critical fire-response requirements between March and May—even as construction had already started.
Castelion’s site developer, Bryce Barlow, wrote to the city on March 23 that the company had not yet finalized the fire-flow response, offering to discuss the question by phone or in person instead.
After a few weeks, the requirements were replaced by city manager Matt Geisel with a statement that hard numbers would appear in the plans later on. Castelion only needed a signed memorandum of understanding to proceed—backed by the governing body’s resolution and a serviceability letter.
“Great news! Saves all of us both legal bills and headaches,” Kreitz wrote in response.
‘A Done Deal’
In August 2025, prior to Castelion’s formal announcement that it had selected New Mexico, Republican state senator Jay Block appeared before the Sandoval County Commission to speak in support of financing Project Ranger. Before becoming state senator, Block was a county commissioner.
The county had approved $125 million in industrial revenue bonds and had passed a resolution giving itself control over the state land picked for the site. The commissioners granted an astounding 95 percent discount on what Castelion would normally owe in property taxes. Finally, the county agreed to abate compensating taxes on out-of-state equipment, lowering the upfront costs for the incoming missile manufacturer to relocate to New Mexico.
Block’s district includes Rio Rancho as of January.
“I strongly supported Project Ranger as it moved through the local approval process, because I believed Rio Rancho and Sandoval County had the workforce, infrastructure, and defense heritage to help Castelion succeed,” Block tells WIRED.
Castelion held its first public information meeting on Project Ranger in October 2025.
“All of this happened behind the scenes. By the time it was public, it was already a done deal,” says Zachary Darden, a Rio Rancho resident who ran an unsuccessful bid for mayor on a platform opposing the development.
In November, emails show Alberto Solís, Rio Rancho’s economic development manager, coordinated Castelion CFO Kreitz’s four-day trip to New Mexico—part of the outreach process required by the state. The CFO asked to attend a Chamber of Commerce “Jingle Mingle” mixer and an event with the Sandoval Economic Alliance, a local nonprofit tasked with recruiting new business to the county.
More than a month after Kreitz’s networking trip, Castelion held its groundbreaking ceremony. Local residents weren’t invited, but many of the state’s most prominent political and business figures were. Block was there as well as US senator Martin Heinrich. So were Gregg Hull, Rio Rancho’s then mayor and Republican candidate for governor, as well as Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham. County and state economic development officials were also in attendance.
“Castelion's Project Ranger shows what a strong public-private partnership can deliver for a local community,” Rob Black, New Mexico’s secretary of economic development, tells WIRED.
Residents living next to the site, though, are contemplating whether the risks are too high to stay. But for most living in Rio Rancho Estates—a low-income neighborhood—the costs of relocation might be too high.
“This land is affordable for people who need it,” says community member Jason Clifford. “We were sold out by our local officials.”

UK's Prince Harry says he fell into depression as he weighed royal future
LONDON, Oct 9 - Britain's Prince Harry fell into depression when he took a break from royal duties in 2019 before he formally stepped down, he told a videocast about grief, where he also discussed feeling "emotionally numb" after his mother died.
Harry, the younger son of King Charles, has been open about his mental health struggles and how the sudden death of his mother Princess Diana in a car crash when he was 12 has affected his life.
"I'd spent so long emotionally numb to a large extent because nobody told me joy was still allowed," he said on a Masterclass videocast called "Redefining Grief: Building Resilience Through Loss".

French student protesters vow to keep up their fight after scoring first win

Unknown Publisher

French student protesters vow to keep up their fight after scoring first win
PARIS, Oct 9 - French student unions vowed on Friday to keep up protests after scoring what they called their first win in a campaign that is increasingly supported by Paris' elite universities, with 141 schools still shut around the country.
The protests have snowballed into a wider movement, with more university students weighing in to express their anger over what they call a dysfunctional system, worsened by spending cuts spurred by France's budget crunch.
Student and teacher unions have called for another round of nationwide school strikes next Tuesday.
France's education ministry is in the process of urgently contacting around 3,000 spare teachers who could be sent to schools with the most pressing needs, often located in low-income areas, Education Minister Edouard Geffray said.
Speaking during a visit to a school in the Paris region that was vandalised during protests, he said more than 100 teaching staff had been injured so far in the nationwide protests.
The movement has fueled similar student protests in Belgium, which on Friday were amplified by a national strike during which scuffles broke out between protesters and police in Brussels.
ELITE UNIVERSITIES ARE WEIGHING IN
Police cleared a blockade at Assas university, a top French law school in central Paris, on Friday morning. Nearby, elite engineering school Mines Paris was also disrupted by blockades.
The Institut Catholique, a private university known for being particularly conservative, said on its website it would switch to remote classes due to a blockade of its campus.
Student unions meanwhile hailed what they see as their first real win, after the government late on Thursday pledged to send some 3,000 teachers, who are fully qualified but have not yet started work, to fill staffing gaps, one of the protesters' main grievances.
The move, which the government called an "emergency plan", shows it is worthwhile for students to continue their protests, Marius Mesnil, from a high school student union, told Franceinfo radio.
"I find it crazy we need to block hundreds of high schools just to get a vacancy plan," he added.
The measure is effective immediately and will cost "several dozen million euros", Geffray told broadcaster TF1 late on Thursday.
MARKETS MONITORING GOVERNMENT RESPONSE TO PROTESTS
Three weeks into the protest, President Emmanuel Macron's government is struggling to work out how to balance demands for more education spending with the need to rein in public debt.
Investors are closely watching the government's next moves in a highly indebted country where street anger has often been tamed with more state spending. This time, France's large pension outlays and its need to rein in public spending leave little room for manoeuvre.
Stephane Boujnah, the head of Euronext, which runs the Paris stock market, said Paris urgently needed to make tough choices.
"What sacrifice are we asking of our own children? ... maybe we need to spend a little less on pensions so that we have a little more money for the children," he told RMC radio.
Nearly 10% of teaching hours are unstaffed at French state high schools, according to education ministry figures, prompting a growing number of wealthier parents to abandon the public sector in favour of private schooling, a trend that some experts say will only reinforce social inequality.
"Let's be frank, families are leaving public schools for our institutions," said Pierre-Vincent Gueret, who heads France's federation of Catholic private schools.
The interior ministry said 71,500 people took to the streets in Paris and elsewhere on Thursday. While most protests were peaceful, violence flared up in some places.
In Belgium, meanwhile, students joined demonstrations alongside striking workers as the country's two largest labour unions staged a national strike on Friday, disrupting public transport, air travel and other sectors.
Thousands of people marched through central Brussels in a protest that was largely peaceful, although some scuffles broke out with police, who used tear gas and water cannons in some instances.
One banner carried by student protesters read: "I skipped class to defend class." REUTERS

"HK$27.6 is equivalent to the fare for Route B13 alone.”  
Ma added that the company has partnered with Alipay to offer a HK$2 voucher to passengers.  
New Lantao Bus will operate a daytime route connecting the port to Wu Kai Sha MTR station.
In addition to franchised buses, six green minibus routes, including three overnight services, and five 24-hour cross-boundary coach routes will serve the crossing.

In Rivne region, a 14-year-old girl will stand trial for the contract killing of a serviceman on behalf of Russia
Kyiv • UNN
In Rivne region, the case of a 14-year-old girl accused of killing a serviceman on the instructions of Russian special services has been sent to court. She is also charged with setting fire to a military vehicle.
In the Rivne region, the investigation into the case of a 14-year-old girl accused of murdering a serviceman of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on the orders of Russian special services has been completed. This was reported by the Rivne region police, UNN writes.
The 14-year-old resident of Rivne, while communicating via video link with her handler, first poisoned the victim with a mixture of alcohol and a narcotic substance on his direct instructions, and then strangled him. The accused is currently being held in a pre-trial detention center
The pre-trial investigation established that the minor met a citizen of the Russian Federation on the Telegram messenger. Acting on the instructions of an employee of the FSB of the Russian Federation, he commissioned the girl to murder a Ukrainian serviceman by poisoning him with methadone. Since the minor had feelings for the handler, he promised to arrange for her departure to territory controlled by the enemy after she completed the task.
Thus, on January 30, the suspect arrived at a rented apartment, where she poured previously prepared alcohol into glasses and added a narcotic substance that she had received from the customers through a logistics company.
Later, a 27-year-old serviceman arrived at the residence. She had met him on the messenger 10 days before the crime. After consuming the mixture, he lost consciousness.
While on a video call with her handler, the minor began strangling the serviceman. As a result of mechanical asphyxia, the 27-year-old man died.
Criminal investigation officers promptly detained the perpetrator.
Police investigators notified her that she was suspected of intentional murder committed to order and by a group of persons acting in prior conspiracy. The court imposed pre-trial detention on the suspect.
The pre-trial investigation has been completed, and the indictment on the intentional murder charges has been submitted to the court. The suspect faces up to 15 years in prison.
The investigators of the Rivne region police investigative department have now established the identities of the handler and the organizer of the contract killing. The criminal proceedings against them are currently under the jurisdiction of the regional SBU officers.
It was also established that, on the orders of the Russian Federation, the 14-year-old girl set fire to a military Opel Campo vehicle in Rivne on November 11. She was promised one thousand dollars for the “job,” but she never received the money.
In addition, the SBU investigators were handling criminal proceedings on charges that the minor had committed high treason under martial law, obstructed the lawful activities of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, and intentionally destroyed someone else’s property by arson; these proceedings have also been submitted to the court.

South Africa's Navi Pillay wins Nobel Peace Prize
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:27:13 UTC
18:27:13 KST

FILE - United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights Navanethem Pillay, center, visits Al- Daraj Elementary Co-ed UNRWA school in Gaza City, Feb. 10, 2011. (AP Photo/Adel Hana, File)
The Nobel Peace Prize was awarded on Oct. 9 to South Africa’s Navi Pillay, the judge who last year presided over a U.N. commission which accused Israel of genocide in Gaza and who headed the Rwanda genocide tribunal.
Pillay headed the U.N. Independent International Commission of Inquiry (COI), which does not speak on behalf of the world body, and which last year found that genocide was occurring in Gaza.
Pillay said at the time that her team had shared “thousands of pieces of information” with prosecutors at the International Criminal Court.
Israel categorically rejected the report’s findings, slamming it as “distorted and false.”
The Nobel committee said that while its prize honoured Pillay’s career of fighting genocide, it was not taking a stand on whether Israel’s actions in Gaza constitute a genocide.
“We are not the court,” Frydnes told AFP.
“It’s her report, the Commission’s report... It will be decided by the International Court of Justice,” he said.
Pillay, currently a judge on the International Court of Justice in a case where Myanmar also stands accused of genocide, has been “instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide are prosecuted,” said Jorgen Watne Frydnes, the chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee in Oslo.
“In historic international court cases, she has shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence,” the committee said.
Pillay’s “independence, her expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time.”
She reacted to the news by making a quip about U.S. President Donald Trump’s well-documented desire to win the prize himself.
“If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump,” the 85-year-old said during a standing ovation captured by Amnesty International Secretary General Agnes Callamard in Nuremberg and posted on the social network X.
The U.N. said her prize was a “testament to the need and to the value of human rights in this world more than ever.”
The International Criminal Court, meanwhile, said her award was of “particular significance” given current attacks on international law.
The Nobel committee echoed that sentiment in its statement, noting that “at a time of existential challenges — including more wars and conflicts than the world has seen in a long time — international law is no longer just a supplement to peace and security.”
The prize for Pillay is sure to anger Trump, whose administration has repeatedly attacked international justice institutions.
“This is a clear message to those who are putting pressure on these institutions, to those who are sanctioning the judges and are attacking the institutions. That needs to stop,” Frydnes told AFP after the announcement.
Since returning to the White House in January 2025, Trump has made no secret of his desire to win the prize, insisting that he was the most deserving candidate and claiming to have ended up to eight wars.
“They have a reputation for maybe not giving it to people like me .. and I think it would be a great discredit to them,” Trump said on Oct. 7.
But his war against Iran, his territorial expansion ambitions as in Greenland, his hard line on migrants and his attacks on multilateralism and the media have, according to experts in Oslo, disqualified him for the prize.
Last year, the prize went to Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, a choice generally considered palatable to Trump.
Machado even gave him her Nobel gold medal, judging he deserved it after the capture of President Nicolas Maduro — though she failed to obtain his political backing in exchange.
The Nobel committee has said it is not swayed by external pressures.
“Of course we have to discuss it, but it’s not like that influences the discussions in the room and decisions that come out,” the secretary of the committee, Kristian Berg Harpviken, told AFP ahead of the prize announcement.

Political parties in Türkiye’s parliament have called for tighter controls on civilian gun ownership and stronger measures against online violence as lawmakers seek ways to prevent attacks in schools.
Members of parliament made the proposals on Oct. 8 during a meeting of a parliamentary commission investigating school violence, which is preparing a report on measures to address the problem.
Their talks followed a stabbing at a middle school in Istanbul’s Başakşehir district on Oct. 6, when a 15-year-old student from another school injured eight students, one of whom later died. The incident came after attacks or shootings were reported in the provinces of Şanlıurfa, Kahramanmaraş, Manisa and Osmaniye in recent months.
Several lawmakers argued that easier access to firearms contributes to the risk of violence. Mehmet Ali Cevheri of the ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) said stricter penalties were needed to address public demand for gun licenses, while Suat Özçağdaş of the main opposition New Party called for restrictions on civilian gun ownership.
Beritan Güneş Altın of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) also urged lawmakers to take clear steps to this end, saying schools could address violence by fostering a culture of peace.
Lawmakers also highlighted the role of social media and digital platforms in exposing children to violent content and cyberbullying.
AKP’s İsa Mesih Şahin proposed introducing digital patrol officers within the police force and called for a review of television series, films and other media that may promote violence through their portrayal of role models. Özçağdaş urged the creation of dedicated reporting mechanisms for digital threats and cyberbullying.
Nationalist Movement Party (MHP) lawmaker İbrahim Özyavuz called for stronger legal protections against threats children face online, while İYİ (Good) Party MP Şenol Sunat said the commission should address algorithmic influence, cyberbullying and online radicalization.
Sunat also called for early warning systems to identify risks before violent incidents occur, improved coordination between institutions and stronger guidance and mental health services.
Social media-driven violence and rampant digitalization belong front and center in the commission’s report, according to Özyavuz.

Estonia to recoup €25 million from Nordica's former aircraft lessor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:26:00 UTC
18:26:00 KST

Estonia to recoup €25 million from Nordica's former aircraft lessor
The liquidation of state-owned aircraft lessor Transpordi Varahaldus will put €25 million into Estonia's budget next year following the shutdown of bankrupt airline Nordica.
The government is expected to authorize Infrastructure Minister Kuldar Leis (Reform) to wind up Transpordi Varahaldus in the coming weeks, following its July decision to liquidate the company, which leased aircraft to bankrupt airline Nordica.
The company's seven aircraft and spare parts have been sold, it has no outstanding debts and its bank accounts hold €25 million. Leis said the money will go to the State Treasury, but its eventual use will remain up to the Ministry of Finance.
"It's yet unclear how that money will be used, as that decision rests with the Finance Ministry, which manages the state's cash flow," he explained. "The money won't come with a label attached."
Transpordi Varahaldus also has claims of €35.7 million against Nordica and €27.5 million against its subsidiary Regional Jet, both of which are bankrupt.
Leis said the state will retain these claims and continue seeking repayment until both bankruptcy proceedings are concluded. The claims will be transferred to the state as part of the liquidation, with either the Finance Ministry or the Climate Ministry responsible for managing them.
"We have no intention of giving up these claims," he said. "The state will continue pursuing repayment itself."
According to the minister, the liquidation process is expected to take nine to 12 months, involving routine legal procedures.
Last flight
Nordica ceased operations in March when the last of its seven 88-seat Bombardier CRJ900NG jets departed Tallinn Airport. The aircraft, owned by state-run Transpordi Varahaldus, had been sold to U.S.-based Regional One last June.
The planes had been leased to Nordica subsidiary Regional Jet. Both companies filed for bankruptcy in November 2024, with Nordica declared bankrupt in January 2025 and Regional Jet, which operated under the Xfly brand, following a month later.
Nordica launched in 2015, ahead of the bankruptcy of Estonia's former flag carrier, Estonian Air. It flew under its own name from Tallinn until 2019, then shifted to subcontracting services. Transpordi Varahaldus also began operations in 2015.

MPs from GERB have officially alerted the European Commission over alleged document manipulation at the Road Infrastructure Agency (RIA). According to them, the alleged manipulation is intended to artificially increase the budget deficit for 2025 and reduce the deficit for 2026, BGNES reported.
“Yesterday, we officially alerted the European Commission. Russians forcibly remove 25 Ukrainians from Kharkiv Oblast – Ukrainian human rights commissioner
Russian forces have forcibly removed 25 civilians, including children, from the occupied part of Kharkiv Oblast to an unknown location.
Source: Dmytro Lubinets, Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights, on Telegram
Quote: "Russia calls this an 'evacuation'. But when people are taken away against their will, intimidated and given no choice, this is not rescue. It is coercion.
Russian military personnel unceremoniously removed 25 local residents from the temporarily occupied part of Kharkiv Oblast, where active hostilities are ongoing [Lubinets did not specify the settlement – ed.]. They include young and elderly people, as well as children. The most alarming thing is that no one knows where these people are now or the conditions in which they are being held. What concerns me most in this case is the fate of the children. They are being taken away and their personal details are being collected, while their parents and family members may not even know where they are.
Without the slightest shame, the occupiers themselves reported on the so-called 'rescue operation' on their Telegram channels. But behind the reassuring word 'evacuation' lies a very different reality: people were deprived of the opportunity to decide for themselves where to go and what would happen to them next. Available video footage indicates pressure and intimidation."
Details: Lubinets said the relatives of the 25 people currently do not know where they are.
In addition, Russian forces have already created a Telegram bot through which they collect people's personal details under the guise of a so-called evacuation. Such information could be used against the individuals themselves and their relatives.
"I urge people not to provide passport details, addresses, phone numbers or documents – either their own or their children's – through this bot," Lubinets stressed.
Such actions violate international humanitarian law. The Geneva Convention relative to the Protection of Civilian Persons in Time of War explicitly prohibits:
- forcible transfers and deportations from occupied territory (Article 49)
- the taking of hostages (Article 34)
- intimidation, terrorism and collective punishment (Article 33).
Lubinets said he had already contacted Russia's human rights commissioner, demanding that she:
- disclose the whereabouts of all 25 people
- provide information about the conditions in which they are being held
- provide the full details of the civilians who were removed
- take measures to facilitate their return to Ukraine.
The human rights commissioner has also appealed to the International Committee of the Red Cross, the United Nations and other international organisations for help.

Driving out on a robot: 60th Brigade evacuates two civilians from Lyman – video

Driving out on a robot: 60th Brigade evacuates two civilians from Lyman – video
Soldiers from the 60th Separate Mechanised Brigade have evacuated two civilians – a man and a woman with shrapnel wounds – from under fire in the city of Lyman, Donetsk Oblast, using an unmanned ground vehicle (UGV).
Source: 3rd Army Corps in a comment to Ukrainska Pravda.Zhyttia (Life)
Details: The 3rd Army Corps said that this method was chosen because of the constant threat posed by Russian UAVs in the city.
Lyman is located close to the line of contact, but around 1,500 civilians still remain there.
The high level of danger has made evacuating residents more difficult, as government emergency services and volunteers are unable to reach the city. The military therefore brought in neighbouring units to escort the civilians along the evacuation route.
The operation was led by soldiers from the Cerberus unmanned ground systems company of the 60th Separate Mechanised Brigade. It was carefully planned with weather conditions and the security situation taken into account. An unmanned ground vehicle was used to rescue the man and woman from a dangerous area of Lyman.
The UGV transported them without the need to deploy military personnel directly into the high-risk area. Operators controlled the vehicle remotely throughout the evacuation.
The evacuated woman had injuries to her arm and leg. The previous day, shrapnel from a drone had wounded her in the shoulder, and she had been forced to treat the injury herself.
She and the man were taken to the 60th Separate Mechanised Brigade's stabilisation point, where they received medical assistance. Both civilians are now safe.
Natalka Bahrii, head of the brigade's civil-military cooperation unit, urged residents of frontline areas to evacuate in good time and heed announcements from local authorities. She said doing so would help avoid putting both civilians and soldiers at risk.
The evacuation was carried out under AB3.Humanitarian, the 3rd Army Corps' humanitarian initiative for evacuating civilians from areas of active hostilities.
Background: Earlier, Ukrainian soldiers evacuated 79-year-old Ela Fedorivna and her 86-year-old husband from the outskirts of Orikhiv in Zaporizhzhia Oblast. They had been the only residents remaining in a destroyed neighbourhood of the city.

Natural gas remains top household energy source in Türkiye in 2025
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:23:15 UTC
18:23:15 KST

Turkish households consumed a total of 1.38 million terajoules of final energy in 2025, with natural gas remaining the dominant energy source, according to data released by the Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK) on Oct. 9.
Natural gas accounted for 52.1 percent of total household energy consumption, followed by electricity at 19.3 percent and solid biomass at 13.3 percent.
Space heating remained the largest area of household energy use, representing 62 percent of total energy consumption. Lighting and electrical appliances ranked second with a 16 percent share, while water heating accounted for 12.7 percent.
Energy used for cooking made up 8.2 percent of total consumption, while space cooling and other uses together represented 1 percent.
Natural gas, the most widely consumed energy source, was used primarily for space heating, which accounted for 74.2 percent of total natural gas consumption. Water heating represented 16 percent of natural gas use, while cooking accounted for 9.8 percent.
Electricity consumption was concentrated in lighting and electrical appliances, which made up 83 percent of total electricity use. Space cooling accounted for 5.3 percent and water heating for 4.5 percent.

Greece is the most popular luxury honeymoon destination for 2027 – with Italy and France also in the top 10
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:23:10 UTC
18:23:10 KST

Greece tops the ranking of the world’s most popular honeymoon destinations for 2027 in Virtuoso’s latest Luxe Report, ahead of Bali and the Maldives.
With its romantic sunset spots and stunning islands that are perfect for lazy beach days, there are plenty of reasons why newlyweds would choose Greece for a luxury honeymoon.
Now, Greece has been named the world’s most popular honeymoon destination for 2027 in the latest Virtuoso Luxe Report, ahead of traditional favourites such as Bali and the Maldives, which placed second and third respectively.
On the honeymoon hotlist, Italy takes fourth place and France eighth, putting three European countries among the top 10 destinations for affluent couples planning a post-wedding holiday. French Polynesia, Japan, Fiji, Thailand and South Africa make up the top 10.
Drawing on insights from Virtuoso's global travel agency members, the annual survey of more than 3,100 advisors across more than 50 countries reveals the destinations and behaviours that are “guiding the choices of affluent travellers worldwide”.
Alongside priorities such as celebrating milestones and the excitement of exploring a new destination, honeymoons also ranked sixth among the top 10 motivations for affluent travel in 2027.
“Greece took the top spot for 2027, ending Italy’s long-standing lead, while Italy remained in the top five and France also placed in the top 10,” said Misty Belles, Vice President, Global Public Relations at Virtuoso.
“Together, the results point to strong demand for destinations that combine romance with culture, cuisine and opportunities to build a more varied itinerary beyond the traditional beach escape.”
Why Greece is the leading destination for 2027
As well as ranking first in the 2027 honeymoons list, Greece was also number four on the report’s 10 most popular global destinations for luxury travel overall.
With its combination of “romance, spectacular scenery, exceptional food, history and culture with an impressive range of luxury hotels”, Greece is “almost tailor-made for honeymoons”, said Kayla Zeigler, Founder and Travel Advisor at Destination Europe, an affiliate of Virtuoso.
Speaking to Euronews Travel, Zeigler said that couples are increasingly “looking beyond the traditional Mykonos and Santorini combination”, which have become “much busier and increasingly oriented toward cruise tourism”.
She revealed that newlyweds are now looking for a “more relaxed, authentic” Greek island experience “without sacrificing luxury”, with Paros, Milos and Crete emerging as new favourites.
Other Greek destinations attracting interest include the “exciting development” along the Athens Riviera, she said, with new luxury hotels giving honeymooners “an attractive alternative” to spending their entire stay in Athens city centre.
“Couples can experience the history and energy of Athens and then retreat to the coast before continuing to the islands,” she said.
“Overall, affluent honeymooners still want beautiful hotels and exceptional service, but increasingly they're also looking for authenticity, privacy and a genuine sense of place – a trend reflected in Virtuoso's 2027 findings.”
What are honeymooners looking for in Europe?
Italy and France have long been top choices for honeymoon bookings. Couples making their first trip to Europe still want “iconic destinations” like Rome, Florence and Paris, Zeigler said. But there has been much more interest in combining them with places that feel “more intimate, authentic and less saturated”.
“In Italy, we're increasingly recommending Ischia over Capri for couples visiting the Amalfi Coast region,” she added. “Capri will always be iconic, but Ischia offers beautiful hotels, thermal spas, wonderful food and a more relaxed island experience.
“We're also selling more Piedmont and Umbria in lieu of Tuscany, alternatives to Lake Como among Italy's other beautiful lakes, and Puglia continues to be an up-and-coming favourite, particularly for its masserias, coastline and food.”
The Dolomites are also “having a moment”, offering spectacular scenery, exceptional mountain hotels, wellness and outdoor experiences. “With Venice, this is a wonderful honeymoon combination.”
There’s a similar shift happening in France, Zeigler revealed. “Couples are looking beyond Paris and combining it with Provence, where the villages, markets, vineyards and countryside lend themselves beautifully to a honeymoon, or the French Riviera for a Mediterranean coastal experience”.
Champagne is a “natural fit” for a celebratory trip, while Burgundy and Bordeaux appeal to couples interested in food and wine. “France makes it very easy to combine a few exciting days in Paris with a completely different, slower-paced experience.”
Overall, one of the biggest changes Zeigler is seeing at Destination Europe is the move towards shoulder and off-season travel.
“June and July in southern Europe are becoming increasingly hot and crowded, and we're booking more honeymoons in April and May, as well as October and even into November,” she said. “Depending on the destination, couples can enjoy more comfortable weather, fewer crowds and better value.
“Overall, luxury honeymooners seem less interested in checking off as many destinations as possible and more interested in slowing down, finding places that still have a strong sense of place, and really experiencing Europe together.”
How is the luxury honeymoon evolving?
Honeymooners are becoming more selective about where they splurge, according to Zeigler, and are balancing standout hotel stays with personal experiences.
“We're seeing couples choose a beautiful suite in a smaller boutique hotel – something charming, full of personality and with a real sense of place – over the grand palace hotel, and then use that portion of their budget for unique, private and personal experiences,” she said.
That might mean booking an exceptional suite for a few nights, then choosing more moderately priced boutique properties elsewhere.
Private boat trips, cooking classes, wine tastings and guided tours are increasingly part of the appeal, alongside time to relax and explore together.
Zeigler estimates honeymoons account for around a quarter of her agency’s bookings, with European trips typically lasting 10-14 nights. Longer journeys spanning several cities, regions or countries have also reshaped budgets.
For many experienced travellers, she sees the honeymoon as the start of a lifetime of shared trips, rather than a single grand adventure.
“Luxury today is becoming less about extravagance at every turn and more about choosing where to splurge, creating meaningful experiences and having the time and freedom to enjoy them.”

Prosecution charges three Israeli Bedouins of supplying weapons to 2024 Beersheba station terrorist

18:21:45 KST

Israel's Southern District Attorney's Office filed indictments on Thursday against three Negev residents accused of supplying weapons to the terrorist who carried out the October 2024 attack on the Beersheba Central Bus Station, killing 19-year-old Border Police officer Shira Chaya Suslik and wounding several others.
They were charged with trafficking and possession of weapons and ammunition, as well as providing the means to commit a terrorist act.
This indictment follows an undercover operation in which Border Police arrested the three suspects, who allegedly sold -- or facilitated the sale of -- a pistol and ammunition for the attacker, Ahmad Said Suliman al-Ukabi, a 29-year-old Bedouin Israeli.
The suspects indicted Thursday are Yahya al-Uqbi, a resident of Hura, and two other Bedouin Israelis, a father and a son, one of whom was a minor at the time of the offenses, and neither of whom is named in the police report.
The investigation revealed that some of the suspects were also engaged in other arms trafficking deals with other Negev residents.
At the time of the attack in early October 2024, the Forum of the Heads of the Bedouin Authorities in the Negev strongly condemned it, saying it did not reflect the human or moral values of the Bedouin community and was in complete contradiction with the common principles of life and peace.
They also warned that we should not allow any “extremist party/group” to take advantage of the situation to deepen societal rifts and sow division between the two peoples, and called for increased cooperation and cohesion against terrorism.
Shin Bet uncovers Bedouin terror cell plotting attacks on police station, Beersheba bus station
Also on Thursday, the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) released a statement announcing that a terrorist cell modeled after the Palestinian Battalions of the West Bank was uncovered in the Bedouin community of Segev Shalom.
According to the statement, five suspects were arrested for interrogation in May and June, with the interrogations revealing that Arab Israeli citizens in the Negev planned to establish a terror battalion in the town of Segev Shalom, just outside of Beersheba, in order to carry out acts of terror.
Jonah Davidov, Jerusalem Post Staff, and Yuval Barnea contributed to this report.

Parashat Bereishit: The world of water
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:21:26 UTC
18:21:26 KST

Few things accompany a person wherever they go and throughout every period of life as consistently as rain and water. We are so accustomed to them that we rarely stop to consider the wonder of their existence. Water surrounds us and is within us. It quenches our thirst, nourishes the earth, and makes life possible. Precisely because of this, it is fascinating to discover how central water is to the Jewish world and how much deeper our connection to it is than mere physical necessity.
Water is also the thread that connects the festival of Sukkot, which we recently concluded, with the first Torah portion, Parashat Bereishit, read on the first Shabbat after Sukkot.
Our Sages taught us (Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 1:2) that on Sukkot the world is judged concerning water, and that during the time of the Temple there was great rejoicing over the water libation on the altar. Even the aravah branches that we take on Hoshana Rabbah are connected by their very nature to water, since willow trees grow along riverbanks. And on Shemini Atzeret, the festival that concludes Sukkot, we already begin to pray for rain.
The first thing we see is a world covered in water
WHEN WE open the Book of Bereishit once again, there is a natural continuation of this theme. When the Torah tells us about the beginning of Creation, the first thing it reveals is a world covered in water:
“Now the earth was formless and void, and darkness was upon the face of the deep, and the spirit of God hovered over the face of the waters. And God said, ‘Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide between water and water.’ And God made the firmament and divided between the waters that were beneath the firmament and the waters that were above the firmament, and it was so.”
The world we know was created through a separation of water from water, between heaven and earth, between the upper and lower realms. Yet precisely because separation is part of the order of Creation, there also exists a longing for connection. Our Sages describe this longing in a remarkable passage cited in the commentary of Rabbeinu Bachya ben Asher on the Torah:
“They said in the Midrash: The lower waters are called ‘weeping waters’ because when the Holy One, blessed be He, divided the waters, He placed some above and some below. The lower waters began to weep, saying: ‘Woe to us that we were not worthy to ascend above and be close to our Creator.’ What did they do? They boldly broke through the depths and sought to rise, until the Holy One, blessed be He, rebuked them. He said to them: ‘Since you have done all this for My honor, the upper waters will not have permission to sing praise until they receive permission from you. Moreover, you will one day be brought upon the altar, in the form of salt and the water libation.’” (Rabbeinu Bachya, Leviticus 2:13)
The profound place of water in Judaism
From this, we can understand something profound about the place of water in Judaism.
WATER IS not merely a substance that sustains the body. It represents a movement of connection between heaven and earth and of life flowing from the upper realms to the lower ones. When rain falls, the heavens and the earth that were separated at the beginning of Creation are, as it were, reunited, and the world enters a state of complete harmony.
This is why our Sages spoke so highly of the day of rain.
As the Talmud teaches: “Rabbi Abbahu said: The day of rain is greater than the day of the resurrection of the dead, for while the resurrection of the dead is only for the righteous, rain is for both the righteous and the wicked... Rav Yehudah said: The day of rain is as great as the day on which the Torah was given... Rava said: It is even greater than the day on which the Torah was given.” (Taanit 7a)
The coming together of the waters creates a state of connection between rain and spirit. This is precisely the essence of the resurrection of the dead – the reuniting of soul and body that had been separated. And when the world reaches its spiritual potential, when spirit prevails over physical matter, there is no longer a place for separation.
The comparison between water and Torah is no coincidence. Both bring life to the world. Rain causes the earth to flourish and makes human physical existence possible; Torah causes the human being to flourish and makes spiritual existence possible. Rain descends from above and reaches the entire earth; Torah descends into the world and gives it meaning, direction, and purpose.
As our Sages taught in Bava Kamma 82a: “For it was taught: ‘They traveled for three days in the wilderness but did not find water [Exodus 15:22].’ Those who expound Scripture said: ‘Water’ means nothing other than Torah, as it says: ‘Ho, everyone who thirsts, come for water [Isaiah 55:1].’ Since they traveled for three days without Torah, they became weary. The prophets among them arose and instituted that they should read [the Torah] on Shabbat and pause on Sunday, read on Monday and pause on Tuesday and Wednesday, and read on Thursday and pause on Friday, so that they would never go three days without Torah.”
This understanding brings us back to the opening verses of the Torah. The world began with water, but the world was not meant to remain a world of water. The Holy One, blessed be He, created separation, established boundaries, brought forth dry land, and created a world in which human beings could live and act. Yet for the world to continue to exist, the waters must descend upon it.
The physical world can exist in a biological sense, but for it to contain human beings, meaning, morality, and purpose, it needs Torah. It is no coincidence that Torah is compared to water. Just as water descends from a higher place to a lower one, refreshes everything, and does not ask who is worthy to receive it (Taanit 7a), so too Torah can reach a person and bring life to their inner world.
After the Days of Awe, when we drew closer to the Creator, and after Sukkot, when we rejoiced and celebrated the beauty of our Jewish heritage, we return to Bereishit.
We read once again how the world was created and discover that from its very beginning, the Torah seeks to remind us of the secret of its continued existence: The world needs the abundance that comes to it from above.
Water sustains the body and the earth. Torah sustains the human being and the world. And a person can receive both, if only they recognize how to make their existence worthy of the purpose for which they were created.■
The writer is rabbi of the Western Wall and Holy Sites.

Burnham’s Labour holds off Greens in London election test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:20:43 UTC
18:20:43 KST

Labour won the parliamentary by-election in the central London constituency of Holborn and St Pancras on Friday, defeating a strong challenge from the left-wing Green Party in a boost for Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali, the local council leader, secured 12,292 votes, beating Green Party leader Zack Polanski, who received 8,928. The seat became vacant after former Labour leader Keir Starmer stepped down as a lawmaker.
The expected victory will strengthen Burnham's position after lawmakers installed him as prime minister amid concerns that Starmer's unpopularity was leaving Labour vulnerable to a challenge from the populist Reform UK party at the next general election.
After losing left-wing support to the Greens earlier this year, Labour appears to have won back many voters, raising further questions about Polanski's leadership. He had promised to make his party an "eco-populist" movement.
The 43-year-old former actor and hypnotherapist, who had some success in drawing voters away from Labour before Burnham came to power, has come under fire after party members passed a motion titled "Zionism Is Racism."
The motion called for "the establishment of a single democratic Palestinian State in all of historic Palestine" and was criticized by Jewish groups, other parties and most Green Party lawmakers.
After the fiercely contested vote, Polanski, who did not vote on the motion, responded to his critics by saying he would stay on as leader. He described the by-election result as part of "Andy Burnham's honeymoon."
However, he did not receive a full endorsement from the party's former leader, Caroline Lucas, who struggled to contain her anger over what she described as his lack of leadership on the Zionism motion at last week's annual conference.
Asked whether Polanski should remain leader, Lucas told the BBC: "I think just let's see what happens in the coming days and weeks."
"I want him to speak now about what has happened, I want him to show the leadership that was frankly missing on Sunday."
Abdi-Wali, who arrived in Britain as a child refugee from Somalia, said her victory was a defeat for "those who seek to divide us."
"We have a responsibility to defend what we've built and pass it on," she said. "Throughout our campaign, we chose hope, and the people of Holborn and St Pancras chose it with us. And now it's time to deliver."
The by-election was an early test for Burnham, whose predecessor, Starmer, stepped down as a lawmaker in September after being ousted as prime minister in July.
Under Starmer, Labour had also ceded ground to the Green Party, which made record gains in London in May's local elections as its appeal grew among younger, left-leaning voters in the capital and other urban areas.
The Greens have since fallen back in opinion polls after Burnham made policy proposals that strengthened Labour's standing among left-leaning voters, including a tougher line on Israel and a more ambitious approach to relations with the European Union.
Polanski, who is Jewish, was repeatedly questioned after the by-election about the conference vote on Zionism. The Green Party leader again appeared to distance himself from the motion, saying only that he believed the displacement of Palestinians and what he called an "ongoing genocide" were racist.
For now, he said, the Green Party should direct its challenge at Burnham's Labour Party and focus on whether the governing party's budget on Oct. 28 delivers on its promises.
"So many people told me on the doorstep that they want to give Andy Burnham a chance," Polanski told broadcasters. "Well, he's got a chance now. Let's see what he does with it."

Taipei textile show generates NT$1.9 billion in business opportunities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:20:22 UTC
18:20:22 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s textile industry generated an estimated NT$1.9 billion (US$60 million) in business opportunities at this year’s Taipei Innovative Textile Application Show, CTEE reported.
The three-day exhibition, which concluded Thursday, featured 410 exhibitors from 12 countries. The event included 977 booths and attracted approximately 30,405 buyer visits.
Sustainability, functional applications, and smart manufacturing were key themes. Exhibitors displayed recycled materials, high-performance textiles, and AI-assisted production technologies.
Textile manufacturers are expanding their use of recycled and alternative raw materials, including discarded fishing nets and agricultural waste, alongside recycled plastic bottles. The industry is also developing textile-to-textile recycling methods and single-material products to improve recyclability.
Companies are expanding the use of functional textiles beyond sportswear and outdoor gear. Specialized markets, including protective equipment, medical products, military and police gear, and aerospace applications, are creating new opportunities for high-performance materials.
Meanwhile, AI and digital technologies are increasingly being used for fabric inspection, quality prediction, and production planning. They help manufacturers improve quality control and streamline production processes.
To mark the exhibition’s 30th anniversary, a special showcase featured more than 500 innovative fabrics, accessories, and yarns. It highlighted Taiwan’s latest advances in performance textiles, sustainable materials, and lower-impact production methods.
Major Taiwanese textile companies expressed optimism about the industry’s outlook for next year. Tainan Spinning Co. Chair Hou Po-ming (侯博明) said the industry faced US tariffs and low-priced imports last year. Textile companies responded by cutting excess capacity, adjusting their product mix, and diversifying their businesses, according to CTEE.
Lealea Group Chair James Kuo (郭紹儀) said the industry had adjusted to the difficulties. He expects the business environment to be more stable and favorable next year, although uncertainties remain.

The ChiNext Index, tracking China's Nasdaq-style board of growth enterprises, gained 0.22 percent to close at 3,043.33 points Friday.
The STAR Composite Index, which reflects the performance of stocks on China's sci-tech innovation board, closed 0.34 percent lower at 1,726.71 points. ■

Houthi strikes on Riyadh airport kill 3 Saudis, cancel flights as war widens

Houthi strikes on Riyadh airport kill 3 Saudis, cancel flights as war widens
- Saudi Arabia said three people, including a pilot, were killed and airlines forced to cancel or delay flights following Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s airport.
- The attacks widened the Yemen war, forced diplomats and schools to take safety measures, and hit transport and oil targets in Saudi Arabia.
- The Houthis and Saudi-backed forces remain locked in fighting, while UN data says more than 200,000 people have been displaced since July.
AI generated
RIYADH – Saudi Arabia said on Oct 9 that three people, including a pilot, were killed in attacks on Riyadh’s international airport, after Yemen’s Houthis claimed targeting the facility.
The conflict between the Houthis and Yemen’s Saudi-backed government has widened, with the Iran-backed fighters staging repeated attacks on Saudi targets since they began a lightning offensive just across the border.
While seizing large swathes of territory along the Red Sea coast in Yemen, the Houthis have also attacked Saudi transport hubs, oil facilities and other civilian targets in the world’s largest crude exporter.
The Saudi civil aviation authority said two attacks on Oct 8 on the Saudi capital’s airport and a Saudia Airlines plane there “resulted in the martyrdom of three citizens”.
The national flag carrier confirmed the death of the plane’s captain, expressing “profound sadness” and citing an “incident” at King Khalid International Airport.
Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government forces it backs have struggled to contain the Houthis’ advance, despite a counter-offensive aimed at recapturing territory, including the area around the Bab al-Mandab strait that is crucial to global energy flows.
But a regional source said on Oct 9 that Riyadh would not bow to the Houthis’ “military blackmail” and would not agree to a truce until the Yemeni government regains all territory it has lost in recent weeks.
The attacks forced diplomats stationed in the Saudi capital to shelter in place and international schools to take safety measures, as explosions echoed across the city on Oct 8.
Numerous flights at Riyadh’s airport were delayed or cancelled, while the airport advised travellers of the “necessity” to contact airlines before their trips.
Singapore Airlines postponed the launch of its services until March 28, citing the conflict. Philippine Airlines cancelled flights to the capital until at least Oct 11.
Saudia, the country’s national carrier, Egyptair, Indigo and Air India cancelled dozens of flights out of Riyadh on Oct 8 in the aftermath of the attacks.
Operations at King Khalid International Airport have shut down for several hours and restarted multiple times during the past few days as incoming attacks from Yemen make it unsafe for planes to land or take off from there.
Last week, Cathay Pacific Airways extended cancellation of its flights to Dubai and Riyadh through Jan 31.
‘Crisis in everything’
The Houthis, whose heartlands are among the Zaidi Shia Muslims in the north-west, have already controlled the capital Sanaa and most of Yemen’s major population centres since the start of the war in 2014.
Riyadh’s military coalition intervened to support the government the following year.
After declaring their counter-offensive against the Houthis, Yemen’s government claimed to have pushed the fighters out of strategic areas on the Red Sea coast and the port city of Mocha.
But the Houthis insist they are holding their territory, and military sources from both sides have not reported any major changes on the ground.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group launched missiles at an airport in Najran and an airbase in Khamis Mushait on Oct 8.
The Houthis have also warned workers to evacuate Saudi Arabia’s oil facilities, having days before hit a major refinery south of the capital.
Admissions by Saudi authorities of civilian targets being hit are relatively rare. There have been few statements on Houthi attacks in recent weeks.
Claims by the warring parties have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast and access for journalists difficult.
In Yemen, one of the world’s poorest countries, ordinary civilians are paying the price for the renewed fighting, with more than 200,000 people displaced since July, according to UN data.
In Yemen’s Taiz, the Houthis are laying siege to the government-controlled city in the country’s west, depriving residents of their main supply route to the government’s temporary capital in Aden.
“There is a crisis in everything: water, gas, vegetables, everything essential”, said Um Rian. AFP

Navanethem 'Navi' Pillay Wins the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:19:34 UTC
18:19:34 KST

Navanethem "Navi" Pillay, a South African jurist and former U.N. high commissioner for human rights, won the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize on Friday “for her efforts to promote peace and international law.”
“Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career. Born into a family of Indian Tamil origin under apartheid in Durban, South Africa, Pillay became a lawyer and legal pioneer, confronting deep structural discrimination, segregation, and exclusion,” said Jørgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee.
“A common thread runs from her early work defending Nelson Mandela and others who stood up against apartheid to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time.”
Pillay, 85, is a judge on the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in the case where Myanmar stands accused of genocide. She was also chair of the U.N. Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory that concluded last year that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza. (Israel at the time dismissed the report as "scandalous" and “fake.") Israel's Foreign Ministry criticized Pillay's win, referring to it as "grotesque weaponization" of the award.
In "historic international court cases, she has shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence," Frydnes said, referring to Pillay as "one of the great defenders of international legal principles in our time."
Reflecting on her win, Pillay said she is often asked when she will stop working. "I can’t obviously stop my work in support of the Nuremberg Principles, because of the people we meet here," she said.
Pillay's career spans more than 50 years
Born in South Africa in 1941, Pillay was the first non-white woman to establish a legal practice in the country, according to the U.N.
In the early years of her career, she acted as a defense attorney for anti-apartheid activists.
Pillay has served as a judge on the High Court in South Africa, the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, and the International Criminal Court (ICC) throughout the course of her career.
She was the U.N. human rights chief from September 2008 to August 2014. Volker Türk, who currently holds that position at the U.N., said Pillay's Nobel recognition is "particularly poignant" as it comes "at a time when human rights are under attack on so many fronts, including from those who wield enormous power."
“It is an award to all those who around the world dedicate their lives to the defense of human rights, often at great risk to their security," he added.
Pillay is the fifth South African national to be awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. She follows in the footsteps of Nelson Mandela, FW de Klerk, Archbishop Desmond Tutu, and Albert Luthuli.
Pillay dedicates award to "survivors of international crimes"
Pillay dedicated her Nobel Peace Prize to “all of the survivors of international crimes” and people defending international criminal justice, “whose compassion and courage continue to ensure that impunity will not be allowed to reign.”
During a press conference at the International Nuremberg Principle Academy, in the German city where the trials of Nazi leaders showcased the enforcement of international law, Pillay referred to the award as a "wonderful surprise" and the "highest honor."
Using her platform to spotlight the international justice system, Pillay told reporters: “We are living through an era when international law and human rights are under significant political attack... This worsening reality is particularly visible with the attacks on the International Criminal Court."
She added that the Nobel recognition has strengthened her "conviction that we must stand together in defense of the rule of law, in defence of independent courts, and an international legal order based on principle."
Bolstering the importance of international courts
When asked during a press briefing if the award sends a message to those who question or sanction international courts, Frydnes told reporters: “This is definitely a message to those who are attacking, undermin[ing] the international system, the international rules-based system, and the institutions."
U.S. President Donald Trump last month called for countries to "immediately" resign from the International Criminal Court (ICC), amid a broader push by the U.S. Administration to dismantle it.
His call was firmly rejected by European leaders and the Trump Administration's sanctions on the ICC have prompted concern from the international community.
Pillay pokes fun at Trump as she reacts to award
Pillay referenced Trump and his well-documented campaign to be awarded the Nobel Peace Prize when she reacted to her own recognition on Friday morning.
In a video shared by Agnes Callamard, secretary general of Amnesty International, Pillay can be seen entering a room at Nuremberg Court to resounding applause from her peers. "If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump," she jokes.
The 2025 Nobel Peace Prize winner, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, famously gave her medal to Trump in January as she pressed the U.S. to support democracy in Venezuela.
While the Norwegian Nobel Institute doesn’t release a shortlist of its contenders each year, the leaders of Israel, Cambodia, and Pakistan have all previously said they nominated Trump. The institute registered a total of 287 candidates for this year’s prize, including 208 individuals and 79 organizations.
Trump said earlier this week it would be a “great discredit” to the Norwegian Nobel Committee if they did not announce him as this year's recipient.

(Xinhua/Wang Ye)
BEIJING, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- A symposium was held in Beijing on Friday to study the first and second volumes of selected works on culture by Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee.
Li Shulei, a member of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and head of the Publicity Department of the CPC Central Committee, attended the symposium and delivered a speech.
The volumes were published in August by the Central Party Literature Press.
Attendees at the symposium said the selections systematically present the fundamental principles, core content and essential requirements of Xi Jinping Thought on Culture, providing an authoritative textbook for its study and application.
In studying the selections, it is important to consciously study and apply Xi Jinping Thought on Culture and better fulfill the cultural mission of the new era, they said.
The attendees called for efforts to gain a deeper understanding of Xi Jinping Thought on Culture as the fundamental guidelines for public communication and cultural work in the new era, as well as its strategic vision for building China into a leading country in culture. They also urged efforts to translate the gains from studying it into concrete actions.
Organized by the Publicity Department of the CPC Central Committee, the symposium was attended by officials from relevant central departments, central publicity and cultural institutions, and publicity departments of provincial-level CPC committees, as well as experts and scholars in social sciences.
The volumes of the selected works contain 78 pieces of the most important and fundamental works by Xi on cultural development from November 2012 to February 2026, featuring reports, speeches, letters and instructions.
Xi Jinping Thought on Culture was formally put forward at a national meeting on the work of public communication and culture in October 2023. ■

DAR ES SALAAM, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- At least 28 people were killed in a head-on collision between a passenger bus and a truck in Tanzania's eastern Morogoro Region, the regional fire and rescue service said Friday.
Joseph Mwasabeja, acting commander of the Morogoro Regional Fire and Rescue Force, said the accident occurred overnight Thursday at Mkambarani along the Morogoro-Dar es Salaam highway.
He said the timber-carrying truck collided with a passenger bus traveling from Dar es Salaam to Mbeya in Tanzania's southern highlands.
The bus caught fire following the collision and was completely burnt out, he said.
He attributed the accident to the truck driver, whose identity had not been established, saying the driver was traveling from Iringa toward Dar es Salaam and attempted to overtake other vehicles without taking adequate precautions, resulting in the head-on collision. ■
