Cambodia's oil, gas import costs jump nearly 54 pct in first 9 months
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
17:19:07 CST
18:19:07 KST

PHNOM PENH, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- Cambodia's total imports of diesel fuel, gasoline, and combustion gas reached 2.82 billion U.S. dollars in the first nine months of 2026, marking a 53.8 percent surge from 1.84 billion dollars during the same period last year, according to the Ministry of Commerce on Friday.
A breakdown of the data shows the kingdom spent 1.47 billion dollars on diesel fuel from January to September, a 48 percent year-on-year increase. Gasoline imports jumped 76 percent to 1.04 billion dollars, while combustion gas expenditures rose 23 percent to 314 million dollars.
Thong Mengdavid, deputy director of the China-ASEAN Studies Center at the Cambodia University of Technology and Science, attributed the spike to a mix of domestic and international factors.
"Rising industrial production, expanding transport and logistics networks, and heightened electricity demand are key drivers of this surge," he told Xinhua.
He noted that the country's accelerating economic momentum is colliding with global fuel price hikes triggered by ongoing conflicts in the Middle East.
According to data from the Ministry of Commerce, on Friday, the retail price of regular gasoline stood at 5,150 riels (1.27 dollars) per liter, a 33.7 percent surge compared to pre-Middle East conflict levels. Meanwhile, diesel prices reached 5,650 riels (1.39 dollars) per liter, marking a 46.7 percent spike.
Cambodia currently relies entirely on petroleum imports, as the Southeast Asian nation has yet to exploit its offshore oil and gas reserves. ■

VIENTIANE, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- Laos is stepping up efforts to address labor shortages.
Speaking at the second ordinary session of the 10th National Assembly, Lao Minister of Labor and Social Welfare Phoxay Sayasone outlined key measures to expand employment opportunities and address labor shortages, according to a ministry report issued on Thursday.
Measures include reserving certain occupations for local workers, particularly those involving cultural promotion, traditional knowledge, and small businesses requiring limited technology or capital.
During the first nine months of 2026, a total of 119,382 people secured employment, including 103,610 who went to work abroad.
To expand self-employment and rural job opportunities, the ministry has conducted pilot programs since 2024, providing vocational training for poor and disadvantaged people, as well as unemployed individuals interested in starting their own businesses.
The ministry plans to continue expanding these initiatives to create more employment opportunities in rural communities and encourage entrepreneurship. ■

Turkish agricultural exports hit record high in January-September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:18:41 UTC
18:18:41 KST

(AA Photo)
Türkiye’s agricultural exports rose 4.4 percent year-on-year to a record $27.1 billion in the January-September period, supported by strong demand from international markets, according to data from the Türkiye Exporters Assembly (TİM).
The country’s total exports increased 5.2 percent from a year earlier to $211 billion during the first nine months of the year, while the agricultural sector accounted for 12.9 percent of overall exports.
Three of the 10 agricultural subsectors recorded their highest-ever January-September export figures, according to the data.
Fresh fruit and vegetable exports surged 42.2 percent year-on-year to $3.2 billion, while aquaculture and animal products exports rose 8 percent to $3.1 billion. Tobacco exports increased 15.4 percent to $929.5 million.
Among the record-setting sectors, Iraq was the largest market for fresh fruit and vegetables, with exports totaling $842 million. Russia was the leading destination for aquaculture and animal products with imports worth $398.1 million, while the United States ranked first for tobacco exports at $157 million.
By province, Mersin led fresh fruit and vegetable exports with $880.2 million, Muğla topped aquaculture and animal products exports with $814.6 million and İzmir recorded the highest tobacco exports at $677.9 million.

Egypt prepares to deploy troops to Somalia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:17:31 UTC
18:17:31 KST

Breadcrumb
As tensions soar in the African horn, Egypt prepares to deploy troops to Somalia
Technical military teams from Egypt, including advisors, trainers and officers, are reportedly busy preparing for the deployment of army troops to Somalia, the first such move in the Horn of Africa nation, since the signing of a joint military cooperation agreement between the two sides in 2024.
The troop deployment will expectedly come in light of bilateral security and military cooperation between the two countries and within the African Union Mission, widely known as AUSSOM.
Egypt has not released any information about the size of the contingent it would deploy within the mission or within bilateral security and military cooperation with Somalia.
The Egyptian troops will reportedly be positioned in the Ceelcade region which used to house the Cisiley Airfield on the immediate northern outskirts of Mogadishu, within the Middle Shabelle region—in the low-lying semi-arid coastal hinterland just north of the Banaadir administrative boundary, around 400 kilometres from the nearest point to Ethiopia's shared border with Somalia.
The deployment of Egyptian troops to Somalia would advance military and security cooperation with Mogadishu at an important time, Somali political analysts said.
"I believe this is particularly so given the security challenges facing Somalia and the turbulent situation in the Horn of Africa as a whole," Somali political analyst and African affairs specialist Hassan Muhammad said.
Speaking to The New Arab, Muhammad expressed hopes that the deployment of Egyptian troops would contribute to strengthening the capacities of Somali security and military institutions and boost stability in the country.
"The success of this cooperation will, however, depend on the presence of clear goals, full coordination with Somali institutions and respect for Somalia's sovereignty and national interests," he added.
Horn of Africa, at a critical moment
An Egyptian military delegation visited the Somali capital on 20 September and met Somali Defence Minister Ahmed Moallim Fiqi, five days after Egyptian officers met senior Somali commanders in Mogadishu to discuss defence cooperation, military training and capacity-building for the Somali National Army.
Such meetings come as Egypt steps up cooperation with Somalia, following the 2025 elevation of relations between the two countries to a strategic partnership.
Egypt has pledged to offer support to Somalia, repeatedly underscoring the importance of preserving its territorial integrity and preventing foreign meddling in its affairs.
The Horn of Africa nation took centre stage in discussions between Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi and visiting CIA Director John Ratcliffe late last month.
Between October 2024 and October 2026, Sisi hosted Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud five times in Egypt, the last time being on 3 October in the northern Mediterranean city of Alamein.
On the following day, Cairo hosted a quadrilateral Egyptian-Somali-Eritrean-Sudanese summit, in which the leaders of the four African countries called for respecting state sovereignty and territorial integrity and expressed opposition to foreign meddling in their countries' internal affairs.
These encounters and messages, Egyptian analysts argue, point to Egypt's determination to keep offering support to Somalia at a testing time.
"Egypt wants to help Somalia protect its territorial waters, fend off internal and external threats, such as terrorism and piracy, and prevent foreign meddling in its affairs," Egyptian security expert, Lt. Gen. Khaled Okasha told TNA.
He described Somalia as Egypt's "strategic depth", given interconnections between stability in this Horn of Africa country and the Red Sea, the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and the southern entrance to the Suez Canal.
"Somalia's disintegration would threaten Red Sea and Suez Canal navigation," Lt. Gen. Okasha added, warning that such a scenario would harm other regional states and simultaneously bleed the international economy.
Strategic 'repositioning'
When they land in Somalia, Egyptian troops will be in the middle of a severely hostile environment, given the intensity of the terrorist threat in the Horn of Africa country where the Al-Qaeda-linked al-Shabaab movement vies for control over territory with the federal government.
Muhammad, the Somali analyst, referred to public support of Egyptian troop presence in Somalia, but said al-Shabaab was still capable of staging painful attacks against government troops and civilians, despite all the security and military measures taken by the government.
"The movement constitutes one of the most outstanding security challenges facing the government now," Muhammad said.
"The fight against the movement requires concerted military efforts, which have to move hand in hand with addressing the political, economic and social problems that negatively affect Somalia's stability," he added.
The expected Egyptian troop deployment occurs while there is a regional military build-up on the Somali coast, especially from Israel which is gaining a military foothold on the coast of the breakaway Somali region of Somaliland after recognizing it late last year.
Moreover, there is major tension between Egypt and Ethiopia and Ethiopia's civil war, pitting the federal government against seven rebel groups in the northern part of the country, is widening in scope.
Cairo and Addis Ababa are locked in a high-voltage conflict over Ethiopia's operation of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), the Horn of Africa country's multibillion dollar hydroelectric project on the Blue Nile, the main tributary of the Nile River which is Egypt's principal source of fresh water, and Ethiopia's plans to construct additional dams on the Nile.
On 5 October, Sisi said his country would not abdicate a drop of its annual share of the water of the Nile River.
"This share is a firmly established historical and legal right that can neither be reduced or infringement upon," Sisi said.
In a televised address on the occasion of the 53rd anniversary of his country's October war victory of 1973 against Israel, he described this right as a "redline" that could not be crossed.
The two countries are also at odds over Ethiopia's quest for Red Sea access, something vehemently opposed by Egypt which is wary of Ethiopian military presence on such a crucial maritime chokepoint which leads to the Suez Canal in the north.
Egyptian military presence in Somalia is part of larger moves, highlighting Cairo's efforts to militarily and strategically reposition itself in the Horn of Africa to protect its vial national security interests, Egyptian analysts said.
It is also part of Egyptian activity in the region, one that has so far also included—apart from the military side—enhanced economic cooperation with regional states, especially Eritrea, Uganda and Kenya.
"Egypt needs this military presence in the Horn of Africa to protect its national security interests and repel threats to this security," Egyptian political science professor Ayman Shabana told TNA.
By deploying troops in the region, he added, Egypt could also offer support to allied countries, such as Somalia and Eritrea which face growing threats and are expected to be at the forefront of effects from the current civil war in Ethiopia.
"Egyptian military presence also sends a clear message to regional parties that they need to think twice before harming Egyptian interests," Shabana added.

Nobel Peace Prize awarded to former ICC judge Navanethem "Navi" Pillay
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:15:45 UTC
18:15:45 KST

Nobel Peace Prize 2026 awarded to Navanethem "Navi" Pillay, former International Criminal Court judge
The Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 was awarded Friday to Navanethem "Navi" Pillay, a South African-born former judge with the International Criminal Court who went on to become the United Nations human rights chief and is still serving with the U.N.'s other judicial body, the International Court of Justice. She also led a U.N. inquiry last year that accused Israel of genocide in the Gaza Strip, and Israel was quick to condemn her receiving the honor on Friday.
The Nobel Committee said it was honoring Pillay "for her efforts to promote peace and international law," and that awarding the prize to someone with her body of work on international justice was a message to those seeking to undermine international law institutions.
The South African-born former United Nations human rights chief, who is 85, was recognized for her efforts to promote peace and international law, said Jørgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee.
"This is definitely a message to those who are undermining the international system and institutions," Frydnes said.
"The system of international law is under tremendous pressure and its institutions are under attack," he said, noting what the committee saw as a shift "towards power politics at the expense of legal frameworks and global respect for law and justice."
The International Criminal Court (ICC) has come under fire from Israel and the Trump administration in recent years, with the U.S. imposing sanctions against the U.N. court last year after it issued an arrest warrant in 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. President Trump accused the court of "illegitimate and baseless actions targeting America and our close ally Israel."
The ICC condemned the U.S. sanctions against its staff and said they were intended to "harm (the Court's) independent and impartial judicial work."
Pillay served as an ICC judge from 2003 until 2008, when she resigned to take on the role of United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights. She was the chair of the U.N. Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory that said last year it had concluded Israel's actions in Gaza amounted to genocide. Israel dismissed the report as "scandalous."
The Israeli Foreign Ministry blasted the Nobel committee for awarding the prize to Pillay on Friday, saying in a statement posted online that "if there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn't just be a contender. She'd be a frontrunner. Her role in the relentless, politically motivated demonization of Israel and promotion of the genoLIE speaks volumes."
It condemned the committee for awarding her as "the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice."
The Trump administration, hours later, announced further sanctions against the ICC. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the ICC a "threat to U.S. sovereignty" and said the new measures were deemed necessary to ensure the court, which the U.S. has never been a party to, can never prosecute a U.S. national.
He said the new sanctions would "ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate," adding: "We expect our allies, many of whom are part of the ICC and that rely on American servicemembers for their defense, to rein in the court. If they do not, the United States will continue its campaign to dismantle the ICC, brick by brick, until Americans are threatened no longer."
Pillay is currently serving as an ad hoc judge for the International Court of Justice (ICJ), which is separate to the ICC, in the case of Gambia v. Myanmar, in which Myanmar's ruling military junta stands accused of genocide over its treatment of the nation's Rohingya Muslim minority in the western state of Rakhine.
Frydnes said the committee wasn't immediately able to reach Pillay Friday to tell her she had been awarded the prize, adding from the podium that if she was watching and saw a call coming in from a Norwegian phone number, to "please pick up."
Pillay soon appeared in a video posted on social media by the head of Amnesty International, being applauded by well-wishers at the Palace of Justice in Nuremberg, Germany, where Nazi leaders were put on trial for their crimes against humanity after World War II.
"Perhaps it was meant to be that I was in this historic courtroom... when the announcement was made and I was informed of the award," Pillay said. "We are living through an era when international law and human rights are under significant political attack ... This worsening reality is particularly visible with the attacks on the International Criminal Court."
"If you clap a little bit louder I may share this prize with Trump," she quipped, drawing laughs from the crowd. She said that when she was informed that she had been awarded the prize, she first thought "it must be a joke," and that as a "lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify this thing."
She noted that she was lauded by the Nobel committee for her courage, which she questioned, saying: "You can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth? You interpret the law, you look at all the facts, so it's an impartial decision you make."
Last year, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado won the Nobel Peace Prize for her struggle to achieve a democratic transition in the South American nation, winning recognition as a woman "who keeps the flame of democracy burning amid a growing darkness."
Machado gave President Trump, who has long said he deserves the prize, her Nobel medal shortly after the United States ousted then-President Nicolás Maduro. But it was largely a symbolic gesture: The Nobel Committee has said the honor itself cannot be transferred.
Nominations can be made by a select group of people and organizations, including heads of state or politicians serving at a national level, university professors, directors of foreign policy institutes, past Nobel Prize recipients and members of the Norwegian Nobel Committee itself.
Four of this year's Nobels were announced earlier this week. The Nobel for medicine went to three scientists whose work led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works. The physics award recognized a scientist's efforts to demystify a rare group of neutrinos. The chemistry prize recognized two scientists for untangling mysterious mirror images in molecules, a discovery that has been used to develop countless drugs.
Canadian poet, essayist and translator Anne Carson won the literature prize Thursday for "bold and inventive" works that fuse the classical and the modern and blur the boundaries of poetry and prose.
The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced Monday.
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million).
Education activist Malala Yousafzai is the youngest Nobel Peace Prize laureate; she won at 17 in 2014.
The United States is the most-credited country, with 24 awards naming U.S. institutions or individuals, ahead of the United Kingdom (13) and Switzerland (11). No laureate listed as American has won since then-President Barack Obama was awarded in 2009.
The prize has gone unawarded on 19 occasions, most of them during the world wars. In 1948, the year Mahatma Gandhi was assassinated, no prize was awarded; he had been nominated 12 times and never won.
In 1939, a Swedish member of parliament nominated Adolf Hitler, then withdrew the nomination, saying it was never meant seriously.

Kyiv's historic market sits nearly empty after upscale food court makeover
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:14:56 UTC
18:14:56 KST

Food court flop? Kyiv’s historic market empties after million-dollar makeover
A man walks past a closed bar at the Bessarabskyi Market in Kyiv, Ukraine on Oct. 6, 2026. (Danylo Antoniuk/ The Kyiv Independent)
Bessarabskyi Market has stood in Kyiv for 114 years. Its upscale makeover lasted less than one.
Less than a year after the late-2025 reopening, most of the restaurants are gone, and the hall is quieter than before the renovation.
Before the makeover, Bessarabskyi was a labyrinth of produce stalls, offering everything from churchkhela — a sweet from the Caucasus — and watermelons from southern Ukraine to pigs' feet and sauerkraut craft beer.
But by the end of 2025, the maze of vendors had shrunk and been partly replaced by a cocktail bar, a performance stage, and 17 new food and drink stalls ranging from a sushi bar to an Indian restaurant.
Today, Bessarabskyi has one eatery left — a fast food chain called Big Mama. The stall sits in a row of identical tiled stalls with wooden countertops, freshly built and all but one shuttered.
The project — which looked to replicate the success of the popular Kyiv Food Market — is nothing short of a failure. In early June 2026, Natalia Dzhulai left her post as manager of the $3.5 million project, and 15 of the new eateries have closed, leaving only a coffee shop and a fast food chain still standing. Natalia Dzhulai refused to provide a comment to the Kyiv Independent as she is no longer part of the project.
Bessarabskyi’s transformation is part of a wider trend. Across Europe, developers have sought to turn grocery markets into profitable food courts. But in wartime Ukraine, the reality of changing a historic market and piece of Kyiv’s heritage into a trendy food court proved more difficult than developers expected.
Why did the food court fail?
Ihor Kravets, an architectural researcher who has been vocal about Bessarabskyi’s renovation, believes that the food court may have been successful had it been launched in 2019.
"Were it not for the blackouts caused by constant attacks, the general emotional exhaustion of the public, and the growing financial constraints facing consumers — the food court could have continued operating despite the other disadvantages."
The wider economy is also strained. Mobilization and the 3 million people who have fled Ukraine have created a shortage of 2.5 million workers in Ukraine’s economy, according to the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development. In March 2026 alone, 300 Kyiv food and drink establishments closed, according to Olga Nasonova, who runs a restaurant consulting business in Ukraine.
But Bessarabskyi’s renovation faced obstacles beyond its wartime circumstances.
Before the opening, the renovation was met with heavy criticism for its lack of transparency. As a municipal enterprise, the renovation needed to be a city-led project, but the public was not shown what the food court would look like. The developers and project managers sought no input from the community, and even to this day it is still unclear who the architect behind the food court actually is.
"The criticism (of the project) started before the opening, and after it the outcry only got stronger, so the operator started from a minus," said Pavlo Peker, an architect who pioneered the project to protect Kyiv’s historic Zhytnyi Market from a similar food court renovation.
Peker attributes the failure of the food court at least in part to the lack of public involvement: "The failure…could’ve been predicted…People don’t like that…Kyivans were just not a part of the process…so the people behind the Bessarabskyi project didn’t really know what the project needed," he said.
The lack of research meant the renovation ended up replicating what already existed nearby, but at higher prices and lower quality. Kravets said. "This was particularly off-putting given the venue's environment: unbearably stuffy in the summer and plagued by icy drafts in the winter."
"Kyivans were just not a part of the process…so the people behind the Bessarabskyi project didn’t really know what the project needed."
In the winter of 2025, Kyiv endured record-breaking cold and blackouts brought on by Russian attacks so severe that Mayor Vitali Klitschko urged those who could to leave the capital.
Some of Bessarabskyi’s new tenants felt that the impossible task of heating Bessarabskyi, a vast brick building with high ceilings, multiple entrances and a heritage status that restricts structural modifications, was the reason the food court lost customers.
"The winter started and it’s impossible to warm a place like Bessarabskyi, so customers stopped coming, and gradually stalls started to close," said Ruslan Kravchenko, the owner of Big Mama. Kravchenko would likely have also had to close up shop, had Big Mama not had a branch nearby with which it could share resources.
Kravchenko’s stall is surrounded by empty seating for the few and far between customers and a new stage added during the renovation.
While Kravchenko was speaking about the lack of customers, a shirtless man holding a plastic beer bottle clambered onto the stage added during the renovation, which after the reopening hosted live music and even a Q&A with former Foreign Minister Dmytro Kuleba but has not held a performance in months. The man’s shouts echoed across the empty building as he was removed from the building by police.
Above the stall, a slideshow of photographs of old Kyiv play on a 2x2 meter screen: Khreshchatyk as a dusty road for carts and horses, Kyiv’s center made up of two-story buildings — and, of course, Bessarabskyi bustling with customers.
Bessarabskyi today couldn't be further away from the one in the photographs.
Even without competitors, Big Mama may soon have to close. "When there were other restaurants, customers would bring their friends, and that would drive business, but now it’s difficult," said Kravchenko.
What does this mean for Bessarabskyi’s produce market?
Although the eateries at Bessarabskyi have proved to be short-lived, more of the produce vendors have remained.
Natalia Vorovyoba is one of two remaining fresh fruit vendors at Bessarabskyi and, like many of the remaining produce vendors, has worked at Bessarabskyi for almost three decades. The renovation, which many hoped would drive profits, made Bessarabskyi unrecognizable, she said.
"The bar in the middle of the market…makes no sense for a grocery market,."
Vorovyoba has managed to remain at Bessarabskyi despite business declining over the years. She now fears that the renovation may have dealt the fatal blow and that she may soon have to leave.
"When I first started working at Bessarabskyi, there were so many people there was barely anywhere to stand. I could sell 60 kilograms of strawberries at once, but there are days now when I don’t get any customers," Vorovyoba explained.
While Natalia Dzhulai, the manager of the food court project, promised that 50 grocery vendors would stay at the market — 90% of the number pre-renovation — now only a handful remain.
"They didn’t tell us what it was going to look like — they said only half of it would be taken by the food market, but you can see it’s clearly more than half," Vorovyoba said.
The future of Kyiv’s grocery markets is uncertain. Some, like Peker, are optimistic that this is just another chapter in Bessarabskyi's history, while others, like Kravets, are less so.
"It’s a very worrying situation. Potential investors have been scared off. The priceless historic building has fallen into neglect, and it’s unclear who will fund its upkeep," Kravets said.
But in some ways Bessarabskyi’s produce vendors are lucky to have survived the market's development at all. Other projects to turn markets into more profitable venues threaten to change the site altogether.
Demiivskyi Market in Kyiv is set to be torn down completely and will be the site of a new 30-story building which will be built by Manhattan Invest.
Other markets in Kyiv have become the sites of Russian attacks. In Kyiv in 2026 alone, Russia destroyed both the Lukianivskyi Market and the massive book and flea market on Pochaina in two separate and direct strikes.

South Africa’s Navanethem ‘Navi’ Pillay wins 2026 Nobel Peace Prize

International jurist Navi Pillay wins Nobel Peace Prize as global rule of law comes under siege
- The 2026 Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to Navi Pillay for her work on promoting peace, and defending human rights and international law.
- The United Nations human rights office welcomed the news of Pillay’s win, acknowledging her longstanding advocacy for human rights.
- Pillaw oversaw the publishing of a report that concluded that top Israeli officials incited acts of genocide in Gaza, accusations that Israel called scandalous.
AI generated
OSLO – The Nobel Peace Prize was awarded on Oct 9 to South Africa’s Navi Pillay, the judge who headed the Rwanda genocide tribunal and who presided over a UN commission in 2025 that accused Israel of genocide in Gaza.
Pillay, currently a judge on the International Court of Justice in a case where Myanmar also stands accused of genocide, has been “instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide are prosecuted”, said Jorgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee in Oslo.
She reacted to the news by making a quip about US President Donald Trump’s well-documented desire to win the prize himself.
“If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump,” the 85-year-old said during a standing ovation captured by Amnesty International secretary-general Agnes Callamard in Nuremberg and posted on social media platform X.
The Nobel Committee said it decided to honour Pillay at a time when international law and institutions are under attack.
Frydnes said: “The system of international law is under tremendous pressure, and its institutions are under attack.
“Navi Pillay is one of the great defenders of international legal principles in our time. Her distinguished career reminds us of the need to support, fortify and expand the global rule of law.”
Her “commitment to justice and human dignity is a source of hope and inspiration to all who seek to bring about a more peaceful world”, he added.
Born into an Indian Tamil family in Durban, South Africa, Pillay, 85, founded her own law firm in 1967 and earned a doctorate from Harvard University in 1988.
The Nobel Committee said: “A common thread runs from her early work defending Nelson Mandela and others who stood up against apartheid to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time.”
A win for human rights
The UN human rights chief said Pillay’s Nobel Prize was “a collective win for human rights”.
Volker Turk, who worked closely with Pillay during her tenure as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights from 2008 to 2014, described her as “the embodiment of international law”.
“The fact that the Nobel Award Commission decided to give this to Navi Pillay is a collective win for human rights, but also for (those) seeking justice and accountability in this world,” Turk said in response to a question about Pillay’s former role as an International Criminal Court judge.
“And it’s clear that we need international criminal accountability mechanisms, including the International Criminal Court, and it’s clear that we have a very strong signal that this is absolutely critical in today’s world,” said Turk.
Pillay was the former head of the UN Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory.
In September 2025, she oversaw the publishing of a report by the UN Commission of Inquiry that concluded that Israel committed genocide in Gaza, and that top Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, incited these acts, accusations that Israel called scandalous.
The Nobel Committee said it is not taking a stance on whether Israel is committing genocide in Gaza in recognising Pillay’s work.
“It’s her report, the commission’s report, and of course, we have great faith in her professionalism, in her integrity, but that work is of a UN inquiry commission,” Frydnes, the committee chair, said.
The awarding of the prize to Pillay is sure to anger Trump, whose administration has repeatedly attacked international justice institutions.
Since returning to the White House in January 2025, Trump has made no secret of his desire to win the prize, insisting he was the most deserving candidate and claiming to have ended up to eight wars.
“They have a reputation for maybe not giving it to people like me, and I think it would be a great discredit to them,” he said on Oct 7.
But his war against Iran, his territorial expansion ambitions in Greenland, his hard line on migrants, and his attacks on multilateralism and the media have, according to experts in Oslo, disqualified him for the prize.
In 2025, the prize went to Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, a choice generally considered palatable to Trump.
Machado even gave him her Nobel gold medal, judging that he deserved it after the capture of President Nicolas Maduro, though she failed to obtain his political backing in exchange.
Unswayed by external pressure
The reasons given by the Nobel Committee for choosing Peace Prize winners have changed substantially since 1901, shifting from promoting peace to defending human rights in a trend that gained momentum during the Cold War.
The Nobel Committee, meanwhile, says it is not swayed by external pressures.
“Of course, we have to discuss it, but it’s not like that influences the discussions in the room and decisions that come out,” the secretary of the committee, Kristian Berg Harpviken, said ahead of the prize announcement.
The prize comes with a gold medal, a diploma and a prize sum of US$1.2 million (S$1.5 million).
The award will be presented at a formal ceremony in Oslo on Dec 10, the anniversary of the 1896 death of the prizes’ creator, Swedish inventor and philanthropist Alfred Nobel.
The Peace Prize is the only Nobel awarded in Oslo, with the other disciplines announced in Stockholm.
Earlier this week, the prizes for medicine, physics, chemistry and literature were announced in Stockholm, with the latter going to Canadian poet Anne Carson on Oct 8 for her modern twists on Greek mythology and antiquity.
The 2026 Nobel season winds up on Oct 12 with the awarding of the economics prize. AFP, REUTERS, BLOOMBERG

Thieves steal 30,000 wine bottles worth €5m in Italy, reports say
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:09:03 BST
18:09:03 KST

Thieves steal 30,000 bottles of wine worth €5m in Italy, reports say
- Published
Thieves have stolen 30,000 bottles of wine collectively worth about €5m (£4.2m) from a prestigious Italian winery, Italian media report.
Marchesi Antinori, one of Italy's biggest family-owned wineries, said the theft at its storage facility in Tuscany took place on Saturday as the company was preparing to ship a consignment to customers abroad.
At least seven masked men are believed to have deactivated the alarms, disabled the cameras and used company forklifts to load two large trucks of the company's prized Tignanello, Solaia and Guado al Tasso Tuscan reds.
Renzo Cotarella, the chief executive, told Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera this was the largest theft of its kind in Italy.
"A theft of this scale and value has certainly never occurred in Italy," he said.
He added that he was hopeful the authorities would be able to trace the stolen wine.
"Two trucks full of merchandise can't just disappear into thin air. The Tuscan roads are full of cameras - perhaps with a bit of luck we'll be able to recover at least some of the bottles stolen from us."
He told the Financial Times: "These wines have a great value and I don't know how they can sell all this wine around the world without being seen."
The company believes the selection of bottles, which usually sell for between €150 and €500 each, suggests the thieves were wine connoisseurs and had inside knowledge.
The theft was only discovered on Monday morning as staff arrived on site. No arrests have been made.
Marchesi Antinori was founded in 1385 and exports to 170 countries. It had a revenue of €263m (£223m) last year.
There has been a spate of wine thefts in Italy this year, including two in the northern Piedmont region where hundreds of thousands of euros worth of bottles were reportedly taken.

Russian attacks kill at least 41, injure 67 across Ukraine as glide bombs strike Zaporizhzhia
At least 41 people were killed and 67 others injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past day, as Russian glide bombs struck Zaporizhzhia, local authorities said on Oct. 9.
In Zaporizhzhia, Russian glide bombs destroyed and damaged residential buildings, killing one person and injuring seven others, including a child, Ivan Fedorov, co-chair of the Zaporizhzhia Oblast Defense Council, reported.
Across the whole of Zaporizhzhia Oblast, two people were killed and 18 injured in Russian attacks over the past day, Fedorov added. Russian forces launched 1,039 strikes against 51 settlements in the oblast.
Russia attacked Ukraine overnight with 136 drones, including 93 jet-powered Shahed-type drones, Ukraine's Air Force said. Air defenses shot down or suppressed 114 drones, including 77 jet-powered Shaheds. The Air Force reported drone strikes at eight locations, while debris from intercepted drones fell at seven locations.
In Donetsk Oblast, Russian attacks killed 35 people and injured another 24 over the past day, Governor Vadym Filashkin said. Of those killed, 32 were in Kramatorsk and three in Bilenke.
In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, two people were killed and three others injured, the regional military administration said. Russian forces launched more than 60 attacks on districts of the oblast using drones, artillery, and aerial bombs.
In Sumy Oblast, one person was killed and 14 others injured, including two children, the local authorities said. Two 12-year-old boys were injured in a drone attack. Russian forces launched nearly 40 attacks against 21 settlements in the oblast over the past day.
In Kherson Oblast, four people were injured, including a child, the regional military administration said. Russian forces targeted critical and social infrastructure as well as residential neighborhoods, damaging 12 private houses, gas pipelines, and vehicles.
In Kharkiv Oblast, three people were injured in Russian attacks on 17 settlements, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said. Two men aged 51 and 53 were injured in Zolochiv, while a 72-year-old woman was injured in Khotimlia. Russian forces used aerial bombs, multiple-launch rocket systems, and drones, including FPV drones, in the attacks.
In Chernihiv Oblast, an elderly man was injured after a Russian drone struck a courtyard in a village in the Liubech community, the regional military administration said. Overnight, a Russian Geran-type drone also struck a hypermarket on the outskirts of Chernihiv, causing a fire.
In Ivano-Frankivsk Oblast, a 67-year-old man was killed in a Russian attack on the city of Ivano-Frankivsk, regional Governor Svitlana Onyshchuk said.

2026 Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Navi Pillay
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:06:43 UTC
18:06:43 KST

2026 Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Navi Pillay
Pillay has been instrumental in ensuring war crimes and genocide are prosecuted, Nobel committee says.
The Norwegian Nobel Committee has awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize to Navanethem “Navi” Pillay.
The committee’s announcement of the 125th Nobel Peace Prize, made on Friday in Oslo, said the award would go to the South African jurist for her work to promote peace and international law.
The committee said in a statement that Pillay, a former United Nations high commissioner for human rights, had been instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted.
“At a time of existential challenges – including more wars and conflicts than the world has seen in a long time – international law is no longer just a supplement to peace and security. It is an absolute necessity,” the statement read.
Committee Chairman Jorgen Watne Frydnes said the system of international law was “under tremendous pressure” and its institutions were “under attack”. It is judges, he continued, “who guard the thin red line between order and chaos”.
Crimes against humanity
A South African of Indian Tamil origin, the 85-year-old Pillay was the first woman to start a law practice in what was then the province of Natal in 1967.
She was a defence lawyer for Nelson Mandela, who previously won the peace prize, and other antiapartheid activists and was the first woman of colour to serve on South Africa’s High Court.
She later served on the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the International Criminal Court and as the UN’s rights chief.
The committee highlighted her role during her time on the Rwanda tribunal in establishing that rape and sexual violence can constitute crimes against humanity and genocide.
Pillay chaired the UN Independent International Commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory, which concluded last year that Israel committed genocide in Gaza.
“We concluded that the State of Israel is responsible for the commission of four genocidal acts in Gaza with the specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza,” she declared in a presentation to the UN General Assembly.
The conclusions found that Israel’s president, prime minister and former defence minister had “incited the commission” of genocide.
Pillay currently sits on the International Court of Justice in the case in which Myanmar stands accused of genocide against the Rohingya.
Ashok Swain, a researcher at Uppsala University in Sweden said that while the prize won’t deliver any concrete change on the ground, the messaging of the award to Pillay is key in the current climate.
“International law … was never perfect, but at least some rules were there. Now it has become a free-for-all, and everyone interprets it the way they want,” he told Al Jazeera. “We have not seen this many conflicts in the world in the last half-century.
Verification
Reacting to the award, Pillay said she thought at first it must be a joke. “Being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify this,” she remarked.
“The last thing I did is the delivery of the report on Gaza, naming what’s happening there as genocide,” she continued. “One of the main reactions to that report is paying tribute to me for my courage. And you can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth?”
The prize, which is worth 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2m), will be presented in Oslo on December 10 on the anniversary of the death of Swedish industrialist Alfred Nobel, who founded the awards in his 1895 will.
Four other prizes were announced earlier this week for medicine, physics, chemistry and literature.
The Nobel committee received nominations for 287 candidates for this year’s peace prize. Other contenders included the International Space Station, emergency teams in Sudan, children’s advocates in Ukraine and two top international courts.
United States President Donald Trump has long coveted the prize and repeatedly said he deserves it despite starting the ongoing US-Israel war on Iran.
Last year’s winner, Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, handed her medal to Trump after the US deposed former President Nicholas Maduro in January.
Pillay joked that she might share her prize with the US leader.
“If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump,” she said in a video posted on social media by the secretary-general of Amnesty International that showed Pillay being applauded after the announcement of the award.

Zelenskyy blasts US over Russia ties as strikes kill 78 in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:06:40 UTC
18:06:40 KST

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused the United States of being unwilling to help Ukraine after Russian strikes killed 78 people and wounded 215 across the country in two days, urging President Donald Trump to increase military support and sanctions against Moscow.
The attacks included a devastating strike on the eastern city of Kramatorsk, where at least 35 people were killed and 20 wounded, according to Ukrainian officials.
The bombardment followed a major Russian drone and missile assault a day earlier that killed dozens, including 22 people in a residential building in Pryluky, about 130 kilometers (80 miles) east of Kyiv.
Speaking to reporters Thursday in Pryluky, Zelenskyy criticized Washington for pursuing potential economic cooperation with Russia while attempting to mediate the war, now in its fifth year.
He also called on the United States to expand Ukraine's access to the Starlink satellite communications network, saying it could help Ukrainian forces identify and target Russian ballistic missile launchers.
"Open Starlink for Ukraine. You did open it when you were responding to Iran," Zelenskyy said. "Give it to us, help us defend our skies and dominate there. And then Putin will sit down at the negotiating table."
The Ukrainian leader questioned U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio's assessment earlier Thursday that the war had reached a stalemate and Washington would continue working toward a settlement.
Zelenskyy argued that Washington's pursuit of economic projects with Moscow contradicted claims that diplomatic progress had stalled.
"So where's the truth here, where's the honesty? Where's the stalemate? ... That's called unwillingness," he said.
"One cannot, on the one hand, negotiate with the Russians about future economic projects, whilst on the other hand say that we find ourselves in some sort of ... diplomatic stalemate," he added.
His remarks followed a Reuters report that senior Russian and U.S. officials, including U.S. Special Envoy Jared Kushner, had discussed bringing an American investor into the Nord Stream pipeline network, which transported Russian natural gas to Germany before Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Zelenskyy urged Trump to increase sanctions pressure on Russia, arguing that stronger support for Ukraine could help bring Russian President Vladimir Putin to the negotiating table.
Ukrainian negotiators are scheduled to travel to the United States on Friday and Saturday for talks. Zelenskyy said he expected European partners to join the discussions, with air defense expected to be a key issue amid continued Russian attacks.
In Kramatorsk, a Russian guided aerial bomb struck the city Thursday, killing dozens and damaging two buses. A subsequent drone attack killed two more people, bringing the reported death toll to 35.
Regional Governor Vadym Filashkin accused Russian forces of deliberately targeting civilians.
"The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians. For them, a bus full of passengers is an attractive target precisely because a single strike can kill as many people as possible," he said on Telegram.
Images released by officials showed bodies scattered across a debris-covered street beside a charred bus. Some victims had not been identified, Zelenskyy said, warning that the attack would not go unanswered.
Elsewhere, a Russian guided aerial bomb killed two people in a village in southeastern Dnipropetrovsk region, while another person died in the western city of Ivano-Frankivsk, local authorities said.
The latest bombardment followed Wednesday's attacks, which killed dozens across Ukraine, including 22 people in Pryluky.
Russia also attacked Kyiv on Thursday morning, killing four people and wounding 19, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
The strikes disrupted water and electricity supplies in parts of the capital, with officials warning that restoring services would take time.
Moscow has intensified drone attacks on Kyiv in recent weeks, targeting warehouses, data centers and other infrastructure while renewing its campaign against Ukraine's power grid ahead of winter.
Russian technology company Yandex said it could not yet determine whether equipment at a data center hit by a Ukrainian drone attack could be restored.
Zelenskyy did not specifically address the strike on Yandex but said Ukraine was mirroring Russian attacks on data centers.
Ukraine has sought to regain the battlefield initiative as Russian territorial advances have slowed this year. However, Moscow's sustained air campaign continues to threaten civilians, critical infrastructure and the country's energy security.

A Princess Diana sex tape? How Britain's biggest tabloid fell for an elaborate hoax
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:06:19 UTC
18:06:19 KST

Any aspiring businessman will tell you that if someone offers you a deal that seems too good to be true, there's a very good chance that's because it isn't true. By the same token, experienced journalists around the world know that when a story sounds too sensational to be real, it's often because it's entirely made up. The people behind the British tabloid The Sun learned both lessons — one about business and the other about journalism — the hard way back in the mid-1990s.
The Sun had no fewer than 4 million loyal readers at the time, thanks in large part to its editors' knack for delivering a steady stream of sensational stories that caused trouble for Britain's rich, famous and beautiful. So when the newspaper's headlines announced in early October 1996 that its newsroom had obtained a steamy video featuring Princess Diana and her longtime lover, everyone simply assumed the scoop-hungry tabloid had finally landed the ultimate story.
The video, just 80 seconds long, purportedly showed Princess Diana undressing and embracing James Hewitt, her former riding instructor, whose name had previously been romantically linked to hers. By the time The Sun published its scoop, Diana was already divorced from Prince Charles. But the newspaper claimed the footage had been filmed five years earlier, while the couple was still married, and that the alleged affair had taken place at Prince Charles' country estate.
As you might imagine, The Sun's report quickly became the talk of Britain. Princess Diana had long been the ultimate prize for tabloids hungry for sensational stories, and so many paparazzi photographers had built their careers around pursuing her that they could probably have filled Buckingham Palace. That relentless pursuit of Diana would also play a major role in her death just a year later.
A Buckingham Palace spokesman issued a statement on Diana's behalf saying she did not recognize herself or Hewitt in the video, but the denial seemed too generic and terse to be convincing. It certainly didn't help that James Hewitt, the man supposedly featured in the footage, said he remembered the incident very well.
The Sun even claimed the video supported allegations Diana herself had previously made that she had been subjected to malicious surveillance orchestrated by her husband, Prince Charles.
But all of this unfolded in just half a day. The Sun's sensational story about Diana and Hewitt lasted only 12 hours before its rival, the Daily Mirror, announced that it would reveal the truth behind the video the following morning.
But the truth came out even before the next morning. It quickly emerged that the people in the video were not Princess Diana and James Hewitt, but actors and models hired through a well-known London agency specializing in look-alikes of members of the royal family and their romantic partners.
In fact, one British television station even broadcast the original recording, this time in color and close-up, to demonstrate how the footage had been manipulated to convince The Sun's staff that it was genuine.
It turned out that the 80-second video was simply an excerpt from a pilot episode of a satirical television series about the royal family, filmed several months earlier. The producers had hired an unknown actor named Gareth to play Hewitt, alongside two different models who had spent years earning a living from their resemblance to Princess Diana.
Christina Hance, 35, appeared in the first part of the video, while Nicky Lilley replaced her toward the end.
Lilley was quick to clarify that she, not Diana, was the woman performing the striptease in the video. Hance, meanwhile, expressed concern for the princess and her children. Having earned a living from her resemblance to Diana for 10 years, she said she did not want to cause the royal family any harm and felt compelled to set the record straight.
Nick Hedges, the director hired to shoot the television pilot, also sounded astonished by the extraordinary turn his footage had taken.
He revealed that the entire day's filming had cost just 650 pounds — roughly one-thousandth of what The Sun had paid for the video — and that the original idea was to shoot a comedy sketch featuring Diana and her lover supposedly being pursued by photographers.
That was also why Hedges himself had converted the footage from color to black and white and copied the tape several times to make it look like a poor-quality recording shot by a paparazzo from a distance using cheap equipment.
Hedges said he had not expected the sketch to be broadcast because, despite the performers' efforts, he felt the result was unconvincing.
Well, it certainly worked on the thoroughly embarrassed staff of The Sun.
Editor-in-chief Stuart Higgins appeared on television and explained that the newspaper had been duped by sophisticated con artists. He apologized to Princess Diana and the royal family.
According to Higgins, the tape had been offered to him the previous week during a secret meeting with two men acting as intermediaries, one of whom he described as a "smart American lawyer."
He also insisted that the newspaper had made every possible effort to verify the tape's authenticity, consulting independent witnesses who had confirmed the identities of the princess and her lover.
But more thorough examinations conducted after The Sun's blunder only made matters worse.
It emerged that none of the "experts" who had authenticated the footage had noticed that the woman in the video was wearing a watch on her right wrist. That was because Nicky Lilley, who was left-handed, habitually wore her watch that way, while Diana wore hers on her left wrist, like most people.
When the dust finally settled on the fiasco, one man was certainly celebrating the whole affair: the editor of the Daily Mirror.
A certain fellow you may have heard of.
His name was Piers Morgan.

Five confirmed dead in Istanbul building collapse as search wraps up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:05:12 UTC
18:05:12 KST

Search and rescue operations have been completed at the partially collapsed seven-story building in Maltepe. (AA Photo)
Search and rescue operations ended in Istanbul’s Maltepe district on Oct. 9 after crews recovered three more bodies from the rubble of a partially collapsed seven-story building, bringing the death toll to five.
The building’s first three floors collapsed on Oct. 8 on Doğu Street in the Cevizli neighborhood. Under the coordination of Türkiye’s Disaster and Emergency Management Authority (AFAD), teams carried out controlled demolition from the upper floors before moving on to remove debris. They periodically paused work to listen for possible sounds beneath the rubble.
The last body was recovered at 6:15 a.m. on Oct. 9, according to the Istanbul Governor’s Office. Crews then conducted a final controlled search to check whether anyone else remained beneath the debris. Four people died at the scene and one died after being taken to hospital. A total of 14 people were recovered from the wreckage.
Although search and rescue operations have concluded, heavy machinery continues to clear debris from the site. Teams also collected samples from columns on every floor of the building for examination as authorities investigate the cause of the collapse.
Emergency crews evacuated 55 residents across three neighboring buildings as a safety precaution. Authorities secured hotel lodging for 44 displaced individuals, while dispatching psychosocial support teams to both hospitalized survivors and those in temporary housing. On-site teams also distributed food and logistical aid to rescue personnel and affected residents.
The operation involved 774 personnel, 237 vehicles, two drones and 10 search-and-rescue dogs, the governor’s office said. AFAD teams from Istanbul and neighboring provinces, firefighters, emergency medical services, police, municipal agencies, the Turkish Red Crescent and other public institutions took part in the response.

Court jails Bulgarian driver for bringing illegal migrants into Estonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:05:00 UTC
18:05:00 KST

Court jails Bulgarian driver for bringing illegal migrants into Estonia
The Pärnu District Court found a Bulgarian citizen guilty in expedited proceedings for bringing illegal migrants into the country and sentenced him to imprisonment.
On 6 October, police detained a Bulgarian citizen near the border of Kose municipality and Järva County, and seven foreign nationals who had entered the country illegally were found in his vehicle.
The court sentenced the Bulgarian citizen to one year and ten months in prison, of which he must immediately serve three months. After that, the man will be expelled from Estonia to Bulgaria and will be subject to a five‑year entry ban. If he commits a new crime, the court may order the full sentence to be served.
The Bulgarian man was recruited to transport illegal migrants through a social‑media job advertisement, said Marko Roose, head of the organized and serious crime group of the Southern Prefecture's criminal bureau.
"During the investigation, we established that the 63‑year‑old Bulgarian living in Germany saw a job advertisement on TikTok and contacted the poster. His bus ticket from Germany to Riga, hotel accommodation, and rental car were then paid for. Following the instructions he received, the Bulgarian drove to an agreed location near the Belarusian border in Latvia, picked up seven foreign nationals who had entered the country illegally, and began driving toward Tallinn until an Estonian police patrol stopped them on the Tallinn–Tartu highway," Roose described.
Other suspects held in custody
This week, at the request of the Prosecutor's Office, the court also took into custody a German citizen and two Pakistani citizens who were caught transporting a total of nine migrants in Tori and Häädemeeste municipalities. The court likewise took into custody two Ukrainian citizens who were caught in Paldiski attempting to transport two illegal migrants onto a ship bound for Sweden. All of these suspects will remain in custody during pre‑trial proceedings.
The law provides for up to three years' imprisonment for illegally transporting a foreigner across Estonia's state border. If the migrants are placed in a life‑threatening or seriously harmful situation, the court may impose up to seven years' imprisonment.
Since the migration pressure began in July, police have detained nearly 320 foreign nationals who arrived in Estonia without a legal basis, originating from African and Asian countries, including Afghanistan and Bangladesh. Around 50 criminal proceedings have been launched related to illegal transport across Estonia's border, with 11 suspects currently in custody for human smuggling, and two people already sentenced to prison.
Profits will be confiscated
Prosecutor Keili Tiirik said smugglers face an increasing likelihood of being caught and losing their freedom. If profits gained from crimes are identified, they will be confiscated.
Roose advises treating vague job offers critically and stopping activity if doubts arise.
If it becomes clear that the job involves picking up foreign nationals who have clearly crossed the border illegally, it is not too late to inform the police and withdraw from committing the crime, Roose said.
The apprehension of illegal migrants and their transporters confirms that the risk of being caught is high for organizers of illegal migration in Estonia. "We have increased checks at key points where people move and in border areas where there is reason to suspect they may be used for illegal migration," Roose said.
If anyone notices suspicious vehicles or unusual groups of foreign nationals who differ from typical tourists, or activity suggesting human smuggling, they should report it to the police at 112, Roose said.

In Montenegro, the founder of the Russian propaganda network &quot;Rybar&quot; was detained
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:02:33 EEST
18:02:33 KST

In Montenegro, the founder of the Russian propaganda network "Rybar" was detained
Kyiv • UNN
Mikhail Zvynchuk, his wife, and three other people were detained on suspicion of hybrid activities. Zvynchuk is under sanctions.
In Montenegro, the head of the Russian propaganda network "Rybar," Mikhail Zvynchuk, his wife, and three other people were detained. Vijesti reports this, UNN writes.
Details
The operation was conducted on suspicion of hybrid activities by the network, which the United Kingdom and the United States associate with the dissemination of Kremlin propaganda and foreign information influence operations.
The British government named Zvynchuk as a co-owner and chief executive of "Rybar." According to the British authorities, the network is partially coordinated by the administration of the president of Russia, receives funding from the state corporation "Rostec," and cooperates with representatives of Russia's security services. Zvynchuk is under British sanctions, while the U.S. Department of State has included him on a list of individuals involved in malign influence operations targeting the electoral process in the United States.
Under the Rewards for Justice program, the United States is offering up to $10 million for information that helps identify or locate foreign actors involved in interference in U.S. elections, including alleged accomplices of "Rybar," or helps prevent such actions.
Additional information
"Rybar" is a Russian media network founded in 2018. It became particularly well known after the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Initially conceived as a platform for military analysis and conflict reporting, it eventually grew into an extensive network of communication channels that Western institutions associate with the dissemination of pro-Russian narratives, propaganda activities, and information influence operations.
Mikhail Zvynchuk is the founder and one of the best-known representatives of "Rybar," as well as a former employee of information structures within Russia's Ministry of Defense. In 2018, together with Denis Shchukin, he created the project, which later became one of the most influential Russian military Telegram channels.

Justice Minister Akın Gürlek spoke about the disputed investment funds.
Justice Minister Akın Gürlek said authorities have expanded their investigation into the disputed investment funds by focusing on individuals who exited the funds between Sept. 13 and Sept. 16 after allegedly receiving advance information, according to the minister’s remarks published by daily Sabah.
Gürlek said investigators are examining investors who withdrew from the funds based on prior knowledge and information allegedly provided to them.

The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office has reportedly submitted the names of the identified beneficiaries to the Savings Deposit Insurance Fund (TMSF), seeking the return of the 187.65 billion liras through voluntary repayment accounts.
According to the report, TMSF has begun issuing formal notifications to people on the list requesting the return of the funds, which will be collected in accounts established for victims.
Reviews found that the individuals in question exited the funds with prior knowledge and in line with the information provided to them.
