Animals crossing: the simple solution to stop roadkill in the Amazon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:00:44 UTC
18:00:44 KST

By about 7am, with dense fog blanketing the landscape, Gabriel Falquetto had already come across several road-killed animals along the ES-164 highway in Brazil’s Espírito Santo state. The biologist was on his way to Kaetés private natural heritage reserve (RPPN) in the Atlantic Forest, where he monitors wildlife and roadkill.
Then he spotted the lifeless body of a primate on the pavement. It was a buffy-headed marmoset (Callithrix flaviceps), a species listed as critically endangered on the International Union for Conservation of Nature red list. An estimated 2,500 individuals remain in the wild, making it one of the world’s most threatened primates.
“It was extremely painful and discouraging,” Falquetto said. “We travel through this region every day monitoring wildlife, and we celebrate every encounter with groups of buffy-headed marmosets in the forest. Finding an individual in those conditions brings a feeling of sadness and helplessness. Beyond the loss of that animal, the incident reminds us of the impacts our activities have on biodiversity.”
About 1,800 miles away, on a road leading to Alta Floresta, a small Amazon town in the far north of Mato Grosso state, there have been no cases like the buffy-headed marmoset’s roadkill recorded since 2024. That year, eight canopy bridges were installed, connecting fragmented forest patches. Camera trap footage revealed that over 15 months the aerial wildlife crossings enabled 15,000 safe crossings by arboreal animals – and in that time there was not a single road kill.
The bridges are part of a programme involving Projeto Reconecta and the municipal government, along with local organisations and business owners who are eager to conserve the unique biodiversity of their town and promote ecotourism, and were alarmed by the growing number of wildlife-vehicle collisions.
Fernanda Abra, an associate researcher at the Smithsonian national zoo and the Conservation Biology Institute in the US, and the founder of Reconecta, recalled that just hours before installing the first bridges in Alta Floresta, she found two Schneider’s marmosets (Mico schneideri) dead. The species is endemic to the Brazilian Amazon and is threatened with extinction.
“A canopy bridge serves two purposes,” Abra said. “The first is to improve connectivity for wildlife, allowing animals to move from one side to the other in these fragmented forest areas. As a result, we also reduce roadkill.”
All bridges have two camera traps, one facing the crossing to record which animals are using it and the other facing the forest to observe which animals arrive there but decide not to use it.
Among the primate species recorded using the bridges during the first months of the programme were the black-faced black spider monkey (Ateles chamek), the Purús red howler monkey (Alouatta puruensis), the tufted capuchin (Sapajus apella), Schneider’s marmoset and the Alta Floresta titi monkey (Plecturocebus grovesi).
Described only in 2019 and soon after classified as critically endangered, the Alta Floresta titi monkey has become the symbol of the initiative, which is now entering a new phase thanks to its positive results.
“In August, we will install eight more bridges in the city’s urban area,” Abra said. “The only difference is that the electric utility will first need to lower the power lines and insulate them so that if animals jump from the bridge on to the wires, they won’t be electrocuted.”
The project under way in Alta Floresta is not Reconecta’s first. In 2021, working alongside the Waimiri-Atroari Indigenous people, the team installed 32 canopy bridges over BR-174, the highway that crosses their territory and the Amazon between the Brazilian states of Amazonas and Roraima.
The Waimiri-Atroari helped Abra identify the best locations for the artificial bridges. Over the past five years, cameras mounted on the bridge poles have documented about 1,250 crossings by primates, including the golden-handed tamarin (Saguinus midas), a species that is not strictly arboreal and often descends to the ground in search of food, making it particularly vulnerable to roadkill.
“The outcomes of the BR-174 project have been incredible,” Abra said. “We were able to test different bridge designs to find out which ones the animals prefer.”
After years of working along Brazilian highways, she had always sought a solution that was simple, low-cost and durable. The current bridge features a multilayer design that accommodates primates with different modes of locomotion – from species that rely on their prehensile tails to move through the canopy, to brachiating species such as spider monkeys, which swing using their arms, both of which are common in the Amazon, as well as species that simply walk across the network of crossed ropes. Other small terrestrial mammals including opossums, sloths and mouse opossums have also been recorded using the bridges.
Abra said it was important to keep in mind that this was a long-term project, and results were not always immediate. BR-174 was built in the 1970s, and animals take time to adapt to a new crossing alternative. Reconecta’s monitoring has shown that use of the structures increases over time.
“Very often, our sense of urgency in conservation doesn’t take into account the timing of the impact,” she said.
In Alta Floresta, tufted capuchins took seven months before using one of the bridges for the first time, which may indicate that each species has its own pace of adaptation.
Home to the world’s greatest diversity of primates, Brazil also has the world’s fourth largest road network – a deadly combination for animals living along forest edges that have been split apart to make way for highways.
“From our human perspective, roads mean connection and development. But for wildlife, they represent disconnection, barriers and a threat to survival,” Abra said.
Nearly 9 million mammals are killed on Brazil’s roads every year, a 2022 study found. A data compilation published in the journal Nature in 2025 found that the country ranked among those with the highest mortality rates of terrestrial vertebrates killed on roads.
Prof Fabiano Rodrigues de Melo, a primatologist at the Federal University of Viçosa in Minas Gerais, said: “Habitat loss is one of the main drivers of population declines, especially among threatened species, but the impact of roadkill is still greatly underestimated.”
Beyond roadkills, highways bring confinement to fauna. Amely Branquinho Martins, an environmental analyst at the ICMBio, Brazil’s federal agency for conservation units, and a coordinator of the Genomics of the Brazilian Biodiversity project, said: “When populations become isolated, they grow smaller and more vulnerable to threats.”
One of those threats is inbreeding, which occurs when closely related individuals reproduce. “Habitat loss and degradation can prevent an individual from one population from migrating to another – what we call gene flow. Without it, the species’ genetic diversity declines,” Martins said.
The consequences continue to multiply in a domino effect, Melo said. The loss of primates, especially fruit-eating species, can alter forest composition, because they play a key role in seed dispersal and even contribute to pollination. “A whole network of ecological interactions is ultimately lost with the disappearance of these species,” Melo said.
One of the hopes for reducing wildlife roadkill is the passage of a bill under consideration in Brazil’s congress that would establish a national road safety plan for wildlife, which calls, among other measures, for the placement of wildlife warning signs, speed-reduction devices and the construction of overpasses, aerial crossings and underpasses along highways.
The bill has been approved by the chamber of deputies and is now awaiting a vote in the senate.
If approved, the canopy bridge model developed by Reconecta could be implemented nationwide. In 2026, Brazil’s national department of transport infrastructure designated the design as the recommended standard for highways.
Abra’s efforts to protect primates have earned international recognition. She received a Future for Nature award in 2019, followed in 2024 by a Whitley award, often referred to as the Oscars of environmental conservation. In June she was named as one of the recipients of the 2026 Wayfinder award, joining a select group who receive funding from the National Geographic Society for their projects.
The support comes at the right time, as Abra plans to expand Reconecta, including new chapters in Suriname and Lucas do Rio Verde, a municipality in Brazil, which will install 10 canopy bridges.
Abra also hopes to bring her canopy bridges to other biomes, including the Pantanal and the Atlantic Forest, helping prevent the deaths of monkeys such as the buffy-headed marmoset.
Expectations are especially high for bridges over BR-262, one of Brazil’s longest highways, which cuts across the Pantanal and is known as the “highway of death”. Approximately 2,000 animals are killed on the road every year.
Abra said: “I envision a future with Reconecta biomes. We already have Reconecta Amazon, and we’ll soon launch Reconecta Pantanal. I also see canopy bridges in the Atlantic Forest for the primates that live there, including muriquis and howler monkeys, which are both highly threatened.”
She stressed that for this vision to succeed, the continued engagement of government agencies, private companies and local communities would be essential, just as it was in Alta Floresta and the Waimiri-Atroari Indigenous territory. “When everyone is involved, everyone values the initiative and works harder to make it succeed,” she said.

====================================================================================================

‘Self-imposed irrelevance’: why the EU is failing to act on growing public criticism of Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:00:44 UTC
18:00:44 KST

When the British government announced sweeping sanctions on trade with illegal Israeli settlements and condemned “ethnic cleansing” in the West Bank by state-backed “settler terrorists”, some EU diplomats hoped this dramatic shift in UK government policy towards Israel would have a galvanising effect on the rest of Europe. So far, it has not.
Although France and Canada joined the UK in pledging to ban goods from illegal settlements and impose sanctions on “those who facilitate them or profit from them”, there has not yet been a wider ripple effect.
A meeting of EU foreign affairs ministers on Monday is likely to showcase the bloc’s stasis in policy towards Israel – a stalemate that is at odds with rising public criticism in Europe of Israel’s government.
A survey of 10 European countries, including Spain, France and Sweden, found large majorities of people had a negative opinion of Israel. Views had become more negative compared with the previous year, according to the Pew Research Center, mostly after the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran, which unleashed a new crisis in the Middle East and a global economic shock. In Poland, negative views jumped eight points to 70% of respondents, in Italy they increased by nine points to 75% and in Germany they also rose by nine points to 73%.
Israel is facing ever deeper isolation in the theatre of public opinion. Five countries chose to boycott the Eurovision song contest this year over Israel’s participation, after organisers declined to exclude it over its conduct in the Gaza war and rising violence in the West Bank. Organisers have now decided that broadcasters will no longer be eligible to host the song contest if their state is involved in an armed conflict or sensitive geopolitical situation.
More than 74,000 people, including at least 21,200 children, have been killed in Gaza since Israel launched its war in retaliation for the Hamas attack of 7 October 2023, in which the terrorist group killed 1,209 people – including 36 children – and took 251 hostages, inflicting a nationwide trauma.
Gaza remains a humanitarian catastrophe, with people facing acute shortages of water, nutritious food and medical equipment and medicines, while contending with disease, unemployment, economic collapse and the threat of death or injury. Israel’s airstrikes continue: the death toll includes 1,400 Palestinians killed since a ceasefire was declared a year ago.
The EU talks on the Middle East will focus on the conflicts in Iran and Yemen, but ministers will also discuss the situation in Gaza and the West Bank in the context of elections in Israel on 27 October and the first legislative elections in Palestine in 20 years, which are expected by late November.
The discussion is expected to expose familiar fault lines in the 27-member EU. One group of countries are vocal supporters of the Palestinian cause: Spain and Ireland were the first to call for a review of whether Israel’s conduct in the Gaza war was in breach of the human rights requirements of its association agreement with the EU, which covers the €68bn (£58bn) trade relationship, cooperation in research, environment and energy.
A second group consistently opposes targeting Israel’s government: Germany and Austria are close allies for historical reasons, while Czechia and Italy are ideologically aligned with Benjamin Netanyahu’s administration.
Among a third, larger group of countries in the middle are several, such as France and the Netherlands, that are increasingly critical of the Netanyahu government’s conduct in Gaza and its plans to build the vast E1 settlement, which threatens to critically damage the two-state solution.
Martin Konečný, the director of the Brussels-based European Middle East Project, thinks the EU has a diplomatic role to play as Israel advances with the controversial E1 plan. However, he does not see any sign of action. “The EU is basically staying in its usual self-imposed irrelevance,” he said.
This is not an isolated view. More than 500 former senior EU officials and diplomats issued a statement this week condemning the bloc’s failure to take action over Israel’s actions in Gaza and the West Bank.
The signatories, which include former prime ministers of France, Italy and Sweden, as well as Josep Borrell, the EU’s former chief diplomat, singled out Germany and Italy for the first time in stark, uncompromising language.
“Germany and Italy continue to systematically block the adoption of any EU measures, thus becoming de facto complicit in undermining both EU values and the two-state solution,” wrote the group, which includes a few dozen senior figures from those two countries.
Given their size, Germany and Italy have been crucial in preventing the EU from forging a weighted majority to impose trade sanctions and ban commerce with illegal settlements.
Michael Doyle, a former EU ambassador who co-organised the statement, told the Guardian the EU was not meeting the obligations of its treaties or international law.
“Unfortunately our often-proclaimed EU values are set aside when it comes to the EU’s collective response to the dire plight of Palestinians,” he said. The widespread disquiet explained “why we get so many signatures from people who don’t normally sign such calls for action”.
The statement was motivated by the absence of proposals from the European Commission, the guardian of EU law that initiates legislation for the 27-member bloc. The commission has declined to table proposals to ban trade with illegal settlements.
The refusal to act has exasperated numerous lawyers and trade experts, who argue the ban is necessary for the EU to comply with a landmark advisory ruling from the international court of justice in 2024 on the illegality of the settlements. It told other countries to “take steps to prevent trade or investment relations that assists in the maintenance of the illegal situation created by Israel in the occupied Palestinian territory”.
Ursula von der Leyen, the commission’s president and a German Christian Democrat who is not afraid to take political risks, has argued the EU cannot act when member states disagree. In her annual state of the union speech last month, she lamented: “When Europe is divided, it cannot change the course of events.” A year earlier she presented proposals to suspend preferential trade with Israel but never found sufficient support from member states.
Advocates of the EU taking a stronger approach are not convinced she cannot act. Konečný said: “It is not guaranteed that the qualified majority would be reached. But once the commission tables the proposal [on banning trade with settlements], that changes the dynamic.”
The blocking European governments may be lagging behind public opinion. Large majorities in Italy (88%) and Germany (83%) say they do not have confidence in Netanyahu “to do the right thing regarding world affairs”, according to the Pew Research Center’s study.
Meanwhile, the question of Israel-Palestine continues to roil the left. This week the Green party of England and Wales adopted a motion equating Zionism with racism, drawing widespread criticism.
The motion from a small political party in the UK was strongly condemned by the head of the Jewish Greens in England and Wales (“a very bad motion”) and the European Greens, which stressed the importance of being “absolutely unambiguous” in the fight against antisemitism.
Peace campaigners think it makes their job harder. The motion “hands ammunition to those who want to paint pro-Palestinian activism as illegitimate”, wrote Yachad, an organisation that seeks to build support among British Jews for a political resolution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.

Bragging rights for Burnham, blues for Farage: conference season winners and losers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:00:43 UTC
18:00:43 KST

Winners
Andy Burnham
Even his fiercest critics would struggle to argue that Andy Burnham’s first conference as Labour party leader was anything but a success. There was the requisite rapture among the Labour faithful after his deeply-personal speech, delivered without a tie or a lectern and, at times, with tears in his eyes. But even figures on the right, such as the broadcaster Piers Morgan, described it as “one of the best, and most powerfully delivered, by a British politician in a very long time”.
The prime minister’s policy offering packed a punch too. He put forward radical progressive policies on social care, promising to “rip the plaster off” and make changes to the pensions triple lock, electoral reform and Europe.
A YouGov poll after the conference showed that it had boosted the “Burnham bounce”, with Labour opening up a five-point lead over Reform UK in the polls. The upcoming budget, and next year’s spending review, will sorely test whether he can keep that momentum going and make good on his promises. Burnham’s success at the Labour conference was capped by a victory at the Holborn and St Pancras byelection a few days later seeing off a challenge by the leader of the Green party Zack Polanski.
Kemi Badenoch
This time last year, Kemi Badenoch was hanging on to her role as leader of the opposition by a thread. But in the past 12 months her personal favourability ratings have continued to improve, according to More in Common research. This was a conference where she tightened her grip over the Conservative party and leaned hard into her own brand, telling GB News’s Christopher Hope: “We are under new management. There’s a new captain, there’s a new coach, there’s a new owner, effectively, which is all me.”
While Badenoch’s speech lacked the emotional firepower of Burnham’s, she was assured and disciplined in her focus on the economy – not mentioning small boats or other elements of the culture wars which have energised her in the past. Promised giveaways to wealthy individuals, such as free childcare for those earning more than £100,000 and abolishing inheritance tax on family homes for the 5% of households that pay it, were designed to appeal to the Conservative’s traditional base, one of the first indications of a resolve to win back the “blue wall”.
The most powerful moment of the speech came as she drew a line in the sand between the Tories and Reform, thunderously telling her audience there would be no uniting the right: “I don’t want to live in a country run by people who threaten journalists, call veterans traitors and debate whether my mixed-race children are English.” Whether she will reject any deal with Reform if the electoral circumstances dictate remains to be seen.
Online, all the time, communications
Both the Conservative and Labour communications teams can congratulate themselves on a job vigorously done in the past few weeks. The coup of the conference season came in the guise of a 27-metre (88ft) graphical retelling of the past two years in British politics in the style of the Bayeux tapestry, as seen through Conservative eyes. Senior party figures and members alike enjoyed the “Birmingham tapestry”, for its pointed jabs at defector Robert Jenrick, but the canniest move was including depictions of high-profile journalists, most of whom duly posted images of the propaganda to their sizeable social media followings.
The team at the Labour party conference successfully projected the “hopey-changey” vibes they had intended, mainly by producing as many posters and placards declaring there was “hope again” as there were participants at the conference. But special mention should also be given to the socials team at Labour HQ, whose snipes during their rivals’ conferences (“Who was less sure whether he’d finished, the shadow chancellor or the audience?”, they asked after Andrew Griffith’s less than assured end of speech exit) was a masterclass in side-eye.
The battle of political ideas
This conference season saw the most sharply defined battle lines between right and left in a generation. Burnham used his speech to attack neoliberalism, saying: “Britain has been on the wrong path for a long time. Deindustrialisation. Deregulation. Privatisation. Austerity. Brexit.”
He was instantly accused by the Conservatives of indulging in a “socialist fever dream” of the 1970s. They went on to proclaim a love of Thatcher while simultaneously belting out the national anthem. In her speech, Badenoch pitched the fight against Labour as “a battle for the soul of this nation”, trotting out the well-worn Tory treatise that “what people earn belongs to them, not government”.
Sidekicks with main character energy
Ed Miliband lolloped through Liverpool’s conference centre with the ease of a man who appears to be very much enjoying his time as foreign secretary. In a lineup easily swallowed by the gravitational pull of the leader’s speech, Miliband delivered a deft piece of politics, telling assembled members they were “right” to be moved by the plight of the Palestinian people.
Over at the Conservative conclave, the Conservatives’ candidate for mayor of London, James Cleverly, also had a jolly time away from the main stage. “[Kemi Badenoch] knows, as I do, that our best bet of getting her into No 10 is getting me into City Hall,” he told a panel convened by the Centre for Policy Studies (CPS).
Losers
Nigel Farage
Reform UK billed its largest ever gathering at the National Exhibition Centre in Birmingham as “the most talked about event of 2026”. Its leader, Nigel Farage, wanted to use the conference to outline a series of policy pledges for a Reform government’s first 100 days in office.
Instead the opening was overshadowed by the suspension of his close aides Dan Jukes and head of policy James Orr, after an undercover investigation by reporters from a group called Verbatim. Reform UK cleared them of breaking laws that ban foreign donations on Wednesday, but the matter remains under police investigation.
Farage’s own speech was interrupted by protesters, who appeared to be roughed up as they were thrown out of the hall. A man was later given a police caution after footage appeared to show one woman having her hair pulled and being hit with a walking stick.
Zack Polanski
Zack Polanski started his run in to the Green party of England and Wales’s conference by asking, unsuccessfully, if it could be delayed so he could focus on campaigning in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection. He may now wish it had been cancelled altogether.
The party’s gathering in Brighton was consumed by controversy, after members voted in favour of an official policy stating that Zionism, the movement for a Jewish state, is a type of racism. Polanski absented himself from the most toxic internal debate the party has faced for years, choosing instead to leave to campaign, and the party is still reeling from the fallout.
Shortly after the Greens’ triumph in February’s Gorton and Denton byelection it was polling above 20%; it now stands on 11%.
Ed Davey
At first it seemed as if the Liberal Democrat leader, Ed Davey, had come through his party’s conference in Brighton relatively unscathed, despite going unexpectedly viral for a speech in which he enthusiastically, if not entirely successfully, attempted to rally a chant of “We care! We fight!”. But his opposition to Labour’s proposals to change the pension triple lock was met with opposition by senior and backbench Lib Dems, with one saying his defence of the current policy “gaslights an entire generation into believing it’s for our benefit”.
John Healey
The chancellor used the word hope 21 times in his personal conference speech that, while warmly welcomed by Labour party members, managed to say very little about actual policy over quite a long period of time. In the days that followed, senior Labour figures privately voiced unease about Healey’s approach to his crucial first budget this month, noting it lacked detail about policy on investment and growth or any pitch-rolling for possible tax rises.
Andrew Griffith
Among all the gaffes, the spills, the wrong names and forgotten policy details of this season of party conferences, one performance really did stand out.
Griffith, the shadow chancellor, was described by Badenoch as having “more business experience than the entire Labour cabinet combined” – attenders at Conservative party conference were left wondering if any of it had involved public speaking. After an address variously described as “an historic clunker”, “curious” and “the worst speech ever heard”, Griffith’s speech appeared to simply peter out and the shadow chancellor wandering awkwardly off stage, leaving the audience not knowing whether to clap, or simply follow him out of the room.

Labour chair of housing committee calls for urgent funds for affordable homes in England
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:00:43 UTC
18:00:43 KST

The Labour chair of the Commons housing committee is urging John Healey to bring forward billions of pounds of planned spending on social and affordable homes in England, after housing associations said they were ready to build tens of thousands more.
Abena Oppong-Asare called for the chancellor to allocate money from the £39bn Social and Affordable Homes Programme (SAHP) as soon as possible, rather than after the election as planned.
Housing associations have said they could build an additional 41,000 homes outside London over the next 10 years if they had more government funding.
They said the extra units would help the government get closer to its target of building 1.5m new homes across this parliament – though the housing secretary, Angela Rayner, recently admitted that it would be difficult to achieve.
Oppong-Asare said: “The government should use the upcoming budget to increase the building of social homes by ensuring a significant proportion of the Social and Affordable Homes Programme is allocated during this parliament.
“Families stuck on social housing waiting lists need to see action now. I urge the chancellor to ensure a significant sum of the £39bn SAHP is allocated during this parliament and that truly affordable social rent homes are prioritised as part of this package.”
Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves, announced the £39bn 10-year fund last year, having changed the government’s borrowing rules to allow her to borrow more for capital projects.
The money was due to be spent on a mix of council houses and a number of other types of affordable housing, including affordable rents and shared ownership schemes.
Before he became prime minister, Andy Burnham had said the scheme should be reallocated entirely to social rent housing.
But when the first £10bn was allocated under his government in August, it went to a mix of councils and housing associations outside London to spend on a variety of types of subsidised homes.
Ministers said the money would help build 70,000 new homes. But housing associations said they could have built an additional 41,000 – including 25,000 for social rent – if the government had given them all the money for which they bid.
They said they could start construction work on 15,000 of those in the next three years – though some associations have come under fire for selling their homes to the private sector.
The National Housing Federation (NHF), which represents housing associations, said ministers would have to allocate an additional £5.3bn from the programme to build the extra homes.
Ministers have said they are planning to allocate £6bn to London immediately. But of the remaining £13bn, they said they planned to hand out “significant sums” in the second half of the scheme, which would come after the next election.
Kate Henderson, the chief executive of the NHF, said: “Housing associations submitted bids with plans to build tens of thousands of affordable homes, but many organisations with sites ready to go and proven track records did not receive the funding needed to deliver these homes.
“With additional investment now, it is possible to help transform the lives of families in urgent need of an affordable home.”
A spokesperson for the Ministry of Housing said: “We’ve already announced nearly £10bn of allocations from the Social and Affordable Homes Programme so we can start building more than 70,000 council, social and affordable homes across England.
“Our record investment will help families trapped in temporary accommodation or stuck on housing waiting lists into safe, secure homes.”

Malaysia has also sought Jakarta's approval to conduct cloud-seeding operations, using Indonesian airspace as authorities work to tackle haze linked to fires in the region.
Anwar also spoke to Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto regarding the haze and agreed to offer support.
Nearly 95,000 hectares burned in Indonesia in July alone, while about 202,000 hectares had burned nationwide by the end of July, the Forest Ministry said.
Indonesia has recorded around 175,000 cases of acute respiratory infections since August across areas affected by forest and land fires.
Meanwhile, neighboring Singapore is hosting Formula 1 race over the weekend and organizers have said they will not delay it despite haze.

Mamdani Demands Trump End ICE Operations in New York After Shooting

2026-10-09

18:00:19 KST

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani wants President Donald Trump to put an end to Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s operations in the city after an agent-involved shooting injured one person on Thursday.
“This is an unconscionable and incredibly serious situation,” Mamdani said in a statement Thursday evening. “I have called the President; when we speak I will demand that he ends all ICE enforcement actions in our city. I will not stand by while ICE agents terrorize our communities.”
New York police said that around 4 p.m., federal agents got involved in a shooting and injured a man in the city’s Marble Hill residential section. The police’s afternoon statement said the shooting victim was conscious and receiving medical attention in a nearby hospital.
But at a press conference Thursday evening before furious protesters, Mamdani said that after his two-hour conversation with Trump and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, he has failed to negotiate the release of the shooting victim.
The response to the shooting tests Mamdani’s charm offensive with the President, who appears unlikely to budge on his immigration agenda despite previous friendliness with the Democratic mayor. Despite wide ideological differences, Trump and Mamdani have had a cordial relationship.
Mamdani, however, remains just as firm on his own side of the issue. A steadfast critic of ICE operations, he has backed calls to abolish the agency. “I have said this directly—whether to the President or to the public—ICE undermines public safety,” he said.
The White House pointed TIME to the Department of Homeland Security’s statement, which attacked New York’s “sanctuary politicians” that limit cooperation with federal agents. Homeland Security Secretary Markewayne Mullin responded directly to Mamdani at a press conference Friday morning, accusing the mayor of “inciting hostilities" and undermining ICE's mission. Mullin said he had spoken with Mamdani multiple times on Thursday night.
Besides Mamdani, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, also a Democrat, released a swift rebuke of the shooting and said she too spoke with Trump and Mullin. “New Yorkers have witnessed far too many acts of violence by a rogue federal agency and untrained agents that operate with impunity,” the governor said. “Federal authorities need to provide answers, and they must do so immediately.”
What happened?
City police commissioner Jessica Tisch said that based on initial information, police received multiple 911 calls around 4 p.m. reporting shots fired and a person shot near 2 Marble Hill Avenue.
Their preliminary investigation showed that federal immigration agents were “conducting a targeted enforcement operation” to take a person in a gray vehicle into custody. Their target, whom Tisch identified as 28-year-old Oscar Belgal, was with a 5-year-old boy, whom police believed to be his son.
Tisch said that one plainclothes federal agent approached the driver’s side window, with his gun drawn, with another plainclothes agent near the headlight, before the vehicle moved forward. According to evidence collected on the scene, Tisch said that at least one ICE agent fired seven rounds, “striking the driver in the neck below his left ear.”
DHS said in its statement that an ICE officer “discharged his weapon” and injured its target, whom ICE agents immediately rendered aid to. “The incident remains under investigation,” the department added.
Tisch added that when New York police arrived on scene, they saw men in various clothes, including “at least one carrying a long gun.” Police also saw the injured Belgal “handcuffed and seated on the ground,” and they “immediately” placed him into a police vehicle and gave aid, before transporting him to New York-Presbyterian Allen Hospital in stable condition. The child, meanwhile, is safe and in the care of a family member, Tisch added.
Mullin said Friday that the ICE officers involved in the shooting were wearing body cameras and that there was footage relating to the incident. “As the investigation moves forward, as I said, we’ll release the information,” he said.
What do we know about the victim?
Tisch said that Belgal had two prior arrests in New York City: “one for robbery in 2023 in which he pleaded guilty to fourth-degree grand larceny and received five years probation; and one for criminal sale of a controlled substance in 2025, which is still pending.”
DHS did not name Belgal, but it described the target of the ICE operation as a “criminal illegal” immigrant from the Dominican Republic “with a prior criminal conviction for grand larceny, and multiple prior arrests for assault, robbery, possession of drugs, and weapons possession.”
The department alleged the shooting victim had ties to the Trinitarios gang, which was involved in the shooting of an off-duty Customs and Border Protection officer last year. It added that police arrested the target on Dec. 7, 2023, “but was released into the community a few days later by reckless Democrat sanctuary policies that put American lives at risk.”
Mullin said Friday morning that Bengal was "affiliated with a gang" and that ICE believed Bengal had knowledge regarding the shooting of a CBP officer last year. He also said ICE had attempted, and failed, to detain Bengal in September.
What have been the reactions?
The New York City shooting is just the latest in a spate of violent incidents involving federal immigration agents. Tallies from the New York Times and ABC News show more than 20 people shot, with at least six killed, including three U.S. citizens: Renee Good, Alex Pretti, and Ruben Ray Martinez.
The city has also become a hotspot for ICE-related activity. As Gothamist reported on Oct. 7, more than 8,800—or nearly half—of all ICE arrests in New York state during the second-term Trump Administration have happened in New York City’s five boroughs.
Lawmakers have since debated the nationwide enforcement of Trump’s immigration agenda, leading to funding battles and partial shutdowns of DHS.
Mamdani and other New York politicians took issue with how the ICE operation could have endangered a child. “There is no explanation for federal officers firing this many rounds into a car that has a 5-year-old,” the New York mayor said in the press conference.
Rep. Ritchie Torres, who represents the Bronx, posted that “firing multiple rounds into a car with a child inside, on a busy residential street in the Bronx, is abhorrent and indefensible.”
Rep. Adriano Espaillat, the Democrat representing the district covering Upper Manhattan and parts of West Bronx, posted on social media that ICE has denied him as well as the victim’s family from visiting and checking on the victim. Espaillat said he met the victim’s 5-year-old son, “distraught and traumatized after witnessing this horrific event.”
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, who represents New York and led the legislative standoff that temporarily blocked funding for DHS, called the shooting “deeply disturbing, especially amid reports that a child was in the car when shots were fired.” The senator called on DHS to release body camera footage and ensure independent investigations.

Why We Must Invest in Scientists, Not Just Science
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:00:01 UTC
18:00:01 KST

We often think of science as a search for answers to a specific issue: a solution to a known problem, or a cure for a particular disease. In practice, scientific discovery is typically more chaotic and uncertain, full of false starts and contradictions. That is why so many of the major scientific breakthroughs in human history have been born out of hunches, the product of imagination or serendipity, coupled with the brilliance and curiosity of a scientist to recognize the significance of a discovery. For instance, graphene was born out of tangential research at the University of Manchester and is now used in everything from medical equipment and electronics to batteries and tennis racquets.
Scientific research invariably raises new questions. What begins as a narrow inquiry opens dozens of new avenues of investigation, each capable of taking the research in an entirely new direction. The pursuit of science is, at its core, less a journey towards a destination than an evolving exercise in enlightened exploration.
It is through patient, painstaking work, driven by curiosity and pursued through personal dedication and sacrifice, that scientific advancement occurs. Yet, too often, our tendency as a society is to celebrate the tangible breakthroughs and neglect the assiduous process that made them possible.
The Nobel prizes are a magnificent celebration of transformative science. But by design, most are awarded decades after the breakthrough discovery being recognized was first made. Scientists, however, are typically most creative and productive early in their careers but fail to receive the financial support essential to reaching their full potential.
This quandary is replicated many times over within the wider world of institutional funding. Public bodies and universities must decide which projects to back before they know where those ideas will lead. And with many talented scientists competing for finite resources, much promising research is lost.
I would argue that this challenge, therefore, is felt most acutely by early-career scientists. The pressure on them is not simply to demonstrate scientific progress, but to produce the kind of science that can be articulated succinctly in a grant application, attached to a clear set of deliverables, and ultimately defended as a sensible investment. Something is lost if we focus too narrowly on supporting only what we can fully justify in advance.
Not every research grant is funded, and difficult choices must be made in the best of funding environments. But the nature of the funding matters too, and philanthropy must help broaden the level of support provided to young scientists.
This is where unrestricted funding plays an especially important role. Unrestricted funding is an investment in the person. It recognizes and supports their talent, ideas, judgment, curiosity, and long-term potential. The money provided can be used to buy new equipment, hire a new staff member, or simply pursue a new line of inquiry. It means having the space and time to evaluate an idea that might otherwise be too abstract for a regular grant application.
Unrestricted funding also provides scientists with freedom in a broader sense: it can relieve anxiety over rent, allow for a much-needed family vacation, or simply reduce financial pressure and give great thinkers more time to think about their science.
This is the principle upon which the Blavatnik Awards for Young Scientists was founded. Awardees receive grants ranging from $15,000 to $250,000, the largest such prizes awarded to early-career scientists. Crucially, there are no conditions attached; it is up to the awardees themselves to decide how and where the money can make the greatest difference for their science.
Philanthropy alone can never be a substitute for institutional or government funding, but it can play a vital role in driving discovery and human progress. It helps to create the conditions for greater risk-taking, unexpected advances, and the encouragement and retention of exceptional scientific talent.
And we have seen what can happen when that freedom is provided. Take the recipients of the Blavatnik Award. These early-career scientists have created over 50 companies, with a combined value exceeding $40 billion. Among these success stories are Amprius, which develops high-energy-density lithium-ion batteries; Editas Medicine, a gene-editing company; and Revolution Medicines, which develops new treatments for cancer.
Commercial return, however, is not the only measure of success. So is a breakthrough that fundamentally changes how we understand the world or a finding that opens an entirely new field of discovery.
Unrestricted funding is not simply the awarding of money. It is the gift of freedom to explore, experiment, and persevere. It provides the freedom to ask questions without knowing where the answers might lead, which is the very essence of science.

America’s Hybrid Hype Has Hit the Used Market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Conventional wisdom is that cars are bad investments. Drive one off the lot, and it starts losing value the minute its wheels touch the road. That makes what’s happening with the 2026 Toyota Rav4 downright weird.
Some used vehicles are listing for $3,000 to $6,000 above brand-new dealership prices, according to new data from the online automotive marketplace CarGurus. The months-old cars are aging like fine wine.
The crossover SUV—one of the top-selling in the US—went all-hybrid last year, after Toyota announced it would drop the gas-powered model from its lineup. That’s likely why we’re catching a glimpse of an economic Upside Down. Kevin Roberts, director of economic and market intelligence at CarGurus, says the situation reminds him of the pandemic-era chip shortage, when a supply crunch for new cars also drove up used prices, and buyers flipped them months later for a profit.
“Hybrid demand is so strong, the Rav4 is still in that 2021 world,” he says. Toyota can’t make new models fast enough.
The leaves are changing, and America’s hot hybrid summer has become a toasty hybrid autumn, for new cars and for old ones. Toyota reported this month that its hybrid sales are up 29 percent in the third quarter of 2026; Kia said its sales more than doubled. Nearly one in six new US cars sold is a hybrid, according to Cox Automotive data.
“The American market has a reputation for gas guzzlers, but we're starting to shake that reputation because of how much we like hybrids,” Roberts says.
The major driver is gas prices. They’ve skyrocketed since the start of the Iran war and the ensuing conflict in the Strait of Hormuz, a global center of oil and gas production and shipping. Nationally, a gallon costs an average of $4.40, up 40 percent from this time last year, according to AAA; Californians pay an average of $6.36. Car buyers are a simple bunch, Roberts says—when prices start rising, they immediately look for more fuel-efficient cars. Soon, drivers actually start buying them.
For now, struggles in the US electric vehicle market are hybrids’ gain. New EV sales are down by almost half from last year, after the Trump administration cut a federal tax credit that made the often-expensive powertrains more affordable. Unlike electrics, hybrids don’t necessarily force drivers out of their familiar gas station routines. (Even plug-in hybrids sometimes need a gas top-up, though smart owners depend mostly on electricity.) Finally, more hybrids are available now than before. A buyer interested in nearly every major sort of passenger vehicle—three-row SUVs, pickups, minivans, or luxury cars—can find one with the powertrain
Interest has spread to the used market, where hybrid prices are up almost 5 percent over last year, according to the automotive data website iSeeCars.com. At $34,500, the average price of used hybrids is higher than used EVs or gas-powered cars. Used buyers seem to be especially keen on long-term fuel savings.
Hybrid tech has been around for decades, but it still may be just the beginning of its reign in the US. “Certainly from a philosophical, functional, and cost perspective, they make the most sense,” says Karl Brauer, iSeeCars’ executive analyst. Several hybrid models already outsell their gas counterparts, including the Toyota Highlander and the Ford Maverick. Soon, he predicts, most US cars will come with a hybrid drivetrain.
US automakers seem to see the hybrid writing on the wall. At the beginning of the decade, General Motors said that 40 percent of its 2025 lineup would be electric. That didn’t happen, and the subsequent pivot left it well behind its Asian counterparts in the new hybrid race. Now, GM has changed its tune. Hybrids “are part of the plan,” an executive told CNBC this week. “We’re not tone-deaf to our customers. We know what they want, and we want to give that to them as quickly as we can.”

Ukrainian strikes kill four civilians across Russia

Ukrainian strikes kill four civilians across Russia
Four civilians have been killed and 17 injured, including a 10-year-old boy, in Ukrainian attacks on several Russian regions, according to local officials.
The fatalities were reported in Belgorod Region and near Moscow, while nine people were wounded in a drone attack on Kaluga Region.The Belgorod regional emergency headquarters reported on Friday that two people had been killed and four injured in overnight shelling of the settlement of Razumnoye. A projectile struck a private house, killing a married couple inside.
Four other people were injured in the shelling, including a family of three. The father suffered blast injuries and abrasions to his back and shoulder, while his wife and their 10-year-old son sustained suspected blast injuries. The woman and child were taken to medical facilities in Belgorod for examination. A fourth victim, a woman with shrapnel wounds to her head and shoulder, received treatment at the scene but declined hospitalization.
One house was completely destroyed, while a neighboring property sustained roof damage, shattered windows, and a damaged fence.
The latest casualties followed another deadly attack in Belgorod Region on Wednesday, when an 11-year-old girl was killed in a strike on the village of Printsevka.
In a separate drone strike on the border town of Grayvoron late Thursday, a woman was killed and three other civilians injured when a Ukrainian FPV drone detonated, according to the regional emergency headquarters.
Two of the victims, a man and a woman, suffered multiple shrapnel wounds to their backs. Another woman sustained shrapnel injuries to her scalp. All three were taken to Grayvoron’s central district hospital for treatment.
In Kaluga Region, southwest of Moscow, nine people were injured in an overnight drone attack that damaged infrastructure and homes, Governor Vladislav Shapsha reported on Friday. Russian air defenses shot down 26 drones across the region, he added.
A separate Ukrainian drone attack killed a 57-year-old man in Podolsk, just south of Moscow, on Thursday, Moscow Region Governor Andrey Vorobyov reported. A 37-year-old woman was also injured, while three cars caught fire and windows were shattered in a nearby apartment building.
The Russian Defense Ministry said its forces had intercepted and destroyed 505 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones across the country overnight, including over border regions, central Russia, Crimea, and the Black and Azov seas.
The attacks come as civilian casualties mount in Russian regions bordering Ukraine. Russian Ambassador-at-Large Rodion Miroshnik said earlier this week that 29 civilians, including two children, had been killed and 206 injured in Ukrainian strikes between September 28 and October 4.
Moscow has condemned Ukrainian attacks on civilians as terrorism.

Chinese AI tool pulled over 'misuse' fears after South Korea hacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
08:54:41 UTC
17:54:41 KST

Chinese AI cybersecurity tool Artex will no longer be open-source after its developer acknowledged that “bad actors” had misused it to launch cyberattacks, following South Korea’s warnings linking the tool to recent bank hacks.
Artex was designed to help organisations strengthen cyber defences by identifying potential weaknesses. However, South Korea’s government said this week it was “highly likely” the tool had been used in data breaches at more than seven financial institutions, including major banks.
The developer, known as “Autumn-27”, said on Thursday that the project would no longer be updated and would become closed-source.
“Given the misuse of the tool, the Artex project will no longer be updated and will be converted to closed-source,” the developer wrote on GitHub, adding that no further public versions or maintenance support would be provided.
The developer said using Artex for cyberattacks was “entirely contrary to” its intentions.
Banks and companies targeted
South Korea’s Financial Services Commission said more than 68,000 people had been affected by the hacks. Shinhan Bank said information linked to loan applications for around 25,000 customers had been leaked, including names, phone numbers and annual income.
Meanwhile in Japan, around 20 companies have reported possible data compromises in similar attacks that could affect millions of customers.
Police chief Yoshinobu Kusunoki said it remained unclear whether the cases were connected.
US cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike said its investigation suggested the attacker had used Artex and was potentially a 26-year-old based in China. It described the suspected threat actor as “likely a Chinese speaker and financially motivated”.
Limits of closing the code
Experts said making Artex closed-source could make it harder for new users to obtain and adapt, but would not remove copies already downloaded.
“Because the code was public, people could download it, change it and run it themselves,” said Poe Zhao, founder of Hello China Tech.
Ilya Kulyatin, CEO of Foundry Labs, said open-source tools can allow users to remove built-in restrictions, making some forms of misuse easier. However, he added, openness also allows researchers to inspect code, identify weaknesses and improve defences.
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung said on Tuesday that as AI makes hacking more sophisticated, the scale of damage is spreading across areas in ways that are difficult to compare with the past.

A 9-billion-year-old signal could help explain dark energy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
08:53:28 UTC
17:53:28 KST

A 9-billion-year-old signal could help explain dark energy
- Date:
- October 9, 2026
- Source:
- University of British Columbia
- Summary:
- A Canadian radio telescope has detected the faint glow of hydrogen from billions of years ago using only its own observations, proving a long-awaited way to map the distant universe can actually work. CHIME can use this hydrogen signal to trace how matter is spread across space and measure how the universe has expanded over time, offering a powerful new way to investigate dark energy.
- Share:
For the first time, the Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment (CHIME) has demonstrated that it can detect the extremely faint radio glow of hydrogen gas from the distant universe using only its own observations.
The result could give scientists a faster and less costly way to investigate dark energy, the still mysterious phenomenon believed to be accelerating the expansion of the universe. Understanding dark energy remains one of the biggest unresolved problems in modern physics. The achievement is also an important milestone for CHIME, which was originally designed with this type of measurement in mind. The findings were published in The Astrophysical Journal.
"Hydrogen is the most common element in the universe and the raw material from which stars form," said co-author Dr. Arnab Chakraborty, postdoctoral fellow at the University of Toronto who first proposed the finding. "Its faint radio emission acts like a cosmic tracer, revealing how matter is distributed across space."
Scientists have proposed competing explanations for the nature of dark energy. Because CHIME can now make these measurements using its own data, researchers can test those ideas independently and gather evidence that could support or challenge existing theories.
"This is a completely new technique for probing the cosmos, delivered by an instrument that was conceived, built and funded by Canadians," said co-author Dr. Mark Halpern, professor in the UBC department of physics and astronomy and CHIME principal investigator. "It's a bold new step in the global cosmology program and a Canadian success story."
Mapping the Universe With Hydrogen
CHIME is a radio telescope located near Penticton, British Columbia, and hosted by the National Research Council of Canada (NRC). The instrument surveys the entire northern sky every day.
The project brings together researchers from across Canada, including scientists at the University of British Columbia, McGill University, the University of Toronto, and the Dominion Radio Astrophysical Observatory (NRC). Other North American collaborators, including Arizona State University, also participate in the effort.
One of CHIME's main goals is to chart how hydrogen gas was distributed in the earlier universe. By measuring that large-scale structure, astronomers can reconstruct how the universe expanded over time and use those measurements to investigate dark energy.
Until now, CHIME researchers needed to compare their radio observations with galaxy survey data collected by other telescopes. Those surveys address similar cosmological questions by observing light from galaxies in much greater detail. However, they can cost millions of dollars more and mainly probe regions of the universe that are hot and dense enough for stars to form.
CHIME instead measures the combined radio emission produced by hydrogen itself. That approach allows researchers to examine much larger regions of the cosmos, reach farther back in time and pursue similar questions at a fraction of the cost, without depending on data from other surveys.
What the Hydrogen Signal Reveals
In an accompanying paper, the researchers analyzed what the newly detected signal can tell scientists about how hydrogen was distributed throughout the universe.
"Our data indicate that roughly two per cent of the hydrogen in the universe was in neutral atomic form at this time, broadly consistent with other measurements," said co-author Dr. Shabbir Shaikh, postdoctoral fellow at Arizona State University. "By measuring how that hydrogen is distributed and clustered, CHIME gives us a new way to test our understanding of how galaxies form and evolve."
The measurement therefore offers more than a new way to study cosmic expansion. It can also help researchers test models of galaxy formation and better understand how matter became organized across the universe.
Finding a Signal Buried in Cosmic Noise
The discovery did not arrive as a sudden breakthrough. Researchers had to use new data processing and analysis methods to extract the extremely weak hydrogen signal from much stronger sources of interference.
That background included radio noise from the universe itself, signals produced by human technology, and even effects created by the telescope. After identifying the possible hydrogen signature, the team spent more than a year testing it to make sure the result was genuine.
Their analysis ultimately showed that the signal came from hydrogen in the distant universe when the universe was about five billion years old. The result was based on 94 nights of observations collected in 2019.
"We worked very hard to convince ourselves that this wasn't a false alarm," said Dr. Chakraborty. "After all the tests, the signal remained. That gave us confidence we were seeing real hydrogen from the distant universe."
Seven Years of CHIME Observations Remain
The new result draws on only a small portion of the information CHIME has gathered since it began operating.
Researchers now have nearly seven years of observations available for analysis. They are working to extend the technique farther into cosmic history, with the goal of studying an era when the universe was only three billion years old.
"For a long time, astrophysicists have believed there is great potential in this hydrogen mapping technique with this kind of telescope. By actually showing that the technique works in practice, we've opened up a whole new window on the universe. We can use it to test our current theories and learn new things about galaxies and other properties of the universe," said co-author Dr. Simon Foreman, assistant professor at Arizona State University.
This project is funded by the Canada Foundation for Innovation, the National Research Council of Canada, the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council and the provinces of British Columbia, Ontario and Quebec, and supported by the Digital Research Alliance of Canada.

New Swiss solar research facility aims to boost agriculture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
08:52:22 UTC
17:52:22 KST

New Swiss solar research facility aims to boost agriculture
Swiss energy group Axpo, the canton of Aargau and the Research Institute of Organic Agriculture have begun construction of an agri-PV research facility to boost agriculture with solar power.
The Swiss dairy foods processor Emmi will use the energy directly on site.
A joint research project aimed at further developing agri-photovoltaics (Agri-PV) is to be launched, Axpo announced on Friday. The research facility currently under construction in Suhr, canton Aargau, combines agricultural use with solar power generation on the same plot of land.
The facility is expected to have a capacity of 600 kilowatt-peak. The module racks stand approximately three metres above the field. A tracking system adjusts the orientation of the solar modules according to the season. The structure is mounted on steel profiles embedded in the ground, as stated in the press release.
The Research Institute of Organic Agriculture (FiBL) is providing scientific support for the project. The total trial area covers 279 acres. The solar modules cover around 120 acres of this area.
The researchers intend to use the eastern section as a reference area. They are comparing the effects on crop yield, biodiversity and water flow. They are also investigating how crops such as cereals and maize react to drought.
More
Swiss Alpine solar farms struggle to deliver on their promise
According to Axpo, the electricity generated is supplied entirely to the Emmi site and consumed on site. This creates a project in Suhr that combines local electricity production, agricultural use and applied research.
The project forms part of the cantonal “AgriSolar Research” programme. It is the second of three planned pilot plants in Aargau. The first plant is situated above an orchard at the FiBL site in Frick.
The canton of Aargau and FiBL are contributing their expertise in agriculture, research and project development. According to Axpo, the company has already gained experience in France and Italy through its subsidiary Urbasolar.

Lithuania moves to lift constitutional ban on nuclear weapons: What it means
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
08:49:00 UTC
17:49:00 KST

Lithuania’s parliament has taken the first step toward removing a constitutional ban on weapons of mass destruction being present on its territory, a move supporters say would allow the country to participate more fully in NATO’s nuclear deterrence arrangements.
The Seimas voted 106-18, with six abstentions, in favour of removing Article 137 of the Constitution. The provision prohibits weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases on Lithuanian territory.
The change is not yet final. Under Lithuania’s constitutional amendment procedure, lawmakers must vote twice, with at least three months between votes. The proposal must receive at least 94 votes – two thirds of the total – in favour in each ballot.
Supporters stress that removing the provision would not automatically lead to nuclear weapons being stationed in Lithuania. Instead, they say, it would remove a legal obstacle to participation in NATO deterrence activities, including exercises involving allied aircraft or ships carrying nuclear weapons.
Why does Lithuania want to change the Constitution?
Conservative Homeland Union leader Laurynas Kasčiūnas, a former defence minister, said Lithuania’s current constitutional restrictions prevent it from participating fully in NATO’s nuclear deterrence plans.
He noted that Estonia, Latvia, Finland and Poland do not have the same constitutional prohibition.
Under the existing provision, nuclear weapons cannot be stationed in Lithuania, and even the flight of aircraft carrying such weapons over Lithuanian territory is prohibited, Kasčiūnas said. The restriction also prevents allied vessels carrying nuclear weapons from entering the country’s territorial waters.
“Given the current restriction, we cannot participate fully in NATO’s nuclear deterrence plans,” Kasčiūnas told parliament, describing nuclear deterrence as a central element of the alliance’s broader deterrence strategy.
Removing the ban would give Lithuania greater flexibility to participate in allied activities intended to deter potential adversaries, supporters argue.
Former Defence Minister Arvydas Anušauskas, also a conservative, said the amendment would enable more comprehensive participation in deterrence exercises, rather than necessarily leading to the deployment of nuclear weapons.
Social Democrat Remigijus Motuzas similarly argued that removing Article 137 would not turn Lithuania into a nuclear-armed state or mean that nuclear warheads would immediately appear in the country.
Would nuclear weapons be stationed in Lithuania?
Not automatically. Removing the constitutional prohibition would eliminate one legal barrier, but it would not itself authorize a decision to deploy nuclear weapons in Lithuania. Liberal Movement leader Viktorija Čmilytė-Nielsen said any future decisions on deploying such capabilities would require separate legislation.
“What specific measures will be needed for our security is something we will decide ourselves, of course together with our allies,” she said.
What about chemical and biological weapons?
Kasčiūnas rejected claims that removing Article 137 would open the door to the use of chemical or biological weapons.
He said Lithuania had ratified international conventions in 1997 and 1998 that have the force of law and prohibit the proliferation, production or use of those weapons.
Who opposes the change, and why?
Opposition to the amendment was concentrated among lawmakers from the opposition Nemunas Dawn party. Fourteen of its members voted against the proposal and two abstained.
Aidas Gedvilas of Nemunas Dawn questioned whether parliament should make such a consequential change without a public vote. He called for a referendum, arguing that alternative approaches were available.
Vitalijus Šeršniovas, a member of the Seimas’ mixed parliamentary group, proposed a narrower solution that would address the need to allow aircraft carrying nuclear weapons to fly over Lithuania without removing the entire constitutional provision.
He also argued that the issue should be decided by referendum.
Three other members of the mixed group and one lawmaker from the Lithuanian Farmers and Greens Union and Christian Families Alliance parliamentary group also voted against the amendment.
The existing Article 137 covers both weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases. The proposal under consideration would remove the provision rather than replace it with a narrower rule.

The plant behind the Kh-101's fuel
The Redkino Experimental Plant in Tver Oblast came under attack overnight, Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ reported. It said the plant makes components of Decilin-M, a fuel for Kh-55 and Kh-101 cruise missiles, as well as additives for diesel and aviation kerosene.
Tver Oblast Governor Vitaly Korolev claimed a plant in Redkino caught fire as a drone attack was being repelled. He did not name the plant. No workers were hurt, he said.
The plant also makes ferrocene derivatives, which serve as burn catalysts in solid-fuel rocket motors, Militarnyi reported. The UK sanctioned it in September 2025. Drones attacked it in September 2023 and twice in one night in June 2024, the outlet said.
In February, drones of the Security Service of Ukraine's (SBU) Alpha unit struck the plant, sparking a large fire, SBU sources told Kyiv Post. The Kh-101 is the missile Russia used against Pryluky on 7 October, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
Yandex loses a second data center
Part of Yandex's data center in Kaluga was damaged in the drone attack, and several modules were completely knocked out, the company's press service told Interfax, Russian newspaper Kommersant reported. Some Yandex services may run with interruptions, no one was hurt, and the company is still assessing the damage, Yandex said.
Kaluga Oblast Governor Vladislav Shapsha claimed nine people were injured in the overnight attack on the region. A day earlier, a drone attack forced Yandex to fully shut its data center in Sasovo, Ryazan Oblast.
A refinery in the north, a depot near Belgorod
Locals reported an attack on the Ukhta refinery in the Komi Republic, followed by a fire, Exilenova+ said. The Lukoil-owned plant can process about 4.2 million metric tons of oil a year, making gasoline, diesel, fuel oil, and vacuum gasoil. The extent of the damage is unclear.
An oil depot north of Belgorod was also burning after the night's attack, the channel posted. Belgorod's regional headquarters claimed two people were killed and four injured, including a child, in the Belgorod district.
A large fire also broke out in Pushkino near Moscow, likely at a truck parking lot, Astra reported. The cause is unknown.
Repeated strikes on Redkino target a specialty fuel that Russia's cruise missiles depend on, while two Yandex data centers hit in two nights bring the war to services ordinary Russians use every day.

Musk names Indian billionaire responsible for Starlink troubles
Elon Musk has escalated his criticism of Starlink’s delayed India launch by singling out Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani, hours after New Delhi rejected claims that its satellite approval process was discriminatory.
“Is Ambani the real boss of India?” Musk asked on X on Thursday, pointing out that his satellite internet service had spent five years complying with Indian requirements but was still unable to begin commercial operations. 
Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries is India’s largest privately-owned conglomerate, with interests in oil-to-chemicals, telecommunications, retail, media, and green energy. He is also India’s second richest man, with a net worth of $86.3 billion, according to Forbes. 
Musk’s tweet drew in Indian opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, who replied: “Welcome to India, Elon. Wait till you discover the other guy.” 
Gandhi seemed to be targeting India’s richest man, Gautam Adani, with the “other guy” remark. Adani hails from the same state as Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, and Gandhi has repeatedly accused him of receiving favorable treatment from the government.
Thank you, Rahul. This is indeed troubling.
— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) October 8, 2026
The world’s richest man had, a day earlier, accused unnamed “oligarchs” of blocking Starlink in order to maintain a “monopolistic chokehold” over Indian consumers. On Thursday, he also sent out a volley of retweets that echoed his views on Starlink’s utility to India. His outburst coincided with the 10th edition of the Indian Mobile Congress that Modi inaugurated in New Delhi.
Starlink, Ambani’s Jio Satellite Communications, and Bharti Group-backed Eutelsat OneWeb are all at broadly the same stage of regulatory approval for satellite internet connectivity in the country, with security assessments underway, according to India’s Communications Ministry.
Starlink has to complete the security assessment, and spectrum assignment, before it can start commercial services, although it holds an Indian telecom license and authorization for its satellite constellation.
The company has built 20 gateway sites with hundreds of antennas in India and introduced India-specific security controls designed to keep Indian users’ data within the country, its Vice President Lauren Dreyer said at the India Mobile Congress just before Musk ignited the fireworks on X.
Reliance Jio did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Musk’s latest remarks.
Musk and Ambani have previously been on opposing sides of India’s satellite-spectrum policy. Reliance had pushed for satellite spectrum to be auctioned, arguing that it would ensure a level playing field, while Starlink favored administrative allocation. New Delhi ultimately adopted the administrative route.
Jio is itself preparing a competing low-Earth-orbit satellite network. RT reported in June that the Indian telecom giant plans a constellation of around 1,600 satellites, potentially costing up to $15 billion, as it seeks to expand from terrestrial broadband into satellite connectivity.

Polish parliament approves ban on nighttime alcohol sales in shops
Unknown

An overwhelming majority of MPs in the Sejm, the lower house of Poland’s parliament, have voted in favour of a bill that would introduce tough new anti-alcohol measures, including a ban on all forms of advertising and on sales in shops during nighttime hours.
The legislation must still pass through the upper-house Senate and will then require the signature of President Karol Nawrocki. However, given the level of support – with only two small far-right groups voting against the bill – it appears likely the measures will be approved.
#PILNE | Sejm uchwalił ustawę wprowadzającą na terenie całego kraju nocną prohibicję, zakazującą reklamy alkoholu i podnoszącą opłatę za sprzedaż alkoholu. https://t.co/OawNUdtqM6
— tvn24 (@tvn24) October 8, 2026
The new restrictions were initially proposed in separate bills submitted by two junior members of Poland’s ruling coalition, The Left (Lewica) and the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), which were combined into a single package.
The measures include a ban on the sale of alcohol for off-premises consumption between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m., with local authorities able to extend those hours up to 9 p.m. to 9 a.m. if they wish. Bars, clubs and restaurants would still be allowed to sell alcohol for on-premises consumption as presently.
Almost 200 Polish municipalities, including large cities such as Warsaw and Kraków, have already introduced their own local bans on nighttime alcohol sales. Kraków saw police interventions at night fall by almost half during the first six months the measures were in place, with other cities reporting similar improvements.
The newly approved bill also includes a complete ban on advertising and promoting alcoholic drinks. Those who violate the prohibition can be fined up to 1 million zloty (€228,400).
Packaging for alcoholic drinks will be required to include warnings about their harmful effect on pregnant women and minors. The legislation also toughens requirements for shop staff to check the age of buyers if they suspect they may be underage.
The cost of licences to sell alcohol will be increased from 525 zloty to 1,050 zloty for drinks with up to 18% alcohol content and from 2,100 to 4,200 for stronger drinks.
Warsaw has announced a ban on nighttime sales of alcohol in shops.
The new measure will come into force on 1 June 2026 and will apply from 10 p.m to 6 a.m. across the entire city https://t.co/A7xVvJMpvU
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 12, 2026
In a vote on Thursday night, the bill won support from 400 of the 433 MPs present in the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament. The only groups that did not vote in favour were the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP).
The legislation now passes to the upper-house Senate, which can suggest amendments but only delay, not block, a bill’s passage. Once finally approved by parliament, it will reach the desk of President Karol Nawrocki, who can sign the bill, veto it, or send it to the constitutional court for assessment.
Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has vetoed a record number of bills. However, given the level of support for the alcohol bill in the Sejm, including from the largest opposition groups, Law and Justice (PiS) and Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), it appears likely he will sign it.
Poles are eating more meat but drinking less alcohol, continuing a long-term trend, new data show.
The average person in Poland ate 82kg of meat last year, up 7.5% from 2024 and 22.7% since 2005.
They also drank 82 litres of beer, down 18.7% since 2018 https://t.co/FxFMupWLRv
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 1, 2026
In June, an IBRiS poll for the Rzeczpospolita daily found that 55% of Poles support some form of ban on nighttime alcohol sales while 43% are opposed. A survey by IBP for Super Express published today showed even stronger support, with 67% in favour of a ban and only 26% opposed.
Recent data released by Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, showed that alcohol consumption among Poles is continuing its recent decline.
In 2025, the average Pole drank 81.7 litres of beer, down 4.9% from the previous year and 18.7% from the peak of 100.5 litres per person in 2018. Likewise, consumption of spirits and liqueurs fell 5.9% year-on-year in 2025 to 3.2 litres per person. That was 13.5% down from a peak of 3.7 litres in 2019.
However, alcohol consumption is still higher than it was two decades ago, with the average Pole drinking 28% more spirits and 1.2% more beer in 2025 than in 2005.
