Over 8,000 Palestinians remain missing 3 years into Gaza genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
08:45:36 UTC
17:45:36 KST

Thousands of Palestinian families remain desperate for answers about loved ones who disappeared during three years of Israeli attacks on Gaza, as widespread destruction, restricted access and limited forensic resources hamper efforts to find the missing.
The United Nations estimates that millions of tonnes of debris cover Gaza, while Palestinian Civil Defense says more than 8,000 people remain missing beneath the rubble. Others may have been detained or remain unaccounted for, leaving families uncertain whether their relatives are alive or dead.
Pat Griffiths, spokesperson for the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) in Jerusalem, described seeing families gather at hospitals when buses carrying released Palestinian detainees arrive in Gaza. Some hold photographs of missing relatives, hoping to discover whether they are among those released.
Psychologists call this experience "ambiguous loss," a form of grief in which families cannot establish whether their loved ones are alive or dead.
"You don't know if your loved one you haven't heard from ... is alive or if they've been killed. You don't know if they're detained or not," Griffiths told Anadolu Agency (AA).
"Thousands of people live with this limbo. This pain of not knowing what to do or how to feel exactly. They're stuck."
Amani Al Naouq, an ICRC spokesperson in Gaza, said families repeatedly approach the organization seeking answers.
"If they are dead, we can be relieved. But the fact that we don't know if they are dead or alive," she recalled families saying. "That's one of the most difficult things for them."
Some continue contacting the ICRC even when answers are unavailable, simply needing somewhere to share their anguish. Others begin accepting that missing relatives have died without receiving confirmation, Al Naouq said.
The search is complicated by the scale of destruction across Gaza, where rubble may contain human remains, unexploded ordnance and evidence relevant to investigations into alleged international crimes.
An April 2026 damage assessment by the European Union, United Nations and World Bank estimated that removing and managing more than 68 million metric tons of debris would cost more than $1.7 billion.
Al Naouq said recovery teams have extremely limited heavy machinery, sometimes relying on just one or two excavators rented from private suppliers. Much of the work is performed with smaller equipment or by hand.
Teams also depend on families to identify where missing relatives were last seen, including specific buildings and rooms. Recounting those moments can force relatives to relive their inability to rescue loved ones.
"It's actually back again an open wound for these families," Al Naouq said.
Griffiths, who recently spent a week in Gaza, described seeing kilometers of rubble, much of it posing dangers from unexploded remnants of war. The ICRC supports the rental of two excavators, but he said the contribution was minimal compared with the need.
"The scale of the task ahead of them, it's daunting. It's huge," he said.
Restricted access prevents recovery teams from safely reaching large areas. DNA testing is also unavailable in Gaza, according to the ICRC, forcing forensic specialists to rely on details such as age, height, dental information, clothing, previous injuries and personal belongings.
Time further complicates identification as remains decompose and rubble movement separates them from their original locations.
"The more time passes, the harder identifying the deceased gets," Griffiths said, warning that searches can continue for decades, as seen in conflicts in Syria, Iraq, Afghanistan and the Balkans.
Mayy El Sheikh, of the U.N. Human Rights Office in the occupied Palestinian territory, recalled interviewing a 37-year-old woman with a disability whose husband disappeared during an attack on his family's home in northern Gaza in 2023. The couple have a 5-year-old son.
Almost everyone in her husband's family was killed. Some bodies were recovered, but his remains were not, El Sheikh said.
The woman believes she knows where he lies beneath the rubble but cannot reach the site because it is beyond the deployment line for Israeli forces, known as the "yellow line."
El Sheikh said the woman felt unable to help her son recover because he had no grave to visit. She also believed she had failed her husband by being unable to recover his remains and honor him through burial.
"For her, the war is not over until her husband is found," El Sheikh said.
Other families have believed missing relatives were dead before recognizing them alive in photographs or videos from Israeli prisons, she added.
The destruction of Gaza's ruins has raised concerns that human remains and evidence of alleged international crimes could disappear.
Francesca Albanese, the U.N. special rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territory, has warned that removing, crushing and relocating rubble in areas under Israeli military control could destroy evidence.
El Sheikh said restricted access, reported debris removal and limited forensic resources have increased the risk that evidence is being lost or damaged. Large areas remain inaccessible to independent observers and investigators.
She also cited reports of remains being returned to Palestinian authorities without identifying information or details about where they were recovered.
"They have returned remains to the Palestinian authorities, sometimes even partial remains with no identification and no clarity on where they were recovered or how they were killed," she said.
Srinivasan Muralidhar, chair of the U.N. Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel, said the commission had received reports of rubble removal that could destroy evidence.
"We are concerned that the removal of rubble could result in evidence getting lost forever," he said.
Evidence recovered from destroyed buildings can complement witness testimony, medical records and forensic findings, helping investigators reconstruct events. Although losing evidence would not necessarily prevent investigations into alleged crimes, Muralidhar said, it could leave important gaps.
He also emphasized families' right to know what happened to their relatives.
"In international law, there is a known concept of the right to the truth. Every family wants to know what exactly happened," he said.
Griffiths called for more heavy machinery, greater humanitarian access and safe passage for recovery teams to reach areas currently beyond their reach.
Muralidhar urged international cooperation to accelerate debris removal while protecting potential evidence and preventing further destruction.
"We have to have cooperation across countries to help clear the rubble quicker," he said, warning that continued attacks could make recovery increasingly difficult.
The ICRC has supported a cemetery for unidentified dead in Deir al-Balah, where recovered remains can be buried individually while information is preserved for future identification.
Forensic teams document available identifying details and assign each unidentified person a unique serial number linked to their burial record. The ICRC is also supporting an information-sharing system connecting recovery teams, forensic authorities and cemetery administrators.
The effort could enable future identification if DNA testing becomes available in Gaza.
During a visit to the cemetery, Griffiths and Al Naouq met a young woman whose husband's remains had been identified using available forensic methods.
"She could visit his grave, she could stand at his grave, to be near him," Griffiths said, describing the closure the burial provided.

U.S. plans to keep V-22 Osprey flying past 2055
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
08:44:54 UTC
17:44:54 KST

- The V-22 program office and Bell Boeing brought 14 new suppliers into the Osprey supply chain to sustain the fleet past 2055.
- About 200 people from six allied nations, seven U.S. agencies and more than 35 companies took part in the Team Osprey Working Group.
The U.S. military’s V-22 Osprey program office and manufacturer Bell Boeing have brought 14 new companies into the tiltrotor’s supply chain as they work to keep the aircraft flying past 2055, after years of gearbox failures, fatal crashes and flight restrictions that have kept large parts of the fleet on the ground.
The new suppliers joined a recent Team Osprey Working Group hosted by the V-22 Joint Program Office, known as PMA-275, and Bell Boeing. About 200 people from six allied nations, seven U.S. government agencies and more than 35 defense, engineering and manufacturing companies took part, according to the program office, which focused the meeting on improving parts availability, component reliability and modernization. The program office did not say when or where the meeting took place, name the new suppliers, or identify the allied nations.
“Synchronizing our global supply chain and integrating technical innovations directly translates to higher material availability on the flight line,” said Col. Robert Hurst, PMA-275 program manager. “Optimizing component reliability across our defense industry partners ensures deployed commanders maintain the rapid expeditionary lift and logistical flexibility required to operate effectively in high-threat environments.”
The Osprey takes off and lands like a helicopter but tilts its rotors forward to fly like a turboprop airplane, giving it more speed and range than conventional helicopters. The U.S. Marine Corps uses the MV-22 as its main medium-lift aircraft to move troops and cargo. The U.S. Navy flies the CMV-22 to deliver people and supplies to aircraft carriers at sea, a job it took over completely when the Navy retired its last C-2 Greyhound cargo planes this year. Air Force Special Operations Command uses the CV-22 to insert and recover special operations forces. Japan is the only foreign operator.
The program has spent the past several years dealing with problems in the Osprey’s proprotor gearbox, the transmission that sends engine power to the rotors. Four V-22 crashes since 2022 have killed 20 U.S. service members, and investigations tied several of them to gearbox failures or to a sudden clutch re-engagement known as hard clutch engagement. After a CV-22 crashed off Japan in November 2023, killing eight airmen, the entire U.S. fleet was grounded until March 2024 and has since flown under range and other restrictions.
Deliveries of redesigned gearboxes with stronger, triple-melted steel components began in January 2026, with about 12 units arriving each month. The Marine Corps’ aviation plan estimates an unrestricted operational fleet by December 2027, while the full gearbox upgrades are scheduled to finish in 2029 for the U.S. Air Force and U.S. Navy and in 2033 for the U.S. Marine Corps.
PMA-275 manages development, purchasing and sustainment for all three U.S. variants and for Japan’s fleet.

On the evening of October 8, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhiy Tykhy stated that the Embassy of Ukraine in Austria had requested clarification from the Austrian side regarding the circumstances of the detention in Vienna of Mykhailo Tkach, head of the investigative journalism department at Ukrayinska Pravda.
"The consul is already in contact with Austrian counterparts and has officially requested access to the detained citizen," the press secretary said on Thursday evening in response to inquiries from journalists.
Earlier, Ukrayinska Pravda reported that Mykhailo Tkach, the head of the outlet's investigative journalism unit, had been detained in Vienna while on assignment to track down fugitive Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko.
The publication’s editorial team stated that it considers the detention unlawful and is demanding Tkach's immediate release, as well as an official explanation regarding the actions of Austrian law enforcement.
Tkach was in Austria with his colleague Yaroslav Bondarenko. The outlet has appealed to Ukrainian diplomats to urgently take all necessary measures to protect the journalists, establish their whereabouts, and facilitate their release.

U.S. Army buys new locomotives to replace aging rail fleet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
08:39:20 UTC
17:39:20 KST

- The U.S. Army has fielded its first new locomotives in more than a decade at Crane Army Ammunition Activity and Blue Grass Army Depot.
- More than a third of the Army’s active locomotives are past their 65-year expected life, and TACOM aims to cut that below 20%.
The U.S. Army has taken delivery of its first new locomotives in more than a decade, part of an effort to replace a rail fleet in which more than a third of the active engines are older than their 65-year expected service life.
The Army’s Tank-automotive and Armaments Command, known as TACOM, said its rail program has fielded two new locomotives and a track-maintenance vehicle at three installations since October 2025. The command’s goal is to cut the share of locomotives past their expected service life to below 20%, to rein in rising maintenance costs and keep equipment moving to ports and railheads when units deploy. TACOM did not say how many locomotives are in the Army’s fleet or how many more it plans to buy.
The Army relies on its own locomotives and rail lines at depots, ammunition plants and major posts to move tanks, vehicles and munitions to commercial railroads and seaports. TACOM handled the requirements, engineering reviews and contract oversight, while the U.S. Department of Transportation’s Volpe National Transportation Systems Center acted as the buying agency.
“Army Rail serves as a critical enabler to deployment activities and power projection of the force,” said Bryan VanGheluwe, section chief for heavy tactical vehicles and Army rail at TACOM. “This effort renewed a commitment to the modernization of the fleet and providing enhanced readiness to move warfighter equipment in support of mission requirements.”
The newest locomotive went to Crane Army Ammunition Activity in Indiana, which accepted USAX 4673 on Feb. 2, 2026. The 120-ton (about 109-metric-ton) locomotive was built by Knoxville Locomotive Works for $2.9 million and designed around the site’s tight track curves and close clearances, with smaller exterior dimensions and special couplers that do not have to line up on the centerline.
Blue Grass Army Depot in Kentucky accepted USAX 1699 on Oct. 23, 2025. The 80-ton switcher, built by SpecSys for $2.1 million, uses the same physical footprint as the classic GE 80-ton locomotive so it can run on the depot’s older, lighter track without wearing it down or risking derailments.
Fort Drum, New York, received a ballast regulator from Knox Kershaw on Nov. 13, 2025, for about $733,000. The machine keeps the gravel bed under the track in shape, and it is fitted with snow-removal attachments so crews can keep the post’s deployment railheads open through the region’s heavy winters.
Before these deliveries, the last major locomotive the Army fielded was USAX 6524, a 140-ton engine delivered to what is now Fort Hood, Texas, on July 30, 2015, at a cost of $1.84 million.
The locomotive purchases are one part of the Army’s push to keep its installation rail networks ready for large deployments. The service has also looked for faster ways to repair rail lines at its installations so damaged track does not slow units heading to ports.

Finland to roll out citizenship test from March 2027
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:39:18 EEST
17:39:18 KST

Finland will begin requiring citizenship applicants to pass a civic knowledge test from March 2027, according to a statement by the Finnish Immigration Service (Migri).
Although the amendments to the Citizenship Act will enter into force from 1 January 2027, there will be a "transitional period for the legislative amendments" that lasts for two months until the beginning of March.
"The new requirement will only apply to you if you submit your application in the Enter Finland online service or a paper application at a service point of the Finnish Immigration Service on or after 1 March 2027," Migri's statement explained.
The introduction of the test is the final part of the government's three-pronged strategy aimed at tightening the rules around obtaining Finnish citizenship. The previous changes focused primarily on periods of residency and financial self-sufficiency.
Self-study learning material coming
Although the exact content of the test has not been announced, it is expected to contain multiple-choice and true-or-false questions about Finnish culture and history as well as human rights and gender equality.
The University of Helsinki is partnering with Migri to "prepare the learning material and questions for the citizenship test", according to the agency's press release.
"The questions in the citizenship test will be based on self-study learning material that will be published on the website of the Finnish Immigration Service at the turn of the year," Migri added.
The requirement to sit the test only applies to citizenship applicants aged between 18 and 64, and it can be taken in either Finnish or Swedish.
Migri also note that, as an alternative to sitting the citizenship test, applicants can also demonstrate their knowledge of Finnish society by completing the matriculation examination in Finnish or Swedish, or by completing a Finnish- or Swedish-language higher education degree in Finland.
Among the other Nordic nations, Sweden, Norway and Denmark also require citizenship applicants to pass a civic knowledge test.

US military to livestream Fort Hood shooter execution
Unknown

2026-10-09

Breadcrumb
US military to livestream firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan
The execution by firing squad of convicted military base shooter Nidal Malik Hasan will be livestreamed, a Pentagon official said Thursday, after US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said it would be carried out in "public."
Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist, shot dead 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009. His execution will be the first by the US military since 1961, and the first it has carried out by firing squad since World War II.
"It will be livestreamed. Details will follow," the Pentagon official told AFP on condition of anonymity.
Hegseth had said in a video posted on X by official Pentagon accounts earlier Thursday that Hasan is "going to get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be, and we'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public."
"People need to understand that...there's serious consequence for these types of things," Hegseth told right-wing influencer Jack Posobiec while aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier.
Hegseth noted that it would be the military's first firing squad execution since the Second World War -- a reference to the case of Eddie Slovik, who was put to death for desertion in 1945.
"I kind of like the mentality we had in World War II, which was win, which was understand when the enemy attacks you, you need to stand your ground," Hegseth said.
In a separate clip, Posobiec asked the Pentagon chief if Hasan had made any final request.
"Don't care. We'll see him on December 3," Hegseth said—the day Hasan is slated to die.
The last US military execution was carried out in 1961, when John Bennett was hanged for rape and attempted murder.
Public executions
According to rights group Amnesty International, at least 17 public executions are known to have been carried out in 2025—six in Afghanistan and 11 in Iran.
The Death Penalty Information Center says that 135 soldiers have been executed by the US military since 1916.
The Pentagon announced earlier this week that US President Donald Trump had approved Hasan's execution for carrying out the attack, which he said was due to US wars on the region and Afghanistan.
Twelve of those he killed and 30 of the wounded were soldiers. Hasan was shot and partially paralyzed by a civilian police officer who responded to the attack.
He was sentenced to death by a military jury in 2013.
Hasan chose to conduct his own defense during the trial but called no witnesses and gave no testimony, and made no attempt to deny the charges. Court-appointed defense attorneys expressed concern that he was seeking execution.
The court that convicted Hasan was told he was opposed to the US military's occupations of Iraq and Afghanistan, and that he had spoken online with an alleged Al-Qaeda figure, radical cleric Anwar al-Awlaki, an American citizen subsequently killed in a US drone strike in Yemen.
While mass shootings in the United States are common, they are relatively rare at military facilities.
In 2025, a soldier opened fire at a US military base in the state of Georgia, wounding five fellow troops before he was tackled and apprehended.
In 2019, a US sailor fatally shot two people and wounded a third at a base in Hawaii, while a Saudi military student shot dead three people at a military facility in Florida the same year.
And a Kuwaiti-born US citizen attacked two military installations in Tennessee in 2015, killing four Marines and a sailor. The FBI concluded the violence was inspired by a "foreign terrorist group."

Russian military blogger detained in NATO country
Mikhail Zvinchuk, founder of the Russian military Telegram channel Rybar, has been detained in Montenegro, local media reported on Friday.
Police and the country’s National Security Agency reportedly carried out the operation in the coastal town of Risan that morning. Zvinchuk’s wife and three associates were also detained, according to the reports.
The operation is being described as targeting alleged “hybrid activity” by the Rybar network, but no specific evidence supporting the accusation has been presented.
The channel, which has around 1.3 million subscribers, had previously also faced US and British accusations of spreading Russian propaganda and conducting information operations abroad. The US State Department had even issued a $10 million bounty in 2024 on any information about the individuals behind the Rybar channel.
Moscow’s embassy in Montenegro is currently inquiring into the circumstances of Zvinchuk’s detention, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova has said.
The Telegram channel Baza has reported that it has been able to independently confirm Zvinchuk’s arrest, stating that he and his wife were detained at 7:30 AM local time at the Mövenpick Hotel in Risan and were reportedly not even allowed to pay for their room or collect their belongings.
The pair have since been taken to Montenegro’s capital Podgorica, where they are currently being interrogated, Baza claimed. Their phones and documents have been confiscated.
Montenegrin media have reported that local security services had been monitoring Zvinchuk’s group for several days before Friday’s detention. The Rybar team is believed to have arrived in the country to film a report about Montenegro’s plans to align its visa policy with EU standards.
The planned video is reportedly being viewed by authorities as an attempt to portray European integration as a threat to the country’s tourism, economy and national interests.
Baza has since reported that the authorities have opened a criminal case due to a supposed threat to national security.Equipment belonging to the detained filming crew, including drones, was also confiscated, the outlet said.
Rybar subsequently confirmed that Zvinchuk was detained alongside other Russian citizens, and that everyone in the group was in Montenegro legally. Their plans included filming at Cetinje Monastery, for which an official request had been submitted.
The project said its team was in contact with the Russian Foreign Ministry, which was working to resolve the situation. Rybar maintained that the group had broken no local laws and said it expected all those detained to be released.
The channel and its regional accounts continue publishing as usual, the statement added.
Montenegrin Prime Minister Milojko Spajic has since also confirmed the detention of Rybar’s head. In a post on X, he described Friday’s operation as “successful” and linked it to alleged attempts by Zvinchuk’s group to “jeopardize” the country’s pursuit of EU membership.
Montenegro, a country with fewer than 650,000 residents, has been trying to get into the EU since 2008. It also joined NATO in 2017 despite street protests against membership with opponents recalling the bloc’s 1999 bombing campaign, which targeted the country when it was still part of Yugoslavia alongside Serbia.

Plague fears fuel online push for antibiotics, emergency kits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
08:36:00 UTC
17:36:00 KST

Reports that a woman working at a plague research institute in Russia’s Irkutsk region died from the disease have fueled a surge in online interest across North America in potential treatments.
Russian authorities have not confirmed that the woman died of plague. The regional governor said Thursday that no health concerns had been identified after officials traced all her contacts.
Despite the lack of confirmation, social media influencers and doomsday preppers are promoting a $300 kit they claim can help people avoid emergency room visits.
“Don’t wait until everybody is scrambling. Prepare before you need it,” reads the caption of a Facebook video viewed more than 161,000 times and posted with the hashtags #Russia and #plague.
The posts include personalized discount codes, suggesting the creators may receive financial compensation when purchases are made.
The Wellness Company, a brand promoted in many of the videos, saw a subsequent spike in online searches, according to Google Trends data.
The company is fronted by Peter McCullough, an American cardiologist who has promoted COVID-19 conspiracy theories and health misinformation debunked by Agence France-Presse (AFP). The company did not immediately respond to questions about the kits.
Rogan O’Handley, known on social media as DC Draino, highlighted the kit’s inclusion of the antibiotic doxycycline to his 2.9 million followers.
Doxycycline is among the antibiotics used to treat plague in countries where cases occur each year, helping contain outbreaks.
“We know how to treat it,” said Isaac Bogoch, an infectious disease specialist at Toronto General Hospital.
“Obviously it can be a very severe infection,” he said, but he warned against taking a course of antibiotics without known exposure.
He said the unconfirmed case in Russia “isn’t the type of infection that would cause a pandemic.”
Paul Keim, a plague researcher and professor at Northern Arizona University, also said there was no reason for people in North America to start taking doxycycline.
“You’re altering the microbiome of your gut, and perhaps creating antibiotic-resistant bacteria in your body that will fight off the drug therapy the next time you really need it,” he said.
The kits are also advertised as containing “hard-to-find” prescription medications such as ivermectin.
But “ivermectin is never really used for a bacterial disease,” Keim said.
The antiparasitic drug is approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to treat certain parasitic worm infections.
Yet it continues to be touted as a solution in health misinformation, in part because authorities rejected its use as an effective treatment for COVID-19 after clinical trials failed to demonstrate sufficient benefits.
This is not the first public health scare to prompt individuals to promote unproven medical solutions.
When a cruise ship passenger contracted the rare hantavirus in May, social media accounts also quickly touted ivermectin as a “cure,” even though there is no established treatment for the disease.
Amid the 2026 Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, videos featuring a doctor recommending vitamin D3 and zinc spread through accounts selling supplements, despite the substances being unable to treat the disease.
“Whenever there is a crisis, especially in the health space, the grifters are gonna come out,” said Timothy Caulfield, a misinformation expert and professor at the University of Alberta.
“They exploit fear and uncertainty to sell unproven products.”

Russian technology and AI company Yandex said on Friday that several modules at its data center in the Kaluga region southwest of Moscow had been completely disabled by a drone attack, the second in two days.
“Part of Yandex data center infrastructure in Kaluga was damaged in a drone attack. Several data center modules are completely disabled,” Yandex told Interfax, warning that some of its services may experience disruptions.
Kaluga region Governor Vladislav Shapsha southwest of Moscow said nine people were injured and infrastructure was damaged by Ukrainian drones. He did not comment on the Yandex data center attack.
The strike comes a day after a Ukrainian drone hit another Yandex data center in the Ryazan region southeast of the capital, where two of the three supercomputers used to develop the company's AI model are housed.
Yandex, whose apps have become an indispensable part of many Russians' lives, said the attacks had struck at the core of its operations and that it was trying to keep its services going.
"Our teams are working day and night to do everything possible to keep services running and to help those affected by the incident. Right now this is our most important task, but unfortunately it is not an easy one," the company said in a statement Friday.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky described the targeted attacks as retaliation to Russia’s recent missile strikes against Ukrainian server facilities in Kyiv.
“We always respond symmetrically,” Zelensky told reporters Thursday.
Russia has conducted a strike campaign against Ukrainian data centers and telecommunications infrastructure over the past month, including targets in central Kyiv.
In the Tver region north of Moscow, a drone reportedly struck an experimental plant described as a major chemical producer of liquid fuel for Russia’s Kh-55 and Kh-101 cruise missiles.
Tver region Governor Vitaly Korolyov confirmed a drone attack on an unidentified factory, saying its employees had been evacuated in advance.
In the southwestern Belgorod region, Ukrainian shelling of a residential home killed a husband and wife and injured four others, including a 10-year-old child.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its air defense systems intercepted 505 Ukrainian drones overnight.
On Friday morning, reports indicated that Ukrainian also attacked a Lukoil refinery in the northern republic of Komi.
Both Russia and Ukraine have expanded drone attacks this year on economic targets, from energy facilities and refineries to ports and vessels carrying oil and grain, e-commerce warehouses and, most recently, data centers.

The incidents have prompted a nationwide security response, with the police deployed to 10,000 schools and the government warning against the spread of misinformation that officials fear could inspire copycat attacks.

These included a 13-year-old from Warsaw who posted a photo of a knife in a class group chat and threatened other students; a 14-year-old in Warsaw detained on school grounds with a knife and firecrackers; and two 15-year-olds from Pruszkow County just outside the capital who posted a video with threats to kill.

Bulgarian Pavilion at Venice Biennale is presented simultaneously in Norway
Unknown

2026-10-09

Author
Vessela Krasteva
Article
Bulgarian Pavilion at Venice Biennale is presented simultaneously in Norway
Bulgaria makes art history at the Italian forum as “Federation of Minor Practices” travels to a third country for the first time
Friday 9 October 2026 11:20
Friday, 9 October 2026, 11:20
PHOTO bulgarianpavilionvenice.art
Font size
Bulgaria’s participation in the 61st Venice Biennale is making its mark on the history of contemporary art, both in Bulgaria and at the prestigious international event itself. For the first time, a project occupying a national pavilion at the Biennale is being presented abroad, outside Italy, in a parallel exhibition that preserves the conceptual integrity of the original.
From 6 to 20 October 2026, Federation of Minor Practices, a project by Bulgarian artists Veneta Androva, Gery Georgieva, Maria Nalbantova and Rayna Teneva, curated by Martina Yordanova and commissioned by Desislava Dimova, is on display at the NOUA cultural venue in Bodø, Norway. The exhibition is part of Arts of Democracy, a new cultural and civic programme exploring the relationship between art, freedom of expression and democracy.
“This is an initiative conceived as a festival week of accompanying events, continuing the legacy of Bodø’s tenure as European Capital of Culture in 2024,” Martina Yordanova told Radio Bulgaria.
Martina Yordanova
PHOTO Mihail Novakov
The curator, together with two of the artists, Veneta Androva and Maria Nalbantova, attended the opening in Norway on 6 October. The Bulgarian Pavilion is the only official exhibition featured in the Arts of Democracy programme.
“Beyond the Arctic Circle, we are presenting a reconstruction of our pavilion, as the original exhibition will remain in Venice until 22 November. In Norway, we are showing the four films by the artists featured in the main exhibition: Spray and Pray, UWU Channel Radiance, Swamp Song and Geography Is Destiny. They are projected on a large screen, just as they are at the Biennale.
PHOTO Bulgarian Pavillion at the 61st Venice Biennale
The other interactive element, created jointly by the artists, is the video game Kazana, presented here on a smaller scale.
“The conceptual framework of Bulgaria’s pavilion in Venice this year moves between the past, the present and the future. What we are showing in Norway is a reconstruction that brings together the project’s key elements, the pavilion’s central message and the themes that intersect throughout the exhibition,” Martina Yordanova explains.
PHOTO Mihail Novakov
Presenting the Bulgarian project in a third country is particularly important for its continued artistic life and its encounter with an even wider international audience. Most national pavilion projects in Venice effectively disappear once the Biennale ends, or are rarely exhibited again in their entirety. The themes explored by the Bulgarian artists, including disinformation and collective care, are especially relevant to the programme in Norway.
It is no coincidence that negotiations for the Bulgarian artists’ participation began as early as March 2025, before the official opening of the Venice Biennale. The invitation came from another Bulgarian curator, Svetlana Kuyumdzhieva.
Svetlana Kuyumdzhieva
PHOTO openartfiles.bg
“She has been working with the Bodø European Capital of Culture 2024 initiative for several years and served as an adviser to its team. As you may know, Svetlana Kuyumdzhieva was the artistic director of Plovdiv European Capital of Culture 2019 and also chaired the jury that selected our project to represent Bulgaria at this year’s Venice Biennale.
“When the Norwegian organisers settled on the theme Arts of Democracy, they asked her whether there were Bulgarian artists and projects that would fit this cultural context. Kuyumdzhieva recommended Federation of Minor Practices.
PHOTO Bulgarian Pavillion at the 61st Venice Biennale
“Protracted negotiations followed. The organisers travelled to Italy specifically to assess whether our pavilion could be presented in Norway, and if so, how. We invested considerable effort in making this possible.
There is also an interesting detail worth mentioning. The table on which visitors play the game Kazana is made of copper. Near Panagyurishte in Bulgaria lies the largest copper mine on the Balkan Peninsula. Here, too, just 30 kilometres from Bodø, there is a copper mine, and the table used in the Norwegian presentation of the project has been made locally from the same material.
Copper is fundamental to the ways we communicate with one another in the modern world. All our technologies are deeply connected to this metal, and communication through them would be impossible without it. Yet copper is also a material of antiquity. In this way, layers of the past, present and future come together in the exhibition, providing a context for our shared experience through art", says Martina Yordanova.
PHOTO Mihail Novakov
Growing interest in Bulgaria’s pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale
This is Bulgaria’s 12th participation in the prestigious art event, and the response so far has been overwhelmingly positive, Martina Yordanova told Radio Bulgaria. More than 30,000 people have visited the Bulgarian Pavilion in the Sala Tiziano at the Don Orione Artigianelli Cultural Centre, which, she says, is evidence of considerable public interest.
“Bulgaria’s participation has received extensive coverage, not only in the Bulgarian media but also internationally. I would like to stress that this is no easy feat, given the enormous competition. There are 99 national pavilions, including those of countries with a strong and long-established presence at the Biennale,” the curator notes.
Looking back at the history of the event, which dates back to 1895, Bulgaria first participated in 1910, when it was one of only four foreign countries represented. For political and economic reasons, that remained the country’s sole participation until 1942. Bulgaria subsequently took part in 1948, 1964, 1993, 1999, 2007, 2011 and 2019.
In 2022, Bulgaria was represented by Here You Are, a project by Mihail Mihaylov curated by Irina Batkova. In 2024, The Neighbours, by Lilia Topouzova, Krasimira Butseva and Julian Chehirian, gave voice to the victims of political repression.
This year, the all-female team behind Federation of Minor Practices has created an imaginary research laboratory exploring possible forms of political imagination grounded in care and collectivity. The project comprises four films addressing digital identity, disinformation, the relationship between labour and violence, and care for the natural environment. They are linked through an interactive environment designed as a computer game, in which visitors become active participants.
The exhibition is shaped by the theme of this year’s Biennale, In Minor Keys, conceived by its curator, Koyo Kouoh.
Tizian Hall
PHOTO bulgarianpavilionvenice.art
On 8 October, the Bulgarian Pavilion team met the public for the last time in the exhibition space before the Biennale closes on 22 November. 
The following week, on 14 October, the entire team will meet Bulgarian audiences for the first time. The event will take place at 2:30 p.m. in the Conference Hall of Sofia University’s Cultural Centre in Sofia. Desislava Dimova and Martina Yordanova will introduce the pavilion, after which each artist will discuss her work.
The meeting will conclude with an open discussion moderated by Daniel Nenchev, Bulgarian National Radio journalist and head of the public broadcaster’s Strategic Development Department. Art historians Vesela Nozharova and Snezhana Kresteva will also take part. Admission is free.

Balkan Developments
Unknown

PHOTO Reuters
Font size
More than 1,000 protest in Blegrade against overseas voting restrictions
More than 1,000 people protested outside the Republic Electoral Commission in Belgrade on October 7 against restrictions on voting abroad ahead of the early parliamentary elections on October 25, BTA reported.
The Republic Electoral Commission changed the locations of polling stations abroad. They are located mainly in Serbian embassies and consulates, requiring some voters to travel long distances to exercise their right to vote. Polling stations abroad are also expected to operate according to Serbian astronomical time. This means that Serbian citizens in countries such as Australia will have to vote at night.
More than 100,000 for Serbian citizens living abroad have registered to vote in the upcoming elections, compared with around 40,000 in the 2023 parliamentary vote. On October 25, the student-led opposition will face the ruling Serbian Progressive Party, led by Aleksandar Vučić.
Kaja Kallas and Marta Kos
PHOTO EPA/BGNES
Brussels calls for swift government formation following elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina
The EU has called on elected representatives in Bosnia and Herzegovina (BiH) to take full responsibility to form the state-, entity- and cantonal level- authorities without delay following the general elections held on October 4, hina.hr reported. According to EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas and Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos, the elections proceeded normally.
The EU is urging BiH to take all necessary steps and implement the reforms required to open accession negotiations. Bosnia and Herzegovina is also encouraged to make full use of the EU Growth Plan for the Western Balkans. To avoid the further loss of funds, the country urgently needs to finalise the legal and institutional framework and proceed with implementing the committed reforms.
Justina Shiroka-Pula
PHOTO Reuters
Kosovo lawmakers elect Justina Shiroka-Pula as President
In the final minutes of October 6, just before the deadline to elect Kosovo’s president expired, the opposition Democratic Party of Kosovo (PDK) backed Justina Shiroka-Pula for the post, averting another snap parliamentary election.
Shiroka-Pula served as Kosovo’s Minister of Energy from 2008 to 2011. She was a member of the PDK until 2014. She has led the Academy of Sciences and Arts of Kosovo since December 2025.
As part of the deal to elect the president, the ruling Self-Determination Movement (Vetëvendosje) supported amendments to the Law on the Specialist Chambers in the Hague, proposed by the PDK, Koha.net reported.
PHOTO abc-corridor.com
Egypt to link Africa with the EU through a trade and logistics corridor in the Balkans
A new private trade and logistics corridor will connect Egyptian ports with the Balkans and EU markets via Thessaloniki, Sofia and Niš. The “Arab-Balkan Corridor” initiative, presented in Cairo, was developed by Dutch company BDS Holding BV in cooperation with the Union of Arab Chambers.
Under the plan, cargo from Egypt will be shipped from the ports of Alexandria and Port Said to Thessaloniki, before continuing by rail and road through Bulgaria and Serbia to European markets.
Sofia is envisaged as a major rail logistics hub, while Niš will serve as a key distribution point for Serbia and the Western Balkans. The route will use existing transport infrastructure. The Niš–Sofia connection is part of a branch of Pan-European Transport Corridor X, BGNES reported.
PHOTO digi24.ro
Romanian President Nicușor Dan signs a law aimed at reducing the country’s bear population
Romanian President Nicușor Dan has signed a law aimed at reducing the country’s bear population. The law authorizes the preventive culling of 859 brown bears by 2027. An additional 110 bears may be culled by the end of 2026 if they pose a threat.
In recent years, bears have increasingly been appearing in populated areas across Romania, while the number of attacks has also risen, including fatal incidents, digi24.ro reported.
Romania is home to Europe’s largest bear population, estimated at between 10,479 and 12,700 animals. Conservationists are protesting against the law and argue that, rather than spending money on culling, efforts should focus on sterilizing bears to control population growth.

Unknown

Seyit Kurt
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
Canada Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canadians will determine the country's future, responding to Elon Musk's remarks supporting the separation of Quebec, Alberta and Saskatchewan from the country.
"The future of Canada will be decided by Canadians, and the priorities of Canadians, the priorities of the people of Quebec," Carney told reporters in Sherbrooke, Quebec, on Thursday.
Carney said Canadians should be free to live in accordance with their language and culture, adding that discussions about the future of the provinces should be "free from interference from foreign governments and large tech firms that think they can tell us what to do."
His remarks came after Musk, the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, voiced support on US social media platform X for the separation of Quebec and the two Prairie provinces.
Musk weighed in on Canada's separatist debate on X on Wednesday, initially writing: "Good. Quebec should separate."
In a subsequent post, he added: "They would be better off. Alberta and Saskatchewan should separate too."
 
Alberta, Saskatchewan premiers respond
Alberta residents are due to vote on Oct. 19 on whether the province should remain part of Canada or whether the provincial government should begin the legal process required to hold a binding referendum on separation.
The two options in the non-binding vote are: "Alberta should remain a province of Canada," and "The Government of Alberta should commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada."
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith has said she will vote for the province to remain in Canada.
Speaking in Edmonton on Thursday, Smith said separatist sentiment in the province had weakened as her government and Carney's federal government worked to address concerns among Albertans.
"The federal government has changed. Their approach to us has changed and they're willing to work together on addressing those issues," Smith said.
Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe, meanwhile, responded to Musk's remarks with a single word on X: "No."

Scientific study reveals scariest horror movie – with one 2026 title breaking heart rate record
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
08:33:04 UTC
17:33:04 KST

The ranking was determined by a study monitoring audience's heart rates and BPM increases while watching horror films.
Halloween is creeping up and many of you will be wondering: “What should I be watching to get in the mood for the big night?”
Well, if you're sticking to rigorous scientific research, we can reveal what the scariest films are – with no accounting for taste or your tolerance for jump scares.
The Science of Scare Project, now in its seventh year, tracks the pulses of hundreds of volunteers, who watch hours of English-language horror movies whilst fitted with heart rate monitors.
Their scientific study establishes a Scare Score system, which combines both heart rate (measured in beats per minute - BPM) and heart rate variability (HRV - measured in milliseconds), which measures the time in between each beat of your heart. Peak heart rate is also taken into consideration, with the highest point proving to be a valuable indicator and leading to an overall ranking of the scariest horror movies.
Scroll down for the Top 20 scariest films according to the study.
This year, 15 new contenders, including breakout hits Obsession and Backrooms, challenged horror favourites, while not yet cracking the Top 20. A24's paranormal podcast horror film Undertone is scientifically the scariest movie of 2026 and took the overall position of 33 in the rankings.
Most notably for this year’s study, Resident Evil broke a jump-scare record held by the film which has remained at the Number 1 spot for the last four years - with Zach Cregger‘s 2026 release recording a heart rate peak of 134 BPM.
For general reference, a normal resting heart rate for both adult women and men typically falls between 60 and 100 beats per minute (healthiest being between 70 and 80).
However, the top spot still belongs to Scott Derrickson’s 2012 supernatural horror film Sinister.
The film raised viewers’ average heart rate by 34%, from 64 to 86 BPM, with its most terrifying moment reaching 131 BPM. Its combination of sudden shocks and lingering dread earned it a Scare Score of 96/100.
Here’s the list of the 20 scariest horror movies according to the study:
- Sinister
- Host
- Skinamarink
- Insidious
- The Conjuring
- Hereditary
- Smile 2
- Smile
- The Exorcism of Emily Rose
- Talk To Me
- Hell House LLC
- The Conjuring 2
- It Follows
- The Dark and the Wicked
- The Descent
- Paranormal Activity
- The Babadook
- A Quiet Place 2
- The Autopsy of Jane Doe
- Insidious 2
Check out the full rankings and methodology in detail here.
As we’ve previously noted when it comes to the Science of Scare’s findings, the results are largely dominated by modern horror films which employ jump scares. It tracks considering the methodology is centred around heartbeats; however, many dreadheads and gorehounds consider the ubiquitous cattle-prod tactic to be cheap and an overused ploy to illicit easy frights. They’re great for a quick adrenaline rush, but many would argue that the jump scare startles rather than actually scares.
Do heart rate modulations necessarily equate to a film being the scariest? It's a valuable metric, but not necessarily synonymous with films that manage to burrow under your skin and set up camp. Those are the long-term scariest.
Still, if the Science of Scare’s study gets people watching the very underrated The Autopsy of Jane Doe, who are we to grumble?

MPs vote to fly rainbow flag at parliament for first time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

MPs vote to fly rainbow flag at parliament for first time
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The rainbow flag will fly at the Dutch parliament building on Sunday, Coming Out Day, after MPs overturned a decision by managers of parliament to drop the plan.
MPs backed the move by 90 votes to 36 in a vote late on Thursday night, public broadcaster NOS reported.
Parliament’s presidium, which runs its day-to-day affairs, initially agreed to the plan but changed its mind after Christian parties were told about the plan, RTL Nieuws reported on Thursday.
The orthodox Protestant SGP led the objections. “The rainbow flag is not a national flag but a flag of interest groups, which has grown into a symbol of activism,” SGP MP Diederik van Dijk told NOS.
Roll-call vote
Kati Piri, MP for opposition party Pro, then tabled a motion saying parliament should “stand up for the rights of the global LGBTI movement” and ensure “an inclusive working environment” for its staff.
Van Dijk responded by demanding a roll-call vote, in which each MP votes individually rather than by party. That meant MPs who had already gone home on Thursday had to return to The Hague.
Most MPs from D66, the VVD, CDA, PRO, PvdD, SP, ChristenUnie, 50PLUS and Volt voted in favour. The anti-immigration PVV, far-right Forum for Democracy (FVD), Denk and the SGP voted against, while MPs from JA21 and the Markuszower group were absent.
Purple Friday
The vote came on the eve of Purple Friday (Paarse Vrijdag), when schools mark LGBTI acceptance. This year it is being held in October for the first time, having been moved from December at the request of schools.
A record 3,130 schools have signed up, including 2,130 primary schools, compared with 2,890 last year, LGBTI rights organisation COC told news agency ANP.
The COC linked the rise to a survey published last month that found acceptance of homosexuality has slumped among teenagers. Only 22% of secondary school boys and 51% of girls now have a positive view, down from 40% and 78% in 2021.

Xinjiang cotton farmer embraces new opportunities through agricultural modernization
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:30:49 CST
17:30:49 KST

Lu Dewen checks the status of cotton at his field in Sandaogou Village of Shawan, northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, Sept. 30, 2026.
As the autumn harvest arrives, cotton fields across Xinjiang turn snow-white. In Shawan, at the foot of the Tianshan Mountains, 35-year-old cotton farmer Lu Dewen is busy managing his cotton-picking team. This year, he planted 1,500 mu (about 100 hectares) of cotton. Since late September, his team's schedule has been filled with harvesting orders from nearby farmers, with some jobs taking them to southern Xinjiang.
Four years ago, Lu's family bought a cotton picker, allowing them to harvest their own cotton and provide services to other farmers. Lu hired four workers and organized them into two shifts to improve efficiency. As cotton harvesting depends on favorable weather, the team must make the most of clear skies. Lu stays in the fields throughout the harvest to coordinate orders, troubleshoot his machine and manage schedules.
Lu began farming alongside his father, Lu Gaolin, 10 years ago, learning every stage of cotton production, from sowing and irrigation to harvesting. "Fluctuations in the cotton market are normal, but farming requires steady, hard work," he said.
Over the years, Lu has witnessed advances in cotton-growing techniques and the wider use of mechanized and intelligent agricultural machinery. His business now extends beyond his own farm to providing harvesting services for other growers. His father has stepped back from daily farm work but still visits the fields during the busy harvest season to check on progress and offer advice.
Shawan is a major cotton-producing area in northern Xinjiang. According to the local bureau of agriculture and rural affairs, the city planted 1.6457 million mu (about 109,713 hectares) of cotton this year, with mechanized operations accounting for more than 99 percent of the work from sowing to harvesting. Feature: Chinese university's Kazakhstan campus fosters talent, strengthens education ties
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:30:44 CST
17:30:44 KST

ALMATY, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- "Dong -- dong as in dongfang, the East."
In autumn-hued Almaty, the sound of students reciting Chinese drifts from a teaching building at Al-Farabi Kazakh National University.
Inside a classroom of Northwestern Polytechnical University's Kazakhstan branch campus, Chinese teacher Li Xiangning is teaching first-year students. Paper cutouts bearing the Chinese character "Fu," meaning good fortune, decorate the windows, while small Jade Rabbit lanterns hang from the door handles. Students repeat after her and carefully take notes.
The branch campus, an important cooperation project agreed upon by China and Kazakhstan during the first China-Central Asia Summit, opened in October 2023. It offers undergraduate, master's and doctoral programs and has trained nearly 300 Kazakh students.
Its undergraduate program mainly enrolls Kazakh students majoring in artificial intelligence (AI) under a dual-registration, dual-degree model, with students spending two years in Kazakhstan and two years in China.
"Here, I can learn both artificial intelligence and Chinese," said first-year student Yelissey Goncharenko, wearing a T-shirt bearing the emblems of both universities.
For second-year student Dinara Kamitkan, Chinese has been a seven-year journey. She began learning through online courses before receiving systematic instruction after entering the branch campus. She can now converse fluently in Chinese.
"I hope that after pursuing further studies in China, I can bring the knowledge and skills I learn back to Kazakhstan and use them to serve more people," she said.
In July, Dinara traveled with friends to Xinjiang in northwestern China, where she was impressed by both the landscapes and the level of digitalization.
"Whether watching videos online or visiting China in person, I can see the changes brought by artificial intelligence," she said.
Northwestern Polytechnical University has strengths in fields including AI, materials science, computer science, and information and communications. For students at the branch campus, learning Chinese also prepares them for further study.
Cooperation between the two universities has expanded beyond education.
In October 2024, the China-Kazakhstan Belt and Road Joint Laboratory on Materials Genome Engineering and Intelligent Science, jointly proposed by the two universities, was approved.
In December 2025, a China-Kazakhstan Agile Remote Sensing Key Payload jointly developed by the two universities was launched and completed in-orbit verification, providing technical support for ecological and environmental monitoring in Kazakhstan.
The branch campus has also begun producing graduates. Li Ziwei, vice dean of the branch campus, said eight master's students graduated in 2023 and 36 in 2024. Some continued their studies, while others found jobs or started businesses in Kazakhstan.
Li said the branch campus will continue improving its talent-training system, promoting educational connectivity under the Belt and Road Initiative and exchanges between young people from the two countries. ■

Hearing tests shed light on marine mammals' exposure to human-made noise
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:30:35 CST
17:30:35 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- Researchers in Australia have conducted the first hearing tests on Australian sea lions and long-nosed fur seals, providing a baseline for assessing how human-made noise could affect the marine mammals.
The researchers from Curtin University and Taronga Conservation Society Australia trained two sea lions and two long-nosed fur seals at Taronga Zoo Sydney to respond to sounds by pressing a paddle when they heard a tone, receiving fish as a reward for correct responses, according to a university statement released on Thursday.
Both species were most sensitive to sounds around 3.2 kilohertz, providing the first detailed baseline of hearing sensitivity for the two species, the statement said.
Understanding what the animals could hear was an important first step in assessing the potential impacts of noise from human activities, said lead researcher Christine Erbe, a professor at Curtin University's Center for Marine Science and Technology.
The researchers also assessed whether long-nosed fur seals could hear noise from boats, ships, aircraft, trains and construction, finding that many of these sounds were audible to the animals when hauled out on land.
The research was particularly important for the endangered Australian sea lion, whose population is estimated at about 12,000 and which relies on hearing to communicate, find food, navigate and detect threats, Erbe said.
The findings, published in the journals Conservation and Animals, could help inform environmental impact assessments and noise management as shipping, coastal development and offshore industries expand, the researchers said, adding the next step is to investigate how noise affects the animals underwater and when it begins to interfere with their behavior or hearing. ■

UN warns over police force as French student protests intensify
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
08:30:04 UTC
17:30:04 KST

The United Nations has expressed concern over police tactics during nationwide student protests in France, where more than 6,800 people have been detained and several injured as demonstrations over underfunded schools enter their third week.
Although most high schools had reopened by Friday, student unions vowed to continue their campaign, arguing that government concessions fall short of demands for more teachers, better classrooms and improved learning conditions.
The protests have attracted tens of thousands of people, university students, teachers and other supporters.
“We are following with concern incidents related to the student protests and high school blockades in France, some of which have turned violent,” Shabia Mantoo, spokesperson for the U.N. human rights office, said Friday.
She urged all sides to keep demonstrations peaceful and warned against the disproportionate use of force by law enforcement, stressing that the right to peaceful assembly must be upheld.
The demonstrations began in late September, with students complaining of teacher shortages, overloaded timetables, deteriorating school buildings and classrooms struggling to cope with rising temperatures.
Police have used tear gas, batons, stun grenades and water cannon to disperse blockades, prompting accusations of excessive force from students and rights groups. Police have opened 18 internal investigations into alleged misconduct.
A 15-year-old student lost a hand Monday after police fired a stun grenade, prompting the government to suspend the weapon’s use.
The Justice Ministry said Friday that more than 6,800 people had been detained since the protests began, with minors accounting for 86% of those arrested.
While most demonstrations have remained peaceful, some have involved vandalism, fires and clashes with police. Authorities reported attacks on education staff and damage to public property, while a school in the western city of Poitiers was set on fire.
The government made its first significant concession late Thursday, when Education Minister Edouard Geffray announced that about 3,000 qualified teachers who have yet to begin working would be deployed to address staffing shortages at the 114 high schools most affected.
The measure takes effect immediately and will cost several dozen million euros, Geffray told broadcaster TF1.
Student unions welcomed the announcement but insisted that it did not resolve the wider problems facing schools.
Marius Mesnil, a high school student union representative, said the decision showed that continued protests could deliver results.
“I find it crazy we need to block hundreds of high schools just to get a vacancy plan,” he told Franceinfo radio.
Mesnil described the offer as insufficient and called for another nationwide wave of school strikes Tuesday.
Other students expressed similar frustration. A 16-year-old in Toulouse said that protesters were saving their energy for the following week, while Alice, a student in Marseille, called the announcement a first step but said more action was needed.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has promised a broader plan to address the crisis by the end of October. Economy Minister Roland Lescure has also said there is room to consider education demands despite constraints in the proposed 2027 budget.
Under the current draft, education funding would rise 1.4% to 90.9 billion euros, the second-largest increase among government spending categories after defense.
The Education Ministry reported that 141 of France’s roughly 3,700 high schools remained closed Friday, down from about 800 a week earlier. However, disruptions continued at universities and other institutions.
Police cleared a blockade at Assas University, one of France’s leading law schools, in central Paris on Friday. Nearby Mines Paris, an elite engineering school, was also affected, while the Institut Catholique moved classes online because of a campus blockade.
Paris has become a focal point of the unrest, with students barricading school entrances and confronting riot police.
At Helene Boucher High School in northeastern Paris, students blocked the entrance with garbage bins Thursday before police moved in with tear gas. Demonstrators later gathered around Place de la Republique and Place de la Bastille, carrying signs demanding more education funding and questioning police conduct.
Some placards read “More money for repression than for our education” and “Who protects us from the police?”
Police used tear gas and water cannon to disperse crowds, while some protesters threw projectiles at officers.
Emma Khelil, an 18-year-old university student who returned to her former high school to support the movement, said she feared police violence.
“We’re here to defend our rights, not to lose an eye or a hand,” she told The Associated Press.
Khelil also described poor school conditions, including water leaks and insulation problems, and said she had occasionally seen rats inside the building.
Dounia Gergeon, a 39-year-old school librarian who joined a demonstration in Paris, said students felt abandoned and worried about their futures.
“They do not feel supported,” she said. “They feel cornered and forced to work under these conditions.”
Lecornu condemned attacks on students, school staff and police officers, along with fires, vandalism and thousands of hours of lost instruction. He accused political leaders of exploiting public anger for electoral purposes ahead of France’s presidential election in April.
“We cannot play with the safety of France’s youth,” he said.
The protests have intensified scrutiny of France’s public spending priorities as the government tries to address education shortages while reducing public debt.
Nearly 10% of teaching hours at French state high schools go unstaffed, according to education ministry figures. The shortages have fueled dissatisfaction among families, with some wealthier parents moving their children to private schools.
Stéphane Boujnah, head of Euronext, which operates the Paris stock market, said France needed difficult spending decisions to protect younger generations from the consequences of mounting debt. He suggested that reducing pension spending could free up money for education.
The Interior Ministry said 71,500 people demonstrated across France Thursday. Student and teacher unions are planning further strikes, raising the prospect of renewed disruption despite the decline in school closures.
The unrest has also coincided with demonstrations and labor action elsewhere in Europe.
In Belgium, two major labor unions organized a nationwide strike Friday that disrupted public transport, schools and air traffic over planned budget cuts and the rising cost of living. Tens of thousands were expected to attend a demonstration in Brussels.
Student protests have also spread across Belgium, with demonstrators demanding more teachers, smaller classes and improvements to school facilities. In Liège, authorities banned public gatherings until Oct. 16 after clashes involving tear gas and water cannon. Nearly 90 people were arrested, and several police officers were injured.
In Italy, students have occupied schools and organized marches over deteriorating buildings, education funding and increased military spending. Activists have explicitly drawn inspiration from the French movement, adopting the slogan “Let’s do as they do in France.”

U.S. destroyer enters Spanish dry dock, a first in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
08:30:03 UTC
17:30:03 KST

- USS Arleigh Burke (DDG 51) entered dry dock at Navantia’s Cadiz shipyard on Oct. 7, the first such docking for a Europe-based U.S. destroyer in the region.
- The ship is one of five U.S. Navy destroyers based at Naval Station Rota supporting NATO air and missile defense.
The U.S. Navy has put the destroyer USS Arleigh Burke (DDG 51) into dry dock at Navantia’s shipyard in Cadiz, Spain, the first time one of its Europe-based destroyers has been dry-docked in the region since the Navy began stationing them in Spain more than a decade ago.
The ship entered the dock on Oct. 7 for planned maintenance and modernization, according to U.S. Naval Forces Europe-Africa. Sailors from the ship, military and civilian staff from the Forward Deployed Regional Maintenance Center and Navantia workers are carrying out the work together. The Navy did not say how long the ship will be out of service, what modernization work is included or what the job will cost.
Dry-docking lets workers reach a ship’s hull, propellers, shafts and other parts below the waterline, work that cannot be done pierside. Being able to do it in Spain spares the Navy from sending a forward-deployed ship back across the Atlantic or relying on more distant facilities, keeping it closer to its operating area.
“The dry docking of Arleigh Burke is a major milestone in expanding U.S. Navy forward-deployed maintenance capabilities in Europe,” said Vice Adm. J.T. Anderson, commander of U.S. 6th Fleet. “By integrating dry docking into planned maintenance periods overseas, the Navy is increasing material readiness for our forward-deployed warships.”
Arleigh Burke is one of five U.S. Navy destroyers based at Naval Station Rota, near Cadiz, and assigned to Task Force 65 as part of the U.S. contribution to NATO’s integrated air and missile defense. The Navy began basing destroyers at Rota in 2014, when USS Donald Cook (DDG 75) arrived as the first of four ships sent under the European Phased Adaptive Approach for ballistic missile defense. In 2023, the United States and Spain agreed to raise that number to six, and USS Oscar Austin (DDG 79) arrived in October 2024 as the fifth.
The ships operate across a wide area, from the Mediterranean and Black Sea to the waters off Africa and up to the Arctic. Oscar Austin was recently in the Red Sea, while USS Roosevelt (DDG 80) has been operating in the Mediterranean.
USS Arleigh Burke, the first ship of the U.S. Navy’s largest destroyer class, has been based at Rota since April 2021, when it moved from Norfolk, Virginia, to replace Donald Cook. Navantia, Spain’s state-owned shipbuilder, builds and maintains ships for the Spanish Navy.

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- U.S. obsession with "absolute strategic advantages" stalls the multilateral arms control process and erodes the international non-proliferation system, a Chinese envoy said Thursday at the UN General Assembly (UNGA).
The United States is "obsessed with absolute strategic advantages," invests heavily every year in upgrading nuclear forces, promotes the Golden Dome anti-missile system, forward-deploys strategic offensive and defensive forces against other nuclear-armed countries, and continues to build nuclear alliances through "nuclear sharing and extended deterrence," said Sun Xiaobo, head of the Chinese delegation to the 81st session of the UNGA Disarmament and International Security Committee.

The United States applies double standards on arms control and non-proliferation, adopts a utilitarian attitude toward the current multilateral arms control mechanism and treaty system, and has repeatedly withdrawn from treaties and organizations, he said.
"This is the fundamental cause for the stalemate of the multilateral arms control process and the erosion of the international non-proliferation system," Sun said.
China advocates that all states should practice true multilateralism, he noted.
Calling the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons the cornerstone of the international nuclear non-proliferation and disarmament regime and an essential pillar of the post-war international security architecture, Sun said the consensus on the prohibition of nuclear tests based on the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty cannot be challenged. ■

Deputy Court President Judge Michal Davidi ordered the extension of Adiel Miost's detention with the consent of his defense attorney, Uri Goldman, and in the presence of police representative Chief Inspector Perry Goldman and Tax Authority investigators Ilan Hirschberg and Amit Keren.
Miost was arrested as part of a joint investigation by the Tax Authority's Haifa Investigations Assessing Office and the Coastal Economic Crimes Unit of Lahav 433.
According to investigators, Miost allegedly traded cryptocurrencies on various exchanges without reporting his activities to the Tax Authority, omitting income from his personal tax returns to evade paying taxes.
He is also suspected of holding undeclared foreign bank accounts and using another person's bank account to conceal his activities and the funds generated from them.
Luxury vehicle, foreign currency seized in investigation

The case is part of a series of investigations into suspected tax evasion and money laundering involving millions of shekels through cryptocurrencies. The cases were developed by the cryptocurrency department at the Tax Authority's Investigations Intelligence Headquarters.
Ashdod businessman suspected of concealing $13 million in cryptocurrency income

At the Jerusalem Magistrate's Court on Tuesday, Judge Hagit Plaut Babad ordered his release under stringent financial guarantees, following a request by Yaniv Shitrit, deputy head of the Jerusalem Tax Investigations Assessing Office.
The conditions included a personal undertaking of NIS 500,000, a NIS 200,000 guarantee provided by his wife and a cash deposit of NIS 50,000.
Pochinsky was also required to surrender his passport and was barred from leaving Israel for six months.
According to investigators, Pochinsky began trading cryptocurrencies in 2019 using various digital wallets.
During the investigation, authorities obtained identification documents from cryptocurrency exchange Binance linking him to an account that conducted extensive trading activity between 2019 and 2021 through wallets he owned.
Investigators also suspect that funds transferred from his exchange account ultimately reached additional digital wallets after passing through several wallets under his control, allegedly to conceal the money.
Searches conducted at Pochinsky's home resulted in the seizure of computer materials and digital wallets.
An analysis of the seized computer materials also revealed an additional digital wallet address.
The investigation into Pochinsky remains ongoing.

A quantum prediction from 1931 just came to life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
08:25:24 UTC
17:25:24 KST

A quantum prediction from 1931 just came to life
- Date:
- October 9, 2026
- Source:
- University of Innsbruck
- Summary:
- Nearly a century after physicist Hans Bethe predicted them, scientists have created and directly observed unusual quantum states known as “Bethe strings” in an ultracold gas. By cooling cesium atoms to near absolute zero and trapping them in thousands of tiny one-dimensional tubes, researchers were able to make groups of atoms bind together without ordinary chemical bonds. These strange clusters could contain six or more particles and even collide with one another without falling apart.
- Share:
Nearly a century after Nobel laureate Hans Bethe predicted their existence, scientists have created and observed unusual quantum structures known as "Bethe strings" using ultracold atoms. The experiment, led by quantum physicist Hanns-Christoph Nägerl, provides researchers with a highly controllable way to explore these unusual quantum many-body states.
In 1931, physicist Hans Bethe proposed that particles in certain quantum systems restricted to one dimension could join together into collective states now called Bethe strings. These structures differ fundamentally from familiar molecules. Rather than being connected through chemical bonds, the particles remain bound because of their interactions with one another, and the resulting states can exist only in one dimension.
For much of the past century, Bethe strings were primarily a theoretical idea. Researchers at the University of Innsbruck have now created and detected these multiparticle bound states in an ultracold gas, working with theory teams from the Department of Experimental Physics at the University of Amsterdam and the Technical University of Munich. The results were published in Nature Communications.
Creating Bethe Strings Near Absolute Zero
To produce the unusual quantum states, the researchers started with a cloud of cesium atoms cooled to within only a few billionths of a degree above absolute zero. They then separated the cloud into several thousand extremely narrow tubes.
Within each tube, the atoms are effectively restricted to moving along a single direction, creating the one-dimensional environment required for Bethe strings to exist. The researchers can also precisely adjust how strongly the atoms interact.
By changing those interactions from repulsive to attractive, the team caused the atoms to bind together. Rather than simply collapsing into one group, the atoms formed bound states of several different sizes. Some of the larger clusters contained six or more particles.
Watching Quantum Strings Collide
The next challenge was demonstrating that these particles were truly bound together.
"One of the simplest experiments was to let the strings expand," says Milena Horvath, one of the lead authors.
The researchers first allowed the atoms to spread out while keeping them trapped inside their one-dimensional tubes. During this expansion, the strings encountered one another and collided, yet the bound structures survived.
"This is a remarkable feature of the strings: they can collide without breaking apart," says Milena Horvath.
The scientists then performed a second version of the experiment in which they removed the confinement and allowed the atoms to expand freely through three-dimensional space. Because Bethe strings can exist only in one dimension, releasing the atoms into three dimensions caused the bound states to fall apart.
The energy that had kept the particles bound was then transformed into motion, making the atoms spread apart faster. Comparing the two types of expansion gave the researchers a clear way to identify the presence of Bethe strings.
When the particles were unbound, as they were when the interactions were repulsive, both expansion measurements produced essentially the same energy. When Bethe strings were present, however, the three-dimensional expansion contained extra energy released as the bound states broke apart.
A New Laboratory for Quantum Many-Body Physics
"Bethe strings were predicted almost a century ago as part of a beautiful mathematical description of quantum many-body systems," says Sudipta Dhar, another lead author. "Now we can create them in the laboratory, manipulate them and make them collide and probe their remarkable collisional stability."
Bethe strings have previously been detected experimentally in solid-state magnetic systems. The new work places these unusual quantum bound states in a very different environment: an ultracold atomic gas where researchers can control the system's geometry, particle density, and interactions with exceptional precision.
"This opens new possibilities for studying how these collective quantum objects form and interact," says lead theorist Alvise Bastianello.
The research was funded by the Austrian Science Fund FWF through a Wittgenstein Prize grant, the European Union through an ERC grant, and the UK Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council. Milena Horvath is a member of the FWF doctoral program Atoms, Light and Molecules (DK-ALM).
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Innsbruck. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Milena Horvath, Alvise Bastianello, Sudipta Dhar, Rebekka Koch, Yanliang Guo, Jean-Sébastien Caux, Manuele Landini, Hanns-Christoph Nägerl. Probing Bethe strings in an attractive one-dimensional Bose gas. Nature Communications, 2026; 17 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-76018-0
