Raytheon wins up to $6.3B to build more SM-3 interceptors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
08:05:21 UTC
17:05:21 KST

- Raytheon received a contract worth up to $6.3 billion over five years, plus two option years, to produce and sustain SM-3 Block IB interceptors.
- The interceptor was first used in combat in 2024, and production will take place mainly in Tucson, Arizona, and Huntsville, Alabama.
The U.S. Department of War and the Missile Defense Agency have awarded Raytheon a multiyear contract worth up to $6.3 billion to build and sustain Standard Missile-3 Block IB interceptors, the ship- and land-launched missiles the U.S. Navy uses to shoot down ballistic missiles in space.
The contract runs five years with two additional option years. It was issued as an undefinitized contract action, which lets Raytheon start work immediately while final terms and pricing are still being negotiated. Neither the Pentagon nor the company said how many interceptors the contract will buy or how quickly deliveries will begin. Production will take place mainly at Raytheon plants in Tucson, Arizona, and Huntsville, Alabama.
The SM-3 Block IB is built to destroy short- to intermediate-range ballistic missiles during the midcourse phase of flight, while they are outside the atmosphere, by hitting them directly rather than with an explosive warhead. It is launched from Aegis-equipped U.S. Navy destroyers and cruisers and from Aegis Ashore land sites, alongside the larger SM-3 Block IIA. The Block IB was first used in combat in April 2024, when U.S. Navy ships intercepted Iranian ballistic missiles fired at Israel, and it has been used again during this year’s war with Iran.
Raytheon said the award supports urgent replenishment of missile defense stocks that have been drawn down in combat.
“This award underscores Raytheon’s commitment to increasing production of critical munitions, ensuring our customers have the defensive capabilities they need, when they need them,” said Raytheon President Phil Jasper. “SM-3 Block IB has proven its relevance in combat and this contract helps ensure we can replenish inventories and keep pace with the evolving threats the U.S. Navy, MDA and their partners face around the world.”
The Pentagon said the multiyear deal is meant to give industry the production certainty to invest in assembly lines, solid rocket motor suppliers and smaller domestic subcontractors, where shortages have limited how fast interceptors can be built.
“Our warfighters must never face a fair fight, and the SM-3 Blk IB has proven its operational superiority to dominate any adversary across the globe,” said Michael P. Duffey, under secretary of war for acquisition and sustainment. “This contract provides production certainty to our defense industrial base, breaks sub-tier manufacturing bottlenecks, and ensures that our fleets and combatant commands have the interceptors required to dominate the battle space.”
The award is the latest under five framework agreements Raytheon signed with the Department of War in February, covering expanded production of Tomahawk cruise missiles, AMRAAM air-to-air missiles, SM-3 Block IB, SM-3 Block IIA and SM-6 under deals of up to seven years. Last week, Raytheon received a contract worth up to $24.4 billion for SM-6 production under the same framework.
The SM-3 Block IB line had slowed before the current buildup. In March, the Missile Defense Agency awarded Raytheon about $267 million for 23 more Block IB interceptors to restart production, bringing that order to 78 missiles, along with an $8.41 billion increase to the ceiling of a contract for SM-3 sustainment and engineering support.

The countries traded accusations after a reported incursion by Eritrean troops this week raised fears of outright war in the region, where the two nations have fought previous conflicts. The stakes have been raised this time around by conflicts in the Horn of Africa region and tensions across the Red Sea.
Ethiopia lost its access to all coastline when Eritrea secured independence in 1993. Addis Ababa argues that restoring sea access is an existential issue but has said it would be restored through peace and dialogue.
Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of supporting a rebel alliance in Ethiopia. Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos said in the letter that Eritrean forces had advanced up to 60 km (37 miles) into the country.
"The all-out invasion of parts of northern Ethiopia by Eritrea is a matter of public record,” the letter said. “It is a blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia’s inherent right to self-defence.”
The letter, dated Thursday, was addressed to French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot. The senior Ethiopian government official who shared the letter said it was also sent to the other members of the UN Security Council.
AT WAR FOR THREE YEARS, SAYS ERITREA
"The Ethiopian regime has been pursuing, in effect, an unprovoked war of aggression against Eritrea for more than three years," Yemane Gebremeskel, Eritrea’s information minister, said in a statement posted on X on Friday.
Citing statements made by Ethiopian officials, Yemane accused Addis Ababa of using the current conflict to take Assab, an Eritrean port, in order to restore access to the Red Sea.
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Eritrean soldiers were seen in northern Ethiopia this week, witnesses told Reuters, days after the neighbours severed diplomatic ties.
Yemane's statement did not address the issue of Eritrean troops deploying in Ethiopia. On Wednesday, he called reports of an Eritrean incursion part of an Ethiopian plan to justify a war of aggression against his country.
FLIGHTS TO MEKELLE TO RESUME
Drone strikes, believed to have been carried out by Ethiopia’s military, targeted Eritrean forces on Wednesday and Thursday as they withdrew from positions near the northern Tigray town of Adigrat, about 30 km (19 miles) from the border with Eritrea, the US-based conflict monitor ACLED said.
An Adigrat resident told Reuters on Friday that they had heard repeated explosions overnight and into the morning from several kilometres outside town.
Ethiopian government forces have continued to gain ground in Tigray in recent days and, in a sign of further consolidation, Ethiopian Airlines said it would resume flights to the regional capital Mekelle on October 11.
Eritrea has denied backing the rebel alliance that has been battling federal government troops since September 23 in the northern regions of Tigray, Amhara and Afar.
After years of war, Eritrea and Ethiopia made peace in a 2018 agreement that earned Abiy a Nobel Peace Prize. Eritrea fought in support of Ethiopia’s federal government during a 2020-2022 civil war in Tigray, but relations soured again toward the end of that conflict.
The fighting that broke out last month has been the biggest escalation of violence since the Tigray war, which caused hundreds of thousands of deaths. REUTERS

Switzerland resigned to spread of invasive raccoons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
08:03:45 UTC
17:03:45 KST

Switzerland resigned to spread of invasive raccoons
With their black beady eyes and Zorro-like masks, raccoons are undoubtedly cute. But they pose a threat to native wildlife and cause considerable damage. Their spread is unlikely to be halted in the Swiss canton of Zurich.
“Not exponential, but gradual” is how Reto Muggler, co-head of the cantonal fisheries and hunting authority, describes the growth of the raccoon population in the canton of Zurich. The number of raccoons shot has remained constant at between one and five for decades.
But he, like other experts, is convinced that their spread can hardly be stopped. “Sightings of young raccoons are becoming more frequent.” However, this could also be due to the fact that there are far more cameras today than there used to be.
More
How Switzerland is battling invasive species
The canton of Zurich does not currently have a specific plan to prevent these cute animals from spreading further. “As the raccoon is hunted anyway as an invasive species, there is no need for that at the moment,” said Muggler.
It is not known exactly how many raccoons now live in Switzerland. The animals have been appearing in hunting statistics for the past ten years. In 2025, a total of 84 were shot, with 54 in Aargau and 23 in the canton of Basel-Country alone. The first Swiss raccoons were sighted in northern Switzerland in the 1990s. They had probably escaped from enclosures.
The animals are native to North America. They were imported to Europe for the fur trade, and in 1934 a number of them were released in Hesse. From there, these omnivores spread throughout Germany. As they have virtually no natural predators in Europe, their numbers have grown rapidly.
Two million raccoons in Germany
Today, there are an estimated two million raccoons in Germany. In some places, they have become a veritable pest. They cause massive damage to buildings and in attics. As skilful climbers, hunters and nest predators, they also pose a threat to native amphibians and birds.
And last but not least, they can transmit the raccoon roundworm, which is dangerous to humans.
Whilst Germany has long since lost the battle against the raccoon, Swiss authorities are attempting to contain them or, rather, to prepare for an infestation. The neighbouring Swiss canton of Aargau, for example, is working with hunting associations to this end.
Hunters have at their disposal 11 specially designed box traps fitted with a catch basket. If a raccoon is caught in the trap, the hunter kills it with a well-aimed shot.

'Fire hoses' are Britain's nuclear submarine's only defence against drone attacks, reports say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
08:03:39 UTC
17:03:39 KST

While drone attacks are becoming a major threat in armed conflicts, Britain's nuclear submarines are revealed to use "fire hoses" to defend themselves against air attacks, reports say.
The Royal Navy nuclear submarines' sailors have allegedly been trained to defend the fleet from drone attacks using 'fire hoses', UK tabloid The Sun reports.
Despite the €6.5 billion Vanguard-class submersibles being armed with nuclear ballistic missiles, they allegedly use high-pressure water jets to defend themselves from air attacks.
These water jets, located on submarine decks as a defensive weapon when the vessels are at dock, are their main defences from drone attacks.
Several layers of defence are present to protect docked submarines, said the Navy, including "physical barriers, patrols, surveillance, monitoring, and counter-drone capabilities", UK newspaper reports. The water hoses are set to be manipulated by sailors standing on deck and aimed at drones that bypass land-based defences.
The fire hoses are designed to defend against small and medium-range FPV drones, while long-range Iranian Shaheds or Russian Gerbera drones would be intercepted by Royal Air Force fighter jets.
"We always thought this would be for small spy drones or civilian dicking around — but the threats moved on a lot", said a Navy source to The Sun.
'At risk of drones'
Faslane base, located north-west of Glasgow in Scotland, is one of UK's most sensitive military sites, home to its nuclear submarine fleet. Even though it is protected from naval attacks because it is far inside a bay, it could be particularly vulnerable to drone attacks.
"Gare Loch has excellent natural protection against enemy submarines, but the topography leaves it at risk of drones", a Navy source told The Sun.
"There are lots of public roads, people can roam on the hills. If several drones were launched nearby, there is less time to react".
"Faslane is very clearly of interest to hostile states. We know it has been targeted before, and it would not be surprising if it was targeted again", Charlie Williams, researcher and defence analyst at the London-based think tank the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), told The Sun.
"It is very surprising they are relying on fire hoses to defend the submarines. We have to hope the Ministry of Defence is investing in the right kind of capability to defend it".
He says Russia has flown hundreds of drones over nuclear sites throughout Europe, including France's Île Longue nuclear submarine base and Royal Air Force Lakenheath in Suffolk.
"The protection of our bases is kept under constant review", said UK's Ministry of Defence spokesman. "Through the Defence Investment Plan, we are investing an additional £470million (€554 million) over the next four years to strengthen the protection of UK military sites".

Huge victory for Spain as two cities crowned greenest in the EU. Which countries missed out?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
08:02:48 UTC
17:02:48 KST

The winner of the European Green Capital 2028 awards is going home with €600,000 to help turn ambition into further action.
The EU's greenest city for 2028 has been crowned, in a sweeping victory for Spain.
The European Commission’s annual European Green Capital and Green Leaf Awards recognise cities that are making measurable environmental progress while improving quality of life for their residents.
Back in June, an independent panel whittled 27 eligible applicants down to eight finalists, judging them on everything from air and water quality to their biodiversity and efforts to cut emissions.
Five were in the running for the Green Capital title: Aalborg in Denmark, Bielsko-Biała in Poland, Košice in Slovakia, Porto in Portugal and Zaragoza in Spain. Another three – Benidorm and Chiclana de la Frontera in Spain, and Estarreja in Portugal – were shortlisted for the Green Leaf awards for cities with smaller populations.
Europe's greenest city revealed
Yesterday (Thursday 8) at a festive ceremony in Guimarães, Portugal, the 2026 prizewinner, Zaragoza, was named European Green Capital 2028.
The city received the first-place prize for its "strong governance and long-term commitment, helping the city respond successfully to growing climate challenges". Zaragoza, which has received a €600,000 prize, was praised for urban biodiversity, green areas and sustainable land use.
It has also implemented a Green Infrastructure Master Plan, which establishes "diverse strategies to maximise and connect green components across the city".
Benidorm and Estarreja also impressed the jury with their strong commitment to creating greener, healthier and more sustainable places to live – and were both awarded the European Green Leaf 2028 title. Each will take home €200,000 for green projects and public activities.
Benidorm stood out for "successfully managing mass tourism pressures" while maintaining environmental protections and sustainable development – while Estarreja was recognised as a "compelling example" of green transformation, successfully moving beyond its industrial legacy.
"Our cities are at the heart of Europe’s environmental transition," says Jessika Roswall, European Commissioner for Environment, Water Resilience and a Competitive Circular Economy.
"They are where we can turn policies into visible change by bringing nature back into our neighbourhoods to cool our streets, reduce air, water and noise pollution, and improve waste management, to create healthier, more sustainable places for people to live and thrive."
Roswell congratulated all three winners, arguing that many cities in Spain and Portugal are "true frontrunners in urban sustainability".
She adds: "I hope their experience will inspire many more European cities and accelerate the transition towards greener, more resilient communities."
How are Europe’s greenest cities judged?
The EU launched the Green Capital Award to recognise cities that are making measurable progress on environmental problems and improving quality of life for their residents.
The main prize is open to cities with more than 100,000 inhabitants. Smaller cities with populations between 20,000 and 100,000 compete for the Green Leaf title.
The expert panel judged applicants in seven areas, including how clean their air and water are, how they protect nature and green space, how they manage waste and noise, how quickly they are cutting emissions and how they are preparing for threats such as extreme heat and flooding.
How are European cities adapting to a hotter climate?
The changes being recognised by the EU are part of a paradigm shift visible in cities around Europe. As summers get hotter and weather patterns become more unpredictable, urban planners are giving more space back to trees, parks and water.
In Barcelona, for example, some streets have been closed to through traffic while others have been turned into parks and pedestrian areas.
Meanwhile, in Milan, the Bosco Verticale has provided a small but important example of ways cities can add greenery even where there’s little room for parks. The two residential towers feature more than 21,000 trees and shrubs on their terraces.
In Breda, the Netherlands, widespread civic involvement has transformed the city since the turn of the century. Concrete tiles have been replaced with grass, flower beds and trees. Homes and schools have added rooftop gardens.
Today, 60 per cent of the city is green space – part of more than a decade of work that helped Breda become the EU’s first National Park City in 2025.
The Green Cities Awards are not only a matter of adding plants to buildings or streets, though. Heilbronn, Germany, won the 2027 Green Capital title after scoring highly for its clean air and water, noise reduction policies and waste reduction, among other things.

There are once again more outage schedules amid Russia's attacks; parts of Kyiv and seven regions are without power
Kyiv • UNN
An energy worker was killed and three injured in the Sumy region. Emergency and hourly power cuts of up to 2.5 groups are in effect in Kyiv and seven regions.
Russian attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure have intensified. An energy worker was killed in Sumy region. As of the morning of October 9, parts of Kyiv and seven regions are without electricity. Emergency and hourly outage schedules are in effect, and the scope of the latter has been increased again. This was reported by the Ministry of Energy and NPC Ukrenergo, UNN writes.
Russian attacks
"In recent weeks, Russia has intensified its attacks on energy infrastructure. The enemy is targeting energy equipment and high-voltage networks that transmit electricity between regions. As a result, the power system has temporarily lost some of its ability to transmit electricity to consumers," the Ministry of Energy said.
Enemy shelling, it was noted, is complicating repair work. As soon as the security situation permits, energy workers begin restoring damaged equipment in order to return power to consumers as quickly as possible, the ministry stressed.
"Yesterday, as a result of a Russian attack on an energy facility in Sumy region, one energy worker was killed and three others were injured. The injured were taken to hospital, where they are receiving the necessary assistance," the statement said.
Where outages and schedules are in effect
"As of the morning, due to shelling of energy infrastructure, some consumers in the city of Kyiv and in the Kyiv, Donetsk, Dnipropetrovsk, Zaporizhzhia, Odesa, Chernihiv and Kharkiv regions remain temporarily without electricity," the Ministry of Energy reported.
As noted, "due to equipment damage and a voltage drop in the high-voltage network, emergency outages are being forced in some districts of Kyiv and Kyiv region. The schedules published in advance are currently not in effect there. The return to predictable schedules will take place after the situation in the power system stabilizes."
"In a number of regions today, hourly outage schedules are being applied to all categories of consumers, along with capacity restriction schedules for industry and business," the ministry reported.
To prevent overloading of equipment damaged by Russian shelling, capacity restriction schedules for industry and hourly outage schedules (up to 2.5 queues) for all categories of consumers are being forced throughout the entire day today in some regions
The day before, Ukrenergo forecast outage schedules of 0.5 to 2 queues for October 9.
Current schedules are posted on the official resources of regional power distribution companies.
Consumption
According to Ukrenergo, electricity consumption has increased. Today, October 9, as of 09:30, it was 11.4% higher than at the same time the previous day—Thursday. The reasons for the changes are a reduction in the extent of forced outages in some regions, as well as cloudy weather and rain in the western regions of Ukraine, which is resulting in low efficiency of household solar power plants and a corresponding increase in the volume of electricity consumption from the general grid. Yesterday, October 8, the daily maximum of consumption was recorded in the evening. It was 4.4% lower than the maximum on the previous day—Wednesday, October 7. The reason for the changes was the greater extent of forced restriction measures applied.
"It is advisable to shift active electricity consumption today to the period when industrial solar power plants operate most efficiently—from 11:00 to 15:00. Please do not switch on several powerful electrical appliances at the same time from 17:00 to 22:00," Ukrenergo said.

Mask and Face must face same consequences: SC stays HC bail, sends Rs 3,000 crore drug case accused to jail
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
08:00:25 UTC
17:00:25 KST

NEW DELHI: “Mask must face the same consequences as the Face”, “If your masters are in jail, you will serve them better by being there, not outside” – were the caustic remarks by Supreme Court on Thursday as it send back to prison an accused who was granted bail by the Punjab and Haryana HC in a huge narcotic drug trafficking case.The case related to seizure of 5,000 tablets of tramadol from one Ashu Arora last February in Amritsar and subsequent unearthing of an inter-state illegal drug trafficking syndicate. Senior advocate Maninder Singh, appearing for the accused, argued that HC had granted bail six months ago putting a premium on the liberty of citizens and because of his illegal custody.A bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana asked, given the gravity of the crime, a Rs 3,000 crore illegal drug trafficking syndicate and seizure of 5,000 Tramadol tablets, can the illegal detention prior to arrest vitiate the arrest itself as has been cited by the HC?When Singh said that his client, Anuj Kumar Singh, was a mere employee of those who were allegedly running the inter-state drug trafficking network, the bench said, “You are a ‘mukhota’ (mask) which was as much involved in the crime as the face itself.”“When your masters are in jail, you can serve them better by being there with them, not outside,” the bench said while expressing serious concern over the menace of narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances in the state. The senior advocate said that there was no evidence of any seizure of drugs from his client.The bench said, “In a game of football, there are 11 players but all of them do not have possession of the ball simultaneously.”
The counsel said his client was not even a 12th player. Switching to cricket from football, the bench said, “He was either a cover or an extra-cover.”The bench said it would cancel the bail, ask the prosecution to complete the trial in one year and if it does not complete, then the accused can apply for regular bail. When Singh protested saying the accused had cooperated with the investigation and regularly attended trial while being on bail, the bench said, “For a Rs 3,000 crore drug trafficking case, one year in jail is nothing.”
It asked the accused to surrender within two weeks and asked him to respond to the Union govt’s appeal against HC order granting bail.When Singh cited the HC’s decision to grant bail because of illegal custody prior to arrest and the premium it put on liberty, the bench said, “We also continuously ruled in favour of preserving liberty if there are other redeeming features. In your case, we do not find your cooperation in investigation or attendance of trial in the face of nature of crime and the restrictions in law to be a very relevant redeeming feature. Your arguments are most persuasive. In any other case we would have agreed with you.”

'We work to pay the bills': Swiss middle class under pressure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

‘We work to pay the bills’: Swiss middle class under pressure
Despite having stable jobs and a decent income, more and more Swiss people are struggling to make ends meet.
Rising fixed costs, fear of unexpected expenses, and cutting back on leisure activities: financial pressure is no longer sparing the middle class, who are voicing their frustration.
In the southeastern town of Vevey, in canton Vaud, amongst the colourful market stalls, the consensus is clear: the cost of living is becoming an ever-greater burden. “Prices are becoming unbearable. Next year, there’ll be something I simply won’t be able to afford,” says one customer.
Another sums up the general feeling: “We want to buy two or three things, but it feels as if we’re trying to buy gold!”
More
‘Anyone moving to Switzerland just for the money often ends up disappointed’
Pensioners and those on very low incomes are among the hardest hit. With a state pension of CHF1,700 ($2,040) per month, a woman from Vevey has taken the drastic step of selling her car. “I can no longer afford the car park, the insurance and everything else,” she said.
Rising costs are no longer affecting only the most vulnerable. The middle class, regarded as the country’s economic engine, is also seeing its purchasing power eroded.
In Lucens, also in canton Vaud, Sabrina Meriem, a home care nurse, and her partner Mathieu Rochat, a municipal landscape gardener, have a combined net income of CHF11,200 a month. Yet, when they add up their taxes, mortgage, health insurance premiums, food and fuel, their fixed expenses exceed CHF7,000.
Rising heating oil prices
The soaring price of heating oil is a particular cause for concern. Mathieu Rochat has therefore decided not to fill his home heating oil tanks completely. “At the current price, I hope to get through the whole winter with what’s left and wait for the price to fall significantly,” he said.
Beyond the numbers, the psychological impact is taking its toll on this family. “We manage to pay our bills; there’s no problem there. But we look at what’s left at the end of the month, and it’s getting less and less. All the extra activities we can do as a family are being cut back,” he added.
More
Having children is a luxury in Switzerland. Is the US next?
For his partner, the anger is more pronounced: “The middle class foot the bill for everyone,” she said. “We’re cash cows. If you’re rich, you can have it all. If you’re poor, you’re lucky to get support. If you’re in the middle, you foot the bill for both the top and the bottom. That’s not right for the society we live in.”
Fewer holidays
According to a survey carried out by market researchers Qualinsight in January 2026, 89% of people in French-speaking Switzerland now keep a close eye on their monthly spending. More than half are cutting back on leisure activities and holidays, while 47% of those surveyed are making concessions on food.
The same picture emerges in Poliez-Pittet, in the Gros-de-Vaud region. Aurore and Lionel Carrard run a family farm. Despite an annual gross income of around CHF280,000, their outgoings regularly reach CHF20,000 a month.
“We work to pay the bills, that’s all,” says Aurore Carrard. “It’s sad to live in a rich country and not be able to say to yourself: ‘this weekend, we’re going to a restaurant’.”
More
Life has become more expensive in Switzerland – despite low inflation
Her husband Lionel shares this frustration. “Back in the day, my grandfather employed my father, and he had staff of his own. As for me, I’m on my own. I’ve only got one employee who stands in for me one Sunday a month.”
“It’s frustrating. Our estate used to be smaller and it supported two families, maybe even more. These days, we’re swamped with work and, at the end of the day, we’re no better off.”
What are the solutions?
In Bern, opinions on the solutions are divided. Social Democrat parliamentarian Benoît Gaillard believes that stricter enforcement of the law could bring down rents and allow for better control of fuel mark-ups.
Yvan Pahud of the right-wing Swiss People’s Party argues instead for reducing taxes to give households some breathing space. This approach draws inspiration from the recent success of a local people’s initiative that achieved a 12% reduction in Vaud cantonal income and wealth tax.
But the outlook remains bleak. Rents, public transport, postal services and energy costs continue to rise. For many Swiss, a sense of declining living standards is taking hold.

Oil Slick Expands Near Sochi After Tanker Fire, Greenpeace Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09

17:00:00 KST

An oil slick in the Black Sea near Russia’s resort city of Sochi has expanded following a fire aboard a tanker attacked by sea drones earlier this week, Greenpeace said Friday, a day after authorities reopened beaches and reported no oil contamination.
The slick grew from 8 to 25 square kilometers over three days, the environmental group said, citing satellite images from Planet Labs.
Greenpeace said the slick extended along the route taken by the Aframax Rio after the attack. Around midday Wednesday, the tanker was near Lazarevskoye, about 50 kilometers from the site of the fire. By Thursday, it was near Tuapse. Environmentalists believe the vessel may be under tow to Novorossiysk.
Sochi and the neighboring federal territory of Sirius closed their beaches on Tuesday after the Liberian-flagged tanker caught fire following an attack attributed to Ukrainian sea drones.
Authorities reopened the beaches Thursday, saying tests found no oil contamination.
Sochi’s administration said seawater samples taken across the city met sanitary standards, according to consumer protection watchdog Rospotrebnadzor. Satellite monitoring also found no oil slicks, it added.
Sirius administration head Dmitry Plishkin said tests found no traces of oil in seawater and air pollution levels remained within permitted limits.
The tanker was attacked on the evening of Oct. 6. The fire sent thick black smoke over Sochi. Russia’s Transportation Ministry said burning oil prevented rescue vessels from approaching the ship. The flames were extinguished on Wednesday.
All 23 crew members, who were Indian nationals, were rescued.
The amount of oil aboard the tanker has not been disclosed. The Mash Telegram news channel, citing unidentified sources, reported that the vessel was fully loaded.
The tanker continued to drift along the coast after the fire. Its operator, Executive Ship Management, said Wednesday that officials and two senior crew members had started inspecting the vessel to assess its condition.
Built in 2004, the Aframax Rio is 247 meters long and 42 meters wide, with a deadweight capacity of 107,100 metric tons.
According to the investigative outlet The Insider, the tanker has called at Russian Black Sea ports and is under Ukrainian sanctions. Kyiv has linked it to Russia’s “shadow fleet,” a network of tankers used to transport oil and circumvent sanctions.

A promising future now looks perilous for election loser Zack Polanski. He sowed, now he reaps | John Harris

16:58:41 KST

As ever, among all the noise triggered by Labour holding the seat of Holborn and St Pancras, the most plain-spoken and undeniable analysis was provided by that sage and national treasure John Curtice, of Strathclyde University. The result, he said, echoed national opinion polls and reflected two undeniable facts: that the Greens are in need of a period of contrition and reflection, and Labour ought to be slightly less than ecstatic.
Andy Burnham’s party, with a majority of 3,364, he said, showed they “are in a much better position than they were six months ago, but still not as popular as they were in 2025”. The Greens, meanwhile, remain “a more significant player than historically they have ever been”, but have lost much of the ground they gained during Zack Polanski’s first year as leader, when the serial failures of the local MP – one Keir Starmer – provided him and his party with such a glorious succession of political opportunities.
Do not forget: the Greens’ success earlier this year in Gorton and Denton played a massive part in Starmer eventually leaving the political stage, and the man he barred from being the Labour candidate snatching his job. But now? Publicly, Polanski seems largely unrepentant about the “Zionism is racism” motion passed at his party conference, and confident he can resume where he left off. But his party’s claim that it tripled its previous vote share in the seat is very specious indeed: as the pollster Peter Kellner puts it, “the leftwing vote two years ago was divided between the Greens’ 10.4% and an independent, Andrew Feinstein’s, 18.9%. Together, they won 29.3%.” The true increase in the leftwing anti-Labour vote, therefore, is only 3.5 percentage points, and Polanski has thus taken such a significant blow that his experience of the next few weeks and months could be very choppy indeed.
Over the last week, I spent two days in the constituency, filming another episode of the Guardian’s Anywhere But Westminster video series, and got a deep sense that our politics remains in a state of unpredictable flux. So many people and the conversations we had come to mind. The young people of colour in the pinched neighbourhood of Somers Town – the urban village right next to Euston station – who were all voting Green, and talked of Gaza and the impossibility of living in our capital. The woman in upmarket Primrose Hill who told us she no longer told people she was Jewish for fear of instant uproar and upbraiding about Israel, a country she had last visited 15 long years ago. But most of all, a 24-year-old trainee teacher called Tom, who reluctantly still lives with his parents, and has no idea how he is going to hold down a job in his home city. He had once been an enthusiastic Green member and activist, he told me, and had every intention of voting for them, until the Zionism motion suggested a party perfectly happy to inflame the UK’s sense of division and polarisation. He decided to switch to Labour.
The searing summer should have provided the Greens with another boost, and a real chance of another byelection win. But now? Polanski – who endorsed the idea that Zionism is a form of racism eight days before his party’s conference began – looks not just morally questionable, but distinctly weak: one central bit of symbolism in this whole affair, let us not forget, was his absence from the Zionism debate and vote at his party conference.
And so to a geographical jump to a few other parts of the country. As I may have written once or twice in the past, I live in Frome, in Somerset: a 25,000-population settlement whose affinity with the Greens has been deepening for the last decade or so. They provide four of the six councillors who represent the town on our new unitary council. The rurality and climate-fear in the villages that surround us chimes with Ellie Chowns’s seemingly out-of-the-blue election two years ago as the Green MP for North Herefordshire and Adrian Ramsay’s success in the East Anglian seat of Waveney Valley. But there are also elements of the maverick, future-facing attitudes that waft down into our neck of the woods from Bristol Central, the seat held since 2024 by Carla Denyer, the former Green party co-leader. I think I know what was holding those two elements together, and partly powering the Greens’ resurgence: a mixture of radical, empathetic social democracy and urgency about the fate of the planet that also seems to have taken root in some of England’s suburbs.
With the possible exception of Bristol, if you wanted to completely wreck the Greens’ successes in all those places, you would bin that approach and accelerate exactly what Polanski has facilitated: not just a politics of no-surrender and provocation, but the entry into the party of embittered former Jeremy Corbyn supporters and assorted ultra-leftists, bringing with them a flimsy, pious gesture politics.
The party’s former leader Caroline Lucas and the longstanding Green activist Rupert Read are about to publish a mini-manifesto titled Climate Popularism: a guide to “breaking the grip of rightwing populism through a new politics of crisis resilience”, to be formally launched on 15 October. Written before the antisemitism meltdown, it rather minces its words about Polanski’s project, but makes it pretty clear why things have now gone wrong. “Some observers have wondered whether this new eco-populism has at times been a little too quiet about the ‘eco’ part,” Lucas and Read write. “On the doorstep, at least, this may be an understandable strategy … [But] as recent heatwaves have made abundantly clear, the salience of climate impacts will make adaptation concerns a doorstep issue before long.”
Lucas and Read make the case for “centrally funded, locally appropriate action to adapt neighbourhoods, infrastructure and ways of life, to prepare for the broad, cascading impacts of human-triggered climate change”. They propose a domestic retrofit programme that would entail a lot of “secure green jobs”. They also write, very perceptively, about an “exhausted majority” tired of our shrill politics, and suggest the “depolarisation” of the climate issue in the face of plain facts – which sounds like the direct opposite of how Polanski operates. There is talk of a politics of “courage, hope, love of place” – and, crucially, a decisive turn into the use of citizens’ assemblies. This is the kind of turn the Greens should undoubtedly take – but even if they do, they will now be starting in a deeply troubled and weakened state.
Burnham, meanwhile, still has no end of work to do. For what it’s worth, many of us have long believed that the substantial presence in British politics of a radical party free of Labour’s pussyfooting around the climate crisis and the harsh realities of inequality was an absolute necessity, and the Greens’ fitful growth was nothing but a good thing. Now, by contrast, as the fallout from Polanski’s sudden crash only deepens, they have a massive amount of self-questioning and reinvention to do. Whether they will even have the inclination is another question entirely.
- John Harris is a Guardian columnist

Delays in the case of medical negligence by Odrex doctors: two consecutive hearings canceled
Kyiv • UNN
The court hearing in the case of medical negligence by Odrex doctors took place on October 8, but the next two hearings will not be held\nbecause of yet another set of motions from the defense attorneys.
On October 8, the Kyiv District Court of Odesa continued hearing the case concerning medical negligence by doctors at the private Odrex clinic, Vitalii Rusakov and Maryna Bielotserkovska. However, the next two hearings, scheduled for October 9 and 13, will not take place due to a motion filed by Maryna Bielotserkovska’s lawyer. The next hearing is scheduled for October 14, UNN reports.
Vitalii Rusakov and Maryna Bielotserkovska are charged under Part 1 of Article 140 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine — improper performance of professional duties by a medical worker. The case concerns the circumstances of businessman Adnan Kivan’s treatment at the private Odrex clinic. According to the investigation, the actions or inaction of the medical workers may have led to the development of postoperative complications and sepsis, which, against the backdrop of the patient’s cancer, could have caused his death. The court must provide a final assessment of the evidence and the issue of the doctors’ guilt.
However, whether the court will manage to reach a decision remains an open question. Due to regular postponements, the hearing of the case is being delayed, while lawyers interviewed by UNN warned of the risk that the statute of limitations could expire.
It should be noted that the hearing in the case also did not take place on October 7. At that time, Bielotserkovska’s defense attorney filed a motion to postpone it. At the same time, one of the lawyers for the accused surgeon Vitalii Rusakov also failed to appear in court.
Let us recall
In September, the court scheduled 13 hearings. Seven of them were postponed or did not take place, including due to motions from the defense. After Rusakov’s lawyers requested the postponement of two consecutive hearings because they were participating in other court proceedings, presiding Judge Viktor Chaplytskyi found the reasons for their absence unjustified and sent the relevant information to the Qualification and Disciplinary Commission of the Bar. It is to assess whether the defense lawyers’ actions show signs of deliberately delaying the proceedings.
Andrii Misiats, acting head of the Higher Qualification and Disciplinary Commission of the Bar, had previously also drawn attention to the possible consequences of lawyers’ systematic nonappearances.
The combination of nonappearances may indicate not an accidental violation, but a certain pattern of behavior by the lawyer and his negligent attitude toward his professional duties

Three years after October 7, prolonged war takes its toll on Israelis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
07:57:36 UTC
16:57:36 KST

Three years after October 7, prolonged war takes its toll on Israelis
Children’s psychiatric emergency visits have more than doubled in Israel, study shows.
As Israel marks the third anniversary of the 7 October Hamas-led attacks, the psychological toll on its society remains visible, with an increase in PTSD among children, more adults struggling with everyday life amid mental health issues, and a rise in suicides among soldiers, experts have told Al Jazeera.
About 1,200 people died in the attacks on villages and army outposts in southern Israel, while Israel’s assault on Gaza has since killed more than 74,000 Palestinians. Gaza has been left almost uninhabitable amid a wave of destruction that a UN commission of inquiry has concluded amounts to genocide. Meanwhile, Israeli society continues to function, but beneath the surface, the attacks, war and missile strikes have compounded the psychological strain among its people.
New research has found that one in five Israelis reports severe difficulties with daily functioning because of their mental health, according to the National Mental Health Barometer, conducted by Clalit Health Services’ Research Institute and the Myers-JDC-Brookdale Institute.
Among children and adolescents, separate Clalit research shared with Al Jazeera recorded a 121 per cent increase in psychiatric emergency visits compared with the period before the war. Behind those figures are families living with bereavement and fears about what comes next.
A family living with loss
During a webinar for journalists organised by Clalit Health Services to mark the anniversary, Irit Ben Arye recounted how her husband, Haim Ben Arye, drove south to help evacuate survivors from Kibbutz Be’eri. It was one of the communities attacked by Palestinian fighters on 7 October 2023.
The 52-year-old bus driver returned home crying, she says. About two weeks later, he died by suicide.
The couple were married for 30 years and had eight children. Irit worries about the lasting effects on them. Recounting to journalists what she told her children following the death of her husband, she said: “You have to ask for help, if something is bothering you, if you’re in pain, in the dark, you feel that you are alone.”
“Cry, ask, break something. Make yourself noticed, make us notice that you are in pain.”
The Ben Arye family are not the only ones experiencing mental distress. In fact, one-third of the Israeli population felt they needed mental health treatment, according to the National Mental Health Barometer report. Half reported that their leisure activities had been affected, while 35 per cent said they had difficulty forming and maintaining close relationships.
Growing up on alert
Israel’s attacks on Iran and retaliatory missile strikes have brought further periods of fear and interruption to civilian life. With missiles and airstrikes raining down on Israel at various times since 7 October, everyday activities can become calculations about access to shelter and the possibility of another attack.
Eric Vermetten, a professor of psychiatry at Leiden University Medical Center in the Netherlands, told Al Jazeera that this type of repeated exposure to danger can lead to long-lasting psychological issues. “Repeated attacks, warning sirens and displacement turn ordinary decisions – where to sleep, whether to send children to school, how to plan tomorrow – into questions of safety,” he said.
“Maintaining that vigilance is exhausting: sleep becomes deeply fragmented, concentration falters and anxiety, irritability or withdrawal can seriously strain relationships,” he added.
Drawing on records from about five million members, Clalit Health Services’ assessment has found that psychiatric emergency visits among children and teenagers more than doubled over this period.
Edgar Jones, professor at King’s College London’s Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology and Neuroscience, told Al Jazeera that people respond differently to prolonged conflict. Some do adapt and develop ways of coping.
But if people experience the destruction of their home or the death of a relative, they may develop post-traumatic illness or depression, he said. “Many of those in this group will become war-weary should their daily lives continue to be disrupted and threatened.”
“Everyone has a breaking point,” Jones said.
The psychological toll on soldiers
The effects of prolonged warfare are also apparent among those carrying out Israel’s military attacks. Soldiers, including young conscripts, have been deployed to Gaza, where a United Nations commission of inquiry concluded that Israel has committed genocide against Palestinians.
“For reservists, moving repeatedly between combat and civilian life may leave little to no time to reconnect with family or make sense of their experiences – loss, guilt, shame, anger, despair – before returning to duty,” Vermetten said.
Jones added: “They may, when reflecting on what they have been ordered to do, or failed to do, experience moral injury”.
“This arises when their actions challenge their view of themselves, sometimes leading to guilt, shame and anger against themselves.”
Israeli parliamentary data recorded 279 suicide attempts among serving soldiers between January 2024 and July 2025. Combat soldiers accounted for 78 per cent of military suicide deaths in 2024. The figures exclude veterans who died by suicide after leaving service.
Vermetten cautioned against treating suicide as an inevitable consequence of prolonged war, but said that “conflict, loss and isolation can increase vulnerability” among soldiers who go on to take their own lives.
A toll across the region
The psychological consequences of Israel’s military campaigns extend far beyond its own population. Since 7 October 2023, its assaults on Gaza and Lebanon, as well as attacks on Iran have brought death, destruction and displacement across the region, leaving children particularly vulnerable to lasting trauma.
UNICEF estimated that in Lebanon, 770,000 children have experienced psychological distress, while almost two-thirds of households reported that their children were anxious or nervous. The conflict has also compounded years of economic crisis, leaving families struggling to meet basic needs as well as support their children.
In Gaza, the scale of destruction and displacement has eroded the foundations on which psychological recovery depends, with hospitals and homes destroyed across the enclave.
UNICEF estimates that more than one million children are in need of mental health and psychosocial support, while much of the population is suffering from hunger, amid bombardment that has continued despite a so-called “ceasefire” last October.
“Children know trauma does not end when the bombing stops,” Jonathan Crickx, UNICEF’s chief of communication in the State of Palestine, said in February.

EU may need to cut winter gas demand by 7% as storage hits record low, IEEFA warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
07:57:13 UTC
16:57:13 KST

The EU could have to curb gas consumption by 7% this winter, the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis warned on Friday, with stocks at their lowest for the time of year on record and the Iran war keeping prices high ahead of a full ban on Russian LNG imports from January 2027.
The EU's gas reserves are emptier than at this stage of any autumn since 2011, meaning the bloc might have to burn 14 billion cubic metres (bcm) less gas than last winter over the coming months, according to the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA), a US-based non-profit that analyses energy markets and backs a shift to cleaner energy.
In a report published on Friday, IEEFA noted that EU gas storage sites were about 72.4% full on 3 October and could supply 7.3bcm less gas this winter, from November to March, than they did last winter.
Combined with the EU’s complete ban on Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports from January 2027, the storage shortfall means the bloc may need to use 7% less gas than last winter.
"This does not mean EU gas storage will run dry this winter,” the report said. However, emptier sites release gas more slowly, which could leave the bloc short in a late-winter cold spell, and a depleted system would need a bigger and pricier refill next summer.
Plugging the storage gap with extra imports instead of cutting demand would cost about €3 billion, IEEFA estimates, a 12% premium on what that volume would have cost last year, as the US-Iran war has lifted prices.
“An increased reliance on gas storage has become a major financial liability for Europe,” the think tank concluded.
War drives up prices
Europe’s gas market has been under strain since the Iran war began on 28 February, disrupting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a route for about a fifth of the global LNG trade.
Dutch TTF futures, the benchmark for gas prices in Europe, hit €84.5 per megawatt-hour in mid-September, the highest since 2022, the year Russia’s invasion of Ukraine began.
They crossed €80 again on Thursday and were trading at around €78 early on Friday.
Since the end of February, imported fossil fuels have cost the EU an extra €100 billion "without a single molecule of energy in addition", European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Tuesday.
EU Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen urged governments last month to keep curbing demand amid "exceptionally low" storage levels, according to a letter seen by Euronews.
Europe’s gas grid operators also warned on Thursday that a severe winter could leave the bloc up to 15% short of the gas it needs.
The storage business depends on gas costing less in summer than in winter, so traders can buy, hold and sell at a profit. However, that gap has narrowed, and at times this year the summer contracts were dearer than winter ones.
"Buying gas to store has become a financial risk rather than a profitable strategy," IEEFA said.
Governments are stepping in. The Hague cleared up to €993 million in June to help state-owned EBN build reserves, while Germany told state-owned importer SEFE to store 8 terawatt-hours of gas by 15 December, and Spain has increased the LNG held at its import terminals by over 25%.
Winter gas use fell from about 222bcm in 2021-22 to 185bcm in 2022-23, as prices soared and emergency savings kicked in, but has risen to around 200bcm in each of the last two winters, "suggesting the era of easy demand cuts may be over", IEEFA said.
With imports flat, storage covered 30% of EU winter consumption last winter, up from 25% in 2021-22, the think tank noted, citing Eurostat.
Rather than spending on more storage, which IEEFA warned "risks locking in fossil fuel infrastructure for decades", it urged investment in renewables, heat pumps, industrial electrification and efficiency upgrades to curb the winter demand peaks that drain reserves.

Suppressing Palestinian resistance: US charity under fire for  AI monitoring of Gaza classrooms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
07:56:29 UTC
16:56:29 KST

A US charity in Gaza plans to record classroom conversations and use artificial intelligence to flag speech deemed “hateful” or “inciting.”
The plans laid out by the founder of the Gaza Children Village in a webinar last month have elicited ethical, safety and privacy concerns from some Palestinian and advocacy groups and at least one of the charity's partners.
There is no indication the charity intends to share its classrooms’ recordings with anybody else, but concerns about the potential misuse of surveillance technology are heightened in Gaza after three years of Israel’s genocidal war. The Israeli military has used AI to sift through intercepted communications to, among other things, identify targets for strikes.
Palestinian rights groups have been critical of the charity's education agenda more broadly, saying it is unaccountable to local and UN agencies that have long managed Gaza’s schools. Who controls education in Gaza is one of many unresolved questions about its postwar governance.
It is unclear when the classroom monitoring is supposed to begin, what specific language will be flagged, and whether teachers, students and their families have been told about the plans.
The charity's founder and CEO is Dr David Hasan, a neurosurgeon born in Kuwait to Palestinian parents who now teaches at Duke University medical school in Durham, North Carolina.
The charity has raised money largely from individual donors, including American Jews, and says it's partnering with North American, Israeli and European aid organisations and hospitals.
The schools' lessons are mostly built around the Palestinian Authority curriculum, but language that he says “glorified violence“ was removed, Hasan has said.
Hasan declined to comment for or provide examples of curriculum changes.
On a webinar last month with humanitarian groups, Hasan said the reason to monitor classrooms is to help train teachers in how to uphold a curriculum that he had previously said was aimed at “de-radicalisation.”
“I know it’s controversial, but trust me, it’s the only way we feel for us to survive and deliver this curriculum,” Hasan said.
The rhetoric of ‘de-radicalisation’ is what Israel and its supporters have often used to undermine Palestinian resistance and rewrite history, which is replete with Zionist atrocities in the occupied Palestinian territories.
Israel has maintained a crippling land, air, and sea blockade on Gaza since 2007.
Since October 7 2023, Israel has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and wounded over 175,000 in its genocide in Gaza, while around 90 percent of the besieged enclave’s infrastructure has been destroyed, according to Palestinian and UN figures.
Monitoring classrooms opens ‘Pandora’s box'
Two people affiliated with the charity expressed concerns when notified about the possibility of classroom monitoring.
“Cameras to monitor the performance of students and teachers is acceptable. But cameras to silence students and teachers from being able to have a free exchange in a classroom are not acceptable,” said Bishara Bahbah, a Palestinian American political activist on the charity's board. He said he wasn't aware of the monitoring plans and that they haven't been raised with the board.
Bahbah said that with so few functioning schools in Gaza, the charity's top priority is getting more kids in classrooms.
An official at an aid group that partners with the Gaza Children Village said the use of cameras could prompt it to reconsider working with them. Using AI to monitor people’s words opens a “Pandora’s box,” said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
Six current and former teachers at Academies of Hope declined to comment.
The system will flag language deemed ‘hateful’
Under the plans outlined by Hasan in various communications, recordings of classroom conversations will be analysed by an AI-powered system to detect “anti-Semitic,” “inciting" or “hateful” language.
If such language is detected, a warning will be sent to Hasan, who can then contact the teacher to understand the context and provide feedback, Hasan said in the September webinar. He said recordings are stored for 72 hours.
Palestinians in Gaza are especially concerned about surveillance technology
Concerns regarding surveillance technology remain acute in Gaza amid Israel's genocidal war and extensive monitoring by Israeli forces.
"Israel has weaponised information to such a dystopian degree that many Palestinians feel they cannot utter a word, type a thought, or twitch an eye without fearing it could be seized upon,” said Amjad Iraqi, senior Israel and Palestinian Territories analyst for the International Crisis Group.
Groups opposed to the charity's curriculum say Palestinians are being stripped of their autonomy in deciding what to teach their children.
“It is very concerning, they’re trying to control the minds of new generations,” said Ines Abdel Razek, co-director of the Palestine Institute for Public Diplomacy, an advocacy group.
The Palestinian Authority, which has limited autonomy in parts of the Israeli-occupied West Bank, and UNRWA should be supported in rebuilding schools in Gaza, she said.

'PERM distinct from H-1B visa': MEA on US move to suspend certain firms from green card programme
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
07:56:18 UTC
16:56:18 KST

File photo: MEA says US move against tech firms may affect green card process, not H-1B status
NEW DELHI: The ministry of external affairs (MEA) on Friday said the US government's decision to suspend several technology companies from the employment-based green card programme would not, by itself, affect existing H-1B visas or the status of visa holders and their dependents.The ministry said the suspension of applications under the Permanent Labour Certification (PERM) programme could, however, affect the permanent residency process for eligible employees of the companies concerned.“We are aware of the US Department of Labour’s decision concerning the Permanent Labour Certification (PERM) programme for certain companies. It should be noted that PERM is distinct from the H-1B visa programme,” the MEA said in a statement.
“The suspension of PERM applications does not, by itself, affect the validity of existing H-1B visas or the status of H-1B visa holders and their dependents, though there could be some impact on the permanent-residency/Green Card process of eligible employees of the affected companies,” it added.The ministry also emphasised the economic benefits of skilled talent moving between India and the US, saying the latest measures did not advance the shared ambitions of the two countries.
“It should also be clear that talent mobility adds value to both economies. While it creates opportunities for Indians, it equally helps US companies with cutting-edge talent, innovation, research, productivity, competitiveness and job creation, besides creating shareholder wealth in the US,” the MEA said.“This is therefore an area of tremendous mutual benefit for the two countries and our expectation is that all stakeholders in this process can appreciate this fact. The steps announced by the US do not advance the shared ambitions of both countries,” it added.
Which companies have been suspended?
The US department of labour has suspended Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini from the PERM programme. The department said it would not accept new applications from the affected companies or process their pending applications amid multiple active federal investigations.US labour secretary Keith Sonderling said the companies had collectively sought millions of foreign workers and received hundreds of thousands of approvals under employment-based immigration programmes.“Since 2009, just these companies alone have requested almost 3 million foreign workers. They received over 230,000 H-1B visa approvals and over 100,000 permanent labour certifications. That's hundreds of thousands of jobs that were taken from American workers,” Sonderling said.The administration has alleged that companies misused employment-based immigration programmes to replace American workers with foreign employees. These are allegations made by US officials; the announcement cited ongoing investigations.
What is PERM, and how is it different from H-1B?
PERM is a labour-certification process that allows an eligible US employer to sponsor a foreign worker for employment-based permanent residency, commonly known as a green card. Before certifying an application, the US department of labour must establish that there are not enough qualified and available American workers for the job and that employing the foreign worker would not adversely affect the wages and working conditions of similarly employed US workers.
The H-1B programme, by contrast, allows US employers to hire skilled foreign workers temporarily for specialised occupations. The PERM suspension does not automatically cancel existing H-1B visas, but it could disrupt a route to permanent residency for employees whose employers are sponsoring them through the programme.The move comes amid a wider crackdown by the Trump administration on skilled foreign labour. A day before the announcement, the US department of homeland security proposed new fees for F-1 international students seeking to participate in Optional Practical Training (OPT), describing the measure as an effort to protect American workers and strengthen the integrity of the immigration system.

Vance described workers coming in on H1B visas as 'indentured servants'. (Photo: Agencies)
NEW DELHI: The ministry of external affairs on Friday slammed US vice-president JD Vance over his description of H-1B visa workers as "indentured servants", calling his remarks "unwarranted" and "deeply offensive".In a statement, responding to Vance’s comments, the ministry said, "We have also seen some comments in this context by the US Vice President. We believe that such descriptions are unwarranted and ignore the fact that Indian professionals in the United States are highly educated and skilled contributors to its economy and innovation ecosystem."The MEA also highlighted the contribution of immigrants to the US economy, saying, "Indeed, the history of the United States itself has been shaped by generations of immigrants whose labour, enterprise and innovation have contributed to its growth and prosperity.""Resorting to terminology that carries painful historical and colonial legacy connotations is deeply offensive," it added.Vance made the remarks while addressing a news conference on visa fraud, alleging that companies bring in foreign workers at lower wages while laying off American employees.“If you are working as an H-1B visa in the United States of America, you’re earning $20,000 less than an American citizen hired in the same position.
If you were brought in by one of these foreign outsourcing firms, you’re making $48,000 less than an American citizen in a similar position," Vance said."So, I’m sure that everybody here understands the game that is being played. You bring in indentured servants from outside the country, you lay off American workers and, if you’re a corporation, you make a ton of money by under cutting the wages of American workers, replacing them with people who frankly shouldn’t be in the United States of America to begin with,” he added.The MEA said that it was aware of the US department of labor’s decision concerning the Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) programme for certain companies."It should also be clear that talent mobility adds value to both economies. While it creates opportunities for Indians, it equally helps US companies with cutting-edge talent, innovation, research, productivity, competitiveness and job creation, besides creating shareholder wealth in the US," the statement said."This is therefore an area of tremendous mutual benefit for the two countries and our expectation is that all stakeholders in this process can appreciate this fact. The steps announced by the US do not advance the shared ambitions of both countries,” it added.The MEA also clarified that PERM is separate from the H-1B visa programme. It said the suspension of PERM applications does not, by itself, affect the validity of existing H-1B visas or the status of visa holders and their dependents, although it could affect the green card process for eligible employees of the companies concerned.“We continue to follow developments around this issue,” the ministry added.The MEA’s response came a day after the Trump administration suspended eight companies, TCS, Infosys, Wipro, HCLTech, Cognizant, Capgemini, Microsoft and Adobe, from participating in the PERM programme.
The US administration’s move is part of a broader crackdown on skilled-worker immigration. US officials have alleged that companies have used the system at the expense of American workers.The US department of labor said it would stop accepting and processing new and pending PERM applications involving the affected companies.PERM is an important step in the employment-based green card process. Employers generally need labour certification from the US department of labor before sponsoring eligible foreign workers for permanent residence.The process requires employers to establish that there are not enough qualified, willing and available US workers for a position and that hiring a foreign worker will not adversely affect wages and working conditions.

South Africa withdraws asylum directive after anti-migrant violence
JOHANNESBURG, Oct 9 - South Africa's Department of Home Affairs said on Friday it had withdrawn a directive allowing the intake of asylum applications, a day after anti-migrant protests turned violent in Johannesburg and Durban.
The directive had sought to implement a July 7 Constitutional Court ruling that said asylum seekers cannot be denied access to South Africa's asylum system solely on procedural grounds, such as entering the country illegally.
Home Affairs said in a statement that the directive was issued as an operational measure, and the implementation had overwhelmed refugee reception offices within days, put officials at risk and led to threats to public safety and order.
The government has blamed disinformation over the court's ruling, adding that it did not automatically grant refugee status, permanent residence or other legal rights to undocumented migrants.
Africa's biggest economy grapples with a surge in anti-immigrant protests that have strained relations with other African countries and forced thousands of foreign nationals to leave.
Migrants are often blamed for unemployment, crime and pressure on public services, accusations that social scientists say are unsupported by evidence.

Germany Extends Protection for Ukrainians to 2028, Tightens Rules for Military-Age Men
Germany has extended temporary protection status for Ukrainian refugees until March 4, 2028, while establishing special conditions for newly arrived men of military age.
The updated regulation, enacted by the Federal Ministry of the Interior and published in the country's official legal gazette, Bundesgesetzblatt, takes effect on October 9.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Under the amended transitional residence framework, men subject to military service must meet specific requirements to qualify for temporary protection.
They are required to show proof of completed military obligations, demonstrate that they crossed the Ukrainian border legally, or provide official documentation certifying exemption from mobilization.
The European Commission planned to update its temporary protection directive in July 2026, requiring newly arriving Ukrainians to present official documentation proving their exemption from military mobilization to obtain temporary protection status in the EU.
The measure was designed to target first-time applicants, both men and women, without affecting the roughly 4.3 million Ukrainians already residing in the bloc with protected status, including over 1.2 million in Germany and nearly 960,000 in Poland.
Scheduled to take effect in March 2027, the policy reflected a broader trend among member states, such as Denmark, which had introduced separate legislative measures to restrict refugee status for military-aged Ukrainian men.

Why has Iraq decided to ban online map service Waze?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
07:48:15 UTC
16:48:15 KST

Why has Iraq decided to ban online map service Waze?
Communications minister points users to Google Maps and a locally developed app as alternatives to the Google-owned service.
Iraq is set to ban the popular navigation app Waze, which was founded in Israel.
Communications Minister Mustafa Sanad announced the move on Tuesday. It has prompted discussions in Iraq over whether the country can build its own alternative and whether banning one app protects users’ location data.
What has Iraq decided and why?
The Ministry of Communications plans to block the use of Waze by the end of December, according to the Iraqi newspaper Al-Mada.
Sanad told the broadcaster Rudaw that it would take effect some time at the start of 2027.
He made the announcement on the sidelines of the Hitex 2026 technology exhibition in Erbil, the capital of the semiautonomous Kurdish region in northern Iraq.
“Because it comes from the entity [Israel] and is Israeli-made, we will ban it at the beginning of 2027,” he said.
What is Waze?
Waze is a widely used navigation app. Hundreds of motorists, including taxi drivers, use it to get around. The service relies on users to report traffic jams, accidents and police checkpoints as they happen.
It was developed in Israel, and Google bought it in 2013 for nearly $1bn.
Waze’s privacy policy lets it collect users’ locations, routes, destinations, search histories and device details, depending on their settings.
Pooled across many users over time, such data have security value because they can reveal movement patterns, peak times and unusual changes.
Rudaw reported that the app has been the subject of security discussions in Iraq over its alerts being used to avoid checkpoints although Sanad did not link the ban to that issue.
Why does the Israeli connection matter in Iraq?
Iraq does not recognise Israel or have diplomatic relations with it and has formally been at war with it since 1948.
A 2022 law criminalises any diplomatic, political, military, economic or cultural ties with Israel. Its penalties include life imprisonment and the death penalty. It was passed by 275 votes in the 329-seat Council of Representatives.
The law applies to all Iraqi citizens, state institutions and media as well as private companies and foreign entities operating in the country, including the Kurdish region.
Sanad has not specifically said Waze must be blocked under the antinormalisation law.
Distrust of Israel has been bolstered by the US-Israel war on Iran. The United States and its allies have targeted Iraq’s Iran-aligned militias with air strikes and economic measures.
During the war, Iraq also faced a serious case of Israeli infiltration. In May, US media reported that Israel had built two secret military outposts deep inside Iraq’s desert to support its war on Iran.
One post was nearly exposed by a local shepherd who stumbled upon it and was killed.
What alternatives is the government offering?
Sanad said users could switch to Google Maps or Iraqi navigation apps.
Communications Ministry spokesman Omar al-Amiri said in remarks carried by Al-Mada that Waze would be replaced by a yet-to-be-named Iraqi app.
He said the app would run without technical problems.
Al-Mada also quoted Iraqi technology researcher Mustafa Kamel al-Sharif as saying a national alternative would take more than an app with an Iraqi map and logo.
It would need accurate geographic databases, a constantly updated road network, routing systems and live data on traffic, accidents and closures, he said.
He also told the newspaper that the crux of the issue lies in how Iraq regulates its citizens’ data and other services may also collect sensitive data similar to Waze.
What remains unclear?
The ministry has not said how the block will be enforced or whether it will cover the Kurdish region. It has also not set out the ban’s legal basis or said when the Iraqi app will launch.
Another unknown is why Google Maps, owned by the same parent company, Alphabet, would remain available or serve as an alternative.
The government has also not answered why Waze is being banned now when its Israeli roots have been long known.

More work visas, less temporary housing: Czechia changes rules for Ukrainians
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:45:06 EEST
16:45:06 KST

More work visas, less temporary housing: Czechia changes rules for Ukrainians
Kyiv • UNN
The Czech government plans to allow Ukrainians with temporary protection to apply for work visas and employee cards. The number of places in humanitarian housing will be reduced from 20,000 to 10,000.
In the Czech Republic, the government approved amendments to several government regulations concerning the possibilities for Ukrainian citizens to stay in the Czech Republic. Among other things, they expand the possibilities for obtaining work visas and residence permits. UNN reports this with reference to Radio Prague International.
Details
The changes, as stated in the accompanying documents, are aimed at facilitating the arrival of Ukrainian citizens in the Czech Republic and are being adopted following recent restrictions on granting temporary protection to people liable for military service. They also take into account the provision of opportunities for a gradual transition from the temporary protection regime to the regime of standard residence permits for certain groups of people who wish to work in the Czech Republic, including after the end of Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Among such standard residence permits, the most common are precisely those that the current government proposal would make more broadly available to Ukrainians in the Czech Republic. These are, on the one hand, a short-term visa for employment purposes and, on the other, a long-term residence permit for employment purposes pursuant to §42g of the Foreign Nationals’ Residence Act, the so-called "employee card" (zaměstnanecká karta).
Restrictions to be lifted
Access to them is also to be opened to people with temporary protection in the Czech Republic — at present, they do not have it.
"The proposed change returns economically motivated migration to the standard framework appropriate to it, separates it from the humanitarian temporary protection regime, and represents a step toward the systematic and proper targeted use of individual residence permits," the authors of the proposal said.
Currently, long-term migration from Ukraine to the Czech Republic is possible, in particular, for the purpose of family reunification, full-time study at a university, or employment. Applications are accepted at Czech consular offices in Kyiv and Lviv.
Ukrainian citizens who are staying in Ukrainian territory (and are entitled to leave it), as well as those staying in other countries, including with temporary protection in other EU member states, may apply at these consular offices for an "employee card" (zaměstnanecká karta), a "blue card" (modrá karta — a long-term residence permit for employment in positions requiring a high level of qualification), and special work visas (mimořádné pracovní vízum) within government migration programs and the established annual quotas, which are fully sufficient.
However, the current rules do not allow Ukrainian citizens who have or previously had temporary protection in the Czech Republic to apply for an "employee card" at Czech consular offices in Ukraine. This restriction is now to be lifted.
"The unemployment rate in the Czech Republic and the shortage of workers in a number of sectors of the national economy are currently, despite the presence of approximately 150,000 people with temporary protection who are employed at this time, at the same level as before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. In 2021, almost 27,700 "employee cards" were issued to Ukrainian citizens. In addition, Ukrainian citizens also actively used short-term work trips on the basis of short-term employment visas, of which more than 185,500 were issued in 2021," the document says.
Humanitarian housing to be halved
Another proposed change concerns halving the number of places allocated for the temporary humanitarian accommodation of newly arrived refugees. People who have nowhere to stay may receive such state-funded housing for up to 90 days after obtaining temporary protection.
There are currently 20,000 such places reserved; there will be 10,000. However, as noted in the cover letter, this will not worsen the actual situation of refugees.
As the authors of the proposal noted, in 2026 approximately 300 people are staying in such accommodation in the Czech Republic; on average, 17 people are placed there each week, representing 1.3% of all those who received temporary protection during the week. In 2024–2025, as of the end of those years, around 500 people were staying in humanitarian accommodation; such accommodation was provided to an average of 45 people per week, which accounted for about 3% of all newly arrived people with temporary protection.
Therefore, the document states, the number of 10,000 reserved places is also expected to be entirely sufficient in the event of an unexpected increase in the number of newly arrived applicants for temporary protection.
