UK's Green Party Jewish leader Zack Polanski loses parliamentary seat election to Labour candidate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
07:36:33 UTC
16:36:33 KST

Andy Burnham's Labour Party won an election for a parliamentary seat vacated by former leader Keir Starmer on Friday, fending off a strong challenge from the left-wing Green Party in a boost for the British prime minister.
Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali, the leader of the local council, won the seat in the central London constituency of Holborn and St Pancras with 12,292 votes, compared with 8,928 for Zack Polanski, the Green Party leader.
The victory, which had been expected, will buoy Burnham, installed as prime minister by lawmakers fearful Starmer's unpopularity was opening the way for a challenge by the populist Reform UK party at the next national election.
After losing left-wing support to the Greens earlier this year, Labour looks to have won many voters back, a result which triggered more questions about the leadership of Polanski, who had promised to make his party "an eco-populist" movement.
The 43-year-old former actor and hypnotherapist, who had some success in drawing voters away from Labour before Burnham came to power, has come under fire after party members passed a Zionism is Racism motion. The move, which called for "the establishment of a single democratic Palestinian State in all of historic Palestine" was criticized by Jewish groups, other parties, and most Green Party lawmakers.
After the fiercely contested vote, Polanski who did not vote, answered his critics, saying he would stay on as leader, and described the result as part of "Andy Burnham's honeymoon."
Yet he did not get a full endorsement from the party's former leader, Caroline Lucas, who struggled to contain her anger over what she said was his lack of leadership over the motion on Zionism at last week's annual conference.
Asked whether he should stay on as leader, she told the BBC: "I think just let's see what happens in the coming days and weeks."
"I want him to speak now about what has happened, I want him to show the leadership that was frankly missing on Sunday."
Labour candidate celebrates victory over Green Party
Labour's Abdi-Wali, who arrived in Britain as a child refugee from Somalia, said her victory was a defeat for "those who seek to divide us."
"We have a responsibility to defend what we've built and pass it on," she said. "Throughout our campaign, we chose hope, and the people of Holborn and St Pancras chose it with us. And now it's time to deliver."
It was an early test for Burnham, whose predecessor, Starmer, stood down as a lawmaker in September after being ousted as prime minister in July.
Under Starmer, Labour had also ceded ground to the Green Party, which made record gains in London in May's local elections with its widening appeal among younger, left-leaning voters in the capital and other urban areas.
The Greens have fallen back in opinion polls since, after Burnham made policy pitches that boosted Labour's standing among voters to the left, including a tougher line on Israel and a more ambitious approach to relations with the European Union.
Bridget Phillipson, Labour's chair, said the election result showed the party's "message of hope is really cutting through," describing the Greens' conference motion as something that held "British Jews to a standard that we do not apply to others."
"We tackled antisemitism in our own ranks but all political parties have to be ever vigilant," she told Times radio, describing a period when Labour had to deal with antisemitism in the party under former leader Jeremy Corbyn.
Polanski distances himself from Green Party vote on Zionism
Polanski, who is Jewish, was questioned repeatedly after the by-election over the conference vote on Zionism and the Green leader seemed again to distance himself from it, saying only that he believed displacement of Palestinian people and "ongoing genocide" were racist.
For now, he said, the Green Party should take their fight to Burnham's Labour and focus on whether the governing party's budget on October 28 delivers.
"So many people told me on the doorstep that they want to give Andy Burnham a chance," Polanski told broadcasters. "Well, he's got a chance now. Let's see what he does with it."

She called on people to stand together in the defence of rule of law.

Why the EU is failing to act on growing public criticism of Israel? - analysis
Jennifer Rankin
in Brussels
When the British government announced sweeping sanctions on trade with illegal Israeli settlements and condemned “ethnic cleansing” in the West Bank by state-backed “settler terrorists”, some EU diplomats hoped this dramatic shift in UK government policy towards Israel would have a galvanising effect on the rest of Europe. So far, it has not.
Although France and Canada joined the UK in pledging to ban goods from illegal settlements and impose sanctions on “those who facilitate them or profit from them”, there has not yet been a wider ripple effect.
A meeting of EU foreign affairs ministers on Monday is likely to showcase the bloc’s stasis in policy towards Israel – a stalemate that is at odds with rising public criticism in Europe of Israel’s government.
A survey of 10 European countries, including Spain, France and Sweden, found large majorities of people had a negative opinion of Israel. Views had become more negative compared with the previous year, according to the Pew Research Center, mostly after the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran, which unleashed a new crisis in the Middle East and a global economic shock. In Poland, negative views jumped eight points to 70% of respondents, in Italy they increased by nine points to 75% and in Germany they also rose by nine points to 73%.
Israel is facing ever deeper isolation in the theatre of public opinion. Five countries chose to boycott the Eurovision song contest this year over Israel’s participation, after organisers declined to exclude it over its conduct in the Gaza war and rising violence in the West Bank. Organisers have now decided that broadcasters will no longer be eligible to host the song contest if their state is involved in an armed conflict or sensitive geopolitical situation.
More than 74,000 people, including at least 21,200 children, have been killed in Gaza since Israel launched its war in retaliation for the Hamas attack of 7 October 2023, in which the terrorist group killed 1,209 people – including 36 children – and took 251 hostages, inflicting a nationwide trauma.
Gaza remains a humanitarian catastrophe, with people facing acute shortages of water, nutritious food and medical equipment and medicines, while contending with disease, unemployment, economic collapse and the threat of death or injury. Israel’s airstrikes continue: the death toll includes 1,400 Palestinians killed since a ceasefire was declared a year ago.
The EU talks on the Middle East will focus on the conflicts in Iran and Yemen, but ministers will also discuss the situation in Gaza and the West Bank in the context of elections in Israel on 27 October and the first legislative elections in Palestine in 20 years, which are expected by late November.
The discussion is expected to expose familiar fault lines in the 27-member EU.One group of countries are vocal supporters of the Palestinian cause: Spain and Ireland were the first to call for a review of whether Israel’s conduct in the Gaza war was in breach of the human rights requirements of its association agreement with the EU, which covers the €68bn (£58bn) trade relationship, cooperation in research, environment and energy.
A second group consistently opposes targeting Israel’s government: Germany and Austria are close allies for historical reasons, while Czechia and Italy are ideologically aligned with Benjamin Netanyahu’s administration.
Among a third, larger group of countries in the middle are several, such as France and the Netherlands, that are increasingly critical of the Netanyahu government’s conduct in Gaza and its plans to build the vast E1 settlement, which threatens to critically damage the two-state solution.
President Pavel returns from holidays as Czechs go to polls
Czechs go to the polls on Friday at the start of two days of voting to fill one-third of the seats in Parliament’s upper house, the Senate, and elect local representatives, AP reported.
The elections are the first test for populist billionaire Andrej Babiš since he returned to power after a decisive victory in parliamentary elections in October 2025.
His centrist ANO (YES) movement hopes to make gains in the 81-seat Senate, which is controlled by pro-western opposition parties. Twenty-seven Senate seats are up for grabs in the two-round election, with runoffs scheduled for next week. First-round results are expected on Saturday.
Babiš has formed a governing coalition with two small political groups whose agenda includes reducing support for Ukraine and rejecting some key European Union policies.
Unlike the government, the opposition and president Petr Pavel remain firm supporters of Ukraine following Russia’s invasion.
But Pavel – an avid biker – attracted a lot of attention in the build up to the vote as it emerged that he would miss the vote due to a long-planned motorcycle trip in Morocco. After days of relentless pressure, he eventually cut the holiday short and reported to vote, acknowledging his original “error” in scheduling.
He said on X:
“Some mistakes can be corrected relatively easily, others with more difficulty, and some cannot be corrected at all.
Fortunately, a mistake in planning can be remedied by changing the plan. Admitting a mistake is not easy, but if a politician values people’s trust, he must prove it.
I know what responsibility is and that any trust is hard to earn, but terribly easy and quick to lose. You pay for mistakes, and I have learned from this one of my own.”
EU grants temporary trade preferences to Armenia after Russian sanctions
Lisa O’Carroll
Senior correspondent
The European Union is granting temporary trade preferences to Armenia following trade restrictions recently imposed by Russia.
In a move which shows how flexible the EU can be, it said the temporary trade preferences “will help alleviate the difficult situation faced by Armenian producers and exporters and support the resilience of Armenia’s economy by facilitating access to the EU market.
The measures, which will enter into force tomorrow for a period of two years, temporarily allow 80% of Armenian exports to the EU, including almost all exports of fresh fruit, vegetables and flowers affected by the Russian measures, as well as over 91% of exports of beverages and spirits.
Armenia is not an accession state, but has been singled out for support as part of the EU a broader solidarity support package
Schröder's cosy encounter with Putin sparks outrage in Berlin
Kate Connolly
Berlin correspondent
The Kremlin’s release of photos showing a cosy fireside encounter between former German chancellor Gerhard Schröder and Russian president Vladimir Putin on the occasion of Putin’s 74th birthday, reportedly at his home in Moscow, has sparked outrage in political Berlin.
We understand that Schröder travelled to Moscow for his latest lucrative business role in Russia. In addition to his positions on the advisory boards of various gas companies – which he has retained, refusing to distance himself from Putin despite his punitive war on Ukraine – Schröder, 82, has now reportedly taken up a position as an advisory board member of the Russian retailer Globus, advising on strategy since September and drawing on his influence and extensive network of contacts.
The pictures, emphasing the political and personal alliance between the two men, jarred with many in Berlin.
Schröder had said in early 2025 that he was too ill to attend a parliamentary inquiry committee into the construction of the Nord Stream 2 gas pipeline between Russia and Germany, citing “burnout”. This is the latest of numerous controversial trips Schröder has taken to Russia, even following the 2022 full invasion of Ukraine.
Katrin Göring-Eckardt of the Greens said she was appalled that Schröder had been “too sick” to attend a commission into the Nord Stream 2 pipeline in person, but was able to fly to Moscow. She called the revelation a “shame for Germany” and a “betrayal of Europe”.
Marie-Agnes Strack-Zimmermann, who leads the European parliament’s Committee on Security and Defence called Schröder “Germany’s most brazen pensioner”.
According to the Kremlin, Putin only learned of Schröder’s presence in Moscow via media outlets, and invited him over to celebrate.
The two pictures posted by the Kremlin show the two pals in open-necked shirts and jackets – Putin unusually casual in blue jeans – warmly shaking hands in front of a blazing fire, a beaming Schröder placing his left hand on the small of Putin’s back. It’s the height of gemütlichkeit.
Mawkish fascination draws the eye to the Russian autocrat’s interior design of which we rarely get a glimpse: a traditional ceramic stove, miniature golden rocking horses dotted about the room, a gleaming samovar, soft furnishings in striking traditional patterns, colourful drapes, and intimate niches.
These details, along with Putin’s almost shy, sheepish grin in the picture, belie the terror he has come to represent. The image is a PR coup for both, helping Putin prove that Russia is certainly not fully isolated, and showing Schröder’s complete indifference to the fact that his proximity to Putin has shattered his domestic reputation.
(Schröder did eventually testify via video link to the Nord Stream committee in October 2025, where he staunchly defended the pipeline’s construction and the formation of the controversial Climate Protection Foundation but denied Russia had exerted undue pressure on either project or on him.)
US imposes sanctions on international criminal court, hours after former judge Pillay wins Nobel
US president Donald Trump’s administration imposed sanctions on the international criminal court on Friday, hours after one of its former judges won the Nobel Peace Prize, putting Washington on a diplomatic collision course with European allies, Reuters reported.
The ICC’s deputy prosecutor, Nazhat Shameem Khan, condemned the sanctions and said they would not halt the tribunal’s work.
The Trump administration has long been hostile to the court and has previously imposed sanctions on its prosecutors and judges. Friday’s move would go far further, by potentially punishing companies that provide services to the court itself.
“President Trump will never allow the international criminal court to prosecute Americans,” secretary of state Marco Rubio said in a statement reviewed by Reuters ahead of the official announcement.
“That is why, today, the United States is sanctioning the international criminal court. We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate.”
ICC Deputy Prosecutor Khan told Reuters the sanctions “must be condemned“.
“The sanctions are intended to undermine the rule of law internationally and the work that an independent judicial institution is doing,” Khan said. “Our work will continue across all our situations, our investigations and our prosecutions.“
Washington has long been angry over ICC arrest warrants issued for Israeli officials including prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and over a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan which the ICC has since closed.
The court, founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide, counts 125 countries as member states, including all EU countries and all members of the Nato alliance apart from the United States and Turkey.
It has received strong public backing in the past from member countries including major US allies, and is based in the Netherlands, an EU and Nato member.
Navi Pillay, the South African jurist who won the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday for her work in international criminal justice, served as a judge on the ICC’s Appeals Chamber from 2003-2008. In its citation, the prize committee said it had sought to “issue a reminder” at a time when “judges and institutions of international law are under political attack“.
Rubio said the sanctions had been structured to give the court and its member states an opportunity to address US concerns.
He did not provide further details, but a senior state department official said the US Treasury would issue a set of licenses “to protect American interests“, an apparent reference to temporary exemptions to some sanctions.
US sanctions typically bar all US-based companies from any work with a sanctioned organisation, forcing banks to shut accounts, insurers to end coverage and software companies to halt cooperation.
The Trump administration previously imposed targeted sanctions on court officials during his first term, which were rescinded under President Joe Biden. Washington announced new sanctions just days after Trump returned to office in January 2025.
Court officials have been preparing for months for the prospect of sanctions on the court itself, shifting office computers from Microsoft software to open source equivalents and making new arrangements for banking and health insurance.
The court’s registrar Osvaldo Zavala Giler called earlier this week for the EU to be prepared to use a so-called “blocking mechanism” that lets it shield European countries from the extraterritorial effects of sanctions.

He is making best efforts to end the Russia/Ukraine war, to stop Iran, the number one sponsor of international terrorism, and he is trying to rebuild Gaza despite the terrorists’ best efforts to control it. China reaches 'an understanding' with the EU to stop trade tensions
Lisa O’Carroll
China has reached an “understanding” with the EU, to avert deterioration in trade tensions after two days of talks in Beijing, according to a Chinese statement.
EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič is due to hold a press conference around 3pm CET, but China says the two sides have agreed a 16 point agreement allowing for a relaxation of restrictions on rare earth exports from China to the EU in return for concessions on electric vehicle exports.
China is “willing... to continue facilitating the approval of export licenses for rare earths and permanent magnets destined for the EU”, a statement from the Chinese ministry of commerce has said following two days of talks in Beijing.
While they acknowledged “differences” between them, the two sides were committed to maintaining trade and to hold a further meeting in March.
China said both sides would adhere to “procedures concerning company price undertakings” of hybrid cars, Beijing’s commerce ministry said, citing a joint statement, suggesting a deal to find minimum prices for hybrid cars exported to the EU.
The talks follow months of rising tensions between the 27-nation EU and the Asian powerhouse that threatened to escalate into a trade war.
Maroš Šefčovič said earlier in the day that the EU’s trade deficit with running at around £1bn a day (€1.18bn) every day was “unsustainable”.

Spanish right-wing parties keep solid lead ahead of November election, polls show
MADRID, Oct 9 - Spain's centre-right People's Party and far-right Vox were on track to win a combined parliamentary majority in a snap general election called by the ruling Socialists for November 29, according to two opinion polls published on Friday.
Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who has been in power since 2018, called the early election this week after parliament rejected his government's proposals to address a mounting housing crisis.
He is gambling that protests over home shortages and surging rents following the eviction of an 87-year-old woman could galvanize leftist voters. Political debate had earlier focused on a migrant crisis and investigations into alleged corruption in his party and alleged influence peddling by his wife and brother.
Sánchez, leading one of Europe's last remaining left-leaning governments, has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing by his party and defended his family's innocence.
A survey by El País newspaper, one of the first to be conducted after the election was called, showed the People's Party (PP) and anti-immigration party Vox combined would clinch 198 seats, above the 176-seat threshold needed to form a parliamentary majority. In the last election in 2023, both parties totalled 170 seats and now Vox would double its support.
The Socialists would fall to 112 seats from 121 three years ago and their options to govern would be severely impacted by the falling support for their far-left government coalition partner Sumar, the survey showed.
In terms of overall votes, the PP would win the election with 31.9% of support, ahead of the Socialists with 28.1%, according to the El País poll. Although both parties lose votes compared with 2023, the Socialists' fall is sharper.
"All the polls we are seeing reflect the same message: Spain wants a change, wants an alternative," PP's parliamentary spokesperson Ester Muñoz told Telecinco TV on Friday.
The PP and Vox currently govern in coalition in four regions in Spain.
Showing a similar outcome, a survey by El Confidencial website gives 200 parliamentary seats to the PP and Vox, which would usher a far-right party into central government for the first time since Spain's return to democracy following the 1975 death of authoritarian leader Francisco Franco. ICE shooting triggers clashes in New York (VIDEOS)

ICE shooting triggers clashes in New York (VIDEOS)
Anti-ICE demonstrators have clashed with police in New York City after federal agents shot and wounded a migrant from the Dominican Republic during his arrest.
Scuffles erupted in the Bronx late on Thursday outside a hospital where a man had been taken earlier in the day after suffering a gunshot wound to the neck.
Several hundred protesters gathered near the medical facility, chanting obscenities and slogans such as “From Palestine to Mexico, all these walls have got to go” and “We want ICE off our streets. No justice, no peace.”
At one point, the crowd attempted to dismantle the barricades set up by the police and engaged in a shoving match with officers. Several people were arrested, according to media reports.
The US Department of Homeland Security, which incorporates ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement), said in an earlier statement that the shooting happened on Marble Hill Avenue at around 4 PM local time on Thursday.
Federal agents opened fire when they tried to detain a “criminal illegal alien” who was in a car with a child in the back seat, the statement read. It didn’t explain what provoked the shooting.
The 28-year-old man had “a prior criminal conviction for grand larceny, and multiple prior arrests for assault, robbery, possession of drugs and weapons possession,” the DHS said.
The wounded migrant is expected to survive. The child, said to be his five-year-old son, was unharmed in the incident.
Democratic New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani used the shooting to launch another attack on ICE, saying in a post on X that he would call US President Donald Trump and demand an end to the agency’s activities in the city.
“I will not stand by while ICE agents terrorize our communities... Get ICE out of our neighborhoods. Get ICE out of our hospitals. Get ICE off our streets. Get ICE away from our children. Abolish ICE,” he wrote.
Mamdani later arrived at the scene and addressed the protesters, saying that “as somebody who is proud to be an immigrant in this city, I know that these kinds of raids, the kind of terrorizing… leaves the 3 million migrants of this city asking if they are safe here, if they belong here, if this too can be their home here.”
The shooting in New York comes less than a month after a similar incident in Austin, Texas, in which ICE agents wounded a Venezuelan national while he was delivering food in his car. The man was later charged with assaulting an officer.
The Democrats have repeatedly called for the abolition of ICE since a wave of nationwide protests over the fatal shootings of two US citizens by federal immigration agents in Minnesota in January.
White House border czar Tom Homan defended ICE and its conduct last month, saying: “You can hate us all you want. We’re not going anywhere.”

Türkiye’s industrial production falls 1.9% year-on-year in August

Mücahithan Avcıoğlu
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
Türkiye’s industrial production fell 1.9% year-on-year in August, with manufacturing output declining despite gains in mining and energy production, according to Turkish Statistical Institute data released Friday.
Manufacturing production decreased 2.5% compared with August 2025, while mining and quarrying output rose 1.7%.
Production in the electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply sector increased 1.3% over the same period.
On a monthly basis, overall industrial production declined 1% in August.
Manufacturing output fell 1.6% from July, while mining and quarrying production increased 4.1%.
The electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply sector posted a monthly increase of 3.3%.

Hungary's 2026 drought is the country's most severe in 126 years, data shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
07:33:15 UTC
16:33:15 KST

The central European nation has been facing a critical water shortage following a drought that began in the second half of 2025.
Hungary has experienced its most severe drought in 126 years in 2026, according to data from its national weather service, HungaroMet.
The Central European nation also recorded its driest summer since 1901 this year, as well as its second hottest.
Following a winter that saw lower rainfall than usual, Hungary was hit by a heatwave in June, followed by further hot spells in July and August. The unusually dry conditions also led to record low water levels on the Danube.
According to a HungaroMet analysis of the summer, average rainfall across the country amounted to just 74.1 millimetres, 36 per cent of the 1991 to 2020 mean.
The seasonal mean temperature was 23.43°C on average across the country, 2.59°C above the long-term norm of 20.84°C.
What's behind Hungary's drought?
HungaroMet said in its analysis that the 2026 drought was the result of prolonged weather patterns and disruptions to the water cycle.
Whilst January saw cold and wet weather, the following months were marked by a severe lack of rainfall and higher than normal temperatures. In April, for example, rainfall was just 10 per cent of the usual amount.
May saw some wetter periods, but the soil had still not recovered enough moisture by the end of spring, and the summer months then brought further spells of unusually dry weather.
By late June, almost the entire country was experiencing a soil moisture deficit of more than 100 millimetres in the top metre of soil. The lack of rainfall, combined with temperatures far above average, increased evaporation losses and caused soil moisture levels to fall sharply.
Between 1 April and 2 September, at least 30 per cent of Hungary's territory experienced moderate or more severe drought conditions for nearly 84 per cent of the period. By the end of August, agricultural drought had reached severe levels across half the country.
Groundwater shortages in Europe
A report by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said that water levels below the ground are continuing to fall, with Central and Eastern Europe among the regions most affected by groundwater shortages.
Soil moisture was already far below normal levels in 2025, and the situation deteriorated further in 2026.
In Hungary, an earlier estimate put the average groundwater level at 1.4 to 1.7 metres below what is considered ideal. Even if autumn brings wetter days, this alone will not be enough to solve the water shortage.
Experts have been warning for years that Hungary would only be able to tackle its water crisis by retaining water instead of allowing it to drain away quickly, whether it comes from rainfall or rivers.
However, achieving this would require changes in farming practices as well as major structural reforms and investment.

Tartu toy museum hosts 10th annual LEGO exhibition
A toy museum in Tartu is hosting its annual LEGO exhibition this weekend, and will be filled with a variety of brick-built displays.
This is the tenth time the event has been held, jointly by Estonian Lego enthusiasts' club EstLUG and the Tartu Toy Museum (Mänguasjamuuseum)
"Our first joint exhibition took place in 2016, when the museum hosted a large display called Legomaania," said Marge Pärnits, the museum's development manager. "By the following year the predecessor of today's exhibition had grown out of it — EstLUG enthusiasts built a city from bricks in the Teatri Kodu hall that made visitors gasp. Since then we have organized a joint event every autumn," she went on.
This year's LEGO world includes rotating carousels, rattling trains and city life, with superheroes joining as surprise guests. A Star Wars theme series will be on display, along with cartoon and film stars, collectible minifigures and themed minifigure collections.
Visitors are invited to the museum's playroom to help build a shared mosaic, and to the single-color building area to show off their own creations. In the Theatre House lobby, fans can buy LEGO bricks and minifigures.
The exhibition runs Saturday, October 10, at 11a.m.–6p.m. and on the Sunday, October 11, 11a.m.–3p.m., with a two-day café, brick sales, and a city built from LEGO including carousels and trains.
Entry is by a special ticket covering the full program at the Teatri Kodu, on Lutsu 2, home of the museum, on the day of purchase. This covers the toy museum's main building exhibitions and playroom building area. Museum cards are not valid for this event. The museum's social media page is here.

Ukrainian drones struck a chemical plant producing fuel for Russian cruise missiles, an oil depot near the border region of Belgorod and infrastructure in the Kaluga region southwest of Moscow overnight on Oct. 9, Russian officials and Ukrainian monitoring channels reported.
In the Tver region, which is situated between Moscow and St. Petersburg, drones hit the Redkino Experimental Plant and sparked a fire. The facility is the region’s largest chemical enterprise, according to Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+.

The facility manufactures Decylin-M, a specialized rocket fuel component used in Kh-55 and Kh-101 cruise missiles, as well as fuel additives for diesel and aviation kerosene, Kyiv Post sources within Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) said in February, after the first strike on the enterprise.

Architecture of Care: 6 Unbuilt Spaces for Childhood from the ArchDaily Community
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
07:30:00 UTC
16:30:00 KST

As cities change, so do our expectations of them. People are asking for more caring spaces: public places open to all ages and genders, nature within reach of every social class, and settings that foster connection. Few design intentions hold these together as well as spaces for children. This selection of unbuilt projects submitted by ArchDaily readers showcases different approaches to care-based architecture. Schools, daycare centers, a library, a youth center, and a new model for orphanages take on the mission of providing a safe and stimulating environment for children at every stage of their development. Not yet built but carefully designed, these proposals offer a glimpse into spaces for play, learning, and calm that fuel creativity in design for people of all ages.
When thinking about children's areas, colors, playful volumes, daylight, and open air come to mind. Some of that is reflected in this selection of conceptual projects, grounded in the local realities of Senegal, Brazil, Vietnam, India, Italy, and Ukraine. The six projects are built around learning, encounter, play, and safety, shaped into curved earthen or brick buildings, colorful playscapes, light-filled interiors, and, most of all, a permanent reference to plant life. Biophilic design, in different contexts, shapes and sizes, seems to be a cornerstone of the environment envisioned for future generations. Whether out of nostalgia, experience or a protective instinct, an enduring connection to nature, or an idea of it, emerges as a common thread in the design of these proposals. They are presented as lived spaces, and their differences reflect the stages of childhood through the integration of movement, atmosphere and the opportunities they offer for the collective care of multiple generations.

lsrael's genocide squeezes Gaza into smaller territory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
07:23:12 UTC
16:23:12 KST

Breadcrumb
lsrael's genocide is squeezing the Gaza Strip into smaller and smaller territory
The ongoing Israeli genocidal war on Gaza has not only transformed the physical landscape of cities and neighbourhoods but has also redefined the relationship between more than two million Palestinians and the land they inhabit.
Areas that once had homes, farms, roads, schools, and public buildings are now rubble, replaced or overlaid with earthen berms, military roads, troop movements, and Israeli observation posts.
Although the Strip's area stays around 365 sq km, the space available for residents, movement, and agriculture has shrunk dramatically.
Before the war, Gaza was a geographically small, densely populated, and relatively contiguous despite the Israeli blockade since 2007.
Now, its landscape is fragmented into destroyed neighborhoods, displacement zones, inaccessible farmland, and areas controlled or restricted by Israel.
The so-called "Yellow Line" is central to this transformation and is linked to the ceasefire in October 2025. For Palestinians, it’s more than a map mark; it's now a reality affecting where they live, move, farm, and rebuild.
A military line within Gaza
The "Yellow Line" marks Israeli military deployment inside Gaza, not an official border but a line separating Israeli-Restricted areas from Palestinian zones, and cuts into Gaza, leaving inhabited, cultivated, or work areas, along with zones under strict restrictions, instead of following the coastal enclave's actual perimeter.
Connected to military positions, berms, roads, buffer zones, and movement restrictions, it impacts Palestinian territory beyond the line.
A research paper released on 30 September 2026 by the Palestinian Centre for Policy Studies, titled "The Engineering of Spatial Control in the Gaza Strip: The Yellow Line Between Temporary Security Arrangement and Permanent Partition", found that the Israeli-controlled or restricted area increased from 53 per cent in October 2025 to 65-70 per cent by August 2026.
The paper pointed to military sites, land demolitions, and restrictions that block residents' access to land used for housing, agriculture, and jobs; the result: a Gaza that has not simply been physically destroyed but spatially reorganised.
Salwa Qudeih, a Khan Younis resident, has lost her house in the yellow area of the city's western part and now faces an uncertain return home.
"Before the war, the land, the houses and the roads were familiar to us. Today, the landscape has changed, and there are places nearby that we cannot reach. Even when we think about returning to our homes, we do not know if the area has ended up behind 'the line' or not," she told The New Arab.
"The problem is not just that our house was damaged; it is that we do not know if the land the house stands on will remain accessible to us at all," she said.
In northern Gaza, Mahmoud Abu Rayash, a resident of Beit Lahia, told TNA that the Yellow Line has become a physical danger rather than simply a mark on a map.
"For us, the Yellow Line is not merely something on a map. It is a place you cannot approach; land that used to be reachable in minutes has now become a danger zone," he said.
"Even if the war ends, how will we return to places we cannot access? And how can a house be rebuilt if the land itself lies within a restricted zone?" he asked.
Cities and neighbourhoods erased
Recently updated satellite imagery also starkly illustrates the scale of Gaza's physical transformation by Israel's genocide.
A United Nations assessment based on images captured in June 2026 found that around 200,000 buildings, or roughly 82 per cent of the Strip's structures, had sustained damage, with more than 134,000 classified as destroyed.
The impact goes beyond buildings lost, as home destruction erases streets, neighborhoods, landmarks, and turns urban and agricultural areas into barren land.
In northern Gaza, Beit Hanoun, Beit Lahia, and Jabalia have changed drastically, with densely populated areas turned to rubble and vacant land, and new military roads, earth berms, and structures emerging.
In Gaza City, neighborhoods like Shuja'iyya, Zeitoun, and Tuffah are heavily damaged. Mass displacement has turned open and agricultural areas into densely populated zones of tents and shelters.
In southern Gaza, Rafah exemplifies destruction, with large parts of the city, Rafah refugee camp, and Tal al-Sultan destroyed or demolished, erasing parts of the pre-war landscape.
Across central Gaza, farmland and open spaces have become displacement areas, and families have lost access to land that once provided homes, livelihoods, and food.
Gaza-based political analyst Mustafa Ibrahim argued that the significance of the Yellow Line cannot be separated from the changes taking place around it.
"The issue is not merely about the Yellow Line as a military demarcation; it is about the changes unfolding behind it, affecting the land, the population and freedom of movement," he told TNA.
"When an entire area is demolished, its residents barred from returning, and fortifications, roads and military outposts are established in their place, you are doing more than addressing security concerns - you are creating a new geographical reality," he said.
Ibrahim believed that controlling territory could be part of a post-war deal, limiting movement and reducing land for housing and agriculture.
"When land beyond the line becomes inaccessible, and reconstruction is tied to areas where access is permitted, geography begins to shape demography. You are effectively determining where people can and cannot live," he added.
The shrinking space in Gaza raises emigration questions, especially after hundreds of thousands lost their homes and livelihoods.
But Ibrahim cautioned against directly equating every geographical change with an intention to displace Palestinians.
"When living space constricts [with the destruction of homes, agricultural land and infrastructure, and with reconstruction tied to specific zones] some residents may indeed consider emigration," he said. "Yet, one cannot claim that the direct aim of every geographical change is the displacement of the population."
From the Nakba onwards
Gaza's shrinking usable space did not begin with the current war.
Before the 1948 Nakba, the Gaza District was larger, including many Palestinian villages and towns that Zionist armed groups occupied and absorbed into their newly enforced state. Hundreds of thousands of Palestinians were displaced into the future Gaza Strip, making it a densely populated refugee refuge.
Under the 1949 Egyptian-Israeli Armistice Agreement, signed in Rhodes, the Gaza Strip's boundaries were set at about 365 sq km under Egyptian control until Israel occupied Gaza in 1967.
Israel also briefly occupied the Strip during the 1956 war before withdrawing in 1957.
"History is crucial to understanding current events because Gaza has seen, time and again, how military arrangements can harden into realities that alter the landscape and the movement of the population," Ibrahim said.
But he argued that the current transformation is different in scale.
"We are not merely discussing a military line; we are talking about destroyed cities, neighbourhoods razed to the ground, agricultural lands rendered inaccessible to their owners, and a population redistributed within a confined space," he added.
The question now is whether the so-called "Yellow Line" will remain a temporary ceasefire arrangement or become a lasting geographical reality.
"The problem lies not merely in declaring the line a new boundary [a move requiring political arrangements and formal recognition] but in the creation of a facts-on-the-ground reality that compels any government or entity responsible for Gaza's reconstruction to contend with a fundamentally altered geography," Ibrahim added.
"If large areas stay sealed, military posts remain, and people are resettled only in certain zones, the Strip could effectively be partitioned without a formal division," he concluded.

Moscow is seeking the extradition of the ICC president who issued an arrest warrant for Putin
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:19:32 EEST
16:19:32 KST

Moscow is seeking the extradition of the ICC president who issued an arrest warrant for Putin
Kyiv • UNN
Russia has asked the Netherlands to detain and extradite ICC President Tomoko Akane and eight court representatives. Japan called the demand unacceptable.
Russia’s Prosecutor General’s Office has asked the Netherlands to detain and extradite International Criminal Court (ICC) President Tomoko Akane, as well as eight other representatives of the institution. UNN reports this, citing Reuters, Bloomberg and the Japanese news agency Jiji Press.
Japan has already criticized Moscow’s actions, calling them unacceptable, and said that further diplomatic measures may be taken.
Details
On Friday, October 9, Japanese Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki said during a press conference that Tokyo regretted Russia’s demand for the extradition of International Criminal Court President Tomoko Akane, who is a Japanese citizen. According to the official, the Japanese authorities have repeatedly contacted the Russian side, emphasizing that the prosecution of ICC representatives is unfounded and unacceptable.
The fact that the Russian side has approached several countries with extradition requests is regrettable
He emphasized that Japan consistently supports the work of the International Criminal Court as a permanent international judicial institution tasked with ensuring accountability for the gravest crimes and upholding the rule of law. In this regard, the Japanese government intends to continue consultations with the ICC leadership and other states parties to the Rome Statute. Tokyo also does not rule out making new diplomatic representations to Moscow over the prosecution of court officials.
Whom Russia is demanding be extradited
On October 8, Russia’s Prosecutor General’s Office said it had sent requests to the Ministry of Justice and Security of the Netherlands, as well as to the competent authorities of a number of other countries, for the detention and extradition of nine representatives of the International Criminal Court. They include current ICC President Tomoko Akane, former Prosecutor Karim Khan and former President of the Court Piotr Hofmański.
The list also includes ICC First Vice-President Rosario Salvatore Aitala, Second Vice-President René Alapini-Gansou, judges Luz del Carmen Ibáñez Carranza, Sergio Gerardo Ugalde Godínez and Haikel Ben Mahfoud, as well as former judge Bertram Schmitt.
By the way, the Russian prosecutor’s office’s statement incorrectly lists some of the ICC representatives’ positions. In particular, Hofmański was described as the current president of the Court, although Tomoko Akane has held that position since March 2024.
The Russian agency currently claims that the officials in question were allegedly involved in the unlawful criminal prosecution of Russian citizens and in decisions to arrest them without sufficient legal grounds.
In December 2025, the Moscow City Court found nine ICC representatives guilty in absentia under several articles of Russian criminal law. They were sentenced to various terms of imprisonment, ranging from three years and six months to 15 years. The charges included unlawful prosecution, unlawful detention and encroachment on persons enjoying international protection.
At the same time, there is currently no information that the Netherlands has agreed to grant Russia’s request.
Why Russia is prosecuting ICC representatives
The confrontation between Moscow and the International Criminal Court intensified after the ICC issued arrest warrants on March 17, 2023, for Russian President Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova, the Commissioner for Children’s Rights. The warrants were based on suspicions of war crimes related to the unlawful deportation and forcible transfer of Ukrainian children from temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine to Russia. The Court said it had sufficient evidence for Putin and Lvova-Belova to bear individual criminal responsibility for these actions.
After that, the Russian authorities began criminally prosecuting ICC representatives and later placed a number of judges and prosecutors on a wanted list.
In June 2024, the International Criminal Court also issued arrest warrants for Russia's former defense minister, Sergei Shoigu, and the chief of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces, Valery Gerasimov. They are suspected of war crimes and crimes against humanity linked to strikes on Ukraine's energy infrastructure.
Moreover, Russia does not recognize the ICC's jurisdiction, citing the fact that it is not a party to the Rome Statute. At the same time, the international court has the authority to consider crimes committed on the territory of Ukraine.
Can the Netherlands extradite the ICC president?
The International Criminal Court is located in The Hague, and the Netherlands is a state party to the Rome Statute. Under Article 48 of this document, ICC judges and prosecutors enjoy international privileges and immunities while performing their official duties. Such guarantees are provided to ensure the institution's independent operation.
Context
Tomoko Akane has headed the International Criminal Court since March 2024. She was elected president of the institution for a three-year term.
In August 2026, the United States also imposed sanctions on Akane. The US administration explained the restrictions by citing its disagreement with the ICC's activities concerning nationals of states that do not recognize its jurisdiction. The International Criminal Court criticized the sanctions, saying that they undermine the independence of international justice. Japan, for its part, expressed regret over the US restrictions and reaffirmed its support for the court.
Let us remind you
In August 2026, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi stated that Tokyo would continue to support the International Criminal Court amid pressure from the United States.

16:18:34 KST

Explainer: Watches win, pharma waits as Swiss-India trade deal turns one
In October 2025, Switzerland, as a member state of EFTA, entered into what was billed as a historic free trade deal with India. One year on, Swiss pharma still wants more intellectual property protection.
The promise of zero tariffs on Swiss watches in India within the next five years fuelled high spirits at a mid-September gathering of Indian and Swiss entrepreneurs hosted by the Geneva Chamber of Commerce (CCIG). In 2025, Switzerland exported CHF295 million ($354 million) worth of watches to India, a figure up 35% since 2023. Switzerland paid 22% import duties on these last yearExternal link.
The event co-organised with the Swiss-Indian chamber of commerce (SICC) came ahead of the one-year anniversary of the trade deal between India and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA). Switzerland is India’s most important trading partner among the group that also includes Liechtenstein, Iceland and Norway.
“This is the most significant trade agreement worldwide”, said Vincent Subilia, the director of the CCIG.
TEPA came into force on October 1, 2025, after 16 years and 21 rounds of negotiations. Finalising the text was particularly arduous mainly due to disagreements between Switzerland and India over intellectual property rights. While Switzerland’s pharma industry is known for its innovative medicines, protected by strict intellectual property rights, India’s drug industry thrives on generic drugs that are marketed once those patents expire.
One of the biggest achievements for EFTA members was signing a deal with India before any other individual member states of the European Union, or the EU itself, and gaining preferential access to 1.46 billion inhabitants. The agreement covers key industries, such as machinery, watches and vaccine production, but leaves questions around pharmaceuticals unresolved.
In early October, on a trip to the Indian capital New Delhi to meet President Droupadi Murmu and Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Guy Parmelin, who holds the rotating Swiss presidency this year, commenting on the deal declared “everything isn’t perfect”. The visit included negotiations on migration and professional youth exchanges. A bilateral agreement to protect Swiss company dividends and further discussions on intellectual property were also on the agenda. Swiss pharma giants Roche and Novartis took part in the trip.
What’s in the free trade agreement?
According to the agreement, 94.7% of Swiss exports will benefit from a reduction in tariffs, with industries either immediately becoming duty free, or gradually over the next five, seven or ten years. Gold and precious metals, dairy products, finished generics and cars coming into India from Switzerland are excluded from the agreement and will continue to be taxed.
Exports of machinery to manufacture semiconductors, high-purity chemical intermediates that are used in pharmaceutical production, vaccines, and aircraft components have all become duty free since the entry into force of the agreement.
For industries including Swiss watches, chocolate, auto components, and dental equipment, tariffs have already been reduced twice: once on October 1, 2025, and once at the start of 2026. These tariffs will continue to be lowered gradually (depending on the category), until they reach zero.
How have Swiss companies benefitted so far?
Swiss goods with an immediate reduction of customs duties have had a head start compared to European Union competitors, because to date the bloc has no trade deal with India. But EU negotiations were finalised this year and an agreement may come into force in 2027. This will narrow the gap between European companies and Swiss ones.
According to Philippe Reich, chairman of the SICC and an India specialist at Baker McKenzie, Switzerland’s multinational corporations have already expanded but small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) will also benefit in the long run.
Swiss-Swedish automation company ABB announced a $75 million (CHF62.3 million) investment to expand its manufacturing and R&D capacity in 2026, and Swiss engineering firm Sulzer opened a new hub in the Indian city of Pune a month after TEPA’s launch. These investments form part of a financial commitment that is spelled out in the agreement. EFTA signatories have committed to promoting their private enterprises and institutional funds to invest $100 billion in India over the next 15 years. According to the SICC, investments announced since TEPA have reached $29 billion in Switzerland alone.
Global geopolitical shifts, including tensions between the United States and China, have been decisive for SMEs that rely on foreign supply chains. Many have shifted investments from China to India to diversify risks.
“These companies may not necessarily leave China, but they are shifting their investments from China to India. India has become more important,” said Reich.
Switzerland Global Enterprise (S-GE), the country’s official organisation for export and investment promotion, has said it has seen signs of increased interest from Swiss companies in the Indian market but definitive conclusions will come once they finalise their analysis of Switzerland’s economic footprint in India.
Beyond larger and more experienced consultancies, the agreement has also led to the flourishing of smaller offices. In May 2026, entrepreneur Ruby Greber set up India Swiss Enterprise in Geneva, to cater to companies looking into expanding in India.
“We help Swiss companies to establish their business in India and vice versa,” Greber explained. The consultancy is still in discussion with potential clients.
What about Swiss pharma?
While part of the pharma industry was covered by the initial deal, others such as generics were excluded. Intellectual property rights remain a key touchpoint.
According to S-GE, no new pharmaceutical companies have moved to India following the agreement. Following the agreement, Roche announced it would invest about CHF1.7 billion in India. This amount will support its existing operations and the expansion of its hub in Hyderabad, in the state of Telangana in southern India, by 2030. But the company says it hasn’t yet observed tangible benefits for its imported drugs.
More
Patent battle in India tests Roche’s grip on rare disease market
Most of the company’s drugs, which range from oncology to antivirals, are imported into India as finished products and currently taxed at around 10%. Some drugs targeting rare diseases and cancer treatments have already become tax-free, but tariffs on most finished drugs will drop by 1% every year over a decade. Generics, insulin and antibiotics are excluded from the free-trade agreement and will continue to be taxed. The agreement will take longer to impact the price of these drugs.
Reich comments the real issue at stake for pharmaceutical companies isn’t so much tariffs but enhanced intellectual property rights protection, which is essential for greater pharma innovator investments in India.
India refused to grant pharmaceutical firms data exclusivity, meaning generic drugs are automatically approved based on the clinical trial data of the original drugs. The country also rejected broader intellectual property rights through which companies can extend patents beyond 20 years and conserve market exclusivity.
More
Why drugs are becoming more expensive to develop
Previously stalled bilateral talks on intellectual property rights between Switzerland and India picked up again in 2025, following the conclusion of the trade agreement. These talks continued during Parmelin’s visit and focused on patents and data protection during clinical trials. A spokesperson for Parmelin confirmed the exchanges were constructive and were due to continue.
“I’m absolutely convinced we will see pharmaceutical R&D in India but this is a work in progress. Companies will first need to feel comfortable about the regulatory environment from an intellectual property perspective to really go in a big way for it. But I think that’s a matter of time,” Reich said. He estimated a five-year timeline for pharmaceutical companies to seriously consider India as a research and production base.

Only one-third of Israelis want Netanyahu to remain in power, Hebrew University study reveals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
07:16:12 UTC
16:16:12 KST

Only about one-third of Israelis want Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to remain in office after the upcoming October 27 Knesset elections, according to a Hebrew University survey published on Wednesday.
Among the roughly two-thirds of interviewees who said they wanted an alternative candidate, about half pointed to Yashar party chairman Gadi Eisenkot as their choice for the next prime minister, and the remainder were divided between former prime minister Naftali Bennett (B'Yachad party) and MK Avigdor Liberman (Yisrael Beytenu).
Worry and uncertainty about the future of the State of Israel
The findings, according to researchers, point to a significant crisis of confidence in the state's future. When asked about their general feelings toward Israel's future, 36% of respondents reported feeling pessimistic, compared with 33% who reported feeling optimistic. Researchers noted that this represented a decline in both optimism and pessimism compared to previous years, indicating greater overall uncertainty.
Under 25% of Israelis believe that their children will live in a better reality than they do now, and less than half of those surveyed reported believing that Israel is safer today than it was before October 7, 2023. What is more, nearly one-third of respondents believe the country is less safe than it was before the war.
About 20% of interviewees said they were considering leaving Israel due to the current security situation and ongoing social issues.
Did Netanyahu achieve 'total victory'?
Asked about Netanyahu's stated objectives for the Israel-Hamas War, less than 20% reported believing that "total victory" was achieved. Approximately half of Israelis said that the government held the greatest responsibility for the security failures that enabled the October 7 massacre and subsequent war; about one-third laid the blame on the security establishment.
More than half of Israelis, both Jewish and Arab, reported believing that the war has increased divisions within Israeli society -- an increase from previous years -- while only about one-quarter believe the opposite, that the war has strengthened national unity.
The study was conducted by Dr. Nimrod Nir of the Agam Institute and Dr. Gayil Talshir of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem on October 5–6, 2026. The sample included 2,437 respondents, all Israeli citizens.
The sample is representative of Israel’s adult population, age 17 and above, in terms of gender, age, religion, region of residence, voting in the 25th Knesset elections, level of religiosity, and ethnic background among Jewish citizens, who constitute 83% of the sample, as well as religious affiliation among Arab citizens, who constitute 17% of the weighted sample.
Data were collected online using the Polyeda platform. The Jewish sample was recruited through iPanel, while the Arab sample was collected through telephone sampling.
The sampling error is ±3.2% at a 99% confidence level.

Israelis unable to compete in FIDE amateur chess tournament taking place in Malaysia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
07:16:07 UTC
16:16:07 KST

The World Amateur Chess Championship, organized by the International Chess Federation (FIDE), is scheduled to take place from November 4 to 13 in Klang, in Malaysia's Selangor state, a country that prohibits Israeli citizens from entering its territory.
FIDE's official announcement states that "all FIDE member federations and all eligible players are invited to participate." However, Malaysia's entry restrictions effectively prevent Israelis from competing in the tournament.
Lior Eisenberg, who has campaigned against boycotts of Israel in sports and culture in recent years, told Walla: "I contacted the tournament organizer with an innocent question about participating, and immediately received a message saying he was sorry, but Israelis would not be able to play because of Malaysia's immigration policy. Right afterward, he deleted the message and added another saying they would get back to me. A place that does not accept Israelis or players from any other country should not be allowed to host a world championship."
The situation in Malaysia is not the only case raising questions about Israeli participation in international chess competitions.
In the Netherlands, controversy recently erupted over Israeli grandmaster Alexander (Aharon) Bagrationi, who was born in Ukraine, represents Israel, and lives in Germany. Bagrationi has previously played for several clubs, including Elitzur Elkana and Elitzur Samaria.
Organizers of the Amsterdam Chess Open contacted the Dutch organization The Rights Forum following allegations concerning Bagrationi's ties to clubs in Judea and Samaria. The organization recommended that he not be allowed to participate in the tournament.
Following the controversy, tournament organizers announced that, beginning in January 2027 and subject to legal review, they intend to bar players representing clubs located in territories that an international court has determined to be under illegal occupation.
Bagrationi rejected attempts to attach political significance to his membership in the clubs, saying they are recognized by both the Israeli chess system and FIDE. He argued that any objections to their recognition should be directed at the international federation.
He will ultimately not participate in this year's tournament but clarified that his decision was due to family commitments rather than the controversy.
The position communicated to Eisenberg by the tournament organizer is consistent with Malaysia's declared policy.
In July, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim reiterated that his country would continue to prohibit Israeli citizens from entering. Malaysia's Interior Ministry subsequently clarified that travel documents issued by Israel are not recognized for entry into the country. Anwar also said that any Israelis found in Malaysia would be deported.
FIDE regulations prohibit event held where Israelis cannot play
The policy also raises questions about FIDE's own regulations.
In 2019, the international federation publicly committed not to hold events in countries that refuse to issue visas or allow entry to all eligible players, regardless of nationality or citizenship. FIDE emphasized at the time that its events could only be held in locations where access was guaranteed to representatives of all member federations.
Israel is generally not considered one of the dominant nations in chess, unlike countries such as India, the United States, China, and Uzbekistan. Nevertheless, it has a significant chess tradition, with numerous grandmasters and players who regularly compete in Chess Olympiads, European championships, and international tournaments.
The central question, however, is not whether an Israeli player is likely to win the amateur championship in Malaysia, but whether an official world championship can effectively be closed to citizens of one of FIDE's member federations.
Eisenberg is now calling for pressure on FIDE to relocate the championship to another country.
"The biggest problem with boycotts and attempts to delegitimize Israel through sports is our complacency," he said.
"It doesn't matter whether a championship is held thousands of kilometers away and no Israelis are expected to attend, or whether it takes place close to home. The same rules should apply. These countries should no longer be allowed to host competitions without guaranteeing that Israelis can participate."
Eisenberg pointed to the 2019 dispute surrounding the World Para Swimming Championships, which had been scheduled to take place in Malaysia.
The International Paralympic Committee stripped Malaysia of its hosting rights after failing to receive guarantees that Israeli swimmers would be allowed to enter the country and compete. The championship was eventually moved to London.
Eisenberg was among those involved in the campaign at the time, and a petition on the issue gathered thousands of signatures.
"What applied in 2019 must also apply today, after the war," he said.
Pakistan refuses to play against Israel in Chess Olympiad
The controversies follow a series of unusual incidents in international chess.
Last month, Pakistan's national team refused to play against Israel at the Chess Olympiad in Samarkand. The president of the Pakistan Chess Federation said the decision was made in accordance with his country's policy and as an expression of solidarity with the Palestinians. Israel was awarded a win by default.
FIDE itself has previously taken a clear position against boycotts of Israeli players.
In September 2025, following an attempt at a tournament in Spain to prevent Israelis from competing under the Israeli flag, the federation announced that it "strongly condemns all forms of discrimination, including on the basis of nationality and flag."
FIDE also emphasized that the same rules apply to Israel as to all other member federations that are not subject to sanctions.
FIDE will now be called upon to explain how that position is consistent with its decision to hold an official world championship in a country that openly declares that Israeli citizens are not permitted to enter.

France will begin training Ukrainian pilots on Rafale jets in November - minister
Kyiv • UNN
France will launch the first training courses for Ukrainian pilots on Rafale fighter jets in November. This was announced by Minister Catherine Vautrin.
France will begin training Ukrainian pilots on Rafale fighter jets next month. The country’s Minister of the Armed Forces, Catherine Vautrin, said this at a parliamentary hearing on Thursday, October 8, UNN reports.
Starting in November, we will begin the first training courses for Ukrainian pilots on Rafale jets, and we clearly see real potential for cooperation and providing solutions
Addendum
Earlier, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported that Ukrainian pilots would soon begin training on Rafale aircraft in France.
Last November, at the French Air Force Base in the French city of Vélizy-Villacoublay, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy and President of France Emmanuel Macron signed a declaration of intent on cooperation in Ukraine’s acquisition of defense equipment.
This document will enable Ukraine to purchase military equipment from France’s defense industrial and technological base to modernize the Ukrainian Armed Forces.
First and foremost, this concerns 100 Rafale F4 aircraft by 2035 for Ukraine’s combat aviation, SAMP/T air defense systems, radars for air defense systems, air-to-air missiles, and aerial bombs. The possibility of transferring technology and jointly producing aircraft, with localization in Ukraine, is also envisaged.

Maastricht area plans 30 care zones to tackle loneliness
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
07:15:15 UTC
16:15:15 KST

Maastricht area plans 30 care zones to tackle loneliness
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
A new plan by care agencies and insurance companies aims to create 30 residential care zones in the Maastricht-Heuvelland area of Limburg, combining health services, activities and accessible living.
The plan, known as the Deltaplan Maastricht Heuvelland, aims to help older people live independently for longer and receive support and care closer to home, largely to tackle loneliness.
The initiative is a collaboration between municipalities, health insurers, residents, hospitals and elderly care advocacy agencies. Health insurers CZ and VGZ have provided €33.4 million for the project.
Nineteen of the 30 zones are currently under development, and organisers say the rest will be up and running next year.
“We have traditionally been accustomed to looking to nursing homes, but in this way, older people can continue living at home much longer, provided it is responsible,” Petra Lamberts, chair of Deltaplan, told regional news outlet L1.
The zones will also organise more activities, for example in a shared communal living room, to tackle loneliness. “Loneliness is a predictor of the need for care,” Lamberts told broadcaster NOS. “People notice minor ailments sooner when they are alone. When they take part in activities, they are distracted, and they are also encouraged to use their skills.”
Informal carers, such as family members, will also be able to hand over some of their tasks from time to time so they do not become overburdened.
A communal living room recently opened in Valkenburg, where local residents can take part in activities and meet for coffee.
The population of the region is ageing faster than the rest of the country. By 2030, one in four residents of South Limburg will be over 65.
According to Lamberts, a year of home care costs around €12,000, while a year in a nursing home costs more than €100,000.

US, Ukraine Set For Talks In Miami Amid Onslaught Of Russian Air Strikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
07:14:17 UTC
16:14:17 KST

WASHINGTON -- The United States and Ukraine will hold talks in Miami on October 9 to discuss proposals aimed at ending the Ukraine war, amid relentless Russian strikes on vital pieces of infrastructure in Kyiv and other cities ahead of winter.
The White House confirmed that envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner would meet with Ukrainian representatives on October 9 to discuss a new joint proposal covering all aspects of the conflict and aimed at ending the war, now in its fifth year.
A senior US administration official told RFE/RL that the meeting would provide an opportunity to identify areas where the conflicting sides could cooperate, even where their positions remain different.
Previous engagements had produced practical results, including prisoner exchanges, the official said.
After the initial meeting, a broader session involving European allies, NATO, and the EU will take place.
Rubio Warning
The talks follow US Secretary of State Marco Rubio's warning that the conflict has reached a dangerous stalemate, with the risk of escalation beyond Ukraine's borders.
Rubio called the conflict "a very dangerous war" and warned that escalation could include Russian sabotage in neighboring NATO countries, a strike, or other actions that could rapidly widen the conflict.
That could "quickly turn what is a war between two countries to a much broader, far more dangerous regional conflict," he said.
"In the end, we do not believe that there will be military solutions.... We think this war needs to end, and the negotiated settlement is sooner and better."
US President Donald Trump said this week that he planned to speak with Russian President Vladimir Putin by telephone soon.
Sources familiar with the plans said the Miami meeting would focus on proposals that US negotiators had begun developing with Russian and Ukrainian interlocutors during recent visits to the region.
The October 9 talks follow several rounds of negotiations held in Florida late last year, including discussions between US officials and Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev in October 2025 and subsequent meetings with Ukrainian officials in November and December that year.
Witkoff and Kushner also visited Moscow and Kyiv in early September as Washington renewed efforts to broker an end to the war. They met with Putin in Moscow before holding talks with Zelenskyy and Ukrainian officials in Kyiv.
Ukraine is expected to be represented by Kyrylo Budanov, head of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's office; Rustem Umerov, head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service and a former defense minister; David Arakhamia, parliamentary leader of Zelenskyy's Servant of the People party; and Serhiy Kyslytsya, first deputy head of the presidential office.
Broader Meeting With NATO, EU
A broader meeting involving national-security advisers from the United Kingdom, France, and Germany, as well as representatives of NATO, the EU, and US European Command, is scheduled for 11:30 a.m. local time. Talks are expected to resume later at 1:45 p.m.
Representatives of the White House National Security Council and the US Treasury Department are also expected to participate.
The agenda also includes a postwar prosperity and reconstruction plan for Ukraine and other aspects of a potential settlement, sources said.
Zelenskyy said on October 8 that Kyiv's negotiators had been briefed on the issues to raise with the American delegation, including strengthening Ukraine's air defenses.
"Yes, our negotiators have also been briefed on this for their talks with the American side. They know what to discuss and which pressing issues to raise with the American side," Zelenskyy told reporters via WhatsApp.
He added that Ukraine would separately discuss funding and air defense with European partners, including ways to secure financial support more quickly.
"Funding issues will be raised there as well -- the details of how to secure the funding sooner. This is very important. And air defense as well," he said.
Zelenskyy said he had also discussed the issues with European Council President Antonio Costa and expressed hope for a positive outcome.
John Herbst, who served as US ambassador to Ukraine under President George W. Bush and is now a senior director at the Atlantic Council's Eurasia Center, told RFE/RL on October 8 that he expected there would be "a good-faith effort by the sides involved," adding he did not expect a major confrontation between Washington and Kyiv over the terms of a settlement.
Herbst said any serious disagreement between Washington and Kyiv would likely increase Europe's role in the negotiations, as European governments would be reluctant to see the United States put undue pressure on Ukraine to make concessions.
Herbst also said the Trump administration wanted to end the conflict and appeared to believe neither side was likely to achieve a decisive military victory.
He also cited remarks by Vice President JD Vance suggesting that Ukraine currently has a military advantage.
Attacks On Ukrainian Infrastructure
In recent weeks, Russia has stepped up its attacks on Ukraine's civilian infrastructure.
Schemes, the investigative unit of RFE/RL's Ukrainian Service, obtained a copy of a Russian-language document from sources in Ukraine's defense forces outlining a potential blueprint for a campaign by Moscow to inflict enormous suffering on civilians with attacks aimed at sharply cutting supplies of power, heat, and water.
Despite Russia's recent missile and drone attacks, Herbst argued, those strikes were not bringing Moscow closer to winning the war, while Ukrainian operations were making it harder for Russian forces to achieve their objectives.
Washington has maintained separate contacts with Russian officials. Russian presidential envoy Dmitriev recently visited Washington for discussions with American officials as diplomatic efforts to end the war continued.
