From Aden to Sanaa, Yemenis struggle to deal with soaring living costs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
05:53:04 UTC
14:53:04 KST

From Aden to Sanaa, Yemenis struggle to deal with soaring living costs
As fighting intensifies, Yemenis face a deepening economic crisis, with unpaid salaries and rising prices.
Sanaa, Aden and Marib, Yemen – As fighting intensifies across Yemen between the government and the Houthis, millions of people are confronting another battle far from the front lines: the deteriorating living and economic conditions in the country.
With salaries for large segments of the workforce either unpaid or irregularly disbursed – and the prices of goods and services rising – Yemen’s economic struggles have been compounded by a divided banking system that has made moving money between different parts of the country increasingly complicated.
From Aden’s struggling shoppers to displaced families in Marib and unpaid public-sector workers in Sanaa, Yemenis are being forced to make difficult choices about what they can afford, and what they must go without.
Aden: Food costs swallow salaries
In Aden, the internationally recognised Yemeni government’s interim capital in the south, the problem is not so much a shortage of goods in markets as people’s inability to afford them.
Salaries have failed to keep pace with the rising costs of food, rent, healthcare and transport, leaving workers with little money left over at the end of the month.
The consequences are evident in the smaller quantities and cheaper products that now make up shoppers’ baskets, and the decisions they are forced to make about what to cut back on.
Bushra Abdullah Abdulwarith is a government employee in Aden. She earns 78,000 Yemeni riyals ($50) a month at the black market exchange rate while typical household food costs in government-held areas run about 130,366 riyals ($83), according to estimates by the Yemen Economic Tracking Initiative. And that’s before she factors in the cost of rent, transport, healthcare and other household expenses.
The economic difficulties facing Yemenis like Bushra illustrate how more than a decade of war has devastated the economy. According to the World Bank, real GDP per capita has fallen by approximately 58 percent since 2015.
The fragmentation of Yemen’s monetary institutions between the government and the Houthis – who have operated their own institutions since seizing the capital, Sanaa, in 2014 – along with the disruption of oil exports, and declining international assistance have all contributed to the economic decline.
Bushra told Al Jazeera that rising prices have forced many households to give up almost all non-essential purchases and cut back on some expensive basics, particularly meat. Other families, she said, have resorted to buying food in smaller quantities, sometimes on credit or loans.
Reduced demand
The impact of rising prices is reflected not only in economic figures but also in the way people shop.
Ayman al-Maqtari, who works at a shopping centre in Aden’s Mansoura district, said that his customers now rarely buy non-essential items.
When it comes to the essentials such as rice, sugar, flour, and cooking oil, he has noticed that customers size up the price of each item before putting it in their baskets. They are also buying smaller quantities, for example, opting for a 5kg (11 pound) over a 40kg (90 pound) bag of rice.
“Many people have come to live day by day, or week by week,” Ayman told Al Jazeera, adding that more families are buying on credit when they run out of money before the end of the month.
The decline in purchasing power is also affecting commercial activity.
Across several streets and shopping centres in Aden, advertisements for discounts and special offers have become increasingly visible in shop windows and on retailers’ social media pages, as businesses attempt to attract customers and boost sales.
Weak demand, retailers say, is particularly evident for items that households can put off buying, such as clothing and household goods. A growing share of family income is spent on food, rent, healthcare and transport.
Limited pay increase
The Yemeni government approved a 20 percent cost-of-living allowance in May for public-sector employees in an attempt to ease the pressure of rising prices. But the amount is calculated based on each employee’s base salary, rather than their total pay, meaning the actual increase is relatively small for many workers.
Bushra, the government employee in Aden, said the increase has done little to improve her family’s financial circumstances. She described the allowance as “a temporary painkiller that does not reflect the scale of the actual pressure on people’s living standards”.
Her experience is far from isolated. In early October, the World Food Programme said its latest monitoring in accessible government-controlled areas showed that 74 percent of households were unable to meet their basic food needs.
One of the places where the crisis is evident is Marib, a government-controlled city east of Sanaa that is home to hundreds of thousands of displaced people. The sharp increase in the population over the war years, in what was previously a provincial backwater, has led to pressure on the city’s housing, employment and public services.
Government employees in Marib see their salaries disappear within the first few days after being paid, labourers struggle to find more than a few days of work and displaced families are forced to choose between buying water and milk.
Salah al-Zuhaifi works for a government institution in Marib. He said the war has separated him from his parents, who live in Houthi-controlled territory.
Alone in Marib, al-Zuhaifi said that inflation had eroded much of his salary’s purchasing power.
“No matter how much you earn, it will not be enough to meet your needs,” he said.
Abu Mohammed Nasser al-Asbahi, another government employee, described a similar struggle.
He told Al Jazeera that he earns 400,000 riyals ($250) a month, but more than half of that goes towards his rent, leaving little for his other expenses.
“We don’t even get to the first one-third of the month before the salary is gone,” he said, explaining that his family spends the rest of the month relying on loans and credit from local shops.
The healthcare sector in Marib has also been affected by widespread household spending cuts.
Pharmacist Khaled Mohsen told Al Jazeera that the rising price of medicines has prompted many patients to decline parts of their prescribed treatment and purchase only what they consider most essential.
People with chronic illnesses, meanwhile, have increasingly begun reducing their medication doses to make their supplies last longer before having to buy more, which creates serious health risks.
Houthi areas
Residents of Sanaa and other areas of Yemen’s populous northwest, controlled by the Houthis – an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God) – since 2014, are also facing a worsening economic and cost-of-living crisis similar to that affecting Yemenis elsewhere in the country.
Several factors are driving the crisis, particularly unpaid public-sector salaries, declining purchasing power, rising prices for goods and services, and the continuing consequences of the division of Yemen’s currency and banking systems in the early years of the war.
Many public-sector employees in Houthi-controlled areas have gone years without receiving regular salaries, with some sectors only receiving limited payments or half-salaries at irregular intervals.
Even when payments are made, they cannot cover families’ basic needs amid the rising cost of living.
Meanwhile, private-sector workers and business owners face growing pressures as a result of declining economic activity, multiple fees and levies, and a shortage of employment opportunities. The conditions have undermined incomes and job security.
The Yemeni riyal’s exchange rate in Houthi-controlled Sanaa is more stable than in areas controlled by the government. The Houthis have imposed strict monetary controls, banning the circulation of newer banknotes printed by the Yemeni government, and have also enforced a largely fixed exchange rate.
However, that does not necessarily translate into stronger purchasing power. Markets face difficulties caused by cash shortages and the division between monetary and banking systems operating in different parts of the country, including increased costs for moving funds.
That directly affects the many households relying on domestic and international remittances.
For residents in Houthi-controlled areas, the result is an economy in which the currency may be relatively stable, but livelihoods are precarious. Years of unpaid salaries and limited employment opportunities have left many families struggling to afford basic necessities, with few options beyond borrowing, cutting spending or relying on support from relatives.

Government rules out fuel excise cut despite business pressure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
05:53:00 UTC
14:53:00 KST

Government rules out fuel excise cut despite business pressure
The government says it has no plans to cut fuel excise despite a proposal from the Chamber of Commerce and Industry to do so, Climate Minister Erkki Keldo (Reform) said.
Lowering both fuel excises to the EU minimum would cut excise revenue by about €210 million a year, Keldo said. The government is observing whether a recent excise duty cut by Latvia will lead to a significant rise in consumers from Estonia heading south of the border to refill.
The Chamber of Commerce and Industry (Kaubandus-tööstuskoda) has proposed lowering the diesel excise rate to the EU minimum for six months, from the current 42.8 cents to 33 cents per litre, at a time of soaring world diesel prices resulting mainly from the Middle East conflict.
"Reducing the excise rate is necessary to preserve businesses' competitiveness and curb inflation," said Mait Palts, director general of the chamber, in a letter to Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform).
The chamber also recommends creating a transparent, operational, data-based mechanism to assess how far diesel excise could reasonably be reduced in the event of sudden and exceptional circumstances — even temporary ones — and raised again once those circumstances have passed..
"Such an approach would ensure that the process of temporarily lowering the excise rate would be more operational, more transparent and based on data, and that the favorable excise rate would apply only during the period when it is economically justified," Palts said.
He added that several EU countries have cut excise, adding 18 out of the other 26 member states have lower rates than Estonia. Latvia's diesel excise duty is currently 33 cents per liter, Sweden's 11 cents, though Lithuania's (50 cents) and Finland's (51.1 cents) are higher.
"If Estonia has a higher excise rate than our nearby region and several other countries have decided to reduce it, even temporarily, this harms the competitiveness of Estonian businesses," Palts said.
Keldo said the fuel price rise is being driven not by taxes but by the world market, where supply has clearly fallen due to the Strait of Hormuz crisis. Higher fuel prices also do not translate to the same increase in tax revenues, since consumption falls, he added. Conversely, excise duty cuts do not fully get passed on to prices at pump, the minister said.
"We have to watch what our neighbors do, and we are watching very closely. Latvia has now made its first excise cuts. The Latvian Competition Authority's latest best knowledge says that 53 percent of the excise cut — essentially only half — reached pump prices," Keldo said.
As of Monday, diesel average €2.09 per liter at pump in Estonia compared with €2.12 in Latvia. The figures for gasoline were €1.94 per liter (Estonia) versus €1.96 (Latvia).
"What this shows is that the market as a whole is dynamic, and regional price differences and market competition affect it — there is no single solution here," Keldo said.
Latvia decided late last month to cut its excise duty rate on diesel fuel and unleaded petrol from October 1 until the end of this year.
Keldo said the chamber's proposal would cost the state budget a great deal. Taking both fuel excises to the EU minimum for all of 2027 would reduce excise revenue by approximately €210 million, he summarized.
The prime minister said the government is watching the fuel market primarily because Latvia is restructuring various taxes and introducing temporary measures; it would be advantageous to know how great the risk of cross-border trade is.
"We are assessing the situation and taking it seriously — what options there are for steps on cross-border trade if Latvia takes steps, or whether we need to take steps ourselves if price fluctuations from the world market affect our own price rises and inflation," Michal said.
Pump prices have risen by more than 60 cents per liter since the start of the Hormuz crisis in late February, and government decisions could affect the price by 10 to 12 cents per liter, he said, "perhaps more under some conditions."
"Possible costs in that case are about €10 million a month if we take excises to Latvia's level, and if we do more, the costs are greater. So about €120 million a year is the so-called minimum option," Michal added.
Keldo has been tasked by the government with monitoring world market fuel prices and the effect of price rises on consumer confidence and inflation.
Ahead of the mid-term elections, U.S. President Donald Trump threatened a diesel export ban on EU states if reserves were not released to counter soaring prices. The G7 countries earlier this week opted to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel from reserves.

How October 7 changed Lebanon and Hezbollah’s political reality
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
05:52:49 UTC
14:52:49 KST

How October 7 changed Lebanon and Hezbollah’s political reality
Analysts say Hezbollah’s decision on October 8 to join a ‘support war’ for Gaza changed Lebanon’s political reality.
Beirut, Lebanon – A day after the October 7, 2023, attack on Israel and the beginning of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, Hezbollah made the decision to join the war, in what it said was support of the Palestinian people. It is a decision that analysts say has forever shaped Lebanese politics.
Experts said the group had underestimated the depth of Israel’s intelligence penetration in the run-up to the war, which later manifested in the bloody September 2024 pager attack and the assassination of much of Hezbollah’s leadership, including Secretary-General Hassan Nasrallah.
“Hezbollah got sucked into a vortex which culminated in the decapitation of their leadership and the invasion of south Lebanon,” Nicholas Blanford, a non-resident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council and author of a book about Hezbollah, told Al Jazeera. “That dealt Hezbollah a major blow to their popular standing and galvanised the election of Joseph Aoun as president and the formation of a new government that took a much stronger line against [the group].”
Hezbollah’s decisions have left the group politically weakened. And while analysts say the group has not been defeated, despite claims to the contrary from some critics, it is no longer the political or military hegemon in Lebanon it once was.
‘A motion of events’
Before October 7, Hezbollah – a group representing Lebanon’s large Shia community – was the strongest political and military actor inside the country. The Iranian-backed group’s influence stretched across the region. Hezbollah was a key ally of the al-Assad regime in Syria and helped it retake territory from anti-Assad opposition groups. It also had connections with allies in places such as Iraq and Yemen.
Hezbollah had key electoral influence in Lebanon, where it often wielded its power to elect or collapse governments. It was also not against deploying its supporters against movements opposed to it, as in 2019 when they took to the streets of Beirut to beat back protesters calling for political reform of the country’s sectarian system, in which Hezbollah has become a key player in the years since the end of Lebanon’s 15-year civil war in 1990.
In the months leading up to October 2023, Hezbollah’s confidence was on clear display. Blanford pointed to examples such as a military parade in south Lebanon conducted by Hezbollah, and the group erecting tents in the Shebaa Farms – on territory that Lebanon considers occupied by Israel.
At the time, Israel was roiled by protests, and Nasrallah was delivering speeches predicting the imminent doom of Israel. The decision to join the fight against Israel in what became known in Lebanon as the War of Support came on October 8, 2023.
“October 7 set in motion a chain of events that Lebanon’s political system was not properly prepared to manage,” Jad Dilati, a political analyst from Nabatieh in southern Lebanon, told Al Jazeera. “Hezbollah opened its support front for Gaza on October 8 completely unilaterally, without any cabinet decision or governmental consensus or even taking into account the positions of the southern [Lebanese] residents who were most affected and still are most affected by these actions.”
“Hezbollah opened the support front on October 8, genuinely believing that it was operating from a position of strength,” Dilati said. “Most of the South believed that Hezbollah was operating from a position of strength after it had spent years building precision missile capabilities, an elaborate tunnel network and these missiles that we were told can hit every building in Tel Aviv.”
Israel’s re-invasion
For the next 11 months, Israel and Hezbollah traded attacks, albeit with Israel hitting Lebanon more than five times for every Hezbollah attack. Tens of thousands from southern Lebanon and northern Israel fled their homes.
But in September 2024, Israel unilaterally intensified attacks. The Israeli-induced carnage came quickly and heavily, with nearly 500 people killed on September 23 alone. When Nasrallah was said to have accepted a ceasefire – according to Lebanese officials quoted in media reports – Israel ordered his assassination and the evacuation of areas of Beirut’s southern suburbs.
“When Nasrallah was amenable to a ceasefire, Israel was on the offensive and wasn’t going to return to the previous status quo,” Blanford said.
Israel invaded southern Lebanon in October 2024 and stayed in Lebanese territory for more than two months after a ceasefire was agreed in November. Despite the ceasefire, Israel continued to destroy homes and infrastructure in southern Lebanon and refused to pull its troops out of five locations on Lebanese territory. Next door in Syria, the fall of the al-Assad regime in December 2024 also dealt a blow to the group, as its land routes to receive weapons and funding from Iran were disrupted.
Over the next 14 months, Israel violated the ceasefire more than 10,000 times. Then in March 2026, Israel reintensified its war on Lebanon. The attacks came after Hezbollah fired rockets at Israel for the first time in more than a year as a response to the myriad ceasefire violations and the assassination of Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, whom Hezbollah viewed as a religious and political leader.
Israel then invaded Lebanon again and launched widespread attacks on the country. It has killed more than 9,000 people in Lebanon since 2024 and displaced more than 1.2 million people, emptying entire regions of the country.
Hezbollah’s legitimacy crisis
Israel now occupies large swathes of Lebanese territory, stretching up to 10 kilometres (more than 6 miles) from the border at some points. Dozens of villages, once filled with agriculture and people, are now uninhabited piles of dust and rubble. Hundreds of thousands remain displaced.
This has had a massive impact on Lebanon. The World Bank says the country’s economy has contracted by more than 6 percent in 2026. After the 2024 conflict, the World Bank said Lebanon needed around $11bn for recovery and reconstruction. That figure is likely much higher now.
In the aftermath of past wars against Israel, such as in 2006, Hezbollah was able to support much of its community and supporters. Providing social welfare has been key to the group’s ability to maintain popularity and belief among its constituents.
But since 2024, the Lebanese state, along with much of the international community, has been working to expand its own services. The state is also openly claiming it is working to disarm Hezbollah, despite the group’s objections, as part of a framework agreement with Israel.
“Hezbollah is in a legitimacy crisis that it has not faced before,” Dilati said. “I wouldn’t say that there is a rupture in the community or a complete political realignment, but a big part of the communities that supported it for decades are saying that Iran left them behind, the war was fought on their land for someone else’s interests, and that they don’t want wars anymore.”
Still, while grumbles against the group are growing louder, analysts said Hezbollah remains the most popular representative among Lebanon’s Shia Muslims.
“Hezbollah is providing for their needs by and large, and there is no alternative politically for the Shia community at the moment,” Blanford said. “What is binding them to Hezbollah is the fact that several hundred thousand Shias were booted out of their homes and are living in non-Shia areas where they do not feel particularly welcome, and this can create a sense of vulnerability that naturally makes them gravitate to Hezbollah as communal protection, rightly or wrongly.”
The group also maintains fighting capacity, and despite critics calling it a spent force, analysts and foreign diplomats say its weakness has been overstated. Much of the group’s future depends on the outcome of regional events, particularly regarding the US-Israeli war on Iran. But analysts said the status quo – in which the state is negotiating with Israel and trying to extend its influence across Lebanese territory, and Hezbollah adapts to waning domestic influence – could work against the group.
“The key thing is this looks like a long occupation, and you may get a situation where people who have not only lost their home but lost their village, orchards, banana plantations, tobacco fields and the rest of it may think life was good before and may start blaming Hezbollah,” Blanford said.

Visitors see Cappadocia from hot air balloons, while others photograph the balloons and valleys or explore the region on ATV and horseback tours. (AA Photo)
Cappadocia is seeing a major autumn tourism boom, with visitors from across East Asia, particularly China, flocking to the UNESCO World Heritage site to explore its iconic fairy chimneys, dramatic rock formations and rich cultural heritage.
A popular destination year-round, the region has welcomed a surge of Chinese tourists traveling over the Oct. 1–7 “Golden Week” public holiday — which marks the founding of the People’s Republic of China — alongside visitors from other East Asian nations.
While some visitors admire Cappadocia’s natural, historical, and cultural sights from hot air balloons, others photograph the balloons from scenic viewpoints and valleys or explore the region via ATV and horseback tours.
East Asian travelers are also keeping local hotels, museums and underground cities busy, starting their activities before dawn and continuing well into the evening.
Indonesian tourist Eda Dewi, who joined a balloon tour, said it was her first visit to Cappadocia and that she was impressed by the region.
“Cappadocia is a wonderful tourism destination. The scenery created by the balloons is even more beautiful,” Dewi told state-run Anadolu Agency.
Chloe Lim, a visitor from Singapore, said she was having a wonderful time making memories with her friends and was thrilled to go on a hot-air balloon tour.
Chinese tourist Fang Mei Son shared that she had been eager to visit Cappadocia for years and expressed her deep love for Türkiye.
Balloon pilot Tolga Eke said Far Eastern tourists had boosted tourism activity in the region in recent weeks.
“Far Eastern visitors have always been interested in Cappadocia. However, their numbers are increasing every day. They prefer these tours because watching the fairy chimneys from the sky is fascinating,” he said.

He said accommodation facilities and balloon tours had recorded occupancy rates close to 100 percent during the first week of October.
“We are very lucky to live in a destination where tourism is possible 12 months a year. October is one of Cappadocia’s golden months. During this peak period, we also received strong additional demand from China because of the ‘Golden Week’ celebrated in China from Oct. 1 to 7,” Dinler said.
“The occupancy rate at our hotels was close to 100 percent during the first week of October. This was also reflected in balloon tours. A guest who takes a balloon tour one day rushes to the sunrise viewing points the next day to watch this fairy-tale landscape,” he added.
Dinler said Japan, South Korea, China, Singapore, Malaysia and Hong Kong were among the region’s key tourism markets, particularly during the winter season.
He said he expected the Chinese market to maintain its momentum during the winter as flight frequencies between China and Türkiye increase.
Dinler added that the Culture and Tourism Ministry’s global promotional campaigns have contributed significantly to the region’s tourism success.

Istanbul air pollution linked to more hospital visits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
05:50:44 UTC
14:50:44 KST

A haze hangs over Istanbul, as pollution affects older people. (AA Photo)
A study linked air pollution to more hospital visits in Istanbul, particularly among people over 65, after examining 3.94 million visits for asthma, acute bronchitis and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).
Istanbul Technical University’s Eurasia Institute of Earth Sciences lecturer Dr. Özkan Çapraz analyzed hospital visits between 2013 and 2017. The research identified particulate matter smaller than 2.5 micrometers (PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide and particulate matter smaller than 10 micrometers (PM10) as pollutants significantly associated with the diseases.
The study assessed children, adults and people over 65 separately, with older people among the most sensitive groups. Levels of particulate matter and nitrogen oxides were highest in winter, followed by autumn and spring, while exceedance episodes declined in summer.
“Hospital visits increased when air pollution was high,” Çapraz told Anadolu Agency.
Human-induced emissions from vehicle exhaust and heating were more strongly linked to health problems than natural sources, Çapraz said. Nitrogen dioxide and fine particles from vehicle exhaust were associated with asthma, COPD and acute bronchitis.
The effects of pollution could appear several days later rather than on the same day, he said. Fine particles can reach deep into the lungs and trigger asthma and COPD, while areas with heavy traffic and household or industrial pollution face greater risks.
Ground-level ozone can irritate the respiratory tract, posing risks to children, older people, asthma patients and those active outdoors. Çapraz said sensitive groups should limit outdoor activity on polluted days.
He recommended hybrid or electric vehicles and natural gas instead of coal or wood for heating, and said industrial areas should be located outside cities.
Earlier research on Saharan dust found no major same-day effect on emergency asthma or COPD visits but a modest increase in acute bronchitis visits.

525 rare manuscripts from scholar İsmail Erünsal made available online
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09

One of 525 rare manuscripts donated by İsmail Erünsal is online. (AA Photo)
A collection of 525 rare works donated by Ottoman book and library history scholar İsmail Erünsal to Istanbul’s Süleymaniye Manuscript Library has been digitized and opened to public access worldwide.
The collection, assembled by Erünsal over decades through his personal efforts, includes unique copies, rare works and manuscripts written in the authors’ own handwriting. Among its highlights is a handwritten copy of the Divan by renowned Ottoman poet Şeyh Galib, believed to have been written when he was only 18 or 19 years old.
Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy said the donation demonstrated the importance of individual contributions to preserving cultural heritage and passing it on to future generations. He thanked Erünsal for donating the collection. “I sincerely thank our esteemed professor, Prof. Dr. İsmail Erünsal, for donating his collection so that these works, which he regarded as a trust belonging to our nation, could be better preserved, passed on to future generations and made available to more people,” he wrote on social media.
The ministry’s Directorate General of Manuscripts Institutions completed the collection’s maintenance, restoration, digitization and cataloging in about two months after it was donated to the Süleymaniye Manuscript Library on Aug. 6.
The digitization project now allows researchers and members of the public around the world to examine the manuscripts remotely, expanding access to works that are significant sources for the study of Ottoman literary and intellectual history.

Basalt columns in eastern Türkiye emerge as new route for climbers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
05:50:24 UTC
14:50:24 KST

Climbers stand at the base of basalt columns in Kars.
Basalt columns formed 6 to 7 million years ago in the eastern province of Kars have become a new route for climbers and nature enthusiasts following their inclusion in academic literature.
The pentagonal and hexagonal prisms took shape during the Late Miocene epoch as cooling lava surfaced near Karagüney village in the Kağızman district. The distinct formations gained wider attention after being published in the Journal of Social, Humanities and Administrative Sciences, bringing them into the scientific literature.
Sitting at an altitude of 1,890 meters, the columns now draw outdoor sports enthusiasts and climbers from Kars and the neighboring province of Iğdır to the region. Their natural appearance and geological structure have made the site a new stop on climbing routes in the area.
Ali Öztürk, a member of the Iğdır Mountain Safari Club, said the geological structure offers a visually striking route for visitors.
“The columns have a very beautiful appearance. We came here with a 10-person team, made an exploration and created a new route,” he said.
Öztürk said climbers continue to chart new paths in the surrounding area and advised outdoor enthusiasts to see the basalt structures.
Amateur climber Hakan Duman said they had added the geological formation area to their routes and invited all climbers to see it.
Basalt columns form when volcanic lava cools and contracts, creating polygonal structures. The Kars formations emerged as lava cooled after surfacing near Karagüney village during the Late Miocene. The columns are found in a limited area at about 1,890 meters above sea level, where their pentagonal and hexagonal shapes are visible across the formation.

Japan's real household spending falls 3.1 pct in August

TOKYO, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- Japan's real household spending fell 3.1 percent year-on-year in August, marking a ninth consecutive month of decline, government data showed Friday.
Average monthly consumption expenditure by households with two or more people stood at 310,975 yen (about 1,960 U.S. dollars), down 1.0 percent in nominal terms, according to data released by the Internal Affairs and Communications Ministry.
On a seasonally adjusted basis, real household spending edged up 0.1 percent from July, marking a second consecutive month-on-month increase.
Spending on food fell 1.4 percent, while outlays for energy and water bills dropped 5.2 percent as cooler temperatures reduced the need for air conditioning.
Spending on culture and recreation declined 4.3 percent, largely due to a pullback in domestic package tour spending following a surge during the previous year's World Exposition in Osaka, according to a ministry official.
Household spending is a key indicator of private consumption, which accounts for more than half of Japan's gross domestic product. ■

WASHINGTON, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- Local authorities in Arlington County, Virginia, on Thursday sued to block construction of U.S. President Donald Trump's planned Triumphal Arch project.
Arlington County is located in Northern Virginia just across the Potomac River from Washington, D.C.
The county government filed the lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia, arguing that the Trump administration's planned 250-foot-tall arch violates environmental laws and requires further review.
"As contemplated, the Arch will dwarf Paris's Arc de Triomphe and directly obstruct the line of sight between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery that was deliberately created to symbolize the nation's post-Civil War reunification," the complaint said.
Construction of the Arch on Memorial Circle will "cause significant harm" to Arlington County and its residents, as the site lies within a busy traffic corridor, according to the five-person Arlington County Board.
The complaint also noted that construction of the Arch will "harm public safety" in Arlington by clogging thoroughfares needed for emergency transport services.
"It threatens to increase noise and air pollution in Arlington by necessitating the diversion of certain flights into and out of Reagan National Airport," it continued.
According to the complaint, the National Park Service failed to take a "hard look" at the environmental impacts of the Arch project, as required by law.
The county filed the lawsuit to halt the agency's "feverish pace" toward construction of the Arch and to ensure that the "hard look" mandated by the National Environmental Policy Act is completed before the agency commences "disruptive and harmful ground-disturbing activities."
Trump first unveiled the administration's plan to construct the Arch in October 2025, at the time hailing it as a monument to the 250th anniversary of American independence.
More recently, Trump announced the Arch would serve as a "top-grade Military Complex/Triumphal Arch," which will store large quantities of ammunition and "house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers."
In early September, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum announced on social media that excavation work could begin over the next two weeks. ■

Xinhua Headlines: Drones tackle toughest rural delivery stretches in China
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:49:25 CST
14:49:25 KST

CHENGDU, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- Express delivery now reaches more than 95 percent of China's administrative villages. In some rural areas, however, getting a parcel to the village requires more than just one mode of transport.
In Zizhong County in southwest China's Sichuan Province, for example, drones are being used on routes where winding roads make the last leg of the journey slow. This county currently has 131 drone routes serving 131 villages and plans to extend them to all 301 villages by the end of the year.
Some 300 km away in Quxian County, drones are also being tested on the return journey, carrying farm produce from villages to township delivery points.
SHORTER WAY IN
The route from Guide Town to Tongjiazui Village in Zizhong requires a delivery vehicle to travel 9.9 kilometers, which takes about 19 minutes, while a drone on this route covers 5.7 kilometers in roughly 6.5 minutes.
Around 85 percent of Zizhong is hilly, and many villages lie on slopes or in river valleys. Some remote villages previously received parcels only once every two or three days. In places without village service stations, residents sometimes had to travel to town to collect them.
Rao Yurong, who grows blood oranges in Yueliangxia Village, recently received a battery-powered sprayer she had bought online. It took the drone around seven minutes to fly from the township station to the village. Notably, Rao previously spent nearly an hour riding an electric bike to town and back to collect a parcel.
JD Logistics opened 78 routes in Zizhong in June and has since expanded the network to 131.
Drones handle only the last section of the journey. Trucks still carry parcels over long distances and from county-level facilities to township stations.
This service also relies on facilities and staff on the ground. Township landing sites and village collection points have been set up, with local workers handling parcel collection and sorting. Sichuan has also introduced financial support for eligible low-altitude logistics projects.
Similar services are being used where water, rather than hills, slows deliveries. In east China's Jiangsu Province, 32 rural drone routes are in regular operation. One route to Mudun Island on Hongze Lake has cut delivery time by approximately 50 minutes compared with the previous ferry-based service.
MAKING RETURN TRIPS COUNT
Most drones flying into villages still fly back empty. According to JD Logistics, about 99 percent of return flights on rural routes carry no cargo.
Quxian is trying to change this.
In August, local villager Yu Fengying sent several kilograms of peanuts and sweet potato starch noodles to relatives and friends outside the area. Instead of riding an electric scooter to town, she used a drone that had just delivered parcels to the village.
About eight minutes later, the package reached a central landing point in town and entered the conventional express network.
JD Logistics plans to expand this service across Quxian and use return flights to carry local products including daylilies, lemons and plums.
Farm produce requiring fast transit may be among the more suitable shipments.
During the 2025 sweet cherry harvest in Hanyuan County, Sichuan, drones carried fruit from mountainous areas to a mail processing center in around 15 minutes. Conventional vehicles needed one to two hours for the same trip.
In the course of a month, more than 550 flights transported 7,586 packages of cherries weighing a total of 22.76 tonnes.
For fresh fruit harvested within a short season, saving an hour or more in transport can help reduce the time between picking and onward shipment.
WHERE DRONES MAKE SENSE
The faster trip does not yet cost less.
On one Zizhong route, JD Logistics puts the comprehensive cost at roughly 5.6 yuan (about 83 U.S. cents) per parcel by drone, compared with 4.4 yuan by vehicle.
Drones carry approximately 30 percent of their available payload on average, while almost all return flights are empty.
Zhang Jianping, director of a low-altitude air traffic institute at Southwest Jiaotong University, said drones are most useful in places where mountains or water make ground transport difficult. Only a few such services have so far reached a scale that can support commercial operations, he noted, while most are still used alongside conventional transport.
Zhang said western mountainous areas have demand for transporting farm produce, daily necessities and engineering supplies, because difficult terrain, large elevation changes and limited road access can make ground transport slower or harder.
Fangxian County in central China's Hubei Province, meanwhile, is using several transport methods rather than relying on one. A national rural-delivery pilot project there uses conventional vehicles, autonomous delivery vehicles, drones and combined passenger-freight-express mail services, depending on local conditions.
Since the pilot began, average operating cost has fallen by 0.2 yuan per parcel, while daily inbound village mail volume has risen by 16.3 percent and outbound volume by 48.9 percent, according to the State Post Bureau.
In Sichuan, drones are also being used to carry matsutake mushrooms, cherries and highland strawberries, as well as bamboo, power-grid components and construction materials.
JD Logistics plans to expand rural drone services to more than 50 counties and districts across the provincial-level regions of Sichuan, Chongqing, Yunnan and Guizhou, all located in southwest China. ■

Japan's Cabinet approves bill for 1st food consumption tax cut

TOKYO, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- Japan's Cabinet on Friday approved a bill to temporarily cut the consumption tax on food and beverages and introduce an income-based benefit program, marking a major step toward securing its passage during the current Diet session.
Under the bill, the consumption tax rate on food and beverages would be reduced from 8 percent to 1 percent for two years starting in fiscal 2027, which begins next April. The bill also provides for annual cash benefits for low- and middle-income earners.
The government aims to submit the bill to the ongoing extraordinary session of the Diet, Japan's parliament, and secure its enactment by the end of the session on Dec. 12.
The tax cut and cash benefit program are expected to require a total of about 10 trillion yen (about 63 billion U.S. dollars) over the two years, raising concerns about Japan's fiscal health, which is already among the weakest of advanced economies.
Opposition lawmakers have questioned how the necessary funds would be secured and criticized the eligibility criteria for the benefits as vague.
The proposed reduction would mark the first cut in Japan's consumption tax rate since the tax was introduced in 1989. The standard rate has been 10 percent since October 2019, while food and beverages are subject to a reduced rate of 8 percent, excluding alcoholic beverages and dining out. ■

Column: China's quiet rise in global appeal
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:49:06 CST
14:49:06 KST

by Nadeem Javaid
Over more than a decade of travelling across China, I have watched a transformation that is difficult to capture in economic statistics alone.
Since 2013, each visit has revealed not simply a richer or more modern China, but a country steadily changing the way it produces, innovates, consumes and, increasingly, how it is perceived by the world.
What strikes me most today is not simply how much China has changed. It is how the nature of that change has evolved.
Perhaps one phrase captures this journey best: from "Made in China" to "Designed in China." For decades, much of the world encountered China through the products it manufactured -- a symbol of extraordinary scale and efficiency. But the China I see today is different. It is increasingly a China of electric vehicles, batteries, renewable energy, artificial intelligence, robotics and sophisticated consumer products. Chinese companies no longer compete only on cost and scale, but increasingly on technology, design, quality and consumer experience.
This is more than industrial transformation. It is reputational transformation.
During a recent visit to Urumqi, the capital of northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, I experienced a demonstration of autonomous driving technology at the airport. What struck me was not simply the technology itself, but how naturally such innovation seemed to fit into everyday life.
It was a small but telling experience: technologies once associated with the future are increasingly becoming part of the present in China. The journey from "Made in China" to "Designed in China" is becoming visible to consumers.
Yet some of the most revealing changes I have observed since 2013 are not inside factories or technology parks. They are in everyday life.
China's cities today offer a dramatically different consumer experience. Coffee shops and cafés have become woven into urban culture. Domestic brands have grown more confident and sophisticated. Digital payments have transformed daily transactions.
What may appear to be small changes tell us something important: development is ultimately reflected in people's everyday lives, and greater choice is perhaps one of the least discussed dividends of growth.
In many interactions, I repeatedly heard an idea that initially sounded unconventional -- the application of market principles within socialism with Chinese characteristics. Yet China found ways to combine market incentives, entrepreneurship and competition with long-term state guidance and national priorities. What appeared contradictory in theory proved remarkably workable in practice.
What mattered was the willingness to experiment, learn, adapt and scale what worked. From the establishment of the Shenzhen Special Economic Zone to today's advances in batteries, electric vehicles and renewable technologies, China's experience shows that institutions and policies must evolve as the economy evolves.
This matters greatly for the developing world.
Much of traditional development discourse focuses on managing vulnerability: poverty, debt and institutional weaknesses. These are real challenges. But developing societies do not only want to manage scarcity. They also want to create prosperity. They ask how to build productive firms, competitive industries and technological capabilities; how to move from imitation to innovation; and how to climb the global value chain.
China's experience speaks directly to these aspirations -- not as a template to copy, but as evidence that transformation at scale is possible.
Pakistan provides a concrete lens. Through years of working on economic policy and observing China-Pakistan cooperation, I have seen how perceptions change when bilateral ties become tangible to people.
The upgrades to the Karakoram Highway, which have reduced travel times between remote regions; energy projects that have eased chronic power shortages; and affordable technology and educational exchanges all speak more powerfully than diplomatic statements ever could.
Of course, China's experience is neither flawless nor simply transplantable. Every country has its own history, institutions and political economy. But when cooperation translates into lived experiences, those experiences gradually shape a country's reputation.
Perhaps this helps explain why China is increasingly viewed in a more positive light around the world.
People are not simply hearing about China anymore. Increasingly, they are experiencing China -- through its technologies, products, brands, infrastructure, universities and, for millions of visitors, through direct experience of China itself. A country once known mainly for producing what the world designed is increasingly designing what the world wants to use.
Reputation is rarely built by slogans. It is built through experience. And the most enduring influence may be the one people can see, use and remember.
Editor's note: Nadeem Javaid is the vice chancellor of the Pakistan Institute of Development Economics and a member of the Planning Commission of Pakistan.
The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the positions of Xinhua News Agency.

WELLINGTON, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- More than two-thirds of New Zealand businesses are concerned about current and future energy costs, with nearly one-third having raised prices because of energy costs or supply uncertainty, a survey found.
The survey of 406 business leaders found seven in 10 businesses considered energy a major or actively managed cost, while the same proportion reported higher energy costs than two years ago, according to a survey released by New Zealand's ASB Bank on Thursday.
One in five businesses had reduced production, working hours or output because of energy challenges, the survey found.
Despite 64 percent of respondents believing their businesses were well equipped to operate through a prolonged power outage, only 37 percent expected they could continue operating for more than three days if their primary energy source failed, the findings showed.
Another 28 percent had identified energy as a risk but had no plan to address it, according to the survey.
ASB Executive General Manager of Corporate Banking Jonathan Oram said businesses need to treat energy as a strategic issue rather than simply an operating cost, citing rising energy costs and potential supply disruptions amid declining domestic gas reserves, the Middle East conflict and global political uncertainty.
Advances in solar power, battery storage and electric vehicles offer opportunities to improve energy efficiency and cut business energy costs by up to 20 percent, the survey said. ■

Police apprehend T1 Mall jewelry heist suspects
Police arrested three men in late September on suspicion of stealing jewelry from a store at Tallinn's T1 shopping mall. The men were remanded in custody with court authorization.
Police have arrested three men suspected of stealing nearly €500,000 worth of jewelry from a store at Tallinn's T1 shopping mall, Delfi writes.
The suspects are two Russian citizens, aged 46 and 38, and a 38-year-old Estonian citizen.
According to Valmar Viitak, head of the serious crimes unit at the Police and Border Guard Board's Northern Prefecture, police were notified on the morning of September 23 that thieves had broken into the jewelry store overnight.
Investigators established that the suspects had entered the store through the shopping center's ceiling and stolen jewelry worth nearly half a million euros.
Over the following two days, police reviewed nearby security camera footage, collected evidence and interviewed witnesses.
On September 25, officers received information that the 46-year-old suspect was planning to leave Estonia and arrested him after stopping a vehicle near Valga, while the other two suspects were detained the same day in Ida-Viru County.
Prosecutor Marko Moorlat, who is leading the criminal investigation, said the evidence indicated that the theft had been carefully planned and required substantial preparation, coordination and prior knowledge of the store.
According to Moorlat, prosecutors believed the suspects posed a risk of committing further crimes or evading criminal proceedings if released, given their backgrounds and the circumstances uncovered during the investigation.
All three men were remanded in custody pending trial at the prosecution's request and with court authorization.

stained bamboo and concealed storage shape MK designers’ handle table

stained bamboo and concealed storage shape MK designers’ handle table
handle table is built around a simple question: what do we need to keep close at hand without having it constantly in sight?
Marek Kounovský designs table around the idea of ‘just enough’
Designed by Marek Kounovský of MK Designers for Prague-based furniture company Frayer, Handle Table is a bamboo coffee table with concealed storage integrated into its geometry. The design explores the idea of ‘just enough’ by balancing function, material, and form without adding unnecessary details.
oil-based stain highlights bamboo’s natural texture and form
For the table, designer Marek Kounovský of MK Designers draws on the Japanese principle of hodo-hodo, which emphasizes moderation, restraint, and balance. Its reduced form highlights proportion, material, and construction, while the integrated compartment provides storage for everyday items without disrupting the table’s appearance.
The bamboo surface is treated with an oil-based wood stain developed through experiments with application methods suited to the material. The finish enhances the bamboo’s natural structure and tactile qualities while keeping its texture visible. Handle Table was first presented at the 14th Czech Design Week international design festival in Prague.

Ziraat Bank has transferred money for about 43,000 fund investors to banks and brokerages for payment, as the ruling party prepares legislation governing interim payouts and the recovery of assets.
The transfers cover 17 funds established by A1 Capital, Bulls and Pardus, the Communications Directorate said on Oct. 8.
The receiving institutions will credit investors’ accounts as quickly as possible, it said.
Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek said the three portfolio management companies were undergoing ordinary liquidation.
The wider process covers 131 funds run by seven companies, affecting hundreds of thousands of investors.
The ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) is expected to submit its bill to parliament on Oct. 9.
Prepared under parliamentary group leader Abdullah Güler, the draft sets out how investors’ claims would be calculated, payments distributed and assets recovered to cover losses.
It provides for interim payments of up to 1 million Turkish Liras per person, without exceeding investors’ net investments or confirmed entitlements. These would be advances against the amounts due from liquidation.
The Capital Markets Board (SPK) could prioritize investors with the smallest net holdings or set a common initial payment threshold.
If available cash were insufficient, it would be distributed proportionately among eligible investors.
To calculate net investments, past cash flows would be adjusted using the average of changes in consumer and domestic producer prices.
Withdrawals would be offset against the earliest contributions first.
The bill would also establish a voluntary repayment mechanism for those who earned above-normal returns by selling fund units at inflated valuations before liquidation or trading shares held by the funds.
Amounts to be returned would be assessed against comparable fund returns, stock indices or other objective market benchmarks.
Assets seized or confiscated in criminal proceedings could be used to cover investor losses.
The Savings Deposit Insurance Fund (TMSF) would sell or liquidate assets that could not be transferred directly to the affected funds.
Şimşek said the TMSF had opened separate accounts for each of the 131 funds, alongside a general account, to receive recovered money and voluntary returns.
Speaking in Istanbul on Oct. 8, he said small investors and money market funds were being given priority, while proceedings involving some portfolio management companies could take longer.
“We are not downplaying the problem,” Şimşek said, pledging further legal and administrative measures to prevent similar problems.
He also said those responsible for market-abusing practices would be held accountable.
Parliament separately rejected opposition motions seeking an inquiry into the fund problems.

The hidden cost of farmed fish: Pollution, forced labor and the depletion of wild fish
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- More than half the seafood eaten worldwide is farm-raised, but much of it fed ‘fishmeal,’ a product made from wild-caught fish.
- Farm-raised fish feed millions and the farms provide employment. But a global investigation into fish farming found overfishing, pollution and labor abuses.
- The investigation found that fish farming is often worsening the very problem it hoped to solve and harming the people it was meant to help.
As of 2022, more than half of the seafood eaten worldwide was farm-raised rather than caught at sea, a fact that has been praised as evidence that fish farming can meet a growing demand for seafood while slowing the collapse of the oceans.
But the unbridled embrace of aquaculture as a sustainable answer to feeding the planet ignores some very real costs.
The most popular types of farmed seafood — salmon, shrimp, trout, seabass, seabream — are fed “fishmeal,” a protein-rich powder or pellet made from the very kinds of wild fish that aquaculture is thought to save.
In fact, fishmeal is fed to two-thirds of global farmed fish. Before they reach market, some farm-raised salmon eat more than six times their weight in wild-caught fish.
With thousands of fish farms worldwide, aquaculture provides millions of people with year-round access to affordable protein. Fish farming is also a crucial source of jobs, especially for women in India.
But a wide-reaching investigation by The Outlaw Ocean Project, a nonprofit news organization based in Washington, D.C., has found that the aquaculture industry’s answer to worries about the world’s oceans — “grow more fish so we can catch less” — is often making the very problem it hoped to solve worse and harming the people it was meant to help.
The investigation
The business of fishmeal — often out of public view — can involve using forced labor, poisoning communities, and eradicating the livelihoods of local fishermen.
Fishmeal production has led to chronic chemical exposure, violent protests — typically spurred by the stench from fishmeal factories — and escalating transnational tensions as countries compete for catch. That price is paid primarily by the poorer countries where the main ingredient of fishmeal is harvested and processed.
The Outlaw Ocean Project mapped roughly the entire global fishmeal industry, including more than 1,400 fishmeal factories across 64 countries. The effort involved dozens of journalists from over 15 countries who visited factories and farms and boarded fishmeal ships at sea.
Using certification documents, ownership records, trade data, audits and government lists of licensed fishing ships, the reporting team was able to connect ships to the plants they supplied and pin down which species were being targeted for fishmeal. This allowed them to determine which fishmeal plants were connected to ships engaged in illegal or unsustainable fishing. Then, they traced the fishmeal to the fish farm and to where the seafood was sold by retailers.
The investigation found that more than 2,400 ships tied to fishmeal production, operating in the waters of at least 30 countries. It found that most of those ships do not fully comply with the Global Charter for Fisheries Transparency, a guide created by leading ocean-focused civil society groups detailing accountability standards for industrial fishing fleets.
For example, less than 30% of the fleets had publicly available location information, and less than 25% had a unique vessel identification number. Such opacity makes the ships difficult to police.
At least half of the species landed by the assessed fishmeal vessels are classified by scientific studies as “overexploited” or worse. Most of these vessels are purse seiners or trawlers, which deploy vast nets to capture dense schools of fish. Both gear types are associated with high levels of waste, routinely hauling in large volumes of non-target species.
At least 165 of the ships were bottom trawlers, a particularly destructive form of fishing that uses weighted nets that scrape the ocean floor, destroying virtually everything in their path.
Concerns about aquaculture extend far beyond the fate of the oceans. In Gambia and Mauritania in western Africa, the industry drives food insecurity as fish that once sustained local communities are diverted into fishmeal factories.
In remote islands in Russia’s far east and in China’s Xinjiang region, the reporting detailed the use of forced labor on ships, farms and in factories. In other countries, including India and Peru, this industry was tied to at least 80 incidents of civil unrest, some violent, usually in the form of labor strikes and protests sparked by the water pollution or the stink from factories cooking tons of decomposing fish.
In Chile in 2024, several hundred demonstrators burned tires and blocked coastal highways and railway tracks to protest the early closure of the fishing season, a move partly driven by overfishing tied to fishmeal.
In Senegal, fishmeal has put local fishers out of work, so they increasingly are selling — or repurposing — their boats to ferry migrants to Spain’s Canary Islands, a stepping stone to Europe. This perilous journey of roughly 930 miles claimed more than 3,000 lives in 2025.
“We’re fishermen, but there’s no fish left here, so we left,” said Cheikhou Omar, a 21-year-old fisherman in 2024 as he sat on a beach in Senegal, rescued after the fishing boat he tried to sail to Spain capsized, killing 30.
The fishmeal industry also contributes to transnational tensions. For example, in 2021, a dozen Turkish bottom trawlers fishing illegally in the Aegean Sea tried to ram a Greek research vessel when the scientists began filming their activity.
In 2018, riots broke out in Saint-Louis, Senegal, after a fisher was shot and killed by Mauritanian coast guards, during what the Mauritanians said was a cross-border raid by a fishmeal boat.
The politics of protein
In her 2021 book “The Fishmeal Revolution,” Kristin A. Wintersteen traces how the Humboldt Current — a cold, nutrient-rich upwelling system along the Pacific coast of South America — was reimagined as a protein mine. That shift, she argues, turned Peru into a fishmeal superpower, responsible for roughly a quarter of worldwide production.
Fishmeal helped fuel the post-World War II expansion of industrial chicken and hog farming, particularly in Europe and the United States. Since then, this model has spread worldwide.
The feed industry has emphasized that it is decreasing its reliance on fishmeal and fish oil — and especially the use of whole fish or fish parts that can be eaten by people. However, as aquaculture grows, global fishmeal production is predicted to rise by nearly 10% by 2032, according to the Food and Agriculture Organization, a United Nations agency.
For example, five of the world’s largest salmon companies increased their use of fishmeal and fish oil made from whole wild fish by as much as 39% between 2020 and 2024, according to a report from the Farm Animal Investment Risk and Return Initiative.
Asked about sustainability concerns tied to her industry, Véronique Jamin, a spokesperson for IFFO, the international fishmeal association, said that fish farming is “the most efficient animal protein system.” She added that her organization’s “role is not to advise which markets should use fishmeal and fish oil.” Attempts to make the industry more sustainable must consider market forces, she said, and seafood companies have to respond to “what people actually want to buy and eat.”
Efforts to move away from fishmeal and fish oil have struggled. Researchers have identified potential alternatives — including seaweed, cassava waste, single-cell proteins produced by fungi and even sewage.
But none are being produced affordably at scale, and the alternatives often lack the nutrients that support the growth of farmed fish.
The role of forced labor
For those toiling at fishmeal plants and fish farms, the work and conditions can be brutal, the investigation found.
In Russia, fish processing workers were held captive in secluded company towns or stuck on ships far from shore. “People have nowhere to go, no money,” one worker told President Vladimir Putin, who participated in a call-in television show about the fishmeal plant in 2016. A second worker pleaded: “Please, help us.”
In China, the aquaculture industry is expanding rapidly in the country’s mountainous and desert areas inland, particularly in Tibet and Xinjiang, two areas known for political repression, with criminal penalties for speaking native languages or practicing religious or cultural traditions.
Because the U.S. government found human rights abuses to be pervasive there, Congress enacted a law in 2021 that banned all goods produced “wholly or in part” by workers in Xinjiang or by ethnic minorities from the region on the presumption that they were made with state-sponsored forced labor. No such law exists for Tibet.
The investigation mapped more than 1,000 fish farms in Xinjiang and Tibet that produce an estimated half-billion dollars’ worth of seafood annually, much of it exported to more than a dozen countries, including the United States. Despite the 2021 law banning goods from Xinjiang, the investigation found that farm-raised fish from that region have reached the United States.
For example, the Xinjiang Tiayun fish farm, which produces 40% of China’s domestically produced salmon, is tied through supply agreements to a brand of seafood called Aqua Star sold by Walmart and the world’s largest food service company, Sysco, which in the U.S. distributes to public schools, military bases and congressional cafeterias.
Sysco said it was unaware of the link to Xinjiang. “We hold all suppliers across our global supply chain accountable” to uphold U.S., international and local laws, and Sysco suspends contracts when they do not, said Ramit Plushnick-Masti, a company spokesperson. Aqua Star and Walmart did not respond to a request for comment.
Xinjiang Tianyun said in a statement that claims of forced labor “are completely factually unfounded.” The Chinese government did not respond to a request for comment.
More than 80% of seafood eaten in the U.S. is imported, and 9% of that comes from China.
Another major supplier of seafood to the U.S. is India, which produces roughly a third of the shrimp that Americans consume, almost all of it grown with fishmeal. The investigation found at least 18 instances of civil unrest and at least 20 cases of water or air pollution tied to Indian fishmeal plants.
In November 2020, Indian government investigators found hidden bore holes where the operator of the United Marine Products fishmeal plant in Goa had been covertly disposing of toxic waste, thereby contaminating groundwater. The plant owner denied wrongdoing.
Shrimp sold by Sysco and at Kroger and Safeway is fed fishmeal from United Marine, according to Bait to Plate, an online tool that maps seafood supply chains. Kroger and Safeway’s parent company, Albertsons, did not respond to a request for comment.
Sustainable practices
Though problems with fish farming have arisen worldwide, for some countries, it aquaculture has been a boon.
In Bangladesh, aquaculture has driven down the price of fish. Even accounting for fishmeal and transportation to the U.S., the production of certain farmed fish, including tilapia and Atlantic salmon, emits less greenhouse gas per pound than beef or pork.
Harvesting bivalves, like clams, oysters, scallops and mussels, is especially sustainable because these species do not require feed. This type of aquaculture also has a low carbon footprint and the shells function as a form of carbon capture, according to a 2020 paper by the scientific journal Nature Food.
In the United States, at least 16 factories processed fishmeal as of 2025, along the Chesapeake Bay in Virginia, the Gulf Coast in Mississippi and Louisiana, and in California, Oregon and Alaska.
Most of these factories use inedible offcuts from fishing because nearly every U.S. state has outlawed the targeting of whole fish for fishmeal. The factories also tend to be better regulated than plants elsewhere in the world.
Long supply chains
As the production of seafood has become more globalized, its supply chains have stretched longer, making it tougher for consumers and grocers to know whether it was harvested sustainably or legally.
Robert K. Stumberg, professor at Georgetown Law and supply-chain expert, said grocers typically buy from wholesalers and rarely track their suppliers. One other reason may be plausible deniability, he added. “Companies can escape blame or the need to fix problems if they’re unaware of them.”
With government oversight of supply chains sometimes lacking, industry-led certification programs have sought to fill the gap and root out unsustainable, unethical or illegal practices.
But critics say these programs generally focus on environmental crimes and overlook labor abuses on ships. On land, at processing plants or farms, certification programs rarely conduct true spot checks to authenticate the reassurances given by managers, said Allie Brudney, a senior staff attorney at Corporate Accountability Lab, a strategic litigation nonprofit.
Instead, the programs frequently alert companies before inspectors show up. At sea, these programs often rely on self-reported information from ship captains rather than having auditors inspect vessels offshore.
Devan Meserve, a spokesperson for the Global Seafood Alliance, which runs the Best Aquaculture Practices program, defended the value of such inspection programs. She said that her organization represents the “most comprehensive program for farmed seafood,” partly because it covers the “entire aquaculture production chain.”
Protecting workers on the fishing vessels that supply feed mills is, however, an “immense challenge,” Meserve added, because audits occur at port. She added that her organization helps the industry counter illegal and overfishing by requiring feed mills to source most of the fish they use in fishmeal or fish oil from fisheries accredited by certification programs like Marine Trust and Marine Stewardship Council.
The risk of false advertising
“Any accounting of the true impact of aquaculture has to start not with the farm, but with the feed,” said Daniel Pauly, project director of the Sea Around Us initiative at the University of British Columbia. “And that kind of accounting offers a very different picture than the industry offers.”
Since 2020, at least nine lawsuits alleging false advertising have been brought against six seafood companies in six U.S. states. Plaintiffs challenged language such as “sustainable,” “eco-friendly” and “wild-caught,” as well as claims of superior worker-safety standards. Five of the lawsuits resulted in settlements, and the companies paid the plaintiffs more than $2 million.
In at least four cases, the use of fishmeal or fish oil and their link to industrial fishing and ecosystem depletion were central to arguments that the products were not environmentally sustainable. Additional allegations included forced labor on fishing vessels and reliance on harmful pesticides and antibiotics.
The Outlaw Ocean investigation assessed more than 500 seafood companies that made marketing claims that were comparable to — or stronger than — those cited in the lawsuits. Over half of those companies had supply chain ties to fishmeal producers involved in crimes, misconduct and unsustainable fishing practices.
Dana Cleaveley, a research consultant formerly with SeaChoice, a Canadian sustainable-seafood group, said that many industries have already had to begin reckoning with the human rights and environmental abuses buried in their supply chains. She cited “sweatshop garments,” “fair-trade coffee” and “blood diamonds” as examples.
Seafood has been slower to face such scrutiny, though, as the world leans further into aquaculture, that may change, she said, particularly if more governments begin restricting imports tied to illegality or unsustainable practices. She added: “That’s when investors will begin to see material, not just reputational risk, and companies will have to adjust.”
But in some quarters, the troubling costs of fish farming remain unaddressed.
In April 2025, President Trump signed Executive Order 14276, “Restoring American Seafood Competitiveness,” which instructed government officials to reduce regulatory burdens and boost the commercial fishing and aquaculture sectors in the United States.
It made no mention of feed or fishmeal.
Urbina is executive editor of the Outlaw Ocean Project. The reporting for this story was part of a larger investigation conducted by an international team of journalists based at the Outlaw Ocean Project.

Are eurozone bond markets warning of a recession as growth slows?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
05:43:25 UTC
14:43:25 KST

Eurostat's cycle clock, which tracks the economy's phases, flags a sharp slowdown in the eurozone. Bond markets highlight French fiscal stress, sticky inflation and ECB hikes. But that could shift soon.
For most of this year, the story in Europe's bond markets has been about inflation. Prices kept rising, the European Central Bank kept raising interest rates, and investors kept demanding more to lend money to governments.
This autumn, a new word may have entered the conversation: recession.
Eurostat's Business Cycle Clock – a real-time tracker that maps the phases of an economy – showed the eurozone in a sharp slowdown at the end of the third quarter.
Some countries, like Italy, may have already entered a recession, while Germany and France are still facing a downturn.
So is the bond market pricing in the start of an economic contraction?
How bonds usually warn of a recession
When investors expect hard times ahead, they usually do two things.
They move their money to the safest borrower they can find, which in Europe is Germany.
And they bet that the central bank will soon cut interest rates to help the economy.
Both moves push German borrowing costs down. If a recession were really on its way, German yields would be falling.
They are not.
Germany's 10-year yield stood at 3.49% on Thursday afternoon, up from about 2.85% at the start of the year. On 28 September, it reached 3.65%, its highest level in about 17 years.
The two-year yield closely follows what investors expect from the European Central Bank, and it is at 3.07%.
That is well above the ECB's deposit rate of 2.50%. In plain terms, investors still expect rates to go up, not down.
"Bunds are still the natural benchmark investors look to when markets get nervous, so some widening against Germany is exactly what you would expect," Ken Egan, head of European sovereign credit at credit rating agency KBRA, told Euronews Business.
"But it does not look like a full flight to safety, because Bund yields have not fallen materially," he said.
The reason is energy.
The war in the Middle East has pushed up oil and gas prices. Eurozone inflation jumped to 3.8% in September from 3.2% in August, according to Eurostat, and energy prices alone were up almost 19% on a year earlier.
The ECB has already raised rates twice this year, in June and in September. Money markets expect roughly one more increase by December.
The real stress is in France, but it's now broadening out
If the bond market is not pricing in a recession, where is the pressure?
The clearest answer is France.
France's 10-year yield is at 4.88%, about 1.39 percentage points more than Germany pays. At the start of September, the gap was about 0.87 percentage points.
This gap is known as the spread. It is the extra price investors charge for lending to one country rather than to Germany, and it is the bond market's way of measuring trust.
France now pays more to borrow than Italy, whose 10-year yield is 4.60%. Paris also pays about 0.5 percentage points more than Athens.
For most of the euro's history, that would have seemed unthinkable.
The French budget deficit is expected to reach 5.4% of the country's economic output this year. It has been above the EU's 3% threshold for the past six years.
The government presented €43 billion of new savings on 1 October, but it is struggling to win support for them in parliament.
The Economist estimates that stabilising French debt at current borrowing costs would require fiscal tightening worth more than 4% of GDP – roughly ten times the savings lawmakers are currently debating.
France is the centre of the stress, but the pressure is spreading.
Italy's spread over Germany has widened from about 0.84 to 1.12 percentage points since early September.
On Thursday, the Italian 10-year yield briefly touched 4.75%, its highest level in a year.
Spain's spread over Bunds has also widened, to around 61 basis points, as the country heads to a snap general election on 29 November.
For Egan, the move "looks like a mix, and it is difficult to separate exactly how much of the move is France-specific."
"A lot of the broader rise in yields reflects the energy shock and expectations for tighter ECB policy, but France clearly carries an additional fiscal and political premium," he said.
Is this stagflation?
A genuine recession risk would leave clear fingerprints: the two-year Schatz yield dropping below the ECB's 2.50% deposit rate, Bund yields falling as French, Italian and Spanish spreads widen together, and money markets swapping 2027 rate hikes for cuts.
None of that has happened yet.
"The traditional warning sign is an inverted yield curve," Egan said.
"But once a recession is being priced in, the curve would normally start to bull-steepen as markets bring forward rate cuts."
In other words, short-term yields would fall faster than long-term ones as investors bet on rate cuts.
Egan said Bund yields would also fall, periphery and credit spreads would widen more broadly, and purchasing managers' surveys would move "decisively into contraction."
"At the moment, that combination is not really there," he said, noting that Bloomberg's one-year euro-area recession probability of 20% "still points to elevated rather than acute risk."
What markets are pricing in instead looks closer to stagflation, an economy losing momentum while inflation keeps climbing.
That scenario would leave the ECB with no good options.
Hiking further would squeeze indebted governments and a weakening economy. Pausing too early would risk entrenching inflation.
Winter could make things worse before they get better.
European gas storage was about 72% full at the start of October, according to Gas Infrastructure Europe, the lowest for the time of year since records began in 2011 and roughly 15 percentage points below the five-year average. A cold winter would tighten an already strained energy market.
"For the ECB, the difficulty is that inflation has moved back above target without the economy obviously overheating," Egan said.
"If higher energy costs continue to feed through while market yields and financing costs are already restrictive, the casualty may increasingly be weaker demand and growth."
So far, investors have sold European periphery bonds on inflation fears.
If they start buying Bunds on recession fears while still dumping French debt, the ECB will face the dilemma it has spent a decade trying to avoid.

Istanbul Airport has overtaken London Heathrow as the world’s most internationally connected airport in aviation data provider OAG’s Megahubs 2026 index.
The airport rose from second place last year. Heathrow ranked second, followed by Amsterdam Schiphol, Kuala Lumpur and Chicago O’Hare.

Houthi attacks disrupt Saudi flights as allies weigh support
