The fruit and vegetables to look out for this month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
05:00:47 UTC
14:00:47 KST

The fresh fruit and vegetables to add to your shopping list in October
Asparagus is "absolutely sublime" at the moment, according to green grocer Jo Toscano.
Asparagus, snow peas and garden peas are increasingly prominent on shelves as spring sets in.
While no-one doubts the convenience of frozen peas, Effie Ramos from organic market garden Remi's Patch in Naarm/Melbourne says there's something special about the ritual of slowing down and popping the pods open yourself.
University of Newcastle nutrition professor Clare Collins says shopping seasonally can help us to introduce variety into our diets.
"If you eyeball all the veggies and fruit, look at what hasn't visited your trolley for a few weeks," she says.
What can you look for?
Vegetables:
- Asparagus
- Garden peas
- Snow peas
- Broad beans, including broad bean tips
- Broccoli
- Cauliflower
- Asian greens such as Chinese broccoli and bok choy
- Capsicum
- Beetroot
- Fresh garlic
- Celery
Fruit:
- Citrus, such as alfourer mandarins, navel and blood oranges
- Mangoes, as availability increases
Asparagus, peas and broad beans
Asparagus is expected to peak in mid-to-late October, Ms Toscano says.
People tend to avoid the thick asparagus spears, but she says they're "juicy and full of flavour".
White asparagus doesn't offer the "great value" of green asparagus, Ms Toscano says "it is divine". She recommends peeling it as the exterior can be "quite fibrous".
Dr Collins says asparagus works well in an omelette, quiche or with a simple cheese sauce.
Garden peas are also in season.
"Fresh peas sort of stay elevated in price but when they're good they're really good and it's worth it," Ms Toscano says.
When garden peas are fresh and young, she suggests using the pods (after they've been shelled) to flavour homemade vegetable stock or blitzing and sieving that mixture to make an intense pea-flavoured cooking liquid.
Broad beans are also "awesome" right now, Ms Toscano says.
Ms Ramos says the leafy green tip of the broad beans have been popular and are "really good, fresh in a salad".
Brassicas and Asian greens (again)
Broccoli and cauliflower "are pretty good value" and Asian greens such as Chinese broccoli are another good buy, Ms Toscano says.
Dr Collins says brassicas, including cauliflower, broccoli and cabbage, can be divisive because they can taste bitter to "super tasters" — people with a more sensitive sense of taste.
"But the good news, especially for parents, is that [through] repeated exposure you increase your tolerance," she says.
Avoid overcooking the produce and try roasting it or masking the flavour with something like a cheese sauce if someone you are cooking for finds it bitter, she suggests.
Seeing red (capsicum and beetroot)
Ms Toscano says lots of red capsicums are coming from Queensland and that there are "bargains to be had" over the next couple of weeks.
Dr Collins says you can use affordable capsicums and Asian greens in stir-fries.
Ms Ramos says it's a good time for beetroot, which can be added to salads, raw or cooked.
"A lot of people sort of underestimate the power of the leaves of the beets. You can have them raw, or I just blanch them with a little bit of olive oil," she says.
Ms Ramos expects an abundance of spring onions, coriander, parsley, which will decrease prices.
October fruit offerings
Grapes have started but they're still very expensive, Ms Toscano says, and the first stone fruit will begin appearing this month.
"With the confluence of WA and Queensland mango seasons in a few weeks, prices are expected to fall," she says.
Cathy Senn from Sensational Berries in Naarm/Melbourne says supplies of Victorian berries will increase as the month continues, adding to those coming from northern Australia.
"Starting with the strawberries and then we'll go on to raspberries and then later on we'll have the blueberries come on and then the strawberries, the blackberries after that," she says.
Citrus varieties are "diminishing", Ms Senn says, pointing to her "about finished" blood oranges, cara cara oranges and ruby grapefruits.
Dr Collins says at this time of year you can often buy bags of great value lemons and oranges. If she's got people coming over, she likes to cook her lemon-and-orange delicious.
"You use the rind, the more rind the better," she says.
Separating the egg white from the egg yolks is "the tricky bit", but it's also a good opportunity to teach kids or grandkids how to do it.

Russia slashes cancer care as defence spending hits post-Soviet record
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
05:00:40 UTC
14:00:40 KST

The federal cancer programme budget falls from 44.9 billion to 3.87 billion roubles in 2027 — a nearly 40-fold reduction against 2025 levels — as defence spending reaches 35% of all federal expenditure, the highest share since the Soviet Union collapsed.
Russia is cutting funding for its national cancer programme nearly twelvefold in 2027, from 44.9 billion roubles (€470.5m) to 3.87 billion roubles (€40.5m), according to the draft federal budget, as defence spending reaches its highest share since the collapse of the Soviet Union.
The reduction is even sharper compared to last year: the programme received 148.5 billion roubles (€1.5bn) in 2025, meaning federal spending on cancer control would have fallen roughly 38-fold in two years if the budget passes as proposed.
Funding is projected to recover partially thereafter — rising to 5.76 billion roubles in 2028 and 12.78 billion in 2029 — but both figures remain far below current levels.
Since its launch, the federal cancer project has funded diagnostic equipment, cancer centres, and early screening programmes.
Under the new 2027-2029 budget, the remaining money is expected to go mainly to diagnostic and radiology equipment, while specialised units in smaller towns and rural areas face cuts, a distribution likely to deepen an already significant gap between cancer care in major federal centres and outlying regions.
Rerouting roubles
Officials have said some costs will be transferred to the compulsory health insurance system (OMS) and other budget lines rather than eliminated entirely.
Patient organisations and some experts have questioned whether the new mechanisms could fully offset the federal reduction, and noted that shifting costs to regional budgets and the OMS ties the quality of care more directly to the financial strength of individual regions.
The proposed cuts come as new data show Russian cancer patients are already bearing a growing share of treatment costs.
A study by the NGO Movement Against Cancer found that between 2019 and 2025, patients bought roughly one in every six or seven packs of cancer medicines out of pocket. In 2025 alone, household spending on anti-tumour drugs rose from 8.8 billion to 11.4 billion roubles, and the number of packs bought independently increased from five million to 5.8 million.
Around 94% of those drugs are on the list of essential medicines and should be provided free of charge.
The study's authors attribute the out-of-pocket spending not to patients choosing more expensive options — most purchases involved generics — but to supply disruptions and gaps in provision.
Russian law guarantees cancer patients free access to the medicines they need, but in practice, patients and doctors have long reported procurement delays and regional budget shortfalls.
State procurement remains substantial: official figures show the government bought 32.8 million packs of medicines worth 336 billion roubles through the OMS system in 2025. But the trajectory in out-of-pocket spending suggests the burden on patients is already rising ahead of the planned federal cuts.
Defence spending in the 2027 draft budget is set to reach 17.1 trillion roubles, or roughly 35% of all federal expenditure — a post-Soviet record.
More than four years of Moscow's all-out war in Ukraine have progressively shifted Russia's public spending, with civilian programmes including healthcare and medical infrastructure taking a backseat to continued expansion of defence outlays.

Revealed: the ‘black box’ wastewater trade that rakes in millions for UK utility companies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
05:00:39 UTC
14:00:39 KST

Water companies in the UK made more than £340m in revenue last year by pouring billions of litres of industrial and commercial wastewater into sewage treatment works that experts say are not designed to remove most chemicals, leaving pollutants to pass into rivers, seas and farmland.
Water companies in England are required by law to take industrial wastewater and issue permits called “trade-effluent consents” that allow businesses to send it to sewage works, though water companies can refuse applications.
However, no independent regulator oversees the trade-effluent process and there is no central register, so Watershed Investigations, the Guardian and the campaign group River Action compiled a database of 26,000 consents, providing the first ever national picture of the system.
The investigation found an annual total of up to 608bn litres of industrial wastewater entering sewage works from sites such as power stations, pharmaceutical plants, food factories, hospitals, abattoirs and waste facilities.
The permits are issued and enforced by the water companies themselves, with environmental regulators having no direct role. “It’s a bit of a black box,” one industry expert said.
Most sewage works only have biological treatment facilities, which are not designed to remove industrial chemicals, including flame retardants, Pfas, solvents and pharmaceuticals. Some permits on the database feature chemicals such as cyanide, chromium, cadmium and mercury. Watershed has mapped every sewage treatment works and the industrial companies permitted to send waste to each one.
Pollutants that survive treatment are discharged into rivers, lakes and seas as “treated effluent”, while those captured in sewage sludge are spread on farmland as fertiliser. The waste also adds to the overloading of sewer networks that triggers raw sewage spills, which have caused outrage, community protests and calls for the industry to be nationalised so that profits can be reinvested in improving the system rather than going to shareholders.
United Utilities made the most revenue from industrial waste last year, at £61.6m, followed by Yorkshire Water at £48.8m. However, these companies included revenues from tankered waste in their figures, while some others did not. Dŵr Cymru Welsh Water, Scottish Water and Wessex Water said they routed commercial tankered waste through separate companies within their groups.
Thames Water has the largest volume of permitted industrial sewage, at 113bn litres, followed by United Utilities at 105bn litres and Severn Trent Water at 79bn litres.
Across the sector, revenues from receiving industrial and commercial wastewater have risen sharply in five years, with Anglian Water’s increasing by 62%.
The industry expert said water companies had “a financial incentive to accept far more toxic material than they should”.
The permit regime was very old and not fit for purpose, they added. “Currently the Environment Agency doesn’t know exactly how much of this waste is going into waterworks each year.”
Waste handlers also drive tankers carrying industrial effluents, landfill leachate and other liquid wastes to sewage works. An Environment Agency (EA) officer said landfill leachate was its “greatest concern” because of the harmful chemical cocktail it can contain.
Both the officer and the industry expert identified Davyhulme wastewater treatment works in Manchester, operated by United Utilities, and Avonmouth, operated by Wessex Water, as big receivers of tankered waste. “Carriers will drive [long distances] to dispose of their wastes here … You can see lines of tankers queueing outside Avonmouth,” the expert said.
Checks by water companies across the sector can just involve taking a sample and carrying out basic pH and metals analysis, but even more advanced testing does not always pick up a wide range of potentially harmful substances, “and by the time you’ve identified [that] it had something nasty in it, it’s already gone”, the EA officer added.
But “ignorance is no defence”, said the officer. “They should be seeking sufficient information from the producer of that waste to satisfy themselves so they can treat it properly.”
The industry expert said the UK needed a dedicated liquid-waste treatment sector rather than relying on a “dilute and disperse” model.
Amy Fairman, the head of campaigns at River Action, said: “Industrial pollution must not become a lucrative business for water companies … Polluters must be held to account and made to pay, rather than passing the costs and consequences down the line.
“The public has a right to know what is being put into our sewage works and where those pollutants ultimately end up. The government has promised to clean up [England’s] rivers through the clean water bill – it must confront this hidden industrial wastewater trade and address the serious failures exposed by this investigation.”
“Water companies should never profit from pollution,” said a spokesperson for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs. “We know the water industry hasn’t been working in the public interest for far too long and that’s why we are reforming it, including how wastewater is disposed of.”
An EA spokesperson said the trade-effluent framework was “developed over 30 years ago”, before many of today’s concerns about Pfas were fully understood, and that it was working to improve how contaminants in wastewater were managed.
A spokesperson for the trade association Water UK said: “Water companies [in England] are legally obliged to accept trade effluent and charges are set by Ofwat. The Environment Agency sets the permit conditions, but they make no account of the fact that sewers are not designed to treat a range of toxic substances such as forever chemicals and mercury, which is still, sadly, used by many dentists.
“That’s why we have long called for the government to ban these toxic substances and to force the manufacturers to pay the costs of removing them from the environment.”
A United Utilities spokesperson said it had “strict consent and control processes” operating under “regulatory requirements designed to protect public health and the environment” and that it “assesses, monitors and treats wastewater”. It added that tankered waste, including landfill leachate, was accepted only at specifically permitted sites.
NI Water said applications involving “priority substances” were referred to the Northern Ireland Environment Agency, and dedicated teams sampled sewer and tanker effluent to “oversee compliance”.
Scottish Water said it assessed trade-effluent applications based on factors including sewer and treatment capacity, protection of infrastructure and staff, and compliance with environmental standards. All water companies included in this article were contacted for comment.
Companies can also discharge industrial wastewater directly into rivers and seas, but this is subject to permits issued by the environmental regulators.
In England, water companies are regulated by Ofwat and the Environment Agency, with policy set by Defra. Ofwat also covers Wales, but environmental regulation sits with Natural Resources Wales and policy with the Welsh government. Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own regulators and publicly owned water companies, with policy set by their devolved governments.

British households would be £5,000 richer if we were more innovative. Let’s unleash our talents | Gordon Brown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
05:00:39 UTC
14:00:39 KST

The coming 10 years are almost certain to be the decade that sees the greatest scientific breakthroughs in a century. The question is whether advances now under way in AI, quantum computing and biology can address cancer, find ways to treat or prevent dementia, and overcome the growing resistance to antibiotics. Can we find sustainable ways to address our energy needs and protect the environment at the same time? Can AI transform the way we deliver education, health and social care to the benefit of millions, as well as advance modern manufacturing strength? And what role can Britain’s inventors, investors and industrialists play in developing these transformative technologies?
While the US and China are the world’s obvious innovation powerhouses, the UK also has enormous assets, as the Innovation Nation Conference in Manchester addressed by the prime minister, Andy Burnham, will hear today. We are home to four of the world’s top 10 universities and 16 of the top 100, five of which are in Europe’s top 10 for spin-outs, startups based on intellectual property produced through a university’s research. With less than 1% of the world’s population, the UK produces 6% of the world’s research papers, nearly 9% of citations and 12% of the most highly cited research.
Our research expertise is one of the many reasons we have been at the forefront of recent inventions: from AlphaFold, which predicts how proteins behave, to viral-vector vaccine technology and AI that detects cancer as reliably as radiologists. Britain already sits at the intersection of AI, quantum computing and synthetic biology. The question then is: why, having led the first Industrial Revolution, should the UK not be the world’s great innovation nation once again?
We know the public have an entrepreneurial spirit, and back this vision. New polling for this week’s conference finds that 75% of people agree that innovation is essential for creating UK economic growth.
But it is disappointing that only 36% of the British public believes the country is a world leader in science. It is time for innovation to move to the forefront of government policy and the 10-year plan the government is preparing. If we were to raise Britain to Swedish or Japanese levels of innovation intensity we would, over time, leave every household £5,000 better off (according to my calculations), and increase our national income by £150bn a year as higher investment in research and development feeds through into productivity. And a jobs plan on the scale that Our Scottish Future has proposed for Scotland would mean about 3m new jobs across the UK.
We can identify the major hurdles to overcome. While the UK is good at startups and spin-outs, we are slow to turn startups into scale-ups, and even slower to turn scale-ups into global success stories. Per head of population, the US has double the number of $1bn companies and nearly three times as many $10bn-plus companies than the UK. And even when we do scale up at home, three-quarters of venture capital investment comes from overseas.
Turning this around will require a government to keep tackling the bottlenecks that are inevitably created from innovation. Speakers from future-facing companies at today’s conference will set out the steps that we need to consider. These will range from making sure firms can access the money they need to grow from UK investors, to new incentives for investors, to public-private partnerships – as happens in Germany, France and Italy – capitalised by the British Business Bank and the national wealth fund. Competition policy must favour new entrants against vested interests and be aligned with a favourable tax regime, such as through research and development credits that favour companies of all sizes.
Research for the conference has identified 127 innovative clusters covering every region and nation of the UK, many of which will succeed if we are willing to give long-term support to the infrastructure, skills training and research and development support from UK Research and Innovation they need to grow. In order to harness this potential, more power needs to be devolved to enable mayors and regional authorities to act locally while ensuring access to global markets.
Britain does not lack genius or great assets. Every nation, including ours, must do more to find its “lost Einsteins” – the young people in lower-income areas who have the talent but not yet the opportunity to show their creative genius. What we need now is to create a chain of hope that connects all people to intellectual discovery and deployment, to startups and scale-ups, and to global leadership – all aligned around a shared national purpose.
Sixty-four years ago, John F Kennedy declared that the US would lead a nationwide effort to be first on the moon. But the space initiative was not his first choice. He had wanted a national project that everybody could feel part of, and revealed he would have preferred to have chosen a project on Earth – if he could have found one with the same power to inspire a national mission that the whole population could enthusiastically embrace.
Today, we can choose to be the innovation nation. “This generation does not intend to founder in the backwash of the coming age,” said Kennedy of the US. And this generation of Britons has no intention of being left behind as the age of AI accelerates. Today’s event, spearheaded by the prime minister in Manchester – itself a city of innovation – will send a message that we mean to be in the global vanguard; not because, as Kennedy said, it is easy to do, but even though it is hard. For the challenge now is to do more than invent the future. We must invest in it, manufacture it and, wherever possible, own it here in Britain.
- Gordon Brown was UK prime minister from 2007 to 2010

05:00:38 UTC
14:00:38 KST

My go-to cheesecake these days is a burnt Basque. It’s so good it doesn’t even need a biscuit base, which might be the very reason some people aren’t fans. But Basque cheesecakes are rarely too sweet, because the burnt top provides just enough bitterness to balance things out and the insides stay ridiculously creamy. If I can give you one tip, though, it’s to make sure you take it out of the oven while it’s still really wobbly, to get the best set. An overbaked Basque is no fun at all.
Toffee apple Basque cheesecake
I’ve given this an easy autumn spin with a generous topping of lightly spiced toffee apple slices.
Prep 5 min
Cook 1 hr 10 min
Chill Overnight
Serves 12
750g cream cheese
220g caster sugar
1½ tsp vanilla bean paste 
4 large eggs, plus 1 egg yolk
300ml double cream
1 tsp fine sea salt
20g plain flour
For the toffee apples
3 eating apples
60g butter
80g dark brown sugar
½ tsp ground cinnamon
120ml double cream
Heat the oven to 240C (220C fan)/465F/gas 9. Scrunch up two large sheets of baking paper, then smooth them out into the corners of a deep 20cm cake tin.
Put the cream cheese, sugar and vanilla in a large bowl or stand mixer, and beat briefly until smooth. Add the eggs one at a time, followed by the extra yolk, making sure you don’t beat at high speed to avoid incorporating too much air. Stir in the cream and salt.
Scoop about an eighth of the batter into a smaller bowl and sift the flour on top. Mix well to ensure there are no lumps, then scrape it back into the main mixture and stir well to combine.
Pour the batter into the prepared tin and bake for 35-40 minutes, until the top is very well browned and the cheesecake still has a huge wobble. (If the top isn’t dark enough, just put it under a hot grill for a couple of minutes.) Leave the cheesecake to cool to room temperature, then chill in the fridge, ideally overnight. The next day, remove the cheesecake from its tin.
To make the toffee apples, peel and core the apples, then slice them thickly into eighths. Heat the butter in a wide pan, then toss in the apples, turning to coat, and cook for three to four minutes, until they start to soften around the edges. Add the sugar and cinnamon, stir to combine, then, once the sugar has melted, pour in the cream. Cook briefly until the sauce is smooth, let it simmer for a minute, then take off the heat and stir in a pinch of salt.
Let the apples cool, then spoon them and some of the caramel sauce on top of the cheesecake. Serve slices of cheesecake with extra sauce, if you like.

Santorini: Wine, gastronomy and unique experiences beyond the famous sunsets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

At the October tourism forum, GNTO representatives presented the travel preferences of tourists from key European markets, and local authorities are preparing 32 short videos to highlight lesser-known aspects of the Greek island.
With a new digital campaign built around 32 short videos, Santorini is seeking to broaden its international tourism profile, highlighting experiences that are often overshadowed by its famous sunsets and luxury accommodation.
The Greek island, renowned for its whitewashed houses perched above the volcanic caldera and its unique views over the Aegean, aims to attract travellers interested in gastronomy, wine, culture, nature and everyday local life.
The new initiative was unveiled at the GNTO Santorini Tourism Forum 2026, held from 5-8 October, with the participation of representatives of the Greek National Tourism Organisation (GNTO), local authorities, industry professionals and around 30 journalists from international travel media.
During the forum, GNTO executives active in key European markets presented the travel trends they are recording in their countries, looking for ways to link Santorini’s already powerful reputation with different types of experience and trips outside the peak summer season.
From volcanic vineyards to gastronomy and culture
Santorini boasts a distinctive wine-making tradition, closely tied to the island’s volcanic soil and climatic conditions.
For centuries, winegrowers have used the technique known as the "kouloura", training the vines into low, circular basket-like shapes to protect the grapes from strong winds and intense sunlight.
The local Assyrtiko grape variety has gained international recognition, and many wineries now offer tours of their vineyards, visits to production facilities and wine tastings.
Santorini’s culinary identity also features hallmark products such as fava, tiny cherry tomatoes and white aubergine, all cultivated in the island’s distinctive terrain.
The importance of local gastronomy has also been recognised by the Michelin Guide, which announced in December 2025 that Santorini and Thessaloniki will be added to its Greek selection for 2026, alongside Athens.
Beyond food and wine, visitors can explore the archaeological site of Akrotiri, a prehistoric settlement preserved beneath layers of volcanic ash, discover traditional villages such as Megalochori, or follow hiking trails overlooking the caldera.
Local authorities also want to strengthen activities such as cooking and pottery classes, which allow travellers to connect with local production and culture.
"Visitors do not simply tick off a standard sightseeing itinerary; they go home holding on to the moments that moved them," said Georgia Nomikou, president of the Municipal Council and the Tourism Committee of Thira, speaking to the Athens-Macedonian News Agency.
She revealed that production is already under way on 32 short social media videos, focusing on the moments and experiences a visitor can enjoy on the island.
What travellers from European markets are looking for
The diversification of travel preferences was a central theme of the forum’s discussions, with GNTO representatives outlining the trends they observe in Europe’s main markets.
In the United Kingdom, one of Santorini’s key markets, head of the GNTO office Eleni Skarveli noted that luxury remains a strong element of the island’s image, but interest is growing in gastronomy, wellness, family trips and holidays that combine several Greek islands.
Similarly, GNTO's representative in France, Emmy Anagnostopoulou, stressed the appeal for visitors who want to discover local cuisine, wineries and cultural heritage.
"These are not tourists who stay shut inside a hotel wearing an all-inclusive wristband; they get out, explore and spend money in the local economy," she said, describing the preferences she observes in the French travel market.
She also underlined that demand for travel outside July and August can help attract more visitors in spring and autumn.
In Austria and Germany, according to GNTO representative Stavroula Skaltza, there is clear interest in wine tourism, gastronomy and wellness, while repeat visitors are looking for new experiences in a destination they already know.
For the Scandinavian markets, GNTO representative Eftychia Aivalioti highlighted the importance of nature, hiking and activities linked to quality and sustainable tourism.
These assessments are based on reports from GNTO offices in the respective countries and reflect the trends that the organisation’s staff identify in their markets.
More visitors in spring and autumn
One of the main goals of the new strategy is to boost tourism activity outside the peak summer months, attracting visitors who are interested in experiences that go beyond a traditional beach holiday.
The development of wine tourism, cultural visits and nature-based activities can offer additional reasons to travel to Santorini during periods with fewer tourists.
Air connectivity is also a key factor. According to the GNTO representative in France, Transavia flights to Santorini have been extended until November, improving options for autumn trips.
New connections are also planned from the British market. Jet2 has announced weekly flights from Leeds-Bradford Airport to Santorini, from 6 May to 7 October 2027.

LRT English Newsletter: ‘Great people’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

LRT English Newsletter – October 9, 2026
You know you live in a small country when an offhand remark by the US president makes front-page news. Donald Trump has been asked about setting up a military base in Lithuania, to which he responded with a non-comital “we’ll look at it”, setting off a week-worth of discourse about what it means and how Vilnius should exploit the moment.
At issue, of course, is Lithuania’s long-term goal of involving the US as much as possible in its own security, even as the Americans are signalling intentions to cut presence in Europe. That requires being exemplary allies, sometimes leading to comical situations. For example, Vilnius was hosting an international conference on disinformation this week that included a panel about how Washington, too, is engaging in “information manipulation and interference”. The incensed State Department conveyed its dissatisfaction to several allies sponsoring the event, according to Politico, and Lithuania’s foreign ministry obligingly withdrew its logos from the conference materials. How dare anyone suggest disinformation is done by our allies, not just our enemies, Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys commented.
Lithuania also took a more serious step to engage American forces. This week, the Seimas held the first of two votes on crossing out an article from the constitution that prohibits weapons of mass destruction (and foreign bases) on Lithuanian soil. The initiative, prompted by vague suggestions that the US might move its nuclear warheads from Germany further east – faces virtually no opposition, save for a few MPs that would prefer a decision by referendum.
The talk of US bases and nuclear weapons, understandably, drew reactions from Moscow – Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov called it “a step toward escalation”.
LESS IS MORE
The government is beginning work on its most important piece of legislation, next year’s budget bill. How generously will Vilnius spend on defence (and tangentially related things) and will it stay in the “5% club”? Under preliminary proposals, Lithuania’s military budget should increase by 36 million euros next year, although it will represent a slightly smaller share of the GDP (still above 5%) than this year – something that will surely upset defence hawks.
There are indications, however, that Lithuania may not be able to sustain that much military spending for long. Preliminary calculations indicate that it will – for the first time in a long time – substantially exceed the 3-percent deficit limit imposed by eurozone rules. Raising taxes being a strong taboo (some creative exceptions notwithstanding), the social democrat-led government may see prodigious military spending clash with its other priorities.
KALININGRAD BORDER
Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas has announced that the military will be helping to guard Lithuania’s western border with Kaliningrad. You may recall that it was the eastern border with Belarus that has been seeing all the action, while the Kaliningrad side has been relatively calm. As Katelynas explained, the move is being made in anticipation of a mobilisation in Russia that could send some military-age men to seek asylum in Lithuania.
There have also been discussions about the “Kaliningrad transit” – the special arrangement allowing Russians to travel between the exclave and mainland Russia. The Seimas considered a proposal to cut the allowed transit time from 24 to six hours, eventually rejecting it. Katelynas now says he wants to monitor the transiting Russians so that they don’t stray from pre-approved routes.
There have also been calls to completely close the Russian border over a reported incident of pneumonic plague in Siberia. The authorities say, however, that the risk of the disease spreading to Lithuania is low.
NATIONAL ROW OVER MIGRATION
Last Saturday, two opposing rallies were held in Vilnius – separated only by a street and a line of policemen – one calling for stopping immigration, the other one censuring racism and xenophobia purportedly spread by the migration opponents.
While both rallies were far from massive – attended by hundreds rather than thousands – migration is proving to be a salient issue. Vytautas Sinica, the nationalist MP who organised one of the rallies, is now polling third in next year’s race for the mayorship of Vilnius.
The current government, while overall not vehemently anti-migration, is declaring intentions to cut annual migrant worker quotas. Meanwhile, business reps have organised a media event to present their warnings of the economic perils that a crackdown on migration might cause. While no one disputes that Lithuania is facing acute labour shortages, politicians still talk about enticing Lithuanians to return as their preferred solution.
EDITOR’S PICKS
– If you go to Bari, look out for this new portrait of a sixteenth-century Polish-Lithuanian queen.
– Did you know that Lithuania experiences natural earthquakes? It took some time to prove they do occur.
– Should we stop turning clocks twice a year? And if so, should we keep the summer or the winter time?
– A massive marine painting looted by the Nazis is back in Klaipėda. Well, kind of back.
– A new way to observe Kaunas.

Gallery: Estonian conducts charity Hamburg shows with Calum Scott, Kontra K
On October 1–3, conductor Kristjan Järvi led three Hamburg charity concerts with the Lufthansa Orchestra featuring British pop star Calum Scott and German rapper Kontra K.
The three-night run at Hamburg's Deutsches SchauSpielHaus was part of Channel Aid – Live in Concert 2026, with seven musicians from Järvi's band Nordic Pulse also joining the orchestra.
The concerts with Kontra K marked his first time performing his music with an orchestra, selling out many of the more than 200 movie theaters across Germany, Australia and Switzerland that streamed them live.
Calum Scott's concert, with orchestral arrangements by Järvi's team, drew nearly 100,000 viewers worldwide on YouTube and TikTok.
'Estonians are already making a mark'
The collaboration was based on Järvi's developing orchestral rituals approach, in which musicians from Nordic Pulse perform as part of the host orchestra rather than as a separate ensemble.
Manager Nora Liisa Suislepp said the Hamburg project clearly shows the scale of what Estonian musicians and creators are doing internationally.
"We often talk in Estonia about how our artists could reach a wider global audience, but sometimes it's worth recognizing Estonians are already doing really exciting things and making a real mark internationally," Suislepp said.
Channel Aid – Live in Concert is a charity concert series supporting children, youth and disabled people, with proceeds from its digital channels funding projects run by the Lufthansa Group nonprofit help alliance.

Taiwan annual export value set to top NT$28.74 trillion for first time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
04:58:22 UTC
13:58:22 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s total export value is on track to exceed NT$28.74 trillion (US$900 billion) this year for the first time, the Ministry of Finance said Thursday.
September exports reached a record NT$2.79 trillion, up 60.9% from the same period a year earlier. The increase marked the 35th consecutive month of annual growth, the longest streak on record, according to RTI.
The ministry attributed the sustained growth to several factors. Global investment in technological innovation and AI has helped offset geopolitical uncertainties and inflation concerns, supporting a relatively stable global economic outlook.
Meanwhile, emerging applications have driven upgrades to electronic components, boosting demand for more advanced products and increasing export values and volumes. Capacity constraints across the electronics supply chain have also kept prices elevated, while new mobile devices and consumer electronics launches have prompted a wave of restocking.
Information, communication and audiovisual products, along with electronic components, remained the country’s two main export drivers in September. Both categories recorded their second-highest monthly export values on record, at NT$1.25 trillion and NT$994 billion, respectively.
Looking ahead, the ministry expects exports to grow 40-44% year-on-year in October, reaching between NT$2.72 trillion and NT$2.8 trillion. If monthly exports remain at a conservative NT$2.56 trillion through the end of the year, full-year exports would exceed NT$28.74 trillion, according to CNA.
Last year, exports reached a record NT$20.47 trillion, up 34.9% from 2024. The ministry said the continued development of AI and the rapid expansion of its applications had driven upgrades to electronic components, complementing Taiwan’s competitive advantages in technology industries, according to Yahoo Stocks.
The ministry acknowledged that its earlier forecasts for this year had been more conservative, as they were based on historical trends that might not fully reflect the scale of AI-driven growth. It added that related investment and applications were expected to continue expanding.

African countries urge Kyiv to return citizens who fought for Russia
African countries are urging Ukraine to return their citizens held in prisoner-of-war camps after being captured whilst fighting on Russia's side.
Source: Bloomberg, citing Musalia Mudavadi, Cabinet Secretary for Foreign & Diaspora Affairs of the Republic of Kenya
Details: The Kenyan government is negotiating the return of five prisoners, Mudavadi told MPs in Nairobi on Thursday 8 October, adding that President William Ruto had contacted Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy about the matter. Botswana's Ministry of Foreign Affairs told Bloomberg earlier that it was seeking the return of one of its citizens from a Ukrainian camp.
African countries said that some of their citizens had been lured to Russia under false pretences and then forced into military service. According to the governments, the men had been promised civilian jobs, such as drivers, security guards or cooks.
Kenya wants the men to be recognised as "victims of international human trafficking" rather than prisoners of war, Mudavadi said. The men "report having been recruited under false promises of employment".
In a statement on Thursday, the Zimbabwean government expressed concern about deceptive cross-border recruitment practices. "Tragically, some recruits have been deployed to active battlefronts in host nations without any prior military training," the statement said, without specifically mentioning Russia or Ukraine.
According to the Ukrainian authorities, Russia has recruited more than 28,000 foreign nationals from 135 countries to fight on its side, more than 5,000 of whom have been killed. The Ukrainian forces have captured fighters from 51 countries.
Ukraine is holding at least 213 foreign nationals as prisoners of war, excluding Russians and North Koreans. Thirty-seven of these are Africans.
Russia has never publicly acknowledged using foreign mercenaries, maintaining its official position that it has sufficient manpower to wage the war.
According to Mudavadi, the youngest Kenyan held in a camp in Ukraine is 23. "The circumstances of their recruitment and conscription are consistent with trafficking in persons," he added.
In a report to parliament, the foreign minister said that around 84 Kenyans had been killed or are missing, while another 34 are receiving medical treatment in Russia. To date, a total of 62 Kenyans who have taken part in the war have been repatriated.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Su Chiao-hui (蘇巧慧), the DPP’s New Taipei mayoral candidate, said Thursday she plans to breathe new life into traditional Chinese medicine culture through industry upgrades.

Su said disputes over licensing requirements for related businesses had persisted for years following amendments to the Pharmaceutical Affairs Act, leaving many family members unable to legally take over family businesses. In 2019, she worked with DPP Legislator Chang Hung-lu (張宏陸) to help resolve licensing issues by securing a ministry interpretation, according to CNA and LTN.

She sees these dishes as an accessible way to introduce traditional remedies to the public and make them a more familiar part of everyday life.
Su also plans to help traditional medicine shops modernize while preserving their character. Building on a previous city renovation initiative, she aims to connect shop owners with design professionals to improve store layouts and interiors. The city would also work with industry associations to provide training and technical support for adopting e-commerce and AI tools.
The proposed upgrades come as Taiwan’s imports of Chinese medicinal materials have fallen 40% over the past 15 years. The National Union of Chinese Medicine Associations attributed the decline to the shrinking number of traditional Chinese medicine shops and warned that the supply of medicinal materials could eventually be disrupted, according to CNA.
Ma Yi-tsai (馬逸才), the association’s honorary chair, said shop owners had told him that most of their customers were over 50, with few younger people visiting their stores. Ma said Taiwan now has about 7,000 Chinese medicine shops, a number that could fall to 2,000 over the next decade as many operate at a loss and struggle to survive.

As freezing winter approaches, Kyiv residents look for shelter elsewhere
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
05:53:50 BST
13:53:50 KST

Russian strikes and approaching winter force some in Kyiv to pack bags and flee
- Published
As Russia's attacks on Ukraine's cities intensify and autumn's cooler temperatures hint at another tough winter to come, Ukrainians are wrestling with how to meet the twin challenges ahead: Russian drone and missile strikes and the biting cold.
"It was a very difficult winter last year in Kyiv," says mother of two Mariia Shostak, who is now packing her bags and leaving her small flat.
With prolonged periods of sub-zero temperatures and frequent power cuts brought about by Russia's attack on the country's power grid, last winter was one of the hardest so far.
"There were some days and weeks that were unbearable. I started thinking I'm not going through another winter like this."
Mariia is not even waiting for winter. Russia's latest assaults on the capital have forced her hand.
"Everything changed in late August and the beginning of September, when Kyiv started being attacked around the clock," she said.
"Earlier, the drones and missiles were intercepted somewhere on the outskirts. Now it was happening in the centre, right above our heads."
After weeks of escalating Russian attacks, which by the end of September had included petrol stations, power plants and key bridges over the Dnipro river, Kyiv mayor Vitaly Klitschko said the city was facing a "very dramatic situation".
The attacks, he said, were "tearing Kyiv apart".
Mariia's children, four-year-old Artur and Kira, who's two, were both born after Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.
Unwilling to subject them to another miserable, dangerous winter, she's taking them abroad. They plan to spend the winter in Hurghada, on Egypt's Red Sea coast. It's cheaper than Europe, Mariia explains, and warmer too.
"I don't feel safe in Ukraine in any way," she says.
Polls show that many Ukrainians are feeling the same way, even if not everyone has yet made such a radical decision.
A September survey by the Gradus research company found that 40% of Ukrainians were considering relocating if living conditions continued to deteriorate; 35% said they would not move elsewhere, while 25% were undecided.
"People are thinking about a combination of stress factors," Evgeniya Blyznyuk, Gradus's founder and CEO, told us. "Not just about electricity and blackouts like last winter. Russians are targeting big logistics centres, which means that the population is worrying about products, about food during the winter."
Russia's recent attacks on Kyiv's bridges, petrol stations and schools have increased the sense of danger and foreboding.
For families with young children, the situation feels especially urgent.
Last winter, Iryna, who asked us not to use her surname, says her three-year-old daughter Polina found it hard to cope.
"Sometimes we didn't have heating for weeks and the temperature inside the apartment was zero or five degrees," she tells us. "So being here with a little child that is sick all the time was not OK."
The family's recent experiences have only compounded Polina's difficulties.
"We had two missile attacks this year," Iryna says.
The first explosion, in early June, blew out several windows in the family's home on the north-western edge of Kyiv. A month later, after some of the damage had been repaired, a second blast, close to the foot of their 10-storey apartment block, propelled a wave of earth into the flat, forcing the family to move into temporary accommodation.
Polina's health has deteriorated. She suffers from extreme anxiety, which has brought on bouts of incontinence, vomiting and uncontrollable shaking.
"Now we have this neurological problem with her so that's the reason we're thinking about leaving," Iryna says. "There are new symptoms after each shelling."
Iryna, whose husband is in the army, has not yet decided where to go. Her work with an international NGO may allow her to work remotely from Poland.
"Our president says that it is better to leave Kyiv because this is target number one," she says.
For other Kyiv residents, the solution lies closer to home: in the vast open spaces of Ukraine's countryside.
Olena Konoplia tells us she spent weeks looking for a suitable location before settling on a cottage in a rural community two hours outside the capital.
"I decided the better option will be a little village without any factories, any [warehouses] and any railway stations," Olena explains.
"Everything that can be a Russian target."
On the day we visited, Olena was busy ferrying supplies to the house and supervising the installation of a new door.
In keeping with Ukrainian tradition, a priest has already been around to bless her new home.
The cottage has gas-powered convection heaters, but in an adjacent barn a stack of firewood will help to keep Olena warm in the event of power cuts. She has already installed high-speed internet, necessary for her work at a Kyiv-based charitable foundation.
At a time when air raid sirens sound constantly in Kyiv and explosions can be heard almost every day, the peace and quiet of the village is what Olena says she needs most.
"After several nights here, when I can sleep, just sleep, without any explosions, without any sirens, I feel better," she says. "I can work, write my articles, I feel good."
Olena's elderly mother will soon be joining her.
"She lives in a pretty dangerous district in Kyiv and it's harmful for her health," she explains.
Of course, not everyone can afford a cottage in the countryside or a months-long trip abroad.
Most Kyiv residents will do what they can to survive another tough winter in the capital, just as they have before.
The authorities are taking steps to prepare. Some of Kyiv's most vulnerable citizens – the elderly and women with young children – are being offered places in converted sanatoriums and rehabilitation centres in the city's forested outskirts.
Meanwhile, a network of around 15 small-scale power plants has been constructed around the city over the past 18 months in an effort to shore up Kyiv's battered power grid.
The plants, constructed in fortified bunkers and protected from drone attack by huge steel cages, are each capable of providing electricity and heat to several hundred of the city's high-rise apartment blocks.
But with energy companies already talking about scheduled power cuts and supermarkets experiencing periodic shortages of some goods, the pressures to leave are growing.
Evgeniya Blyznyuk says she does not expect to see a mass exodus from the capital and says most people have yet to make up their minds, reluctant to jeopardise their jobs or take children out of school.
"They will postpone it until conditions become really unliveable," she says.
Additional reporting by Mariana Matveichuk and Anastasiia Levchenko.

From barbershops to nature courses: How community-driven campaigns are rethinking men’s mental health
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
04:53:43 UTC
13:53:43 KST

As waiting lists for mental health care continue to grow, community-driven campaigns across Europe have been finding unique ways to support men in particular.
At a small barbershop in Brixton, south London, men’s lives are being transformed. Not just through a new haircut or fresh beard trim — but by opening up about their mental health.
“People confide in barbers and often share things that perhaps they wouldn't with their partners or friends,” Ben Theophanous, owner and co-founder of Curfew Grooming, told Euronews Health.
“The relationship is often strong, but there is an element of superficiality that provides a unique platform for sharing feelings,” he added.
Curfew Grooming is one of more than 100 barbershops across the United Kingdom to receive Mental Health First Aid (MHFA) training through the 12th Man Campaign — a community-driven initiative founded in 2013 by mental health nurse Nick Little and his late friend Oz Osborne.
The campaign takes its name from the football term for a team’s fans and provides support for men by normalising talking about mental health in everyday spaces.
These spaces include barbershops and tattoo studios — places where there’s already a one-on-one dynamic. Employees who volunteer take an online course, which guides them through how to spot signs that a customer might be struggling; how to ask meaningful questions and how to direct them to the right resources if needed.
“We're just handing the responsibility to men in society to look out for their friends and their family. To recognise mental health more in their lives and to talk about it,” Nick Little told Euronews Health.
Nearly 1 in 7 people around the world are living with a mental health condition, but men are still less likely than women to reach out for help — and three times more likely to die by suicide, according to the Office of National Statistics.
Those who are looking for professional help encounter another issue: long waiting times. For example In the UK, people were eight times more likely to wait for over 18 months for mental health treatment on the National Health Service than those waiting for physical health treatments, according to data analysed by the charity Rethink in 2025.
Increasingly, community-led initiatives are stepping in as a way to fill these gaps in the system — not to replace professional services, but to put more preventative measures in place before people reach crisis.
“Let's put trust in society and invest in our community businesses, because that's the front line,” Little said.
Engaging men with nature
Similar community-based and male-focused initiatives are happening all across Europe.
In Denmark, many of these have used the Vildmandsprojektet (Wild Man) project as a blueprint; a 9- to 12-week nature-based rehabilitation program for men in crisis.
Co-founded by nature psychologist Simon Høegmark in 2014, its development was partly inspired by Høegmark’s own personal experiences with mental health.
Over a decade ago, he travelled to Norway to hike and regain his “footing.”
“After several days of heavy thoughts, I reached the summit of a mountain overlooking Lysefjord. For a brief moment, the thought of jumping crossed my mind,” he recalled.
But as quickly as these thoughts took over, the views of Lysefjord became awash with light — and something inside Simon shifted.
“The sun broke through the clouds, illuminating the entire landscape. I experienced a moment of self-forgetfulness, a sense of connection, and a love for life,” Høegmark told Euronews Health.
While the experience did not immediately resolve his psychological crisis, it allowed the beauty of nature to take over — its stillness settling the thoughts in his head and replacing them with a sense of hope.
“I saw my situation more clearly. I decided to investigate why encountering nature can affect people so profoundly, and how nature can be professionally utilised as a framework for recovery and rehabilitation,” he said.
After launching the Vildmandsprojektet project in 2014, Høegmark conducted many studies alongside a team of researchers to monitor its effects. One such study involved 114 men, who showed significant improvements in their physical and mental quality of life, as well as a reduction in self-perceived stress symptoms after taking the course.
“These improvements were evident immediately after the course and — on several measures — six months later,” Høegmark said, also noting a lasting sense of community even after the courses had ended.
“This serves as a vital bridge between a time-limited public program and everyday life, where habits and relationships need to endure,” he added.
The project ran from 2014 for a period of over eight years, during which time around 700 men participated in its courses. Since then, its Nature, Body, Mind, and Community (NBMC) method has been adopted by more than 50 Danish municipalities and adapted for both men and women.
While Høegmark cautions that Vildmandsprojektet was never intended to replace psychiatric treatment, it has proved itself to be an accessible format for men that might otherwise be reluctant to engage with mental health services.
“My professional interpretation is that [the NBMC method] can strengthen participants' sense of agency and ownership regarding their own wellbeing,” said Høegmark.
“However, the method must be used as a supplement within a cohesive health service framework that includes clear referral pathways should a participant require more specialised care,” he said.
The growing importance of community-driven care
Alongside local initiatives, nationwide healthcare systems have also begun looking into community-driven care as a tool to alleviate wait times.
One example of this is social prescribing, which the NHS has been offering as a way to connect patients with activity groups. These can include gardening, walking, art and crafting clubs — anything that encourages reconnection with the outside world.
“The reason I'm so in favour of this more community-driven style of support is that the format can be more relevant to everyday life, more aligned with people's hobbies and things that they normally would do anyway,” Stella Chan, a professor of evidence-based psychological therapies at the University of Reading in England, tells Euronews Health.
“It's less stigmatising and also easier to assess,” she added, which can in turn help ease resistance.
While some have argued that social prescribing is not enough — and avoids addressing more serious underlying societal issues like economic inequality — research suggests it’s become an important way to bridge medical and non-medical support.
“Mental ill-health and mental disorders are among our major global health challenges, and we need both robust treatment and far more prevention,” Høegmark said.

US midterms: key takeaways from Senate debates in Michigan, Georgia and Maine

- 1. Affordability, affordability, affordability Affordability was a major topic across all three debates on Thursday night, as voters consistently name the cost of goods, gas, housing and healthcare as their top concerns in this year’s midterms. “Can you afford your gas? Can you afford your groceries under this guy who’s going to rubber stamp everything Donald Trump tells him to rubber stamp?” El-Sayed asked during the Michigan debate, the first of two in one of this cycle’s most fiercely contested races. Both Rogers and El-Sayed said they support suspending a fuel tax to alleviate costs, while El-Sayed argued that the Iran war, which was driving up gas prices, needs to end. El-Sayed attacked Rogers for growing his personal wealth while in office as a US representative. Rogers called El-Sayed “bought off” by billionaire George Soros, Hamas and Hezbollah. “We cannot afford Abdul, and we cannot risk his ideology,” Rogers said.
In Georgia, Ossoff repeatedly asked Collins to justify his support for Trump’s global tariff policies, which the senator said have “crushed Georgia families” and “strangled” economic growth. “Let’s see if he has the courage to explain his votes,” Ossoff said, adding later: “Still have not heard an explanation for the tariffs.” Collins, who is trying to cut into Ossoff’s lead, blamed inflation on Biden administration policies, singling out spending measures that his opponent had supported. Later in Maine, where polls show a tight race, Jackson focused his remarks on pocketbook issues, including the sharp spike in heating oil costs and high energy prices. Collins defended her record and argued that Maine had benefited from the $50bn rural health transformation fund that was appended to Trump’s signature tax cut and spending bill, the so-called Big Beautiful bill.
- 2. It gets personal in Georgia In the Georgia debate, a question about data centers erupted into a pointed, personal exchange between Ossoff and Collins. “Mike Collins voted to take that money out of your pocket and out of your community and give it instead to data center developers,” Ossoff said. He then accused Collins of being a “bigot” who has “hired half the Third Reich” – a reference to the congressman’s history of employing staffers who have expressed white nationalist, antisemitic, and extremist views online. “If John Lewis were marching today from Selma to Montgomery,” Ossoff said of the late civil rights icon and long-serving Georgia congressman, “Mike Collins would be grabbing a billy club. His office has been in cahoots with some of the most notorious white supremacists on the country.” Collins was asked directly about his son-in-law’s social media posts promoting white nationalist and antisemitic views. “You know, Rick, that’s my family,” Collins replied. “That’s the craziness that Jon Ossoff has been spewing out there.” Collins noted that a New York man had recently been charged after threatening to kill him, and added: “I’ve condemned racism, antisemitism, hate; I don’t care where the source is. And I tell him that too, it’s wrong. We have no place in this world for that.” Collins, meanwhile, sought to cast Ossoff as “radical” and an “extremist” whose record in the Senate had left the state “less safe, more expensive and worse off”.
- 3. Labatt and Red Wings in Michigan Tariffs were also a topic of heated debate in Michigan, which shares hundreds of miles of border with Canada. This week, Rogers publicly backtracked on previous support for Trump’s tariffs on the US’s northern neighbor, saying in a campaign ad that “Canada is not our enemy” and that the “tariff war” needed to end now. During Thursday night’s debate, Rogers said he had spoken to the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, this week to advocate for a deal between the two countries. There are tariffs in place that are “too high and not helpful for us”, Rogers said. El-Sayed said he supports targeted, logical tariffs that protect Michigan manufacturing, but nothing like the “ham-fisted, chaotic, self-serving” tariffs Trump put in place. He called out Rogers for “flip-flopping” on the issue, saying he was only reversing his stance because of “sagging poll numbers”. “He’s doing an ad drinking a Labatt and talking about the Red Wings, pretending like he was not for this the entire time,” El-Sayed said. “Be serious, my guy.”
- 4. Accusations fly in Maine In Maine, discussions about gas prices and the war in Iran raised notable tension in the second debate between Jackson and Collins, who is seeking a sixth term in her seat.
“She’s the Chairman of Appropriations,” Jackson said. “Money has to come through them for these wars – she still can do something.”
Collins, who plans to continue leading the Appropriations committee if re-elected, said she had repeatedly supported war powers resolutions to halt Trump’s military action in Iran. But Jackson pushed further, accusing the senator and her husband of profiting from the war. She could use her leverage to stop this war, but instead they’re making money,” he said, prompting a furious response from Collins, who called the allegation “absolutely outrageous”. “You owe me an apology,” she said.
- 5. Reproductive rights under the spotlight in Maine In Maine, both candidates were also pressed to address inconsistencies in their positions on reproductive rights, a crucial issue for voters in the state. “Our records have changed,” Jackson said. “Mine has gotten better – hers has gotten worse.” He pointed to Collins’ vote to confirm supreme court justice Brett Kavanaugh, who helped overturn Roe v Wade in 2022. Collins, one of just two Republican senators who supports abortion rights, has said she does not regret her vote for Kavanaugh, even though she believed he had given her private assurances before his 2018 confirmation that he would not overturn the landmark ruling.
Collins sought to turn the issue back on her opponent, noting his past stances on abortion that have left many voters wary.
“From 2000 until he ran for the house seat in 2013 was very anti-choice,” she said, accusing Jackson of having held “extremist” views on abortion. “He was for a bill that would not allow abortion when the mother’s life was at risk.”
She also pointed to legislation she helped write that sought to “codify Roe v Wade nationwide,” but the bill never made it passed the Senate.
- 6. Mittens off in Michigan In Michigan, Rogers repeatedly attacked El-Sayed by attempting to tie him to Muslim terrorist groups, including Hamas, and suggested government surveillance would only bother someone if he or his family had something to hide. Rogers brought up El-Sayed’s mom and sister, prompting El-Sayed to say at one point that Rogers should just come out and say what he’s been dancing around all night, after Rogers’ repeated references to terrorist groups. “He wants this to be about anything but his own record,” El-Sayed said. Rogers claimed El-Sayed refused to condemn a terrorist attack in Michigan earlier this year and the 7 October Hamas terrorist attacks in Gaza, although El-Sayed said he had condemned both. But, El-Sayed added: “I’m not somebody who tries to make political theater out of other people’s pain.” He also retorted to Rogers: “Did you sell your yachts?” Rogers responded: “I never owned a yacht in Florida, brother.” After a 30-second commercial break, moderator Rick Albin said that in his 30 years of hosting debates, he’d never seen the sparring continue during the break, but tonight, it had.

ICE Agent at NYC Shooting Has History of Alleged Violence and Illegal Arrests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
04:46:11 UTC
13:46:11 KST

An Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent on the scene of a shooting in upper Manhattan on Thursday has repeatedly been accused in federal court of unlawful arrests and using force during arrests in New York and Minneapolis, a WIRED investigation finds.
On Thursday afternoon, ICE agents shot a man, identified by city authorities as Oscar Belgal, in Manhattan’s Marble Hill neighborhood, near the Bronx. Mayor Zohran Mamdani said agents surrounded the man’s car, in which a 5-year-old child was sitting, before firing multiple rounds—as many as seven, witnesses told local media. Belgal, the New York Police Department said, was hospitalized after reportedly being shot in the neck. The child appeared unharmed.
Footage from the scene shows a man in a high-visibility yellow construction vest brandishing a modified AR-15-style rifle with a pistol grip, sling, and holographic sights. That man, according to court documents, social media posts, and publicly available personal information reviewed by WIRED, is Brenden Cuni—an ICE supervisor with the agency’s National Fugitive Operations team who has been involved in several arrests in the New York City region and Minneapolis during Operation Metro Surge last winter.
Cuni identified himself as an ICE agent to NYPD officers, a law enforcement source tells WIRED, and was the only federal agent captured on video brandishing a weapon on scene. In a statement, the Department of Homeland Security claims that ICE agents were attempting to apprehend an undocumented immigrant from the Dominican Republic with a prior conviction for grand larceny.
A WIRED review of federal court cases, social media, and other public records suggests that Cuni has repeatedly been at the center of illegal ICE street arrests in New York and beyond. Court filings accuse him of using a Taser on a handcuffed man, while activists have alleged he is one of the agents seen forcing a pregnant woman to the ground during a Minneapolis operation. In recent months, federal judges have repeatedly found arrests involving Cuni unlawful. One judge called an arrest warrant he signed “fraudulent,” while another said that video evidence contradicts his sworn account of an arrest; in a third case, the government withdrew his sworn statements as inaccurate.
Cuni has been a DHS agent for nearly a decade. According to court declarations he signed, Cuni began his federal law enforcement career with Customs and Border Protection as a Border Patrol agent in San Diego in 2018 before becoming a deportation officer in 2020. In December 2024, he was promoted to a supervisory detention and deportation officer, and in May 2025, he joined the National Fugitive Operations team.
Cuni’s work history before his time with DHS remains unclear. Felician University, a private Catholic university in New Jersey, listed him as a member of its 2018 baseball roster. On that site, Cuni lists his home town as New Rochelle—a suburb just north of the Bronx.
Cuni has been named in multiple lawsuits alleging violent arrests, both first reported last spring by The City and Documented as part of an investigation into hundreds of ICE street arrests in the New York area. Lawyers for a 21-year-old Bronx man claim that during his arrest in October last year, Cuni tripped him hard enough to break a tooth, then shocked him with a Taser about six times while he was handcuffed on the ground, and later called him a “maldito Mexicano”—damned Mexican. A medical record, obtained by THE CITY and Documented, noted injuries “from taser by ICE agents.”
The following month, another man alleged that ICE agents tackled and shocked him with a Taser three times during an arrest in Queens. According to the man’s petition, ICE’s arrest report lists Cuni among the arresting officers and acknowledges agents used a Taser. The filings do not say who fired it.
Court records also place Cuni in Minneapolis last December, leading a three-person ICE team at a scene where 60 to 70 people had gathered. Agents were trying to arrest a woman who had spray-painted an ICE vehicle; she escaped. Federal prosecutors charged a protester at the scene with assaulting Cuni, alleging that the man had helped tackle him after Cuni pepper-sprayed him. A judge later dismissed that charge with prejudice, writing that the evidence was “weak” and that none of the federal officers who reviewed videos of the encounter “saw a ‘tackle’ or other kind of assault.” Activists later alleged that Cuni was one of the agents seen in video of the encounter forcing to the ground a woman they say was pregnant. WIRED could not independently confirm that identification.
In at least three federal cases this year, judges or the government have found problems with Cuni’s statements or arrest paperwork. In one case, Judge Gary Brown of the Eastern District of New York found that Cuni searched five databases for a Bronx man and found nothing, then signed a warrant saying the searches had confirmed he was undocumented. ICE later added the man to those databases and searched again, creating the record Cuni had already said existed. Brown ruled the arrest and detention illegal, saying that Cuni had tried to “reconcile these falsehoods” after the fact.
In August, US District Judge Brian Cogan, also of New York’s Eastern District, said doorbell footage “largely contradicts” Cuni’s account of Fernando Fabian Chaglla’s arrest. Video reviewed by WIRED shows Chaglla being handcuffed less than three minutes into the encounter. Cuni later said he had typed Chaglla’s name and birth date into Mobile Fortify, an ICE face-recognition app; the search showed no record of lawful entry, but it did show a federal work permit. Cuni said he took the lack of records documenting his entry into the US as evidence that Chaglla was undocumented and acknowledged that he handcuffed him before filling out the warrant by hand. Cogan ruled that the arrest was unlawful.
A little over a week later, Cuni testified that he didn’t recall himself or the agents under his command ever making a warrantless arrest. “In all of the cases that I am aware of, I issued an I-200 prior to the arrest,” he assured the attorneys deposing him. “Now, if you’re questioning my credibility, I don’t know, but again, I’m—can only tell you what I’m aware of.”
In a third case, in June, government lawyers withdrew what a federal judge described as “inaccurate, sworn representations” by Cuni and other officials, including a claim that a detained man had skipped his ICE check-ins.
Cuni did not immediately respond to WIRED’s multiple requests for comment.
An Instagram account apparently associated with Cuni, previously using the handle “shooter.cuni”—now “shooter.914,” seemingly reflecting the Westchester County, New York area code—contains scores of photographs and videos of Cuni with firearms at shooting ranges across the Northeast. Among the items depicted on the account are a mug that appears to be from ICE’s New York City Fugitive Operations team, a silver and black Rolex watch that closely matches one Cuni appears to be wearing in videos from the Marble Hill shooting, and an AR-15-style rifle with a pistol grip, short barrel, holoscopic sights, and olive-colored sling that appears to match the one he wielded at the shooting scene.
Another photo on the Cuni-linked Instagram account, posted on September 4, depicts a GA Precision Templar VII bolt-action rifle with a telescopic sight mounted on a bipod stand at a gun range. “Cuni” is emblazoned on a suede cushion on the rifle’s stock, and a blue “shooter Cuni” lanyard is visible on a separate cloth ammunition sling. The post’s caption reads, “the finest form of relaxation.”

Syria’s new rulers restrict women’s access to universities
Unknown

Syria’s new rulers restrict women’s access to universities
Syria’s new Islamist government has barred women from enrolling in several university and technical programs, drawing public criticism.
The rules for the 2026-2027 academic year affect several institutions, including two universities established in July under Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa.
Al-Sharaa, a former leader of the Islamist group Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), rose to power following the overthrow of Bashar Assad in December 2024. He was appointed transitional president in January 2025 and has since pledged to build an inclusive government.
According to documents published by the Ministry of Higher Education, women are excluded from military engineering programs, as well as legal and social sciences, management, and economics at the National University for Defense Sciences. Another institution, the Syrian University for Security Sciences, reserves several programs for men, although women remain eligible to study cybersecurity.
The restrictions extend to technical institutes specializing in oil and gas, railway transport and radio and television directing. Under the previous academic year’s rules, women could still enroll in certain oil and gas programs, including accounting and precision instruments.
Criticism has come from students and educators. “No one has the right to force me to choose a particular field of study or exclude me from another,” Israa Salloum, a high school graduate preparing to apply to university, told AFP.
A constitutional declaration adopted in March 2025 guarantees women’s right to education.
The rules contrast with recent efforts to expand women’s participation in law enforcement. In September, Syria graduated its first class of 150 female police officers following six months of training.
Since taking power, Syria’s new authorities have faced criticism over measures affecting women’s freedoms. In September, a prominent Damascus school reportedly announced plans to separate male and female students from middle school onward. Four feminist and civil society organizations also accused the authorities in August of restricting freedoms and imposing forms of social control that particularly affect women.
The new admission rules do not include a blanket ban on women studying law or engineering, with such programs remaining available at other Syrian universities.

Migration pressure could rise sharply in the coming weeks as people try to leave Belarus ahead of winter, Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) chief Egert Belitšev said.
Belitšev said Russia has deliberately eased entry requirements and increased flights from countries like Ethiopia. Its ally Belarus facilitates onward travel to Europe. Travel is organized right up to the EU border and can cost up to €10,000 per person.
Estonia does not border Belarus. Latvia does. Most of the nearly 200 illegal migrants apprehended in Estonia since summer came via that route.
Estonia has a population of 1.3 million. Ethiopia has 130 million. More than a million refugees from neighboring countries live there.
Speaking to "Esimene stuudio," Belitšev said six direct flights a week operate between Ethiopia and Moscow, with no Russian visa required. Passengers intend to reach the EU.
"The Russian Federation has deliberately made entry requirements significantly easier for these countries and increased the frequency of flights," Belitšev said.
From Moscow, people travel by bus to Belarus. The authorities there make no pretense of stopping them. They help.
Russia is using Belarus to pressure Europe. "Is it dependence, or the feeling that working alongside the 'master' will bring wealth and success? This is the path Belarus has chosen," Belitšev said.
Organized crime generates substantial profits
Human trafficking is the preserve of organized crime, and it is highly profitable. The authorities in Russia and Belarus take a cut.
"If you think about someone using the migration route through Belarus to reach Europe, it is not simply a matter of buying a ticket to Moscow and arranging the rest yourself," Belitšev said. Criminal organizations handle the whole journey. Each person pays €5,000 to €10,000.
On Tuesday, news emerged that the PPA had caught migrant smugglers red-handed. "Figuratively speaking, it is impossible to stop any pattern of criminal activity without cutting off the heads at the top," Belitšev said.
The main tactic is to detain them, hold them in custody and bring them to trial quickly. Where possible, criminal proceeds are seized. In mid-September, a court sentenced a convicted smuggler to seven months in prison and a six-year ban on entering the Schengen Area.
Local governments and administrative courts not accustomed to workloads
The PPA is under considerable pressure, but has not yet had to leave tasks undone. "However, many other institutions are also affected by the migration attack," Belitšev said.
Many arrivals claim to be minors, attempting to exploit EU child protection systems. That creates problems for local governments, which are responsible for guardianship. The first-tier administrative courts are also unaccustomed to such heavy workloads.
Belitšev said the situation could get more complicated in winter, when migration pressure has usually declined. Few people want to hide in Belarusian forests in sub-zero temperatures.
"Our advantage is that we have four seasons," he said.

Authorities have placed 10 other Chilean districts on high alert as risks of potential mudslides and rain-related emergencies threaten to batter the region.
Heavy rains battered Chile’s capital Santiago and its surrounding regions on Thursday, triggering mudslides that swept cars through streets, flooded homes, forced residents to evacuate and injured at least six people, according to authorities.
Chilean President José Antonio Kast declared a state of emergency in Las Condes, a wealthy suburb east of Santiago, giving government agencies more power to respond as torrential rains turned key roads into impassable waterways.
The district's mayor, Catalina San Martín, said 14.4 centimetres of rain had fallen in recent days — about nine times the average October rainfall — leaving the area “totally drenched.”
The Mapocho River, which runs through Santiago, overflowed, prompting evacuation orders.
Chile’s disaster-response agency put 10 other districts on high alert for more landslides and ordered schools to close on Friday.
Rain storms earlier this week had already damaged a few dozen homes across central Chile and left nearly 12,000 customers in Santiago without power, officials said. The downpours were expected to ease on Friday.
No deaths were reported on Thursday as a result of the heavy rains. The injured however included a one-year-old child, who suffered broken bones. Firefighters said they'd rescued or evacuated more than 1,000 people.
The floods come as a powerful El Niño gains strength.
The naturally recurring warming of tropical Pacific waters scrambles rainfall patterns worldwide and often brings wetter springs to the Southern Hemisphere.
The World Meteorological Organization said on Thursday that this year’s El Niño was expected to peak in December and could be among the most intense since at least 1950.
