I hitchhiked from Sydney to Perth, and found comfort in the company of strangers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:00:33 UTC
23:00:33 KST

I’m alone, hunched over by a dusty road junction, and feeling the bite of the morning sun. I’ve already been waiting here, on the outskirts of Esperance on the south coast of Western Australia, for more than three hours. Another wave of traffic approaches. I smile, stretch out my arm and raise my thumb.
Most drivers who pass wave or give me a thumbs up. One gives me the finger. There isn’t much traffic. Someone tosses a water bottle out their window at me.
Just as I start to catastrophise in the dust, a four-wheel-drive quietly pulls off the road and comes to a stop behind me. I hoist my backpack around my shoulder, run over and jump in the passenger seat, thanking the driver profusely.
One of my stranger interests is hitchhiking. I’m drawn to the idea of abandoning control and finding comfort in a stranger’s company. It’s a subculture, an art, and a way of travel that satisfies wanderlust like no other trip. Plus, it costs nothing.
Once a popular way to travel in the 70s and 80s, these days it’s pretty rare to see a hitchhiker on the side of Australian roads. For starters, its reputation was overwhelmingly tarnished by its association with serial killer Ivan Milat, who murdered several hitchhikers in the early 90s. Australia is also one of the few countries in the world that make it legally fraught to hitchhike, with laws explicitly naming hitchhiking as an offence, though legislation differs between state and territories.
According to Hitchwiki (Wikipedia for hitchhiking), most jurisdictions essentially prohibit a pedestrian from standing on or moving on to a road to hitchhike, though the wording and what legally constitutes “the road” varies. However, in the ACT hitchhiking is legal in most circumstances and Tasmania removed any reference to hitchhiking from its road rules in 2019.
But safety and legal baggage aside, there are some signs hitching is making a comeback. Online resources such as the hitchhiker community Hitchwiki and its offshoot, Trustroots, which has more than 120,000 members, are steadily growing. And according to the University of Western Australia’s Dr Fang Liu, who studies adventure tourism, social media accounts sharing extreme ways of travelling are demystifying and normalising hitchhiking.
“Young international travellers are seeing people online and think, ‘Oh, I can do that too,’ but they may be unprepared and unaware of the risks,” she says.
“In a lot of places there’s no [phone] signal and you might have to wait hours for someone to stop. By then you’ve probably already dehydrated. Social media doesn’t convey that.”
Inside strangers’ cars
I introduce myself to my latest ride. The driver is Doug Hilton, the boss of Australia’s national science agency, CSIRO. His job will make for good conversational fodder, but more importantly, he’s driving 500km west to Albany, his car has air conditioning, and the dusty intersection is in the rear-vision mirror.
I’ve hitchhiked in Australia a few times before, once up Tasmania’s east coast and across Flinders Island on the Bass Strait, and another time from Canberra to Sydney. But never as far and never as ambitious as this latest leg – the plan is to go all the way from Sydney to Perth, mostly inside strangers’ cars.
It’s the final leg of my journey and things have taken a fortunate turn.
‘Here we feel so safe’
Five days earlier I’m fresh and clean-shaven, standing outside Broken Hill in outback New South Wales. I wait just five minutes before an SUV with a bull bar doubles back and offers me a ride.
Inside is Miranda and her two children, originally from Zimbabwe. The car is crammed with pillows and baggage, but they find room for me. While I ram my backpack into the boot, Miranda’s teenage daughter moves to the backseat, squishing in beside her younger brother and an Esky packed with yoghurt cups and juice boxes.
The family immigrated to the US a few years ago, but because of gun violence and immigration crackdowns decided to leave. “I never would have picked up someone there, but here we feel so safe,” Miranda says, the desert rushing by.
They now live in the regional Queensland town of Chinchilla, where Miranda says they’ve been embraced by the community. “We are so happy here,” she says. “Every day I thank God for where we have ended up.” From the backseat, her daughter says she wants to study medicine when she finishes high school.
After four hours of meandering conversations between long silences, we part ways somewhere in rural South Australia. They’re headed to Adelaide to visit a family friend and make the most of school holidays. I’m going west.
‘Milat changed things’
Soon I’m racing through rolling hills of green oats and yellow canola flowers draped in golden afternoon light. Hulking wind turbines spin on the hilltops. Mike, 67, is in the driver’s seat of his Toyota troop carrier. He spends his retirement restoring century-old farm tractors and is headed to Cowell to pick up some engine parts. He says by sundown we’ll be in Jamestown, a small town with a pleasant campground by the river.
“You’re the first hitchhiker I’ve seen in decades,” he says. “Milat probably changed things.”
Ivan Milat was convicted of the murder of five female and two male backpackers between 1989 and 1992 in NSW, several of whom had been hitchhiking. It’s alleged he’s responsible for dozens more unsolved murders or disappearances.
There’s no denying the act of hitchhiking is inherently risky. But I am a white male. Whatever the risks I face, they are not the same dangers a woman or female-presenting person can encounter hitchhiking alone. Hitchwiki offers specific safety advice for female hitchers, but maintains “you have a right to be respected and it is not true that while hitchhiking you expose yourself to a risk at your own wish”. They also point out that women will usually spend less time waiting to be picked up.
On my journey I follow the general rule of thumb when it comes to hitching safely: I stand well off the road, in places with good visibility, with enough room for cars to pull over, and slow-moving traffic. I stick to footpaths where I can.
When a car does pull over I give the driver a once-over and follow my gut. If I feel uncomfortable or unsafe, I know I’m under no obligation to get in the car. Though that’s a hypothetical. Every experience I’ve had has been positive so far.
Over beer and dinner at the Jamestown pub, I learn about Mike’s extended family and how proud he is of his overachieving daughter. The next morning I tag along with him further west, snaking up a mountain pass before plunging into a treeless and barren plain below. Across the Spencer Gulf, grey and faint in the distance, is the Whyalla steelworks. Last month more than 500 of the plant’s employees lost their jobs.
“People are feeling pissed off – there’s only bad news now and the major parties have no solutions,” Mike says. Talking about politics is a staple of the journey, though in a stranger’s car I prefer to do most of the listening. “Still, we are a lucky country, it’s just a lot of us don’t realise how lucky,” Mike says. An hour later we part ways.
‘Middle of everything’
By midday I meet Neil, a 79-year-old widower on the final leg of a four-month road trip across the continent. Neil, who lives in Geraldton in Western Australia, has stopped in his ute. His first joke is about hitchhiking.
“A hitchhiker gets into a car,” Neil tells me. “He says to the driver, ‘You’re fairly brave picking up a hitchhiker these days. For all you know, I could be a mass murderer.’
“The driver turns to him and says, ‘Well, what are the chances of us both being axe murderers?’”
As we get comfortable, Neil’s running commentary begins. There’s a “ripper” wheat crop over there and another a few kilometres later, much the same. Over there is a slag heap from an abandoned iron ore mine. But where are all the sheep? And what could that truck be hauling?
I learn about his life, too. Marrying at 21, raising a family, working 96-hour weeks driving trucks and saving prudently. We talk about relationships, love and getting to the “pointy end”. His motto is: “If you never go, you never never know.”
At dusk we pull off the Eyre Highway at a truckstop and Neil disappears into his camper trailer for the night. I pitch my tent beside it. The ground is gravel and my sleep is restless. In the morning we set off at dawn and I doze off in the passenger seat.
By the time I wake the sun is high and the landscape has transformed, thickets of silver saltbush and red dirt as far as the eye can see. We’ve reached the Nullarbor, a vast arid plain stretching 1,200km across southern Australia. “Middle of nowhere,” I say. “Nah mate, middle of everything,” Neil replies, road trains swooshing by endlessly.
Towing his camper, Neil sticks to about 80km/h for safety and fuel efficiency, so it’s slow going. In the afternoon we drive down the 90 Mile Straight, the longest straight road in the southern hemisphere, and that night, under a gibbous moon, we share a dark beer, dinner and a Magnum mini vanilla ice-cream by the fire, all courtesy of Neil.
Three days and 1,900km since we met, Neil pulls up outside a campground in Esperance. We take a selfie and exchange a warm handshake. I know it’s probably the last time I’ll see him.
A birding detour
I don’t know it yet, but Doug from the CSIRO, 62, will be the last driver to pick me up before I hit Perth.
I bookend my journey by talking to Doug about his passion for moths, his dream of inventing a way to eradicate feral cats, and the benefits of therapy to his mental health. Among other scientific pursuits, he’s on his way to Albany to meet with two Menang Indigenous elders who co-authored a paper with him about moths in the region, including three newly discovered species of primitive jaw moths.
In the afternoon I take up his invitation to join him bird watching by the ocean. We park at a headland, Doug grabs a Nikon Z9 with a huge telephoto lens out of the boot, and we start walking through thick coastal scrub. At sunset we witness a brown blur scurry across a dirt track. Doug misses the photo but is nonetheless ecstatic and wraps his arm around me in joy.
Apparently we’ve just seen one of Australia’s rarest birds, the noisy scrubbird, presumed extinct until it was rediscovered in 1961. The significance of the sighting is lost on me but Doug assures me I’ve just hit the peak of my bird-watching career. I didn’t know I’d started it.
We pull into Albany at dark and Doug drops me off at a hostel. It reeks of marijuana and there’s no hot water but I’m just happy to be sleeping on a thick mattress. When I wake up it’s miserable outside so I make the call to take the bus for the final six hours of the route to Perth. I’m comfortable, but it’s decidedly dull as the sprawling suburbs of the world’s most isolated capital city start rolling by. I’ve spent 4,360km travelling across the most isolated inhabited continent on Earth, yet for all the distance, I’ve rarely felt alone.

====================================================================================================

Pete Hegseth’s plan to livestream execution puts US in dubious company
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:55:07 UTC
22:55:07 KST

If the US defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, goes ahead with plans to livestream the execution of a soldier radicalised to extremist Islam who killed 13 people at a military base in Texas, his country will join a motley assembly of lesser powers and rogue actors who have conducted public executions in recent years.
Only two countries currently systematically carry out capital sentences in public: Iran and Afghanistan. In 2025, the Taliban authorities carried out six such killings and the regime in Tehran 11, according to Amnesty International.
In April last year, the Taliban executed four men accused of murder in three different cities. All were shot dead in crowded public sports stadiums. Such events were common when the hardline Islamist militia movement was in power in the late 1990s. Then as now, the Taliban claimed a due court process had been followed.
In July, two young men accused of killing police officers were hanged by Iranian authorities in the central square of Isfahan, Iran. Human rights monitors have reported about 30 public executions in Ithe country in the last five years, with an intensification in recent months after massive popular unrest earlier this year and the war with the US and Israel. Historically, many hangings have been carried out using a crane as a makeshift gallows.
Saudi Arabia appears to have ended the practice after decades of beheading convicted criminals in a square in the capital, Riyadh, and sometimes publicly in provincial cities.
Legal experts and historians argue that public executions perform different functions. If the rule of law is shaky or there is doubt about the efficacy of the criminal justice system, they offer authorities seeking to win support a way of convincing the community that criminals will be punished. Such public spectacles can also be a way of cowing a population through terror.
Armed militant groups have frequently resorted to public executions – often in an effort to assert their authority.
Islamic State, which ruled a swath of Iraq and Syria between 2014 and 2019, conducted thousands of executions for alleged offences ranging from homosexuality to theft. Many of the executions took place in public or were videoed. A large number were deliberately choreographed to provide a spectacle for broadcast to terrorise enemies and potential dissidents as well as to radicalise IS supporters and attract new ones.
In October 2025, as Hamas sought to reassert its control over the population of Gaza, it carried out a public execution of six men apparently accused of collaborating with Israel. In 2017, the group had executed three men accused of the same crime, partly livestreaming the event on Facebook.
The execution of Maj Nidal Hasan, a former army psychiatrist, at Fort Hood in Texas would be the first public execution in the US in many decades.
In the US, the practice of public executions was largely stopped in the 1930s, though in 2001, some survivors and victims’ relatives were allowed to watch the execution by lethal injection of Timothy McVeigh, convicted of the 1995 bombing of a government office in Oklahoma City.
Hasan’s execution has been scheduled for 3 December. Hegseth, who has the authority to decide the conduct of the killing, has said that “of course” it would take place at the same time and in the same place as Hasan’s attack 17 years ago and would use firearms, as Hasan did.
Hasan can launch appeals within the civilian federal court system that could delay the execution for many years.
In 2025, Amnesty International recorded 2,707 executions, the highest total globally since 1981, and an increase of two-thirds on the previous year. The sharp rise was mainly due to more than 2,100 executions by Iran, its highest number of executions in decades.
Amnesty said authorities had placed the death penalty “at the centre of flawed public security and ‘tough on crime’ narratives to assert control, project state power and score political points”.
“This trend was strongest in countries where the authorities have tightened their grip on power by restricting civic space, silencing dissent and displaying disregard for protections established under international human rights law and standards,” the campaign group reported.

ICE agent shoots man in car with five-year-old child in New York: Mayor

03:25:33 UTC
12:25:33 KST

ICE shooting of New York man in car with five-year-old sparks protests
Mayor Zohran Mamdani says immigration agents fire at car with child inside. DHS says man was an arrest target.
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent has shot a man in New York City as he sat in a car with a child.
Citing an “unconscionable and incredibly serious situation”, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said early reports indicated that agents surrounded the man and a five-year-old in his car on Thursday in the Marble Hill neighbourhood before firing multiple rounds.
The child was believed to be physically unharmed, the mayor added as he said he has called United States President Donald Trump and would demand that he end all ICE enforcement actions in the city.
“I will not stand by while ICE agents terrorise our communities,” Mamdani said.
Protests followed on Thursday evening with demonstrators saying the shooting illustrated the dangers of Trump’s immigration crackdown, and some scuffles with police broke out.
“We are heartbroken and enraged,” said City Council member Carmen De La Rosa, who represents the area.
Speaking at the scene in the evening, Mamdani said: “Today’s shooting is only further devastating confirmation of what we have long known, which is that ICE operates with impunity, that they sow chaos and terror across our country, that they have killed far more of our neighbours than they could ever have claimed to save.”
He demanded the agency “must be abolished”.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul said she spoke with Trump and US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Thursday night.
“I expressed outrage on behalf of New Yorkers and urged them to halt ICE enforcement operations in New York,” she said in a statement.
“I also asked that any body camera footage of the shooting be released to the public, so we can establish the facts and get to the truth.”
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, said its officers were conducting a “targeted enforcement operation” in the Bronx about 4pm to arrest a 28-year-old Dominican national with a criminal conviction identified as Oscar Belgal by city police.
It said an officer “discharged his weapon” and “the criminal illegal alien” was injured. The DHS added that the incident remains under investigation.
Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said Belgal was pulling into a parking space when a federal officer in plain clothes approached with a gun drawn, followed by another federal officer who also wasn’t in uniform.
Belgal started to pull the car forward, and then at least one of the officers fired seven rounds, hitting the man below his left ear, Tisch said, confirming that the child was unharmed and was with a relative.
According to a statement by the New York Police Department, the man remained conscious and was receiving medical treatment at a nearby hospital.
ICE under scrutiny
The shooting took place after months of mounting criticism of the agency.
In January, federal immigration agents shot dead two US citizens in Minneapolis: Renee Nicole Good, a 37-year-old mother of three, killed by an ICE agent on January 7, and Alex Pretti, a 37-year-old intensive care nurse, shot by a US border agent.
After Good’s killing, Trump officials labelled her a “domestic terrorist” even as video of the shooting cast doubt on their claims she had tried to run over an agent.
The federal government removed local authorities from the investigation, rejected calls for a civil rights probe and sent hundreds more agents to Minnesota, bringing the total to 3,000, as protests against the killings and the immigration crackdown spread to hundreds of US cities.
Trump blamed the shift in US opinion about the immigration agency on unfair media coverage, urging DHS and ICE to publicise the “violent criminals” they arrest.
ICE has been tasked with deporting one million people a year.
The agency doubled in size in the first year of the second Trump administration to more than 22,000 agents by January and is now the highest-funded federal law enforcement agency with about $75bn allocated to it over four years under a tax bill Trump signed last year.

UK arrests two men for breaking into US intelligence hub
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
03:20:46 UTC
12:20:46 KST

UK arrests two men for breaking into US intelligence hub
British counterterrorism police have arrested two Latvian nationals accused of breaking into a military installation housing major US and NATO intelligence operations, just days after British authorities alleged an Iranian-linked terror plot at an airbase hosting American warplanes.
The two men, aged 32 and 36, were detained early Thursday inside RAF Molesworth in Cambridgeshire after security personnel discovered an abandoned vehicle and a breach in the base’s perimeter fence, according to police.
Both suspects reside in the UK and were initially detained on suspicion of trespassing and criminal damage. They were subsequently arrested under the National Security Act on suspicion of entering a prohibited site for a purpose prejudicial to Britain. Their identities and possible motives have not been disclosed.
RAF Molesworth, roughly 70 miles north of London, hosts US military intelligence operations covering Europe and Africa, as well as NATO’s Intelligence Fusion Centre. Although officially designated a Royal Air Force station, the facility is operated by the US military and does not function as an active airfield.
Counterterrorism investigators have taken over the case, but British authorities have not publicly presented evidence that the breach involved espionage, terrorism or a foreign government.
“We’re very aware of the recent heightened interest and concern around military sites,” Commander Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said. However, she acknowledged that “at this stage there is nothing to suggest this incident is connected to the events at RAF Fairford.”
The latest incident follows a much-publicized security scare at RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, where five men were arrested on September 27 after police discovered three suspicious vans near the base, which had been used by American bombers during the US-Israeli war on Iran.
The arrests initially sparked allegations of a possible terrorist bombing or drone attack, with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham suggesting there were “strong indications” of Iranian involvement. Tehran denied the accusations.
Police subsequently acknowledged that no explosive devices had been discovered, with the investigation finding only quantities of petrol in the vehicles. All five suspects were released on bail within days, prompting further questions about the initial assessment of the threat.
Two additional men, including a dual British-Iranian national, were subsequently arrested in connection with the alleged plot. Both have also been released on bail, bringing the total to seven suspects released without charges.
The Fairford scare also coincided with Washington’s abrupt withdrawal of its B-1 strategic bombers from the UK installation. US President Donald Trump linked the decision to security threats, while US Secretary of State Marco Rubio played down a direct connection between the alleged plot and the redeployment.
In the latest Molesworth case, investigators also summoned explosives specialists to examine the abandoned vehicle, briefly imposing a security cordon around nearby roads. The restrictions were lifted after nothing suspicious was found.

From Ra’anana around the world and back: Edan Leshem takes a swing for Sharsheret - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
03:20:43 UTC
12:20:43 KST

For Edan Leshem, Friday’s Sharsheret tennis tournament in Ra’anana will bring him back to a place where his own tennis journey began.
More than two decades after he first picked up a racket at the Ra’anana tennis center as a five-year-old, Leshem will return to those courts in a very different role.
Rather than competing for himself, the former Israeli professional will be helping run the tournament, working alongside his longtime coach and colleague Ron Becker to make sure the players have the best experience possible.
For Leshem, now 29, it is a fitting way to give back to a sport that has been such a major part of his life.
“I feel it’s a great cause and that I really want to help,” Leshem said. “I’m just there to support the players and give them the best experience of the tournament.”
The inaugural Sharsheret Israel Tennis Tournament 2026, taking place this Friday at the Ra’anana Tennis Center, will bring together women from the community for a day of competitive tennis, social connection and support while raising awareness and funds for Sharsheret’s work supporting women and families affected by breast and ovarian cancer.
Sharsheret provides resources for Jewish women at risk of breast, ovarian cancer
Founded in 2001, Sharsheret provides personalized support, education and community programs for Jewish women and families dealing with breast and ovarian cancer, as well as for those facing hereditary cancer risk.
Its services include peer support, mental health and genetic counseling, educational programming and practical assistance throughout diagnosis, treatment and survivorship.
The organization launched an Israel initiative in 2024, expanding its support network and programs to women, men and families in Israel.
That includes connecting people with peers who have experienced cancer themselves, developing support groups and providing educational resources around breast and ovarian cancer and genetics.
That community component is particularly important to the Ra’anana tournament. The event is not simply about raising money or playing tennis.
It is designed to bring together women who may have shared experiences with cancer and give them an opportunity to connect in an environment centered around activity, friendship, and strength.
While all the players in Friday’s event will be female, the spectators will include women, men and children of all ages, cheering on their wives, moms, daughters, sisters, grandmothers, aunts, cousins and friends.
Leshem became involved after tournament co-chair Ariella Eltes approached him about helping organize the event. He quickly volunteered to take responsibility for the tournament structure, including organizing the groups and managing the competition.
He will be joined by Becker, the coach Leshem first worked with after moving to Ramat Hasharon at age seven.
A full-circle moment for Leshem
It is a remarkable full-circle moment for a player whose own relationship with tennis began almost by accident.
Leshem was an energetic five-year-old living near the Ra’anana tennis center when his grandfather, who played tennis himself, suggested the sport as a way to channel some of that energy.
What began as an activity to tire out a young boy eventually became a professional career.
By the time Leshem was seven, he had begun working with Becker and found himself surrounded by other young players who were competing seriously. He quickly discovered that he could hold his own.
“I realized I’m not that bad,” Leshem recalled. “I can play some tennis.”
The competition became addictive. He began playing national tournaments, then traveling internationally, and eventually established himself as one of Israel’s leading players of his generation.
Leshem reached the final of the Israeli national championships as a teenager, facing Israeli star Dudi Sela, and also trained with Amos Mansdorf, one of the most accomplished players in Israeli tennis history.
He joined Israel’s Davis Cup team at 17 and went on to represent his country on the international stage. His professional career included appearances in ATP events and extensive competition on the ITF and Challenger circuits.
His best period came in 2017, when he climbed into the world’s top 250, reaching a career-high No. 249 in the ATP singles rankings in December of that year. He also reached a career-high No. 349 in doubles in 2018.
Along the way, Leshem collected several ITF titles and competed against or practiced with players who would go on to become some of the biggest names in the sport, including Alexander Zverev, Andrey Rublev, Jannik Sinner, Carlos Alcaraz and Hubert Hurkacz. He also shared the court with players such as Kei Nishikori and Marcos Baghdatis.
One of his most memorable experiences came at an ATP event in Tel Aviv, where he competed in front of a home crowd. At the 2022 Tel Aviv Open, his home tournament, he qualified for the main draw having received a wildcard.
He defeated seventh seed Lorenzo Giustino and third seed Luca Nardi. He recorded his first ATP career win defeating compatriot, wildcard Yshai Oliel.
As a result, he climbed close to 70 positions up the rankings to No. 377 and became the No. 1 Israeli player in singles. He also won his first Davis Cup match in South Africa in 2018, another moment that remains particularly meaningful to him.
Those experiences gave Leshem a firsthand look at both the rewards and the enormous challenges involved in trying to make it as a professional tennis player.
His career also gave him an intimate understanding of the difficulties facing Israeli tennis players.
Leshem believes the country has plenty of talent, but not always the infrastructure necessary to develop it.
“When I was competing, we had a lot of players,” he said. “Everybody just wanted to play and compete and everybody was fighting. I think that’s what creates a lot of players.”
Today, he believes there is less of that healthy competition.
Tennis has become more social, he said, while competitive tennis has become increasingly expensive and difficult. Travel, coaching, training and education can all create obstacles, particularly for young Israeli players trying to compete internationally.
Leshem experienced those challenges himself.
While some of the players he competed against eventually reached the highest levels of the sport, traveling with coaches, physiotherapists and larger support teams, Leshem often traveled alone. The cost and logistics of competing internationally were significantly more difficult for an Israeli player who had to fly between tournaments.
He remembers looking at players who had far greater resources and wondering whether he could reach the same level without the same support.
Those experiences have helped shape what he wants to do now.
After a fall down a staircase on the way to a match resulted in a lower-back fracture and a disc injury, Leshem eventually realized that a comeback was no longer realistic. Instead, he began building a new career around the sport.
He started slowly, developing his coaching experience and building his own tennis club in Ra’anana.
The goal, he says, was never simply to produce professional players.
“I wanted to build a community of people who love the sport and want to enjoy it,” he said. “It gave me so much joy.”
That philosophy makes the Sharsheret tournament particularly meaningful to him.
Tennis, Leshem believes, offers far more than competition. It provides exercise, social connection, resilience and independence. Unlike team sports, there is nowhere to hide on a tennis court.
“If you have a bad day, it’s all on you,” he said. “So you have to be very resilient and very independent.”
That same quality can make the sport a valuable escape for people dealing with difficult circumstances.
For someone recovering from illness or cancer, Leshem said, tennis can provide a temporary break from everything happening outside the court.
“You go, you play tennis, you focus on the strokes, on the movement, you kind of forget everything around,” he said.
“Sometimes it’s just a nice way to get away from all those troubles.”
The Sharsheret tournament also provides something beyond the tennis itself: an opportunity for women who have shared difficult experiences to come together in a positive environment.
Leshem said many of the participants already know one another and have similar stories, making the tournament an opportunity to reconnect, share experiences and simply enjoy a sport they love.
“I think it’s a very nice way to connect them with each other, to share stories,” he said. “They get the chance to meet all their friends at the same place with something that they all enjoy doing, which is playing tennis and talk.”
That idea is central to Sharsheret’s broader work. Cancer can be an isolating experience, even when surrounded by family and friends. Sharsheret’s peer-to-peer model allows people to connect with others who understand the experience firsthand, while its educational and genetic counseling programs help families navigate issues that extend beyond the immediate medical treatment.
In Israel, where the organization is still expanding its presence, that network is becoming increasingly important.
Tournament raises awareness and creates a supportive environment
The tournament therefore serves two purposes at once. It raises funds and awareness for Sharsheret, while also creating precisely the kind of community environment that the organization seeks to foster: one in which women can talk, support one another, remain active and see themselves as more than their diagnosis.
For Leshem, that sense of community is ultimately what makes the event special.
The former professional has spent years experiencing tennis from the perspective of a player trying to win. He has also experienced the pressures, sacrifices, and limitations that come with attempting to reach the highest levels of the sport.
Now, back on the same Ra’anana courts where his journey began, he gets to see tennis from another perspective.
He gets to help other people enjoy it.
And on Friday, he hopes plenty of people will come out to join them.
“The more people who come, the event will get better and support the cause,” Leshem said. “If anybody watching this wasn’t planning on coming and wants to come, we will be happy to have them with us on Friday.”
For a player whose childhood introduction to tennis began with a grandfather looking for a way to keep an energetic five-year-old busy, it is another chapter in a relationship with the sport that has lasted more than 20 years.
This time, however, the goal is not to win a match.
It is to help make sure everyone who steps onto the court has a reason to feel like a winner.
Sharsheret hosts community sports events in the US and now in Israel to raise funds and support national breast cancer, ovarian cancer, and genetics programs. The upcoming Sharsheret Israel Tennis Tournament Benefit is scheduled for this Friday, October 9, 2026, at the Ra’anana Tennis Center. For more information, please visit sharsheret.org/israel-tennis

====================================================================================================

Top Jewish influencers say opting out is not an option when antisemitism is prevalent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
03:20:04 UTC
12:20:04 KST

Jonah Platt wants potential guests on his podcast to know that “private” solidarity is no solidarity at all.
Platt, a social media influencer and the host of “Being Jewish with Jonah Platt,” said in an interview with the Jewish Telegraphic Agency that he is frustrated with the steady stream of personal messages and other signs of support from celebrities and thought leaders, both Jews and allies, who appreciate his program showcasing Jewish identity and pride - but then decline to come on it.
When declining, they tell him they are too scared for their safety or careers. They’re “afraid it will attract anti-Israel masses to their social media, afraid it will affect them commercially or afraid they’ll get death threats,” he explained.
The would-be guests often say they’ll support the Jewish community privately but not publicly. But to Platt that’s an empty offer. “Having private solidarity doesn’t move the needle when public spaces are being entirely surrendered to fear,” he said.
An AP-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research survey released in July found that 4 in 10 Jews are less likely to wear anything identifying themselves as Jewish than they were before the deadly Hamas attacks on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, in just one sign of concerns about being Jewish publicly. In the three years since, a handful of Jewish influencers have tried to give Jews the support to come out and be proud.
”I think the more Jews speak about their own story, and the more we share it, the more we own it, the stronger we will be as a people and the more people will react positively,” said another influencer, Israeli activist Hen Mazzig, who interviews celebrities and pushes for Jews to express public pride in their heritage.
'Humanizing the Jewish experience' through social media
Despite the difficulties Platt and Mazzig encounter when encouraging people to speak out, they have still made a mark. On Instagram alone Hen Mazzig has 459,000 followers and Jonah Platt has 229,000. Mazzig’s show interviewing Jewish people about their identity, art and culture, “And They’re Jewish,” was just picked up by ChaiFlix, the Jewish and Israeli Netflix.
Platt’s podcast, meanwhile, is often the No. 1 ranked Jewish podcast on Apple podcasts. Views on YouTube for multiple episodes are above 50,0000, with nearly 1,000 comments on single episodes. And he has succeeded in attracting at least some high-profile guests - including Cindy Crawford, Jason Alexander and Mayim Bialik.
Platt developed his podcast in October 2024 as a safe space for Jewish and allied celebrities and thought leaders to share their stories around Jewish identity to help combat rising antisemitism and Jewish hate.
“It humanizes the Jewish experience for the audience, “ he said, especially when listeners can think, “Wow, this person whose movies I love is going through such a horrible time and is experiencing all this stuff, too. I had no idea.”
Platt said appearing on his podcast pays dividends. With only a tiny number of exceptions, according to Platt, everyone who’s been on his show has told him, “This has been so amazing. Everybody wherever I go is telling me how much they love this conversation.”
Platt said his guests find that the typical listener feedback is positive. Some of the responses they’ve received include: “It makes me feel seen. It makes me feel less alone. It makes me so proud to support you, and now I’m gonna buy tickets to every movie you’re ever in and have your back all the way!”
Positive impacts for guests on Platt's social media
A number of Platt’s interviews confirmed that they saw spikes in positive attention after appearing on his show.
“Not only is Jonah a fantastic host with whom I felt so safe, but after my episode aired, I have had so many people commenting online or coming up to me and thanking me for making them feel less alone,” Seth Rudetsky, SiriusXM’s Big Fat Broadway host and Jewish Broadway Alliance founder, wrote to JTA in an email.
Sarah Hurwitz, a former White House speechwriter, said that after her appearance on Platt’s podcast in February 2025, she saw sales of a book she published in 2019, “Here all Along,” go up.
“The fact that my sales were double, then triple what they were the week before the episode aired really does seem meaningful,” she said.
Platt said he’s heard of minimal negative pushback. “I can really only think of one instance where I heard back from a guest who said there’s some specific clips based on things they said that are getting them some hate online that they’re unhappy about it, but certainly didn’t regret appearing on the show,” said Platt. “They’re just like, I can’t keep promoting these clips anymore.”
That experience stands in stark contrast to what many other Jewish performers have found in other contexts, however. In recent weeks, Pink lost 100,000 followers overnight for airing her objections to Macklemore’s anti-Israel advocacy when he was opening for Ed Sheeran. (Stadium owners told Sheeran that Macklemore would not be welcome, and he dropped the rapper from his tour.) Jerry Seinfeld is still headlining the MEO Commedia a La Carte Fest in Portugal, but he’s facing boycott calls and several comedians have dropped out because of opposition to Seinfeld’s pro-Israel views.
But staying silent won’t change that reaction, according to Mazzig, co-founder of the Tel Aviv Institute think tank focusing on antisemitism.
“When Oct. 7 happened, a lot of people were hoping [increased Jewish hate] would be over in a few months,” Mazzig said. Three years later, it is evident that antisemitism is not diminishing, he said.
Mazzig, who is gay, likened the prescription for Jewish pride to the journey gays have undergone.
“It’s what Harvey Milk said about the gay community,” said Mazzig, referring to the trailblazing Jewish San Francisco city supervisor who was assassinated in 1978. Milk believed it’s important for gay individuals to come out to their friends, neighbors, and community, so they aren’t defined by what misconceptions others perceive about them. “And I think for us as Jews, we have to do the same thing,” said Mazzig.
Inspiring Jewish college students in the US
Hearing from proud Jews is especially important for college students, according to Andrew Pessin, a philosophy professor at Connecticut College and the founding director of the Institute for the Critical Study of Antizionism. As far as he can tell, his is the only classroom on campus where students can learn about Zionism in a positive way and have multi-sided discussions.
Pessin said that his Jewish students tell him his class is a safe haven. He said he’s heard things like, “Thank G-d for your class, because I am surrounded by hate on this campus,” and that there, “I realize I’m not alone, and this is actually a safe space for me.”
Avital Goldberg-Curran transferred from Connecticut College after experiences at New York University that left her feeling threatened. She was pleased to see Pessin’s name as a faculty member. “My rabbi would talk about him as a hero. A proud Jew,” she said.
“At NYU, there were days that I felt unsafe going to class because there were mass protesters in the lobby screaming death to Israel and Jewish people,” says Goldberg-Curran, an American history graduate of Connecticut College. “There were multiple times that I took a lap around the block and waited for the protests to be broken up by the police before I went inside because I didn’t know if there were weapons.”
Goldberg-Curran follows Platt and Mazzig and said their podcasts and writings remind her of the importance of being a proud Jew in difficult times.
“They very much inspired me while I was at NYU to lean more into Judaism and being observant,” she said. “I very much sought out observing Shabbos and visiting the Chabad house and surrounding myself with Jewish people.”
She added, “I think it’s been a very important takeaway that in times of struggle, we should be finding each other and leaning into them.”
Pessin believes being vocal on Jewish hate is important for his own self-worth. “If I don’t speak up, I’ll have changed myself,” he said. “If I see something, I have to speak up and say otherwise. If I don’t, it harms me on the inside.”
That feeling of being at peace with and connected to your inner self is part of what Platt guests get from being on his show.
“They feel good for having told their story authentically and being truthful to who they are, and in some cases, spoken about things in a setting where they feel comfortable to speak about things they don’t talk about elsewhere,” said Platt. “So for a lot of people, it’s been cathartic or healing to be on the show.”

Facebook and Instagram-owner Meta has banned advertisements by ByteDance, the Chinese parent of TikTok, on its platforms in the United States and a handful of other countries, a company spokesperson said on Thursday.
The move marks an escalation in the long-running rivalry between Meta and ByteDance, whose video-sharing app TikTok has emerged as one of Meta's most formidable competitors for user engagement, creators and advertising dollars.
Meta's ban takes effect immediately in the US, Canada, Egypt, Indonesia, Japan, Thailand and Vietnam, and extends to third-party advertisers running campaigns that link to TikTok and other ByteDance properties in those countries, Meta said.
"We don't have to run ads from a competitor whose goal is to pull people off our apps," Meta said. "Declining promotional services to a competitor is a normal business practice across industries. We will continue to compete on product quality and user experience."
TikTok and ByteDance did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment on Meta's move.
TikTok's website shows that it does not support links that open or log users into other social media apps. However, users can still add links to their profiles that direct people to those platforms' websites.
Urge for Tiktok, Youtube to take on teen safety
Meta has been urging TikTok and YouTube to follow steps it agreed to take on teen safety in August following a settlement of up to $18 billion with US states over social media harms to children.
Meta in August agreed to impose daily usage limits and restrict nighttime usage by children who use Facebook and Instagram, and enhance measures to prevent children from accessing age-restricted content.
TikTok has not publicly commented on Meta's campaign, but it reached a settlement with Alabama in September that requires the social media platform to impose new usage limits and enhance age-verification measures for users in the state, resolving claims that it endangered children and misled consumers about its safety.
TikTok operates in the US as a majority American-owned joint venture after a deal aimed at safeguarding US user data and averting a US ban on an app used by more than 200 million users in the country.
Bloomberg News first reported Meta's ban earlier on Thursday.

His work places Ukraine among the causes being discussed by Nobel observers this year, alongside humanitarian responses to the war in Sudan, press freedom and international justice.

Ukraine’s abducted children in Nobel spotlight

The issue has also drawn the attention of US First Lady Melania Trump, who has advocated for the reunification of children separated from their families by war.
Recognition of Kuleba’s efforts would put international attention on the fate of Ukrainian children and the continuing challenges of securing their return.
The International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants in March 2023 for Russian President Vladimir Putin and Russian official Maria Lvova-Belova over alleged war crimes involving the unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children.
Russia denies that its transfers are unlawful, describing them as evacuations or humanitarian measures. Ukraine maintains that children were taken without proper consent and has demanded their return.
Trump seeks Nobel recognition despite unfinished wars
Much of the attention surrounding this year’s prize has focused on Trump, who has repeatedly claimed that he deserves the award for helping resolve international conflicts.
The US president has claimed credit for ending up to eight wars, although several of those conflicts have continued and his role in resolving others remains disputed.
His promise to end Russia’s invasion of Ukraine has also gone unfulfilled, with Russian attacks continuing despite months of US-led diplomatic efforts.
Speaking Wednesday, Oct. 7, Trump questioned whether the Nobel Committee would recognize his achievements.
“They have a reputation for maybe not giving it to people like me,” he said, adding that denying him the award would be a “great discredit” to the committee.
Trump has previously criticized the Nobel selection process, maintaining that his diplomatic record deserves international recognition.
Nobel observers, however, have pointed to his administration’s military campaign against Iran, territorial ambitions involving Greenland and confrontational approach to multilateral institutions as factors weighing against his selection.
His response to Friday’s announcement has itself become a subject of discussion among Nobel experts.
Nobel Committee faces political pressure
The Norwegian Nobel Committee maintains that its decisions are independent of political pressure.
However, the selection comes amid questions about how Washington might react if Trump is overlooked.
Last year’s prize went to Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, who subsequently presented her Nobel gold medal to Trump in recognition of his role in the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.
The gesture did not transfer the Nobel title, which remains with Machado.
The committee’s secretary, Kristian Berg Harpviken, said political considerations and possible reactions may be discussed, but maintained that such pressure does not determine the outcome.
The 2026 prize will be selected from 287 candidates – 208 individuals and 79 organizations – whose identities remain officially confidential, AFP reported.
The winner will receive a medal, diploma and monetary award at a ceremony in Oslo on Dec. 10.

SINGAPORE, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- Singapore and Mongolia will open applications for carbon credit projects on Oct. 30 under a bilateral implementation agreement, Singapore's Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry and National Environment Agency said in a statement on Thursday.
The projects will generate carbon credits aligned with Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. Under Singapore's International Carbon Credit Framework, the credits may qualify for use by Singapore-based companies liable for carbon tax to offset up to 5 percent of their taxable emissions.
Interested parties may apply for authorization of eligible carbon credit projects in Mongolia. The two governments will review applications jointly on a rolling basis.
The agreement is Singapore's sixth bilateral implementation agreement under which Singapore has opened applications for carbon credit projects, following similar agreements with Ghana, Bhutan, Peru, Rwanda and Thailand. ■

Unknown Publisher

12:10:12 KST

WELLINGTON, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- New Zealand's food and fiber exports reached a record 65.2 billion NZ dollars (36.6 billion U.S. dollars) in the year to June 30, up 8 percent from a year earlier, a senior official said Friday.
The result was 4.8 billion NZ dollars higher than the previous year and exceeded the Ministry for Primary Industries' June forecast of 64.3 billion NZ dollars, Agriculture and Forestry Minister Todd McClay said in a statement.
"The Middle East conflict and trade policies in some key markets have disrupted supply chains and pushed up inflation and input costs," McClay was quoted as saying.
Strong demand for New Zealand's food and fiber products, along with tight global supply, supported prices, McClay said.
Dairy export revenue rose 6 percent to 28.8 billion NZ dollars, while meat and wool exports increased 20 percent to 14.8 billion NZ dollars. Horticulture export revenue grew 5 percent to 9.3 billion NZ dollars, statistics showed.
In the year to June 30, food and fiber exports rose 20 percent to 5.3 billion NZ dollars to the European Union, 11 percent to 1.1 billion NZ dollars to the United Arab Emirates, and 24 percent to 541 million NZ dollars to India, ahead of a bilateral free trade agreement with India taking effect on Oct. 20, McClay said.
The government is targeting a doubling of the value of New Zealand's exports by 2034, he added. (1 NZ dollar equals 0.56 U.S. dollar) ■

Ukraine, Europe, US officials to meet for talks to end war
October 9, 2026
Ukrainian and European officials are set to meet US President Donald Trump's envoys in Miami on Friday to discuss "new ideas" to end Russia's war in Ukraine.
Ukraine's President Volodomyr Zelenskyy confirmed the meeting on Thursday evening, after a Russian attack on buses killed 30 civilians in the frontline city of Kramatorsk in eastern Ukraine.
Before the strikes in Kramatorsk, a Russian missile hit a five-storey apartment block in the northern Chernihiv region, killing 22 Ukrainians, including five children.
More than 70 people have been killed in Russian strikes on Ukraine in the past two days, Zelenskyy said.
What did Zelenskyy say about the Miami meeting?
"The Ukrainian negotiating team is due to meet Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff in the US tomorrow," Zelenskyy said. "The meeting is expected to last two days. We are also counting on a European team to join our negotiating group."
Zelenskyy's chief of staff, Kyrylo Budanov, and other top officials, including Rustem Umerov, Sergiy Kyslytsya and David Arakhamia, will also attend, the Ukrainian president said.
"They will discuss new ideas and proposals that American negotiators began developing with the Russians and Ukrainians during their recent visit to the region", one of the US sources familiar with the talks told AFP.
"They are all nervous about the winter. It will be a tough winter if the war does not stop," the US source said.
Zelenskyy blames US for inaction
Amid rising civilian casualties and fears of further escalation, Zelenskyy urged the US to accede to his request to expand Ukraine's access to Elon Musk's Starlink satellite service, which would help it target Russian ballistic-missile launchers.
"Open Starlink for Ukraine. You did open it when you were responding to Iran ... I've said quite openly — give it to us, help us defend our skies and dominate there. And then Putin will sit down at the negotiating table," he said.
Zelenskyy went on to accuse the US of being unwilling to pressure Russia into negotiations, adding that enabling Starlink would cost Washington nothing.
"So where's the truth here, where's the honesty? Where's the stalemate? ... That's called unwillingness," he said.
Ukraine president rejects Rubio claim that war is deadlocked
Zelenskyy was responding to remarks on Wednesday from US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who said the war in Ukraine was at a stalemate.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Thursday that he agreed with Rubio's assessment, adding that he saw no immediate prospect for a three-way summit between Russian President Vladimir Putin, Zelenskyy and Trump.
"One cannot, on the one hand, negotiate with the Russians about future economic projects, whilst on the other hand say that we find ourselves in some sort of ... diplomatic stalemate," Zelenskyy said, countering the US narrative. "We are not a diplomatic dead end," he said.
Zelenskyy also called for tougher sanctions to cripple the Russian economy, a point Ukrainian officials are expected to press US envoys on at the meeting.

Nava Koster, an Israeli stranded in Dubai since Tuesday, told Walla on Wednesday that the alternative flight she had booked for Thursday had also been canceled. “The flight we bought tickets for tomorrow has also been canceled. All the rescue flights have been canceled,” she said.

I believe we are not the only group of Israelis still stranded in Dubai.”

Israelis stuck without medication, unable to afford return tickets
The situation is particularly difficult for two members of the group who are nearing 80 and need medication. “For them, the prolonged wait and uncertainty are not merely a matter of convenience,” Koster wrote in a message to Walla.
She asked Walla to investigate how many Israelis remain in Dubai, how many are able to board flights described as rescue flights, and what assistance is available to those who cannot afford thousands of dollars for replacement tickets.
“There is a large gap between reports of ‘rescue flights’ and the reality on the ground,” she said. “We are still here, waiting for a solution and a way to get home.”
Arkia cancels rescue flights
Meanwhile, Israeli airline Arkia announced that its rescue flights from Dubai to Israel had been canceled.
“Authorization to operate the flights was valid until yesterday, but in the evening, the authorities decided to revoke the permits for Israeli airlines to operate flights from Dubai. Since then, Arkia has worked with all relevant parties and done everything possible to obtain renewed authorization and operate the flights. Unfortunately, these efforts have not succeeded as of this hour, and we are therefore forced to cancel the flights,” the airline said.
Eshet Tours said: “We understand the distress and uncertainty passengers are experiencing following the cancellation of flights from Dubai to Israel, and we are continuing to work to help bring home those who have not yet returned. The company has been, and remains, in regular contact with passengers through the tour guide and its emergency hotline. Some members of the group have already returned to Israel. Unfortunately, the cancellation of the flight on which some passengers were due to return has further delayed their return. We are addressing the situation continuously and assessing the available alternatives to find the best solution for their return as soon as possible. The company continues to assist all passengers who remain abroad and stay in contact with them until they return to Israel.”

Editor's Notes: American Jews are changing after Oct. 7, but we cannot abandon them - comment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
03:03:43 UTC
12:03:43 KST

At the National Conservatism Conference in Jerusalem this week, Israeli historian Gadi Taub described progressive Jews whom he accused of appeasing antisemites as “no longer our friends.” I respect Gadi and think highly of his work. I disagree with writing those Jews off, and I worry that we are missing how much American Jewish life has changed since October 7.
NatCon, part of the national conservatism movement founded by Yoram Hazony, brought together politicians and thinkers from Israel, the United States, and Europe. They offered plenty of advice on how other people should run their independent nations. Some arguments made me reconsider assumptions; others troubled me. I also heard Israelis on the Right struggling with things said by people they had expected to agree with. Those conversations were worth having.
I was born in Chicago and grew up in Israel. I still consider American Jewry a community I belong to. Since October 7, I have seen leaders become more outspoken in Israel’s defense and more restrained in their criticism, even when some constituents wanted them to be harsher. They deserve recognition, including when the changes fall short of what Gadi or I would like.
Rabbi Ammi Hirsch, senior rabbi of Manhattan’s Stephen Wise Free Synagogue, has urged Reform Judaism for years to strengthen its commitment to Zionism and Jewish peoplehood. In 2023, I reported his warning: “I fear that we are losing the soul of the Reform movement.” He wanted Reform Jews to place responsibility for their own people at the center of their Judaism.
On Yom Kippur 2024, he told younger Jews: “We wanted you to be Zionists.” He also acknowledged flaws in his synagogue’s educational approach. This May, more than 350 rabbis, cantors, educators, and other participants gathered at his Re-CHARGING Reform Judaism conference, which adopted resolutions renewing commitments to Zionism, Jewish peoplehood, and Israel education. I see Reform rabbis reconsidering what they teach and how they speak about Israel, with a stronger emphasis on Zionism and Jewish solidarity.
Hirsch is asking what his movement taught its children. Conservatives should ask themselves the same question. Younger Republicans and Democrats are both becoming more critical of Israel. Could failures in education explain part of this? I want young people to know our history well enough to argue with us intelligently.
The Anti-Defamation League also came in for plenty of criticism at NatCon. The ADL is a major institution devoted to monitoring and combating antisemitism, with an annual US incident audit dating to 1979. As a journalist, I consider its research among the most important and systematic bodies of evidence we have for understanding antisemitism in America.
I have known Jonathan Greenblatt, its CEO and national director, for many years. We have had serious disagreements about the ADL’s positioning and its responses to Israel’s internal affairs. I often felt it was reading Israel through American political categories and failing to understand how different Israeli society is.
Since October 7, Greenblatt has become, in my view, one of Israel’s most articulate and influential defenders on American television. He has been a staunch supporter, explaining Israel’s predicament to audiences well beyond the Jewish community. I also see a change in the organization. In 2025, he explicitly pledged to concentrate its energies on Jewish safety while continuing to oppose other forms of bigotry. Singling out the ADL for attack while overlooking that work and that shift is unfair.
American Jewish leaders are also holding together communities whose members disagree sharply about Israel. They need room to speak honestly. Asking them to defend every Israeli policy would make that work harder. Our relationship should accommodate criticism, including criticism I find unfair. I would keep the conversation going even with Jews whose politics have barely moved.
Israel needs allies. We should be open to politicians and parties who reconsider their positions and act accordingly. My mentor on these issues is Dani Dayan, chairman of Yad Vashem, Israel’s Holocaust memorial. He has taught me to examine the country, the party, and the individual. Dani once avoided visiting Germany and Austria; their acceptance of historical responsibility persuaded him to reconsider.
In May 2023, I reported on two MPs from Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany party, known as AfD, and an aide who toured Yad Vashem. Dayan and the senior staff declined to meet them, and a request for a memorial ceremony was refused. He hoped the visit would change their views.
I’m open to parties changing. I’d like to see something more substantial than their English-language websites. If a party claims to have dealt with antisemitism, will it remove an antisemite when doing so costs votes? How does it speak about the Jews in its own country?
An Israeli handshake has political value. Before offering it, we should consult the local Jewish community. Its members hear the local speeches and will still be there after our delegation has gone home. Their disagreements with Netanyahu should not affect whether we listen to their evidence.
We are prepared to recognize changes in prospective allies abroad. American Jewish leaders deserve the same attention. And our obligations to fellow Jews extend to those who continue to disagree with us. They are our brothers and sisters, and I’m not willing to give them up.

The war in Gaza, relations with Israel, and the war in Iran were at the center of one of the sharpest exchanges Thursday night between incumbent Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff and Republican challenger Rep. Mike Collins in their Georgia Senate debate.
Ossoff, Georgia's first Jewish US senator, was asked directly whether he believed Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. The question came one day after the third anniversary of the October 7 massacre and referenced criticism he has faced from some members of Atlanta's Jewish community after voting to block an arms shipment to Israel.
Ossoff did not answer yes or no.
"The question of genocide is a question of whether a government has the specific intent to destroy a national or ethnic group, and that is a question for the International Criminal Court," Ossoff said. "There is no doubt in my mind that Israeli forces prosecuting the war in Gaza violated the law of armed conflict and international humanitarian law."
"I care deeply about the security of the Israeli people, among whom are members of my family," he continued. "I also care about innocent Palestinian life and make no apology for my votes."
Moderator Rick Folbaum also asked Ossoff whether he was alarmed by growing anti-Israel sentiment within the Democratic Party and whether he would vote yes or no on the administration's latest $2.8 billion weapons package for Israel. Ossoff did not directly answer either question during his response.
Instead, he attacked Collins over his support for sanctioning and defunding the International Criminal Court.
"His view is that there should not be accountability for crimes against humanity no matter who commits them," Ossoff said.
Collins: 'He talks one way, and he votes another way'
Collins responded with a sharp political and personal attack, tying Ossoff to figures on the left wing of the Democratic Party.
"Jon Ossoff has been out there and recruited support and endorsed this Abdul El-Sayed. He hates Israel, loves Iran. That's his pick," Collins said, referring to the Democratic Senate candidate in Michigan.
He also mentioned Hasan Piker and accused Ossoff of moving "as far left as he can go."
"He talks one way, and he votes another way," Collins said.
The exchange then shifted immediately to antisemitism and extremism. Folbaum asked Collins about his son-in-law, described in the question as a white supremacist social media influencer, and about members of Collins's staff who had been linked to racism and antisemitism.
"I've condemned racism, antisemitism, hate. I don't care where the source is," Collins said. "It's wrong. We have no place in this world for that."
Ossoff fired back, alleging that "neo-Nazi propaganda is disseminated to an audience of millions from your home."
He also accused Collins's office of intervening at the Justice Department on behalf of a Holocaust denier and of working with white supremacists. Those were allegations made by Ossoff during the debate.
Ossoff on Iran war: 'We were lied into' it
Another major point of disagreement was the war in Iran.
Ossoff repeatedly attacked Collins for supporting the conflict, saying the congressman had "voted seven times for the war in Iran." Early in the debate, Ossoff linked the war to higher gas and diesel prices in Georgia and later said the United States should "end this disastrous war in Iran."
He sharpened that criticism later in the debate.
"It's been a disaster, and so has this war, a war, by the way, that we were lied into," Ossoff said. "They told us last year that they'd obliterated Iran's nuclear program. This year, they told us it posed an imminent threat."
"So on top of the tariffs now we have eight months of war, 18 Americans killed in action, hundreds wounded, Iran still has its uranium, Iran still has its drones and missiles, diesel's at an all-time high, unleaded gas is at four dollars."
Ossoff returned to the issue while discussing US service members.
"When I talk to military families across the state, they want to know that their government is being honest with them about why we go to war," he said. "This war has been a disaster. Eighteen Americans have been killed. Hundreds have been wounded. The president declared victory on day four of this conflict."
Collins, by contrast, defended Trump's decision to go to war.
"The president had every right to go in there and make sure that Iran does not get a nuclear weapon," Collins said. He argued that the International Atomic Energy Agency had already sounded alarms that Iran was close to obtaining one.
"Iran doesn't only want to decimate and kill Israel. They want us as well," Collins said. "We've been at war with this regime for 47 years. They've been killing American service members for 47 years. And they were this close to getting a nuclear weapon, and they would have used it."
The contrast between the two candidates returned in their closing statements. Ossoff again said Collins had "voted seven times for the war in Iran," while Collins portrayed Ossoff as aligned with figures on the Democratic left who, he argued, held hostile views toward Israel.
The debate was the first televised meeting between the two ahead of the November 3 midterm election. Ossoff has served in the Senate since 2021, while Collins, a Republican member of the House, is seeking to unseat him and flip the seat to the GOP.
The debate was held in the Atlanta area, moderated by Rick Folbaum and broadcast across Georgia by Gray Media.

El-Sayed says he would not arm Israel after Iranian attack

Examining NYT report alleging top US Embassy aide in Jerusalem suppressed Israel cables - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
03:02:58 UTC
12:02:58 KST

The New York Times published a serious accusation on Thursday: that David Milstein, a senior adviser to US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, suppressed or altered diplomatic reporting to make Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government appear more favorable to Washington.
Such an allegation deserves scrutiny, as does the way a newspaper presents the evidence and the response of those it accuses.
The Times reported that Milstein had delayed, blocked, or rewritten embassy communications about Israeli settlements, settler violence, and humanitarian conditions in Gaza. It said its investigation drew on interviews with 15 US officials and dozens of internal documents.
These are substantial claims that should be examined on their evidence rather than accepted or rejected because of the politics surrounding them.
Huckabee disputed the account. According to coverage of the investigation, the ambassador categorically rejected the allegations and challenged their factual basis. In his public response, he criticized the newspaper’s handling of his comments.
Readers must be able to distinguish evidence, interpretation, and disputes
That complaint raises a question distinct from the accuracy of the investigation itself: Did readers receive the substance of the ambassador’s response, or only excerpts that left important elements out?
When a report makes consequential allegations about officials representing the United States, selected quotations should accurately convey the substance of their replies. Readers need to understand what was denied, what explanation was offered, and whether reporters sought to test that explanation against the documents and accounts on which they relied. Publishing a rebuttal is not merely a formality to be completed before returning to the accusation.
The presence of anonymous sources and internal documents strengthens a report only to the extent that they support its specific conclusions. Neither the number of interviews nor the forcefulness of an official’s denial settles the matter. What matters is whether readers can distinguish firsthand evidence, interpretation, disputed accounts, and facts that remain unknown.
The Times also discussed Milstein’s connection to conservative commentator Mark Levin. Milstein is Levin’s stepson, and Levin is a prominent supporter of Israel and Netanyahu. Their relationship may be relevant background, but family ties do not establish that Levin directed Milstein’s work, shaped embassy communications, or influenced what information reached the Trump administration.
If the report is suggesting such influence, readers deserve to know what supports that suggestion. Documented communications or testimony linking Levin to specific decisions would be significant. Without that connection, placing family relationships alongside allegations about altered diplomatic reporting risks encouraging an inference that has not been demonstrated.
Diplomatic cables routinely reviewed and revised
Diplomatic cables are routinely drafted, reviewed, challenged, and revised within institutions serving elected administrations. Political appointees and career diplomats may disagree about assessments or priorities. Such disagreements are not automatically improper. Deliberately suppressing material information, particularly if it leaves policymakers with a distorted picture of conditions on the ground, would be a much more serious issue.
Any assessment of Milstein’s conduct should therefore distinguish ordinary internal editing from instances in which important information allegedly failed to reach its intended recipients. What authority did he hold? Which changes were requested, and why? Who approved them? Were relevant assessments ultimately delivered through other channels? These details would help readers judge the weight of the accusations.
The Times reportedly acknowledged uncertainty about whether the alleged interventions changed White House policy and how much Huckabee knew. These limitations should remain prominent. Allegations that someone sought to influence diplomatic reporting do not automatically establish that US President Donald Trump or his advisers made decisions on a distorted record.
The newspaper’s investigation may contain valuable findings, and officials’ denials should not automatically outweigh testimony from people familiar with embassy operations. At the same time, Huckabee’s objections about the use of his statement warrant a fair hearing. The credibility of either side depends on the completeness of the underlying record, not on which side delivers the sharper criticism.
Reporting on Israel and US policy carries unusual political weight. Readers should not have to infer connections from proximity, search elsewhere for a central rebuttal, or confuse the possible motives of officials with proof of specific misconduct. Clear sourcing, meaningful context, and faithful representation of responses are basic safeguards against those problems.
The full published allegations and Huckabee’s complete remarks should be assessed together. Serious charges require substantial evidence, and those accused deserve to have their answers represented accurately. A newspaper asking the public to trust its investigation must make it possible to evaluate not only its conclusions, but how it reached them.

US-based Kashmir filmmaker Arfat Sheikh walks free from ICE detention
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
03:00:50 UTC
12:00:50 KST

Award-winning Kashmiri filmmaker Arfat Sheikh has been released from US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention on bond after being detained on September 24, according to a statement by a campaign of his friends and relatives to free him.
Sheikh, whose work has explored conflict in his native India-administered Kashmir, was detained by ICE, part of the Department of Homeland Security, while coming off a plane from California at the Washington Dulles International Airport, the campaign said.
It said Sheikh's bond was granted on Tuesday and he was released on Thursday, adding that the deportation case against him continues.
The campaign said Sheikh, who lived in Alexandria, Virginia, entered the US in 2019 on a student visa to pursue graduate studies in film at Georgia State University and filed for asylum in 2020.
The campaign said he had a pending immigration application and was authorised to work and live in the US.
DHS said on Wednesday Sheikh was arrested on September 24.
It said Sheikh "legally entered the US on a temporary basis and illegally overstayed his lawful admittance." A pending application does not confer legal status in the US, DHS said, adding he will receive due process.
President Donald Trump's administration said in August it was working "to identify and revoke the non-immigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the US claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently."
Trump has pursued an immigration crackdown and deportation drive that he says aims to improve domestic security.
Rights advocates say the crackdown has violated due process and free speech rights and created an unsafe environment, particularly for ethnic minorities, who have raised concerns about racial profiling.
Saffron Kingdom
Sheikh's first feature film, 2024's "Saffron Kingdom," won Best Feature Film at the Chicago Filmmakers Awards, the LA Film and Documentary Awards, the Melbourne Independent Film Festival and the Wake Forest Film Festival.
Sheikh, who hails from India-administered Kashmir, won the Emerging Filmmaker Activist Award at the Teaneck International Film Festival.
The film explored conflict in Kashmir through the journey of a family from Srinagar in India-administered Kashmir in the 1990s to Atlanta in 2019.
Muslim-majority Kashmir is claimed in full by both Hindu-majority India and Islamic Pakistan, but each control only part of it and have fought wars over the territory. India revoked Kashmir's constitutional autonomy and annexed it in August 2019.
A significant proportion of Muslim Kashmiris favour the right to self-determination as promised by several UN Security Council resolutions, seeking either full independence or accession to Pakistan.
In May 2025, India and Pakistan fought a brief war using missiles, fighter jets, drones and other weapons, which ultimately led to US involvement.
US President Trump helped broker a ceasefire during the military confrontation, an intervention later publicly praised by Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, while India maintained that the truce was reached through direct bilateral military communications and that Trump had played no role in it.
Sheikh, who grew up in India-administered Kashmir during the 1990s, told TRT World in a 2024 interview that his film "Saffron Kingdom "was born from his desire to reclaim his people's narrative, who have often been negatively depicted by Indian cinema."
"This film is my way of breaking Bollywood's hegemony over our narrative. It's about debunking the lies they have been peddling for years," he said.
In the interview he recalled traumatic memories of being locked in a room with his family while the Indian military tortured his uncle.
His father, a renowned Kashmiri musician, was murdered while travelling to northern Indian state of Punjab. "His death was reported in newspapers, but each paper had its own version of events. We were not even given his body," he said.

Can China use its widening US yield gap to boost the yuan’s global role?
Beijing could leverage the yuan’s low interest rate to increase the currency’s worldwide use, an expert says
The 10-year US Treasury yield was 5.22 per cent on Thursday, compared with 1.69 per cent for Chinese government bonds on their first trading day after the National Day holiday – a gap of about 3.5 percentage points, compared with a record 3.7-percentage-point gap on September 9.
Jiang Zhenlong, an associate research fellow at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences’ Institute of Finance and Banking, argued that higher US yields weakened the appeal of yuan assets and added pressure on the exchange rate and capital flows, but also raised dollar funding costs.
“The China-US yield inversion presents an asymmetric effect: pressure on the asset allocation side and benefit on the financing side,” he wrote in the latest issue of China Money Market, a central bank-affiliated magazine.

Storm Simon seen exploding into major hurricane before hitting Mexico

Unknown Publisher
