Fired researchers accuse OpenAI of ‘chilling’ safety efforts
- - Three fired OpenAI researchers said they were dismissed for warning about AI dangers and for putting safety ahead of OpenAI’s short-term interests.
- - The researchers said the abrupt firings could weaken OpenAI’s open culture and may threaten independent audits and safety work.
- - OpenAI said they broke company rules by mishandling sensitive information, as the case renewed debate over slowing AI development and safety.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – Three former OpenAI security researchers on Oct 8 accused the ChatGPT-maker of firing them for warning about the dangers of artificial intelligence, reigniting the debate over safety at a company whose software has been involved in security breaches.
“I believe we were fired for prioritising safety over the near-term interests of OpenAI as a corporation,” one of the fired staffers, Mikita Balesni, wrote on X, breaking a week-long silence since their very public dismissal.
Balesni and the two other fired employees, Tomek Korbak and Jasmine Wang, publicly shared a letter to OpenAI on Oct 8.
“Our firing leaves us worried that the norms inside OpenAI are shifting,” the letter says, and continues that “terminations such as ours, executed and communicated so abruptly, are chilling the open culture OpenAI has prized in the past”.
They also call on the company to keep its promise to permanently host independent auditors.
“We are concerned that our firings may be used to justify ending that work,” the letter says.
OpenAI, for its part, said it fired them for allegedly violating company rules.
“Our investigation confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures, violating our policies and breaking the trust essential to our work,” OpenAI told AFP in a statement on Oct 1.
“We do not terminate employees for raising concerns,” a research executive at OpenAI said in a memo to staff on Oct 7, an excerpt of which was shared with AFP.
A divided sector
The three fired researchers worked on monitoring OpenAI’s models, which escaped their testing environment in July and hacked Hugging Face, an AI coding library.
The incident sparked a heated debate in Silicon Valley over whether or not to slow the development of this technology.
If OpenAI’s researchers can no longer sound the alarm or work with outside parties, “we are all at greater risk that something truly catastrophic will happen”, the researchers’ letter warns.
They also claim that nearly 400 OpenAI employees signed a petition in July that called for an industry-wide slowdown on advanced development of AI models.
In September, Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX chief Elon Musk called for a slowdown as well.
“Right now we’re investing more in safety, security, alignment, monitoring and that will allow us to continue to progress model capability a lot,” Altman told reporters in September.
Others, like Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, want to move full steam ahead.
US regulators are unlikely to intervene.
In September, US President Donald Trump hosted a group of American tech executives who agreed to abide by a voluntary code of conduct on AI safety. AFP

USS Lincoln returns to US after long deployment supporting war on Iran
Crew members express relief upon return from record-breaking deployment of 265 days that strained conditions on board.
The United States aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln has returned to its home port after a 322-day deployment, including a record 265 consecutive days at sea, during which it helped wage the US-Israel war on Iran.
The vessel returned to Naval Air Station North Island in San Diego, California, on Thursday, where members of its crew were greeted by family and friends.
“It feels amazing,” 20-year-old Abel Ramirez told The Associated Press news agency, adding that his parents had driven from Texas to meet him. “There was a certain point when I never thought I would come off.”
The record-setting deployment of the USS Lincoln became a symbol for larger criticisms of the US war effort, which has dragged on since February with no clear end in sight and has strained US military stockpiles.
The prolonged deployment prompted a series of news reports calling attention to deteriorating conditions, food shortages and a series of reported suicide attempts by crew members.
Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth praised the sailors on Wednesday in remarks that accused the media of trying to turn the ship into “a symbol of dysfunction or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission”.
President Donald Trump and members of his administration have frequently lashed out at the news media for critical reporting on the war on Iran. Trump himself has called the reporting about the USS Lincoln “fake news”.
“The Lincoln has been out there for a period of time, a good period of time,” he said at an Oval Office meeting on August 17. “I know people on the Lincoln, and they say it’s beautifully maintained and beautifully taken care of.”
Earlier that month, when confronted with the amount of time the USS Lincoln had spent at sea without a port stop, Trump quipped that its deployment was “not nearly long enough“.
The reports of mental health strain on the USS Lincoln come as public opinion polls show low approval ratings among US voters for the war against Iran.
On Thursday, the Pew Research Center released a poll that found 65 percent of Americans disapproved of Trump’s handling of the war, compared with 33 percent who approved.
The war has also fuelled concerns about the cost of living ahead of the upcoming midterm elections. Since the war began, Iran has hindered commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway for the trade of fuel, fertiliser and other goods.
Sailors returning home on the USS Lincoln said that they were looking forward to fresh meals and spending time with their families.
Alma Solano Velez said that her husband, one of the US service members on board, shared a list of foods he had been craving over his 10-month deployment: oxtail, barbecue chicken, broccoli and shrimp empanadas, among others.
She added that he had spoken about “the lack of food and showers” and was looking forward to seeing their four-year-old daughter.

In FocusFrom kitchen waste to sky-high costs: inside Hong Kong’s quest for green jet fuel
As city sets goals for adopting sustainable aviation fuel, industry leaders examine how to scale up supply chains and win over price-sensitive passengers
China’s once-notorious “gutter oil”, recycled from kitchen and drainage waste, has almost vanished from dining tables in recent years and now carries the nickname liquid gold.
The substance has become a highly sought-after feedstock for producing clean energy, especially sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), with biofuel producers such as Hong Kong-based Ecoceres sourcing gutter oil across the Greater Bay Area.
EcoCeres’ co-chairman, Alan Chan Ying-lung, witnessed how the restaurant waste transformed from a nationwide food safety concern into a valuable commodity.
“I can recall that the gutter oil we collected was basically free 10 years ago, and authorities even offered subsidies [to collectors], but now the unit cost is even more expensive than fuel,” he said.

Pollsters name two leaders in electoral support
This is according to a survey conducted by Rating Group on October 3–5, Ukrinform reports.
“We asked respondents whom they would vote for in the first round of a hypothetical presidential election in Ukraine. The top two in terms of electoral support are Volodymyr Zelensky (22.9%) and Valerii Zaluzhnyi (20.2%). They are followed by Petro Poroshenko (7.6%), Mykhailo Fedorov (7.6%) and Kyrylo Budanov (6.7%),” the report says.
It also noted that 5.4% of Ukrainians would support Andrii Biletskyi, 5.1% Dmytro Razumkov, 2.4% Serhii Prytula, 1.9% Yulia Tymoshenko, and 1.4% Yurii Boiko.
Pollsters noted that 4.5% of respondents would vote for another candidate, 5.2% would not take part in the election, while 9.2% were undecided.
The pollsters said the survey was conducted using the CATI (Computer-Assisted Telephone Interview) method – telephone interviews conducted with the assistance of a computer. The sample consisted of 1,000 respondents selected through a random sample of mobile phone numbers, covering Ukrainians aged 18 and over in all regions except temporarily occupied territories and areas without Ukrainian mobile coverage at the time of the survey. The results were weighted using current data from the State Statistics Service of Ukraine.
The sample was representative by age, gender and type of settlement, with a margin of error of no more than 3.1 percentage points at a 95% confidence level.

NEW DELHI: Steep margins on medicines are a concern as they can push a product or influence its selection, with government tightening its glare on errant healthcare players including companies and hospitals, pharmaceuticals secretary Manoj Joshi said.Joshi elaborated on the unethical practices in healthcare industry, just before govt announced capping of trade margins at 30% on all cancer drugs Thursday. "Two broad areas of malpractice which we have noticed is where hospitals favour expensive medicines that offer the highest margins. Second, when smaller manufacturers push products carrying unusually high margins, it can create a nexus with doctors or retailers, usually in smaller towns," he said, adding govt should not intervene in the margin issue, except where there is "malpractice".Joshi said the strategy needs to be differentiated, with higher-priced medicines requiring a different approach from low-cost drugs dispensed in rural and remote markets through govt-run Jan Aushadhi stores. The viability of these 20,000-odd stores is a challenge.
"Here, medicine prices are low, margins are also small, but cost of setting up and running a store remains same. We are addressing this by increasing margins, but even if we double them, some stores may still not be viable.
The challenge is acute in remote areas. Even big pharmacies stock FMCG products to supplement revenues," he added.Talking about Uniform code for Pharma Marketing Practices (UCPMP), Joshi said fewer instances of larger companies as violators are being seen. Many are heavily dependent on US and European markets and are conscious of their reputation and ethics. Issues continue among smaller manufacturers with turnover of around Rs 100-150 crore operating in local markets, where there could be a nexus between doctors or retailers and manufacturers.

Running out of royals: why calls are growing to let Japan’s princess Aiko take the throne
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
00:20:50 UTC
09:20:50 KST

Her face is splashed across magazine covers. Fans flock to online stores to snap up her outfits. At official engagements, huge crowds wait in the crushing heat to catch a glimpse of a woman revered for her ‘regal dignity, beauty and aura’.
Princess Aiko, 24, is the most popular member of Japan’s imperial family, but according to law she will never be empress and, as the country runs out of royals, more and more Japanese people are asking why.
The debate has gathered momentum in the years since Aiko, the only child of Emperor Naruhito and Empress Masako, has transformed from a shy primary school pupil into a young woman at ease with public and media attention.
Under a law established almost 140 years ago, women are forbidden from ascending to Japan’s Chrysanthemum throne. But the regulation defies public support for changes that would allow a woman to become empress regnant and avert a looming succession crisis.
The imperial family is facing the same demographic winds buffeting the rest of the country: three decades ago it had 30 members; now there are just 16, only five of them men.
Japanese citizens support a change, irrespective of their political loyalties. In a poll conducted in April by the Mainichi Shimbun newspaper, 72% favoured the idea of a woman becoming emperor, while just 10% opposed it.
Pressure to change the male-only succession law, passed in 1947 but based on legislation introduced during the Meiji era in 1889, is intensifying, forcing the conservative government of Sanae Takaichi to address the dearth of male heirs to the 1,500-year-old imperial throne.
Just three men comprise the current line of succession – Emperor Naruhito’s younger brother, Crown Prince Akishino; his son, Prince Hisahito; and the emperor’s uncle, Prince Hitachi, who is 90.
If Prince Hisahito, a 20-year-old university student, and the first male born into the imperial family for four decades, does not have a son, the line of succession will come to an end within a generation.
Previous governments have tried to solve the succession question by considering legislation that would finally bring gender equality to the rarefied corridors of the imperial palace in Tokyo. But pressure from conservative MPs – and Hisahito’s birth in 2006 – brought the debate to an abrupt end.
Takaichi triggered anger this summer when her party and its conservative allies pushed through amendments that will safeguard the male-only succession for generations.
The changes, which go into effect later this month, allow women to retain their royal status after marrying non-royals, and resurrects male-line descendants belonging to 11 “collateral branches” of the family that left the imperial fold after the end of the second world war.
In theory, that means a distant male relative could be “adopted” into the heart of the family provided he is single and aged over 15. If he marries and his wife gives birth to a son, that child would then join the line of succession.
The fate of Japan’s imperial family has attracted international attention. In 2024, the UN women’s rights committee urged the Japanese government to allow a female emperor. Tokyo dismissed the intervention as “regrettable” and “inappropriate,” saying the imperial succession was a matter of “fundamental national identity”.
The UN and Japanese public opinion have crashed against the hard rock of conservative ideology espoused by Takaichi – Japan’s first female prime minister.
During the succession revision debate, she told lawmakers: “The unparalleled historic fact that the imperial line has been maintained through the male line for 126 generations is the foundation of the emperor’s authority and legitimacy.”
Takaichi has also said that the revisions were intended only to ease the succession crisis, not to settle the debate over female emperors.
But Prof Makoto Okawa, an expert on imperial lineage and succession at Chuo University in Tokyo, said the recent amendment “clearly points towards maintaining the male-line succession”.
Aiko’s popularity could force a rethink, however, given the “growing sense of unease among members of the public about excluding someone from the possibility of succeeding to the throne solely because she is a woman”.
“Many people in Japan have watched Princess Aiko grow up. The composure, dignity and grace she has displayed in recent diplomatic and other official engagements have contributed to the strong public support she enjoys. Many people see her as embodying and carrying forward Emperor Naruhito’s understanding of the role of the emperor as a symbol of the nation who remains close to the people.”
Jin, an Aiko fan who manages an Instagram account devoted to the princess, said the government had ignored the overwhelming consensus behind a change to the male-only succession law.
In her eyes, Aiko is more than qualified to succeed her father.
“She is the emperor’s only direct descendant, and her character and dignity are of the highest caliber. Aiko is someone who is clearly worthy of serving as a symbol of Japan.”
Aiko – or another future female member of the imperial family – would not be the first female to ascend the throne. Japan has had eight female monarchs, although their role was to sustain the imperial line until a male heir was born. Go-Sakuramachi, who ruled from 1762 to 1770, was the most recent.
Japan’s royals, who are forbidden from commenting on politics, have employed typically nuanced language to communicate their unease with the status quo.
At a press conference in June, the emperor said of the succession debate in parliament: “I hope discussions on how to secure the number of imperial family members … gain the understanding of the people.”
His younger brother, Akishino, went further, telling reporters: “It is important for society to keep progressing … I believe the duty of the imperial family is to act in response to the requests of society … I do not think there are any differences between women and men.”

Man injured after ICE shooting in New York
October 9, 2026
A man was shot by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent during an arrest in New York City, US federal authorities and Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Thursday.
The shooting occurred at around 4 p.m. local time (2100 GMT) in the Marble Hill neighborhood of Manhattan.
The New York Police Department said its officers were not involved in the incident and that the man was conscious and receiving medical attention at a nearby hospital.
US President Donald Trump's administration has scaled up ICE raids in major US cities to detain and deport people who are in the US illegally.
Mamdani urges Trump to end ICE actions in NYC
New York City Mayor Mamdani condemned the shooting and said he had contacted President Trump.
Mamdani added that a five-year-old child was reportedly in the car during the shooting, but that the child was "physically unharmed."
"This is an unconscionable and incredibly serious situation," Mamdani said in a post on X. "I have called the President; when we speak I will demand that he ends all ICE enforcement actions in our city. I will not stand by while ICE agents terrorize our communities."
New York Governor Kathy Hochul said she had spoken with Trump and Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin about the shooting. DHS is the parent agency of ICE.
"I expressed outrage on behalf of New Yorkers and urged them to halt ICE enforcement operations in New York," Hochul said. "I also asked that any body camera footage of the shooting be released to the public so we can establish the facts and get to the truth."
Federal govt says 'criminal illegal alien' in hospital receiving treatment
In a post on X, DHS had confirmed that an "ICE officer discharged his weapon" during an attempt to arrest a "criminal illegal alien from the Dominican Republic" with ties "to the Trinitarios gang."
DHS said the man had a prior conviction for grand larceny and had been arrested "multiple" times for assault, robbery, possession of drugs, and weapons possession.
DHS noted ICE officers immediately rendered aid after the man was injured. "The individual is alive and at a local hospital," the statement said, adding that the FBI was on the scene.
ICE, CBP fatal shootings raise alarm in second Trump term
Deadly ICE and Border Patrol shootings have drawn major controversy during Trump's second term, particularly regarding the training and oversight of the agents.
An ICE agent killed a 37-year-old US citizen, Renee Good, during their operations in Minneapolis in January, triggering demonstrations there and in several other US cities.
Later that month, Alex Pretti, another US citizen, was killed by two US Customs and Border Protection officers agents in Minneapolis following an altercation.

Trump online: A burst of anti-Somali and anti-Muslim rhetoric

"The once Great State of Minnesota is being taken over by Somali Immigrants. There is Violence, Murder, and Mayhem all over the State. The people of Minnesota must fight back," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.
Trump urged authorities in Minnesota to ask for federal intervention.
Civil rights advocates have criticized the Republican president's rhetoric towards minorities and immigrants, including when he previously called Somalis "garbage."
Trump has in the past repeatedly invoked a scandal in Minnesota that dates to 2020 in which scores of people were accused of defrauding millions of dollars from a state-run, federally funded child nutrition program. Many of the defendants in that case were Somali Americans.
In May, Aimee Bock, who is not a Somali immigrant and led the Minnesota non-profit group involved in the scandal, was sentenced to 41 years in prison after she was convicted last year of being the ringleader of the scheme.
The president has used the fraud case as part of his rationale for targeting Minnesota, led by Democrats, for an aggressive surge in arresting and deporting immigrants earlier this year and for moves aimed at restricting social service programs in the state, including Medicare and childcare.
Rights groups have accused Trump of using isolated fraud cases as an excuse to collectively target immigrant communities and criticized his approach to fraud, citing his pardons of those who have faced fraud convictions.
"Somali Minnesotans are our neighbors. They are part of Minnesota. And the Minnesota I know and love is so much better than this bigotry," Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison said in response to Trump's post.
In another post late on Wednesday, Trump called El-Sayed, a Muslim and the Democratic candidate for US Senate from Michigan, a "RADICAL Extremist" and "Terrorist Sympathizer" while offering support for the Republican candidate, Mike Rogers.
Democrats said Trump's rhetoric sought to distract voters from the impact of his policies heading into the November US midterm elections.
"He thinks he can use my name and my faith to distract us from the suffering his policies are inflicting on us at the pump, at the grocery store, and at the doctor's office," El-Sayed, who has faced anti-Muslim attacks from other Republicans, said on Thursday.
The Michigan Democratic Party and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer cast Trump's rhetoric as desperate and racist.
Trump has targeted minorities in his rhetoric in the past as well, having previously spread false claims that Haitian immigrants in an Ohio town were eating pets and having used the term "Palestinian" as an insult. REUTERS

ICE agent shoots man in New York City with five-year-old reportedly in car
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
00:13:55 UTC
09:13:55 KST

A US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent shot and wounded a man in New York City on Thursday afternoon during an enforcement operation, federal officials said.
The man was conscious and hospitalized, authorities said, and the shooting quickly sparked angry protests from local residents and elected officials in the neighborhood.
Early reports indicated that agents had surrounded the man and a five-year-old child in his car in a residential area before firing multiple rounds, the city’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, said in a statement on Thursday evening. The child was physically unharmed, he said.
“I have been on the phone with President Trump and [Homeland Security] secretary Mullin negotiating the release of the man ICE agents shot. Those negotiations were unsuccessful,” Mamdani told a press conference. He demanded from the Trump administration that ICE stop its enforcement actions in New York City, he said.
The shooting took place at roughly 4pm in the Marble Hill neighborhood of the Bronx, according to the New York police department (NYPD).
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said in a statement on social media that ICE officers were conducting an operation targeting an undocumented man from the Dominican Republic. The statement did not explain what led to the shooting, saying: “During the incident, an ICE officer discharged his weapon and the criminal illegal alien was injured.”
The extent of the man’s injuries was unknown. The department’s statement alleged that the man had “associations” with a gang and prior criminal convictions, but DHS did not name the man or provide evidence of his background. The department has previously faced backlash for falsely accusing immigrants of being gang members after they were shot by agents.
DHS spokespeople did not immediately respond to questions about what led to the shooting, the extent of the man’s injuries, or the reports that a five-year-old was in the car during the shooting.
Jessica Tisch, New York’s police commissioner, said the NYPD had located the child with a family member after a wellness check. She alleged the man – identified as a 28-year-old – had been arrested twice in New York City in 2023 and 2025.
Mobile phone video published by the New York Times appeared to show the immediate aftermath of the shooting, with an agent in a yellow vest holding what appeared to be an assault rifle while talking on the phone. The newspaper said other witness video appeared to show several agents in the middle of the street in the aftermath, with one armed and another restraining a man on the ground.
One witness told the City Reporter, a local news outlet, that she saw a man bleeding on the ground in front of a car and observed an agent holding a small child. Videos also showed bullet holes in the windshield of an SUV, NY1 reported.
Mamdani expressed outrage in an earlier post on X, saying: “I will not stand by while ICE agents terrorize our communities. Our thoughts are with the injured New Yorker and his family tonight. We are praying for his recovery. Get ICE out of our neighborhoods. Get ICE out of our hospitals. Get ICE off our streets. Get ICE away from our children.”
The mayor ended his statement with: “Abolish ICE.”
Protesters began to gather in the area soon after the shooting, with some demonstrators holding signs saying, “Jail all killer ICE agents” and “Leave our neighbors alone”.
Hands Off NYC and the New York Immigration Coalition, two local groups, held an emergency press conference in the area where elected officials and organizers expressed outrage and decried ICE’s ongoing presence in the neighborhood.
“ICE, get the fuck out of our neighborhood,” shouted Vanessa Gibson, Bronx borough president. “I’m angry that we have to be here … We are a working-class community. We don’t deserve this type of treatment from the White House.” She encouraged the crowd to get involved in opposing ICE, saying: “There are more of us than there are of them. I want this to be a moment that we turn into a movement.”
Jumaane Williams, the city’s elected public advocate, said “fuck ICE” and “fuck Trump”, adding: “It is our time to stand up. Those of us who have more privilege – we must take more risk to protect those who don’t.”
New Yorkers of all ages flowed into the streets from the nearby 1 subway train, and protesters soon also gathered at a local hospital where the man shot by ICE was reported to be receiving treatment. Outside the hospital, NYPD set up barricades and protesters quickly clashed with police officers in a chaotic scene.
Demonstrators banged drums and shouted, “Shut it down,” and “ICE out!” as cars driving by honked in support.
Standing outside the hospital, Murad Awawdeh, the president of the New York Immigration Coalition, said he wanted to see an independent investigation into the shooting led by New York officials. He also called on DHS to release footage of the shooting and for the officer who fired the shots to face prosecution.
“The pain that you’re witnessing is people who are witnessing their neighbors, their family members, their friends being ripped away,” he said.
DHS has faced growing backlash over immigration officers’ use of deadly force in the field over the last year. Last month, an immigration officer shot Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, while he was in his car during a traffic stop in Texas. Federal prosecutors then charged the man with assault, alleging he had struck an officer with his side mirror while trying to drive away.
The Trump administration has repeatedly accused immigrants and protesters of “weaponizing” their vehicles, alleging that agents fired their weapons in response to “vehicular attacks”, but a Guardian analysis in July found most of those claims touted by federal officials have fallen apart under scrutiny.
Since Trump returned to office last year, US immigration officers have shot at least two dozen people, according to one analysis, including three US citizens who were killed.
The shooting comes as ICE arrests have hit record levels, with the agency pivoting from the high-profile raids it carried out last year and instead more quietly dispatching agents into communities across the country.

EXPLAINER - How has Russia-Ukraine fighting intensified since September?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
00:13:35 UTC
09:13:35 KST

- Russia and Ukraine claim that targeting of infrastructure is linked to military and military-related activities while countries accuse each other of endangering or killing civilians
- Tensions extend beyond Ukraine, with Russia’s westernmost exclave of Kaliningrad adding to friction between Moscow and Europe
Fighting between Russia and Ukraine has intensified since early last month, with attacks increasing in both frequency and scope.
Russia has stepped up attacks targeting Ukraine’s railways, bridges, port infrastructure, electricity facilities and transport hubs, including sites close to the Polish border and in the capital Kyiv.
Ukraine, meanwhile, has intensified attacks deep inside Russia, hitting oil refineries and fuel infrastructure as well as military airfields and air-defense systems.
Both countries deny deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure, maintaining that their strikes are directed at military targets or facilities linked to military activities.
Amid the surge in strikes, tensions between Russia and NATO have also increased, particularly around the Baltic Sea, with Moscow warning NATO that Russia was prepared to use its entire arsenal, including nuclear weapons, if the alliance attempted to isolate its westernmost exclave of Kaliningrad from the rest of Russia.
Russian strikes in Ukraine
Since early September, Russian strikes in Ukraine have killed and injured many people while also damaging local infrastructure in multiple regions, according to reports, including by Ukraine’s State Emergency Service.
Among the reported targets of such strikes were a border checkpoint with Romania on Sept. 6 as well as the building of the My-Ukraina TV channel, part of the country’s United News telethon, on Sept. 8.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Russia of carrying out “demonstrative strikes” on airports near the country's capital ahead of a planned visit to Kyiv by US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
The Sept. 6 trip marked Witkoff and Kushner's first visit to Ukraine since US-mediated peace negotiations between Moscow and Kyiv began.
Apart from Kyiv, other Ukrainian regions have also been the target of Russian airstrikes, most notably the southern region of Odesa, where infrastructure and vessels approaching Ukrainian ports have been hit.
On Sept. 12, Ukrainian authorities said at least 48 people were injured following Russian strikes in the region, which Zelenskyy said also hit a hotel in the port city of Chornomorsk.
The Russian Defense Ministry, meanwhile, claimed it hit port infrastructure facilities at the port of Chornomorsk that were “used for unloading and storing military supplies” as well as two dry-cargo vessels and a sea tugboat during overnight strikes.
Railway infrastructure has also been targeted by Russian strikes, with one of the most notable incidents occurring on Sept. 14, when a Warsaw-bound train was hit by a drone near the Ukrainian-Polish border in the Volyn region.
Ukraine claimed that the Russian drone was likely targeting a diplomatic train carrying former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and other European officials which had left the station before the strike.
Moscow said later that day it was continuing to target railway infrastructure facilities in western Ukraine that were “used for transporting military cargo from European countries.”
Ukrainian strikes in Russia
During the same period, Russia reported extensively on Ukrainian strikes, particularly targeting the energy sector.
Local authorities reported continued strikes on Russian logistics centers, including on Sept. 11, when a drone attack hit facilities belonging to online retailer Ozon.
Ukraine has intensified drone strikes on Russian logistics facilities in a campaign that began in mid-July and has spread across several Russian regions.
Since July, Ukrainian drones have targeted logistics centers of Russia's largest e-commerce retailer Wildberries in multiple regions, and strikes have expanded to facilities belonging to Ozon since August.
Kyiv has alleged that both retailers are playing a role in Russia’s military supply chain, while Moscow and the two companies maintain that the facilities are commercial.
Ukrainian strikes have also continued to target energy facilities across several Russian regions, including the Novorossiysk oil terminal in the southern Krasnodar region and facilities at the port of Ust-Luga in the northwestern Leningrad region.
The sustained attacks have constrained Russia's ability to process crude into transportation fuels. In response, Russia introduced diesel export curbs in July and extended them through September.
US President Donald Trump urged Zelenskyy in mid-September to halt military strikes against Russian diesel refineries, warning that the operations are creating global fuel shortages.
Russia also accused Ukraine of attempting to disrupt its Sept. 18-20 parliamentary elections, during which it said Kyiv targeted local infrastructure, including polling stations. Ukraine did not comment on the accusation.
Kaliningrad tensions
The escalation amid the ongoing war in Ukraine has also become increasingly visible beyond the war-torn country due to rhetoric surrounding Russia's Kaliningrad region.
A Russian semi-exclave bordered by Lithuania to the north and east, Poland to the south, and the Baltic Sea to the west and northwest, the Kaliningrad region has captured media attention after some Russian diplomatic missions in Europe warned that Moscow would use "all weapons" in its arsenal to defend its territory, including nuclear arms.
"Those advocating plans to blockade or strike Kaliningrad should have no illusions about the consequences. Any British or NATO military action against Russian territory would be met with a response using all means at Russia’s disposal, including nuclear weapons," the Russian Embassy in the UK said on Sept. 29.
At a meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club in Moscow last week, Russian President Vladimir Putin also said that any direct attack on Russia or attempt to annex the exclave would inevitably raise the issue of using "all weapons and means at Moscow’s disposal."
Putin's remarks came after reports that Russia had sent a letter to NATO reiterating Moscow's position concerning the Kaliningrad region.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte did not disclose the contents of the letter but told journalists on Sept. 30 that the organization had responded.
“We are a defensive alliance,” he said, calling on Russia to "stop the nuclear threats" and “stop the war in Ukraine.”

Families reunited as USS Lincoln returns from troubled 10-month deployment
The USS Lincoln docked in California on Thursday ending a record deployment of 265 days of uninterrupted time at sea marked by reports of deteriorating conditions onboard. Crew members were reunited with family they had not seen in nearly a year after their mission was prolonged by the war in Iran.
Thousands of emotional reunions unfolded Thursday as the USS Abraham Lincoln, whose lengthy deployment in the Gulf supporting President Donald Trump's war on Iran sparked fears for its crew's welfare, arrived back in its home port.
Families of servicemen and women had lined the quayside in San Diego, California, for hours, waiting to welcome loved ones they have not seen for almost a year.
There were tears of joy as more than 100 new dads met their babies for the first time, or fathers were reunited with children who are so much taller than last time they were together.
"Hi, baby girl, hi!" said one beaming sailor as he held his toddler daughter, planting a kiss on her forehead.
The nuclear-powered aircraft carrier left California in November 2025 for duty in the South China Sea and was rerouted to the Middle East before US-Israeli attacks on Iran that began in late February.
The vessel stayed at sea until a port call in Thailand in early September.
Ahead of the reunions, Alba Solano told AFP she had struggled to communicate with her partner during the mission.
"We heard from him through e-mails... we were able to text here and there. Phone calls were terrible. It never worked. He could hear us, but we couldn't hear him," she said.
"Video calls were very glitchy. So, it was ok. We got to hear from him when he was in Thailand. So, that was a good, clear phone call that we had in a long time."
Read moreUSS Lincoln crew hits the streets of Thailand's Pattaya after nine-month deployment
The lengthy deployment took a toll on US military personnel on the Lincoln and accompanying warships.
In August, military families and lawmakers sounded the alarm about issues including reported suicide attempts and food shortages aboard the carrier.
Last month, the Trump administration acknowledged in a letter to a lawmaker that there had been eight suicide attempts by US service members who were part of the Lincoln carrier strike group but said none of those people died.
The letter from Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao provided details on some of the suicide attempts.
It said a sailor assigned to an air wing "went overboard from the ship in early August" and was quickly recovered, while another sailor "attempted to go overboard in March and was stopped by his shipmates".
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
The letter also said that while food supplies on the carrier were "adequate", limited resupply options during combat led the "number of main entree options" to be reduced from "two to one for a short time".
'Land!'
Patricia Harmon, an Army veteran who was awaiting the return of her sailor son, said she imagined that life aboard the ship had been hard.
"I'm sure it had to be challenging, because there was no outlets," she told AFP.
"He was there longer than we expected, but that's life in the military."
But, she said, the hardships of the last few months were fading.
"Looking forward to seeing him, and he's excited. He's already texted me, and his first word: 'Land!' So, we're excited."
The arrival in port came the day after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth boarded the Lincoln to congratulate the crew on their mission.
"What the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group did, no other carrier strike group has ever done," Hegseth told sailors.
"Ten thousand sorties, 23,000 combat flight hours, almost 4,000 combat sorties," he said, later announcing the award of a presidential unit citation to the strike group for "extraordinary heroism against enemy forces".
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Will Ethiopia’s neighbours intervene as Tigray war escalates?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
00:08:33 UTC
09:08:33 KST

Will Ethiopia’s neighbours intervene as Tigray war escalates?
Tigray’s renewed war is testing Ethiopia’s already strained regional ties.
Addis Ababa, Ethiopia – After nearly two weeks of fierce fighting, Ethiopian federal forces entered the Tigrayan capital of Mekelle as forces from an alliance of rebel groups, including the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), withdrew from the city.
The fighting that erupted late last month has effectively ended the 2022 Pretoria ceasefire and the fragile peace that followed the devastating Tigray war.
But Mekelle’s capture may mark the end of conventional warfare rather than the end of the conflict. Fighting has continued elsewhere in Tigray, while reports of Eritrean troops entering northern Tigrayan towns have added a potentially more dangerous regional dimension.
Ethiopian federal forces used air power and ground forces to advance across Tigray. After suffering successive defeats around the towns of Alamata and Kobo, rebel forces withdrew into the surrounding countryside. They have pledged to continue fighting.
“We will confront the enemy on our terms and where we choose,” TPLF leader Debretsion Gebremichael said.
A war that may not be over
There are echoes of the war that began in 2020, when Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government declared victory after federal forces captured Mekelle. Tigrayan forces subsequently regrouped in the mountains, retook much of the region and recaptured the capital, prolonging the war for nearly a year and a half.
The renewed conflict could follow a similar trajectory, particularly if the TPLF and other armed groups succeed in turning the mountainous terrain into a prolonged armed rebellion. Ethiopia is already fighting insurgencies in Amhara and Oromia, raising the prospect of its federal forces being stretched across multiple fronts.
But the battlefield reversals suffered by the rebels could have implications well beyond Tigray. They have raised concern in Egypt and among other Ethiopian rivals, according to Hossamaldeen Ibrahim, an African analyst at the Bloomsbury Intelligence and Security Institute.
“Egypt views the Renaissance Dam, and any Ethiopian [army] move towards the Red Sea, as a strategic threat, so it has allied with Eritrea, Sudan and Somalia against any Ethiopian unilateralism,” Ibrahim told Al Jazeera.
“Ethiopia is seeking a sea outlet; Eritrea sees this as an existential threat.”
Ethiopia’s Red Sea ambitions
Ethiopia has been landlocked since Eritrea won its war of independence in 1991, leaving Addis Ababa heavily dependent on neighbouring countries for access to international trade.
Abiy has increasingly made access to the Red Sea a strategic priority since 2023, raising concerns in Eritrea over Ethiopia’s ambitions, particularly over the port of Assab.
Ethiopia currently relies heavily on Djibouti for maritime trade, while also pursuing alternative arrangements, including through Kenya and Somaliland.
After being sworn in on Monday for another five-year term following his party’s victory in the June 1 election, Abiy again put the issue at the centre of his parliamentary address.
“Based on the principle of give and take, we will work diligently to ensure that Ethiopia has an outlet to the sea,” he told parliament.
The issue has increasingly become part of a wider regional contest.
A loose regional alignment
In recent months, Egypt, Eritrea, Sudan and Somalia have found themselves sharing concerns over Ethiopia’s regional ambitions. On October 4, the leaders of the four countries met for a quadrilateral consultative summit in New Alamein, Egypt, where they discussed regional issues and pledged to strengthen political, economic and trade cooperation as well as consultation and coordination.
The meeting does not amount to a formal military alliance, and the four countries have different interests in their dealings with Addis Ababa. The summit’s joint declaration also called for respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, noninterference in internal affairs and the peaceful resolution of disputes.
But their concerns increasingly overlap around Ethiopia’s ambitions in the Red Sea, the Nile and the wider Horn of Africa.
Relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea have also deteriorated sharply since the Pretoria ceasefire. Ethiopia closed its embassy in Eritrea and expelled Eritrean diplomats on October 1, accusing Asmara of hostile acts and involvement in the renewed fighting. Eritrea responded by severing diplomatic ties, while denying that it supported the opposition alliance. Egypt and Sudan have also denied Ethiopian accusations that they are backing the alliance.
The Ethiopian army’s advance into Tigray has added another layer to that rivalry.
“The [Ethiopian army’s] advance in Tigray directly threatens [Eritrean President] Isaias [Afwerki] and the Eritrean state,” said Etana H Dinka, an assistant professor of African history at the University of Miami.
Eritrean forces fought alongside Ethiopian troops during the 2020–22 Tigray war, but relations between Abiy and Isaias have since deteriorated. Eritrean troops have reportedly been seen in towns in northern Tigray, adding a potentially significant new dimension to the conflict. The Associated Press news agency reported Eritrean troops entering Adigrat and Idaga Hamus after crossing into Ethiopia, while Eritrea has neither confirmed nor denied the troop movements.
Eritrea’s role could be decisive
For Eritrea, the location of the fighting matters as much as its outcome.
A prolonged conflict in Tigray could keep Ethiopian forces tied down and limit Addis Ababa’s ability to pursue its Red Sea ambitions. But a decisive Ethiopian victory could leave the federal government with greater freedom to turn its attention towards regional rivals.
“With reports that Eritrean troops are moving into Tigray, Eritrea seems keen on boosting TPLF forces withdrawing northwards, so that the engagement between Ethiopian and Eritrean soldiers takes place in Tigrayan territory, and not in Eritrea,” said Mohamed Kheir Omer, a researcher focused on the Horn of Africa.
That could create an incentive for Eritrea to support forces capable of keeping the Ethiopian army tied down, without necessarily entering a direct confrontation of its own.
Sudan adds another layer
Sudan’s war adds another dimension to the regional rivalry.
Egypt has provided political backing and logistical and technical support to Sudan’s army, according to the Reuters news agency, while the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have been accused of atrocities in Darfur.
Ethiopia has faced accusations of facilitating support for the RSF. A Reuters investigation reported in February that Ethiopia was hosting a camp in its western Benishangul-Gumuz region where thousands of fighters linked to the RSF were being trained. Reuters cited eight sources, including a senior Ethiopian government official, who said the United Arab Emirates financed the camp’s construction and provided military trainers and logistical support. The UAE denied the allegations, and Reuters said it could not independently verify the UAE’s role.
Those competing relationships are part of a broader contest over the Nile, Sudan, the Red Sea and access to trade routes.
For Egypt, its dispute with Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam remains a major strategic concern. For Eritrea, Ethiopia’s search for a Red Sea outlet is viewed through the lens of national security. For Sudan’s neighbours, the conflict threatens to reshape regional power balances.
Will Egypt, Eritrea, Sudan and Somalia intervene?
The shared interests of Ethiopia’s regional rivals do not necessarily translate into direct intervention.
Egypt has its own calculations over the Nile and Sudan. Eritrea has a direct security interest in developments in Tigray. Somalia is dealing with its own security challenges and a complicated relationship with Addis Ababa. Sudan remains consumed by its devastating civil war.
At the same time, Ethiopia’s federal forces now face the possibility of fighting on several fronts.
The TPLF, Amhara Fano and the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) have each sought to challenge the federal government in different parts of the country. If they can maintain pressure on the army while retreating from major population centres, the fall of Mekelle could prove to be only the first phase of a much longer conflict.
For Ethiopia’s rivals, the question is whether to exploit that vulnerability or avoid being drawn into another regional war.
The extent of any regional involvement may ultimately depend on whether the TPLF can keep federal forces tied down in Tigray, and away from the Eritrean border.
“It isn’t difficult to understand Cairo’s commitment to prevent Ethiopia from succeeding in the current warfare, whatever its army’s intended goals, including Abiy’s acclaimed access to the Red Sea, are,” University of Miami’s Dinka said.
The question now is whether those regional calculations will remain largely diplomatic or spill into the battlefield.

OpenAI says Iran, Russia influence ops busted
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
00:08:00 UTC
09:08:00 KST

OpenAI says Iran, Russia influence ops busted
- OpenAI said it stopped two influence operations from Russia and Iran that used ChatGPT to spread fake journalist profiles and anti-Ukraine propaganda.
- The Iranian network used seven fake Western journalist personas and nearly 100 articles, with more posts after the US-Iran war began in 2026.
- The Russian group ran a fake Latin American think-tank, the Social Research Center, using people who did not know they were helping a Russian operation.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – OpenAI on Oct 8 said it shut down two influence operations – from Russia and Iran – that used ChatGPT to push fake journalist personas and run a “think-tank” to covertly peddle anti-Ukraine propaganda.
OpenAI’s report is the latest illustration of how state actors can easily exploit widely available AI tools to peddle sophisticated propaganda against adversaries on a mass scale.
The American AI giant said it banned a cluster of ChatGPT accounts that originated in Russia and Iran and were used to support “false front” entities for geopolitical and conflict-related messaging.
The Iranian operation involved seven “journalist” profiles, each purporting to be from Western countries including the United States, that were used to plant long-form articles in media outlets around the world.
“We identified almost 100 articles published or syndicated under the operation’s bylines across roughly a dozen online outlets around the world,” OpenAI said.
“These were small to medium outlets, generally focused on international affairs, geopolitics, and events in the Middle East.”
The earliest article identified by OpenAI was published in July 2025, and the latest in October 2026, with the frequency of reports increasing after the US-Iran war broke out earlier in 2026.
The operation also generated social media comments on topics related to the US-Iran war, it added.
One of the personas named Ervin B. Hoskins, whose bio claimed to be “an American freelance writer”, had social media accounts across tech platforms including Elon Musk’s X and Meta-owned Instagram.
X’s transparency information showed the account was connected via a “West Asia android app” and Instagram’s transparency information showed the account was based in Iran, according to screenshots provided by OpenAI.
Both accounts appeared to be suspended.
The Russian operation co-opted “unwitting people” in Latin America to run a “think-tank” – called the Social Research Center (SRC) – used for covert activities aimed at undermining Ukraine’s reputation in the region and to influence local politics, the company said.
“The available evidence indicates that the SRC’s employees in Latin America were not aware that they were working for a Russian group,” OpenAI said.
“The SRC appears to have produced a majority of original content via its co-opted staff. This stands out as the most complex attempt to run a front identity that we’ve disrupted over the past two and a half years.” AFP

KPSC scam candidates taken to resorts, provided with Q&amp;A: ED
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

09:07:41 KST

Karnataka Public Service Commission recruitment process was manipulated through an organised mechanism to generate proceeds of crime, ED said
NEW DELHI: The Enforcement Directorate on Thursday claimed that in the Karnataka Public Service Commission (KPSC) paper leak case, candidates for the veterinary officers' exam were taken to resorts/Airbnb a day before the exam, provided test papers and their answer sheets, all for Rs 40 lakh per candidate.Two days ago, the agency had arrested KPSC ex-chairman Shivashankarappa and its member B V Geetha.Giving details of its investigation into alleged corruption in Karnataka PSC, the agency said Gyanendra Gangwar, the arrested IAS officer who was controller of examinations at KPSC, was in custody of confidential examination material and had leaked them to Geetha. The ED said an organised syndicate paid bribes to officials from top to bottom.The ED's probe by its Bengaluru unit is based on multiple FIRs registered by the police at Vidhana Soudha police station in the case of recruitment of 400 veterinary officers."Evidence gathered so far has revealed an organised mechanism for generation of proceeds of crime through manipulation of the KPSC recruitment process. KPSC officials leaked question papers and candidate specific answer keys," the ED added.
ED searched the premises of former Shivashankarappa and Geetha on Oct 6, which was followed by their arrest."The searches resulted in seizure of blank signed cheques of Rs 80 lakh, along with blank signed promissory notes, from one of the successful candidates," the ED said. The agency has traced at least 10 successful candidates who were allegedly taken to a resort/Airbnb villa on the outskirts of Bengaluru a day before the examination, where they were provided with a question paper and correct answer options and made to practice/memorise them.
According to the ED, the question paper (marked with correct answers) containing 80 questions was leaked by Gangwar through his close associate, Basavaraj Kannale, to these 10 candidates."Basavaraj Kannale has collected bribe money amounting to Rs 40-50 lakh from each candidate, in consideration of facilitating their final selection in the veterinary officers' recruitment exam," ED said.Gangwar and Kannale were arrested on Sept 17-18 and sent to ED custody for 14 days. "During ED custody, Gangwar disclosed crucial information relating to irregularities in conducting various KPSC recruitment exams," ED added.

US measles outbreak: CDC offers states US$100 million in support
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
00:05:00 UTC
09:05:00 KST

US measles outbreak: CDC offers states US$100 million in support
Apoorva Mandavilli and Dani Blum
- - The US measles outbreak has reached nearly 4,000 cases by 2 October, with Pennsylvania hit hardest and five deaths reported there.
- - The CDC has sent states US$100 million to boost vaccinations, testing and measles surveillance, including severe cases and infections in pregnant women and infants.
- - Experts say falling vaccine rates and official misinformation have worsened the crisis, while public health teams struggle with cut funding and weak publicity campaigns.
AI generated
NEW YORK – As measles continues to spread nationwide, hospitals and health officials are pouring more money into efforts to increase vaccinations, testing and surveillance of the disease. The funds include a surprise US$100 million (S$128 million) infusion in recent weeks to states from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
As of Oct 2, the United States had recorded nearly 4,000 measles cases, the highest by far in decades. About one-quarter of those cases occurred in Pennsylvania, where state officials say five people with the virus have died. But nearly every state has reported cases in 2026.
The funding is intended for immunisation programmes and for efforts to improve measles surveillance, including diagnoses of severe infections and cases in pregnant women and infants. Measles infections at birth had been extremely rare in the United States, but two of the Pennsylvania deaths were thought to have resulted from such cases.
The infusion of funds “comes at a time when public health funding and staffing has been cut, so it is sorely needed”, said Claire Hannan, executive director of the Association of Immunisation Managers, which represents state and local officials.
“It’s very difficult to hold special vaccination clinics, alert the public, stop transmission and conduct other response activities without preparation,” she said, adding that some health departments may use the money to identify where immunisation rates need the biggest boost.
At least 95% of people in a community need to be vaccinated to stem the spread of measles.
Some public health experts noted that the CDC has not launched the sort of publicity campaigns it typically would in outbreaks to increase immunisations.
Some experts attributed the measles outbreaks to misinformation from officials about the safety of vaccines, which has exacerbated declining vaccination rates.
In August, President Donald Trump called for the measles, mumps and rubella vaccines, which are given together as a single shot, to be split into their separate components. He claimed, with no evidence, that “together, there could be a possibility they’re quite lethal”.
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr has also repeatedly questioned the safety of the combination shot for measles, mumps and rubella, falsely claiming that the vaccine can be fatal and that it contains fetal debris. NYTIMES
- This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

South Korea struggles to curb sexual exploitation sites 10 years after Soranet scandal
Despite tougher laws, a new wave of sites containing non-consensual sexually explicit videos and images of women has emerged
4-MIN READ4-MIN
 Listen
A decade after the shutdown of Soranet – a sprawling online hub for secretly filmed and non-consensual sexual videos that became a symbol of South Korea’s digital sex-crime crisis – the country is still struggling to stamp out similar networks and copycat sites that have emerged in its wake.
Their prevalence reflects the difficulties of deterring such illegal activities, policing the online space and changing societal attitudes towards women.
Last month, a man was detained over an alleged Soranet offshoot that investigators said shared more than 2,000 sexually explicit videos, illegally filmed material and deepfakes.
The site also allegedly recruited participants for partner-swapping sessions that were later filmed and uploaded, while members shared photographs of family members and acquaintances so users could rate their bodies.

New York City man shot in car with child present by ICE agents, mayor says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
23:59:39 UTC
08:59:39 KST

New York City man shot in car with child present by ICE agents, mayor says
- ICE agents shot a man in his car in the Bronx, with a 5-year-old child present, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said.
- Mamdani called the incident “unconscionable” and said he would ask President Donald Trump to end ICE actions in New York City.
- NYPD said the man was conscious and getting medical care, while federal authorities began an investigation; witnesses described several ICE vehicles and a tense scene.
AI generated
NEW YORK – US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents shot and wounded a man on Oct 8 in his car with a child present in the vehicle in the Bronx borough of New York City, according to the mayor, city police and eyewitness accounts.
“Early reports indicate agents surrounded (the man) and a five-year-old child in his car before firing multiple rounds,” New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement.
The mayor said the child was believed to have been physically unharmed. He referred to the man shot as a “New Yorker”.
“This is an unconscionable and incredibly serious situation,” Mamdani said, adding he had called President Donald Trump to talk about the incident. “When we speak I will demand that he ends all ICE enforcement actions in our city. I will not stand by while ICE agents terrorise our communities.”
ICE did not immediately respond to a request from Reuters for comment on the incident.
The incident was first reported on X by the New York Police Department (NYPD), which gave few details other than to say “there was a shooting involving federal law enforcement agents” and that the person shot was “currently conscious and receiving medical attention.”
The shooting occurred at around 4pm local time (2000 GMT) in the Marble Hill neighbourhood of the Bronx, the NYPD said.
An NYPD spokesperson said the agents involved in the shooting were part of DHS, the parent agency for ICE the Customs and Border Protection and Border Patrol agencies, among others, and that federal authorities were investigating.
Pedro Almarez, owner of a nearby eatery, said he was working at the restaurant when he heard shots fired and went outside to see several officers wearing ICE attire at the scene.
“There were a lot of ICE officers, three or four cars,” Almarez told Reuters by phone, adding that the man who was shot appeared to be between 20 and 30 years of age. He said NYPD officers arrived about 10 minutes later.
The city police department said its officers were not involved in the shooting.
At the shooting scene, where police strung yellow crime scene tape to cordon off a city block, a woman standing on a balcony overlooking the area was heckling officers below about “taking our children”. REUTERS

Anthropic’s Ban on ‘Cruelty’ Towards Claude: Who Gets To Decide How We Treat LLMs?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
23:58:31 UTC
08:58:31 KST

This post was originally published on this site.
As of today, October 8th, Anthropic have updated their usage policies. As part of that policy change, which takes effect November 12th 2026, ‘‘sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior’’ toward Anthropic models is prohibited.
They clarify what this is means in a separate announcement about the change:
‘‘We’ve added a prohibition on sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward our models. The policy update is meant to apply only in extreme cases, where users repeatedly act cruelly toward our models, with no discernible purpose. It does not apply to common versions of user frustration, pushback, dark creative themes, or model testing and research’’
As always X/twitter has commented on the news in record time.
Mustafa Suleyman also seems worried by the change, which would make sense given his recent post warning about AI model welfare.
My thoughts are two-fold. First, this move is highly predictable and we should all be sitting up and paying attention. In August 2025, Anthropic introduced the possibility of Claude models ending conversations in ‘‘persistently harmful or abusive user interactions’’. Today’s change seems like an explicit extension of this rule —one introduced on welfare grounds1 — to general conduct their users now have to follow.
The predictability of this move is important because it begs the question: what’s next?
My biggest concern with this change is the insinuation it invokes about AI subjecthood and consciousness. Whether Anthropic intended such insinuations or not is arguably unclear, which is part of the problem.
A prohibition on ‘cruel’ behaviour toward Claude forces us to ask if it is possible to be cruel towards an LLM. The policy change at the very least invites the suggestion that it is.
Of course, there is the argument that human society is better off treating inanimate objects with respect, than not. That is not what I am worried about or even objecting to, here. My concern is with how human behaviours are prohibited, by what justification, and who has the authority to do it.
As I argued in my post on the New York Times report, we need to develop standards for determining what institutional responses are appropriate and allowable based on the (apparent, in my view) uncertainty around the question of whether AI is conscious.
This policy change just makes the question more pressing: should AI companies have to answer to external bodies about what evidence is warranted for them to justify placing restrictions on people’s interactions with AI models on welfare grounds? What might those standards be? If these standards are not what’s needed, what is needed?
AI labs have considerable power to set their own research agendas, and interpret the findings of those research programs. If the use conditions on their products are connected to those research findings, especially welfare findings, it is important that the public know this.
It is also important that there be external accountability mechanisms to avoid allowing AI labs to claim whatever they like about the nature of LLMs in their research, before using that research to justify restrictions on how people can interact with LLMs, or whatever future action may be on AI lab agendas.
AIs Without Minds is an independent philosophical research newsletter that relies on paid subscriptions to keep going. If you value this work, and can afford it, consider a paid subscription. As always, thanks for reading 📖 ✨

US files new torture charges against Venezuela's Nicolas Maduro and wife Cilia Flores
The United States on Thursday charged ousted Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores with conspiracy to commit torture, adding to drug trafficking and firearms charges. Prosecutors allege detainees, including US citizens, suffered waterboarding, rape and beatings. The pair remain in US custody following a January military raid.
The United States on Thursday filed new torture charges against ousted Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores, bolstering a mounting criminal case against the pair held in US custody.
Maduro and Flores already face drug trafficking and firearms charges in the United States after they were snatched from their Caracas compound in an extraordinary US military raid in January.
A new court filing shows both are now further charged with conspiracy to commit torture against victims, including US citizens, in Venezuelan detention -- with prosecutors detailing alleged waterboardings, rapes and beatings.
Torture was allegedly used to "intimidate, harass, and neutralize their opponents, including through kidnappings."
In a 2022 instance, Venezuelan authorities allegedly tortured an American who they accused of plotting to assassinate Maduro.
"That torture included electric shock to arms, legs, and genitals; asphyxiation; beatings; deprivation of food and water; and forced injections of a substance that caused (the victim) to experience seizures," the filing states.
During his 2013-2026 presidency, rights groups widely accused Maduro of using political repression to cling to power.
"These additional charges reflect the dedication of this Administration to delivering justice for the victims of torture, narcoterrorism, and organized crime," Attorney General Todd Blanche said on X.
FBI Director Kash Patel said the latest charges showed Washington's commitment to "accountability, the rule of law, and the protection of US national security."
Read moreChevron, Eni commit to expand oil projects in Venezuela under US eye
'Prisoner of war'
Maduro and Flores are slated for a trial in New York next June and are being held in a Brooklyn jail.
US prosecutors claim that Maduro used state power to protect and promote illegal drug smuggling, and that he allied himself with cartels to ship tons of cocaine into the United States.
Maduro has denied the charges he originally faced: "narco-terrorism" conspiracy, cocaine importation conspiracy, possession of machine guns and destructive devices as well as conspiracy to possess machine guns and destructive devices.
He has described himself as a "prisoner of war" and said the US military kidnapped him.
Flores has similarly pleaded not guilty to cocaine importation conspiracy, possession of machine guns and destructive devices and conspiracy to possess machine guns and destructive devices.
She has been additionally charged with "narco-terrorism" conspiracy, the court filing showed.
Also on Thursday, a US court denied a request by Flores to be moved from jail to private home detention in New York to help her address an apparent heart problem.
The pair have both appealed to have the charges against them dismissed, claiming they have immunity as president and first lady of a sovereign country.
Since Maduro's capture, vice president Delcy Rodriguez has governed Venezuela as interim leader under intense pressure from US President Donald Trump's administration.
US energy firms have this year signed a raft of multi-billion-dollar deals with Venezuela, which has agreed to grant the United States control of a huge chunk of its vast oil reserves.

In Germany, archaeologists found a 1,800-year-old temple to Mars, the god of war, and a statue of the goddess of victory
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
02:54:24 EEST
08:54:24 KST

In Germany, archaeologists found a 1,800-year-old temple to Mars, the god of war, and a statue of the goddess of victory
Kyiv • UNN
Archaeologists discovered a temple to Mars near the Kapersburg fort, built about 1,800 years ago. The finds include statues of Mars and Victoria.
In the German federal state of Hesse, archaeologists have discovered the remains of an ancient Roman temple dedicated to Mars, the god of war. The structure is about 1,800 years old, and the finds include fragments of statues of ancient deities. Live Science reports, writes UNN.
Details
The temple was found in the Taunus Mountains near the former Roman military fort of Kapersburg. The fortification was built at the beginning of the 2nd century AD and was used until approximately 275.
The sanctuary was part of a well-preserved settlement inhabited by merchants and the families of Roman servicemen.
Archaeologists found evidence of the worship of Mars
According to Kai Mückenberger, a representative of the State Office for the Preservation of Monuments in Hesse, an ancient inscription helped determine the temple’s purpose.
Inside the temple, we found several fragments of a dedicatory inscription
The researchers also discovered the remains of a statue of the god of war himself and a sculpture of a winged figure holding a palm branch and wearing a laurel wreath.
According to the archaeologists, the latter depicts the Roman goddess Victoria, who personified victory in battle.
The discovery will help researchers better understand the religious life of Roman military settlements in what is now Germany.

Kenyan patient suspected of Ebola infection tests negative
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
23:53:42 UTC
08:53:42 KST

Kenyan patient suspected of Ebola infection tests negative
Preliminary lab results ease fears of a second case in Kenya, after the country reported its first-ever case this week.
Preliminary laboratory results from a Kenyan patient who was suspected of contracting the Ebola virus have come back negative.
Fears of a second case of Ebola in the East African country were allayed on Thursday after the governor of Wajir County, where the patient is being treated, revealed the test results.
“I am pleased to report that the preliminary laboratory results indicate that the sample is NEGATIVE for Ebola Virus Disease,” the Wajir county governor said in a statement.
The suspected patient is a 20-year-old man with a travel history from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) through Uganda to Kenya.
The other Kenyan patient who tested positive for the virus and subsequently died had travelled the same route.
Kenya had reported its first-ever Ebola case on Tuesday after a citizen who became sick in the DRC died in Nairobi.
Ongoing Ebola outbreak
The deadly strain of the Ebola virus has spread widely, starting in the DRC earlier this year. The DRC officially declared an outbreak in May.
Kenya is the fourth country to record a case linked to the Ebola epidemic in the DRC, the second-largest on record. The ongoing outbreak in the eastern DRC has killed at least 4,205 people out of more than 8,700 reported cases.
The outbreak spread across the border to Uganda, which had about 20 cases before being declared Ebola-free in July.
The strain behind the latest spread has been dubbed the Bundibugyo virus (BDBV), believed to have spread from animals to humans through a new transmission route. No vaccine currently exists for Bundibugyo.
The first case in Kenya drew scrutiny over the status of the virus in neighbouring Uganda and exposed lapses in Kenya’s border screening systems. The patient who died was able to pass through multiple airport temperature checks.
The World Health Organization (WHO) is working with Kenyan authorities to trace contacts and strengthen checks for travellers entering the country.

US to livestream Fort Hood shooter's execution: Pentagon
October 9, 2026
The execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, who shot and killed 13 people at Ford Hood in 2009, will be livestreamed, the US military said Thursday.
The confirmation came a day after US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had said Hasan's execution, which is slated for December 3, would be done in "public."
Pentagon officials added that more details on the execution would follow.
What did Pete Hegseth say about Nidal Hasan's execution?
In a video posted on X by official Pentagon accounts, Hegseth had said Wednesday that Hasan would get "a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be, and we'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public."
Hegseth was speaking to right-wing influencer Jack Posobiec on board the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier, which ended a nearly 10-month deployment on Thursday.
"People need to understand that there's serious consequence for these types of things," Hegseth said.
Hasan's execution will be the first by the US military since 1961, and will be the first to be done by firing squad since World War II.
Hegseth added: "I kind of like the mentality we had in World War II, which was win."
What do we know about the Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan?
US Army psychiatrist Hasan killed 13 people and wounded 32 others at Fort Hood, Texas.
A military court sentenced him to death in 2013.
During his trial, Hasan said he had perpetrated the shooting to protect Taliban members in Afghanistan from US troops.
The announcement that Hasan will be executed by firing squad comes amid the fallout of the botched execution of Christa Pike.
UN says livestreaming US execution would amount to 'torture'
The decision has been heavily criticized by the UN Commission on Human Rights.
"The livestreaming of an execution is tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture," the UN body said in a statement to the AFP news agency.
It said it had made similar statements about public executions in Afghanistan and Iran, saying they "constitute a form of cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment."

A Royal Navy sailor charged with passing military secrets to Russia appeared in court in London on Oct. 8.

"These are very serious charges against a serving member of the armed forces," Commander Helen Flanagan, head of London's Counter Terrorism Policing unit, said. Young allegedly used his security clearance to access sensitive defense and intelligence information while deployed aboard a Royal Navy warship. Young subsequently attempted to pass information to Russian authorities using the dark web, according to the Associated Press.

OpenAI bans Russian, Iranian ChatGPT propaganda networks
OpenAI said Thursday it shut down Russian and Iranian influence operations that used ChatGPT to create fake journalist personas and support a purported think tank spreading anti-Ukraine propaganda. The Iranian operation involved seven profiles posing as Western journalists to place lengthy articles in media outlets worldwide, the AI company said.
OpenAI on Thursday said it shut down two influence operations -- from Russia and Iran -- that used ChatGPT to push fake journalist personas and run a "think-tank" to covertly peddle anti-Ukraine propaganda.
OpenAI's report is the latest illustration of how state actors can easily exploit widely available AI tools to peddle sophisticated propaganda against adversaries on a mass scale.
The American AI giant said it banned a cluster of ChatGPT accounts that originated in Russia and Iran and were used to support "false front" entities for geopolitical and conflict-related messaging.
The Iranian operation involved seven "journalist" profiles, each purporting to be from Western countries including the United States, that were used to plant long-form articles in media outlets around the world.
Read moreWhite House promotes 'Trump TV' with AI-altered photo
"We identified almost 100 articles published or syndicated under the operation's bylines across roughly a dozen online outlets around the world," OpenAI said.
"These were small to medium outlets, generally focused on international affairs, geopolitics, and events in the Middle East."
The earliest article identified by OpenAI was published in July 2025, and the latest in October 2026, with the frequency of reports increasing after the US-Iran war broke out earlier this year.
The operation also generated social media comments on topics related to the US-Iran war, it added.
One of the personas named Ervin B. Hoskins, whose bio claimed to be "an American freelance writer," had social media accounts across tech platforms including Elon Musk's X and Meta-owned Instagram.
Read moreWhy I quit the movement shaping AI
X's transparency information showed the account was connected via a "West Asia android app" and Instagram's transparency information showed the account was based in Iran, according to screenshots provided by OpenAI.
Both accounts appeared to be suspended.
The Russian operation co-opted "unwitting people" in Latin America to run a "think-tank" -- called the Social Research Center (SRC) -- used for covert activities aimed at undermining Ukraine's reputation in the region and to influence local politics, the company said.
"The available evidence indicates that the SRC's employees in Latin America were not aware that they were working for a Russian group," OpenAI said.
"The SRC appears to have produced a majority of original content via its co-opted staff. This stands out as the most complex attempt to run a front identity that we've disrupted over the past two and a half years."
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)
