Trump rules out US strikes on Iran before midterms as US Treasury imposes new sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
22:19:55 UTC
07:19:55 KST

US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that the US will not launch an attack on Iran before November's US midterm congressional elections, asserting that the two countries are having "productive" talks about ending the six-month-old war.
"We are having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran," Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social. "We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd."
The war, which began in February when the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran, has helped drive Trump's domestic approval ratings downward and is weighing heavily on his fellow Republicans as they seek to preserve their narrow legislative majorities in November's election.
Some 60% of Americans - including one in four Republicans - disapprove of how Trump is handling the situation in Iran, according to a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll. The conflict has pushed gasoline prices sharply higher at a time when voters say their top concern is the cost of living.
Trump has repeatedly said he expects oil prices to drop after the elections, but he has not offered a detailed plan for exiting the war.
Proposals exchanged aimed at ending war, opening Strait of Hormuz
Iran and the US have exchanged proposals in recent weeks aimed at ending the war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global energy shipping route. Trump rejected Tehran's latest offer.
Iran's state media reported on Thursday that Tehran would not abandon uranium enrichment or hand over its uranium stockpile, citing the head of the country's Atomic Energy Organization, days after US Vice President JD Vance told Reuters that Iran must make "meaningful" reductions in its enrichment capacity.
The US, Israel and Western allies have long accused Iran of seeking nuclear weapons, an accusation Iran has denied.
US imposes fresh sanctions on Iran's shadow fleet
The US imposed fresh sanctions on Iran on Thursday, targeting individuals, networks and 17 vessels for transporting Iranian crude, oil products and petrochemicals, the Treasury Department said, as Washington stepped up economic pressure on Tehran.
The sanctions are part of the department's "Operation Economic Outcast," which aims to cut Iran's funding for the war with the US, missile construction, cyberattacks and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, or IRGC.
"Today's action represents the most significant blow yet to Iran's remaining illicit maritime infrastructure by neutralizing the vast majority of the shadow fleet," a Treasury official told reporters on a call. "Treasury is cutting off the regime's last major source of illicit revenue and strengthening international pressure to hold Tehran accountable."
The move tightens the squeeze on Iranian oil sales after the US reimposed its blockade of Iranian ports on July 14 following the breakdown of a memorandum of understanding between Tehran and Washington to end the war.
Iran has only about 20 million barrels of crude oil left on vessels outside the blockade, off Singapore, Malaysia and China, the Treasury official said. The world uses about 100 million barrels of oil per day.
A second Treasury official said Iran has stopped loading and offloading crude oil vessels due to the blockade and sanctions.
Trump said on social media on Thursday that the US is having "productive discussions" with Iran over the war that began on February 28. Trump said the US will not attack Iran before the midterm elections on November 3.
An analyst said the fact that the US is sanctioning vessels after Iran has delivered virtually all of its oil at sea means the impact will be muted.
"This is economic warfare conducted in the rearview mirror, designed to generate headlines rather than results," said Brett Erickson, a managing principal at Obsidian Risk Advisors.
Vessels targeted by the US sanctions include the Comoros-flagged Paritosh, the Panama-flagged Bitu, and the Bahamas-flagged Gas Lucky.

UK: Two Latvian men arrested for breaking into RAF base
October 9, 2026
Two Latvian men have been arrested for breaching the perimeter fence at an RAF base used by the US military, UK police said Thursday.
The two UK residents, aged 36 and 32, were arrested by counterterrorism police at the Royal Air Force (RAF) Molesworth base in southeastern England, 70 miles north of London.
Police said they were being held on suspicion of trespassing, causing criminal damage and entering a prohibited place "for a purpose prejudicial to the UK."
A former World War II airbase, RAF Molesworth, is now a non-flying facility that is managed by the US Air Force.
It houses intelligence personnel from US Africa Command and the NATO Intelligence Fusion Center, which provides information to the Supreme Allied Commander in Europe.
The incident comes after several men were arrested amid an alleged terror plot at another UK air base last month.
What do we know about the incident at RAF Molesworth?
According to a statement from Counter Terrorism Policing London, officers from the Ministry of Defense Police and Cambridgeshire Constabulary began investigating an incident at approximately 10 p.m. local time on Wednesday after an abandoned vehicle was found near the edge of the base.
Police later discovered a small hole in the perimeter fence and arrested the two suspects at around 2 a.m. on Thursday.
The men were initially arrested on suspicion of trespassing on a prohibited site and criminal damage. They were later arrested on charges of entering a prohibited place with the intent to harm the UK.
Both men remain in police custody. Due to the nature of the offense, the matter is being investigated by counterterrorism police.
Is this related to the RAF Fairford incident?
On September 27, authorities discovered three suspicious vans near RAF Fairford, a British air base from which US bombers launched strikes against Iran. This triggered a widespread investigation that led to seven arrests.
Last weekend, the US Air Force brought home all the bombers deployed to the base.
Commander Helen Flanagan, head of the counterterrorism unit, said that while UK authorities are "very aware of the recent heightened interest and concern around military sites", there is "nothing to suggest" the incident at RAF Molesworth is related to what happened at RAF Fairford last week, although she added that the investigation was still in its "very early stages."
The US European Command acknowledged the incident but declined to comment on specific force protection measures.

Breaking: Data centre operator pulls share market float due to lacking investor demand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
22:12:14 UTC
07:12:14 KST

Data centre operator Firmus pulls blockbuster ASX float after lacklustre demand
In short:
The mega float of data centre operator Firmus has been pulled.
It follows poor interest from investors amid concerns about the company's debt and a lack of detail.
What's next?
The company says it will pursue private funding.
AI data centre company Firmus has withdrawn its application to list on the ASX, scrapping what was set to be one of Australia's biggest share market floats.
The company cited recent market volatility and conditions, saying the offer would not appropriately reflect its long-term growth prospects.
Firmus said it would now pursue private market funding while considering other options.
"We will provide additional information to shareholders as those options progress," the company said in a statement.
Firmus, the AI factory builder backed by chip-making giant Nvidia, was set to be the biggest float in the Australian share market since Telstra in 1997.
The company's founders, co-chief executives Oliver Curtis and Tim Rosenfield, targeted a $44 billion valuation, but prospective investors pulled back based on the high sale price of $11 a share and concerns over an AI bubble.
Yesterday, reports emerged that Firmus and its advisors were considering reducing the size of the initial public offering (IPO) and lowering the per-share price from $11 to $8.25.
Many investors were also focused on Mr Curtis's criminal background — he is a former investment banker who served one year in prison a decade ago for insider trading.
With AI infrastructure demand accelerating across the Asia-Pacific, Firmus's website says its broader portfolio spans seven AI factories across four countries: Australia, Singapore, Indonesia and Malaysia.
It said two sites were operational in Australia and Singapore and five were "under development, targeting ready-for-service over the next 24 months".
Its website also spruiks its relationship with US chip giant Nvidia, which has a 7.2 per cent stake in Firmus.
Institutional investors raise doubts
Today, after Firmus announced the IPO had been pulled, UniSuper chief investment officer John Pearce said it was disappointing.
"The ASX needs new stories and this could have been one if it was correctly priced," he said.
Ahead of the announcement, he had released an investment update detailing potential investors' doubts about the AI company and why the super fund would not directly invest in it.
"Firmus is a neo-cloud company, and that means it provides cloud services, in very simple terms, to AI companies," he said.
"The capital raise will be about $7 billion and that will give Firmus a total market value of around $44 billion."
Mr Pearce said even though UniSuper was not directly investing in Firmus, UniSuper would own some shares if the float proceeded "because we have index strategies in our portfolios and Firmus will ultimately be a part of the major indices".
He said the reason UniSuper was doubtful about investing was the high valuation.
"We think that Firmus indeed has a compelling story. It just doesn't have a compelling valuation,"
he said.
"At the current valuation, it's priced to perfection. So much has to go right to justify the valuation.
"Furthermore, we're quite concerned that Firmus will have to keep coming back to the market for a lot more debt and more equity to fund its expansion plans."
Morningstar senior market strategist Lochlan Holloway yesterday raised concerns over the company's debt levels.
"The neo-clouds are heavily geared," he wrote in an economic note.
"The model is to borrow against customer contracts to buy chips, then use the rent to repay the loans."
Once its data centres are built, Firmus expects to be carrying about $US30 billion ($43 billion) of debt, about six times the $US5 billion of operating earnings it forecasts for 2028.
"Borrowed money alone does not make a bubble, and plenty of infrastructure is sensibly funded with debt. But credit is the common thread running through essentially every boom and bust cycle," Mr Holloway said.
Loading...
CDC was set to build data centres with Firmus but scrapped the deal.
CDC chief strategy officer Jack Dan told a federal parliamentary inquiry into AI that they initially partnered with Firmus when its "focus was a lot more on Australia and creating sovereign AI capability".
"Their business model has then since evolved, and probably the most blunt way of putting it is we have a very clear business model and a very clear mission for our company, and when things start diverging significantly from that, we continue to follow our core mission," he said.

====================================================================================================

Armored assaults aren’t dead. Robots got the credit, but it was Ukrainian infantry in armored trucks that reversed a year of Russian gains near Lyman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
22:11:18 UTC
07:11:18 KST

- Defying the trend toward footborne infantry assaults, the Ukrainian 3rd Army Corps deployed armored vehicles for Operation Vivaldi
- The operation was a reminder that vehicles are still useful despite the ever-present danger from drones
- But vehicles need a lot of support to give them a fighting chance
Armored vehicles aren't dead in Ukraine—they just need a lot of help. That's one of the biggest lessons from the Ukrainian 3rd Army Corps' Operation Vivaldi, its recent successful counteroffensive just north of the town of Lyman in eastern Ukraine's Donetsk Oblast.
Russia spent 18 months building its salient toward Sloviansk; Ukraine took much of it back in three. By 30 September, three of four planned phases in, the operation had returned 176 sq km to Ukrainian control, taken 250 Russian prisoners, and cost Russia more than 5,000 killed and wounded, Ukraine's presidential office said. It also foiled a Russian plan to break into the rear of the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk urban area, the office said.
Defying critics who insisted vehicles couldn't possibly survive in the drone-patrolled gray zone, the 3rd Army Corps repeatedly deployed mechanized forces as it counterattacked across a roughly 100 sq km salient the Russian 20th and 25th Combined Arms Armies had extended toward Sloviansk, one of the last two big free cities in Donetsk Oblast.
Maneuvering for months under a veil of secrecy, the 3rd Army Corps found and exploited gaps along the flanks of the 20th and 25th CAAs, ultimately breaking into the Russian armies' rears and forcing them to pull back across the Zherebets River in order to avoid encirclement.
Armored vehicles were key to the Ukrainian effort. They sped assault troops into battle, dropped them off under fire, and then supported them as they clashed with the Russians. "Maneuver warfare isn't going anywhere," stated Ryan O'Leary, a US Army veteran who once commanded volunteers in Ukraine.
Ukraine is now sending its tanks into battle with drone escorts: they can drive into a Russian kill zone and come back alive
3rd Army Corps commanders knew they were taking a risk deploying armored vehicles in a Russian-controlled salient patrolled by first-person-view drones from Russia's elite Rubicon Center drone unit. But they clearly believed that, with adequate support, the vehicles could accomplish their missions—and survive.
They were right. A dramatic video shot by 3rd Army Corps troopers depicts the troopers disembarking from their armored trucks and rushing into the fight while small arms fire clatters all around them.
Given the intensity of the Russian fire, a mechanized assault "was the only real way to push positions in an effective manner to keep losses low as well as gain and hold momentum and aggression," O'Leary wrote. Walking into battle under the cover of trees might help the infantry avoid the attention of overhead drones, but it takes too long to sustain an aggressive assault, and it can be difficult to mass enough footborne infantry to overcome stiff enemy defenses.
"This is something that hasn't changed even with the advent of drone warfare coming of age," O'Leary added. "Suppression tactics and such have changed and now there is more than just indirect fires and counterassaults that you must be able to suppress and plan for."
But the concept of the infantry-carrying armored vehicle "isn't going anywhere," O'Leary stressed. "Especially when it takes a drone tens of minutes to get to target area, acquire target and hit the target. Right now, the front is extremely susceptible to maneuvering forces on assaults if it is planned right and executed properly."
The 3rd Army Corps' Operation Vivaldi is an excellent example of an operation that was planned right and executed properly—in ways that helped the corps' mechanized forces fight and survive.
Trending Now
Careful preparation
The corps explained that it deployed footborne scouts to find the best paths for follow-on vehicular assaults—and subsequent medical evacuations. Scouts "conducted recon of the front lines, ensured the breakthrough of equipment and led adjacent units along secret paths while evacuating the wounded," the 3rd Army Corps stated.
Before the armored vehicles rolled into action along the pre-scouted paths, the 3rd Army Corps deployed robotic engineering vehicles to clear Russian mines. After that, the corps sent in old BTR-60 wheeled armored vehicles modified for remote control and packed with anti-tank mines. These "robotic kamikaze complexes ... were used to demolish the enemy's strongest fortifications," the corps said.
Only after the assault routes were scouted and cleared of mines and Russian strongpoints did the manned vehicles and their precious infantry cargo roll out. We don't know how many losses the 3rd Army Corps' mechanized infantry suffered on the attack, but we do know they ultimately prevailed—when the battered Russian 20th and 25th CAAs retreated.
In Ukraine’s Vivaldi offensive, nobody rides in the BTR-60s. Bulgaria’s old troop carriers go into Russian bunkers packed with mines
"Recent Ukrainian operations demonstrate that maneuver is not dead," stressed Mick Ryan, a retired Australian army general. "Despite the difficulty in ground operations maneuver observed in eastern Ukraine over the past few years, offensive operations are still possible in modern war. But they need the intellectual effort to develop new techniques to make them viable and repeatable at scale."
In addition to the reconnaissance and robots-first engineering and suppression tactics the 3rd Army Corps employed, Ryan recommended commanders deploy more drone-grounding electronic warfare and use AI tools to help plan attacks.
But ages-old human elements are still essential, Ryan wrote. "Developing viable methods for offensive tactical and operational maneuver in the 21st century also demands the inclusion of older ideas about the employment of mass, logistic support and casualty evacuation [and the] maintenance of morale and leader's provision of purpose to their people."
Even when the assault route is clear, it's understandably terrifying to ride in an armored vehicle across drone-patrolled terrain. But a good leader can motivate their troops to try.

The 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature is announced in Stockholm, Sweden, Oct. 8, 2026. Canadian writer Anne Carson has been awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature, becoming the second Canadian author ever to receive the honor, the Swedish Academy announced on Thursday. (Xinhua/Lyu You)
STOCKHOLM, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- Canadian writer Anne Carson has been awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature, becoming the second Canadian author ever to receive the honor, the Swedish Academy announced on Thursday.
The prize was awarded to Carson "for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature," the academy said.
Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy, said at a press conference that she had informed Carson of the award by telephone. Carson was "taken by surprise, but very happy," she said.
Born in Toronto, Canada, in 1950, Carson writes primarily in English. Her major works include the 1998 verse novel "Autobiography of Red" and the 2001 "The Beauty of the Husband: A Fictional Essay in 29 Tangos". ■

WASHINGTON, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- U.S. Vice President JD Vance said Thursday that nine universities, including Harvard, Yale, Stanford, and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), merit an investigation for alleged J-1 visa fraud.
"While we see a lot of H-1B visa fraud, we also see a lot of J-1 visa fraud. And this is where some of America's most elite universities bring in foreigners again to undercut the wages of American residents. Now, there are nine universities in particular that we believe merit an investigation," Vance said at a press conference.
Those universities are Harvard, Yale, Stanford, Brown, the University of Pittsburgh, the University of California-Davis, the California Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and the MIT, according to the announcement.
"Something weird is going on at these universities. They're using these visas way too much. They're using them to undercut the wages of American grad students and American researchers, and it simply has to stop," Vance said.
At the press conference, Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling said he is suspending from the Permanent Labor Certification Program some of the largest IT outsourcing firms in the world: Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCLTech, and Capgemini.
Sonderling also noted that "due to multiple active federal investigations," the Department of Labor is suspending Microsoft and Adobe from the program.
Since 2009, these companies have requested almost 3 million foreign workers. They've received over 230,000 H-1B visas approvals and over 100,000 permanent labor certifications, according to the secretary.
The H-1B visa is a non-immigrant U.S. work visa that lets American companies hire foreign workers for specialized jobs. It is widely used by U.S. technology companies to attract highly educated and skilled foreign talent.
Since U.S. President Donald Trump returned to the White House, his administration has tightened immigration policies, cracking down on undocumented immigrants and increasing scrutiny of U.S. visa holders. ■

====================================================================================================

More young men than ever are gambling, but not to win
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
22:05:04 UTC
07:05:04 KST

Gambling rates in young men soar as betting becomes ticket into social circles
Australians spend an eye-watering $30 billion each year on gambling. We are, comfortably, the world's most profligate punters.
It is a challenging figure to quantify, but observing the front bar of your local pub can help to understand who, and where, that 10-figure sum comes from.
As the AFL and NRL finals played out, venues across the country were packed to the brim, most in attendance in varying stages of desperation for their team to score.
While all were focused on the game, most kept one eye on their phones, hoping one or more legs on a bet had come off.
While winning money would seem like the obvious goal, it is increasingly no longer the only one.
Win or lose, having a bet on is increasingly part of the social life of thousands of men across the country.
The local watering hole
The ABC visited a pub in Bunbury, WA's largest regional city, during the recent finals series, where almost every table of men had a bet on.
Roy, who was having a casual Thursday night drink with his friend, had two multi-bets on, despite not supporting either team.
"[I have a bet on] for all games, regardless of who's actually playing," he said.
Across the room, sitting together at a small table, eyes darting between the 90-inch screen on the wall and the smaller one in their hands, Adam and Dylan spoke about how gambling applications on their phones had impacted their habits.
"I had multiple apps, but I've deleted most of them," Adam said.
"I used to be pretty bad, but I've slowed down now."
Dylan said inducements from his application of choice, Sportsbet, were frequent.
"Sportsbet loves me … I don't get any messages aside from them," he said.
"It's a love-hate relationship … I'll never learn my lesson."
The ABC also spoke to a table of women who were not gambling.
Tanika said that while she did not bet, it was something that surrounded her.
"A lot of my friends gamble … my brother and my dad do it as well," she said
"I think it's just like one of those things, like the social, the footy club, everyone's doing it."
Mateship and the multi
In January, the federal government's gambling reforms will come into effect, including an opt-out service for online betting advertising.
Experts are pushing for public access to the data collected by gambling companies, in a bid to allow more targeted research and support.
But they are also pressing the government to address the social drivers of gambling's rapid growth among young men.
Vincent Mancini, a senior research fellow at The Kids Research Institute, said a growing number of young men considered betting part of their identity.
"The gambling industry has built sports gambling participation into the expression of manhood," Dr Mancini said.
Sports betting sits alone in this sense, with poker machines and horse or greyhound racing lacking the same cultural cachet.
Dr Mancini said gambling had become so synonymous with socialising, it was no longer about the win.
"When we speak to a lot of young boys, they realise that they're eventually going to lose the money," he said.
"But it's what they're getting along the way. It's the social [interaction], it's the banter, it's the friendships."
Sports betting surging
The 12 months to March this year saw participation in online gambling surpass venue-based gambling, like poker machines or casino gaming, for the first time in Australia's history.
Again, WA provides an interesting case study, boasting both the nation's most restrictive betting laws and its second-highest rate of gambling, according to the Australian Gambling Research Centre.
That is despite WA banning poker machines in 1962, limiting their use exclusively to Perth's Crown Casino, in an attempt to curb gambling losses.
As other states look to introduce stricter controls on poker machines, data shows online gambling will likely undermine reforms.
It is a trend and discussion that is front of mind for football clubs like the Busselton Magpies, and others all over the country.
"In our club rooms, we've got probably seven TVs that run every game of football while we're playing and training," club secretary Ray Gannaway said.
"Of course there's every betting agency in our face at every break, at every change."
He said the club has been working with the AFL to run mental health programs for younger players across all age groups, with gambling forming a big part of those conversations.
"We just aim to make sure our players are well informed about the ramifications if gambling becomes an addiction," he said.
"We're well aware that the boys will team up and have a punt on special occasions."
Mr Gannaway wants gambling advertising banned, and understands why young men get addicted.
"Exposure is what gives conversation, so take the exposure away, we stop talking about it," he said.
Australia's identity crisis
The other key factor is the prominence of gambling in Australia's cultural life, from two-up and its links to Australia's mining and wartime history, through to the national status of events like the Melbourne Cup.
Legalised casinos took gambling from back rooms and SP bookmakers to social and commercial hubs in every major city.
Curtin University gambling researcher Louise Francis said the industry had traded on that history to legitimise near-universal access to electronic betting.
"We're talking, like, highly sophisticated gambling machines, highly sophisticated wagering, the multi-bets," she said.
"And how they know that they can send things, you know, inducements to one person, not another — they can latch on to people.
"That's not tossing up two coins in a two-up ring; we can't compare the gambling of 200 years ago to today."
Dr Francis said the federal government's most recent reforms should have been a "blanket ban."
"I think they find it increasingly difficult to stand up to an industry that is so pervasive and powerful, and it is not just a gambling industry.
"We are talking about a sporting industry, we're talking about broadcasters that rely on that advertising revenue … it's a whole ecosystem."
Advertising ban unlikely
One million Australians either suffer from, or live with someone suffering from, severe gambling harm.
Dr Francis said the industry's resistance to advertising restrictions showed how important marketing is.
"Sometimes you see industry say, 'Oh, advertising is not that big, people would do it anyway if we didn't advertise,'" she said.
"It's a huge component of how they engage with the population … if it's not that important, don't advertise."
Independent Senator David Pocock said the Albanese government's reforms were too "weak" to have a meaningful impact.
"The parliament recommended a complete advertising ban and an end to all inducements for a reason," Mr Pocock said.
"The changes won't drive the deep cultural change we need to stop Australians being the biggest losers in the world when it comes to gambling losses per capita."
But Communications Minister Anika Wells said the government's reforms struck the appropriate balance.
"Children should be able to know the players and follow their team and celebrate a goal without gambling being an inextricable part of that," she said.
"These reforms also introduce choice; if you do not want to see gambling ads online, you will not have to."
The gambling industry body Responsible Wagering Australia warned against further reform.
"We risk pushing Australians towards illegal offshore websites where they lose the safeguards Australians rightly expect," they said.
"The industry has already taken significant action to reduce wagering advertising, voluntarily cutting free-to-air television advertising spend … on top of the federal government's new restrictions from 1 January 2027."

Fort Hood shooter’s firing squad execution to be livestreamed, Pentagon says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
22:01:15 UTC
07:01:15 KST

Fort Hood shooter’s firing squad execution to be livestreamed, Pentagon says
The Pentagon said on Thursday the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan would be livestreamed on December 3 after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth vowed to make the execution "public". Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 in a 2009 shooting at the Texas military base. The UN on Friday condemned the decision as "torture".
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
The Pentagon said on Thursday the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan will be livestreamed, a decision the UN on Friday condemned as "torture".
"The livestreaming of an execution is tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture," the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights said in a message sent to AFP.
The UN body said it had made similar statements about public executions in Afghanistan and Iran, saying they "constitute a form of cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment".
Hegseth, speaking to the conservative TV outlet Real America’s Voice News on Wednesday, said the execution of Hasan will take place at Fort Hood on December 3. Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others in a shooting at the military base in 2009.
“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public,” Hegseth said.
Hegseth spoke to the outlet aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier while visiting the long-deployed crew, who supported the Iran war, before their arrival at their home port in San Diego.
When asked if Hasan had made any final requests or reached out to the Trump administration, Hegseth simply replied: “Don’t care. We’ll see him on December 3rd.”
Officials in the Pentagon clarified Thursday that the execution will be livestreamed and that more details would follow.
Read moreFort Hood shooter sentenced to death
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell had said Monday that President Donald Trump had approved the execution of Hasan.
Trump has previously been critical of public executions in Iran, at times using the possibility of protesters being killed by the Iranian government as a possible rationale for military action. Those warnings preceded his ultimate choice to attack Iran at the end of February over its ballistic missiles and the risk of it developing nuclear weapons.
“We’ve been told that the killing in Iran is stopping,” Trump told reporters on January 14 of this year. “It’s stopping and there’s no plan for executions.”
He repeated that claim on January 20 at a White House press briefing, saying: “We let them know that if that happens, that will be a very bad day for them. And they decided not to do it. They didn’t hang the people.”
Slightly more than a month later in his State of the Union address, Trump said, “We stopped them from hanging a lot of them with the threat of serious violence.”
The White House on Thursday immediately referred questions about the plans for the livestreamed execution to the Pentagon.
However, experts on military law said Hasan could choose to resist execution and file a habeas petition in civilian court, which could significantly delay the execution.
“It frankly might outlast the current administration, and who knows if the next one will have the same penchant for executions,” Eugene R. Fidell, a visiting lecturer at Yale Law School specialising in military law.
Watch moreHegseth says Fort Hood shooter's military execution will be 'livestreamed'
Hasan, an Army psychiatrist who held the rank of major, walked into a medical building where soldiers were were waiting in long lines to receive immunisations and medical clearance for deployment. He shouted “Allahu akbar” – Arabic for “God is great!” – and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun.
During the trial it was revealed that Hasan spent weeks planning the deadly attack, and his preparation included videotaping a sales clerk showing him how to change the magazine on the pistol that he purchased. He would later go to a gun range outside Austin and ask for advice on how to reload with speed and precision from an instructor.
Soldiers later testified that Hasan’s rapid reloading made it all but impossible to stop the shooting. Investigators recovered 146 shell casings inside the building and dozens more outside, where Hasan shot at the backs of soldiers fleeing toward the parking lot.
Hasan said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims. A military judge barred him from presenting that as a defence during his trial. Hasan made almost no effort to defend himself in court, telling jurors when he acted as his own counsel that evidence would show he was the shooter and describing himself as a soldier who had “switched sides”.
Hegseth said the military hasn’t executed a service member by firing squad since World War II. The last military execution took place on April 13, 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was executed by hanging.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

China breakthrough projected to put sustainable aviation fuel gross profit margin past 50%
Biomass-to-jet fuel conversion method could boost production and help meet global aviation industry’s net-zero carbon goals, researchers say
Chinese researchers have developed a catalyst that converts synthesis gas into sustainable jet fuel – an advance that could boost production, help meet net-zero carbon goals and yield a gross profit margin above 50 per cent.
Based on a techno-economic analysis that modelled a planned 100,000-tonnes-per-year jet fuel plant, the researchers estimated they could achieve a gross profit margin of over 50 per cent.
“The excellent pilot test results and the positive techno-economic and life-cycle assessments underscore its strong potential for industrial deployment,” the team said in a paper published in the peer-reviewed journal Nature Communications in September.

Hundreds of farmers rally in Paris against EU-Mercosur pact and import fears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
21:57:17 UTC
06:57:17 KST

France saw hundreds of farmers gather outside the National Assembly in Paris on 8 January, to protest against the EU-Mercosur trade deal and demand greater protection for French agriculture.
Around 100 tractors entered the capital before dawn despite a police ban. Some reached the Arc de Triomphe and the Eiffel Tower before farmers gathered outside parliament, carrying flags and banners warning of the growing pressure on their livelihoods.
The protest was organised by Coordination Rurale, whose members travelled from several French regions to demand stronger protection for domestic agriculture. They also criticised the government's response to an outbreak of lumpy skin disease affecting cattle.
The EU-Mercosur agreement would expand trade with Brazil, Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay. French farmers fear competition from cheaper beef, poultry and sugar produced under different environmental and animal-welfare standards.
Brussels says European food-safety rules would still apply and that sensitive agricultural imports would be subject to quotas.
Tensions rose outside parliament when National Assembly President Yaël Braun-Pivet was booed by demonstrators. President Emmanuel Macron, meanwhile, said France would oppose the agreement ahead of a crucial European vote.
The protests extended across the country, bringing together around 2,200 farmers and 625 tractors in 39 departments, according to the Interior Ministry.
Coordination Rurale called for an end to the demonstrations later that day but insisted the fight was far from over.

The world is preparing for a record-breaking El Niño – scientists have warned of extreme heat, floods and economic losses
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
00:56:24 EEST
06:56:24 KST

The world is preparing for a record-breaking El Niño – scientists have warned of extreme heat, floods and economic losses
Kyiv • UNN
El Niño could become the strongest on record, causing heat, droughts and floods. The previous event cost the global economy $4 trillion.
The current El Niño climate phenomenon could become the strongest ever recorded, causing abnormal heat, droughts and floods in various regions of the planet. Bloomberg reports this, citing forecasts by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), writes UNN.
Details
In the summer, water temperatures in the tropical Pacific Ocean already exceeded normal levels by 2°C. According to researchers’ forecasts, the deviation could reach 3.7°C in the last three months of the year, while the previous record was 2.6°C in 2015–2016.
The ocean from which El Niño draws its water is the warmest we have ever measured. There is simply more heat that can be released
El Niño is already affecting the global economy
In Brazil, heavy rains have complicated sugarcane harvesting and threatened the future coffee crop. In Indonesia, drought is exacerbating forest fires, while in California, an increased fire risk is expected in 2027–2028.
Researchers estimate that the previous powerful El Niño in 2015–2016 resulted in the loss of nearly $4 trillion in potential global economic output over the following three years.
Meteorologists forecast that the current phenomenon will last at least until February. At the same time, Europe’s Copernicus climate service estimates the probability of a new global temperature record being set in 2026 at 26%.

Long-Range Anti-Ship Missile Will Integrate onto B-52
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
21:51:52 UTC
06:51:52 KST

The Air Force’s B-52 bomber may soon be able to carry up to 20 stealthy long-range anti-ship missiles to strike moving targets at sea, a key capability in a potential fight with China.
An Oct. 7 notice from Naval Air Systems Command states that the command plans to award a contract to Lockheed Martin to integrate its Long-Range Anti-Ship Missile on the B-52.
The anticipated award “is for efforts associated with LRASM integration on the B-52 aircraft platform, to include missile software updates, associated testing, test asset repair, and failure review boards,” the notice states.
The B-52 can already carry up to 20 Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missiles, on which the LRASM is based. The two missiles share similar dimensions.
Naval News first reported on the possibility of integrating the LRASM onto the B-52 in 2019, though the idea languished for several years. But the ability to put LRASMs on the B-52 would have massive implications in a large-scale conflict, retired Air Force Col. Mark Gunzinger, a former B-52 pilot, told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
“A handful of B-52s will be able to deliver more weapons on maritime targets and do so over much longer ranges than the Navy’s carrier-based aircraft per day,” said Gunzinger, now as the director of future concepts and capability assessments for the Mitchell Institute of Aerospace Studies.
Spokespeople for NAVAIR and Air Force Life Cycle Management Center did not immediately responded to a request for comment. Lockheed spokesperson Scott Swofford declined to provide any further details about the effort, deferring to the Pentagon, but did tout LRASM’s capabilities.
“As a precise, stealthy and survivable cruise missile, LRASM provides multiservice, multiplatform, and multimission capabilities for offensive anti-surface warfare,” Swofford said. “By leveraging Lockheed Martin’s expertise in successful cruise missile productions, LRASM brings low-risk and long-term, flexible capabilities to the warfighters’ anti-surface warfare environment that no other inventory weapon provides.”
A Necessary Tool
The Oct. 7 notice continues a push to integrate LRASM onto the bomber fleet—the Air Force revealed in June that a B-2A Spirit employed a LRASM to strike a decommissioned amphibious transport vessel during a Pacific exercise, the first time the U.S. military has acknowledged the B-2’s use of that missile.
Such a pairing is important, Gunzinger said.
“The Air Force’s bomber force will be our military’s predominant maritime strike force, considering the number of anti-ship cruise missiles they can carry per sortie and deliver over intercontinental ranges, if necessary,” Gunzinger said. “And LRASMs will give our bomber force the ability to strike moving targets at sea with unprecedented accuracy.”
The move will expand commanders’ options to strike maritime targets while launching from airbases in lower threat density areas, he said, without putting aircraft carriers at risk.
LRASM Development
- 2009: DARPA and the U.S. Navy initiate the program to develop advanced anti-ship strike capabilities.
- 2012: DARPA cancels the supersonic LRASM-B variant to focus exclusively on the subsonic, stealthy LRASM-A based on the JASSM-ER.
- 2013: Lockheed Martin completes the first successful air-launch flight test of the missile from a USAF B-1B bomber.
- 2015: The Pentagon officially designates the stealthy anti-ship missile as the AGM-158C.
- 2017: Lockheed Martin receives the first low-rate initial production contract
- 2018: The U.S. Air Force achieves Early Operational Capability with the AGM-158C on the B-1B Lancer.
- 2019: The U.S. Navy achieves Early Operational Capability integrating the missile onto F/A-18E/F Super Hornets.
- 2024: The U.S. Navy completes four-missile salvo testing and begins flight testing the round on the F-35C
- 2025: Initial flight testing expands to the F-35B short-takeoff/vertical-landing variant.
- 2026: Lockheed Martin expands factory capacity and contract modifications to boost annual production.
Sources: Lockheed Martin, Air & Space Forces Magazine, USNI
LRASM and JASSM
Lockheed produces both the the AGM-158 JASSM and the AGM-158C LRASM. There is also the AGM-158-JASSM Extended Range variant, which can hit targets out to 500 miles.
Currently, the B-1B Lancer, B-2A Spirit, B-52H Stratofortress, F-15 variants, F-16 variants, and C-130 Hercules can carry the JASSM.
The Air Force is also integrating the JASSM onto the F-35A Lightning II and the B-21 Raider.
The LRASM’s range hovers close to the baseline JASSM variant, just beyond 200 miles.
Air & Space Forces Magazine recently reported on JASSM and LRASM production progress based on Pentagon acquisition reports released in July.
The reports noted that, as of April, the Navy and Air Force were expanding their production plans for the shared munition. Lockheed had delivered a total of 5,348 JASSMs to both services. The company’s current production capacity is 600 JASSMs a year, with short-term plans to boost that to 860 missiles annually.
That’s key, as a recent Center for a New American Security report estimates that the Air Force has ripped through a quarter of its JASSM inventory during Operation Epic Fury.
Lockheed announced a new AGM-158 JASSM-FLEX variant in September at the AFA Air, Space & Cyber conference. The new variant lets users swap out the nose and launch options for various payloads and other configuration needs, which might include an LRASM option.
“The AGM-158 FLEX airframe concept was driven by a strategic need to keep pace with rapidly evolving threats, insert emerging technologies quickly, manage obsolescence, and provide, at scale, a cost-effective missile family that can be repurposed for a wide range of missions while delivering timely, relevant capability to the warfighter,” a Lockheed Martin spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine via email.
The Air Force spent $200 million in fiscal 2025 for a second-source engine for the LRASM and JASSM-ER. Lockheed plans to spend between $8 and $9 million through 2030 to boost production on existing lines.

The European Parliament recognized Russia’s new State Duma as illegitimate and called on the EU to cease contacts with its deputies
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
00:48:02 EEST
06:48:02 KST

The European Parliament recognized Russia’s new State Duma as illegitimate and called on the EU to cease contacts with its deputies
Kyiv • UNN
The European Parliament called the elections to the Russian Federation’s State Duma fraudulent and did not recognize its new composition. The EU was urged to cease official contacts with the deputies.
The European Parliament adopted a resolution refusing to recognize the results of the elections to the Russian State Duma and the legitimacy of its new composition. The document was supported by 482 MEPs, Meduza reports, as cited by UNN.
Details
Forty-one MEPs voted against the resolution, while another 39 abstained. The document called the Russian elections "fictitious," noting that the voting took place in an atmosphere of fear and against the backdrop of a full-scale war against Ukraine.
MEPs emphasized that voters had no real political alternative, independent media and authoritative observers were absent, while critics of the Kremlin ended up in prison, in exile, or were killed.
The EU is urged to isolate Russian lawmakers
The European Parliament called on EU member states to refrain from official contacts with deputies of the new State Duma. The lawmakers also opposed Russia's return to full participation in international sporting and cultural events.
The lawmakers separately called for continued support for Russian democratic forces that openly oppose the war in Ukraine.
At the same time, the lawmakers link the normalization of relations between the EU and Russia to the fulfillment of a number of conditions. These include restoring Ukraine's territorial integrity, releasing prisoners of war, and paying reparations.

Pentagon says execution of Fort Hood shooter will be livestreamed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
21:46:59 UTC
06:46:59 KST

Pete Hegseth has said the execution of Nidal Hasan, the former army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, will be a public event when the sentence is carried out later this year. A defense department official later confirmed the execution will be livestreamed.
In an interview with Real America’s Voice, the Pentagon secretary said the firing squad will carry out the sentence at Fort Hood, Texas, at 1pm on Thursday, 3 December. This would be the first US military execution in more than 60 years.
“It was a radical Islamist attack in uniform inside the ranks, and so he’s going to get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be, and we’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth said.
Hasan opened fire at a medical processing center on the Texas base on 5 November 2009, killing 13 people and wounding dozens more. A military jury sentenced him to death in 2013, and he has been held at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas ever since. He exhausted his appeals last year, which cleared the way for Donald Trump to approve the sentence this week on a recommendation from Hegseth.
Investigators had found that Hasan had exchanged 18 emails with Anwar al-Awlaki, a radical cleric who was subsequently killed in a US drone strike, in the months before the attack. At his court martial, Hasan said he had acted to stop American soldiers from deploying to Afghanistan to kill fellow Muslims, before his own impending deployment. A review led by William Webster, a former FBI director, concluded that the bureau should have investigated his correspondence more thoroughly.
In the interview, Hegseth said Barack Obama had called the attack “workplace violence”. The Pentagon initially treated the shooting as a workplace-violence incident rather than a terrorist attack, a classification that affected the victims’ eligibility for Purple Hearts and other combat-related benefits.
But there is no record of Obama himself using the phrase. At a memorial days after the attack, he instead described the victims as Americans who had been unable to escape “the horror of war”, while calling the shooting a tragedy and saying the killer would face justice.
The last known case of a military firing squad in the US was in November 1945, but the Trump administration has sought to bring it back in Trump’s second term to expedite capital punishment cases. Five US states allow for firing squads: Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah.
Abroad, Amnesty International’s most recent annual review lists Afghanistan, China, North Korea, Saudi Arabia, Somalia, Taiwan, the United Arab Emirates and Yemen among the countries that still use firing squads.
Asked whether Hasan had made a final request or reached out to Trump, Hegseth replied: “Don’t care. We’ll see him on December 3.”

The US State Department’s 2026 Trafficking in Persons (TIP) Report, released on Thursday, moved Hong Kong from the Tier 2 Watch List, where it had been listed for two consecutive years, to Tier 3.

EU Cuts Russian Rare-Earth Supplier Linked to Defense Industry From Draft Sanctions List at Estonia’s Request

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08

06:41:21 KST

- Category
- World
EU Cuts Russian Rare-Earth Supplier Linked to Defense Industry From Draft Sanctions List at Estonia’s Request
The EU removed one Russian company and an associated individual from its proposed 22nd sanctions package at Estonia’s request because the company supplies strategically important rare-earth materials to an Estonian processor, ERR reported on October 8.
The sanctions package, agreed by EU ambassadors on October 7, includes 743 individuals and 826 companies linked to Russia’s military-industrial complex.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Radio Free Europe reported that the final list was one individual and one company shorter than an earlier version. The outlet’s journalist Rikard Jozwiak later wrote that the Russian company supplies rare-earth materials to Silmet, which processes them for wind turbines and other uses in the EU.
Kerstin Lepik, spokesperson for Estonia’s permanent representation in Brussels, confirmed the decision to ERR.
“Yes, we asked for one Russian company and a related individual to be removed from the sanctions list approved today by the ambassadors of the COREPER II member states,” Lepik stated.
She explained that the company supplies materials to Estonia-based NPM Silmet that are considered strategically important for Europe. Industries dependent on NPM Silmet include electric vehicle manufacturing, wind turbines, electronics, automotive production, and aviation across the EU.
NPM Silmet is actively seeking alternative sources for materials currently imported from Russia, Lepik added. Estonia plans to reconsider adding the Russian company and the associated individual to the sanctions list next year.
According to Radio Free Europe, the companies included in the proposed sanctions package appear on a Russian government list of enterprises belonging to the country’s military-industrial complex and may therefore receive state support.
The sanctions still require formal approval by the EU Council at foreign ministers’ level and are expected to enter into force in the coming days. They include asset freezes, travel bans, and restrictions on providing funds or economic resources to listed entities and individuals.
Ukraine had previously described the sanctions as the EU’s largest package yet targeting Russia’s military-industrial complex. Ukrainian sanctions commissioner Vladyslav Vlasiuk noted that the package covers about 1,700 entries, with roughly 60% of the measures based on proposals submitted by Kyiv.

Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus slams EU over isolation of Turkish Cypriots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
21:38:19 UTC
06:38:19 KST

Esra Tekin
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
The Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC) on Thursday criticized the EU for its decades-long isolation of the Turkish Cypriots.
References made by the European Commission in a letter on the lifting of the unjust isolation imposed on the Turkish Cypriot side are completely inconsistent with the realities on the island, the TRNC Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
“The letter in question has gone on record as the clearest evidence that the EU will not take any positive steps for the Turkish Cypriot people in the future either,” the ministry added.
The statement underlined that the references made by the European Commission in its letter do not in any way reflect the realities on the island, adding that this “once again demonstrates that the EU will not change its biased and insincere stance on the Cyprus issue.”
It underscored that the Turkish Cypriot people for years have been forced to live under inhumane isolation and embargoes in violation of international law and human rights.
The restrictions imposed in areas ranging from education and sports to culture and economic life violate the fundamental human rights of the Turkish Cypriot people, it said.
It also said the EU’s position is a clear indication of its desire to preserve the unjust status quo on the island and of a structure that has yielded to vetoes by the Greek Cypriot side.
“There is an obvious reality: the people of the TRNC are still being subjected to inhumane isolation before the eyes of the EU and the international community,” the statement said.
 
EU shows ‘no willingness’ to ease isolation
The TRNC statement described the European Commission’s references to 2004 European Council decisions aimed at ending the isolation of Turkish Cypriots, as well as its claims about “building bridges” and “enhancing dialogue,” as “nothing more than an attempt to create a false impression.”
“The EU has taken no concrete steps, and has demonstrated no sincere approach, political will or vision, to eliminate the unjust restrictions imposed on the Turkish Cypriot people and the inhumane obstacles created by the Greek Cypriot side.
"The EU, which supports the Greek Cypriot leadership that even prevents our young people and athletes from establishing ties with the world, is the biggest protector of the status quo on the island," it added.
“We cannot take seriously the European Union and its so-called representative, (European Commission Vice President and EU Special Representative for Cyprus) Raffaele Fitto, which disregard the will, sovereign equality, and equal international status of the Turkish Cypriot people and distort the realities on the island through biased reports, letters and statements.”
The statement said the Turkish Cypriot people and the TRNC will continue their struggle under their own state structure, with the strong support of the Republic of Türkiye, and will remain determined to defend their rights on the basis of sovereign equality despite all embargoes and attempts at obstruction.
“The TRNC will not accept these empty, delaying tactics and approaches aimed at concealing the existing injustice on the island. There is one fundamental truth that the international community must understand: unless these outdated embargoes imposed on the Turkish Cypriot people are completely lifted, and our sovereign equality and equal international status are recognized, the EU’s declarations of ‘goodwill’ will have no validity in our eyes.
“At the same time, it is impossible to understand the portrayal in the press and public of a false impression that positive developments are taking place within the EU regarding the isolation. Far from taking steps to lift the isolation of Turkish Cypriots, the EU will show no willingness even to ease it.”
 
Decades-long problem
Cyprus has been mired in a decades-long dispute between Greek Cypriots and Turkish Cypriots, despite diplomatic efforts by the UN to achieve a comprehensive settlement.
Ethnic attacks starting in the early 1960s forced Turkish Cypriots to withdraw into enclaves for their safety.
In 1974, a Greek Cypriot coup aimed at Greece’s annexation of the island led to Türkiye’s military intervention as a guarantor power to protect Turkish Cypriots from persecution and violence. As a result, the TRNC was founded in 1983.
It has seen an on-and-off peace process in recent years, including a failed 2017 initiative in Switzerland under the auspices of guarantor countries Türkiye, Greece, and the UK.
The Greek Cypriot Administration entered the EU in 2004, the same year Greek Cypriots single-handedly blocked a UN plan to end the longstanding dispute.

laterna magika brought projected images into live perfomance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
21:35:41 UTC
06:35:41 KST

laterna magika brought projected images into live perfomance
josef svoboda and alfréd radok brought live performance and film together, creating a stage where bodies, images and space could occupy the same visual field.
Laterna Magika made the screen part of the stage
Developed by stage director Alfréd Radok and scenographer Josef Svoboda for Czechoslovakia’s pavilion at Expo 58 in Brussels, Laterna Magika brought live performance, film projection, music, dance and stage technology into a single theatrical language, turning the relationship between the physical stage and the projected image into the central subject of the performance. The project continued beyond the exhibition, becoming an independent company of Prague’s National Theatre in 1959, developing a theatrical language that still offers a useful way of thinking about spectatorship, scenography and the way projected images can alter our experience of physical space.
The idea that a filmed image could interact with a performer on stage as if they occupied the same world shaped Laterna Magika. In the original Expo program, filmed figures appeared to speak to the actress performing live, while projected sequences were carefully timed with acting, music and dance. The screen became part of the action, giving the audience something else to follow alongside the performers in front of them. An image could respond to a performer, extend a movement or introduce another version of the same space, while the physical stage remained visible at the same time.
For the audience, watching the performance meant moving between different layers, paying attention to what was happening in front of them and to what was happening on screen. Looking at Laterna Magika today, this way of working feels particularly relevant because screens have become part of so many physical environments, from theaters and museums to public spaces and buildings. Svoboda and Radok were already exploring what happens when an image is given a physical role within a space, and when the audience has to consider the performer and their projected image as two parts of the same scene.
josef svoboda and the architecture of the image
Josef Svoboda worked at Prague’s National Theatre from the late 1940s and became head of its artistic-technical operations, where he pushed the theater workshops toward a more technologically ambitious model capable of responding to increasingly complex stage designs. His approach treated light, projection, movement and technical infrastructure as active components of the stage environment.
His work with Alfréd Radok at Expo 58 grew out of this broader interest in expanding what scenography could do. The two developed an interplay between live action and filmed sequences in which the projected image could heighten or contradict what was happening on stage, producing a visual language that depended on precise timing and coordination between different media. The National Theatre later described Laterna Magika as having evolved from these principles, with each production exploring a different way of connecting stage and image.
Svoboda’s thinking also extended into the technical systems that made these relationships possible. His work on Polyekran, which involved combining multiple projection surfaces into a larger image composition, was developed around the same period, although the National Theatre makes an important distinction between Polyekran as a technical system and Laterna Magika as a theatrical form. Both belonged to Svoboda’s broader investigation into how projected images could alter the perception of space.
a theater built around spectatorship
Seen through contemporary scenography, Laterna Magika belongs to a longer history of treating the stage as a space that can direct and shape attention. The audience moves between what is physically present and what appears on screen, following performers, images, light and movement as they occupy and alter the same space. In this sense, Laterna Magika changes the role of the spectator, who has to follow both the performer and the projected image and understand how the two relate to each other. The stage becomes something that has to be read as much as watched, with projection, movement, light and physical space working together to determine what the audience sees.
from expo spectacle to an evolving theater
The original program was designed for an international exhibition and carried the representational ambitions that came with that context, yet its theatrical language continued after Expo 58. Laterna Magika became an independent company of the National Theatre in Prague in May 1959, initially continuing with revue-like programs before gradually developing longer productions and a broader theatrical repertoire. One of its most enduring productions, Wonderful Circus, premiered in 1977 and remains in the repertoire. Its arrival marked a shift toward multi-theme productions, while the company continued to develop the relationship between live performers and projected imagery as a defining part of its stage language.
Svoboda became Laterna Magika’s artistic director in 1973, at a moment when the company was searching for a new direction, and remained closely connected to its development for the rest of his career. His influence also extended beyond individual productions into the question of where this kind of theater should exist: during the development of Prague’s New Stage in the early 1980s, he pushed for the building to accommodate Laterna Magika, helping reshape the project around the needs of the company. The New Stage opened in 1983 and became closely associated with Laterna Magika, giving the company a permanent architectural setting for a theatrical form that had originally been conceived for a temporary exhibition. This particular form of scenography helped generate the architectural conditions in which it could continue to develop.
the stage after the stage
Looking at Laterna Magika today makes sense because so much of contemporary performance is once again concerned with the relationship between the physical and the projected image. Projection, LED screens, virtual production and responsive lighting are now part of the visual language of theaters, exhibitions and architecture, making Svoboda and Radok’s experiments feel less like an isolated moment in theater history and more like an earlier chapter in a conversation that is still taking place.
What is striking is how much of that conversation was already present in Laterna Magika. The technology has changed, but the basic setup remains recognizable: a performer shares the stage with an image, the image changes our perception of the space, and the audience has to decide how to look at both at the same time. Looking back at the work now allows us to see where some of these ideas came from, before projection became such a familiar part of the environments we move through today.
This is also what makes Svoboda’s approach to scenography worth revisiting. He treated the stage as something that could change through light, movement, projection and technology, giving the image a physical presence within the performance. At a moment when screens are increasingly built into the spaces around us, Laterna Magika offers a useful point of reference for understanding how that relationship between image, space and the spectator developed in the first place.

After 6:00 p.m., Telenor reported that normal connections between telephone networks had been restored. However, trains were still operating with delays in the evening. Railway officials expected a return to the regular timetable the following morning.
Norway's Communications Authority, Nkom, said that the incident was not related to an attack. Telenor also denied the cyberattack theory, but the exact cause of the major technical failure has not yet been identified.

Trump envoys, European officials to discuss ‘new ideas’ for Ukraine peace in Miami
US President Donald Trump’s envoys will meet Ukrainian negotiators and European officials in Miami on Friday to discuss a new proposal to end Russia’s war in Ukraine. Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will present ideas developed during recent talks with both sides, one source said Thursday.
President Donald Trump's envoys will meet Ukrainian and European officials in Miami on Friday to discuss "new ideas" and seek a unified proposal to end the war with Russia, two US sources told AFP.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed the talks after a day in which a Russian strike on buses killed 30 people in the frontline city of Kramatorsk, one of the deadliest attacks in weeks.
"The Ukrainian negotiating team is due to meet Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff in the US tomorrow," Zelensky said Thursday. "The meeting is expected to last two days. We are also counting on a European team to join our negotiating group."
Zelensky said his chief of staff, Kyrylo Budanov, as well as Ukraine's top officials: Rustem Umerov, Sergiy Kyslytsya and David Arakhamia will take part in the talks in Florida.
Watch moreBlack sea and black ops: How exposed is Europe to Ukraine war spillover?
The US-led peace efforts to end the Ukraine war have been largely stalled, with Washington focused on its conflict with Iran despite Kyiv saying Russia has ramped up aerial attacks.
But US officials said they were making a fresh effort in an enlarged format, following visits to Moscow and Kyiv by last month by Witkoff, Trump's business friend-turned-roving envoy, and the president's son-in-law Kushner.

The Kremlin said last month that three-way talks on ending the war could take place in October.
Previous rounds of talks have failed to yield tangible progress towards peace, with Moscow unwilling to drop its maximalist conditions to end the fighting.
Trump said earlier this week that he had a call scheduled with Russian President Vladimir Putin, although it was expected to focus on the reported death of a researcher at a Russian plague lab.
In a sign that Ukraine was under discussion, Witkoff was seen by AFP reporters traveling with Trump on Air Force One on Wednesday on a campaign trip to Texas for the US midterm elections.

Syria weighs deploying thousands of troops to Yemen – Axios
Syria could join a Saudi-backed military offensive against the Houthis in Yemen by deploying thousands of troops, Axios has reported, citing US officials.
Yemen’s internationally recognized government forces have launched a major counteroffensive to recapture territory seized by the Iranian-backed Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah, including areas around the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The Saudi-led coalition has backed the operation with extensive airstrikes against Houthi positions.
According to an Axios report, Riyadh and Damascus are discussing the deployment of up to 20,000 Syrian troops. Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, who previously led the Islamist group Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), is reportedly considering the proposal but has yet to make a decision.
The issue came up during al-Sharaa’s meeting with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Riyadh on Tuesday, the sources said. Saudi Arabia is seeking to reinforce Yemeni government forces, which US officials described as less well-trained than the Houthis.
Washington does not oppose the proposal in principle and sees it as a way to bolster the offensive without deeper American involvement, according to Axios. US Central Command has also been consulted on how Syrian troops could be deployed.
The Syrian units under consideration reportedly include thousands of Islamist foreign fighters who fought against former President Bashar Assad under the HTS umbrella before his overthrow in December 2024. Their involvement could deepen sectarian divisions, as the fighters include Sunni Islamists, while the Houthis follow Zaydi Shiite Islam.
Reuters separately reported that Damascus was considering military assistance, including defensive support for Saudi Arabia or participation in operations inside Yemen. However, Syrian presidential adviser Ahmad Zaidan denied that Riyadh had requested troops, describing the reports as baseless.

The renewed fighting follows Houthi territorial gains along the Red Sea coast in September, threatening shipping through Bab el-Mandeb, a vital trade route connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. Unproven ‘cures’ pushed online amid Russia plague concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
21:18:06 UTC
06:18:06 KST

Unproven ‘cures’ pushed online amid Russia plague concerns
- - Unconfirmed plague reports from Russia have driven online interest in expensive “cure” kits, with social media posts urging people to buy before a crisis.
- - Experts say North America does not need plague treatment kits. They warn against using doxycycline or ivermectin without real exposure or medical need.
- - Misinformation sellers use fear to profit during health scares, repeating a pattern seen with hantavirus and Ebola claims.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - Reports that a woman employed at a plague research institute in Russia’s Irkutsk region died from the disease has spiked online interest in possible treatments for the illness in North America.
Russia has not confirmed the woman died of plague and the governor of the local region said on Oct 8 that no health issues were detected after all her contacts were traced.
But on social media, influencers and doomsday “preppers” are pushing the necessity of purchasing a US$300 (S$384) kit claimed to help people avoid emergency room visits.
“Don’t wait until everybody is scrambling. Prepare before you need it,” says the caption of a Facebook video viewed more than 161,000 times under the hashtags #Russia and #plague.
The posts include personalised discount codes, suggesting the creators may receive financial compensation if a purchase is made.
The Wellness Company brand promoted in many of the videos saw a subsequent spike in online searches, according to Google Trends data.
The company is fronted by Peter McCullough, an American cardiologist who has promoted Covid-19 conspiracies and health misinformation debunked by AFP.
It did not immediately respond to questions about the kits.
Rogan O’Handley, known on social media as DC Draino, highlighted the kit’s inclusion of the antibiotic doxycycline to his 2.9 million followers.
The antibiotic is among those used to treat plague in countries that see cases each year, helping to contain outbreaks.
“We know how to treat it,” said Isaac Bogoch, an infectious disease specialist at Toronto General Hospital.
“Obviously, it can be a very severe infection,” he said, but he warned against taking a course of antibiotics without known exposure.
He said the unconfirmed case in Russia “isn’t the type of infection that would cause a pandemic.”
Paul Keim, plague researcher and professor at Northern Arizona University, also said there is no reason for people in North America to start taking doxycycline.
“You’re altering the microbiome of your gut, and perhaps creating antibiotic resistant bacteria in your body that will fight off the drug therapy the next time you really need it,” he said.
Ineffective remedies
The kits are also said to include “hard-to-find” prescription medications such as ivermectin.
But “ivermectin is never really used for a bacterial disease,” Keim said.
The anti-parasitic drug is only approved by the US Food and Drug Administration to treat worm diseases.
Yet, it continues to be the go-to solution touted in health misinformation – in part because authorities dismissed it as an effective treatment for Covid-19 following unsuccessful clinical trials.
This is not the first public health concern that prompted individuals to offer unproven medical solutions.
When a cruise ship passenger contracted the rare hantavirus in May, accounts also immediately touted ivermectin as a “cure” even while there is no known treatment.
Amid the 2026 Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, videos of a doctor recommending Vitamin D3 and zinc spread from accounts selling supplements, despite these being unable to treat the disease.
“Whenever there is a crisis – especially in the health space – the grifters are gonna come out,” said Timothy Caulfield, a misinformation expert and professor at the University of Alberta.
“They exploit fear and uncertainty to sell unproven products.” AFP
