Taxes account for over 53% of labour costs in Spain, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:11:03 UTC
04:11:03 KST

In 2025, Spain's Finance Ministry argued that its tax cuts for middle-income earners had delivered €38 billion in savings
More than half of the total cost of employing an average worker in Spain goes to public authorities, according to the Juan de Mariana Institute, a liberal think tank highly critical of the government.
The institute estimates the tax burden at €53.60 for every €100 in labour costs. The figure comes from a report the think tank describes as an "economic autopsy" of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's time in office, as reported by The Objective.
The report, written by the institute's head of research, Diego Sánchez de la Cruz, estimates that €21,144 of the average employee's €39,481 annual labour cost goes towards taxes and social security contributions — equivalent to a tax burden of €53.60 for every €100 in labour costs.
The think tank describes the report as an "economic autopsy" of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's time in office, according to The Objective.
The calculation includes social security contributions, income tax, VAT and other taxes, using the employer's total labour cost rather than gross salary as its basis.
The institute previously documented 141 tax increases between 2018 and 2026.
It also estimates that the average taxpayer pays €460,600 in taxes over their lifetime, equivalent to almost 30 years of Spain's most common salary, or 16.4 years based on the average salary.
Higher tax revenues, spending and debt
According to the report, revenue from taxes and social security contributions has risen by 39.7% since 2018, an increase of around €168.17 billion. The figure is nominal, meaning it also reflects inflation and employment growth. The tax-to-GDP ratio has increased from 34.9% to 37.1%.
The report acknowledges that healthcare spending has risen by 43% and education spending by 40%. However, it argues that public services have deteriorated, citing a 28% increase in surgical waiting lists to 853,509 patients, an average wait of 102 days to see a specialist, and the results of the 2025 PISA report.
Public debt stands at €1.763 trillion, around €600 billion more than eight years ago. The report also notes that one in every four euros spent on pensions is funded through government contributions.
Housing and wages
According to the study, median rent (€1,080) now exceeds the median salary of a young worker (€1,048), while only 15.2% of young people live independently, the lowest figure since 2006.
The author attributes this to a housing shortage, noting that 1.16 million new households have been formed since 2021, compared with just 465,000 completed homes on the open market.
The report also blames rent caps introduced under Spain's housing law, linking them to a 43% drop in new rental contracts in Barcelona, 44% in Navarre and 51% in A Coruña.
On employment, the report acknowledges a 66% increase in the minimum wage but describes it as leading to "unprecedented wage compression". It also claims unemployment figures are distorted by inactive workers on permanent seasonal contracts.
The institute describes the period as "devastating" and criticises the state's response to crises including Covid-19, the DANA floods and the crisis in Ceuta as "non-existent".
The report comes shortly after Sanchez called an early general election following the defeat of his government's decrees.

Protesters blame 'vulture funds' for Spain's housing crisis
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
20:10:06 BST
04:10:06 KST

Protesters blame 'vulture funds' for Spain's housing crisis
- Published
Pierina Nicuray, a 21-year-old university graduate, has spent a week camped out in Madrid's Puerta del Sol square.
Like many of the hundreds of others who have pitched their tents here to protest at Spain's housing crisis, she has no doubts when it comes to diagnosing the cause.
"It's the same problem as always," she says. "A lack of homes."
She adds: "Landlords are taking advantage of the situation to raise rentals, and then there's also Airbnb."
Jorge Moreno, a 19-year-old film-dubbing student who has also been living in a tent here in central Madrid for the last few days, agrees.
"There are so many homes standing empty because they have been bought by vulture funds and investment funds which hike up the rent of people living in properties until they get rid of them," says Jorge, who lives with his mother and fears it will be a long time before he can afford a home of his own.
"They've been making a business of housing for a long time," he adds. "But it's an abusive business which stops Spaniards from being able to live in a decent home."
His and Pierina's diagnoses are frequently voiced by fellow protesters, ordinary Spaniards and even the Spanish government.
On presenting a recent package of emergency measures to tackle the housing problem, Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said he was legislating "against those who consider housing just another object on the market with which to speculate".
Those reforms were rejected by Congress, prompting Sánchez to call a snap election next month.
Nicuray and Moreno can point to the single case that sparked the current Spanish housing protest movement as proof that profit-driven practices are at the heart of the crisis: the 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her home after the investment firm that had bought it tried to persuade her to leave, then sharply increased her rent, which she was unable to pay.
Although the social backlash that followed caused the company to invite Abascal to return to her old home, she never did, dying in hospital on Wednesday.
Many others have their own stories of struggling with a soaring rental market.
Carmen Pérez is a retired widow, originally from Ecuador, who has been living in Spain for 17 years.
When she arrived, housing was relatively cheap and accessible, but - as costs have risen - she has been forced to move in with her daughter and son-in-law as she looks for somewhere affordable to rent.
"When a property is listed to rent, there's always a long waiting list," she says. "And the rent is always too high for me. All of this has affected my health - I've got depression, I don't have any stability or security."
Spain has seen an average rise in rental costs of 84% over the last 10 years, according to property outlet Idealista.
In the centre of the southern city of Málaga, the increase has been 113 %, and, in Marbella - just under 150%.
Such numbers have made housing Spaniards' biggest concern.
A recent study by the Centre for Sociological Research (CIS) showed how the broader Spanish population, like the protesters, want to see action taken against those perceived to be powerful movers in the housing market.
Some 72% wanted higher taxes introduced for those with 10 or more properties; 76% wanted limits on short-term tourist accommodation; and 40% supported the expropriation of empty homes.
However, Jorge Galindo, director at the Esade centre for economic policy, says that available data makes it difficult to know exactly how many Spanish properties are owned by so-called "vulture funds" and being used for speculation.
He points to Bank of Spain figures from 2024 showing that only 8% of properties for rent are owned by companies.
Galindo says he concludes from the data available that there is not a notable accumulation of property to rent among a small number of owners in Spain.
"When it comes to explaining the rise in rentals, that is not the big cause," he says. "What explains it is the shortage of supply compared to demand over recent years."
The Bank of Spain appears to agree, and has estimated that the country has a housing shortfall of around 750,000 homes.
The institution's deputy governor, Soledad Núñez, warned in September that by 2028 that could rise to one million.
There are 3.8 million empty properties in Spain, according to the National Statistics Institute (INE), but a large number of those are in depopulated rural areas and therefore have little relevance to the current crisis, which is most acute in urban hubs.
Other explanations for this high number include properties awaiting renovation, or legal disputes between family members who have inherited them.
Demographic changes play a major part in the imbalance between supply and demand.
Between 2021 and 2025, there were about 1.2 million new households in Spain, driven in great part by the arrival of migrants who have played a major role in the country's recent economic growth.
However, house building has not kept pace, with fewer than half-a-million new homes during that period.
That was partly because Spain's construction industry had shrunk in the wake of the Eurozone crisis, while the cost of materials rose substantially after Covid, and a lack of political consensus put legal obstacles in the way of building.
"It was not a priority for us to build new houses," Galindo says. "But, once the demographic boom came, we realised how costly it was for us."
He adds that short-term tourist accommodation, like Airbnb, which has been identified by both the Spanish government and many activists as a culprit, is likely to have had a more localised effect, pushing up prices in specific urban areas rather than having an overall impact.
Meanwhile, the crisis has been aggravated by lagging salaries.
A study by El País found that, in real terms, the average Spaniard had 5% less spending power than a decade ago, due to taxes, social security and inflation. The average monthly salary in the Madrid region is €1,550 (£1,314; $1,738).
"No worker should have to spend 75% or 80% of their salary on rent, because what are they supposed to eat?" says Francisco Pardo, an 81-year-old retired taxi driver, who sympathises with the protesters, during a visit to the tent city in Madrid.
"Many workers don't even earn €2,000 [per month]."
The case of Maricarmen has suddenly made the housing crisis an urgent topic of discussion, not just in Madrid's Puerta del Sol but across the country.
The question now is whether a consensus can be reached on how to solve it.

UK Announces $71M Winter Aid, New Sanctions on Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:08:04 UTC
04:08:04 KST

UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband pledged £54 million ($71 million) to Ukraine ahead of winter and unveiled fresh sanctions against Russia on Thursday, Oct. 8, during his first visit to the country since taking office.
Miliband announced the measures alongside President Volodymyr Zelensky and Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, with whom he toured the site of a deadly Russian missile strike in Pryluky, in the Chernihiv region.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Five winters on, the people of Ukraine are still living under constant threat of Russian strikes, energy blackouts and death,” Miliband said, according to the UK governmental website.
“My message to [Russian President Vladimir] Putin is clear – You cannot wait us out,” he continued, reaffirming UK’s support for Ukraine despite ongoing hybrid warfare threats from Russia, which have significantly intensified in recent months.
The UK pledged another £6 million (approximately $8 million) to Ukraine specifically for the “pursuit of justice” for Russia’s war crimes. As of Oct. 2, Ukraine had opened nearly 244,000 criminal cases over crimes committed by Russian forces and their accomplices on the country’s territory, including almost 227,000 war-crime investigations.
Strike on Pryluky left 22 people dead
The strike on an apartment building in Pryluky coincided with Russian Putin’s 74th birthday, and it left at least 22 civilians dead, including five children.
Zelensky Visits Pryluky With UK’s Miliband, Thanks EU for €1.2B Tranche for Drones
According to Zelensky, 54 people were injured just in that strike alone, while the overall number of Russian attacks left 78 people dead and 215 injured nationwide in recent days. He described the attacks as a severe escalation and “terror directed against people and life,” warning that world leaders must not ignore what is happening.
During their visit earlier on Thursday, the three leaders spoke with survivors of the attack and with emergency workers who had taken part in the rescue effort.
“Russia could end this war tomorrow,” Miliband said. “Instead, we’ve seen escalating attacks, including on key infrastructure and Ukrainian cultural landmarks.”
According to him, the UK’s support for Ukraine is rooted not only in European and NATO security, but also in a wider global effort to defend justice and the rule of law.
How the funding will be allocated
The new funding comes as Ukraine continues to appeal to its Western allies for air defense and financial support ahead of the upcoming winter, when Russia is expected to intensify its campaign against critical infrastructure, including the power grid and water-supply systems.
Of the total pledged, £20 million (about $26 million) will go toward Ukraine’s energy security; to support crews carrying out emergency repairs to the power grid after Russian strikes, provide backup generators and solar power for use during blackouts, as well as to fund technologies to help Ukraine diversify its energy sources.
The remaining £34 million (roughly $45 million) will be allocated for heating and water systems. According to the UK’s government, the amount also includes direct cash assistance.
Aid will be delivered together with the Ukrainian government and partners including UNICEF, the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) and the Ukrainian Red Cross.
Fresh sanctions on Russia
Beyond financial support, Miliband announced fresh sanctions on around 40 individuals and entities in Russia’s financial, oil, and technology sectors.
With the latest package, more than 90% of Russia’s total oil production capacity is now covered by UK sanctions, according to the government.
So far, Britain has sanctioned more than 600 vessels and over 3,500 targets in total under its Russia sanctions regime.
On Oct.1, the UK has announced a new package of 31 sanctions, focusing on global disinformation networks and individuals responsible for the torture of Ukrainian civilians and the forced deportation of children.
Late September, when the EU compromised on the extension of the sanctions on about 3,000 individuals and entities in exchange for the delistment of two Russian oligarchs closely connected to Putin, the UK pledged to keep its own sanctions in place.
The measures are intended to send a message to Russian diplomats and those who support Russia’s war to step back from escalation and move toward a ceasefire.
According to Sybiha’s statement on X, the meeting coincided with the sixth anniversary of the Agreement on Political Cooperation, Free Trade and Strategic Partnership, which Ukraine and the UK signed in London.
Since then, he said, relations between the two countries have reached a new level, strengthened by the historic 100 Year Partnership Agreement that their leaders signed in Kyiv last year.
“We also launched the second meeting of the Political Pillar of the Ukraine-UK Strategic Partnership Dialogue and agreed to continue expert-level discussions in Kyiv,” Sybiha said, expressing gratitude to the UK for its “comprehensive support” – which currently equates to £25 billion (about $33 billion), including £16 billion (roughly $21 billion) in military support.

Astronomers discover record-breaking ancient cosmic outburst
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:07:21 UTC
04:07:21 KST

At some point around three billion years after the big bang, some celestial object in a faraway galaxy suddenly went pop and shot out a brief-but-powerful blast of radio waves, lasting just a fraction of a second. That blast kept traveling across the intergalactic vastness of space and time until, in March 2024, it breezed by Earth, with a small fraction of its energy trickling into the dishes of the MeerKAT radio telescope array in South Africa.
For Themiya Nanayakkara, an astronomer at Australia’s University of Sydney, MeerKAT’s detection was a moment of peak excitement. Fast radio bursts (FRBs), as these types of emissions are called, are common, occurring roughly 5,000 to 10,000 times per day across Earth’s sky. But this one’s sheer faintness signaled it was very old, originating long, long ago from somewhere far, far away.
But just how old was it, and where did it come from? Looking at the power of the burst and the amount of its light that had been stretched, or “redshifted,” by the expansion of the universe around it as it traveled, Nanayakkara and his colleagues were able to find out. As they describe in a new paper in Science, this FRB occurred in a far-distant galaxy some 10 billion years ago. That esteemed cosmic vintage makes this the oldest FRB ever detected by far. This event, in fact, is twice as old as the previous record holder.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Despite intensive scrutiny in the quarter-century since their discovery, FRBs remain rather mysterious. For starters, astronomers still don’t know their astrophysical origins. One leading idea posits they’re produced by magnetars, small remnants left behind by massive stars that detonate as supernovae, but many details are murky, and not all FRBs seem to fit the “magnetar” mold. Detecting and measuring FRBs and their host galaxies can help solve the puzzle, Nanayakkara says. In this case, he and his colleagues traced this one back to a galaxy that appears relatively primitive compared with others from its early cosmic epoch: this galaxy has a lower mass and less heavy elements than its contemporaries but higher amounts of star formation.
None of that is necessarily unexpected for the formation of an FRB-birthing magnetar. But this record-setting FRB still significantly pushes back the baseline for when these bursts can occur in cosmic history. And according to Nanayakkara, this in turn raises the possibility that even older (and fainter) FRBs have passed by Earth unnoticed.
“Our telescopes need to be extremely sensitive to detect them,” he says. Thankfully, MeerKAT exists to help. “The same thing applies when trying to find their host galaxies. Since these galaxies are also very far away, they can be extremely faint, making it challenging to follow them up and study their properties.”
The clamor to find and study increasingly distant FRBs isn’t just a matter of curiosity, either: These short, sharp bursts can also serve as potent probes of otherwise-invisible matter spread between galaxies. As an FRB travels, its radio waves interact with the dilute, dark plasma that astronomers call the intergalactic medium; the FRB’s shorter waves interact more with the plasma, slowing their propagation so that they arrive at Earth later than their longer-wavelength counterparts. Measuring this dispersion allows astronomers to learn just how much of this material any given FRB has traversed on its long journey to our planet.
“Our discovery is particularly important because we have shown that we can do this across approximately 80 percent of cosmic history,” Nanayakkara says. “The further back we push FRB detections, the further we can map this otherwise unseen matter.”
To accomplish this, Nanayakkara recently secured time on NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). Once a year for the next three years, his team will be able to focus JWST onto the faraway astrophysical source of some especially ancient FRB, seeking to break the cosmic distance record yet again.
“We are currently waiting for our radio telescopes in Australia and South Africa to detect such a burst. As soon as we find one, we can trigger JWST observations to study its host galaxy and hopefully push the boundary even further,” he says. “The more distant FRBs we find, the stronger the constraints we can place on the objects and emission mechanisms that produce them, the environments in which they occur and the distribution of matter across the universe.”

Cuba records more than 11,000 dengue cases, over 9 times the expected average
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:07:13 UTC
04:07:13 KST

Mariam Ashalem De Andres
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
Cuba has recorded more than 11,000 dengue cases in 2026, more than nine times the average expected, according to media reports on Thursday.
The island recorded 11,235 cases in 2026, equivalent to 9.2 times the expected average based on data from the previous five years, reported the Infobae news outlet, citing data on the Global Dengue Observatory.
The number of cases has increased sharply in recent months, with 4,102 recorded in September, compared with 3,214 in August.
Figures for July, August and September are estimates because Cuban authorities have not published updated official data on the progression of the disease.
The tracking system said transmission in Cuba is currently at its peak, with October traditionally marking the period of highest incidence of the disease.
The rise in cases comes amid a worsening energy and fuel crisis on the island, which has affected efforts to control the mosquito that transmits dengue.
Prolonged power outages have forced families to keep doors and windows open during hot nights, potentially increasing exposure to mosquitoes, according to the report.
Fuel shortages have also affected fumigation operations, limiting efforts to reduce mosquito populations and prevent the spread of the disease.
The situation has also been compounded by shortages of medicines and laboratory supplies, including drugs used to control fever and pain and reagents needed for blood tests.
Cuba’s Health Ministry acknowledged in September an increase in dengue and other mosquito-borne diseases but did not provide an updated nationwide tally.
Earlier data from the Global Dengue Observatory showed 7,133 dengue cases by mid-September, representing 7.4 times the expected average for that period.
Dengue is a viral disease transmitted primarily by infected Aedes aegypti mosquitoes. Most people recover without serious complications, but severe dengue can cause bleeding, shock and organ damage and may require hospitalization.
The World Health Organization has identified dengue as one of the fastest-growing mosquito-borne viral diseases globally, with cases increasing substantially in recent decades.

KOROLOVA Becomes Highest-Ranked Ukrainian DJ Ever, Reaching No. 36 in DJ Mag Top 100
Ukrainian DJ KOROLOVA has climbed to 36th place in the 2026 DJ Mag Top 100 DJs ranking, marking the highest position ever achieved by a Ukrainian artist on the international list.
According to NV, the achievement also establishes a new record for Ukrainian DJs featured in DJ Mag’s annual ranking, which recognizes leading performers in the global electronic music industry.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Known for blending melodic techno with progressive house, KOROLOVA, whose real name is Olga Korolova, has released tracks including Be Strong, Shining, and Heal My Mind.
Reacting to the announcement, KOROLOVA expressed her excitement and thanked fans for their continued support, emphasizing that the achievement would not have been possible without them.
“I’m in shock. Literally SHOCKED. I ranked 36th in the DJ Mag Top 100 DJs worldwide. Actually, no, we ranked 36th together. Every single one of you who supported me, voted for me, believed in me, and showed me so much love—this would never have happened without you,” she said.
“I’m so incredibly happy right now, I can’t stop crying. I still can’t believe it… Out of hundreds of thousands of DJs around the world, WE MADE IT TO #36. I love you all so, so much, and I can’t even put into words how grateful I am for every single one of you,” KOROLOVA added.
The result marks KOROLOVA’s third consecutive appearance in the DJ Mag Top 100 DJs ranking, with the Ukrainian artist climbing 14 positions from 50th place in 2025. Last year, she had already risen ten spots compared to her debut in the ranking.

Philippines ex-President Duterte fit to stand trial, ICC rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:06:08 UTC

Philippines ex-President Duterte fit to stand trial, ICC rules
The former president is able to understand the charges and follow the proceedings, panel of experts find.
Judges at the International Criminal Court (ICC) have found former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte fit to stand trial and able to face charges of crimes against humanity related to the so-called “war on drugs” he waged while in office.
The ex-leader is accused of murder and attempted murder for his alleged involvement in dozens of killings. He denies the charges, but faces a maximum sentence of life imprisonment if convicted.
The court in The Hague said on Thursday that independent medical experts had examined the 81-year-old’s health and concluded he was mentally fit to understand evidence and discuss his defence with his lawyers.
“The chamber was satisfied that the accused is able to effectively exercise his fair trial rights in the proceedings,” the court said.
His legal team had previously attempted to get the case thrown out on medical grounds, arguing that serious memory loss had left him unable to absorb new information or reliably recall the past.
The trial is scheduled to open on November 30.
Duterte, who served as president from 2016 to 2022, was arrested in the Philippines in March 2025 and sent to the ICC’s headquarters in The Hague following a lengthy ICC investigation.
Last month, he appeared in person for the first time at the ICC.
Duterte denies the charges against him, saying he only ordered police to act in self-defence as part of his anti-drugs offensive. Judges also denied a request for him to be released from custody.
Estimates of the death toll in the crackdown on drugs during his presidential term vary, from the more than 6,000 reported by the national police to up to 30,000 claimed by human rights groups.
Prosecutors say that police and government hit squads carried out dozens of killings at his orders, motivated by the promise of money or to avoid becoming targets themselves.
Throughout his presidency, Duterte enjoyed a high approval rating from the public, allowing him to push for his brutal anti-drugs agenda.
He became the first Asian ex-leader to be arrested by the ICC, which prosecutes individuals for the world’s worst crimes, such as war crimes and crimes against humanity.

France ready to help defend Saudi oil infrastructure in 'strictly defensive manner': Paris
Unknown

France is willing to help protect Saudi Arabia's energy infrastructure in a “strictly defensive” capacity, the country’s foreign ministry has said amid heightened regional security tensions.
“We assure Saudi Arabia of our full solidarity in the face of these attacks,” a ministry spokesperson said on Thursday.
The spokesperson said France was willing to participate in protecting energy infrastructure, particularly facilities in Yanbu and the East-West pipeline.
“Our willingness to participate, in a strictly defensive manner, in the protection of energy infrastructure, particularly Yanbu and the East-West pipeline in Saudi Arabia,” the spokesperson said.
The remarks came after Houthis in Yemen on Monday warned airlines that Saudi airspace could become a “theatre of military operations.”
Saudi Arabia reported three deaths on Wednesday in attacks targeting its airports, including one in the capital Riyadh.
“We have very firmly condemned all these attacks by the Houthis, which must stop, particularly the latest attacks you mentioned yesterday,” the spokesperson said.
On the Strait of Hormuz, the ministry said the international community had a collective interest in restoring maritime traffic and upholding international law.
“We, the international community, have a collective interest in strictly upholding international law [...] to restore the flow of maritime traffic along the Strait of Hormuz,” the spokesperson said.
France is also participating in the EU's Aspides maritime security operation in the region, the spokesperson said, without disclosing the French assets involved.
“France is participating, with assets that it is not for me to comment on, in the Aspides operation,” the spokesperson said.
The spokesperson said France had supported the mission since its launch in February 2024 and would continue to support its implementation and any possible evolution depending on regional security conditions.

In memoriam Denis O’Brien (1936-2026)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:05:20 UTC
04:05:20 KST

Denis O’Brien, scomparso pochi giorni nel suo castello in Francia (era nato nel 1936), è stato una delle figure più luminose negli studi nella storia della filosofia antica della seconda metà del XX secolo e dei primi decenni del XXI, cui ha dedicato studi fondamentali e originali. Formatosi al Trinity College di Cambridge con W. K. C. Guthrie, quindi Fellow del Gonville and Caius College della stessa Università, poi ricercatore e direttore di ricerca nel CNRS in Francia, prima presso il Centre Léon Robin, in seguito, fino al pensionamento, nel Centre Jean Pépin, ha scritto opere decisive su Empedocle (Empedocles’ cosmic cycle. A reconstruction from the fragments and secondary sources, Cambridge University Press, Cambridge 1969, riedito nel 2009; Pour interpréter Empédocle, Les Belles Lettres, Paris; Brill, Leiden 1981), su Parmenide (Études sur Parménide, publiées sous la direction de P. Aubenque, Tome I: Le poème de Parménide. Texte, traduction, essai critique par D. O’ Brien, Vrin, Paris 1988), Platone (Le non-être. Deux études sur le ‘Sophiste’ de Platon, Academia Verlag, Sankt Augustin 1995), Plotino (Plotinus on the origin of matter. An exercise in the interpretation of the ‘Enneads’, Bibliopolis, Napoli 1991; Théodicée plotinienne, théodicée gnostique, Brill, Leiden 1993) e sulle teorie fisiche antiche (Theories of weight in the ancient world. Four essays on Democritus, Plato and Aristotle. A study in the development of ideas, 4 voll., Les Belles Lettres, Paris; Brill, Leiden 1981 ss.), oltre a numerosissimi saggi e articoli in volumi e riviste (si veda https://independent.academia.edu/DenisOBrien3).
Non è questo il contesto adatto per ripercorrere l’influenza e i risultati di questi studi essenziali; ricorderò però che a Denis O’Brien è capitato il caso, più unico che raro, di vedere confermata la sua interpretazione di Empedocle, almeno nei suoi termini generali, dal ritrovamento di alcuni versi precedentemente ignoti del poema empedocleo (il celeberrimo Empedocle di Strasburgo). Non si tratta di una soddisfazione da poco. Ma l’insieme dei suoi scritti, spesso polemici nei confronti delle posizioni di altri commentatori, del passato e del presente, testimonia di un’attività di ricerca instancabile e inflessibile, rigorosa e coerente, sempre spinta dall’esigenza della verità e non della semplice φιλονικία. Molto della sua vita di studioso si potrà trovare nella splendida Apologia pro vita sua che O’Brien ha composto e inserito in apertura del volume a lui dedicato Agonistes. Essays in honour of Denis O’Brien, edited by J. Dillon and M. Dixsaut, Ashgate 2005.
Nella mia mente resta oggi come ricordo indissolubile degli anni ’90 del Novecento una grande aula alla Sorbona, nei locali dell’Università di Parigi 1, con Monique Dixsaut e Denis O’Brien a dirigere dalla cattedra importanti seminari internazionali, sempre affollatissimi, con ospiti di prestigio, argomenti difficili, molte domande e interminabili discussioni (quasi sempre presenti, in quelle occasioni, gli amici Pierre-Marie Morel e Dimitri El Murr): Monique Dixsaut con una sigaretta in mano, il braccio disteso in basso; Denis O’Brien con un sorriso perennemente ironico, pronto e reattivo a ogni stimolo intellettuale. Lo spirito e il desiderio più autentico della ricerca della verità, l’attenzione instancabile alla ricostruzione filologica e alla comprensione filosofica dei testi, l’esigenza inflessibile dell’esame degli argomenti dei filosofi, considerati in sé e nel loro contesto, la finissima sensibilità storica e l’acutezza dello storico delle idee – sono tutte caratteristiche che hanno animato il suo magistero, come sanno bene tutti coloro che hanno avuto la fortuna di frequentarlo e di seguirne l’insegnamento. A tutto ciò si accompagnavano alcune doti umane rare che caratterizzavano in modo specifico e unico la sua personalità: l’ironia, sempre intelligente e rispettosa degli altri, la generosità intellettuale, che ne faceva un interlocutore prezioso e non comune, la curiosità, che è tratto distintivo degli esseri intelligenti.
Gli studi di filosofia antica perdono un protagonista assoluto; ma coloro che lo hanno conosciuto e amato, che da lui hanno imparato, che con lui hanno avuto la fortuna di discutere, potranno misurare la grandezza di questa perdita nell’intimità della propria coscienza.
Francesco Fronterotta

A Raid on a Gay Bar Risks Taiwan’s LGBTQ-Friendly Reputation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:01:00 UTC
04:01:00 KST

A patron at a well-known gay bar in Taipei recalls being “extremely shocked and confused” when around 30 police staged a dramatic raid on October 3 and took dozens of people away for questioning.
The raid occurred just four weeks before Taipei’s annual Pride celebration. Footage of officers using demeaning language and what attorneys have described as unlawful treatment spurred an estimated 100 protesters to march on precinct headquarters the next day.
While several officers have been disciplined, LGBTQ+ advocates say the issue goes beyond the actions of a few. They are calling for structural changes to protect the rights of sexual minorities in a city that has come to be known for tolerance.
“This incident exposes a serious gap. A city can celebrate LGBTQ+ communities publicly but still not ensure everyone is treated equally by institutions like the police,” Sean Du, secretary-general of the Taiwan Tongzhi Hotline Association, Taiwan’s largest LGBTQ+ advocacy group, said.
Taiwan has built a reputation as one of Asia’s most LGBTQ+-friendly societies in the decades since the police crackdowns and harassment of the martial law era that ended in 1987.
Taiwan became the first in Asia to legalize same-sex marriage in 2019. For queer travelers from countries in the region where same-sex relations are stigmatized or even criminalized, Taipei has become something of a liberal bastion. The island also boasts Asia’s largest Pride parade, held annually on the last Saturday of October, with an estimated 150,000 attending last year.
The Raid
The raid targeted Commander D, a 14-year-old BDSM-themed club in Wanhua District’s Ximending area. Wanhua Precinct police said they had received 13 complaints about Commander D from members of the public between January 1 and Saturday, October 3.
Police visits are not unusual at Taipei clubs; officers typically check IDs before heading on their way. But this time officers came armed with a search warrant approved by the Taipei District Court.
Lin, 34, a clinical psychologist and founder of the independent Threads publication Taipei Rainbow Party Weekly, said he had witnessed numerous nightclub inspections before but that Saturday’s was a “fundamentally different” encounter, one that left some of his friends traumatized.
More than 30 police, including uniformed and plainclothes officers, flooded Commander D at around 4:30 p.m., stopping the music and turning on the lights, Lin said. Videos shared on social media by others showed officers ordering customers to squat down and put away their phones.
Police told the media they had found used condoms and that some customers were nude. Those not wearing clothes were not allowed to put them back on, while those who had hastily gotten dressed were made to remove their clothes to preserve evidence, Lin recounted.
Of the 58 customers police say were inside, around two-thirds were shirtless and most of the rest in their underwear. Only a few were completely naked, Lin said.
Police did not initially display the warrant to those gathered, witnesses said. A video shared on social media shows police repeatedly ordering customers to stop talking, telling them to challenge the operation in court.
Officers also mocked a man for being in a wheelchair, questioning whether he was able to have sex. When a manager came to the man’s defense, he was handcuffed and made to kneel on the floor, local media cited eyewitnesses as saying.
Patrons had their belongings searched and were subjected to a urine test for drugs. After several hours, 51 people were loaded into police vehicles and taken to the precinct for further questioning as “witnesses.”
Commander D did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Did Police Overstep Their Authority?
Several police actions that day were legally problematic, according to Lingwei Li, founder and managing lawyer at Zenkuan Law Firm and founder of the Taiwan Nonbinary Queer Sluts, Taiwan’s first support group for nonbinary people.
A warrant to search the premises does not automatically entitle police to search every customer’s property, and individual searches require separate criteria or consent, Li said.
Compulsory drug tests, meanwhile, should be limited to persons placed under arrest, not witnesses. Li told The Diplomat they were not aware of any legal basis for barring witnesses from using their phones.
Police also blurred the line between a witness and a suspect, Li said. A witness cannot simply be detained unless they fail to appear without good reason after being formally summoned to testify and a warrant has then been issued.
Addressing the question of nudity, Li said the Social Order Maintenance Act requires more than mere nudity to qualify as an offense, including conduct that offends public decency and continues despite a warning. “This case involves an abuse of police authority,” Li said. “Evidence indicates that the police prohibited the nude individual from putting on clothes, which also contradicts the requirement of ‘failing to heed warnings.’”
“Ordering people who were already dressed to undress is not preserving evidence. It’s humiliation.”
Officers Disciplined
Wanhua Precinct’s investigation found four officers had used inappropriate language. “They have been dealt with strictly,” the precinct told The Diplomat. Each received two reprimands. The official who supervised the operation received a demerit, while the precinct chief himself was issued two reprimands after voluntarily requesting disciplinary action.
“The precinct respects diverse communities and will undertake a thorough review of officers’ on-site enforcement procedures,” the statement said. “It will comprehensively strengthen education and training and require officers, when carrying out their duties in the future, to continue to respect the cultures of a diverse society, in order to safeguard residents’ rights and interests and prevent similar controversies from occurring again.”
No charges have been filed yet in connection with the raid. In a separate statement, police said Commander D’s owner, surnamed Zhong, 44, was referred to the Taipei District Prosecutors’ Office on suspicion of violating public decency, according to a press statement viewed by the Central News Agency.
Commander D had been in the news before. During a September 11 session at the Taipei City Council, Councilor Hung Chien-yi repeated a parent’s claim that minors were entering bars and displayed photos of a venue media identified as Commander D.
The club denied these claims and insisted its staff check IDs before allowing patrons to enter. It’s not clear if those allegations were related to the raid last week.
On October 7, a civil society group filed a criminal complaint with the Taipei District Prosecutors’ Office over alleged police misconduct during the raid, the precinct told the Diplomat. The police said the matter was now subject to investigative confidentiality.
In remarks to the press on October 4, Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an said an investigation should follow any suspected misconduct but stopped short of criticizing the Commander D search. After more footage of the operation emerged, Chiang issued an apology and said all Taipei residents are entitled to equal rights. He said he had instructed the police department to improve force discipline to prevent discrimination in the future.
Chiang’s office had not responded to a request for comment by publication time.
Discrimination
Du, the secretary general of Taiwan Tongzhi Hotline Association, believes there was “concrete discrimination” on display on October 3. “And there are sufficient grounds to investigate whether an LGBTQ+ venue was subjected to differential policing,” he told The Diplomat.
The precinct’s acknowledgment is just one step, he said. “We need to look at whether the venue’s gay and BDSM character contributed to it being presumed criminal. Would a comparable non-LGBTQ+ venue face police action with the same frequency and scale? Was it necessary to take dozens of patrons away?”
Du called for an independent investigation, arguing discrimination often goes beyond individual officers’ conduct. “We aren’t claiming every officer had an anti-LGBTQ+ motive. Discrimination also involves assumptions and unequal standards and treatment.”
The Commander D episode recalls a police investigation into Body Fresh, an LGBTQ+ venue in the city of Taichung, that subsequently closed following allegations that it was facilitating commercial sex. Advocates argued authorities had singled out the business while heterosexual-oriented venues avoided similar scrutiny.
“The similarities are frustratingly striking, and traumatizing to many in the community,” said Li, the Zenkuan Law Firm attorney. “In both cases, morality charges were applied to consensual adult conduct in a space serving LGBTQ+ people. Complaints and political pressure, not an identifiable victim, led to enforcement,” they added.
Lin, one of the eyewitnesses, believes the raid has injected energy into the upcoming Pride. “Taipei is, in fact, still friendly and still inclusive. Although society still needs some time to digest what happened in this incident, the social mobilization that followed was faster and more diverse than before,” he said.

Canadians ‘worried’ about US travel as Trump’s policies make travelers feel unwelcome: Former premier

Fahri Aksüt
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
US President Donald Trump’s immigration and border policies make Canadians uneasy about traveling to the US for the first time, a concern reflected in tourism figures, former Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said.
Trudeau, speaking at the opening session on Friday of the World Travel & Tourism Council’s (WTTC) 26th Global Summit held in the Maltese capital of Valletta, stated that for the first time, many Canadians are “worried” about crossing the border.
“In the past number of years, the US hasn’t been very good at making travelers feel welcome, whether it’s the thickening of the borders, the worries about what can happen if you get arrested at the border,” he said. “Because, for decades, generations, Canadians and Americans criss-crossing our shared border, the longest unmilitarized border in the world, has been something we almost took for granted, and the family, personal, and business connections have been huge and strong.”
Trudeau stated that the real issue is Washington’s attitude towards Canada, particularly “this disrespect that the president has shown, in terms of saying it’s not a real country.”
“I think, first of all, (it’s important to) understand that some governments get along, some governments don't get along, and that's the reality,” he said. “Looking at what, how people are feeling — like, even when we were facing difficulties with the United States, we didn't impose penalties or raise prices or make it more difficult for people to travel to the United States, for example.”
The former prime minister noted that the number of Canadians traveling to the US declined by more than 20% and that, to compensate, American tour operators, airlines, and hotels lowered their prices, but to no avail in changing Canadians' travel preferences.
“At places like Florida, Arizona, even nearby places like Maine or elsewhere, (they’re) coming to tell Canadians, ‘it’s okay, we still like you, Please come back’ — we know Canadians still like Americans, Americans still like Canadians, but conflict between governments and disrespect from the US government has caused Canadians to say, ‘Okay, let's look at other places to go,’ and that has been a really important shift, but also a telling one, that how the mood of a country, how people are made to feel welcome, is an extremely important part of tourism,” he said.
He recalled that early bookings for the North American World Cup were affected because travelers felt hesitant about entering the US.
“Now, the US actually was very successful in welcoming lots of people from around the world who had a wonderful experience discovering North America, discovering how wonderful and nice Americans are. But at the same time, in the run-up to the World Cup, we saw that bookings were down, we saw people worried about going to the United States, not sure if they wanted to go to the United States, and there was a point at which people were worrying that it might not be a huge success. It ended up being a success, but countries need to be a little more consistent. If they want tourism dollars, they have to show themselves as being open to the world, which is something that Canada always did well,” he added.

The Great Healthcare Cost Hike Is Here
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
18:59:22 UTC
03:59:22 KST

American healthcare, the priciest healthcare system in the world, is set to get even more expensive
In the coming weeks, the roughly 160 million Americans who get health insurance through work will log into their benefits portals and pick a plan for 2027. Even for people used to rising healthcare costs, what they see may come as a shock. Employer health plan costs are projected to rise 8 to 10% next year, the largest increase in more than 20 years and double the average increase of the 2010s.
This spike is just the second in a series of three successive shocks to healthcare costs and coverage. The first came in January 2026, when the 24.3 million ACA Marketplace enrollees saw their after-subsidy premiums rise by an average of 114%. The second is the sharp increase in premiums and out-of-pocket costs for those who get insurance at work, the third year in a row of elevated increases. The third comes next January, when Medicaid work-reporting requirements take effect, which CBO projects will eventually push nearly 6 million people out of coverage.
History suggests that the American political system makes a bold attempt to reform healthcare about once a generation. President Harry Truman fought for national health insurance in 1945. President Lyndon B. Johnson signed Medicare and Medicaid into law in 1965. President Bill Clinton pushed for reform in 1994. And President Barack Obama passed the Affordable Care Act in 2010. With healthcare costs already among voters' top concerns, these shocks may create the next generational window for reform.
In the meantime, here’s how the looming healthcare hike will impact insurance costs, wherever you get your coverage.
If you buy your own insurance
The enhanced premium tax credits were first passed in the 2021 American Rescue Plan Act pandemic relief bill, then extended in the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act. They expired on December 31, 2025, after Congress declined to renew them in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA).
KFF estimates this decision raised after-subsidy premiums by 114%, or about $1,000 a year. In response, some people left the market and enrollment fell 12%, from 21.8 million to 19.2 million. New Mexico, the one state that replaced the federal subsidies with its own money, was the only state where enrollment grew. Others traded down to skimpier plans, but still are paying more. The share of enrollees in the least generous bronze plans went from 30% to 40%, and the average deductible rose by more than $1,000 to $3,786.
Even after all that switching and leaving, the average premium paid by people on the Marketplaces hit $178 a month in 2026, 58% higher than in 2025 and above the $164 people paid in 2021, the last year before the enhanced credits. Those who left were healthier than those who stayed, so insurers have proposed another 15% increase for 2027, stacked on top of this year’s 20%
If you get insurance through work
About 160 million Americans get health insurance through an employer. Most employers hold open enrollment for two or three weeks starting in October or November, for the plan year beginning Jan. 1.
The best data we have on 2027 costs comes from the large benefits consulting firms. They project total costs will rise 8 to 10% next year, the largest increase since 2003 and double the average increase of the 2010s. These firms point to more use of care, expensive new drugs, GLP-1s, hospital consolidation, and AI-assisted billing. For a typical worker, an increase that size works out to roughly $400 to $500 more next year.
And these totals understate the full cost increase, since many employers have made plans less generous to hold costs down. One common change is to raise deductibles, which shifts costs onto workers. Another is to cut back on what's covered. The share of large employers covering GLP-1s for obesity, for example, has fallen from 72% to 60%. Remove those changes, and the consulting firms estimate costs would have climbed another one to three percentage points.
If you’re on Medicaid
The third shock is to the Medicaid program. Starting January 1, 2027, OBBBA requires the 44 states (including Washington, D.C.) that expanded Medicaid to require adults covered by the expansion to document 80 hours a month of work, school, or community service. The CBO estimates that the requirement will push about 5.7 million people off Medicaid by 2034, leaving 5.3 million more people uninsured.
Most of those people should not lose coverage. The evidence suggests they will meet the criteria and lose coverage anyway because of the paperwork burden. When Arkansas imposed a work requirement in 2018, employment did not change. Instead, more than 18,000 people lost coverage within seven months, even though 95% either met the requirement or qualified for an exemption.
The work requirement is not the only Medicaid cut. OBBBA also requires eligibility checks every six months instead of once a year, shortens retroactive coverage, and limits the provider taxes states use to fund their share of the program. Counting those provisions, CBO projects 7.5 million more people will be uninsured by 2034
All of this means we are in the middle of the great healthcare cost hike. In January, after-subsidy premiums on the Marketplaces rose 114%. This fall, we expect the 160 million people who get insurance at work will see the largest increase in a generation. Next January, work-reporting requirements will start pushing millions of people off Medicaid. These shocks will strain family budgets.
They will also create a generational opportunity for reform. The best thing we can do is seize it.

After botched US execution, Christa Pike walking, mentally ‘foggy’, says lawyer

- - Pike was given two lethal pentobarbital doses on Sept 30 and was later due to have life support removed, but she woke up and started talking on Oct 6.
- - Her lawyers want Governor Bill Lee to commute her sentence, while Tennessee has paused executions and ordered evidence from the failed execution to be preserved.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - The convicted US killer who survived a botched execution was walking around her hospital room though she was mentally “foggy,” her lawyer said in an interview broadcast on Oct 8.
Christa Pike, 50, had been considered braindead following two lethal doses of the drug pentobarbital on Sept 30 that failed to kill her.
Doctors had been planning to remove life support on Oct 6 when she unexpectedly woke up and started talking, her lawyers have said.
“She is up and walking for the first time today, but just around the room, you know, not very far,” lawyer Stephen Ferrell told the BBC.
“She’s also somewhat foggy. She can lose her train of thought really easily, and forgets where she’s going.”
“There could be some permanent damage. We don’t know that yet,” said Ferrell, who has not personally seen Pike or spoken with her, but is getting updates from colleagues who have.
Pike was sentenced to death in the state of Tennessee for murdering a classmate, a crime committed when she was a teenager.
Since the botched execution, her lawyers have repeatedly called on Governor Bill Lee to commute her sentence to life in prison.
Lee has suspended executions in Tennessee pending an independent investigation.
‘Uncharted waters’
Whether the state will eventually attempt to execute Pike again was not known.
“We are very much in uncharted waters,” Ferrell said.
Pike is the only inmate to ever survive after being injected with lethal doses of execution drugs, according to the Death Penalty Information Centre (DPI).
Other cases of botched executions in the United States were because the procedure did not go according to plan though those inmates ultimately died, according to DPI.
There were seven executions that were halted when personnel were unable to set IV lines for the lethal injection.
On Oct 7, a court ordered Tennessee corrections officials to preserve all evidence related to Pike’s botched execution including medical supplies, waste, and audio and video recordings.
Excluding Pike’s case, there have been 30 executions in the United States this year, all by lethal injection.
The most recent was that of Jamaal Howard, who was put to death in Texas on Oct 7 for killing a store clerk during a 2000 robbery.
The death penalty has been abolished in 23 of the 50 US states, while three others – California, Oregon and Pennsylvania – have moratoriums in place.
The Pentagon said this week that President Donald Trump has approved the execution of Nidal Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist who shot dead 13 people and wounded more than two dozen at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009.
Hasan’s execution by firing squad, set for Dec 3, would be the first carried out by the US military since 1961. AFP

Netanyahu’s ex-military secretary says PM’s office falsified Oct. 7 records
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
18:58:11 UTC
03:58:11 KST

Maj. Gen. (res.) Avi Gil, who served as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s military secretary before and during the October 7 attack, said Thursday that a stenographer in the Prime Minister’s Office told him she had been instructed to change the recorded time of a key phone call on the morning of the massacre, an act he described as “falsification.”
Gil told Channel 12 that, in January 2024, the stenographer entered his office and said she had been ordered by the prime minister’s chief of staff to change the time of a four-minute call from 6:40 a.m. to 6:29 a.m. “She told me, ‘I’m not allowed to change it. The computer shows and says 6:40 to 6:44,’” Gil said. “Those are facts, and there is no dispute about them.” He said he immediately documented the account in a handwritten note to the attorney general and recommended that any future commission of inquiry demand the original recordings rather than relying solely on transcripts. Earlier reporting by ynet had detailed suspicions surrounding an effort to change the time of the call.
“The first thing I asked myself was why anyone was dealing with the transcript of a four-minute conversation on the morning of October 7,” Gil said. “Who cared about it, and what was in that conversation that made it important?” He added that, in his view, “someone was dealing with certain narratives” months after the attack. “This is changing a transcript, changing the truth. Factually, there was an instruction to change the time of a call.”
Gil also said that before October 7 security officials had periodically recommended targeted operations in Gaza that the political leadership chose not to approve. “There were recommendations from time to time to carry out targeted operations in Gaza. Those recommendations were not accepted,” he said. “I’m talking about the facts, and the leadership has broader considerations. There were actions that were recommended and not approved, and I stand behind what I’m saying.”
The former military secretary also confirmed an earlier report that then-Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar had delivered a warning to Netanyahu in July 2023 that Israel was facing the danger of war. According to the warning previously reported by Yedioth Ahronoth, Bar told Netanyahu: “I am giving you a warning of war today. I cannot give you an exact day and hour, but this is the warning.” Gil stressed, however, that it was not a specific warning of an impending attack from Gaza. “Was there a specific, focused warning from Gaza? Absolutely not,” he said. Bar has separately said he instructed that Gil be updated at 5:15 a.m. on October 7, although Netanyahu’s first documented conversation with Gil came at 6:29 a.m.
Gil said he received a call from the Shin Bet chief’s office at 6:12 a.m. that morning and was told of suspicious signs in Gaza, including unusual SIM card activity and movement underground, alongside indicators that appeared to reduce the urgency because similar behavior had previously occurred during Hamas exercises. He said the Shin Bet planned further assessments and had ordered an operational team south as a precaution. “While we were talking, the many alerts began at 6:29 a.m.,” he said.
Looking back at the preceding night, Gil rejected the idea that Netanyahu would ordinarily have been awakened based on the intelligence picture then available. He said the intelligence officer who saw the overnight message understood that the word “routine” appeared repeatedly and that there was no indication of immediate urgency. 
“Cases in which a prime minister, in a phone call, decides against all the heads of the security establishment are rare, if they exist at all,” Gil said. “The chief of staff and the head of the Shin Bet do not call the prime minister directly. That is what the military secretary is for. There is one address.”
Gil was also asked about reports that Netanyahu may have received warnings from Egypt or the United Arab Emirates before the massacre. He said he was not in the office on the dates associated with the reported Emirati meeting and therefore could not say what occurred. But he pointed to recent reports of an Egyptian aircraft arriving in Israel and departing shortly afterward. “A plane like that does not come for a training sortie,” he said, while stressing that he did not know who, if anyone, had met its passengers.

South Africa vs Australia Test series, everything you need to know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
18:54:40 UTC
03:54:40 KST

Australia is back in South Africa for one of the most eagerly anticipated Test series in recent history.
It has been eight long years since Australia last toured South Africa in red-ball cricket, in a series that will forever be remembered for its ignominy.
Sandpapergate is what that contest will be remembered for, but even before that, it was crossing a red line in despicable behaviour unbecoming of the sport.
Here's everything you need to know ahead of the three-Test series.
When are the Test matches?
The two teams will play three Tests.
The first is at Kingsmead in Durban from October 9 to 13.
The second is at St George's Park in Gqeberha from October 18 to 22.
And Newlands in Cape Town will host the third from October 27 to 31.
What time are the Test matches?
The Durban Test starts at 6:30pm AEDT and will likely run through to 2am AEDT.
That AEDT time relates to New South Wales, the ACT, Victoria and Tasmania.
In Queensland, the action begins at 5:30pm.
In South Australia, at 6pm.
In the Northern Territory, at 5pm.
And the first ball will be bowled at 3:30pm in Western Australia.
How can I watch the Test series?
The entire series is live on Fox Sports and Kayo.
ABC Sport will also have live radio commentary on the ABC Listen App or online.
You can also follow every ball in our live blog on the ABC Sport website.
Who is playing in the series?
Australia's squad: Pat Cummins (c), Scott Boland, Alex Carey (wk), Cooper Connolly, Cameron Green, Sam Harper (wk), Josh Hazlewood, Travis Head, Matthew Kuhnemann, Marnus Labuschagne, Nathan Lyon, Nic Maddinson, Michael Neser, Matt Renshaw, Steven Smith, Mitchell Starc, Beau Webster.
South Africa's squad: Temba Bavuma (c), Marques Ackerman, David Bedingham, Corbin Bosch, Gerald Coetzee, Tony de Zorzi, Simon Harmer, Marco Jansen, Keshav Maharaj, Aiden Markram, Wiaan Mulder, Senuran Muthusamy, Anrich Nortje, Dane Paterson, Kagiso Rabada, Ryan Rickelton (wk), Tristan Stubbs (wk), Kyle Verreynne (wk).
Australia's record against South Africa
Australia has won 54 of the 102 Test matches between the two teams, with 21 draws and 27 defeats since their first meeting in 1902.
On South African soil, Australia also has a winning record, with 29 victories against 16 defeats and nine draws.
Australia has won six of the 11 Tests played at St George's in Durban, including winning each of the last three Tests it has played there, while South Africa has won three with two draws.
The two teams also drew a Test at the city's old Lord's ground in 1921, before the venue's demolition in 1922.
South Africa has a much better record at St George's Park in Gqeberha though, winning four of the seven matches played there, including the last two.
Before 2021, Gqeberha was Port Elizabeth, but is now known by its Xhosa name, and this is the first time Australia will play in the city under its new name.
Australia has a great record at Newlands though, winning 10 of the 14 Tests played in the shadow of Table Mountain. However, it has only won one of its last four Tests at the ground considered one of the most beautiful in the world.
The two teams last played a Test in June 2025, when South Africa shocked Australia at Lord's to win the World Test Championship.
In the 2022/23 summer of cricket, Australia claimed a 2-0 Test series victory over South Africa on home soil.
The last time Australia played a Test series in South Africa was 2018, and it's safe to say things were … complicated.
The fiery 2018 series
It is fair to say the 2018 series was combative, fiery, febrile and chaotic.
Australia won the first Test at Kingsmead in Durban, but not before David Warner and Quinton de Kock almost came to blows in a stairwell at the end of the fourth day.
South Africa won the second Test in Gqeberha, but man of the match Kagiso Rabada, who took 5/96 and 6/54, was subsequently banned for barging into Steve Smith after dismissing him in the first innings.
Rabada was then handed a reprieve after an appeal involving one of South Africa's highest-profile lawyers, freeing him to play the next two matches.
The third Test was in Cape Town where, in the shadows of Table Mountain, Australia's descent into the dark arts was exposed.
On the third day, host broadcaster Supersport captured Cameron Bancroft rubbing the ball with a square of sandpaper to help encourage the prodigious reverse swing that had featured throughout the series thus far.
While South Africa romped to a 322-run win and a series lead, the full extent of Australia's cheating was exposed, leading to a moral reckoning about the team's approach back home, with then-prime minister Malcolm Turnbull leading the criticism of the offending players.
Smith, Bancroft and Warner were all sent home in disgrace, and an under-manned Australian team was thumped by 492 runs at the Wanderers in Johannesburg.
What's happened since?
Australia has toured South Africa twice since the 2018 Test series, in 2020 and 2023 for limited-overs matches, with Smith and Warner both involved.

In Bordeaux, masked perpetrators set fire to rubbish bins near a police station. The fire spread to the building, and three police officers escaped through an emergency exit.

Details

The fire spread to the rest of the building before it was brought under control; three police officers had to escape the flames through an emergency exit.

Over eighty citizens killed or missing in Russia-Ukraine war: Kenya
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
18:51:14 UTC
03:51:14 KST

Kenya has recorded 84 of its citizens as killed or missing in the Russia-Ukraine war, Foreign Minister Musalia Mudavadi told lawmakers.
Appearing before a joint Senate committee on labour and defence, Mudavadi, who also serves as prime cabinet secretary, said 354 Kenyans have been documented as involved in the conflict.
“The ministry has records of 354 Kenyan nationals involved in the Russian-Ukraine crisis and the record is as follows,” he told senators on Thursday.
“On the front lines, we have indications of 77. In camp, 38. Those who are in unknown locations or unclassified, it's estimated at 52. Those killed or missing in action, 84.”
Mudavadi said 34 Kenyans had been hospitalised, 62 repatriated, five identified as prisoners of war, one detained and another had completed a military contract.
He said some families only approach authorities after losing contact with relatives in Russia, complicating efforts to establish their whereabouts.
“We therefore encourage families to engage with the department as soon as possible,” he said.
Mudavadi said the State Department for Diaspora Affairs collects identification and travel details before referring cases to Kenya's Embassy in Moscow for verification.
Russia halted new recruitment
Mudavadi told lawmakers that his visit to Moscow in March 2026 resulted in Kenya being placed on a Russian military recruitment stop list intended to prevent further enlistment of Kenyan nationals.
“During my official visit to Moscow in March this year, 2026, we secured Kenya's inclusion on Russia's stop list,” he said.
“The Embassy of Kenya in Moscow has since confirmed that no additional Kenyan nationals have been enlisted in the special military operation following the implementation of the stop list.”
Mudavadi said Russian authorities were considering requests to terminate military contracts individually, with decisions resting with military unit commanders.
He also said Russia's defence ministry had declined to cover the cost of returning the remains of deceased Kenyans, leaving Nairobi to negotiate burial, cremation or repatriation arrangements with Russian authorities and affected families.
Kenya is also engaging Ukrainian authorities through its embassy in Vienna, which is accredited to Ukraine, over Kenyan nationals detained during the conflict.
The Senate committee is examining concerns surrounding the recruitment of Kenyans into Russia's military and efforts to locate and bring home those affected by the war.

Katie Lynch wants to see AFL 'harness the momentum' of Pride Round
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
18:50:44 UTC
03:50:44 KST

The Gold Coast Suns' Katie Lynch says Pride Round comes at exactly the moment needed every season.
Two weeks out from the men's season finishing and a month before the women start finals, it provides an injection of enthusiasm, celebration and joy.
"A different energy comes into the competition on Pride Round," Lynch told ABC Sport.
"Because so many of our players connect with the movement and understand the power of the round for the community and who we represent," Lynch told ABC Sport.
However, Lynch would like to see that movement grow beyond the AFLW competition and across the whole AFL, to include not just the men's teams but all club staff and fans of the game.
The dedicated league-wide Pride Round was introduced annually in 2021.
It celebrates inclusion and diversity over two weeks, while honouring the contributions of the LGBTQ+ community to the game and providing a platform for education on queer issues, particularly those entwined with the game.
"I think that can be perhaps transferred across more of the whole code essentially," Lynch said.
"A pride round in the men's would be awesome to see, and I know from my experience, it's nothing but a positive experience, and so I can see that going enormously well and being enormously helpful for the entire code."
Some LGBTQ+ Australian Rules fans and community members have felt the pang of exclusion from the sport in recent years.
In the past three years, there have been 10 cases of AFL-listed players or coaches sanctioned for homophobic language, including Suns players Max Knobel this year and star defender Wil Powell in 2024.
When put to Lynch whether an extended Pride Round would help in this regard, she said the game of Aussie Rules had always been excellent at creating a space for people to connect, converse and interact, and that Pride Round was an incredible vehicle to do that around LGBTQ+ issues and experiences.
"We know that the players and the code have significant ability to influence, of course, and we've seen that probably have a negative effect on our fans more recently," she said.
"So I think for me, it's how do we shift that dial to come back the other way?
"And that's why I talk about things like visibility and representation."
She said it was also a great opportunity to connect more fans to the game, and have them feel seen within it.
This year Lynch helped design the club's Pride guernsey alongside her teammate Lily Mithen and good friend and tattoo artist Mady Peters.
It resembles patchwork tattoos and stickers, including a tramp stamp on the back, which Lynch says is proof they had a lot of fun putting it together.
But more than that, Lynch said it felt special to have her friend Peters "who doesn't even know what a drop punt is" now have an attachment to the game of AFLW through the Pride movement, where she is represented as a queer person.
Lynch said she noticed the boost in attendance during Pride Round, including within her own friend group.
"My friends are great, very supportive of me … but if they're going to come to a game, it's Pride Round," she said.
"Pride Round has the power to bring people, even loose fans of AFL, to the game … and not only to experience the joy of it but they're there because they feel like they belong there."
She wants that "special feeling" to reach even further.
"That's what I've felt, particularly this year, is the support for us and this Pride Round has been enormous, and it's growing," she said.
"The opportunity now is to harness the momentum we've got and use it in a growth capacity.
"We'll probably never know the enormity of pride and visibility, particularly as players … I feel there's so much impact that I don't see, but I know is there."

BLADE’s Hunter WOLF drone heads to Pentagon field trial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
18:43:42 UTC
03:43:42 KST

- BLADE’s Hunter WOLF unmanned ground vehicle advanced to Phase II of the Department of War’s GroundBreaker 1 demonstration at Camp Grafton, North Dakota.
- Live trials run Oct. 19-23, and successful vendors may be invited to propose for a prototype Other Transaction Authority award.
BLADE, the robotics company formerly known as HDT, said its Hunter WOLF unmanned ground vehicle has been selected for the second phase of GroundBreaker 1, a U.S. Department of War demonstration in which service members will put industry-built ground robots through field trials at Camp Grafton, North Dakota, on Oct. 19-23.
The company said Hunter WOLF advanced after government evaluators reviewed the solution brief it submitted in Phase I. During Phase II, evaluators will judge the vehicle’s technology maturity, operational readiness and ability to work with other military systems. Companies whose demonstrations pass that evaluation may be invited to a third phase to submit full proposals for a prototype Other Transaction Authority agreement, a contracting route the Pentagon uses to buy prototypes faster than through standard procurement. BLADE did not say how many vehicles it will bring to Camp Grafton.
GroundBreaker 1 is a joint Department of War effort to speed the military’s adoption of unmanned ground vehicles. The government asked for proposals in August through the Department of War Drone OTA Consortium, and only consortium members were eligible. The solicitation sought complete systems able to handle at least one core mission, including reconnaissance and surveillance, moving supplies and equipment, explosive ordnance disposal and route clearance, search and rescue, perimeter security and casualty evacuation. At Camp Grafton, service members will operate the vehicles in realistic field conditions and give feedback on how easy they are to use and how well they perform. Other companies are also competing; startup Liminal Industries said last month that its DUEL-V vehicle had advanced to Phase II.
“Hunter WOLF was built for exactly this kind of challenge,” said Tom Van Doren, president of the robotics sector at BLADE. “This is a mature, mission-ready platform that has been tested alongside warfighters in demanding environments. GroundBreaker 1 gives us the opportunity to demonstrate why the Hunter WOLF is ready to support the warfighter now.”
The Hunter WOLF is a six-wheeled, diesel-electric hybrid robot that BLADE says can carry 2,800 pounds (1,270 kg) of cargo and supply electrical power to other equipment. It can be driven by remote control or operate autonomously, and it takes modular payloads for logistics, reconnaissance, casualty evacuation and communications relay. The company says the vehicle has been used operationally in Ukraine, along with service in military exercises and training events.
GroundBreaker 1 is the second U.S. military ground robot effort Hunter WOLF has joined in recent weeks. BLADE was one of six companies the U.S. Army selected in August for its Infantry Last Tactical Mile initiative, which is testing robots that resupply troops and evacuate casualties near the front line. The vehicle has also been through a series of U.S. Army evaluations this year, including an August event with the 82nd Airborne Division at Fort Polk, Louisiana, and the company has said it has supported the U.S. Marine Corps and Australian forces.

The Block's contentious new build site has a feral cat problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
18:42:24 UTC
03:42:24 KST

in brief
- Dozens of cats are believed to be living on and around The Block's next build site in Melbourne's north-west.
- Advocates are seeking a pathway to trap, treat and rehome them.
Heritage concerns aren't the only challenge facing The Block's next build, with a population of unowned cats becoming the latest flash point.
Animal welfare advocates have urged the television network behind the reality television series to step up and help rescue the feral felines — dozens of which are believed to be living on and around the site in Sunbury in Melbourne's north-west.
The Nine Network says it is aware of the cats living at Jacksons Hill, which formerly housed an asylum and psychiatric hospital, and is assessing the situation.
The cats are currently cared for by a group of volunteers, who hope to reach an agreement with the local council, Hume City Council, to legally rescue and rehome them.
SBS News has contacted Hume City Council for comment.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Under Victoria's Domestic Animals Act, the management of feral cats — which have a significant impact on wildlife — is typically the responsibility of local councils, unless they are on crown land, like in national parks, where the duty is shared with the state government.
When cats are collected by council pounds or rescue shelters, they muust be held for eight days before they can be rehomed, or if necessary, euthanised.
The holding period for euthanasia doesn't apply to cats that are deemed "wild, uncontrollable or diseased".
State Animal Justice Party MP Georgie Purcell has written to Nine and The Block, calling for a comprehensive welfare plan to coordinate rescue and veterinary support for the cats.
"While The Block isn't responsible for causing this problem, they can be part of the solution, and this is a chance for them to show some goodwill to the community, respect for animals rather than just profiting off development," she said.
"Site clearing, demolition, construction traffic, fencing and the broader transformation of the site will only disturb and displace these cats and make any rescue attempts even harder."
Purcell said at minimum, the show should fund veterinary assessments and provide financial assistance to foster carers for the cats.
Under Victoria's framework, independent rescuers are often left to manage financial, logistical and legal risk, where shelters are unable to take entire colonies.
A spokesperson for Nine said the network was aware of the cats near the site and was "assessing the situation prior to their safe removal" and the start of construction, slated for the new year.
"We intend to keep all relevant stakeholders engaged throughout this process," the spokesperson said.
Volunteer rescuers want a clear legal pathway to manage established cat colonies to enable humane trapping, veterinary treatment including desexing and rehoming, without people having to bear the risks.
The Cat Protection Society of Victoria, which is not aware of this particular colony but rehomes around 600 to 700 stray cats a year, said doing this sort of work requires significant help from volunteers.
"Most strays also require behavioural work, some quite substantial. We're very fortunate to be supported by a cat-loving community who provide volunteer hours and financial assistance," the society's operations manager Alison Thompson said.
The upcoming Block season has already faced backlash from the local community over concerns about the site's historical significance.
In 1864, the site, then known as Caloola, opened as an industrial school, according to the Victorian Heritage Register. Over the next century, it was redeveloped as an asylum, then a psychiatric hospital, and later as a training centre for people with disabilities.
Victoria University was given some of the site in 1944, but stopped using it as a campus in 2009. The Victorian goverment bought the site in 2018 to "return most of it to community use", according to the state's transport and planning department.
An application for adaptive re-use and conservation to create six private residences, adding swimming pools and undercover parking has been lodged with Heritage Victoria. The regulator has extended submissions for community engagement.
