Over 130 children remain in mandatory evacuation zone in de-occupied part of Kherson region
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
18:42:00 UTC
03:42:00 KST

Over 130 children remain in mandatory evacuation zone in de-occupied part of Kherson region
Elvina Osmanova, head of the Kherson Regional Military Administration's Department of Internal and Information Policy, said this in a comment to Ukrinform.
"Due to the difficult security situation, mandatory evacuation of residents and a ban on entry for families with children have been introduced in some settlements of the Kherson, Beryslav and Kakhovka districts. Currently, 132 children remain in the mandatory evacuation zone," Osmanova said.
Specifically, two children remain in the Mylivka community, while 14 children have been evacuated; 125 children remain in the Kherson community, while 540 have been evacuated; two children remain in the city of Beryslav, and three in the village of Stanislav.
According to Osmanova, courts have ruled that the children remaining in Beryslav and Stanislav should be removed from their families without terminating parental rights, as their parents refused to evacuate. However, the children have not yet been evacuated due to the difficult security situation.
"Evacuation is complicated by mined routes, the threat of Russian drone strikes and artillery shelling. Each such operation requires special caution and careful coordination," she said.
Osmanova stressed that despite the danger, the evacuation is continuing. The main task is to evacuate people from areas under fire and save their lives, with the safety of children being the top priority. She stressed that the evacuation of children remains under the constant supervision of the Kherson Regional Military Administration.
As reported, more than half a tonne of food was delivered by drones to frontline Beryslav in the Kherson region, where about 300 civilians, including two children, still remain.

South Africa: Anti-migrant protests turn violent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
18:42:00 UTC
03:42:00 KST

South Africa pulls asylum directive after violent protests
Published October 8, 2026last updated October 9, 2026
South Africa has halted a new directive for the processing of asylum applications after violent protests broke out in Johannesburg and Durban.
The directive was issued by the Department of Home Affairs in response to a court judgment.
The court had ruled that asylum seekers could not be denied access to South Africa's asylum system solely on procedural grounds, such as entering the country illegally.
Offices for asylum seekers were quickly overwhelmed, and that placed officers at serious risk, the Department of Home Affairs said.
That's because the court ruling led to days of protests in the major coastal city of Durban, which then spread to Johannesburg's Soweto township on Thursday.
Rioters torched 14 cars in Durban and 10 in Soweto. Shops were looted in both locations.
What else do we know about protests in South Africa?
The unrest in Durban followed a protest by a group demanding that a refugee center stop processing asylum applications. Vehicles were overturned and set on fire. Foreign-owned shops were also looted.
Meanwhile, in Soweto, residents clashed with foreign shop owners, and gunshots were heard, according to the broadcaster Newzroom Afrika.
"It's reported that there were clashes between foreign nationals in the area and South African nationals," Johannesburg Metropolitan Police Department spokesman Superintendent Xolani Fihla in an interview with SABC television. "At the present moment, I can confirm that no injuries have been reported."
What is the court ruling that sparked protests?
The court ruling that sparked the flare-up of xenophobic tensions deemed certain provisions of the government's refugee policy to be unconstitutional.
Recently, this ruling has led hundreds of people, reportedly including those who do not qualify for asylum, to flock to government refugee centers.
On Wednesday, the government emphasized that the judgement "does not grant refugee status or permanent residence automatically to anyone who enters South Africa."
Xenophobic sentiment in South Africa: What to know
South Africa has experienced months of anti-immigrant protests this year. Populist and anti-immigrant groups have demanded that undocumented foreign nationals leave by June 30.
Amid international criticism, tens of thousands of people have fled the country, while some were repatriated by their governments.
Although South Africa has a third of its population unemployed, it remains the largest economy in Africa and continues to attract migrants.
Migrants are often blamed for taking jobs, fueling crime, and straining public services. However, social scientists have said these accusations are not supported by evidence.
Edited by: Sean Sinico and Roshni Majumdar

Trump awards top US science, technology medals to Musk, 5 tech executives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
18:40:52 UTC
03:40:52 KST

Rabia Iclal Turan
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
US President Donald Trump on Thursday awarded the nation’s highest science and technology honors to six tech executives, including Elon Musk.
At the New Golden Age Summit at the Institute of Peace in Washington, DC, Trump presented the National Medal of Science to Musk of SpaceX, Google co-founder Sergey Brin, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and AMD CEO Lisa Su.
Dell Technologies founder Michael Dell and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella received the National Medal of Technology and Innovation.
“Few Americans in history have done more to advance America’s national interest than Elon,” said Trump, calling Musk “our modern-day Thomas Edison.”
“The entire world is now running on Nvidia,” he said about Huang’s company.
“With the help of the brilliant men and women here today, we will always be on top. There is nobody that can compete with us, nobody,” he said. “From day one, my administration has taken decisive action to ensure that America continues to dominate the frontiers of science and technology.”
Trump said he signed an order on quantum computing and “set the goal of delivering a quantum computer for scientific discovery by 2028.”
He said his administration created the Genesis Mission “to solve some of the biggest mysteries in science and technology with superintelligence.”
“Last week we brokered the White House accord on superintelligence, keeping America at the forefront,” he said.

5 Palestinians killed, over dozen injured in Israeli attacks across Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
18:40:48 UTC
03:40:48 KST

Laith Al-jnaidi and Sahin Demir
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
At least five Palestinians, including a woman, were killed and more than a dozen others injured in Israeli attacks across the Gaza Strip on Thursday, according to medical sources and witnesses.
The attacks targeted the Tel al-Hawa neighborhood and the Al-Tawam and Amer Project areas in Gaza City, the Al-Sudaniya area in the northwest, as well as Al-Mawasi in northwestern Rafah and areas around Bani Suheila and northeastern Khan Younis.
A medical source told Anadolu that Palestinian Mohammed Rajab Warsh Agha died from injuries sustained in an Israeli airstrike on a tent sheltering displaced people at the Egyptian Camp in the Al-Tawam area of northwestern Gaza City.
Earlier, a medical source at the Palestine Red Crescent Society’s Northern Field Hospital said two Palestinians had been injured in the strike, one critically.
In another attack, two Palestinians were killed and three others injured, one critically, when an Israeli drone struck a civilian vehicle in the Tel al-Hawa neighborhood of southern Gaza City, a medical source told Anadolu.
The casualties were transferred to Al-Shifa Hospital, according to the source.
Earlier Thursday, a Palestinian woman was killed and her husband and two children were injured when Israeli artillery struck their tent in the Amer Project area of northwestern Gaza City.
A medical source at Al-Shifa Hospital identified the woman as Ahlam Mubarak, 30, and said her husband was seriously injured.
Separately, a young Palestinian, Ahmed Khamis Abu Naja, died from injuries sustained in an Israeli airstrike on a vehicle in Gaza City about a week ago.
Witnesses also told Anadolu that Israeli naval forces opened fire and launched shells off the Gaza City coast, while artillery fire targeted the Al-Sudaniya area in the northwestern Gaza Strip.
In southern Gaza, seven Palestinians were injured when Israeli artillery struck a house in the Al-Mawasi area northwest of Rafah, according to medical sources.
Local sources said the Israeli army also demolished residential buildings and other structures in areas where its forces are deployed northeast of Khan Younis.
Witnesses said Israeli forces dropped smoke bombs near the Bani Suheila roundabout east of Khan Younis, causing several tents sheltering displaced Palestinians to catch fire.
As of Wednesday, Israeli violations of the ceasefire agreement had killed 1,467 Palestinians and injured 5,161 others, according to the Gaza Health Ministry.
Since October 2023, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and over 175,000 injured in Israeli attacks on Gaza, while around 90% of the enclave’s infrastructure has been destroyed, according to Palestinian figures.

Italian language courses for Tunisian diplomats kick off in Tunis
Embassy: 'Knowledge of languages strengthens dialogue and consolidates ties'
08 October 2026, 20:41
ANSA English Desk
Share
Link copiato
- ALL RIGHTS RESERVED
Italian language courses for Tunisian diplomats are set to begin at the International Diplomatic Academy in Tunis. The Italian diplomatic mission announced this, noting that, “as a result of the collaboration between the academy and the Italian Embassy in Tunis, the initiative is part of a centuries-old tradition of linguistic exchanges between the two shores of the Mediterranean.”
“Knowledge of languages strengthens dialogue and consolidates ties—both between countries and between diplomatic corps—in the spirit of promoting the Italian language worldwide and of the first International Conference on the Italian-Speaking World, to be chaired in Rome in November 2025 by Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani,” the embassy emphasizes, concluding by thanking the academy for its hospitality and wishing all participants success in their work.

Javelin ramps up: missile output nearly doubles in 2 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
18:39:57 UTC
03:39:57 KST

- The Javelin Joint Venture says it has nearly doubled Javelin missile production capacity over two years, with all ramp-critical test stations due by year-end.
- Raytheon invested $22 million in its Tucson launcher factory as production of the lighter Lightweight Command Launch Unit for the U.S. Army ramps up.
The Javelin Joint Venture, the Lockheed Martin and Raytheon partnership that builds the Javelin anti-tank missile, says it has nearly doubled its annual production capacity for complete Javelin rounds over the past two years to keep up with demand from the U.S. military and foreign customers.
Lockheed Martin announced the milestone on Oct. 8 but did not give a current production rate or say how many missiles the joint venture now builds each year. The companies said the increase came from ramping output on the existing production line and across Javelin’s supply chain, and from Lockheed Martin investments to speed up long-lead parts and equipment.
“By scaling our Javelin production line to meet increasing global demand, we’re extending Javelin’s legacy of performance excellence for years to come,” said Rich Liccion, vice president of the Javelin Joint Venture and Lockheed Martin’s Javelin program director. “Our increased output ensures that warfighters worldwide continue to rely on an anti-tank missile system that has delivered unmatched precision for over 30 years.”
The joint venture said it will finish building all the test stations critical to the ramp by the end of the year. Those stations check that each missile and its components meet environmental, performance and functional requirements before delivery, and after they are complete the program plans to upgrade 16 more stations that duplicate essential capabilities and replace aging equipment.
The production push is tied to the largest single-year Javelin production contract to date, a follow-on award in May 2025 under an indefinite-delivery, indefinite-quantity contract first awarded in May 2023. The joint venture has built more than 55,000 Javelin missiles and more than 12,000 reusable command launch units since the weapon entered service.
The Javelin is a shoulder-fired, fire-and-forget missile that locks onto a target before launch and guides itself, letting the gunner take cover immediately after firing. Its effective range runs up to about 4 km (2.5 miles), and it has been used heavily by Ukrainian forces against Russian armor since 2022.
Alongside the missile ramp, the joint venture is increasing production of the Lightweight Command Launch Unit, the new sight and firing unit soldiers use to find targets and launch the missile. The first units were delivered to the U.S. Army in May. The launcher gives twice the target detection and recognition range of the legacy unit while being 30% smaller and 25% lighter, and it works with all current, past and future Javelin variants. Raytheon has invested $22 million to modernize the launcher factory in Tucson, Arizona, where annual production is ramping in coordination with the U.S. Army.
“Delivering the LWCLU into soldiers’ hands underscores our commitment to accelerating meaningful capability upgrades,” said Jenna Hunt Frazier, president of the Javelin Joint Venture and Javelin program director at Raytheon. “Our investment in modernization and production capacity ensures the Army can field this advanced launcher more quickly, giving soldiers better awareness and greater lethality on today’s battlefield.”
Javelin missiles are built by Lockheed Martin in Orlando, Florida, and Raytheon in Tucson.

Billionaires donate millions supporting California law requiring voters to show IDs before casting ballots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
18:39:55 UTC
03:39:55 KST

Billionaires across the US are spending vast sums to support California’s Proposition 39, a measure that would require voters to show identification before casting their ballots.
The measure is being promoted as a way to “[increase] trust and confidence in our elections”, and comes amid a nationwide push by the Trump administration to restrict voting. California Republicans have long sought to advance a voter ID initiative in the state.
The campaign has received more than $36m, according to a report from CalMatters, including $17m from Richard Uihlein, a prominent conservative donor and owner of a shipping supply company. Joe Gebbia, a co-founder of Airbnb and Trump administration official, has given $8m, and Cameron and Tyler Winklevoss and Nicole Shanahan have also made significant donations. The yes campaign has far outraised its opponents by as much as $13m, according to CalMatters.
California voters do not currently have to show identification at the polls, but are required to provide a driver’s license or state identification number or their partial social security number when registering to vote. In addition to requiring ID at the polls, Prop 39 would also mandate that mail ballots include the last four digits of a government-issued ID number on an envelope.
The Republican lawmaker Carl DeMaio authored the proposition after unsuccessfully fighting in California’s Democratic-dominated statehouse to advance legislation implementing voter ID requirements in response to a demand from Trump. He has argued the initiative could be a bright spot for Republicans in an election where the party is expected to see significant losses.
“It’s not the same as the Trump Save Act. It is a more nuanced, balanced approach customized for California. It keeps mail-in ballots, but requires citizenship verification, requires voter ID,” DeMaio recently said. “This is a gamechanger.”
The state Democratic party, the ACLU and the League of Women Voters oppose the measure.
Supporters have said the proposition has bipartisan support.
A recent poll from the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies found that Prop 39 was losing some of the support it had attracted in late summer and was trailing by a 13-point margin. But other polls from late September showed it with a lead. A bilingual statewide survey of 600 Latino likely voters in early August found they were evenly divided on the measure.

Zelensky sends delegation to meet Trump envoys as he hints at secret US-Russia economic talks
A Ukrainian delegation will meet with U.S. President Donald Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in the United States on Oct. 9 to discuss proposals for an energy and Black Sea ceasefire, President Volodymyr Zelensky told reporters on Oct. 8.
The talks come amid growing uncertainty over Trump's latest push to end Russia's war against Ukraine, with officials in both Washington and Moscow casting doubt on the prospects for progress.
"Meetings are expected to take place over two days," Zelensky said. "And we are counting on a European team to join our negotiating group and the American negotiating group."
The Ukrainian delegation will include Foreign Intelligence Service Chief Rustem Umerov, Zelensky's Chief of Staff Kyrylo Budanov, and other senior officials, the president said.
The meeting follows comments by U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who said on Oct. 8 that ending Russia's war against Ukraine through negotiations was currently unattainable.
Rubio said that the goal remained out of reach because Russia insists on gaining full control over Ukraine's Donetsk Oblast without fighting, a demand Kyiv has rejected.
The latest rounds of peace negotiations have stalled over Moscow's territorial demands. The Kremlin has repeatedly rejected a ceasefire and demanded that Kyiv surrender the partially occupied Donbas, a strategically important region in eastern Ukraine. Moscow is effectively seeking territory that Russian forces have failed to capture militarily.
Ukraine has instead called for a ceasefire along the current front line.
Responding to Rubio, Zelensky said that Washington could not simultaneously discuss future economic projects with Russia while describing diplomacy as being at an impasse.
Asked what kind of economic deals Washington and Moscow might be discussing, Zelensky told reporters that Ukraine "knows a lot" but was not ready to discuss the matter publicly.
"I'm simply not ready to talk about it publicly or in detail," the president said.
The latest diplomatic effort began in early September, when Trump's envoys traveled to Kyiv and Moscow seeking progress before the U.S. midterm elections.
The visits produced one tangible outcome: an agreement in principle to hold a trilateral meeting between Ukraine, Russia, and the U.S.
A month later, however, even that meeting remains uncertain.
Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov said on Oct. 7 that there were currently no plans for U.S.-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine.

Blackouts return to Kyiv as Russia prepares to freeze civilians over the winter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
18:35:58 UTC
03:35:58 KST

Power outages have returned to Kyiv after Russian attacks damaged the energy infrastructure supplying the capital, with authorities warning that the situation could worsen as Russia intensifies its campaign against Ukraine’s energy system ahead of winter.
Russia has repeatedly targeted Ukraine’s power, heating, and other critical infrastructure to disrupt the systems civilians depend on and create a humanitarian crisis during winter. Ukrainian officials have repeatedly warned that this winter will be especially severe, as Russia has expanded its strike capabilities since the summer and Ukraine continues to face shortages of air-defense systems needed to protect its energy infrastructure.
Ukrenergo said on 8 October that emergency outages were being imposed in parts of Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast because of falling voltage in the high-voltage network. Previously announced hourly schedules were suspended, with predictable schedules to resume once the system stabilizes.
In the evening, further disruption came after a Russian attack on an energy facility important to Kyiv. Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal said that energy workers were working to restore power.
Kyiv has been under Russian attack throughout the day, with four people killed and 19 injured.
The attack continues into the evening of 8 October, with air raid alerts active across most of the country.
Kyiv loses power, water, and public transport
The damage throughout the day quickly spread beyond electricity.
The Kyiv City Military Administration said power disruptions temporarily halted metro trains and escalators. Part of the capital’s public transport system was also suspended because of the lack of electricity.
Reduced power to water infrastructure caused lower pressure on the right bank of the Dnipro, particularly in the Holosiivskyi, Sviatoshynskyi, Solomianskyi, and Shevchenkivskyi districts. Some buildings could temporarily lose water, the administration warned.
Russia is hitting the energy system as winter approaches
The outages come as Russia has stepped up attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure ahead of the heating season.
Ukrenergo said Russian attacks had caused new power outages in Donetsk, Kharkiv, Sumy, and Zaporizhzhia oblasts. The company said damaged equipment was already limiting the grid’s ability to supply consumers and warned that further Russian strikes could rapidly change the situation.
For 9 October, Ukrenergo announced all-day power restrictions in affected regions, including hourly outages for some consumers. Industrial and business consumers will also face restrictions. The company urged Ukrainians to conserve electricity, particularly during the evening peak from 5 p.m. to 10 p.m.
Ukraine’s energy authorities have been warning about the consequences of repeated Russian attacks for months. In late September, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said attacks on energy facilities had been occurring almost daily since the summer, with the September 29–30 attack marking the first massive combined strike on the energy system since the previous heating season.
The renewed strikes mark the beginning of Russia’s winter campaign against the energy system, with Russian missiles and drones increasingly targeting power-generation and transmission infrastructure in Kyiv and surrounding regions.
Russia has openly threatened another winter of blackouts
The campaign follows years of Russian attacks aimed at disrupting the infrastructure that keeps Ukrainian homes heated and supplied with electricity and water during the winter.
In August, Russia’s Defense Ministry openly taunted Ukrainians over its attacks on energy-related infrastructure, posting images of attack drones with the message that Ukrainians would “get a freeze” in winter.
Russia’s strategy has repeatedly linked attacks on electricity infrastructure to disruptions in heating and water supplies. This makes damage to the power grid particularly consequential as temperatures fall: a strike on an electrical facility can leave not only homes without lights, but also affect water pumps, heating systems, transportation, and other essential services.
The return of blackouts to Kyiv before the heating season is fully underway is an early indication of the pressure Russia’s renewed energy campaign is putting on Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure.

EU countries brace for €100B-€200B smaller budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
18:35:25 UTC
03:35:25 KST

BRUSSELS ― EU governments expect the proposed size of the bloc’s next seven-year budget to be slashed by €100 billion to €200 billion from the previous plan announced in June, 12 EU diplomats told POLITICO.
Ireland, which holds the presidency of the Council of the EU and is steering the talks, will unveil the proposal on Saturday, setting the scene for fraught discussions among EU leaders at their summit next week.
The bloc is split between so-called frugal countries — Germany, Austria, the Netherlands and others — that want to slash several hundred billion euros from the nearly €2 trillion proposal on the table, and a rival coalition of southern and eastern countries, the Friends of Cohesion, that opposes the cuts.
Advertisement
Dublin is expected to cut the budget by between €100 billion and €200 billion as a goodwill gesture to the German camp, the diplomats said. However, the Irish plan to shield agriculture and regional spending from major cuts as a concession to the Friends of Cohesion.
At next week's summit, EU leaders will react to the latest numbers, known as the "negobox" because it gives governments something to negotiate on, and signal early whether an agreement is possible by the end of the year.
Governments are rushing to secure a deal among themselves before national elections in France, Poland and Italy in 2027 threaten to derail the negotiations.
As a neutral broker in the discussions, Ireland hasn't publicly disclosed its intentions on the negotiating document.
Dublin’s European Affairs Minister of State Thomas Byrne told the European Parliament earlier this week that EU member countries have made “substantial progress” toward an agreement. But he warned: “we cannot satisfy everybody.”
Germany and its allies criticized the previous Cyprus Council presidency for cutting only €32 billion in the last negobox in June.
Advertisement
Ireland’s looming cuts
The frugals’ calls for budget savings have ignited fears among the Friends of Cohesion.
The 17 countries — including heavyweights Italy, Spain and Poland — issued a joint statement last week opposing cuts to agriculture and cohesion.
In a concession to this camp, Ireland is expected to propose budget savings in other policy areas. Governments are bracing for major reductions to the Global Europe fund, the EU’s €200 billion pot of development aid and external relations cash, and the €410 billion European Competitiveness Fund to boost the bloc’s industrial capacity.
In 2025, the European Commission proposed five new levies that are expected to generate €66 billion per year. | Michele Spatari/NurPhoto via Getty Images
Cuts to administrative costs, with €118 billion earmarked for the EU’s institutions and staff, are also popular among EU governments, though they will yield fewer savings.
However, frugals have warned against shielding agriculture and cohesion from a smaller budget. They argue instead that more money should be steered away from traditional priorities towards new challenges such as defense and competitiveness.
"We are very concerned that Ireland would decide to smash funding for research and external action, which is a major issue for development, our economic interests and migration," said one EU diplomat, granted anonymity like others in this article to speak frankly about their expectations for the sensitive negotiations.
Advertisement
Tax game
Another sensitive issue is EU-wide taxes — known as "own resources" — to finance the budget and reduce national contributions.
In 2025, the European Commission proposed five new levies that are expected to generate €66 billion per year. During negotiations, governments opposed levies that would overwhelmingly affect their economies.
Several European governments lobbied Ireland to remove a corporate tax, known as CORE, that is unpopular across the bloc. But Dublin is expected to refrain from doing so, and keep the Commission's five levies in the negobox.
To make CORE more palatable, Dublin might exempt small and medium enterprises from the scope of the levy. It could also make tweaks to a tobacco levy that is opposed by many.
Instead, the European Parliament’s proposed taxes on digital levies, online gambling and crypto firms are expected to be left out entirely from the negobox.
An EU diplomat criticized these incremental changes as “disappointing and minimal.”

South Korea conducts 1st test launch of hypersonic glide vehicle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
18:30:31 UTC
03:30:31 KST

Saadet Gokce
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
South Korea conducted its first test launch of a hypersonic glide vehicle Thursday, a presidential spokesperson said.
The test was conducted to verify core hypersonic technologies, including flight trajectory and speed, for a strategic asset capable of surprise precision strikes against enemy targets, Kang Yu-jung said, according to the Yonhap news agency.
“The HGV successfully separated from its booster and seamlessly executed its planned flight path under hypersonic conditions,” she said.
“This successful launch marks a major milestone in that preparations are complete to secure a new deterrent capable of striking critical targets across the theater of the Korean Peninsula,” Kang added.
She said the launch aimed to test super-high-temperature thermal protection materials, guidance and control systems, as well as irregular maneuverability at low altitudes.
President Lee Jae Myung, Defense Minister Kang Shin-chul and other officials witnessed the launch, according to Kang.
HGV missile systems use a booster to accelerate and ascend into the upper atmosphere before separating from the booster and gliding at lower altitudes at hypersonic speeds.
While the location was not officially disclosed, Yonhap reported that the launch took place on a barge at a test center operated by the Agency for Defense Development in Taean, about 130 kilometers (81 miles) south of Seoul.
Lee commended the HGV development team, stressing that national security should be protected through the country's own strength.
“The government will fully support the development and operational deployment of advanced weaponry so that our people can live without concern,” Lee said, according to Kang.
Lee later inspected the military's Hyunmoo-5 surface-to-surface missile, known as the “monster missile” for its massive weight and destructive power.
It was the first time the government officially referred to the previously undisclosed weapon by its name, Hyunmoo-5.
Yonhap said the launch was “widely seen as a countermeasure” to last month's land mine explosion on South Korea's side of the Military Demarcation Line that severely injured two South Korean soldiers.
Seoul accused Pyongyang of deliberately planting two mines inside the Demilitarized Zone, while North Korea rejected the accusation, calling it “blame shifting.”
On Saturday, North Korea also launched an intermediate-range strategic missile capable of changing its flight trajectory at low altitude and using artificial intelligence technology during a firing drill off its east coast.

Elective egg freezing costs thousands, but most women never use them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

In short:
Only one in four women from Australia or New Zealand who freeze their eggs for non-medical reasons return to use them, according to a study.
The study's lead author cautions that elective egg freezing doesn't provide a guaranteed path to parenthood.
What's next?
Experts say there's a need for more accurate, evidence-based information about the process.
Anna Parle describes herself as an "early adopter" of egg freezing.
She froze her eggs 12 years ago when she was 37 and still single, aware her fertility was starting to decline.
Knowing she wanted to be a mum, Ms Parle asked herself: "How do I keep this dream of mine alive going into my late-30s?"
"It was a great backup plan because it took a lot of the pressure off," she said.
After meeting her now-husband, Ms Parle retrieved her frozen eggs and used them to conceive her sons, giving birth to one at the age of 40 and the second when she was 42.
Elective egg freezing is becoming an increasingly popular option for women, like Ms Parle, looking to extend their reproductive years.
Also known as planned or social egg-freezing, it preserves the biological age of the egg, which is generally a stronger indicator for successful pregnancy than a woman's age.
A single egg-freezing cycle in Australia costs between $7,000 and $12,000 up front, then an extra $500 to $1,000 a year in storage fees.
But a study published this week in Human Reproduction found just over one in four women from Australia or New Zealand who electively freeze their eggs return to use them within 10 years.
Study lead author Oisin Fitzgerald, research fellow at University of New South Wales Sydney, said it highlighted the need for people to set realistic expectations about the likelihood they would thaw their eggs within a decade, or that the procedure provided a guaranteed pathway to parenthood.
Higher return rate than expected
Dr Fitzgerald said elective egg freezing had become "very very, popular" over the past five years.
In 2009, 55 women underwent planned egg freezing, compared to 4,919 women in 2023.
Dr Fitzgerald analysed data from the 20,209 Australian and New Zealand women who underwent planned egg freezing for non-medical reasons between 2009 and 2023.
As egg freezing grew more popular over the latter part of the study's time period, more people were followed over five years than over 10.
"If we looked at how many returned after five years, it was 22 per cent and then after 10 years it was 28 per cent," Dr Fitzgerald said.
Most people who thawed their eggs returned after 4.9 years.
Of the people who used their frozen eggs, about half used donor sperm and a third went on to have a live birth.
Devini Ameratunga, a Brisbane-based reproductive endocrinologist not involved in the study, said the return rate was higher than she expected.
"In general, we tend to counsel patients that about 10 per cent of people come back and use their eggs," she said.
"This new paper really gives us Australian and New Zealand data, and it's quite a significantly higher number of people that do come back."
Egg freezing decision information
Egg freezing is a complicated decision, said Sherine Sandhu, a research fellow at the University of Melbourne who led the development of a new egg freezing decision aid to help people make informed choices about the procedure.
Dr Sandhu said most women who froze their eggs electively in Australia did so because they did not have a partner to co-parent with.
Other reasons included pressure from their "biological clock" and to avoid potential future regret.
Hannah (not her real name) described her own decision to freeze her eggs at 34 as "empowering", allowing her some time to consider her options following a relationship breakdown.
But four years on, Hannah is unsure about whether she will use them.
"I'm getting older and I'm not sure if I actually even want kids," she said.
"I really don't know what I'm going to do; you can only keep them on ice for so long."
Hannah is not alone. More than three in four of the women Dr Sandhu's team spoke to while researching the egg freezing decision aid felt "high uncertainty" about what to do.
"If you can understand what your decision means and the implications of it, you are less likely to regret it," Dr Sandhu said.
Dr Ameratunga said it was important for patients to have access to accurate, evidence-based information, which they could then discuss with their doctor.
"Medical misinformation is quite high in society at the minute," she said.
Egg freezing offers 'no guarantee'
Planned egg freezing was often portrayed as an insurance plan, Dr Fitzgerald said.
But his study highlighted that the procedure had limitations, with success heavily influenced by the age someone froze their eggs and the number of eggs thawed.
Ms Parle, who spent about $30,000 on egg freezing and four rounds of IVF, knows how lucky she is.
She is well aware not everyone who freezes their eggs has the same unwavering confidence in their decision or the same result as her.
"I had a very positive egg freezing experience, very successful IVF journey, and I'm very mindful of the fact that it's not how it always goes," she said.
"It's not always a guarantee."

How Madonna and Gandalf ended up on Troye Sivan's new album
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

How Troye Sivan landed Madonna and Sir Ian McKellen on one album
Troye Sivan has felt the rush and isn't slowing down anytime soon.
His fourth album, She's The Best, has pushed the 31-year-old singer-songwriter further from his YouTube roots and deeper into the inner circle of "it girls" within modern alternative pop.
Now based in New York — though he still has his stunning pad in Melbourne's Fitzroy — Sivan has found himself out of the nightclub and keen to honour the people who always have his back: his girls.
"I feel so comfortable in the orbit of these people and just want to celebrate them and say thank you," Sivan tells triple j Mornings's Lucy Smith.
"I think that, in the album, there's a lot of feeling not very safe. I don't know if it's maybe because of work, it definitely has gotten worse over time, the feeling of just not really knowing how to exist in spaces.
"Especially queer spaces sometimes can be just uncomfortable for me, which is a shame.
"Knowing that the true safety has always come from the girls. I wanted to honour that."
Sivan is no stranger to collaborations, featuring on songs with peers including Charli xcx, Ariana Grande, Tate McRae, Alessia Cara and more.
She's The Best is no different, with collaborations with Nicole Kidman, Sir Ian McKellen and Lily-Rose Depp – and an approved sample from Madonna.
Bringing Music to the Party
Sivan initially produced second single Party without the sample of Madonna's 2000 hit Music, until his friend and longtime collaborator Leland absentmindedly fused the two while they worked.
"We ended up on version 17 or something like that before we started even mixing it," Sivan says.
"It was really just chipping away at it and at one point Leland started singing Music. And I was like: 'Wait, yes.'
"The song's about partying and everything like that. Immediately it breaks down to this hot and heavy breath section, then Music starts to play and it places me in the club."
Going from dancing to Madonna in his living room as a child to having her music on one of his songs became a beautiful full-circle moment.
"As far as the process of actually getting her to do it, it was random … she made it very, very easy and was down," Sivan says.
"It's hilarious because my little brother Tyde is a producer on that song. So I'm like, 'Bro, your first cut has Madonna on it'. I'm happier for him than I am for myself."
Troye's knight in queer armour
Party's music video, directed by Gordon von Steiner, is an elaborate, cinematic castle party featuring Sivan's siblings and friends.
Filmed at Berkeley Castle in Gloucestershire, two hours out of London, Sivan and von Steiner explored the idea that letting loose is an "innate human desire" and how that would look in the Middle Ages.
The final piece of the puzzle came in the form of a booming voiceover from the person most synonymous with mythical celebration: Sir Ian McKellen.
Sivan's only connection with Sir Ian was working alongside him in Waiting For Godot in 2010, when teenage Sivan was plagued with indecision about coming out as gay to his parents.
"I was backstage with Sir Ian McKellen and all of these incredible people that I realised were queer and older than me," Sivan says.
"And I think it instilled a lot of hope in me.
"I was like 'I think the first person that I come out to in the world might be Sir Ian McKellen'.
"Because I really wanted to tell him, just to kind of like get some advice or something. I couldn't do it. I couldn't get the courage."
Troye Sivan had to truly shoot his shot to get Sir Ian to narrate the Party music video, more than 15 years after they worked together.
The highly decorated 87-year-old delivered.
"I get an email with a link, and I click it and I can see that it's from his email and I download it and it's a video," Sivan says.
"He sent me a video back, and it's him in full Gandalf garb. He's got a massive, long beard and in the beginning of the video he's also talking like Gandalf. And he says my name in this booming voice, and I was like, 'Oh my God, what is happening?'
"But basically, he just sent me a really sweet video message of him saying yes, that he would love to do it.
"I guess they're filming right now in New Zealand, so he used the Lord of the Rings voiceover crew and mics, and then I was emailing with the production team of Lord of the Rings being like, 'Hey, do you mind sending me the voiceover clips?'.
"So yeah, very cool. Very, very cool."
Whether it's the queen of pop or the wizard protector of the One Ring, Troye Sivan's recognition of the people who influenced him throughout his life is deeply felt on this album.
It's hard to argue with Sivan when he tells us they are all the best.
Troye Sivan's fourth album She's The Best is out today.

Philippines pushes 4-nation power grid as Middle East war threatens ASEAN bloc’s energy supplies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Faisal Mahmud
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
The Philippines is pushing to accelerate a four-nation electricity interconnection project linking Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines as Southeast Asia confronts energy supply disruptions stemming from the US-Israeli war against Iran, according to the state-owned Philippine Information Agency (PIA).
Energy Secretary Sharon Garin announced the initiative Wednesday during the 44th ASEAN (Association of Southeast Asian Nations) Ministers on Energy Meeting in Manila.
The project would connect electricity networks through high-voltage submarine cables, allowing cross-border power trading among the four countries.
Garin described the initiative as the Philippines' principal gateway to the proposed ASEAN Power Grid, alongside an existing electricity trading arrangement linking Laos, Thailand, Malaysia and Singapore.
"Every interconnection brings that day closer when hydropower from one neighbor's mountains lights a hospital across the border,” said Garin.
Singapore's Energy Minister Tan See Leng stressed the need for common regulations governing submarine cables, including installation, maintenance and infrastructure protection.
The meeting in Manila brings together energy ministers from ASEAN's 11 member states to discuss regional electricity connectivity, energy security and financing for infrastructure projects.
The Philippines became the first country to declare a national energy emergency following the US-Israeli attacks on Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz in February. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. issued the declaration on March 24.
More than 50% of ASEAN's imported crude oil comes from the Middle East, while supply disruptions could threaten volumes equivalent to nearly 28% of regional oil consumption, according to the ASEAN Centre for Energy.

Rami Levy faces class-action lawsuit over wage deductions from supermarket cashiers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
18:18:53 UTC
03:18:53 KST

Two former Rami Levy cashiers who challenged deductions totaling NIS 303.20 from their pay will now represent a wider group of workers after the Jerusalem Regional Labor Court on Tuesday approved their case as a class action over register shortages.
The ruling turns a dispute over small deductions from two workers’ wages into a case that can now be brought on behalf of cashiers across the nationwide chain. The court said the workers had a reasonable chance of winning the case and that a class action was the best way to hear it.
The case now covers Rami Levy employees who worked as cashiers from seven years previous to the filing of the request in 2023 and had money deducted from their wages because their registers came up short. The workers had sought to include all company employees affected by the alleged practice, but the court limited the group to cashiers.
The case was brought by Meir Adri and Baruch Shaltiel. Adri worked as a cashier for about five months in 2018, when the company deducted NIS 45.70 from his April salary after a shortage was recorded at his register. He denied signing the company’s authorization form. The court did not decide at this stage whether the signature was his, but said two different dates on the document raised doubts about its authenticity.
Shaltiel worked for Rami Levy for nearly six years, most of the time as a cashier. The company deducted NIS 200 and NIS 57.50 from his wages after shortages were recorded in July and November 2016, according to the ruling.
Rami Levy faces class-action lawsuit
Israeli law generally allows employers to deduct money from a worker’s pay only in specific circumstances. One exception applies when a worker has agreed in writing that a debt is owed to the employer. Even then, no more than one-quarter of the worker’s pay may be deducted.
Rami Levy argued that register shortages were clear debts that workers had agreed in writing to repay after an internal check. It said its procedures required the money to be counted again and the area around the register to be searched. Shortages above NIS 100 were sent to a security officer for further examination.
The company also said it did not deduct money when a worker refused to sign and argued that each shortage had to be examined separately, making the case unsuitable for a class action.
The workers argued that being responsible for a register did not mean every shortage became their personal debt. They said money could be missing because of an ordinary mistake, a counterfeit banknote, a customer misleading the cashier, another worker using the register, or an error when the money was counted.
They also alleged that workers were pressured to sign deduction forms at the end of late shifts, after the store had closed and while their colleagues were waiting to leave.
At this stage, the court largely accepted the workers’ account. It said money can be deducted from wages as a debt only when the amount is clear and either proven or not disputed. A register shortage, by contrast, often requires an investigation to establish what happened and who, if anyone, was responsible.
The court found that Rami Levy had effectively imposed what it called a system of “absolute responsibility,” under which cashiers could be required to cover shortages even when their cause could not be identified.
It also found that a worker’s signature did not necessarily amount to free consent. Signing the company’s procedures was part of being hired, while the deduction forms were sometimes presented under pressure after a shortage was discovered.
The ruling does not mean that a worker can never be held responsible for money lost during a shift. An employer can still seek repayment if it can prove that the worker caused the loss. It cannot, however, decide on its own that a disputed register shortage is the worker’s debt and simply deduct it from the worker’s pay.
The class action will deal only with money deducted from wages. The original request also alleged that some cashiers were made to cover shortages in cash, but that claim was not included in the part of the case approved by the court.
The workers’ lawyer must submit a public notice for the court’s approval within 30 days. The notice, which will explain the case and workers’ right to leave the group, must then be published in two daily newspapers.
Rami Levy must file its defense in the class action within 30 days, after which the court will decide how the case will proceed.
The company was also ordered to pay NIS 25,000 in legal fees for this stage of the case and NIS 4,000 in expenses to each of the two cashiers who brought it.

US State Department restores Israel to highest anti-trafficking ranking for first time since 2021
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
18:18:48 UTC
03:18:48 KST

The US State Department has returned Israel to Tier 1, the highest category in its annual Trafficking in Persons Report, after five consecutive years in Tier 2.
The 2026 report, published Thursday and covering government efforts from April 1, 2025, through March 31, 2026, found that the Israeli government fully meets the US minimum standards for eliminating human trafficking and recorded several key achievements during the reporting period.
The report said police opened 42 trafficking investigations in 2025, including 33 involving sex trafficking and nine involving forced labor, more than double the 20 investigations opened in 2024.
It said prosecutors also charged 19 alleged traffickers, compared with 13 the previous year. The State Department highlighted what it described as a February 2026 indictment against an employer accused of the forced labor of numerous foreign workers, the first such indictment in more than a decade.
However, the report also identified significant continuing shortcomings. It said courts convicted six traffickers during the reporting period, down from 11 in 2024, and recorded no forced-labor convictions. Of the nine sentences imposed, five included at least one year in prison.
US recognizes Israel's progress against human trafficking
The State Department concluded that Israel had not adequately held labor traffickers criminally accountable.
The report said the government officially recognized 90 trafficking victims in 2025, down from 115 the previous year. It credited Israel with formalizing procedures for identifying Palestinian trafficking victims, increasing funding for victim-protection services and expanding the number of labor inspectors.
At the same time, nongovernmental organizations cited in the report said the government continued to apply a high evidentiary threshold when deciding whether to recognize victims, sometimes requiring third-party witnesses and retraumatizing applicants. The organizations said foreign and Palestinian victims remained under-recognized and that government services were difficult to access outside Tel Aviv.
The report also warned that Israel’s increased reliance on private agencies to recruit foreign workers had left workers vulnerable to exploitation and debt bondage.
According to a government-commissioned study cited in the report, 73% of surveyed construction workers recruited privately had paid more than $4,000 in recruitment fees, while approximately 20% said their employers had taken their passports or other documents.
Nongovernmental organizations cited by the State Department said some foreign workers had paid illegal recruitment fees exceeding $25,000.
Enforcement against trafficking for prostitution, protection of victims remains deficient
Separately, a State Comptroller report published in July found that police translated only 44% of their already limited intelligence on trafficking in persons into operational activity in 2024. The comptroller said enforcement against trafficking for prostitution, protection of victims, and treatment services remained deficient and incomplete.
Under the State Department’s methodology, governments are placed in four categories: Tier 1, Tier 2, the Tier 2 Watch List and Tier 3. The rankings measure government efforts to combat trafficking rather than the prevalence of trafficking within each country.
Tier 1 means that a government meets the minimum standards established under the US Trafficking Victims Protection Act, enacted in October 2000, shortly before the UN General Assembly adopted the Palermo Protocol against human trafficking.
Previous State Department reports show that Israel held a Tier 1 ranking from 2012 through 2020. It was downgraded in 2021 after the department found that its efforts were not sufficiently serious and sustained, and remained in Tier 2 through the 2025 report.
In a statement issued Thursday, the Justice Ministry welcomed the upgrade and highlighted the increase in investigations, expanded victim services, additional inspectors and the establishment of dedicated police and prosecution positions.
“We have received full recognition of Israel’s status as one of the world’s leading countries in the fight against human trafficking,” Justice Minister Yariv Levin said.
“I thank all the partners in this work, who joined forces toward the important goal of combating human trafficking, preventing exploitation and ensuring proper protection and assistance for those harmed by this serious phenomenon.”
Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar also welcomed the decision in a post on X, saying he was “proud to see Israel return to Tier 1.”
Sa’ar thanked US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the State Department “for recognizing Israel’s unwavering commitment to the highest standards in the fight against human trafficking.”
“Israel is determined to combat this abhorrent phenomenon, protect its victims, and hold perpetrators accountable,” he wrote.

Privacy law violated after data of 21,000 special education students leaked, Justice Ministry says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
18:18:36 UTC
03:18:36 KST

The Education Ministry violated Israel’s privacy law and data-security regulations after sensitive personal and medical information about approximately 21,000 special education students reached unauthorized people, the Justice Ministry’s Privacy Protection Authority said Thursday.
The students were registered in the ministry’s ultra-Orthodox (haredi) education district. The exposed information included identifying details, home and school information, religious affiliation, and medical information specifying each student’s disability, according to the authority.
The finding followed an administrative review by the privacy regulator. The authority classified the leak as a serious security incident, but its announcement did not specify a fine or say whether further enforcement action would follow.
The authority opened its review in March 2025 after the leak was reported in the media and the information was found to have circulated online. Its investigation traced the file’s creation to around May 2024, when Education Ministry employees sought to build a digital form to streamline the placement of special education students in the haredi sector.
The employees extracted information from a ministry system and created a file containing the students’ sensitive data. They then connected it to a form that educational institutions could use to enter information.
Data reached members of public, unauthorized individuals
The Education Ministry told the authority that the data file was intended to work behind the scenes, allowing the form to retrieve information from it. In practice, however, both the form and the underlying file were set so that anyone with the link could access them. The file was not password-protected and could be viewed or downloaded, while the link itself could be forwarded to others.
The link was sent in May 2024 to relevant staff at haredi educational institutions through both official and private email accounts. The authority found that the data ultimately reached members of the public and other people who were not authorized to receive it.
The ministry argued that the leak was probably caused by an isolated error in the permission settings for one of the forms. According to its account, the error allowed an outside user to search for and locate the data file after opening a link.
The authority nevertheless found wider failures in the ministry’s handling of the system. The information had been extracted by an employee who was not included on the current list of people authorized to use it. The ministry had also failed to maintain a required description of the database, a compliant information-security policy, and a current security risk assessment.
The regulator also found failures in the way access permissions were managed, the system was operated, and the data were transmitted. Sending the information through an open link without accepted encryption measures violated the rules governing the transfer of information over the internet, it said.
The ministry database contains sensitive information about more than 100,000 people and is therefore subject to a high level of security requirements under the regulations, according to the authority.
The ministry argued during the review that its certification is under international information-security standards, which exempt it from some of the regulations. The authority rejected that argument, saying certification under an international standard does not by itself replace compliance with Israeli privacy rules.
Files contained records on 21,439 children
It concluded that the ministry violated Section 17 of the Protection of Privacy Law, which makes the owner of a database responsible for securing the information it holds, as well as several provisions of the data-security regulations.
When the leak was first reported in March 2025, N12 said the file contained records on 21,439 children, including names, identification numbers, dates of birth, addresses, and medical information. Parents said the disclosure had exposed private diagnoses within their communities and could affect their children and families in haredi social and matchmaking circles.
Because the incident occurred before Amendment 13 to the Protection of Privacy Law took effect, the authority said it conducted the review under the law and enforcement powers in force at the time.

Open letter to the US administration: The G20 invitation to Putin should come with conditions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08

Open letter to the US administration: The G20 invitation to Putin should come with conditions
Russian President Vladimir Putin arrives for his inauguration ceremony at the Grand Kremlin Palace in Moscow, Russia, on May 7, 2024. (Sergei Bobylyov/Pool/AFP/Getty Images)
David J. Kramer
Former Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Ukraine, Russia, Belarus, and Moldova
The Trump administration recently announced that it has invited Russian President Vladimir Putin to December's G20 summit in Miami.
This invitation erodes the well-deserved isolation of Putin for his brutal and unprovoked invasion of Ukraine. Putin last appeared on U.S. soil for a bilateral meeting with President Donald Trump in Anchorage, Alaska, in August 2025. That meeting produced no progress toward ending the war that Putin started against Ukraine.
If anything, the Russian bombardment of Ukraine has only increased over the past year.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, not Putin, is the leader who should be invited to the G20 gathering. Zelensky leads a country of incredibly brave and determined people whose fight for their freedom should inspire us all.
"The only issue on which G20 leaders should engage Putin is ending his war against Ukraine."
If the invitation to Putin is not rescinded, as a bipartisan group of U.S. Senators urged, it should be made conditional on the following two points:
First, Putin should announce and observe an immediate, unconditional, and full ceasefire to the war he started, not simply one restricted to energy facilities, as proposed by President Trump, but rejected by Putin. He should not be allowed to set foot on U.S. soil again as long as his forces continue to attack Ukraine.
Second, Putin should commit to meeting face-to-face at the G20 with President Zelensky, along with President Trump and leaders from the European Union, to negotiate a permanent end to the war.
European nations have borne the brunt of assistance to Ukraine after direct aid from the United States ended last year, and they deserve a seat at the table. Any negotiation should ensure the full sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ukraine, the return of Ukrainian prisoners of war and kidnapped children, the right for Ukraine to determine its own future, and reparations for the damage Russia has caused.
Putin started the war against Ukraine in 2014, not just in 2022, and bears responsibility for the deaths and injuries of hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians, to say nothing of more than 1.5 million Russian soldiers.
Putin has been indicted by the International Criminal Court for war crimes, specifically for directing the targeted abduction of tens of thousands of Ukraine's children and their transport into Russia. He created the worst security crisis on the European continent since World War II, and it is he who refuses to end the fighting.
President Zelensky and Ukraine, by contrast, have repeatedly demonstrated flexibility and willingness to end the war, though not on the condition of Ukraine's capitulation to Russia.
At last month's United Nations gathering, 51 countries backed Ukraine in a joint statement, urging the Kremlin to agree to a full ceasefire and enter meaningful negotiations. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov countered that Russia would not pause its "special military operation" even during negotiations, once again illustrating that Russia, not Ukraine, is responsible for prolonging this war.
As the group of bipartisan Senators noted, allowing Putin to participate in a G20 Summit in the United States "raises serious concerns about legitimizing and normalizing a government that continues to attack Ukrainian civilian targets every day."
President Zelensky stated that the invitation for Putin to attend the G20 meeting could be “one of the best opportunities proposed by the U.S. side. I believe this is an opportunity for a trilateral meeting that could yield results."
When Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the invitation to Putin, he described it as "an opportunity for him (Putin) to engage not just with the (American) president but with other world leaders." The only issue on which G20 leaders should engage Putin is ending his war against Ukraine.
If Putin agrees to that, then the Trump administration will deserve credit for helping end the war Putin started. However, in the more likely scenario that Putin doesn't agree, he should stay in Moscow, while the West ramps up assistance for Ukraine and tightens sanctions on Russia to help Ukraine achieve victory.

We have always found a route to yes, says air regulator
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:11:52 BST
03:11:52 KST

The Military Aviation Authority has yet to meet an uncrewed system for which it could not find a path to approval, its head of regulation and certification told the Apex Europe conference in London on Wednesday, and he asked industry to keep testing that.
Commodore Neil Mathieson closed a panel on the interoperability of uncrewed systems with a short message to the companies in the room. “From a safety perspective, industry keep challenging us. I do like a challenge. We have not found any case yet where we have not found a route to yes,” he said.
Certification is triggered by a combination of size, speed, complexity and the job an aircraft is doing, by his account, with casualty evacuation and anything carrying a person taking a system firmly into the regulated category. Most of what Britain currently flies sits below that threshold, leaving one of the roughly 180 uncrewed systems in the inventory holding a certification. “Of 180 odd uncrewed systems in the UK inventory, only one is certified,” he said.
The question that prompted the answer came from the floor, from a representative of a company with an American parent and a British arm set up last year, who argued that the heavier end of the market will bring a different set of regulatory demands than the small systems dominating the discussion. He gave the example of an autonomous aircraft carrying four hundred kilograms and asked how the behaviour of the latches holding that load could be guaranteed unless the software had been engineered to a standard such as DO-178C, the civil benchmark for airborne software.
Commodore Mathieson agreed with him and set out where the heavier end of the market takes the regulator. “If we are going to get into those large uncrewed systems flying around in unsegregated airspace, potentially they will have to be certified to the same level as crewed platforms, because none of you in this room want to take off from Heathrow Airport on your way to Orlando and be hit by something that I have not certified properly that’s flying in civil airspace,” he said.
“At the moment, though, defence goes back to the demand signal. There is no demand signal in defence right now. Everyone is concentrating on the smaller stuff,” he said. “When that day comes, and it will come, we are going to have to certify things to the same standards as we’ve certified MQ-9B.” A panellist put that day at the start of next year, and observed that collaborative combat aircraft are now eight or nine tonne jets.
The MQ-9B he referred to flies in British service as Protector RG1, and its certification is the proof that the route exists. It was designed from the outset to operate in unsegregated airspace, and getting it there took sustained work between the manufacturer, the Military Aviation Authority and civil regulators, which is a reasonable guide to what the next generation of large uncrewed aircraft will need.

New Kyiv Business Centre opens in Ukraine
The inaugural meeting has been held at the centre, which provides a permanent foothold in Ukraine for UK companies.
The UK’s first dedicated business centre for industry in Ukraine has now opened, offering companies a permanent presence in Kyiv to deepen industrial ties with our ally.
The Kyiv Business Centre (KBC) is the first of its kind in the Ukrainian capital and is the result of close collaboration between the National Armaments Director (NAD) Group, industrial partners and finance industry, demonstrating the sustained commitment to Ukraine under the 100-Year Partnership.
The KBC gives UK companies, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), a base from which to build trusted relationships with Ukrainian partners, access battlefield insight and pursue co-development, co-production and investment opportunities.
Until now the cost, security requirements and administrative complexity of operating in Ukraine have made it prohibitively difficult for smaller firms to establish a presence in the country.
Luke Pollard, Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, said:
  Britain has stood firmly with Ukraine since the first days of Russia’s illegal invasion, and with the Kyiv Business Centre now open, we are helping to unlock new opportunities for investment, growth and long-term recovery.
By supporting UK companies in Kyiv, we are deepening the 100-Year Partnership and turning our shared resolve into shared innovation.
The KBC’s operating model is built around three principles: industry, innovation and investment, giving members access to a networking platform to help form partnerships, raise investment and scale-up production and capability.
National Armaments Director Rupert Pearce met with senior industry figures and SMEs to mark the start of the centre’s work connecting UK and Ukrainian industries.
NAD Rupert Pearce said:
  This new facility is not just a centre; it’s a permanent gateway transforming the UK’s ability to collaborate meaningfully with our Ukrainian partners now, and for the long term.
Until now the costs, security considerations and other restrictions created by Russia’s full-scale invasion have made it difficult for firms, especially smaller firms, to work in Ukraine.
Our previous Trade Missions successfully addressed some of those challenges - this centre breaks down those barriers, giving UK firms a permanent centre in Kyiv embedding real opportunities for innovation, investment and export.
It builds on more than 40 major UK-Ukraine industrial partnerships already in place and on the success of the MOD’s trade missions to Ukraine. The KBC also supports Ukrainian firms seeking UK industrial partners or establishing UK-based subsidiaries.
UK companies interested in doing business in Ukraine can find out more by emailing enquiries@kyivbusinesscentre.com, or visiting www.kyivbusinesscentre.com.

Top bosses at Goldman Sachs are in line to share a bonus pot worth up to $500m (£378m) this year, marking one of the biggest payouts in the Wall Street bank’s history.
The eye-watering sum will be shared between 20 bankers, with its chief executive, David Solomon, due to take about $100m (£75.6m) of the reward, which is made up of Goldman Sachs stock.
That is more than double the value of the record $47m (£35.5m) annual pay packet he was granted last year.
The $500m bonus pot is the culmination of a long-term investment plan first crafted by the bank in 2021.
The final sum, which is due to be confirmed later this month, is tied to how high Goldman’s share price has climbed over the past five years, as well as how its stock price has performed compared with peers such as JP Morgan and Bank of America over that period.
Goldman Sachs said the bonuses were meant to persuade bosses to stay at the bank “in an increasingly competitive market”.
The bank’s president, John Waldron, who is widely expected to succeed Solomon as chief executive, is also in line for a payout, alongside other top bosses such as the co-heads of global banking and markets, Ashok Varadhan and Dan Dees.
News of the bumper bonus, which was first reported by Bloomberg, comes days before Goldman is due to report third-quarter earnings on 13 October.
The bonuses reflect the value of Goldman Sachs stock, which has surged roughly 146% over the past five years, and climbed about 300% since Solomon took the helm as chief executive.
A spokesperson for the bank said: “The board created these awards to achieve three principal objectives: align compensation with rigorous performance thresholds, ensure leadership continuity and enhance retention of our top talent in an increasingly competitive market. It’s no secret our firm has performed exceptionally well in the years since.”
The payouts are the latest in a string of large payouts for executives in the US, particularly on Wall Street.
The US lender Citigroup announced earlier this year that its chief executive, Jane Fraser, had been paid a record $42m (£31.8m) for 2025. Meanwhile, JP Morgan’s chief executive, Jamie Dimon, took home a total pay package worth $43m (£32.5m) last year, up 10% from a year earlier. Dimon’s own long-term incentive award is worth about $270m (£204.1m), according to Bloomberg.

====================================================================================================

Kilauea’s display is revealing why volcanoes spew like a fountain show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
18:05:31 UTC
03:05:31 KST

Kilauea has been erupting almost continuously for nearly 200 years, and volcanologists have seen a lot of sides to Hawaii’s most active volcano. But in the last year, Kilauea started doing something new: firing up frequent fountains of lava.
The volcano’s fountain era kicked off at dawn on December 23, 2024, with an eruption inside the summit crater of Halema’uma’u. Since then, Kilauea has put on a recurring pyrotechnic display of lava fountains, researchers report October 8 in Science. It produced 54 different lava fountains by September 2026, some of which shot as high as 457 meters into the sky.
During an eruption, which can last from hours to days, months or even years, occasional lava fountains aren’t unusual. But it’s rare to see repeated fountains — distinct bursts separated by minutes to weeks — during a single eruption. At Kilauea, these clustered spurts have only occurred three times since 1823, and never with such frequency.
Thanks to their rarity, researchers have known relatively little about what initiates, sustains and ends these episodic fountains, say Ashton Flinders, a research geophysicist at the U.S. Geological Survey’s Hawaiian Volcano Observatory, based in Hilo, and colleagues. There have been two prevailing ideas: Water dissolved in magma — the underground, molten mix of rock and gas — rising from deep inside the volcano suddenly escapes as the pressure changes, leading to a burst of pyrotechnics; or a carbon dioxide–rich foam atop the trapped magma, like the pressurized froth over a shaken bottle of soda, suddenly and violently expands.
Kilauea is the perfect laboratory in which to assess these hypotheses, the researchers say. It has been intensely studied by scientists and monitored by instruments for decades. Scientists continuously collect data on its seismic activity, temperature, low-frequency acoustics, how much the ground swells or deflates and the gases that escape. Using these data, researchers have begun to form a picture of what’s causing the relentless spewing.
Before each fountain, the team found, the floor of the bowl-shaped caldera would swell and tilt, suggesting magma was gathering beneath. As the eruption matured and the fountains continued, a pattern emerged, first appearing before the fourteenth fountain. Just before that eruption, the team detected a repetitive sequence of minutes-long bursts of seismic energy and low-frequency acoustics.
Those signals, the researchers say, are linked to the buildup and release of trapped gases in magma, which make it rise and fall through narrow volcanic vents in the rock like a piston in a car. The team also noted that while the volcano burped some sulfur dioxide gas, there was relatively little carbon dioxide, suggesting that the foam hypothesis wasn’t at work.
This is just a preliminary glimpse into this phenomenon, and a lot of questions remain, Flinders and his colleagues say.
