Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's former military secretary, Avi Gil, told N12 News and Israel Hayom on Thursday that Netanyahu's chief of staff allegedly tried to change the official record of the prime minister's schedule.
Shortly before leaving his position, Gil made sure the entire contents of his notebooks were digitized and stored on a classified computer in the Military Intelligence Directorate. "A state commission of inquiry will receive everything I have on the day it is established, including what I have to say," he clarified.
He explained in the interview that at the end of October 2023, weeks after the start of the war, several people approached him about collecting transcripts of the day.
Recounting the hours leading up to the attack, Gil said intelligence reports circulated through the security establishment's systems overnight, reaching computers in the offices of the head of the Research Division and the Military Intelligence Directorate.
At 3:55 a.m., an intelligence assistant received an alert about a message detailing suspicious actions near the Gaza border that were called "routine," and it said another consultation would take place later that day. Based on that, the assistant decided not to wake either the prime minister or the military secretary, believing the situation was not urgent enough to warrant doing so.
'We are at war'
At 6:12 a.m., Gil said he was awakened by a phone call from the office of former Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) chief Ronen Bar, who asked him to return the call using the secure red telephone. When asked what the call was about, Bar replied in one word: "South."
At 6:17 a.m., he called back and was briefed on suspicious indicators, including the activation of SIM cards and reports of Hamas operatives moving underground.
At 6:29 a.m., he woke Netanyahu with a phone call over a non-secure line and informed him: "Hamas has launched extensive fire, a large-scale surprise attack. I am gathering information and will call you as soon as possible."
Eleven minutes later, at 6:40 a.m., he called the prime minister again and told him: "We are at war."
"In January, one of the stenographers approached me and told me she had been instructed to retrieve the transcript of that 6:40 a.m. phone call and had been instructed [by Netanyahu's then chief of staff, Tzachi Braverman] to change the time of the call from 6:40 to 6:29," Gil said in the interview.
Asked why someone would want to change the times, Gil said, "Someone was dealing with particular narratives," adding that he quietly flagged the incident to the attorney-general during a meeting.
"It was important for me to document it so that if someone later came along and presented evidence of things that I had documented differently, that I remembered differently, and that contradicted the transcripts of organizations and the memoranda recorded by people in various places, we would have an example of it, the falsification," he stated.
He said that aside from the change made to the time stamp of the phone call, he did not know of other changes.
"Nevertheless, I have one recommendation for the commission of inquiry that will be established, and for the State Comptroller, who obtained transcripts: Do not rely solely on the transcripts," he urged. "Demand the original recordings. Listen to them."
Regarding the hostages, Gil stated that Israel could have returned the hostages earlier; he said, "We could have."
PM's ex-military secretary: 'What the public is being told is not what actually happened'
Gil also rejected claims that betrayal had led to the massacre.
"There was no betrayal," he clarified, warning that those spreading such allegations were undermining the resilience of Israeli society. "There were failures. The system failed utterly... Anyone who alleges betrayal without a shred of evidence is not only spreading a lie, but is also harming the resilience and strength of this wonderful thing called Israel."
Gil said that he thought he would be speaking to a state commission of inquiry about the massacre, which is why he kept his accounts of the day private. He now believes that one will never be formed, which is why he felt he needed to speak about his experience on October 7.
"Three years have passed since October 7, and two years since I retired from the IDF. I hoped a state commission of inquiry would be established to investigate everything. Unfortunately, that hasn’t happened, and I doubt it will.”
"In the past few weeks, I realized I had to come out and say what I knew. Because we saw what happened recently when there is no investigation," he said, referencing the incident of the flydubai flight.
“What the public is being told is not what actually happened,” he added. “This isn’t my truth. It’s the country’s truth.”
"I think we are tearing Israeli society apart because of the lies," he said, adding that there are discrepancies between what the public has been told and what actually happened, calling for the formation of a state commission of inquiry.
Gil told reporters that Netanyahu had heard several warnings before the October 7 massacre about suspicious activity in Gaza, but they were all shot down. "October 7 was Israel’s failure. Netanyahu heard it all from agency heads, everything that was known. There were suggestions to do targeted strikes in Gaza from time to time, but they were all denied."
He also recounted that in July 2023, while Netanyahu was hospitalized, former Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) head Ronen Bar requested to speak with him and warned of the possibility of war.
Touching on the recent reports of warnings given to Netanyahu from Emirati President Mohammed bin Zayed and Egypt, he stated that he had not been in the PMO during the dates of the talks between the prime minister and MZB, and had not been aware until recently of matters with Egypt.
However, he said that a plane often used by Egyptian intelligence had landed in Israel for about an hour, citing recent reports. "An aircraft like that came for a purpose. I believe someone in Israel can shed light on what happened, one way or another."
Gil concluded by placing the responsibility for the failures of October 7 on Netanyahu.
"I do not understand in what world it is possible to separate the concept of leadership from the concept of responsibility," he said. "There is no leadership without responsibility."

No connection to RAF Fairford

Astronomers detect mysterious burst of energy from a galaxy far, far away
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
18:00:25 UTC
03:00:25 KST

A long time ago in a galaxy far, far away, a mysterious flash of energy was released into the universe.
Astronomers have now detected that flash – a burst of radio waves which travelled for more than 10bn years before reaching Earth – what they believe to be the most distant fast radio burst (FRB) ever recorded.
FRBs are intense bursts of radio waves that can emit as much energy in milliseconds as the sun does in months or years. These mysterious pulses were first discovered in 2007 and have puzzled scientists ever since, with speculation from some that they could have an alien origin.
In a new study published in Science, researchers have detected an FRB that originated when the universe was only about 3bn years old, meaning it has travelled through “approximately 80% of cosmic history”.
The burst, dubbed FRB 20240304B, is believed to be the farthest yet detected, more than double the previous distance record.
The scientists detected the burst using the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa and subsequently identified its host galaxy using Nasa’s James Webb space telescope (JWST).
Dr Themiya Nanayakkara of the University of Sydney, one of the lead researchers on the paper, said when the burst was produced, “there was no Earth, there was no sun”.
Data from the JWST indicated that the burst originated from a “young, very small galaxy which is forming stars at a very high speed, with not many metals around it”.
There are several theories as to what the source of FRBs is, including that they originate from magnetars, neutron stars with a very powerful magnetic field.
“Whatever the mechanism that causes this radio burst has to account for that fact that it can be produced in … very young galaxies with very low amount of metals,” Nanayakkara said.
More than 10,000 FRBs have been detected since 2007. Some repeat continuously, Nanayakkara said, while “some of them repeat for a while and then stop … and then there are some FRBs that only go once and we never see again”.
Whether the new distant burst is a one-off flash or will yield recurrent signals remains to be seen.
“[But] the fun thing about FRBs is that we don’t need to know what is causing them to do some of the science we are doing now,” Nanayakkara said.
This particular burst “has been travelling for 80% of the age of the universe”, he said, adding that further detections of distant FRBs would enable scientists to map unseen matter in the distant universe.
Prof Matthew Bailes of Swinburne University, one of the astrophysicists who first discovered FRBs, described the new paper as “a validation of how powerful the FRBs are for probing the universe”.
Bailes described them as “a very fundamental way of counting how many atoms there are in the universe”. FRBs are affected by the particles they travel through, enabling scientists to quantify matter that cannot be seen through optical telescopes.
Dr Sara Webb, an astrophysicist also at Swinburne University who was not involved in the research, said: “You can use them essentially as a line-of-sight count for how much matter they had to go through [to get to Earth].”
The discovery suggests that “FRBs might have been very common in the early universe”, she added.

====================================================================================================

Brain scans find tau buildup in nearly two-thirds of patients with late-onset psychosis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
18:00:13 UTC
03:00:13 KST

A study in Japan found that people whose psychosis began after age 40 were far more likely than healthy older adults to show buildups of amyloid-beta and tau, two proteins linked to Alzheimer’s disease and other forms of dementia. Many patients showed tau buildup without the amyloid that marks Alzheimer’s, suggesting that more than one type of brain disease may be involved. The paper was published in Molecular Psychiatry.
Psychotic disorders, which involve symptoms such as hallucinations and delusions, usually begin in adolescence or early adulthood. In some people, however, these symptoms first appear after age 40, and sometimes after age 60. These cases are referred to as late-onset psychosis.
Late-onset psychosis often looks different from psychosis that begins earlier in life. Older patients tend to have more prominent persecutory delusions, such as the belief that others are out to harm them, along with fewer negative symptoms, such as emotional flatness and social withdrawal, and less disorganized thinking. These differences have raised the possibility that late-onset psychosis may involve partly distinct changes in the brain.
Small brain imaging studies have reported changes in white matter, particularly in rear regions of the brain, and altered blood flow in some people with late-onset psychosis. A large Swedish study also found that people who develop psychosis after age 60 have a higher risk of later dementia. Studies of patients’ brains after death have found several neurodegenerative diseases in such cases, including disorders involving abnormal tau buildup that differ from Alzheimer’s disease.
Most of that evidence comes from autopsies, because tools for detecting the full range of tau buildup in living people have been limited. The research team previously developed florzolotau, a radioactive tracer used in brain scans that binds to tau and can detect both the type of tau buildup seen in Alzheimer’s disease and the types seen in several other neurodegenerative diseases.
Study authors Manabu Kubota and Shin Kurose of the National Institutes for Quantum Science and Technology in Japan and their colleagues used this tracer to investigate the brain changes underlying late-onset psychosis. They hypothesized that amyloid-beta and tau buildup would be more common in patients with late-onset psychosis than in healthy older adults.
Participants were 37 patients with late-onset psychosis and 47 healthy older adults who served as a comparison group. Patients’ average age was 70, compared with 66 for the healthy participants, and 27 patients and 22 healthy participants were women. Most patients had been diagnosed with schizophrenia (20) or delusional disorder (13), and none had evidence of cognitive impairment or neurological disease when their symptoms began.
In 24 of the patients, symptoms started after age 60, while in the remaining 13 they started between 40 and 60. Compared with the healthy participants, patients scored lower on tests of thinking skills and had less education.
All participants underwent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and two positron emission tomography (PET) scans, which use small amounts of radioactive tracers that bind to specific proteins in the brain. One scan detected amyloid-beta, and the other used florzolotau to detect tau. Both proteins occur naturally in the brain, but they can build up abnormally, with amyloid forming plaques characteristic of Alzheimer’s disease and tau forming tangles seen in Alzheimer’s and a number of other neurodegenerative disorders.
Three raters examined the amyloid scans and classified each participant as amyloid-positive or amyloid-negative using standardized procedures from the Japanese Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. Tau positivity was determined with a computerized, point-by-point analysis of each person’s tau scan.
Thirteen of the 37 patients (35%) were amyloid-positive, compared with only one of the 47 healthy participants (2%). All of the amyloid-positive patients had developed psychosis after age 60. Tau buildup was even more common: 65% of patients were tau-positive, compared with 15% of healthy participants.
The patients fell into three groups of roughly equal size. Twelve of the 13 amyloid-positive patients were also tau-positive, a combination consistent with Alzheimer’s disease, while half of the 24 amyloid-negative patients showed tau buildup without amyloid, which may point to other tau-related diseases. The remaining 12 patients showed neither.
The tau patterns varied widely from patient to patient. As a group, patients showed more tau tracer in the parietal cortex, a region toward the top and back of the brain involved in attention and integrating information, and this difference held even when the analysis was limited to amyloid-negative participants. Among amyloid-negative patients, tau levels did not differ between those whose symptoms began before or after age 60.
Among the 13 amyloid-positive patients, those with more parietal tau tended to score lower on a test of executive function, the mental skills used to plan and control behavior. Tau levels were not linked to the severity of patients’ psychiatric symptoms.
The authors concluded that late-onset psychosis “may be associated with heterogeneous tau-related neurodegenerative processes,” meaning that a variety of tau-related brain diseases may be involved. They suggest that for some patients, late-onset psychosis may be an early stage of a dementing illness, though following patients over time will be needed to test this.
There are some caveats to consider. The study was relatively small, and the authors describe the findings as exploratory. Because no autopsy data were available, it has not been confirmed which specific diseases the tau patterns represent, and interpretations of the non-Alzheimer’s patterns rest on the tracer’s ability to distinguish different types of tau.
The patients and healthy participants also differed in age, sex, and education. Most results held when the researchers adjusted for education or excluded younger male controls, though the difference in tau in the occipital lobe among amyloid-negative patients weakened to a trend in both analyses. The study captured patients at a single point in time, so it cannot show whether those with tau buildup will go on to develop dementia, and two of the authors hold patents on compounds related to the research.
The paper, “High prevalence of tau pathologies in late-onset psychosis: A PET study,” was authored by Manabu Kubota, Shin Kurose, Kenji Tagai, Yuki Momota, Masanori Ichihashi, Hironobu Endo, Chie Seki, Sho Moriguchi, Yasuharu Yamamoto, Yuko Kataoka, Ryoji Goto, Takehiro Tamura, Hiroki Shiwaku, Kiwamu Matsuoka, Hisaomi Suzuki, Mitsumoto Onaya, Takahiko Tokuda, Hiroyuki Uchida, Hidehiko Takahashi, Kazunori Kawamura, Ming-Rong Zhang, Makoto Higuchi, and Keisuke Takahata.

The duality of Australia's newest cricket captain Sophie Molineux
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

The everyday version. Quiet, composed, down-to-earth. Calmly answering questions, even the difficult ones, unfazed.
Those level-headed qualities come in handy when she's on the field, allowing her to think clearly and execute at critical points in the game.
Then there's Molineux's alter ego. The outgoing, bubbly personality that her teammates know well and us outsiders get a glimpse of every now and then.
Whether it be dressing up as 80's icon Jane Fonda in neon lycra to lead a stretch session on tour, opening the batting in a game of street cricket outside the Old Mates pub in New York, or celebrating hard after a T20 World Cup win … It's fun and it's rather infectious.
In 2020, Molineux danced on stage with Katy Perry at the MCG. In 2026, she channelled Shane Warne on the Lord's balcony, holding a stump aloft as a beer was poured over her head.
During her six months in the job as the nation's newest captain, this contrast has made a real impact to the team environment. And it speaks volumes that two of her peers that watched from the sidelines in July as Australia reclaimed the T20 crown were filled with pride.
Loading Instagram content
Instead of feeling bitter they'd been left on the bench while the rest of the side beat England in the final by seven wickets, Grace Harris and Megan Schutt reflected on how much this victory meant to the entire group. The first with Molineux in charge.
"That was good fun," Harris remarked.
"It's not unlike Soph to get amongst the celebrations and it's great to see an Aussie captain kind of relax a bit too — you've got to enjoy the wins.
"To go through the World Cup and not even look like losing was really cool and a real answer to the criticism we've had in recent times," Schutt added.
"It was a euphoric feeling for Soph. There were so many people that doubted the decision to make her captain, when we knew internally why she was picked for that role. To be able to put it to them a bit felt good and we're so proud of her.
"Following the game when the crowd had dispersed, it was late at night, and we were sitting on the ground with the trophy basically having a gratitude session for the last six weeks.
Most had thought the experience of vice-captain Tahlia McGrath or all-rounder Ash Gardner would put them next in line. McGrath had even filled in for Healy 15 times previously. Perhaps even 24-year-old Annabel Sutherland would have been a good pick, as a long-term nod to the future?
All three had certainly played more international matches than Molineux, whose career has been hampered by a string of injuries since her debut in 2018. Due to serious foot, knee and shoulder issues, Molineux had only accumulated a total 58 caps when she was appointed.
Social media was rife with criticism. Were others more worthy? Would she be able to stay fit and be a consistent presence in the team?
"I was aware of the criticism, and I understood completely why it came and why people wouldn't have expected my appointment," Molineux tells ABC Sport.
"I would have loved to have played another 100 games for Australia by now but that hasn't been my journey and I can't change that.
"I wouldn't even want to change that because through those injuries and setbacks I learned a whole lot about myself — what's important to me and a big part of that was leading.
"Making sure that whatever environment I was in, that I could contribute and make others feel safe. It set me up, in a way, to be able to do this job.
"At the same time, I was pretty determined to prove it all wrong, and it probably fuelled me to nail the preparation for the T20 World Cup."
After two consecutive semi-final exits at ICC tournaments, there was extra pressure on Australia to perform. Despite this, Molineux excelled.
The left-arm orthodox bowler finished in the top three wicket-takers (11 in 7 innings with best figures of 2/6) and was credited by her teammates for spearheading their most consistent and dominant campaign yet.
Which is saying something, as this was their seventh T20 title. The result felt like vindication for her family too, who have supported her through every one of her setbacks.
Loading Instagram content
"They ride it with you, the highs and the lows," Molineux said.
"Throughout the World Cup they were in the stands watching and for them to be able to experience it was really special to me.
"They were the first ones to the games and the last ones to leave.
"I'm forever grateful for my family's support and Mum and Dad were so excited and happy when I was appointed as captain … Their opinions to me were most important."
As the summer of cricket approaches, with next year's Women's Ashes on the horizon, we wonder, what kind of leader does Molineux want to be?
"I just want to be authentic. I want to be me," she responds.
"I've played under some amazing captains in Meg Lanning and Alyssa Healy. They were strong players who wanted to take the team on their shoulders and lead through their actions. I've learned a lot from them, but I don't want to lose too much of who I am.
"I am from country Victoria. I play cricket because I love the challenge and the people. The memories and the experiences. So, I don't really want to lose that sense of fun.
"Although the job can be serious at times, it's getting that balance right."

Unless you're Hanson, migration can be a dangerous sinkhole
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

analysis
Unless you're Pauline Hanson, the migration debate can be a dangerous sinkhole
When, way back, the opposition started talking about cutting immigration, it would have thought on the basis of polling it was tapping into a vein of political gold.
But since then, Pauline Hanson has taken ownership of the mine and pretty much locked it away for One Nation.
Simon Welsh, from the Redbridge Group political consultancy, says: "The Liberals talking about migration doesn't create more Liberal voters, it creates more One Nation voters.
"Immigration offers people a simple explanation for the pressures they are feeling. When the major parties talk about it, it validates that. [Voters] then ask, who is the strongest voice on immigration? It's a massive strategic error [by the major parties]," Welsh says.
Also, and crucially, the opposition may not have initially appreciated how a migration policy can open a political sinkhole that it's easy to be pushed into and hard to scramble out of.
We're seeing that this week, now opposition leader Angus Taylor has finally released the Coalition's plan.
Taylor late to the conversation
One Nation and the government already had their policies out, so Taylor appeared very much a follower rather than leader on the issue.
His policy would cut net overseas migration (NOM), currently a little under 300,000, to 100,000 in each of the first two years, rising to 160,000 by the fourth year (NOM is "the net gain or loss of population through immigration to Australia and emigration from Australia").
For Liberals looking to compete with One Nation, Hanson's offering goes further, with a negative NOM initially, rising to 130,000.
The real problem for the Coalition, however, is that it is very difficult to win a policy argument when there are multiple moving parts, vocal stakeholders, many potential losers and outcomes that rely on assumptions that may or may not stand the test of the real world.
The migration system certainly needs significant reform. The government, which ordered a major inquiry led by former public servant Martin Parkinson that reported in 2023, should have done more years ago; instead it was playing catch up in its recently announced changes.
But whatever changes are made will have intended and unintended (and unforeseen) consequences, triggering intense debate.
As the Parkinson review put it: "Our work reinforced that, while there often was strong agreement between stakeholders about broad objectives and high-level issues, putting migration into practice involves making difficult decisions about trade-offs and balancing competing, equally valid, concerns."
The thrust of the Parkinson review was similar to that of the opposition's policy — moving away from the high proportion of temporary visa holders that underpins our labour market — although that review was more detailed and nuanced.
Backpackers in, guest workers out
Taylor condemns the "guest worker" economy, saying "Australia should be a home, not a hotel". In the 1980s, the emphasis in the migration system was on permanent arrivals. Over subsequent years there has been a major trend, under Liberal and Labor, to people on temporary visas, which are more demand-driven.
In trying to cut migration, there are various big "levers" that can be pulled — visa classes with large numbers, including the working holiday program, foreign students and those on temporary graduate visas. Whichever levers are chosen will have consequences and bring reactions.
When the government announced in its recent policy overhaul a tightening of working holiday numbers, farmers and others in the regions screamed blue murder, saying there'd not be enough people to pick the fruit or serve in local cafes.
The backpackers have been protected under Taylor's policy. The Nationals insisted on that.
As it looked for levers, the opposition went after (among others) those on temporary graduate visas — people who have finished their studies but have visas to stay and work for a period. They fill many jobs, including in the gig economy.
Business organisations have attacked the Coalition's proposals as potentially denying them workers they need. They are not buying Taylor's argument that having more skilled workers as part of a more limited overall intake will serve their needs better.
And in some parts of the economy — the aged care sector, for instance — it's relatively unskilled labour that's required. The opposition argument is that aged care workers could switch to the skilled stream, but how many would? The bar would be higher.
Former immigration official Abul Rizvi, writing in Guardian Australia, says: "There is no chance a NOM figure of 100,000 a year over two years can be delivered if the labour market remains at around its current [tight] state … The Coalition would be overwhelmed by pressure from the business community to increase its target."
The policy would hit foreign students, not so much directly as indirectly. The opposition says there would be only a modest cut in the number of students allowed in. But there would be a disincentive effect from a tougher approach to family members accompanying students (as the government is taking) and from scrapping temporary graduate visas. International education is a big industry for Australia, so these changes would have potentially serious implications for export income as well as for university finances.
Loading
Coalition wants to move past immigration
More widely, the consequences of the opposition's migration policy for particular sectors and regions are unclear. To what extent the policy would dent the wider Australian economy, which has been held afloat recently on the large intake, will be a meaty debate from now until the election.
Unfortunately for the Liberals, one of those central to the policy's framing, spokesman Jonno Duniam, is preparing to depart parliament just as the difficult selling job gets underway. Duniam, leaving for family reasons, is among the opposition's few strong performers and the timing of his exit, although long known, couldn't be worse.
One gets the impression that while the Opposition originally saw the migration issue as a political honey pot, now its attitude has changed. It knew, given the clamour, it had to produce a detailed policy and is now anxious to get it out of the way. Remember, only a few weeks ago it was flagging it would withhold the bottom-line figures until closer to the election when it would have the latest data. Now we have been given those numbers.
Taylor just wants to get this done and move back onto the more fertile (for him) and less tricky economic ground as soon as he can.
Michelle Grattan is a professorial fellow at the University of Canberra and chief political correspondent at The Conversation, where this article first appeared.

How Australian mortgages compare to the US, Japan and South Korea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

How Australian mortgages compare to the US, Japan and South Korea
As interest rates started to rise earlier this year, Andrew Clifford decided he needed to protect his family from being stretched any further.
In March, he changed his mortgage from a variable to a fixed rate for the next two years.
That was well before the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) lifted the cash rate last week to its highest level in 15 years, from 4.35 per cent to 4.6 per cent.
"I'm relieved I locked it in … [but] it's only the people with mortgages that are doing the heavy lifting of trying to beat inflation," Mr Clifford said.
"If I could have got a 25-year fixed-rate home loan like they do in the US, I'd be all over it."
Under a fixed-rate mortgage, lenders charge the same interest rate for the life of the loan.
Under a variable-rate mortgage, lenders can charge different rates over the life of the loan.
Most Australians with a mortgage have a variable rate, with less than 5 per cent on a fixed rate, according to the RBA.
Research suggests Australians would benefit from longer fixed-rate home loans, similar to the US, South Korea, and the European Union, where fixed-rate mortgages of 10–50 years are commonplace.
How does Australia compare to other countries?
In the US, government-sponsored entities such as Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac guarantee about 70 per cent of mortgages.
According to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, this reduces risk for lenders and has made loans more affordable for consumers.
In addition, a secondary debt market allows lenders to move risk off their books by selling mortgage-backed securities to investors like pension funds and insurance companies.
These conditions allowed US lenders to offer 30-year fixed-rate mortgages, University of NSW economist Richard Holden said.
"They were founded with the idea home ownership was an important kind of social concept.
"And giving borrowers certainty about their future mortgage repayments.
"There are pros and cons but we don't have anything like that in Australia."
Professor Holden said moving to a long-term fixed rate would mean borrowers could not benefit when interest rates fell, such as between 2015 and 2021.
"You would have felt pretty silly if you'd borrowed at, just for the sake of argument, 6 per cent fixed rate … then watched interest rates plummet," he said.
"Then you are sort of saying, 'Well, new borrowers can borrow at 2 per cent, and I'm locked in at 6 per cent.'"
Loading...
University of Sydney's Doowon Lee said in Japan most mortgages had a variable-rate for 35 years.
He said this was because Japan's interest rates had been extremely low for phe last 30 years.
Dr Lee said that during that period, some lenders offered Japanese nationals and permanent residents full loans with no deposit.
"So you have for 35 years close to 0 per cent interest rate. [But] now it's a different story because Bank of Japan has been raising the interest rate," he said.
In South Korea, most mortgages were variable, but the gap between the rate offered on fixed and variable loans was smaller, Dr Lee said.
The most common fixed-rate loans were between five and seven years, he said.
Dr Lee said the smaller gap between fixed and variable rates was due to investor demand in Korea being affected by a rental scheme called "jeonse", often a two-year lease agreement.
It allows someone to rent a property by paying 50–70 per cent of its value, which is returned after the tenancy ends.
Jeonse make up about 70 per cent of rental agreements in South Korea's capital, Seoul, according to the Asia Society.
The not-for-profit said the arrangement worked for landlords because they got access to a large amount of interest-free money to save in a high-interest account or to invest, while tenants could spend two years saving to buy their own property.
"The investor side demand is slightly lower in Korea. So that does create the banks to compete for customers, and that sometimes creates smaller spread [between variable and fixed loans]," Dr Lee said.
What would it take to change?
Professor Holden said for Australia to move to a 30-year fixed-rate home loan system, like the US, the entire mortgage lending market would need to change.
If the Australian government issued more 30-year debt, it would signal to mortgage lenders that offering 30-year mortgages was less risky.
Professor Holden said government "scaffolding" would be required to encourage Australian banks to offer the product to lenders "because there's nothing stopping them doing it right now".
Moving to a South Korean model would require government intervention, Dr Lee said
Over the last decade, the South Korean government has had a target to increase borrowers on fixed rates, offering fixed-term rates as long as 35 years.
By the end of 2026, it aims to have at least a third of all mortgages as fixed-rate loans, Dr Lee said.
Other factors, such as South Korea's capital gains tax treatment, reduced investor demand in the housing market, he said.
"In Korea, if you sell your house within a year, then you'll be taxed at close to 70 per cent. If you sell it within two years, it's close to 60 per cent.
"So it totally discourages people buying a house [and] flipping it within one or two years.
"Thereby a five-year [loan] becomes more viable. So again, those are sort of government policies changing how the mortgage borrowers are actually going to a specific bucket of years rather than short-term versus midterm."

Hurricane Isaias charges towards the US Gulf Coast with dangerous winds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
17:58:07 UTC
02:58:07 KST

Hurricane Isaias charges towards the US Gulf Coast with dangerous winds
The storm is forecast to strike Florida, Alabama and Mississippi with up to 10 inches of rain this weekend.
Hurricane Isaias has intensified into the first hurricane of the Atlantic season as it barrels over record-warm water toward the northern shoreline of the United States Gulf Coast, prompting school closures and local government shutdowns.
According to the Miami-based National Hurricane Center, the storm is forecast to make landfall in parts of the Florida Panhandle, southern Alabama and southern Mississippi late Friday or early Saturday. The low-lying areas are especially vulnerable to flooding and storm surges.
The center warned residents in likely impact zones on Thursday to complete all emergency life-safety and property protections without delay.
It has also issued a hurricane watch from Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, through Indian Pass in the northwestern part of Florida in anticipation of torrential downpours and the substantial risk of localised flash and urban flooding.
A rainfall total of 3-6 inches is forecast with isolated peaks up to 10 inches.
“We are expecting Isaias to be a dangerous hurricane when it makes landfall,” Michael Brennan, director of the National Hurricane Center, said in a Thursday morning update, adding that he expects “up to near-major hurricane strength” by Friday as the storm pounds north of Mexico’s Yucatan Peninsula.
On Thursday morning, Isaias was packing maximum sustained winds of nearly 130km/h (80mph) with higher gusts. Heavy rain and flash flooding also threaten the inland areas throughout the weekend, extending as far as the Tennessee Valley and potentially encompassing a broad stretch from the inland southeast up through the southern Appalachian Mountains.
Ahead of the storm, oil and gas producers shut down a significant share of offshore production in the US Gulf, which accounts for almost 15 percent of crude pumped annually in the US.
As of Wednesday, about 25 percent of the oil production in the region had been temporarily halted, taking about 511,000 barrels a day off the market, according to the Marine Minerals Administration. It said eight of the Gulf’s 371 manned oil platforms had been evacuated.
With oil prices already high, the production cuts are steep enough to affect markets, though other Gulf hurricanes have caused larger disruptions, said Jim Burkhard, global head of crude oil market research for S&P Global Energy. More concerning, he said, is whether Isaias strikes as a powerful storm near refineries.
When Isaias was first declared a hurricane on Wednesday, it marked the latest date for an Atlantic season’s first hurricane in 121 years, falling just short of the record set in 1905, according to data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The season normally runs from June 1 through November 30.

Trump promises not to attack Iran before November’s US midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
17:56:44 UTC
02:56:44 KST

Donald Trump has promised not to attack Iran before November’s US midterm elections, outlining a pause on the protracted war he has struggled to end after almost eight months.
In a Truth Social post on Thursday, the US president said Washington was “having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran”, which he claimed was “in very bad condition, both Economically and Militarily”.
The strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas passed through before the war, was all but closed after the US and Israel struck Iran in late February.
On Thursday, however, Trump suggested that oil was moving through the strait in record volumes: “22 Million Barrels, last night alone”, he claimed, “with not one barrel coming from, or going to, Iran”. The figure could not be independently verified.
“We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd,” Trump wrote. “IRAN WILL NOT HAVE A NUCLEAR WEAPON!”
The US first imposed a blockade on the strait of Hormuz in April after talks in Islamabad collapsed, and reinstated it in July after a short-lived June deal to end the fighting. Fighting flared again in early September, when US forces struck rocket launchers on Iran’s Larak Island and Tehran responded with missiles aimed at American military bases in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates.
Trump’s public position on the elections has shifted over the past month. On 2 September, as the US exchanged fire with Iran for the first time in weeks, he told reporters he was “not affected by the election”, adding that he was not on the ballot himself but intended to help his party.
A week later, before heading to the Republican “midterm convention” in Dallas, he said he expected the war to end almost as soon as the voting was over, and accused Tehran of holding out in the hope that a change of power in Congress would leave it free to pursue a nuclear weapon. He also conceded that US oil prices were unlikely to fall before polling day.
A Reuters/Ipsos survey from late September found that only about a third of Americans approved of the strikes on Iran, while more than four in five expected the conflict to last for an extended period, and that approval for Trump among Republicans had fallen from 82% to 73% in a week.
Polling averages now show Democrats leading Republicans by roughly nine points on the generic congressional ballot, according to forecaster Nate Silver, the widest margin of this election cycle.
The Wall Street Journal reported in September that JD Vance, the US vice-president, and secretary of state Marco Rubio had privately warned Trump the conflict could extend through the remainder of his presidency.
Trump’s post did not say what the US would do after 3 November.

Ex-ILVA furnaces to shut down Friday

The furnaces of the troubled former
ILVA steelworks in Taranto will be shut down Friday after a
Milan court on Monday rejected a second petition against the
order.
                                    
Lay-off notices will start to be issued.
                                    
The government-appointed administrators of the plant and AdI
S.p.A., the company that owns it, had requested a suspension
pending a decision by the supreme the Court of Cassation on the
appeal against the closure of the facility's hot area.
                                    
The Cassation is set to hold a hearing on the case on October
20.
                                    
The original decision was made in July, when a Milan court
upheld a motion presented on health grounds by members of a
parents' association and a child with a rare genetic mutation
and said that activity at the hot area must stop within three
months unless all the asbestos on the site is removed and
measures to bring particulate emissions within safe limits are
taken.
                                    
The ruling ramped up existing uncertainty about the future of
the plant and implementation of a plan to decarbonize it and
make it electric, with fears thousands of jobs could be lost.
                                    
Italy's steel federation Federacciai said in August that its
board has tasked its president, Antonio Gozzi, to express an
interest in taking over the former ILVA steelworks with the
authorities on behalf of a consortium of Italian companies.
                                    
Premier Giorgia Meloni's government has not ruled out State
involvement.
                                    
Indian group Jindal, Czech group CE industries, and US-based
private investment group Flacks have also expressed interest in
buying the plant.
                                    
The Taranto factory, once Europe's biggest steelworks, has been
dogged by economic problems in recent years and linked to high
cancer rates in the Puglia port city.
                                    
ADI was put into State-controlled administration early in 2024
after ArcelorMittal's ownership of the group ended
acrimoniously.

Trump made ‘clear’ that media ban was due to critical coverage, court told
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
17:56:04 UTC
02:56:04 KST

Donald Trump continues to be the strongest witness for the media companies arguing that they were unfairly barred from the White House at his direction, a lawyer representing CNN, MS Now and Politico told a federal judge on Thursday afternoon.
The media coalition was in court asking the judge to extend the temporary restraining order (TRO) he issued on 24 September requiring the White House to lift the ban for 14 days. That temporary reprieve was scheduled to expire on Thursday, but district court judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, said he would extend it until Tuesday and that he would probably rule on a motion for a preliminary injunction by that day. That means the White House will be forced to allow journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico to continue accessing the building until at least Tuesday.
Theodore J Boutrous, who has represented numerous media companies that have sued the Trump administration over access issues, said the president made abundantly clear in a recent interview with Time magazine that he chose to bar the three news organizations because of their critical coverage of him. (Under binding court precedent, news organizations cannot be removed from the White House for editorial or viewpoint-based reasons.)
Asked by Time for the “impetus” for the ban, Trump replied: “It’s just bad story after bad story, and when I say bad story, I can handle bad stories. I’ve got a lot of bad stories. Most of them are fake, and it’s not only CNN, and it’s not only MSDNC [sic]. It’s a lot of other people.” He made no mention of national security concerns, one of the primary reasons that has been given by government lawyers as a rationale for the ban.
“The case has gotten stronger for the plaintiffs thanks to President Trump,” Boutrous told the judge, citing what he said was “a confession of viewpoint discrimination and retaliation”. He added: “It’s really just absolutely clear … President Trump, to give him credit – he’s not hiding it.”
While the judge didn’t give a strong indication of which direction he was leaning, he accepted Boutrous’s argument when questioning the lone lawyer representing the White House, Michael Velchik.
“The decision-maker seems to have said I’m taking this action because of X and Y, and the government is saying: ‘No, it’s Z,’” the judge said. “It just seems like that fact pattern is a hard one around.”
Velchik, who began his argument by saying “the White House is a sacred place,” said a failure to adhere to basic standards of journalistic conduct was also one of the precipitating factors in the decision, something he said was in line with Trump’s comments criticizing the way that these three specific news organizations operate.
He also faulted the media companies for not responding to post-hoc letters giving the plaintiffs a chance to rebut the charges against them, something that Boutrous later described as a “sham process”.
In his ruling granting a TRO for the media plaintiffs, Kelly said the White House had violated constitutional requirements for due process by not giving the companies adequate notice for what the standards for acceptable conduct are and not giving them a chance to protest against the potential sanction in advance.
Nothing from Thursday’s hearing seemed to indicate that the judge had changed his thinking on that important standard, suggesting he is likely to adhere to his earlier decision-making and extend the lifting of the ban.
The judge told the government’s lawyer that they “still have a notice problem, it seems to [him], or at least a notice issue”. Kelly said the standards for adequate advance notice laid out in a binding circuit case involving a similar White House access issue “are probably the biggest hurdle you have”.

- At least 33 dead after Russian glide bomb strikes Kramatorsk buses
- Russian drone barrage on Kyiv kills 4, injures 19, disrupts electricity, water supplies
- Polish SIM cards found in Russian drones downed in Poland
- US, Russia confirm Trump's latest Ukraine peace push is falling apart
- Ukraine strikes Russia's Omsk oil refinery in Siberia, General Staff confirms
- UK ramps up sanctions against Russian shadow fleet, crypto industry, big oil
A Russian glide bomb strike on two minibuses in Kramatorsk killed 33 people on the morning of Oct. 8, Ukraine's emergency service (DSNS) said.
Twenty-two more people were injured in the Russian attack, Donetsk regional governor Vadym Filashkin said. Fire broke out in at least two busses following the Russian strikes, according to DSNS.
"Russia comes to the Ukrainian land with death. She hits our cities, kills our people and multiplies her crimes every day," Filashkin said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said that doctors were still fighting for the lives of some of the injured people and warned that the number of dead may still increase. Two dead people could not yet be identified due to the severity of their injuries, he added.
"This strike will not go without our response. Russia is trying to destroy all life in Donbas, and the world needs to react to this," Zelensky said.
The Kramatorsk and Sloviansk military administrations ordered the stop of all public transport.
"The Russians are targeting civilians. For them, a bus with passengers is an attractive target precisely because one hit can kill as many people as possible," Filashkin said.
Across Ukraine's Donetsk Oblast, four more people had been killed and six injured by Russian attacks as of the morning of Oct. 8, prior to the Kramatorsk strike, according to the governor.
In total, Russian forces shelled settlements in the Donetsk region 31 times over the last day, and 256 people, including 32 children, were evacuated from the front line, according to the Donetsk governor.

Shortly after, KMDA announced that the right bank of Kyiv may experience interruptions in water supply, as the power decrease in the electricity grid also meant a decrease in pressure of the water supply network. This applied especially to the Holosiivskyi, Sviatoshynskyi, Solomyanskyi and Shevchenkivskyi districts.
The drop in voltage from external power supply centers also temporarily halted Kyiv Metro train services and escalator operations, the KMDA said.
DSNS also said that a fire broke out at a logistics facility in the Buchanskyi district in Kyiv Oblast following a Russian drone strike.
In Sviatopetrivske in Buchanskyi district, a school-kindergarten and a nearby playground in a residential complex were damaged in the attack, Kyiv Oblast Governor Tymur Tkachenko said. In another settlement in the district, a woman was injured and hospitalized, he added.

US, Russia confirm Trump's latest Ukraine peace push is falling apart
Ending Russia's war against Ukraine through negotiations is currently unattainable, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Greek media outlet Kathimerini on Oct. 8, casting further doubt on President Donald Trump's latest push to broker peace.
The comments confirm earlier Kyiv Independent reporting that Washington's latest effort to advance negotiations faces growing uncertainty.
At this point, there appears to be no prospect of a negotiated settlement, Rubio said. He added that the goal remains out of reach because Russia insists on gaining full control over Ukraine's Donetsk Oblast without fighting, a demand Kyiv has rejected.
The latest rounds of peace negotiations have also stalled over Moscow's territorial demands.
The Kremlin has repeatedly rejected a ceasefire and demanded that Kyiv surrender the partially occupied Donbas, a strategically important region in eastern Ukraine. Moscow is effectively seeking territory that Russian forces have failed to capture militarily.
Ukraine has instead called for a ceasefire along the current front line.
The diplomatic effort now faces another obstacle: Moscow has given little indication that it intends to take part in further talks. Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov said on Oct. 7 that there were currently no plans for U.S.-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine.
"There are currently no plans to hold talks in this format," Ryabkov told reporters.
The latest effort began in early September, when Trump's envoys traveled to Kyiv and Moscow seeking progress before the U.S. midterm elections. The trips produced one tangible outcome: an agreement in principle to hold a trilateral meeting between Ukraine, Russia, and the U.S.
A month later, however, even the trilateral meeting remains uncertain.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Oct. 8 that Ukrainian negotiators will meet with Trump's envoys in the U.S. later this week to discuss the prospects for peace talks with Russia.

Ukraine strikes Russia's Omsk oil refinery in Siberia, General Staff confirms
Ukraine's General Staff confirmed that its forces struck Russia's Omsk oil refinery in Russia's Omsk Oblast on Oct. 8.
"The destruction of such facilities is the exercise by Ukraine of its inalienable right to self-defense in accordance with Article 51 of the UN Charter and is aimed at reducing the military-economic potential of the Russian Federation," the General Staff said.
Ukrainian drone manufacturer Fire Point had previously reported an attack on the refinery, saying that the refinery was hit with its own long-range FP-1 attack drones.
Videos and images from local residents, shared by Ukrainian monitoring channels, show explosions, fire, and smoke rising from the area surrounding the oil refinery.
Omsk Oblast Governor Vitaly Khotsenko confirmed that there was a drone attack on the region. Ukrainian authorities have not yet confirm a strike on the refinery.
Omsk is located in southwestern Siberia, north of the Kazakh border. The city of more than 1 million people is some 2,500 kilometers (about 1,550 miles) east of Ukraine controlled territory.
The Omsk oil refinery is owned by Russia's state-owned energy giant Gazprom. It's the country's largest refinery by refining capacity, processing more than 21 million metric tons of crude oil per year.
The plant produces a wide range of fuels, lubricants, and petrochemical products and is involved in supplying the Russian military, Ukraine's General Staff said after Ukraine struck the refinery on July 6. According to the military, the facility has a refining depth of about 99%, one of the highest rates in Russia.

UK ramps up sanctions against Russian shadow fleet, crypto industry, big oil
The U.K. published 38 new sanctions listings on Oct. 8, targeting ships helping Russia evade existing sanctions and a range of companies in Moscow's military-industrial complex, energy, and cryptocurrency sectors.
"The message is simple: if you help Russia fund or equip this war, you will face the consequences," reads a U.K. government press release.
Among the businesses in the new sanctions listings are three cryptocurrency exchanges and two payment platforms.
Xeltox Enterprises, one of those listed entities has "been involved in obtaining a benefit from or supporting the government of Russia by carrying on business in a sector of strategic significance (...) the financial services sector," reads the U.K. government's sanctions listing.
Russia has increasingly sought to use cryptocurrency, which is hard to track, to circumvent global sanctions, and the new U.K. sanctions target the "A7" network, which is at the heart of Moscow's attempts to evade financial sanctions.
That has prompted the U.K., the U.S., the EU, and Ukraine to target crypto schemes in recent sanctions packages.
Also featuring on the listings are two further oil companies: Zarubezhneft and INK Capital.
"The U.K. was the first country in the G7 to sanction the top four Russian oil companies," reads the press statement.
The U.K. has also added 12 ships to its list of sanctioned vessels accused of being part of Russia's shadow fleet — dilapidated vessels suspected of helping Moscow evade price caps and bans on its trade in oil and gas.
That takes the number of ships sanctioned by the U.K. to 645 and the total number of Russia sanctions to 3,537.

Wired for War: The German spymaster caught in Mossad’s web
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
17:53:45 UTC
02:53:45 KST

Wired for War: The German spymaster caught in Mossad’s web
It took a bungled kidnapping for Germany’s former spymaster to be charged with espionage and treason, but August Hanning’s ties to Israeli spies and criminals should have set alarm bells ringing in Berlin long ago.
Hanning, who led Germany’s Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND) from 1998 to 2005, was arrested on Tuesday and charged with espionage, the disclosure of state secrets, and treason.
Prosecutors have alleged that Hanning bought state secrets from his former BND aide – identified as ‘Manfred D’, who remained in the agency after Hanning’s departure and served several of his successors. They claim Hanning acquired nearly 2,000 BND documents between 2010 and 2022, which he then leveraged in his work as a private security consultant at-large to the rich and powerful.
Hanning, part of the woodwork on the security conference circuit, used this material to prepare a report for an employee of a foreign intelligence service, and maintained “close contact with a representative of another foreign intelligence service,” to whom he passed information obtained by Manfred D “for several years.”
Prosecutors haven’t publicly identified which foreign services Hanning collaborated with, though media reporting suggests one is believed to be the Foreign Intelligence Service of Azerbaijan, a country Hanning has openly lobbied for since the mid-2010s. As for the other, Hanning’s involvement in a bizarre kidnapping plot suggests one obvious culprit.
The Israeli kidnapping plot
German investigators picked up Hanning’s trail last September, when Hamburg police searched his apartment as part of an investigation involving multi-millionaire Christina Block, whose father built Germany’s most popular steakhouse chain, as well as a burger franchise, boutique hotels and gastro-resorts.
Ms. Block has been in a custody dispute with her ex-husband, Danish banker Stefan Hansel, since 2021. She is currently on trial for ordering the kidnapping of her two youngest children from their father’s care in Denmark. According to prosecutors, Block hired Hanning’s consulting firm, System 360, to carry out the abduction in 2022, but Danish police intervened before the System 360 team could snatch the children.
Hanning apparently gave up on the direct approach and decided to outsource the job to his contacts from the world of intelligence. These contacts were Yaakov Perry, the former chief of Israel’s Shin Bet domestic intelligence agency, and Danny Yatom, the former head of Mossad.
Block’s trial is ongoing and details are murky, but the allegations are as follows: Hanning hired Perry and his private intelligence firm, CGI Group, to assemble an eight-man team to kidnap the children; the German spymaster requested that Yatom be involved; Perry brought in David Barkay, a former member of the IDF’s Unit 504 intelligence wing and alleged Mossad agent; Barkay led the team that carried out the kidnapping on New Year’s Eve, 2023.
Barkay’s team assaulted Hansel and dragged the children – a ten-year-old boy and 13-year-old girl – across the German border on foot, taping their mouths shut and threatening to kill them if they screamed for help.
Hanning denies any role in the kidnapping, as does Yaakov. Barkay has confessed to orchestrating and carrying out the operation, but has not implicated Hanning or Yaakov. Yatom has told Israeli media that he has “no connection to this case,” and furthermore, that his relationship with Hanning was a strictly professional one dating back to the late 1980s.
However, Yatom invited Hanning to join the board of his private cybersecurity company, World Health Energy Holdings (WHEN), in 2021. Speaking to the Jerusalem Post at the time, Hanning said that his “contacts with states, law enforcement and intelligence agencies” would be valuable to WHEN, a company that markets spyware to businesses seeking to monitor their employees.
Hanning added that he maintained “very close working relationships, even friendships” with Yatom and other Mossad officials long after he left the BND. Both men are still listed as board members on WHEN’s website.
The gray man
During his tenure at the BND, Hanning was the consummate ‘gray man’ of intelligence: a gaunt and bespectacled bureaucrat in the mould of John le Carre’s ‘George Smiley’. Le Carre met Hanning several times, and described the German spymaster as “courtesy itself.”
Yet his “career was clouded by speculation about his loyalties, with persistent whispers of too-close-for-comfort ties to Israel and Russia,” according to a recent Irish Times report. Prosecutors have ruled out any suspicion that Hanning colluded with Russian agents, according to German media, leaving only one possibility.
Hanning once remarked that “a good agent is one who doesn’t draw attention to himself.” In the murky world of Israel’s ‘private’ intelligence sector, however, Hanning could hardly have chosen a more conspicuous duo to work with than Yatom and Perry.
The Congo debacle
Perry’s private intelligence firm, CGI Group, is an outfit that will sound familiar to readers of our ‘Wired for War’ series. Founded by former Israeli spies and specializing in illegal or quasi-legal private spycraft, the company boasts that it hires “senior personnel from elite IDF units, the General Security Services and the Mossad.” Among them are:
- Yaakov Perry, president, Shin Bet Director from 1988 to 1995
- Zvika Nave, founder, described by CGI as serving “in many classified positions in the defense system”
- Oren Ziv, Italy manager, described by CGI as a “key figure in Israeli diplomacy and national security”
- Alon Pinkas, consultant, former foreign policy adviser to Israeli Prime Ministers Ehud Barak and Shimon Peres, former Israeli Consul General in New York
Before its alleged involvement in the Block kidnapping, CGI Group became infamous when it attempted to steal $60 million from the Bulgarian government in 2019. Some 30 years earlier, Israeli businessman Gad Zeevi attempted to buy a stake in Bulgaria’s national airline, but the deal fell apart and Zeevi claimed that he was owed $10 million in compensation from Sofia. International arbitrators agreed, but Bulgaria refused to comply with the judgment, and the Israeli government refused to chase the Bulgarians down for the money.
Zeevi reached out to Perry and Nave, who came up with a long-shot scheme to collect the debt. CGI Group would ask the government of the Congo to order $60 million worth of weapons from Bulgaria, with Yatom acting as a go-between. Once the Bulgarians had sent the arms and the Congolese government transferred the money to his account, Yatom would hand it to Zeevi, minus a generous cut for him and his co-conspirators in CGI Group.
It was never clear how CGI would convince the Congolese to order weapons that would never be paid for, and the plan never came to fruition. Zeevi and CGI Group threatened to sue each other for damages, but the case never made it to court.
Yatom and CGI Group refused to comment, giving similar answers as they did when questioned about the Block kidnapping. “I don’t want to talk about my business activities,” Yatom told Israel’s Globes news outlet in 2022. “We don’t talk to the media,” Nave said.
Red flags ignored
Despite the fact that Yatom and the CGI spies colluded to defraud a NATO and EU member state in 2019, German investigators didn’t ask questions when Hanning joined Yatom’s company two years later. No investigation was opened when he spoke to the Israeli media of his “close friendship” with the former Mossad chief behind the swindle. Hanning’s ties to the Israeli intelligence underworld, apparently the subject of “persistent whispers” in the corridors of the BND, were evidently brushed aside or ignored.
None of this is to say that Shin Bet or Mossad is, without a doubt, the “foreign intelligence service” that Hanning passed secrets to. However, his contacts with Perry and Yatom certainly point that way, as does his work to advance Israeli foreign policy goals.
Hanning aided Israeli efforts to push the US into war with Iraq in late 2002, when he told then-CIA Director George Tenet that the BND had “plausible and convincing” evidence that Saddam Hussein was developing chemical and biological weapons. Hanning’s source, an Iraqi defector codenamed ‘Curveball’, later admitted to fabricating the claims.
Hanning now sits on the board of ‘United Against Nuclear Iran’, a Washington-based think tank funded by pro-Israel megadonors Miriam Adelson and Thomas Kaplan, which has explicitly advocated for military strikes on Iran since 2008. Adelson and Kaplan supply around three quarters of the group’s funding, with the remainder coming from smaller Jewish organizations and individual donors.
Europe’s wilful ignorance
Anyone following our ‘Wired for War’ series will recognize the pattern here. Over and over again, the actions of private Israeli spy firms are ignored by European governments, even when the Israeli state itself is involved in the skulduggery. The British government has refused to investigate Israeli meddling in Scottish elections, in order to “avoid giving offense” to the perpetrators. The EU has stayed silent on Israeli interference in elections in Cyprus and Slovenia, and on the proliferation of Israeli spyware throughout the union.
Meanwhile, governments at the EU and national level continue to sound the alarm about Russia’s invisible and unprovable “hybrid war” against the West. Fires, false drone sightings, and even natural disasters are all presented as examples of this shadow war, while the most blatant malfeasance from other foreign powers is ignored.
One day before Hanning’s arrest, his successor at the helm of the BND, Martin Jaeger, warned German MPs that Russia is “waging a shadow war,” and that “no other country currently poses such a direct, comprehensive, and concrete threat to Germany.” Had he looked at the company August Hanning kept, he might have reassessed his position.

Callous Kallas: The bitter diplomat dragging the EU down the warpath with Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
17:53:32 UTC
02:53:32 KST

Callous Kallas: The bitter diplomat dragging the EU down the warpath with Russia
Kaja Kallas, the Estonian diplomat and former prime minister currently serving as the vice-president of the European Commission, has shown a deeply confrontational attitude towards Russia and the Russians.
It is perhaps worth pausing here to note that this is particularly personal, given her family history. Her mother, Kristi Kallas, was only six months old when she, together with her mother and grandmother, was deported to Siberia during the Soviet mass deportations of March 1949. She remained there until she was ten, and later studied medicine and worked as a pediatrician.
Her father, Siim Kallas, had a very different experience with the Soviet system. He was a member of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union from 1972 to 1990 and held senior positions in the financial system of Soviet Estonia, including heading the Estonian branch of the USSR Savings Bank. He later became President of the Bank of Estonia, Prime Minister of Estonia and a Vice-President of the European Commission.
These two sides of her family history – one marked by deportation and the other by a successful career within the Soviet system – form a striking background to Kaja Kallas’s present-day political position.
Last month, Kallas described the German people as being blind to the Russian threat because of their resistance to providing further financial support to Ukraine. Now, I suppose Russian people are also considered blind because of the convincing victory of President Vladimir Putin’s party in September’s legislative election. I am definitely not blind.
Kaja Kallas is not alone in her hostility towards Russia. Other senior EU officials, including European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, have supported substantial financial and military assistance to Ukraine. The EU has committed up to €90 billion in support for Ukraine for 2026 and 2027, including funding for both defense and general budgetary needs.
The question Europeans should be allowed to ask is how these decisions affect their own societies. Public money is limited, and European citizens also need investment in healthcare, education, transport, housing and infrastructure.
Since 2022, Europeans have been paying a heavy price for the transformation of their energy system. The decision to move away from Russian pipeline gas was made in the name of security, and the EU has succeeded in diversifying its supplies. But security has come at a considerable economic cost. The European Commission reports that although wholesale energy prices have fallen substantially from the extraordinary peaks of 2022, industrial gas and electricity prices remain two to four times higher than in the EU’s main trading partners. The Commission warns that this continues to threaten the long-term competitiveness of European industry.
The EU’s energy import bill reached €604 billion in 2022 before falling to €427 billion in 2024. Meanwhile, industrial energy prices remain considerably above their pre-crisis levels. Germany, the industrial heart of Europe, has felt the consequences particularly sharply. German industrial energy consumption fell by 9.1% in 2022 and another 7.8% in 2023, with the German Federal Statistical Office explicitly linking these declines, particularly in energy-intensive industries, to significantly higher energy prices and associated production reductions.
Germany’s broader economic performance tells the same story. Its economy contracted for a second consecutive year in 2024, while manufacturing gross value added fell by 3%. The Federal Statistical Office identified high energy costs, together with stronger international competition and other structural pressures, among the factors weighing on the economy. Manufacturing remained under pressure in 2025, when value added in the sector fell another 1.3%.
Europe faces an uncomfortable question: Is it prepared to accept permanently higher energy costs while production and investment increasingly move towards countries where energy and manufacturing costs are lower? It is one thing to pursue energy security; it is another to allow the foundations of European industry to become the price of achieving it.
The issue of NATO and Ukraine is equally contentious. The argument that NATO expansion towards Ukraine ruined Moscow’s relations with Europe is not just a Kremlin talking point – reputable Western analysts, like Professor Jeffrey Sachs, have repeatedly argued the same point. Even if that analysis remains disputed, it is an argument that deserves to be heard in any serious discussion of the origins and continuation of the war, which continues to have devastating consequences for Ukrainians.
European leaders should be asking what policies can bring the conflict closer to a negotiated settlement rather than simply allowing the confrontation to continue indefinitely.
Perhaps the most revealing part of this story is that the argument is no longer simply between the EU and its critics. It has begun to unfold within Europe itself.
Defense spending in the EU is rising at an extraordinary pace. According to the Council of the EU, member states spent €418 billion on defense in 2025, and expenditure is estimated to reach €454 billion in 2026 – 75.3% higher than in 2021. Defense investment alone is projected to reach almost €163 billion in 2026.
But the question of who decides how this enormous effort should be organized is becoming increasingly contentious. In September, Kaja Kallas withdrew plans for a new high-level advisory group on European defense after several member states objected. Reporting by Defense News and Euractiv identified Germany, France and Italy among the governments pushing back against the initiative. The German position was that NATO remains the primary framework for military capability and defense planning.
The disagreement was not about whether Europe needs defense. It was about who should set priorities, how decisions should be coordinated, and whether another Brussels structure was the right way forward. Even as European governments prepare to spend hundreds of billions more on defense, there is no agreement about the political direction those resources should serve.
The EU, in other words, is having two conversations at once: how much it should spend, and what kind of Europe that spending is meant to create.
Ms. Kallas, Europe needs diplomacy as well as security policy. European citizens need their governments to protect their interests, use public money responsibly and keep open the possibility of a peaceful future.
If the EU continues indefinitely along the present path, the economic and political consequences for European societies will deserve much greater public discussion.
EU citizens have the right to ask difficult questions about how their money is being spent and what kind of Europe they want to build. They may disagree strongly about Russia, Ukraine and NATO, but that does not make their questions illegitimate.
I was born in Ireland and have been affiliated with Russia for thirty years. I have been living here for the last eight years. From that perspective, I believe Europeans should be able to discuss these issues without being dismissed as blind, naïve or sympathetic to one side simply because they question current policies.
Europe has enormous resources and enormous human potential. With wiser choices about priorities, Europeans should be able to expect excellent healthcare, education, transport and infrastructure alongside a responsible security policy.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.

Diia explains how to file Europrotocol in event of traffic accident
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
20:52:45 EEST
02:52:45 KST

The Diia app now features a function for filing a Europrotocol report, which allows users to report a traffic accident via their smartphone without calling the patrol police or filling out a paper form.
According to a statement from the Diia press service on Thursday, to use the service, users must update the Diia app and navigate to the "Services," "Driver," and "Europrotocol" sections.
Next, users should verify the details; specifically, information about the drivers, vehicles, and insurance policies will be automatically retrieved from government registries.
The press service added that drivers will need to fill out the details of the accident and upload photos of the damaged vehicles at the scene. Subsequently, drivers will receive the other driver's consent and signature via a QR code or a notification in the Diia app.
It is noted that after completing these preliminary steps, users will need to sign the document using Diia.Sign and submit it. It is expected that after both parties have successfully signed the document, the app will automatically submit the Europrotocol to the Motor Transport Insurance Bureau of Ukraine (MTIBU), and MTIBU will subsequently forward it to the insurance companies.
"Next, contact your insurance company for further instructions," Diia said.
According to the press release, before filing the claim, you should ensure that no one is injured, that only two vehicles were involved in the accident, that neither driver is under the influence of alcohol or drugs, that both have valid MTPL insurance policies, and that they have reached an agreement regarding the circumstances of the accident.
It is expected that drivers who have the following in Diia at the same time can complete the Europrotocol: a verified RNOKPP (IPN), a digital passport (ID card), foreign passport, or residence permit, a driver's license, and a vehicle registration certificate – as the owner or authorized user – as well as a valid MTPL policy for the vehicle involved in the accident.
"In other cases, fill out a paper Europrotocol or call the police," Diia said.

The Guardian view on cancers in under-50s: the risks of obesity must be confronted | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
17:50:05 UTC
02:50:05 KST

The latest findings about the rise in cancers in people under 50, from the World Cancer Research Fund (WCRF), are extremely concerning. While a cancer diagnosis is bad news at any time, it is a particular blow for those in younger age groups where most people are in good health. Overlapping trends observed in England, the Netherlands and the US include a troubling rise in the incidence of colorectal (or bowel) cancer. Other diseases that have increased in England include uterine and kidney cancers.
These diseases are still rare in young people: 10 times more adults in their 50s, 60s and 70s are diagnosed than those in their 20s, 30s and 40s. Earlier detection is thought to be one factor behind the rise in younger patients. Diagnosing more cancers sooner is an explicit policy goal in England, where late diagnosis and lower uptake of screening are two reasons for mortality rates that are higher than elsewhere in Europe.
But diagnostic improvements are unfortunately not the main reason for increased cases. While research is ongoing and many questions remain, evidence points to obesity and poor diet causing cancers as well as heart disease and type 2 diabetes. The Prospect-UK trial is currently seeking 250,000 participants for a longitudinal study into early-onset (under-50) bowel cancer. It will scrutinise information about nutrition in more detail than has been done previously, including what people are eating less of.
The success of international efforts to cut lung cancer through targeting smoking set a powerful precedent for public health campaigning. This took longer than it should have done, due to tobacco industry lobbying. But it remains the gold standard of regulation combined with messaging, to bring about behaviour change. The WCRF data shows that lung cancer rates in under-50s have continued falling.
So far, efforts to cut obesity have had nothing like the same impact. The patterns are not the same everywhere; one recent study found that in some countries a rapid rise had been replaced by a levelling-off. But English-speaking countries have some of the worst records, and the lack of strong action in the UK is among the big disappointments of health policy in the last decade.
Politicians from Boris Johnson to Wes Streeting have committed to obesity action plans, only to water them down in the face of opposition from the food and drink industries. Last year, scientists wrote to Mr Streeting to protest that the government had done “virtually nothing” to alert consumers to the carcinogenic properties of the nitrites added to bacon and ham.
There is a grim irony in dramatic advances in cancer research and treatment coinciding with the rise in early-onset cancers. For many doctors and patients, this a period of hope. But politicians and health bosses must guard against a situation in which some groups have improved prospects, while others face increased risks linked to socioeconomic disadvantages.
In relation to obesity and diet, the close link with poverty points to the need for ministers to view public spending holistically, and to recognise that the NHS is not the only institution with the capacity to improve health. While more research into early-onset cancers is needed, existing data tells us a great deal. Governments should be as bold in tackling the causes of obesity as they once were in confronting big tobacco.
