The Guardian view on Ethiopia’s return to conflict: civilian catastrophe and a spiralling regional polycrisis | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
17:49:38 UTC
02:49:38 KST

When the Nobel peace laureate is announced on Friday, the committee will be hoping that its choice ages better than 2019’s. Ethiopia’s prime minister, Abiy Ahmed, won the prize for ending the 20-year border conflict with neighbouring Eritrea – signing a peace agreement with President Isaias Afwerki. A year later, their new relationship facilitated a war with the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) that killed as many as 600,000 people, displaced millions more, led to atrocities by both sides, and pushed Tigrayans into famine.
Both sides bear responsibility for failing to properly implement the deal that ended that conflict in 2022, and the African Union and US did little to ensure that a piece of paper became a durable settlement. Now violence has resurged in northern Ethiopia, and old foes are forming bizarre new pacts. Last month, seven Ethiopian regional groups announced an “Alliance for Survival” to remove the federal government. Mr Abiy’s coalition is held together by his patronage, but so far may be faring better than his rivals, united solely by shared loathing of him and riven by deep disputes. The TPLF, which controls Tigray, has previously battled the Fano militia of Amhara, and their territorial dispute endures. Ethiopia accuses Eritrea – previously accused of atrocities against Tigrayan civilians – of backing the rebel alliance. Despite Asmara’s denials, there are multiple reports of Eritrean troops in Tigray.
The Ethiopian prime minister demands his landlocked country should gain access to the Red Sea, to Eritrea’s concern and anger. The Eritrean president’s control of the coastline, opposite Houthi-held stretches of Yemen, means that Washington is now keen to engage with his regime and unlikely to challenge him. Ethiopia’s complex internal politics are interlocking with geopolitical turmoil. Addis Ababa also accuses Egypt and Sudan of backing the TPLF. They deny it, but Cairo is furious over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance dam on the Nile. Khartoum too fears losing water, and says Ethiopia is supporting the RSF rebels in the civil war (Addis Ababa denies it). The UAE, having lost a foothold in Yemen, has increased support for Ethiopia.
The concern now is not merely the grave risk of full-scale war within Ethiopia, or between Ethiopia and Eritrea, but that a spiralling regional polycrisis is hitting already beleaguered communities. Agricultural production has not recovered from the last war. Now the fertiliser and fuel crisis born of the Iran war, the evisceration of aid budgets and the impact of El Niño are intensifying the crisis. The UK and others must urgently provide humanitarian support.
Though the escalating violence is alarming, with hundreds reportedly killed, this conflict has not yet fully ignited. In 2020, Tigrayans believed they had to unify for collective survival. This time the TPLF itself is deeply split, with veteran commanders reportedly arrested for questioning the new war, and soldiers and civilians showing little appetite for a conflict fuelled by factionalised, self-serving and corrupt leaders. A truce is not impossible and must be a priority. Ethiopia needs relief, reconstruction and a political reconfiguration. But its conflict cannot be separated from the broader picture, as wars in Sudan, Somalia, Yemen, Iran and beyond enmesh to devastating effect. The longer that ambitious leaders convince themselves that interference elsewhere can advance their own power and resources, the deeper and more intractable it will become.

Lithuania plans to deploy up to 100 soldiers to support border guards along its frontier with Russia's Kaliningrad Oblast, Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas said on 7 October.
Lithuanian Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas has described the deployment as a preventive measure linked to possible Russian mobilization and a recent incident on the Latvia-Belarus border, where masked, armed escorts tried to push a group of migrants into Latvia. Katelynas said Lithuania could face people trying to avoid mobilization and seeking asylum.
Kaunas said he had granted permission to use Lithuanian soldiers to strengthen border protection for the next several weeks.
“The order starts being implemented immediately,” he wrote on Facebook.
Russia denies a new mobilization
The Kremlin denies a new mobilization is coming. In early September, Russian President Vladimir Putin called reports of one "complete nonsense" and "an information attack on Russia." Ukraine's military and foreign intelligence services say Russia's General Staff has prepared a scenario to mobilize 600,000 people over 2026 and 2027. On 28 September, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that "in effect, the Russians have already begun additional mobilization."
Frontier-station patrols for a couple of weeks, possibly longer
On 8 October, the Lithuanian army said soldiers were being brought in to help the State Border Guard Service from that day. A company-sized unit was planned for the assignment, initially for two weeks, with the option to extend. Soldiers will patrol with border guards in frontier-station areas, while mobile patrols, mobile observation posts, and military police crews may be added as needed. The army described the deployment as preventive and a normal form of interagency cooperation.
Kaunas had told LRT TV the soldiers would stay until 16 October. On the morning of 8 October, he said the deployment "was supposed to start" overnight and that he would check with the army. On 8 October, the Lithuanian army said soldiers were being brought in to help the State Border Guard Service from that day. Kaunas also said that “on the Kaliningrad side” there were no physical barriers, unlike the border with Belarus.
Lithuania says its border guards are stretched
On 8 October, Katelynas said the border guard service’s capacity was insufficient, with shifts growing while officer numbers were not increasing. He said the threat level had not changed. In a Facebook post the previous day, he said the situation at Lithuania’s border was calm and there was no reason to panic. He said Russia was planning mobilization after the elections and that Lithuania may face people trying to avoid it and seeking asylum.
Lithuania's State Border Guard Service had turned back 1,693 people trying to cross illegally from Belarus this year and about 26,300 since the migration crisis began, as reported by ELTA on 8 October. Katelynas said 43 migrants tried to enter southern Lithuania last week and were turned back.

‘Regional proxy contest’: What’s fuelling Ethiopia-Eritrea tensions?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
17:48:13 UTC
02:48:13 KST

Eritrea and Ethiopia, two neighbouring countries in the Horn of Africa, have a long history of conflict in a region of growing strategic importance due to its proximity to the Red Sea and the Bab al Mandab Strait, a vital global maritime chokepoint.
Eritrea’s three-decade war of independence from Ethiopia, fought between 1961 and 1991, resulted in hundreds of thousands of deaths on both sides. Unresolved border disputes later triggered another war between the two countries from 1998 to 2000.
In 2018, the two countries signed a peace agreement that ended the two-decade stalemate. The breakthrough earned Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed the 2019 Nobel Peace Prize.
But the same Ethiopian leader now faces the prospect of another military confrontation with Eritrea, which has reportedly deployed its forces in northern Ethiopian towns as it seeks to align with Tigray rebel forces fighting against Addis Ababa.
“Tensions between the two countries are escalating largely because all sides have their own reasons,” says Yunus Turhan, an associate professor at Haci Bayram Veli University who specialises in Gulf-Africa relations.
According to Turhan, Eritrea's shifting position in Ethiopia's internal conflict, from supporting the central government to backing the Tigray rebels, has coincided with landlocked Ethiopia's ambitions to gain access to the Red Sea, further escalating tensions between the two neighbours.
Current global economic dynamics have made maritime security a geopolitical priority, intensifying competition among regional and global powers over strategic chokepoints such as the Bab al Mandab Strait.
“The Horn of Africa sits on this route giving local disputes wider strategic weight,” pulling both global attention and foreign intervention into its conflicts, says Turhan.
‘Worst assumptions’
Asmara, which was excluded from the 2022 Pretoria peace negotiations between the Abiy government and the Tigray rebels, has closely followed developments in the war-torn Tigray region, which borders Eritrea, according to Turhan.
Although Eritrea supported Abiy's government against Tigray rebels during the previous conflict, its position began to shift as Ethiopia increasingly turned its attention to Assab, a strategically important Eritrean port on the Red Sea.
Despite internal divisions and some defections to the Ethiopian government, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the main rebel group opposing Addis Ababa's policies, has remained active even after the Pretoria agreement, Turhan says.
According to Turhan, Eritrea came to see the TPLF as a natural ally in its efforts to prevent Ethiopia from seizing Assab.
“The timing of the current escalation is hardly coincidental,” he adds, referring to the recent formation of an alliance between the TPLF and six other opposition groups seeking to oust Abiy.
But Turhan also points to Abiy's ability to rally different factions around his leadership by turning contentious issues into national causes.
These range from the construction of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, which heightened tensions with Egypt, to Ethiopia's ambitions for Red Sea access, which have contributed to the current escalation with Eritrea.
On October 5, during a parliamentary speech after being sworn in for another five-year term, Abiy again raised the sensitive issue of Ethiopia's access to the sea. Referring to the country's landlocked status, he said a nation of 150 million people could not live in a "geographic prison", remarks Asmara could interpret as a potential threat.
Ethiopia, meanwhile, may view the formation of the new rebel alliance as evidence of Eritrean interference in its internal affairs.
Against this backdrop of growing mistrust, compounded by the ongoing war in Yemen across the Red Sea from Eritrea, “each move by either side is taken by the other as confirmation of its worst assumptions,” Turhan tells TRT World.
Red Sea access
Eritrea and Ethiopia did not sign a peace treaty after the civil war ended in 1991. Two years later, Eritrea held a referendum that paved the way for its independence.
After the 1993 referendum, the two countries signed the Friendship and Cooperation Agreement and the Transit and Port Services Agreement.
These agreements recognised Eritrea's sovereignty over its Red Sea coastline while granting Ethiopia tax-free and customs-free access to the Eritrean ports of Assab and Massawa.
However, Ethiopia’s current leadership questions the legitimacy of the 1993 agreements, arguing that the transitional authorities at the time lacked the constitutional mandate to make binding decisions concerning the country’s territorial sovereignty, particularly over the port of Assab, says Kaan Devecioğlu, coordinator of North and East African Studies at ORSAM, an Ankara-based Turkish think tank.
“Ethiopia’s current leadership argues that the two countries need to negotiate a new agreement on access to the Red Sea,” Devecioğlu tells TRT World.
He says that reports of Eritrean troops allegedly entering Ethiopian territory, coupled with accusations of Eritrean support for armed opposition groups, could provide Addis Ababa with an opportunity to invoke Article 51 of the UN Charter and frame potential military operations as acts of self-defence.
Under such a scenario, Ethiopia might seek to extend its military operations toward Assab and other strategically important border areas, potentially linking its security concerns to its longstanding ambitions for Red Sea access, he argues.
As tensions escalate in the Horn of Africa, external actors are also playing an increasingly important role in shaping regional dynamics, Devecioğlu notes.
He says that the UAE and Israel, given their strategic ties with Ethiopia, may have interests that align with Addis Ababa's position in its ongoing tensions with Eritrea, although this does not necessarily imply direct involvement or explicit support in the current conflict.
On October 4, the leaders of Eritrea, Somalia, Egypt and Sudan issued the El Alamein Joint Declaration, reaffirming their commitment to regional sovereignty and territorial integrity while asserting that coastal states alone govern the Red Sea.
Sudan has been engulfed in civil war since April 2023, while Somalia has been grappling with Somaliland's separatist ambitions, which have received public backing from Israel.
This can not be "coincidental", says Devecioglu signalling potential support to Eritrea from Somalia, Egypt, which have issues with Ethiopia over its big dam project that might cut Cairo’s access to the Nile River, and Sudan, where UAE back the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) against Sudanese Armed Forces.
Turhan shares Devecioglu's assessment.
He says Egypt has developed an alliance with Eritrea and Somalia, while Saudi Arabia reportedly leans toward Asmara.
According to Turhan, the Al Alamein declaration makes clear that “the Red Sea governance belongs to coastal states alone, a rebuff to Addis Ababa”.
“The Nile dispute and Sudan's war bind these camps together, turning Assab port quarrel into a regional proxy contest,” he says, emphasising that Ethiopia's pursuit of Red Sea access has become both a cause of the latest escalation with Eritrea and a factor intensifying it.
“Open war becomes likely if Eritrean units fight openly inside Tigray or if Ethiopian strikes reach Eritrean soil,” Turhan tells TRT World.
“Any move toward Assab would be the point of no return”, potentially transforming Ethiopia's internal tensions into a direct war with Eritrea and drawing regional powers into the conflict, he adds.

NATO attempts to cool tensions with Russia ahead of key nuclear exercise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
17:47:53 UTC
02:47:53 KST

Crew members of aircraft carrier USS Harry S. Truman are pictured during a NATO vigilance activity in the Mediterranean on May 23, 2022. | Andreas Solaro/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — NATO is seeking to reassure Russia that an upcoming nuclear drill in Italy is nothing to fear, with tensions high between the alliance and Moscow.
NATO announced Thursday that 17 allies will participate in the annual Steadfast Noon exercise from Oct. 13-23. But this year, the exercise follows a tense exchange of letters between Moscow and NATO after allies conducted exercises near Russia’s Kaliningrad exclave in August.
“We have been doing this every year and … this is also a clear message to nations like Russia that there is no need to worry,” said Nassima Barrows, NATO’s nuclear policy director. “This is predictable and there is no reason to miscalculate.”
Advertisement
“Its purpose is really essentially to train our allied forces so that we are ready and prepared, and we ensure the safety and security of our nuclear capability,” she told reporters.
Following the previous NATO exercises, Moscow sent a letter to the alliance threatening to hit allied territory and mentioning the use of its nuclear arsenal — a move that NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte publicly rebuked last week.
Tensions are rising as European countries accuse Russia of sabotage and growing so-called hybrid attacks across the continent.
“Our intention is to really keep things calm,” said a senior NATO official, who was granted anonymity to speak freely. Russian officials “keep ratcheting up this mood of tension and we are going to keep trying to calm the mood.”
U.S. Col. David Bull, chief of NATO’s nuclear operations, said the exercise has garnered “similar” participation to previous years and involves everything from a “simulated alert to [a] live flight exercise” — but “no live nuclear weapons.”
It will also feature dual-capable aircraft and ground troops to support the exercise and train on loading, fueling, and maintaining planes, a senior NATO military official added.
Russia’s embassy to Belgium said that it took note of the NATO statement, but added: "these exercises — given that NATO considers our country as the main threat to security — do not contribute to reducing tensions on the continent and are part of the Alliance's nuclear policy, to which Moscow's negative attitude is well known."

ink traces and rotational gestures shape polkadot design’s visual identity for athens epidaurus festival
polkadot design creates 2026 visual identity for the athens epidaurus festival, one of greece’s most important cultural institutions and one of europe’s longest-running festivals.
traces of ink turn performance’s physicality into graphic form
Athens Epidaurus Festival is one of Greece’s most important cultural institutions and one of Europe’s longest-running festivals. For 70 years, it has brought together leading Greek and international artists in theater, music, and dance. This year’s Festival visual identity was created by Polkadot Design. A human gesture, a trace of ink, and a manual process form the basis of a visual language that reflects the physical nature of the performing arts.
Movement makes the poster an open-ended visual experience
The process behind the identity was entirely manual: a rotational gesture leaves a trace of ink, transforming movement into a contemporary visual language. For Polkadot Design Studio, the poster is not a static object, but an invitation to the viewer to move beyond the role of passive observer and actively participate in giving the work its final meaning.

Ukrainian medics learn about the Dutch model of care for premature babies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
17:45:00 UTC
02:45:00 KST

Ukrainian medics learn about the Dutch model of care for premature babies
As reported by an Ukrinform correspondent in The Hague, during the visit Ukrainian medics learned about the organization of the neonatal intensive care unit and the approaches used by their Dutch colleagues to treat and care for premature babies. Dutch specialists demonstrated advanced technologies and shared a new approach that involves actively engaging parents in their child’s care. The approach was explained by Kiki Ruhe, a Dutch nursing scientist and Neonatal Intensive Care Nurse.
“Previously, parents were welcome, but they were not directly involved in caring for their tiny newborns. We now have a great deal of research showing that involving parents is beneficial for the parents themselves, for the children, and for medical staff,” Ruhe said.
She explained that the family integrated care approach includes, among other things, 24-hour access for parents to the unit, access to essential facilities, participation in medical rounds, and training in how to care for their child.
According to Ruhe, parents are taught practical skills such as feeding a baby with a syringe, changing diapers, practicing Kangaroo Care, and performing other procedures depending on the newborn’s condition.
The unit cares for babies born from approximately 24 weeks of gestation. It currently has between 18 and 25 operational beds, out of a designed capacity of 36.
Ruhe also said that during the visit, Ukrainian specialists mainly asked practical questions, particularly about medical equipment and respiratory support for newborns.
According to her, the smallest baby she treated at the unit weighed 410 grams.
“Working with such patients requires significant effort and involves gradually engaging parents in their care,” she said.
The experience-sharing program for Ukrainian medical professionals was organized by the Ukrainian Academy of Pediatric Specialties and the NGO Early Birds.
“We are grateful to the team at Emma Children’s Hospital for their openness and for the opportunity to learn about the work of the neonatology department. Here, we saw how the family-integrated care approach is implemented in daily practice: parents are part of the team caring for a premature baby. Particular attention is paid to training healthcare professionals, including communication with families. As a parent-led organization, it is important for us to learn from this experience so that we can help promote the implementation in Ukraine of approaches that support children and their parents,” said Oleksandra Balyasna, co-organizer of the program and head of the Early Birds NGO.
Among the Ukrainian specialists taking part in the visit was pediatrician and anesthesiologist Iryna Kondratova, who previously headed the Kharkiv Regional Perinatal Center. During the intense shelling of Kharkiv in 2022, she and her team remained at the hospital around the clock, caring for women in labor and saving newborns.
“Ukraine needs a comprehensive system of medical and social support for children who are born prematurely, have severe illnesses, or receive incurable diagnoses. The focus of this system should not be only on the child, but on the entire family,” she said.
1 / 11
According to Kondratova, Ukraine has individual elements of support for such children, but they are not integrated into a single system. This includes support from the moment a child is born, assistance to the family during treatment and preparation for discharge, further outpatient follow-up, assessment of the child’s development, and, when necessary, palliative care.
She was particularly impressed by the way the neonatal intensive care unit in Amsterdam is organized. According to her, the focus is not only on the child, who may require mechanical ventilation, continuous monitoring, and a large amount of medical equipment. The mother, father, and other family members can remain close to the child.
“This is not even a hospital room in the way we understand it. It is more like a three-room apartment built around the family. And if there are older children in the family, they can stay here as well,” the doctor said.
She also highlighted how thoroughly the needs of medical equipment are taken into account when the space is designed. In one of the rooms, she counted 22 electrical outlets around the child’s bed alone.
“An engineer or a builder simply would not understand all the requirements involved. Doctors and nurses need to be consulted before implementing this philosophy. This is all about the family, dignity, and the best practices in the world, so that the family does not feel abandoned. I find it truly remarkable,” she said.
Kondratova also highlighted the role of nurses in the Dutch healthcare system. According to her, the visit to the neonatal unit and children’s hospice made it clear that a significant share of the workload is carried by nursing staff.
As reported by Ukrinform, in December 2025, the renovated Neonatal Intensive Care Unit, along with the hospital’s mobile neonatology team, was officially opened at the Okhmatdyt National Specialized Children’s Hospital under Ukraine’s Ministry of Health.

Iran will not abandon uranium enrichment or hand over its enriched uranium, the head of the country’s Atomic Energy Organization, Mohammad Eslami, has said, rejecting a US demand for “meaningful” reductions in Tehran’s enrichment capacity.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on Thursday that Tehran could respond within days to Washington’s latest response to an Iranian proposal that would allow the strait to reopen within seven days if specified conditions were met.
The parallel diplomatic efforts have placed the nuclear dispute alongside broader negotiations over security, hostilities and freedom of navigation.
Iran rejects weapons claims
The United States, Israel and other Western countries have long accused Iran of seeking the capability to develop nuclear weapons, pointing in particular to Tehran’s enrichment of uranium to 60 percent — well above the level generally required for civilian nuclear power and below weapons-grade enrichment of about 90 percent.
Iran has consistently denied seeking nuclear weapons and maintains that its nuclear program is intended for peaceful purposes.
Iranian officials have previously indicated that Tehran could agree to dilute its most highly enriched uranium as part of a broader agreement.
US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that Washington was engaged in productive discussions with Iran and would not launch an attack before the US midterm congressional elections in November.
The latest statements underscore the gap between Tehran and Washington over the future of Iran’s enrichment program even as both sides continue diplomatic contacts on wider regional issues.

President Donald Trump said Thursday that the U.S. will not attack Iran before the Nov. 3 midterm election, explicitly tying the timing of potential further military action to the domestic political calendar.

Trump's declaration came after he told reporters late Wednesday that his administration was considering renewed strikes against Tehran before the election, helping send oil prices higher amid fears of further escalation. Brent crude rose more than 4% Thursday to above $104 a barrel.
Trump said the U.S. naval blockade of Iran would remain in place and reiterated that Tehran would not be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon.
It's a shift from his posture less than a day ago. At a campaign rally Wednesday night, Trump said a deal with Iran was "not really something that I wanted to do."
The more diplomatic tone comes as voters are already casting midterm ballots and public support for the war has fallen. Just 31% of Americans supported U.S. military action against Iran in an August Reuters/Ipsos poll, down from 37% in March, while 83% expected the conflict to be prolonged.
The war has helped push fuel costs higher, compounding Republicans' vulnerability on affordability as they fight to retain control of Congress. Poll after poll has ranked the cost of living among voters' top concerns heading into the Nov. 3 election.
Gas prices have climbed roughly 40% from a year ago, according to AAA data. The national average stood at $4.36 a gallon Thursday, up from $2.98 just before war began in late February.
The political fallout is showing up on the campaign trail. Numerous GOP candidates in competitive congressional races have tried to distance themselves from Trump, often on the Iran war.
Inside the White House, the election calendar has reportedly loomed over the administration's Iran strategy for weeks. Reuters reported in September that top Trump aides were pushing to keep the war contained through the midterms to limit Republican losses, while leaving open heavier U.S. strikes after votes are tallied.
Trump's latest statement does just that. Meanwhile, the U.S. is sending roughly 9,000 sailors and Marines and a third aircraft carrier to the region, a buildup that could put three U.S. carriers in the Middle East by late October, the Associated Press reported last week.
The president also claimed Thursday that 22 million barrels of oil moved through the Strait of Hormuz overnight, with none coming from or going to Iran. CNBC has not independently verified that figure.
Kpler data show about 11.3 million barrels per day of crude oil and petroleum products exited the strait during the week ended Tuesday, while total oil flows from the region stood at 20.4 million barrels per day.

NATO announced plans to begin its annual nuclear deterrence exercises in Italy on Tuesday, as growing concerns over Russia heighten security tensions across Europe.
Its "Steadfast Noon" drills will run from Oct. 13 to 23 and will involve 17 nations, it said Thursday.
"The exercise is a long-planned, routine training activity that is part of NATO's efforts to maintain readiness and test procedures that contribute to the alliance's deterrence and defence," said a NATO statement.
"No live weapons are used in Steadfast Noon. The exercise is not linked to current world events and is not directed against any country," the alliance added.
But NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte commented that while NATO was a "defensive alliance" the exercise "helps us ensure a safe, secure, effective, and credible capability to preserve peace, prevent coercion and deter aggression. It also sends a clear message of unity and resolve".
Russia, embroiled in an invasion of Ukraine since 2022, has accused NATO of staging "provocative" actions around its exclave of Kaliningrad.
It has warned that it is ready to use "its entire arsenal."
NATO condemned the comments, but its officials say the alliance has not seen major changes in Russia's nuclear posture.

Fabien Mandon is pictured upon arrival at the Elysée Palace in Paris for a defense council meeting on Sept. 16, 2026. | Benjamin Vodant/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
PARIS — France's top general Fabien Mandon admitted on Thursday that the Franco-German next-generation battle tank project had failed.
It's one of the first times a French official has publicly acknowledged that the plans have faltered, after months of speculation about the fate of the Main Combat Ground System.
"The outcome isn't good. We had hoped to build a future tank in cooperation with the Germans, but unfortunately, we have to acknowledge that the Germans have withdrawn from the project," the French chief of defense staff told lawmakers during a hearing on next year's budget.
Advertisement
MGCS — which involves KNDS France, KNDS Germany, Rheinmetall and Thales — has been bogged down by years of delays, industrial disputes and political tensions. POLITICO reported in June that the next-generation tank project was increasingly doomed.
Mandon's admission comes only a few months after another high-stakes Franco-German defense industrial program — the Future Combat Air System — abruptly ended.
However, answering a question from a far-right National Rally lawmaker, the French general pushed back against the word "failure" to describe the MGCS's fate.
"It's not a complete failure; it's an important decision by Germany, but our land forces have worked together for several years to determine what a future main battle tank should look like," he said. "It wasn't a waste of time. But from an industrial standpoint, this isn't good news."

Residential buildings are seen without power during widespread outages following Russian attacks on Kyiv, Ukraine on Oct. 8, 2026. (Olga Rudenko / The Kyiv Independent)
Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
The Russian attack on Ukrainian energy infrastructure on Oct. 8 has caused widespread power outages across the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, home to over 3 million people.
"There was an attack on one of the energy facilities important for the city of Kyiv," Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal said. "Energy workers are doing everything possible to restore electricity as quickly as possible."

Ahead of winter, the sound of generators returned to Kyiv throughout affected neighborhoods, as businesses sought to keep operating. In the dark of the evening, buskers continued to perform on the capital's main street of Khreshchatyk.

Earlier on Oct. 8, Ukraine's largest private energy company, DTEK, announced emergency power shutdowns in parts of Kyiv Oblast, including the Brovary, Bucha, Vyshhorod, and Boryspil districts.
The Kyiv Oblast Military Administration said Russia had significantly intensified attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure in recent weeks, targeting power lines and transformers and disrupting electricity transmission to consumers.
Energy workers are operating around the clock to repair damaged equipment and stabilize the grid, the administration said.
The disruptions followed a morning of repeated Russian drone strikes on Kyiv and the surrounding region that killed and injured civilians and damaged buildings and infrastructure.
Russian drone strikes on Oct. 8 killed four people and injured at least 19 in Kyiv, the city's Mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said.

UK plans to announce ban on workers’ non-compete clauses in push for growth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
17:34:20 UTC
02:34:20 KST

Andy Burnham gives a TV interview following his meeting with the German chancellor in Berlin on Oct. 8, 2026. | Pool photo by Sean Gallup/AFP via Getty Images
LONDON — The U.K. government is planning to commit to a full or partial ban on non-compete clauses in workers’ employment contracts, six people with knowledge of the discussions told POLITICO.
All six of the people, who were granted anonymity to discuss government policy, said they believed an announcement is due imminently and could be made as soon as Friday. Three of those people said they believed the announcement was likely to be fronted personally by Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who is expected to give a speech Friday.
The government of Burnham’s predecessor, Keir Starmer, set out options in November 2025 to limit the use of non-compete clauses, which aim to restrict a person’s ability to work for or set up a competing business after they leave their job.
Advertisement
The founders of more than 20 U.K. tech start-ups wrote to the government last month saying the restrictions, along with long notice periods and enforced gardening leave, were and “undermin[ing] the innovation that drives economic growth”.
The options set out 11 months ago ranged from a total ban on non-compete clauses to a partial ban, such as allowing non-compete clauses only for workers earning more than a set salary threshold, or limiting their length.
However, two of the six people quoted above said that the government would stop short of backing a specific option at this stage.
Ministers are expected to set out a broad intention of ensuring that non-compete clauses are no longer a hiring problem for start-ups and innovative firms, but finer details will be worked out further down the line in consultation with industry.
No. 10 declined to comment.
The announcement comes after Chancellor John Healey said he wanted to tackle the costs for businesses in his budget on Oct. 28. One of the six people quoted above said: “They want to sell it as pro growth and freeing up the labour market.”
Advertisement
AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said last week that the government was “working extremely rapidly” on potential changes to the system.
Non-compete clauses are common in the financial services industry. The lobby group TheCityUK opposed a ban earlier this year, arguing that non-compete clauses “promote competition and innovation in high-value industries” as they are often the “only way to pre-emptively protect confidential information and intellectual property.”
The government argued last year that even though non-compete clauses are “unenforceable” as a starting point under current law, ministers were “concerned about the behavioural effect of including a non-compete clause in an employment contract. Even if broadly drafted and unlikely to be enforceable, workers may perceive the clause as binding and comply with it for fear of legal repercussions.”

Germany has decided to withdraw from a project with France to develop a future battle tank, French Chief of the Defence Staff Gen. Fabien Mandon said Thursday, the French broadcaster BFMTV reported.
“The Germans have decided to leave the project,” he said, referring to the Main Ground Combat System (MGCS).
“This is not a complete failure, it is an important German choice. Our land forces have worked together for several years to consider what a future battle tank should be,” he said at a National Assembly hearing.
Mandon stressed that the work had established the tank’s main principles, while acknowledging that the withdrawal was “not good news from an industrial point of view.”
The MGCS program was launched in 2017 to replace France’s Leclerc and Germany’s Leopard 2 tanks with a ground combat system centered on a new tank.
The project has faced delays and disagreements on industrial work-sharing, financing and technological choices, with deployment pushed toward 2040 or 2045, the broadcaster reported.
Mandon said France still needed a heavy combat capability, emphasizing the continued relevance of tank firepower.
He urged complementary platforms incorporating robots, artificial intelligence and greater data sharing, potentially requiring fewer personnel to operate.
“We will have a gradual withdrawal of the Leclerc starting in 2038. In 2027, we must launch the studies to be ready for this deadline,” he said.
The announcement marks another setback for Franco-German defense cooperation, coming four months after the failure of the Future Combat Air System project.
That program, also launched in 2017 and involving Spain, was intended to develop a next-generation fighter aircraft to replace the Rafale and Eurofighter sometime in the 2040s.

A code orange drought alert will remain in effect in Belgium's Flanders region despite recent rainfall and further precipitation forecast in the coming days, authorities said Thursday.
The decision was made by the Flemish Drought Commission following an exceptionally dry September, Flemish Environment and Agriculture Minister Jo Brouns said in a statement cited by broadcaster VRT.
Authorities said the hydrological situation remains "vulnerable," with water levels and flows in several waterways still at very low levels for this time of year.
Groundwater reserves have also shown limited recovery.
About 84% of monitoring points are recording low to extremely low groundwater levels compared with seasonal averages.
The situation is particularly concerning in the Yser basin, where high salinization pressure continues to pose a threat.
While the expected rainfall may bring temporary improvements in some areas, authorities said it will not be sufficient to replenish water reserves structurally.
Several drought-related measures, as a result, remain in force.
Temporary bans on water abstraction apply to a number of non-navigable waterways, while water-saving measures remain in place on navigable waterways, including restrictions on lock operations and vessel draft.
The drinking water supply remains secure, although authorities stressed the need for continued vigilance in all supply areas.

66% of France's groundwater sites below monthly norms, authorities say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
17:32:35 UTC
02:32:35 KST

Seyma Erkul Dayanc
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
Two-thirds of groundwater monitoring sites in France were below monthly normal levels as of Oct. 1, the French Geological Survey (BRGM) said Thursday, according to broadcaster BFM.
“With 66% of observation points having levels below monthly norms, the groundwater situation remains very concerning,” the geological survey said in its monthly bulletin.
It said groundwater levels were continuing to decline across France, while the usual trend at this time of year would be the beginning of seasonal replenishment.
France experienced its hottest summer on record, with an average 24-hour temperature of 24C (75.2F), 3.6C (6.5F) above the 1991-2020 average, according to the report.
Low rainfall during the summer contributed to severe drought conditions, which have continued into October.
According to the VigiEau water information service, 79 French departments were under “crisis” restrictions and 14 under “heightened alert” measures at the start of October, limiting water use.
Some 94,000 people in metropolitan France were without running water at the end of September, 30,000 more than at the beginning of the month, according to the Environment Ministry.
Groundwater levels were degraded across most of the country, the BRGM said, with some exceptions in the southeast, including the Vistrenque aquifers in the Gard region and the Astien sands around Valras-Agde in the Herault region.
The survey also identified particularly low levels in several aquifer systems, including those in Limousin, Morvan, Livradois, Forez and Vivarais, as well as Champagne, Jura, Vosges, Lorraine and northern Alsace.
The BRGM said “inertial” aquifers, which can take months or years to respond to changes, continued to decline, while levels in almost all “reactive” aquifers, which can respond to rainfall within weeks, were also falling.

Kenya reported its first imported case this week involving a patient who died after traveling from Congo.
The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo Ebola virus, for which no vaccine or treatment has been approved.
In August, Congo was allocated 70,000 Ervebo vaccines from the global Ebola virus disease vaccine stockpile for use in the current outbreak. The vaccine is approved for use against the Zaire Ebola virus.
More than 7,700 healthcare and other frontline workers have so far been vaccinated, Mankoula said.
The Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations announced in August a $16.5 million partnership with African biopharmaceutical company Minapharm Group to develop their Bundibugyo vaccine candidate.

Mobile network outage halts trains across Norway, disrupts emergency calls

Necva Tastan Sevinc
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
A major outage in Telenor's mobile network halted train traffic across Norway and disrupted calls to emergency services Thursday, public broadcaster NRK reported.
Rail infrastructure operator Bane Nor said all trains were being stopped because train controllers could not contact emergency services.
The suspension was imposed for safety reasons in case a serious incident occurred, communications adviser Olav Nordli told NRK.
Train operator Vy said trains were at their nearest stations or approaching them, warning passengers to expect delays and cancellations.
Passengers could leave trains or wait for services to resume, Vy communications director Elin Myrmel-Johansen said. The operator arranged buses from Oslo to nearby major cities.
Telenor said the fault began at 3.15 pm local time (1315GMT) and affected calls to and from customers using its network. Some calls to emergency numbers also failed.
The company reported at 6 pm that SMS and mobile network services had returned to normal, but voice traffic problems remained unresolved.
“There are no indications that there is any hacking or attack underway,” Telenor communications manager Vetle Andersen told Norwegian newspaper Aftenposten.
The Norwegian Communications Authority said Telenor customers could still experience difficulties reaching emergency numbers despite improvements.
Police in Oslo and several other districts warned that callers might be unable to reach the emergency number 112 or the non-emergency number 02800.
The Norwegian Directorate of Health said the medical emergency number was also affected. It advised callers who could not get through to try again or use a phone connected to another mobile network.
The Directorate for Civil Protection said the separate emergency communications network used by emergency responders remained operational.

"We cannot continue to introduce new forms of fiscal
flexibility," Dombrovskis told a press conference following the

"Indeed, this could cast doubt on our collective determination
to adhere to the fiscal rule framework, at a time when the
credibility of our commitment to the sustainability of public

adopt the correct interpretation of flexibility, noting a

"garnered widespread support, notwithstanding the traditional
reservations of the 'frugal' countries," said Giorgetti
following the Eurogroup meeting in Luxembourg.

interpretation of the factors relevant to compliance with the
current Stability Pact.

the right approach—sound technical arguments will lead to a
correct interpretation of the rules, including within the
framework of the energy clause already approved, in a manner
consistent with the sustainability of public finances."

NATO Could Close Russia’s Baltic Sea Access Within Hours After Attack, Estonian FM Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08

- Category
- World
NATO Could Close Russia’s Baltic Sea Access Within Hours After Attack, Estonian FM Says
NATO could close Russia’s access to the Baltic Sea within hours if Moscow launched an attack on the alliance, cutting a maritime route that carries about 60% of Russia’s seaborne oil exports, Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna told The Times on October 7.
The Times reported that an allied blockade of the route between Estonia and Finland would sever one of Russia’s most important economic and military corridors. Russian vessels departing St. Petersburg use the Baltic route to reach open waters, while the same passage also connects Russia with Kaliningrad.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“We are able within a few hours to form a force of 50,000 experienced soldiers,” Tsahkna told The Times. “We could close the exit to the Baltic Sea within a few hours. This is a vital artery for the Russian economy.”
Tsahkna emphasized that such measures would follow a Russian attack triggering NATO’s Article 5 collective defense clause, rather than serve as a pre-emptive action by the alliance.
He described portraying NATO as an offensive organization as “absurd,” while noting that the alliance has operational plans for responding to Russian military aggression.
“If Russia starts a war, then we have plans and practical measures that we can take,” Tsahkna stated.
According to The Times, NATO members have not attempted to close the route under current conditions because they continue to operate under international rules governing maritime access.
Tsahkna argued that a direct Russian attack would fundamentally change that calculation.
“They will lose their vital artery. The Black Sea is already closed. For Russia, [the Baltic Sea] is existential,” he told The Times.
A few months earlier, Tsahkna had argued that Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries and military facilities were hitting a key economic lifeline for Moscow. He noted that up to 60% of Russian oil exports pass through the Gulf of Finland, the same Baltic corridor he now describes as vital to Russia’s economy.

Ukraine’s Drones Reach Russia’s Arctic Gas Capital—Now Locals Are Being Paid $12,000 to Shoot Them Down
Russia’s far northern Yamalo-Nenets region is offering mobile fire groups $12,000 for every incoming drone they destroy, underscoring growing concern over Ukrainian long-range strikes reaching some of the country’s most remote oil and gas infrastructure, according to The Barents Observer on October 8.
The regional government announced the new reward after a Ukrainian drone reportedly reached Novy Urengoy, widely known as Russia’s “natural gas capital,” roughly 3,000 kilometers, or about 1,860 miles, from the Ukrainian front.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The $12,000 reward will be divided among members of a mobile fire group that successfully destroys an incoming drone. There is one major condition: the payment will only be made if the facility being defended escapes damage.
Authorities are also offering financial incentives simply to join the units. Employed residents who sign up can receive $1,200, while unemployed recruits are eligible for $1,800. Membership in a mobile fire group requires signing a contract with Russia’s Defense Ministry.
The measures show how far Russia’s drone-defense problem has spread from the Ukrainian border. Yamalo-Nenets lies thousands of kilometers from the battlefield in the Russian Arctic, yet the region has already begun periodically issuing drone alerts and restricting civilian aviation when UAV threats are reported.
That matters because the region is one of the centers of Russia’s energy industry. Yamalo-Nenets contains major oil and natural gas production infrastructure, while large liquefied natural gas projects—including Yamal LNG and Arctic LNG 2—are located in its northern areas.
Previously, reports emerged that Russia’s federal budget received about $5.43 billion in oil and gas revenue in September, down 22% from the same month in 2025.

US imposes fresh sanctions on Iran's shadow fleet
WASHINGTON, Oct 8 - The Trump administration imposed fresh sanctions on Iran on Thursday targeting individuals, networks and 17 vessels for transporting its crude, oil products and petrochemicals, in the latest act of US economic warfare on Tehran, the Treasury Department said.
The sanctions are part of the department's "Operation Economic Outcast," which aims to cut Tehran's funding for the war, missile construction, cyberattacks and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps or IRGC.
"Today's action represents the most significant blow yet to Iran's remaining illicit maritime infrastructure by neutralizing the vast majority of the shadow fleet," a Treasury official told reporters in a call. "Treasury is cutting off the regime's last major source of illicit revenue and strengthening international pressure to hold Tehran accountable."
The move boosts pressure on Iranian oil sales after the US re-imposed its blockade of Iranian ports on July 14 following the breakdown of a memorandum of understanding between Tehran and Washington.
Iran only has about 20 million barrels of crude oil left on vessels outside of the blockade, a Treasury official said. The world uses about 100 million barrels of oil per day. REUTERS

This September was the hottest ever on record for the U.S.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
17:28:31 UTC
02:28:31 KST

September 2026 shattered the record for the hottest September ever recorded in the contiguous U.S., according to new data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. It marks another sobering record for an already historically hot year.
This past January through September were the hottest first nine months of any year in the U.S. since at least 1895.
Overall, the contiguous U.S. averaged a balmy 69.42 degrees Fahrenheit (20.79 degrees Celsius) in September—more than 4.5 degrees F (about 2.5 degrees C) higher than the historical 20th-century average.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Whether 2026 will break the record for the U.S.’s hottest year—currently standing at 55.48 degrees F (about 13 degrees C), set in 2024—depends on the temperatures for October, November and December. As Scientific American previously reported, climate predictions are complicated. But what is clear is that such a warm September only makes the situation more dire.
Leading up to now, the period of the first eight months of the year, January–August, was exceptionally hot. If the period of September–December averages around 50.5 degrees F (10.3 degrees C)—a warm but not unusual scenario for recent years—the U.S. is likely to break its record, climatologist Zeke Hausfather previously told Scientific American.
Crowning 2026 as the hottest year would only be part of the picture; climate change doesn’t care about records.
As Climate Central scientist Zachary Labe previously told Scientific American, “Whether 2026 ultimately ranks as number one or number three doesn’t distract from the bigger story that temperatures are rising across the country and leading to major impacts for communities.”
Editor’s Note (10/8/26): This is a breaking news story and may be updated.

====================================================================================================

Israeli startup developing minimally invasive alternative to bowel surgery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
17:28:02 UTC
02:28:02 KST

An Israeli medical technology company founded by a Toronto surgeon has raised $5 million to develop a device that could allow doctors to create an opening in a patient's abdomen to drain the bowel without conventional surgery or general anesthesia, the company said Thursday.
Phantom GI, founded in Tel Aviv in 2025 by Dr. Eran Shlomovitz, Dr. Eliyahu Bechor and CEO Ido Sadan, said the seed round was led by Pitango HealthTech, with participation from RAD BioMed and RUNI Ventures. The company's device is designed to create a stoma through a single puncture in the skin under X-ray guidance.
About three years ago, Dr. Eran Shlomovitz treated a cancer patient in serious condition who was suffering from a bowel obstruction. The patient was supposed to undergo an ostomy – a surgery designed to create an opening in the abdominal wall that allows intestinal waste to drain, also known as a stoma – but her condition was too severe for her to undergo the operation.
Shlomovitz, a general surgeon at the University Health Network in Toronto and an associate professor at the University of Toronto, obtained the patient's consent to try an experimental approach: using existing medical equipment off-label to drain the bowel through a minimally invasive procedure under local anesthesia. The procedure was successful.
The patient was able to eat and function again, and many more patients were referred to Shlomovitz for the same procedure.
The device, which is undergoing a patent application process, is designed to enable the creation of a stoma without conventional surgery or general anesthesia, using a single puncture through the skin under X-ray fluoroscopic guidance.
In 2024, Dr. Eli Bechor, a senior surgeon at Beilinson Hospital in central Israel, trained under Shlomovitz in Toronto. The two then began developing Shlomovitz's technique and, after several attempts, concluded that new technology would be needed to deliver optimal treatment.
A mutual acquaintance introduced them to CEO Ido Sadan, an engineer by training who works in medical devices, and the three joined forces.
According to estimates, in the United States alone, about 50,000 patients each year suffer from malignant bowel obstructions and are not suitable candidates for conventional surgery because of their complex medical conditions. Another significant target group is cancer patients with abdominal tumors who undergo surgical removal.
"Today, when a tumor is removed from the bowel and the ends are reconnected, there is always a risk of a life-threatening leak at the connection site," Sadan explains.
Sadan said that in previous treatments, patients required additional surgery under anesthesia to close the stoma and restore the intestine. Their device, he said, is designed to eliminate the need for that second surgery.
According to Sadan, the device "inserts a supporting tube, or stent, through the skin to drain the bowel without having to bring the intestine outside the body or perform another operation. Once the intestinal tissue heals, the stent can be removed through a simple outpatient procedure."
Asked whether the new technology could help Crohn's disease patients, Sadan said Crohn patients have much to gain from the treatment, but some are reluctant to have a stoma created because they fear they may be left with it for the rest of their lives after surgery.
Phantom GI is currently in the preclinical stage. The startup expects to begin a clinical study in Canada in early 2027, followed by a larger trial whose results will form the basis of its application for FDA approval.
"The Phantom GI team is challenging a surgical paradigm that has remained almost unchanged for decades. The shift to a percutaneous approach – through the skin – could significantly reduce the complexity of treatment and expand access to patients who currently have no suitable treatment options," says Dr. Yonatan Glazer, a partner at Pitango HealthTech.
Phantom GI has presented long-term preclinical evidence and advanced a broad patent portfolio to the international Patent Cooperation Treaty stage.

Syria calls for independent probe into sinking of ship in Black Sea
Syrian authorities questioned why search and rescue operations were called off before the fate of 10 sailors was known.
Syria has called for an “independent and transparent” investigation into the sinking of a cargo ship in the Black Sea, demanding answers over the fate of the ship’s 10 crew members, including nine Syrians and an Egyptian, who remain unaccounted for.
The Togolese-flagged Alfa Watan, went down in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone early on Tuesday, amid a rising number of drone strikes hitting Black Sea shipping during the Russia-Ukraine war.
It is unclear who carried out the attack.
Mazen Aloush, from the Syria’s port authority asked the International Maritime Organization (IMO) and Bulgarian authorities to find out why a search and rescue mission was called off, before the missing sailors were found.
“Their fate is still unknown” said Aloush, adding that “the reasons that led to the suspension of search and rescue operations” had to be established.
The attack on Tuesday also hit the Palau-flagged Able, setting it ablaze. Eighteen Turkish and Indian crew members were rescued from the burning vessel, while the Alfa Watan sank.
Both commercial ships were managed by Turkey-based companies, according to the Equasis merchant shipping database.
The Syrian sailors’ union said contact with the ship’s crew had been lost and no survivors had been found after search operations were halted.
Aloush condemned the targeting of a civilian commercial vessel saying it was a serious breach of maritime security and a threat to sailors.
He said Syrian General Authority for Ports and Customs was closely monitoring the incident.
He urged authorities to use all available technical means to locate and inspect the wreckage to help establish what caused the ship to sink.
He called for international and maritime bodies to strengthen measures to help commercial shipping as attacks in the Black Sea rise.

EU debates harsh working conditions for fishers: 'I had no other choice'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
17:25:46 UTC
02:25:46 KST

Endless weeks, shifts of up to 24 hours and even no drinking water: these were some of the hardships aired last week at a debate held by the EU Fisheries Committee with sector representatives.
"The food was in very poor condition and I could only drink seawater that had been filtered. I had no other choice, it was never properly clean," recalled Fredi Seprizal, an Indonesian who endured what he describes as "modern slavery" at sea and who spoke during the debate 'Boosting the social dimension of sustainable fisheries', held last week in the European Parliament.
Seprizal's was one of the most striking testimonies at the meeting, which took place on 30 September and was organised by Carmen Crespo (EPP), chair of the European Parliament's Committee on Fisheries (PECH), and Virginia Battu-Henriksson, a member of the cabinet of the Commissioner for Fisheries and Oceans, Costas Kadis.
The sailor told MEPs about the conditions he endured for 16 months on board a Chinese vessel. He explained that he worked between 16 and 20 hours a day and, at times, for 24 hours straight, with rest periods of between three and six hours. Seprizal also denounced the lack of adequate safety equipment and said he feared for his life while he was on the high seas.
The aim of the meeting was to examine fishermen's working conditions and the fight against forced labour. Survivors of labour exploitation, international organisations, trade union representatives and members of the fisheries sector came together to call for stronger guarantees for those working in the industry.
"Europe cannot compete by lowering its standards, but by turning them into its greatest asset," said Crespo, stressing that the European fleet must maintain its requirements on sustainability, safety and labour rights. "Defending a competitive fishing sector also means defending its workers against unfair competition and ensuring supply chains that are transparent, responsible and free from exploitation."
The need for "effective protection"
The experiences shared during the meeting, according to a statement (source in Spanish) by the Organisation of Associated Producers of Large Frozen Tuna Vessels (OPAGAC), are in line with the findings of a study presented by Sallie Yea, professor and researcher at Charles Sturt University, based on interviews with 121 fishers and 32 family members from the Philippines, Indonesia, Cambodia and Fiji.
According to her research, 94% of the fishers interviewed had at some point suffered non-payment of their wages, and all of them had seen their contracts changed to less favourable conditions.
In addition, one in every four fishers interviewed had witnessed the death of a fellow crew member, while deaths were recorded on one in every four vessels analysed.
"We need to move from purely formal compliance to the effective protection of labour rights, including checks on contracts and wages, arbitration mechanisms to resolve labour complaints, protection against reprisals and accountability mechanisms for recruitment agencies, and not only for fishing fleets and seafood companies," Yea argued at the meeting.
During the Fisheries Committee's round table, representatives from the International Labour Organization (ILO), the European Transport Workers' Federation (ETF), the Environmental Justice Foundation (EJF) and Oxfam called for stricter enforcement of labour standards.
Economist Tariq Haq, from the ILO, recalled that the Work in Fishing Convention lays down the minimum requirements for working on board, but has been ratified by only 27 member states.
The EU also has a regulation (source in Spanish) on forced labour, which will be phased in until December 2027. For OPAGAC, which promoted the meeting together with Hands for the Oceans, access to the European market should be made conditional on compliance with the same standards that apply to the European fleet.
"We hope that the EU rules on due diligence and forced labour can become a turning point," said Julio Morón, director-general of OPAGAC, to ensure that European consumers do not eat fish caught using forced labour and modern slavery.
In that context, Seprizal's words still resonate. During the debate he went so far as to say: "The thought of jumping off the ship or setting it on fire crossed my mind; but I could not escape because the captain kept hold of my documents. I even had to pay to get them back."

Senior US Embassy official in Jerusalem suppressed diplomatic cables to shield Netanyahu government: Report
Unknown

US suspends Microsoft and Adobe from visa programme amid fraud claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
17:25:02 UTC
02:25:02 KST

US suspends Microsoft and Adobe from visa programme amid fraud claims
Visa probe also targets universities for allegedly exploiting international students to reduce US wage costs.
The United States government is suspending several major tech companies, including Adobe and Microsoft, from a programme that gives skilled foreign workers a path to permanent residency amid allegations of fraud.
The move comes as the White House ramps up pressure on companies to hire more Americans. “Our message to Microsoft is: You’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers,” US Vice President JD Vance said at a news conference on Thursday.
Vance claimed that the Redmond, Washington-based tech giant laid off 6,000 American workers while obtaining 6,300 H-1B foreign work visas and almost 3,000 permanent residencies known as green cards.
“You cannot lay off American workers and replace them with foreign indentured servants,” Vance said.
Across the technology sector, there have been more than 131,000 layoffs in 2026 alone, according to Layoffs.fyi, which tracks job cuts across the tech and startup industries.
“When someone comes in, they are completely subordinate to that company. If they lose that job, they have to leave the country.”
Microsoft pushed back on Vance’s claims in a blog post, saying that “80 percent of the visas were to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees.”
“The remaining filings for new employees were for individuals already legally in the United States who decided to come work for us, and they equal only 1% of our U.S. workforce. They are not new arrivals to our country,” the company said in the post.
Microsoft is No 5 among US employers when it comes to using H-1B visas, according to data from US Citizenship and Immigration Services. Amazon is No 1.
Adobe did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.
Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling also said that several major information technology firms will be suspended from the programme as well. Among them are Indian tech giants Infosys and Tata Consultancy Services.
The H-1B programme has long been a target of supporters of US President Donald Trump who say that the programme undercuts American workers and is rife with abuse.
H-1B visas are meant for high-skilled jobs that are difficult to find US workers to fill. Technology companies are the biggest users, with nearly three-quarters of approvals going to workers from India.
The Department of Labor also said it had uncovered $22bn worth of visa fraud.
“Today we are protecting something far more valuable than any dollar amount. We are protecting the American worker,” Sonderling said.
The news came hours before Trump was to honour Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella with the National Medal of Technology and Innovation. India-born Nadella was one of six business leaders to be awarded on Thursday. Five of the leaders were foreign-born, including Tesla boss Elon Musk and Google co-founder Sergey Brin.
Crackdown on universities
During the news conference, officials also announced a crackdown on alleged J-1 visa fraud involving nine universities, including MIT, Harvard, Yale, Stanford and Cal State, amid allegations that they brought in international students to undercut US wages. A J-1 visa allows foreign nationals to enter the US temporarily for education or cultural programmes. Universities use these visas to bring in international PhD candidates or scholars.
Vance claimed that when schools employ an American as a researcher, that person earns $20,000 more than someone brought in under a J-1 visa.
Al Jazeera asked for data supporting this claim, but the White House did not respond.
Microsoft’s stock slumped 1.5 percent on the heels of the news, while Adobe was up 2.1 percent in late day trading on Thursday.

US suspends major IT firms from green card programme, including Microsoft, Adobe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08

02:22:18 KST

The US government is suspending Microsoft, Adobe and several large IT firms from a programme that allows skilled foreign workers to gain permanent residency, senior US officials announced, citing alleged fraud and as part of an effort to push companies to hire more Americans.
"Our message to Microsoft is: You're a great American company, but you've got to hire great American workers," US Vice President JD Vance said on Thursday.
Secretary of Labour Keith Sonderling added that some of the largest IT firms in the world would also be suspended from that programme, including Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini.
"We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labour certification applications involving these companies," Sonderling said.
Microsoft did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Under the PERM process, employers seek certification from the Department of Labour that there is no qualified, willing or available US worker for a specific job. It's a step required before filing petitions for most employment-based green cards.
Vance also said nine universities, including Harvard, Yale and Stanford, would be investigated for allegedly bringing in international students to undercut American wages. Labour Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito said subpoenas had already been served.
"We will investigate whether foreign influence, improper financial relationships, or visa abuse are compromising federally funded research," D'Esposito said.
"If an American university is breaking the law to save $1 while exposing American research to a foreign adversary, that is not academic excellence. It's institutional betrayal."

Human cost of Russia’s war

Zelensky also briefed the EC President on meetings with US officials planned for the coming days, particularly Oct. 9-10, noting that a Ukrainian delegation is already on its way.

Mélenchon declares ‘Bastille retaken’ after major student rally in Paris
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
17:21:29 UTC
02:21:29 KST

The mass student-led movement emerged over a range of issues including long school days, overcrowded schools, teacher absences.
Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of the hard left France Unbowed party took to X on Thursday to declare the Bastille had been "retaken", after students staged demonstrations across the country — including a major rally at Paris' infamous Place de la Bastille.
Thursday's major protests were part of the student-led movement which began on 17 September in the suburbs of Paris, before gradually developing into a broader campaign addressing issues including long school days, overcrowded schools, teacher absences.
The mass gathering which took place at the place de la Bastille started off peacefully, before clashes with the police later erupted, with tear gas and a water cannon fired at protesters.
On social media, Mélenchon stated "powerful demonstration by the youth who carry their demands in the most beautiful way possible! Immense pride. See you on Tuesday, October 13, at the call of the youth unions and workers."
The storming of the Bastille in 1789 marked a major turning point in the French Revolution and became a symbol of the people’s resistance to royal authority.
The leader of France Unbowed and his allies have been accused by their opponents of stoking unrest and manipulating young people for political gain. Mélenchon has rejected these criticisms, underlining that despite the fact that his party supports the protests, they were independently launched by students.
The student and professional union coalition has called for another day of protests and strikes on 13 October, with a further major mobilisation planned for 17 October.
Meanwhile, later in the day, France's Education Minister Édouard Geffray announced in an interview with broadcaster TF1 later that 3,000 substitute teachers would be deployed to schools facing critical shortages.
What did protestors say on the ground?
Cathy, a history teacher in a secondary school located in Paris told Euronews she had decided to accompany her students to the Bastille rally, because she backed their demands in favour of a change in France's education system.
"The students have demands that are very close to the ones teachers have been putting forward years. The system is degraded and it's because there has been no response for so long, that this is happening," she stated.
Meanwhile, one schoolboy warned that it was "normal" if violent outbursts occurred, if students' demands were "not be heard."
"All the revolutions in history have served a purpose. In 1789, there were a lot of deaths. We don't want to have deaths, but we could revert to violence as a means of expression. The goal is not to perpetrate violence to hurt people, but it's to use violence to change the system that harms us", he said.
Despite this, many other school pupils said they backed peaceful protests and strongly condemned police violence.
Many students questioned by Euronews at the rally had not heard of the government's mass online consultation, which was launched earlier in the week in order to collate student opinions and drive possible policy proposals. France's Education Ministry said it surpassed 40,000 responses within days of its launch.
Breaking down the numbers
According to the Interior Ministry, 71,500 people took part in Thursday's protests, with 24,500 in Paris. Meanwhile, an estimated 55,000 people took part in protests outside schools, amid school blockades that were staged across the country.
The Education Ministry said 375 schools were fully or partially closed for the day.
Authorities also reported an increase in what they described as cases of "urban violence", saying they took place on the "margins' of peaceful student demonstration, acting as a 'stain on their legitimate expression.'
Police have made more than 6,600 arrests since late September, when students, most of them under 18, began protesting to demand more education funding, according to the Interior Ministry.

US judge orders return of Egyptian deported to Equatorial Guinea
A US judge has ordered the Trump administration to facilitate the release and return of an Egyptian man who was deported to Equatorial Guinea this year and has since been jailed there.
Ahmed Soliman is one of hundreds of migrants sent from the US to African countries under so-called third-country deportation deals that the US government has used to accelerate removals.
Human Rights Watch said in a report published on Thursday that 536 people had been deported to African countries "that are neither their country of citizenship nor habitual residence" between January 2025 and August 2026.
Last month, Soliman said he had faced rough treatment by Equatorial Guinean police officers. Video obtained by Reuters showed police pulling firearms on migrants including Soliman.
After Reuters published its story, Soliman was taken into custody and has been held incommunicado at a gendarmerie station that has also been used to detain human rights activists.
In a ruling seen by Reuters on Thursday, US judge John C. Hinderaker said the Department of Homeland Security must facilitate Soliman's release from custody and his return to the US. That includes arranging any travel documentation he would need to return.
The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Equatorial Guinea has also not responded to requests for comment about Soliman's case.
Soliman wrote in a declaration to an immigration judge last year that he feared being killed in Egypt because he is gay.
Reuters has documented 40 cases in which migrants granted US legal protection after being persecuted for their LGBT status were deported to third countries in Africa that either criminalize same-sex relations or have been described by the State Department as hostile to LGBT people.
