Not since 9/11 has the UK faced such a security crisis – and threat to our liberal principles | Gaby Hinsliff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:55:39 UTC
01:55:39 KST

The first time the window-rattling roar of a B-1 bomber woke me up this summer, I thought for one crazed second we were under attack. By the second time, I’d learned to recognise the sound of US planes taking off from their base at RAF Fairford for what it was: a reminder that although Britain wants no part in this war with Iran, we cannot quite escape the consequences.
We’ll feel them at the petrol pump, or in the supermarket this autumn, or in this winter’s heating bills. But living under the flight path adds an extra edge to it. The skies finally fell silent last week, but only because the bombers have been hastily summoned home after an alleged terrorist plot to attack Fairford, in which (according to the prime minister) there are “strong indications that Iran played a part”. If Fairford is now a target of war, did that threat disappear when the Americans did? Nobody knows.
Rural Oxfordshire is peppered with military bases, and after 15 years here I don’t bat an eyelid at helicopters practising low-flying drills, uniforms on the school run, or the stash of Day-Glo marshmallow cereal our local supermarket used to keep for homesick Americans. But the Fairford incident follows a serious security breach at RAF Brize Norton last year – and though this involved pro-Palestinian protesters rather than the Russians, it didn’t inspire confidence – and news this summer that the Manchester synagogue attacker had scoped out the security arrangements for the nearby Shrivenham defence academy. Bases nationwide are on high alert, with two Latvians arrested on Thursday on suspicion of trespass inside RAF Molesworth in Cambridgeshire, home to a Nato intelligence hub. At Fairford, it was a farmer who sounded the alarm, raising some difficult questions about how vigilant to be in small rural communities where strangers tend to stand out. I don’t want to become paranoid about every passing dog walker, or leap to ridiculous conclusions on hearing a Russian accent. But not since living in London in the aftermath of 9/11 have I felt more alert to anything seemingly out of the ordinary.
And that, of course, is how terrorism works. It’s not just the attacks themselves, but the fear and distrust they engender. For a while after the 7/7 bombings, people would change train carriages rather than stand next to some poor kid with a rucksack. At the height of the Troubles in Northern Ireland, Irish émigrés in Britain faced hostility. Sadly, it’s usually minorities who are singled out for suspicion or – in areas prone to far-right protests or antisemitic attacks – forced to wonder which of their neighbours might have joined the marches, or daubed graffiti on Jewish-owned shops. This time, there’s a particularly grim risk of a backlash against asylum seekers, with Reform pouncing on unproven reports that Tehran may be using small boat crossings to smuggle covert operatives into Britain. (For the record, those arrested and released on bail in connection with the alleged Fairford plot have British nationality. However, a Kuwaiti citizen recently convicted of a terror plot against the Israeli embassy and two Iranian nationals recently charged with allegedly plotting to target Jews in Manchester reportedly got here in dinghies.) Whatever the truth, Tehran must be delighted to see such destabilising ideas spread.
For the second time since 9/11, Britain faces a dilemma over how much of a securocracy – a country dominated by security concerns, whose citizens live at a pitch of constantly heightened anxiety – it should become in response to increasing threats. As Andy Burnham will remember, the “war on terror” forced the last Labour government, of which he was part, into a painful rolling back of civil liberties at home. Since the threat this time is less from an ideology than from three hostile nation states with domestic reach – namely Russia, Iran and China – the coming dilemmas may be more over the movement of technology, assets and people.
Historically, Britain’s economy has been a relatively open one, even after Brexit. We let Gulf states buy our football clubs, Russian oligarchs prop up the prime London real estate market, and Chinese money bail out our cash-strapped universities and build our power stations, despite concerns about espionage, censorship and interference in domestic politics. (Tom Tugendhat, the shadow foreign affairs minister and longstanding China hawk, revealed last week that he still gets letters from Beijing to the family home “that say, basically, ‘we know where you live’”.)
London’s tech startups, expanding faster than they could hire domestically, snapped up skilled young Russian coders understandably anxious to escape a country at war. We didn’t slap tariffs on cheap Chinese EVs when the EU did, despite concerns they could kill off domestic car manufacturing – or even that some of their software might still be controllable from China, because trade wars are generally bad for business. (Though the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, suggested recently that that debate is not entirely closed.)
We chose not to become a fortress because for a long time, the benefits of being open to the world felt worth the risks, but perhaps also as a statement of our values. But there is an increasingly live debate in Whitehall about whether, in retrospect, autocracies saw that openness as a weakness to exploit. If nothing else, they’re certainly weaponising it now: both Iran and Russia are throttling shipping routes in the strait of Hormuz and Black Sea respectively, with consequences for oil and food prices that are now ringing serious alarm bells within governments.
Though it’s not entirely clear yet what Burnham makes of all of this, there are early signs of attitudes hardening. The Cabinet Office recently summoned CEOs of critical infrastructure companies to brief them on the threat of Russian sabotage, while last week MI5 issued a rare public warning to academics against working with a Chinese organisation regarded as a front for espionage. The concrete barriers hurriedly going up around Fairford last week may be a harbinger of what is to come: a signal that as the world moves closer to a war footing, our relaxed way of life may have to change.
But there’s a difference between being vigilant and being paranoid, let alone xenophobic, and we are going to need to hold that line in months to come. No foreign national in the UK should ever be persecuted for the sins of their country of origin: there’s no going back to the dark days of 1939, when Jewish refugees fleeing Nazi Germany and Austria were shockingly interned in Britain as “enemy aliens”. New powers of surveillance should always come with new safeguards.
And this government should remember that if the “war on terror” taught us anything, it’s that security crises test liberal principles to breaking point. I just hope Burnham is ready for that.
- Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

African Union urges for ceasefire compliance in DR Congo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:54:38 UTC
01:54:38 KST

African Union urges for ceasefire compliance in DR Congo
The African Union (AU) has called on parties to the conflict in the east of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DR Congo) to respect ceasefire agreements and refrain from actions that could undermine peace efforts, according to a statement released on Wednesday.
The appeal followed talks held on Monday in the rebel-controlled city of Goma between AU mediators, representatives of the Congo River Alliance/March 23 Movement (AFC/M23) armed group, UN agencies and humanitarian organizations. The discussions focused on the security situation, humanitarian conditions and efforts to advance peace negotiations.
AFC/M23 captured Goma and Bukavu, the respective capitals of North and South Kivu provinces, during a major offensive in early 2025 and now controls large parts of both regions.
The DR Congo’s mineral-rich east has been plagued by decades of violence, with dozens of armed groups, including M23, fighting Congolese government forces for power and control of resources such as gold and coltan. Clashes escalated in early 2025, leaving thousands dead and resulting in large-scale displacement, according to UN agencies. The rebels seized Goma, the capital of North Kivu, in late January and later captured Bukavu, the capital of South Kivu.
Ceasefire efforts have repeatedly faltered, including Qatar-facilitated talks in Doha. In February 2026, the parties agreed on arrangements for a ceasefire monitoring mechanism, a step welcomed by the African Union. Congolese authorities have long accused Rwanda of supporting the militants, allegations backed by a UN panel of experts. Kigali has denied the claims.
The accusations have strained Rwanda’s relations with Western partners, including Belgium. In March 2025, Kigali severed diplomatic ties with Brussels, accusing it of harboring “neo-colonial delusions” and interfering in the conflict. The two countries, however, restored diplomatic relations in September 2026.
In December 2025, Congolese President Felix Tshisekedi and his Rwandan counterpart, Paul Kagame, ratified a US-brokered agreement committing Kigali to withdraw its forces from the border and end alleged support for M23, while Kinshasa pledged to curb militias hostile to Rwanda. US President Donald Trump has said the pact, which includes calls for a joint security mechanism, gives Washington rights to local mineral wealth. The fighting has continued despite Trump’s claims that he ended the decades-long conflict.
The AU panel called for “strict respect for ceasefire commitments, full cooperation with verification mechanisms, and restraint from actions that could undermine the peace process.” It also urged the parties to continue negotiations under the Doha peace process.
The mediators called for stronger protection of civilians, particularly women and girls, measures to prevent sexual violence and accountability for abuses. They also stressed the need for safe, humanitarian access to affected communities and the protection of schools and essential services.
The appeal comes following the resumption of fighting in North Kivu province in September, with clashes reported between Congolese government forces and AFC/M23 rebels in the Masisi, Rutshuru and Walikale territories.
On September 20, the Congolese army accused the rebels of launching attacks on several fronts in violation of ceasefire agreements reached through the Doha and Washington peace processes. The rebel group has also accused government-aligned forces of carrying out attacks.
The country also continues to struggle with an Ebola outbreak. Although the health authorities said last week that the outbreak had passed its peak, the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) warned that declining case numbers did not mean the disease was under control.
The agency said insecurity in affected areas continued to hamper surveillance and efforts to contain the virus. As of October 6, the country had recorded 8,728 confirmed cases and 4,205 deaths, with a fatality rate of 48.2%.

US judge orders return of Egyptian deported to Equatorial Guinea
DAKAR, Oct 8 - A US judge has ordered the Trump administration to facilitate the release and return of an Egyptian man who was deported to Equatorial Guinea this year and has since been jailed there.
Ahmed Soliman is one of hundreds of migrants sent from the US to African countries under so-called third-country deportation deals that the US government has used to accelerate removals.
Human Rights Watch said in a report published on Thursday that 536 people had been deported to African countries "that are neither their country of citizenship nor habitual residence" between January 2025 and August 2026.
Last month, Soliman said he had faced rough treatment by Equatorial Guinean police officers. Video obtained by Reuters showed police pulling firearms on migrants including Soliman.
After Reuters published its story, Soliman was taken into custody and has been held incommunicado at a gendarmerie station that has also been used to detain human rights activists.
In a ruling seen by Reuters on Thursday, US judge John C. Hinderaker said the Department of Homeland Security must facilitate Soliman's release from custody and his return to the US. That includes arranging any travel documentation he would need to return.
The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Equatorial Guinea has also not responded to requests for comment about Soliman's case.
Soliman wrote in a declaration to an immigration judge last year that he feared being killed in Egypt because he is gay.
Reuters has documented 40 cases in which migrants granted US legal protection after being persecuted for their LGBT status were deported to third countries in Africa that either criminalize same-sex relations or have been described by the State Department as hostile to LGBT people. REUTERS

Brussels is steering Europe toward totalitarianism and a “Euro-Gestapo” while lecturing Russia on democracy, Slovak MEP Lubos Blaha has warned.
Blaha made the remarks during a European Parliament debate on Tuesday, responding to EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, who denounced Russia’s recent parliamentary elections as undemocratic.
The politician questioned why Brussels was focusing on Russia while cracking down on dissent within the bloc.
He cited arrests of pro-Palestinian protesters in Germany and the imprisonment of Estonian opposition figures, who he claimed were jailed for opposing war with Russia.
“Are you going to set up the Euro-Gestapo here, Mrs. Kallas, and lock up everyone who wants peace?” he asked.
"Will you set up a Euro-Gestapo here, Ms Kallas, and lock up all of us who want peace?" Slovak MEP Blaha calls out warmongers von der Leyen and Kallas. "You criticize the Russians for holding elections, but you do not mind that Zelensky has been governing for a third year without any elections, without a mandate. You hypocrites."
— Chay Bowes (@BowesChay) October 7, 2026
The Slovak lawmaker also questioned why Brussels was debating Russia’s elections while Europe faced mounting unrest.
“You may not have noticed, but Spain is in the streets, France is in the streets, and you are here dealing with Russian elections. You must be joking,” he said.
Blaha went on to accuse Brussels of double standards over Ukraine’s suspended presidential elections.
“You blame the Russians for having elections, but you don’t mind that [Ukraine’s Vladimir] Zelensky has been governing for three years without any elections, without a mandate,” he said. “You are hypocrites!”
Zelensky’s presidential term expired in May 2024, but elections have remained suspended under martial law.
Blaha also cited the annulment of Romania’s 2024 presidential election, claiming the vote was canceled because “the wrong candidate won.” Romania’s Constitutional Court scrapped the result over alleged irregularities and accusations of Russian interference after EU- and NATO-skeptic Calin Georgescu won the first round. Pro-EU candidate Nicusor Dan won the rerun in May 2025.
The MEP argued that Russia had held elections despite the ongoing conflict and daily Ukrainian missile and drone attacks on its territory.
The September poll saw the ruling United Russia party win nearly 58% of the party-list vote.
Blaha also defended Russian President Vladimir Putin, contrasting his popularity with that of Western European leaders.
“You have nothing to criticize Putin for, Mrs. Kallas,” he declared. “Unlike you and your Merzes and Macrons, he has the support of his own population.”
Recent polls have put German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s approval rating at a record low of 10% in October, while French President Emmanuel Macron’s support fell to 17% in September. Neither Kallas nor European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen was directly elected to her current position by voters, having assumed office through the EU’s institutional appointment process.
Blaha belongs to Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico’s Smer-SD party, which opposes EU sanctions on Russia and has criticized Western military assistance to Ukraine.

Uncrewed Systems Centre to pull drone buying together
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
17:53:14 BST
01:53:14 KST

The Uncrewed Systems Centre is the body expected to bring coherence to British drone procurement, and a newly arrived two-star officer has just taken it over, the Military Aviation Authority’s head of regulation and certification told the Apex Europe conference in London on Wednesday.
Commodore Neil Mathieson said the centre had not come up at the conference until that point, and that conversation about it tends to settle on the building it occupies when the value of it lies elsewhere. “The beauty of it is to cohere all these things, so we’re buying the right stuff with the right networks, with the right architectures,” he said.
The task in front of it is considerable, and he described it plainly. “We’ve got British Army regiments out there who are operating four or five different types of drone. They then come together at brigade level with other regiments who have also got four or five different types of drones. They don’t talk to each other. They don’t communicate in the same webs and the same networks. They then get to division level, and you’re suddenly faced with hundreds of these things,” he said, adding that doctrine and policy have not yet caught up with the rate at which equipment is arriving.
Speaking with his safety regulator hat off, he said the authority sees all of this and can advise on it while sitting outside the procurement chain. The same question arrives again further up the scale, he said, asking how a Royal Navy collaborative combat aircraft will talk to a Royal Air Force one. Companies telephone the authority announcing they will be flying at next year’s Steadfast Defender, at which point the useful questions are who is sponsoring them and how they intend to do it.
Colonel Thomas Erlenbruch of the Bundeswehr’s Cyber and Information Domain Service made the same case from the German side, and put it in terms of what a soldier can reasonably be trained to do.
He said: “Open interfaces are really, really important to be able to bring data from one system to the other, because we cannot forget that with all the autonomous systems, we also need a C2 system to get all the information they collect into, or to give missions to those systems for targeting. That’s one major user requirement, that I don’t have to train 50 different systems on the battlefield, but that I may be able to use one main system to be able to control all these different things out there, and that comes back to the standards and the interfaces. That’s the only way to be able to do it, because otherwise I cannot train my personnel to use it.”

Israeli forces killed at least 69 in southern Syria since 2024
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:52:25 UTC
01:52:25 KST

Breadcrumb
Israeli forces killed at least 69 people in southern Syria since fall of Assad
Israeli forces have killed at least 69 people in southern Syria since the ouster of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, a rights monitor has found, saying that the killings come amid a rise in ground incursions, detentions, raids on homes and checkpoints being installed.
The Syrian Network for Human Rights (SNHR) told The New Arab that the deaths and attacks were part of a pattern of assaults and operations carried out by the Israeli army in the south.
The director of the organisation, Fadel Abdul Ghani, said the Israeli army has carried out “repeated ground incursions, detentions, raids, searches of homes, built checkpoints, restricted the movements of residents and demolished civilian property using force”.
According to Abdul Ghani, data documented by the organisation shows that the number of Israeli attacks surged in 2025, particularly during the latter half of the year.
Records show that from 9 June to 5 July 2025, there were at least 22 ground incursions in Quneitra, Daraa, and the Damascus countryside. During this time, at least one civilian was killed and around 13 were detained.
On Monday, at least three people have been shot by Israeli forces in Quneitra province, with one of them being identified as a child.
The Syrian Network for Human Rights has called for urgent investigations, accountability and for the protection of civilians in a bid to stop any future violations.
Legality of Israeli incursions
Abdul Ghani called for an investigation into the legality of Israeli attacks in Syria.
“We must distinguish here between the legality of use of force inside Syrian territory, the rules governing the behaviour of forces towards civilians, Israel’s responsibility as a state, and individual criminal responsibility for possible war crimes,” he said.
Article 2(4) of the Charter of the United Nations prohibits threats or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state.
Should Israel invoke the right of self-defence under Article 51 of the Charter, “it must be evaluated in the light of legal considerations governing the exercise of this right, foremost among which is the existence of an armed attack, necessity and proportionality,” Abdul Ghani explained.
He also said that the 1974 Syrian-Israeli disengagement agreement established a separation zone that is supposed to be free of military forces, except the United Nations Disengagement Observer Force (UNDOF).
He noted that the presence of Israeli forces and the military operations carried out within the separation zone have raised concerns over compliance with the conditions of the agreement.
Further questions have also been raised on whether Israeli attacks and incursions could be considered an occupation.
Abdul Ghani said there are certain guidelines and frameworks which outline what constitutes an occupation, noting that article 42 of the Hague Regulations state that this includes when a territory is effectively under the authority of an enemy army.
While he stopped short of calling the attacks an occupation, he demanded Israel to “stop the use of force and incursions that are not based on a legitimate legal basis, respect the disengagement agreement, stop arbitrary detentions, and reveal the names and whereabouts of detainees and the legal basis for their detention”.
He also called on detainees to be able to communicate with their families and lawyers, and for the ICRC to be able to reach out to them.

‘Hard to scare me’: Eisenkot says threat against him left on fallen son’s grave
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:49:48 UTC
01:49:48 KST

A threatening message aimed at former IDF chief Gadi Eisenkot was recently left on the grave of his son Gal, who was killed fighting in Gaza in December 2023, Eisenkot revealed for the first time in an interview with Yedioth Ahronoth. “Someone made the effort to go to the cemetery and leave a threatening message aimed at me on Gal’s grave,” said Eisenkot, who now heads the Yashar! party. “I debated what to do about it, and in the end I decided to do nothing. At this stage of my life, it is very difficult to frighten me.”
The revelation came during an interview in which Eisenkot also made serious allegations over the record of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s conduct before the October 7 massacre. He said he suspects documents provided to investigators were falsified. “I see something here with potential criminal implications,” Eisenkot said. “In my assessment, reports were falsified.”
Eisenkot said his suspicions were based partly on material provided to the state comptroller, which he compared with information he had seen as a member of Israel’s wartime Cabinet and a parliamentary intelligence subcommittee. “When I take what was distributed to the state comptroller, and I know as a Cabinet member and a member of the intelligence subcommittee what material was there, I have a very deep suspicion of document falsification,” he said. “In my view, this is a document that someone cooked.” His allegations have not been established as fact, and the material presented does not identify who may have altered any document.
The document on Netanyahu’s desk
One document at the center of the dispute concerns possible action against Hamas’ senior leadership. According to the material cited in the interview, it was prepared by Netanyahu’s military secretary following a security assessment convened by the prime minister on October 1, 2023, six days before the Hamas-led attack. It included the instruction: “Advancing operational readiness for the recommended targeted killings, Hamas leaders, with emphasis on an emergency scenario.”
The document appears to indicate that senior security officials had recommended preparing for strikes against Hamas leaders shortly before October 7, potentially conflicting with Netanyahu’s account of what he was told before the massacre. Eisenkot also said he believes Netanyahu’s opposition to a state commission of inquiry stems from a desire to avoid scrutiny over the information available to his office before the attack. A broader investigation by Yedioth Ahronoth journalists Ronen Bergman and Yuval Rubovitch into Netanyahu’s version of events is due to appear in the newspaper’s 7 Days weekend supplement.
‘My youngest son will fight there’
The interview then turned personal when Eisenkot produced an April 2004 article from Yedioth Ahronoth, written when he was a young brigadier general commanding IDF forces in the West Bank. 
“Terrorism will continue for many more years,” he said at the time, before adding: “The bitter truth is that there is no ‘total victory’ in this struggle. Our role is to minimize Palestinian achievements.”
He made another prediction in that interview that would later prove painfully personal: “I expect that even my youngest son, who is now 5, will fight in the West Bank or Gaza.” That child was Gal Meir Eisenkot, who was killed nearly two decades later while fighting in Gaza. Now, Eisenkot says, even his son’s grave has become a target in the political battles surrounding him.

Brazil’s voters have moved camps
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

01:46:45 KST

Brazilians awoke on Monday to a changed political map. Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro, who is under house arrest for attempting to overturn the last presidential election, has received 47 percent of the vote in the first round of this year’s presidential election, while the incumbent, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, received 45 percent. Brazil appears poised to join the growing ranks of rightward-veering countries.
In fact, Bolsonaro’s first-place finish understates the scale of Brazil’s political shift. The far-right Liberal Party (PL) also won five governorships outright and its allies took Sao Paulo, Goias and three other states. It would hold 28 of 81 seats in the Senate, the largest faction in a legislative session since 1988. Lula’s former minister of finance Fernando Haddad lost Sao Paulo in the first round, and in Rio de Janeiro, a PL candidate who trailed the former mayor by 18 points last month, nearly beat him outright.
With a presidential runoff set for Oct. 25, Bolsonaro is the clear favorite. Lula could still close the gap, but he has no room for error. Every first-round leader since 1989 whose election went to a runoff has gone on to win the second round.
Illustration: Mountain People
Demography explains part of this shift. Brazil’s median age is 36, up from 29 in 2010. Brazilians are wealthier than they were when Lula’s left-wing Workers’ Party (PT) first won power in 2002, and evangelical Christians make up more than one-quarter of the population. With crime topping voters’ concerns, many put public order ahead of redistribution, the PT’s strong suit.
The PT has never found the right language to reach such voters. It is fielding an 80-year-old candidate for a fourth term because it never created a succession plan. Talented figures have long been sidelined or driven away, and women remain scarce at the top. The PT campaigned with radio jingles and rallies, while the right dominated online, ultimately making inroads in many PT strongholds.
The right also nationalized local politics. Gubernatorial and senate races became plebiscites on Lula, allowing the Bolsonaro brand to carry candidates who had been unknown just months earlier. Many voters cast ballots for the right as a protest against Lula. Since that kind of behavior is generally reserved for the runoff, it suggests that their minds are made up.
The Supreme Court became another liability for Lula. Justice Alexandre de Moraes led the coup case against Bolsonaro and ordered his arrest. Though Moraes was appointed by former president Michel Temer in 2017, many voters came to see him as a figure of the left. The collapse of Banco Master reinforced that view. The bank had a contract worth about 129 million reals (US$26 million) with the law firm of Moraes’ wife, although they deny wrongdoing. While Flavio was also implicated in the same case, through messages about the banker Daniel Vorcaro funding a film on his father, the right nonetheless casts the judiciary as part of Lula’s camp.
The PT does have a narrow path to victory, but the arithmetic is unforgiving. Minor presidential candidates took about 8 percent of the vote, and most of their supporters lean right. Bolsonaro needs only one-third of them, whereas Lula must either win two-thirds of them or draw several million new voters from the more than 33 million who stayed home. He becomes a slight favorite only if about 7 million additional voters turn out and break heavily in his favor, which would require a mobilization in the northeast far beyond anything seen in 2022.
Lula’s campaign must make the runoff about the Bolsonaro family. It can call attention to the fact that Flavio’s brother Eduardo lobbied Washington for the tariffs and sanctions that hit Brazilian exporters hard last year. Moreover, the Bolsonaros are well-known allies of US President Donald Trump, and Brazil’s intelligence agency reportedly told European officials that the US is interfering in this election. Such charges make sovereignty a live issue for Lula to seize on.
However, to address concerns about his age and give centrist voters permission to support the left, Lula should commit publicly to serving only one more term and naming a successor. He also must take a stronger line on public security and safety — an issue that the PT has always ceded to the right.
To that end, the federal government’s meaningful action against the financial networks of Brazil’s largest organized-crime operation the Primeiro Comando da Capital, allows Lula to campaign on his law-enforcement record, in addition to the PT’s redistributive economic policies. The PT also needs to court evangelical women and gig workers directly, such as by addressing living costs and promoting more portable benefits.
Whatever happens on Oct. 25, the harder work comes after. The PT must position itself for the Brazil that actually exists: an older, wealthier, more devout country preoccupied with crime. That would require a new generation of leaders.
Brazil is part of a broader, hemispheric pattern. In October last year, midterm elections left Argentinian President Javier Milei in a stronger position. Soon after, Hondurans voted out the governing Libre party and elected a conservative president. In Chile, the conservative President Jose Antonio Kast won in December last year. In Peru, President Keiko Fujimori, the daughter of a far-right former president convicted of serious human-rights abuses, won a runoff. And in Colombia, the right-wing candidate, President Abelardo de la Espriella, narrowly beat Ivan Cepeda, ending the left’s hold on power. Security and the cost of living decided most of these contests, and the left had little to offer on either issue.
Poland offers another warning. In 2023, a broad coalition led by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk ousted the illiberal Law and Justice (PiS) party, largely by mobilizing women and young voters who had previously stayed home. However, the new government’s efforts to restore judicial independence and reverse the previous PiS takeover of public media drew charges of partisanship, and last year, Poles elected a right-wing candidate in President Karol Nawrocki, who is blocking much of the government’s agenda. Ousting an illiberal government turned out to be the easy part. Holding on to power usually requires progress on kitchen-table or quality-of-life issues. As important as institutional repairs might be, they rarely mobilize voters.
Still, South Korea offers a different lesson. When right-wing former president Yoon Suk-yeol declared martial law in December 2024, the people took to the streets, and legislators climbed fences to reach the parliamentary chamber and overturn the edict. The decree lasted only a few hours, and Yoon was ultimately removed and prosecuted.
Similarly, in Brazil, the Supreme Federal Court and the electoral court held the line after former president Jair Bolsonaro’s attempted coup in January 2023. However, the judiciary’s expansive role in the crisis created a populist backlash that produced the new right-leaning Senate. Sometimes, institutions can preserve their legitimacy only by avoiding perceptions of overreach.
The lesson, in Brazil and elsewhere, is that democrats cannot count on the courts to save them. They must win on the issues that voters care about, starting with crime, while protecting the independent institutions that they would need while in opposition. Brazilians would choose their next president in a little over two months. For the PT to find its way back onto solid ground would take considerably longer — even if it ekes out a comeback victory this time.
Robert Muggah, cofounder of the Igarape Institute and the SecDev Group, is a member of the World Economic Forum’s Global Future Council on Cities of Tomorrow and an adviser to the Global Risks Report.

Its central tool at sea is the “cabbage strategy”: the Chinese People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) layers fishing boats, maritime militia, coast guard cutters and warships around Taiwan’s contested waters in overlapping rings. Each layer normalizes daily coercion, narrows Taiwan’s freedom of movement and chips away at its maritime sovereignty — all while staying below the threshold of armed conflict. This is “gray zone” warfare at its most cost-effective — one of Beijing’s most promising

What would make your life easier? Martin Lewis asks public for ‘small ideas’ to improve UK
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:46:44 UTC
01:46:44 KST

Every day, people run into what the finance expert Martin Lewis calls “the life-potholes of unintended consequences” – clunky systems and poorly conceived rules that make life harder than it should be. His latest project, the Small Ideas Initiative, will attempt to address that, with a cross-party panel of politicians and policymakers crowdsourcing ideas for everyday fixes to take to government.
The ideas could cover anything from health and schools to policing, tech and money. Lewis is encouraging people to submit ideas for “practical, low-cost, non-controversial ways to improve the UK” before 12 November.
“If we can fix some of those frustration points, we can make people’s lives easier, save time and help everyone get on with work or the things they enjoy,” said Lewis.
“There’s just a sense that there’s so many little things to fix,” said Polly Mackenzie, who worked with Lewis to come up with the idea. Mackenzie, who was director of policy to Nick Clegg during his deputy premiership, says the initiative could be an avenue to regaining trust in public institutions.
“I think this is about rebuilding confidence in the idea that government can sort stuff out, rather than rebuilding confidence on any one political party having the right ideas,” she said.
Mackenzie will sit on the panel, which will choose about 50 ideas to take to the government, councils and regulators. Alongside Lewis, the initiative is run by the innovation charity Nesta and the public participation charity Involve.
The Reform MP Danny Kruger, the former Conservative MP Penny Mordaunt, and the Labour mayor of West Yorkshire, Tracy Brabin, are among those sitting on the panel alongside Mackenzie. She said the group had “a real interest and capability in getting involved and sweating the small stuff”.
The ideas they are looking for will be “no-brainers” that are not party-political and would be easy fixes. Mackenzie said a good example was when she and Lewis first set up the Money and Mental Health Policy Institute and discovered through a survey that GPs had been charging to fill out debt and mental health evidence forms.
“People in debt crisis were having to pay 80, 100, 150 quid to get forbearance for their debts, which is just wrong-headed,” she said. In 2019, two years after the Money and Mental Health Policy Institute started its campaign, the law changed.
Before the initiative’s launch, people in north London shared the policies they would consider submitting. Clare, a railway worker, suggested the government should increase rubbish collections during heatwaves, saying her bins had been “a buffet for flies” this summer. Mark, who works on a market stall, said he would ask the government to put more bins in and around train stations. “There are no bins. I know it’s for security reasons, but I think they could find a way,” he said.
Kwajo Tweneboa, a social housing campaigner who will also sit on the deciding panel, said relatively small changes could make a “massive difference”.
“One small change I’d like to see is housing providers aiming to fix repairs properly, rather than repeatedly applying plaster fixes that don’t address the underlying problem and prolong the misery for tenants,” he says. “I’ve seen how something that should be a straightforward repair can drag on for months, with residents having to repeatedly chase their landlord while the problem gets worse.
“It’s about listening to those everyday experiences and turning simple, practical ideas into policy that can make a tangible difference to people’s lives.”

A Chinese militia boat was spotted along with two other vessels off Taiwan’s east coast in August, a surveillance report showed, the first known sighting of such a craft in the area.
The Apex Aviation report identified the Minfudingyu 07902 (閩福鼎漁07902) as a fishing boat that doubles as a Chinese militia vessel, which was seen operating with a Chinese coast guard cutter and a research vessel in mid-August.
China has stepped up activity off the nation’s east coast since June with regular coast guard patrols.
Photo: Apex Aviation via Reuters
Officials in Taiwan said they believe China is practicing for a potential maritime blockade using overlapping military, paramilitary and civilian assets.
China was “using law enforcement and scientific research as cover for harassment, seeking to expand their scope of operations during a non-conflict scenario to create an illusion of de facto jurisdiction,” the Ministry of National Defense said.
Such actions undermine international order and challenge Taiwan’s maritime rights, the ministry said, adding that the military was using reconnaissance tools to track Chinese activity in coordination with other agencies, including the Coast Guard Administration.
In a practice dating to the 1950s, China’s maritime militia, more commonly observed around South China Sea flashpoints, consists of fishing vessels whose crews receive training and support to operate in disputed waters, often alongside China Coast Guard ships.
Analysts said the fleet helps Beijing assert maritime claims while maintaining a civilian appearance.
The Minfudingyu, the China Coast Guard cutter 2502 and the research vessel Xiang Yang Hong 03 (向陽紅03) were operating near Taiwan in mid-August, two senior Taiwanese officials briefed on the matter said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Authorities identified the fishing boat as part of the Chinese People’s Liberation Army’s maritime militia fleet, which Taiwan was tracking and which was operating “in coordination with Chinese coast guard maritime harassment drills,” one official said.
“The purpose of militia boats is to conduct substantive harassment,” the official said.
The other official said the three craft were operating “in an area not commonly used by Chinese vessels” and had been “designated for heightened monitoring.”
The Apex report said a reconnaissance aircraft the company operates detected a Chinese maritime group more than 30 nautical miles (55.6km) off Hualien County.
The patrol by Apex reflects Taiwan’s efforts to involve civilian firms in technologies relevant to the government’s whole-of-society resilience initiative, although the company said its patrols are independently run and not carried out for the government.
Chinese warships, coast guard vessels, research ships and some civilian vessels continue to operate in overlapping ways, “creating pressure in the waters surrounding Taiwan,” Apex defense and security director Honor Hung (洪曉榮) said.
The three Chinese vessels were spread over a roughly 10-nautical-mile radius, Honor said, adding that one surveillance tracking could not determine their missions or any coordination among them.

Exports hit record amid AI demand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:46:40 UTC
01:46:40 KST

Taiwan’s exports rose to a record last month as booming demand for artificial intelligence (AI) servers and other high-tech products powered shipments, putting the economy on track for another year of exceptionally strong trade growth.
Exports jumped 60.9 percent from a year earlier to US$87.22 billion last month, the highest monthly figure on record, the Ministry of Finance said yesterday.
Shipments have risen for 35 straight months, extending Taiwan’s longest uninterrupted growth streak.
Photo: CNA
The latest surge was led by AI-related products, with demand offsetting uncertainty over global trade policy and geopolitical tensions, Department of Statistics Director-General Beatrice Tsai (蔡美娜) said.
Exports of information, communications and audio-video products more than doubled from a year earlier, with shipments of graphics cards, servers, storage devices, switches and routers all posting triple-digit growth, the ministry said.
Electronic components were also a major source of momentum, rising 45.3 percent as AI applications and preparations for new consumer electronics products boosted demand, it said.
Third-quarter exports surged 44.6 percent year-on-year to US$244.92 billion, exceeding the government’s August forecast and suggesting room for an upward revision to its 11.05 percent GDP growth forecast for this year.
“The growth momentum is expected to continue in October,” Tsai said, adding that exports are expected to rise to 40 to 44 percent from a year earlier, potentially reaching another record.
Shipments of non-tech products also improved, although textile products bucked the trend, ministry data showed.
The US and Southeast Asia were the biggest contributors to last month’s export growth, with shipments to the US more than doubling, while exports to Southeast Asia jumped 93.4 percent from a year earlier.
The markets accounted for about 70 percent of the increase in total exports as global supply chains continued to realign, Tsai said.
Shipments to China, including Hong Kong, as well as Europe and Japan also posted double-digit gains.
Imports rose 51.7 percent to a record US$63.59 billion last month, leaving Taiwan with a monthly trade surplus of US$23.63 billion, also an all-time high, the data showed.
The outlook for exports remains strong for this quarter as cloud-service providers and governments accelerate investment in AI infrastructure, which is supporting demand for semiconductors, servers and related components, Tsai said.
The year-end shopping season in China, Europe and the US should provide an additional boost, she said.
Still, shifts in global trade policy and geopolitical tensions remain key risks to the outlook, Tsai added.
In the first nine months of this year, exports soared 46.2 percent from the same period last year to US$661.55 billion, topping the full-year figure of US$640.69 billion last year.
Imports rose 41.3 percent to about US$501 billion over the same period, the data showed.

Do not pave the way for competitors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:46:40 UTC
01:46:40 KST

Now that businessman Elon Musk has approached Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC) to discuss collaboration on his Terafab project, the issue Taiwan should be focused on is not whether TSMC would establish more factories in the US, but whether cracks are beginning to appear in the division of labor underpinning the chip foundry.
TSMC is evaluating a potential investment in Texas — but the structure of the partnership, ownership stakes, manufacturing processes and timeline have yet to be determined, Reuters said.
It is too early to conclude that TSMC’s potential Texas fab would be Terafab, but when a hyperscale artificial intelligence (AI) customer wants not only to buy chips, but also to own a semiconductor fab, the larger question is: Is TSMC dealing with a major customer or future competitor?
The Terafab project, a massive chip factory designed to build more than 1 terawatt of AI computing power annually, is different from a typical start-up foundry. Tesla’s job openings describe it as a highly vertically integrated semiconductor manufacturing hub, bringing logic chips, memory, advanced packaging, testing and photomask production under one system, and requires 2-nanometer-class Gate-All-Around process capabilities. That would bring Tesla’s autonomous driving and robotics, SpaceX’s space computing, and the AI computing needs of Musk’s AI start-up, xAI, into a single supply chain. When a company needs enough computing power to support an entire fab, semiconductor manufacturing could shift from an outsourced project to strategic infrastructure.
However, a fab cannot simply be replicated with money. Extreme ultraviolet lithography machines can be purchased and fabs can be built, but the hardest things to acquire are process integration, yield ramp-up, equipment management, materials qualification and the discipline of mass production accumulated over decades. This is precisely why Musk needs TSMC. If the arrangement follows a model similar to Japan Advanced Semiconductor Manufacturing Inc or European Semiconductor Manufacturing Co, with the customer taking an equity stake while TSMC retains majority ownership and operational control, it would still be an extension of an existing business model.
However, if Terafab holds the controlling stake while TSMC provides process technology and operational expertise, the implications would be entirely different. TSMC’s most valuable asset is its ability to integrate processes, equipment, materials, yields and customer confidentiality into a manufacturing system capable of sustained operation. If that capability is exported to a customer-controlled factory, the moat of the chip foundry would be redefined.
Taiwan should not focus solely on how much advanced process technology is being moved overseas. It should also ask who controls the fab, which generation of process technology is being transferred and whether the other party is gaining access to production capacity or manufacturing capabilities. Manufacturing for a customer overseas and assisting that customer in acquiring the ability to manage an advanced fab are vastly different things. What the nation needs to preserve is its Taiwan centered ecosystem of research and development, process integration, key talent and supply chain collaboration.
Musk on Saturday last week wrote on X: “Just discussions, but something may come of it.” If the outcome is simply another major customer, TSMC would secure a long-term order. However, if it instead helps a customer develop advanced semiconductor manufacturing capabilities, what would be rewritten is not merely the story of a fab in Texas, but the division of labor that TSMC founder Morris Chang (張忠謀) created.
TSMC can manufacture more chips for the AI era, but it should not, in building fabs for its customers, pave the way for competitors.

Senegal, Morocco replay their title match in court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:46:39 UTC
01:46:39 KST

Senegal and Morocco played a chaotic Africa Cup of Nations final in January and they were contesting the title again yesterday — this time at the Court of Arbitration for Sport.
A turbulent match, provoking violent clashes between Senegal fans and Moroccan police, and a controversial fallout was being relitigated at sport’s highest court in Switzerland nearly nine months after the referee’s final whistle blew in Rabat.
The authority of that referee, Jean-Jacques Ndala of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, could be decisive in Senegal’s appeal to regain the trophy that was stripped from players who earned it on the field of play with a 1-0 win over Morocco after extra-time.
Photo: AFP
The result was overturned in March to a 3-0 win for Morocco by a Confederation of African Football (CAF) appeals panel because Senegal’s team walked off to protest a penalty being awarded, causing a 15-minute delay in play.
A one-day appeal hearing was scheduled with three judges behind closed doors yesterday at CAS’ headquarters in Lausanne.
No target date has been set by the court for a verdict that should finally crown the champions of African men’s soccer. The next Africa Cup of Nations tournament is scheduled to start in June next year, cohosted by Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda.
Leaders of the Senegalese and Moroccan soccer federations were expected to skip the hearing that clashes with a three-day CAF soccer summit in Cape Verde being attended by FIFA president Gianni Infantino.
Soccer’s rule book, The Laws of the Game, is clear about the referee’s decisionmaking power.
“The decisions of the referee regarding facts connected with play, including whether or not a goal is scored and the result of the match, are final,” Law 5.2 states.
Senegal beat hosts Morocco in a game eventually completed to referee Ndala’s satisfaction, despite the chaos.
The referee restarted play once Senegal’s players had returned to the field after protesting a penalty-kick awarded to Morocco deep in stoppage-time.
Before the referee could decide to abandon the game, which would have gifted the title to Morocco, Senegal’s Sadio Mane helped persuade his team to finish the game as tensions rose in the stadium.
The game restarted with the spot-kick that could have won Morocco a first title since 1976.
What Brahim Diaz did next entered soccer history. The Real Madrid forward placed a delicate slow chip shot, designed to deceive the goalkeeper who typically dives to one side and watches the ball slowly arc into the middle of the goal.
Senegal goalkeeper Edouard Mendy stood up straight and easily caught the ball.
The game went into extra-time and four minutes later Senegal midfielder Pape Gueye surged forward to fire a rising shot into the Morocco net. It was the only goal.
More than US$1 million in total fines for the two federations, plus players and Senegal coach Pape Thiaw, were imposed 11 days after the game by Cairo-based CAF disciplinary judges.
The judges dismissed a request by Morocco to have the result annulled and be declared the winners because of the Senegalese walk-off.
There were appeals to CAF and, two months after the final, Senegal were ruled to have forfeited the game.
CAF appeal judges cited tournament rules that if a team “refuses to play or leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorization of the referee, it shall be considered loser and shall be eliminated for good from the current competition.”
Senegal’s government promised to help “pursue all appropriate legal avenues” to regain the title and called for an investigation “into suspected corruption” within African soccer.
The case fueled the sense that 2030 FIFA World Cup cohost Morocco has extensive influence within CAF and FIFA.

TRC to sell limited-edition railway boxed lunches
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:46:37 UTC
01:46:37 KST

The Agriculture and Food Agency collaborated with Taiwan Railway Corp (TRC) to launch limited-edition railway boxed lunches in celebration of Double Ten National Day, which feature traceable, Taiwan-grown produce.
The boxed lunches use regional specialty ingredients such as Taiwan quinoa, glue berry, squid and eel, each having two main dishes.
For example, the meals available at TRC’s Taichung catering services branch has braised pork ribs and stir-fried baby squid as its dual entree, with braised tofu skin, fried taro balls and seasonal vegetables as side dishes.
Photo: Wu Po-hsuan, Taipei Times
People can buy the meals at TRC’s six local catering services branches in Taipei, Keelung’s Cidu District (七堵), Taichung, Kaohsiung, Hualien County and Taitung County until Nov. 7.
Agency Deputy Director-General Huang Chao-hsing (黃昭興) said each boxed lunch is priced at NT$199 and uses only traceable, Taiwan-grown ingredients.
The combination of ingredients was designed by TRC’s nutritionists based on the balance of nutrients and calories, he said.
TRC deputy general manager Huang Chen-chao (黃振照) said TRC has been implementing the Hazard Analysis Critical Control Point system across the six local services branches to ensure food safety.
He thanked the agency for assisting TRC in sourcing local food ingredients, adding that the company expects more collaborations with the agency.
Key ingredient suppliers also spoke.
Chiu Ming-chung (邱茗莊), head of the 29th coarse grains production and marketing group in Yunlin County’s Yuanchang Township (元長), said that the tofu skin used in the meals is made solely from “Kaohsiung No. 10” soybean, which has a richer aroma than imported soybean.
Tao City Veg chairwoman Yuka Yu (尤優佳) said that Tao City Veg is a major greenhouse vegetable farming company in central Taiwan with 20 hectares of cultivation area.
Its vegetables are supplied to more than 4,000 catering channels, including Din Tai Fung, she said.
Mr Djulis Co owner Ljuwa thanked the agency for helping integrate Taiwan quinoa — a traditional indigenous ingredient — into railway the boxed lunches for the first time.
Taiwan quinoa is mainly produced in Taitung and Pingtung counties, he said.
Taiwan quinoa and millet constitute the two critical economic crops for mountainous indigenous communities, where farmlands are limited and mechanized agriculture is not as applicable as in low-lying areas, Ljuwa said.
The agency said 20,000 boxed lunches would be produced during the event period, adding it expects the event to help Taiwan-grown produce become a regular part of railway lunchboxes.

SOCIETY
Total population falls
Taiwan’s population dropped for the 33rd consecutive time last month to 23,213,251, a decline of 11,470 from the previous month, Ministry of the Interior data showed. There were 7,704 births last month, an increase of 212 from August, bringing the total number of births in the first nine months to 69,446. There were also 16,712 deaths last month, an increase compared with August and the same period last year. Meanwhile, 70,672 people moved to Taiwan last month, down 8,408 from the same month last year, but up 4,273 from August, the data showed. However, 73,134 people left Taiwan, resulting in a net outflow of 2,462 people. Accounting for births, deaths and migration, the total population fell by 11,470 compared with August.
Photo: CNA
ENVIRONMENT
Night markets give vouchers
An eco-friendly campaign offering vouchers at 40 night markets across Taiwan is to be held over the next four Saturdays, the Administration of Commerce said yesterday. Visitors who bring reusable bags, utensils or cups can exchange NT$100 for NT$200 worth of vouchers to be used through Nov. 8, it said. Staff at night markets would verify the eco-friendly items and distribute the vouchers, it said. Those who spend NT$500 or more at the same night market can also present an invoice, receipt or proof of purchase at the campaign service desk to receive a Taiwanese-style mesh reusable shopping bag, it added. Each night market would have a limited supply of 60 shopping bags and each participant would only be able to claim one per day.
LITERATURE
Writers’ festival to open
The Taiwan Writers Festival is to bring together authors and translators from the US, Australia, South Korea, Japan, Singapore, Finland and Poland to meet and hold discussions with their Taiwanese counterparts next month, organizers said yesterday. From Nov. 6 to 22, participants would join sessions exploring how literature looks back on the past while tackling present-day questions about technology, the environment and social change, curator Yen Hung-ya (閻鴻亞) said. Among the international guests is US author Barbara Demick, said the National Museum of Taiwan Literature, which is organizing the festival. Demick will join a panel with China-born journalist Annie Zhang (張潔平) and Taiwanese journalist Jason Liu (劉致昕) to explore how writers navigate power, crises and truth in their work, the museum said.
PUBLISHING
Magazine marks 50 years
The government-funded Taiwan Panorama magazine is celebrating its 50th anniversary with an exhibition of some of its best photographs of Taiwan’s social, economic and political development over the past half-century. The free exhibition is to be held at Taipei’s Huashan 1914 Creative Park from today through Oct. 19. It would feature four sections exploring everyday life, public infrastructure and resilience, democracy and freedom, and Taiwan’s presence on the world stage. Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Francois Wu (吳志中) said that since its inauguration in 1976, Taiwan Panorama has documented Taiwan’s stories through different eras. As the magazine is set to end its print edition and transition to a digital format at the end of this year, Wu said its vast collection of stories and images would continue to live on through digital platforms, online exhibitions and more diverse content.

Samsung profit rises on chip windfall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:46:36 UTC
01:46:36 KST

Samsung Electronics Co reported a nearly nine-fold rise in quarterly operating profit, although that was still shy of sky-high expectations elevated by relentless spending on artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure.
The world’s largest memorychip maker yesterday posted a record preliminary operating profit of 107.4 trillion won (US$80.1 billion) for the quarter through last month, but even those record results still fell short of the average analyst forecast.
Revenue was 195 trillion won, also lower than expectations.
Photo: AFP
“Samsung has delivered a record profit and still fallen short of expectations, which tells you just how demanding the AI trade has become,” eToro Group Ltd lead Asia Pacific analyst Josh Gilbert said.
Technology providers are rushing to secure supplies of memory needed to power AI services. High-bandwidth memory (HBM) — the critical chips used alongside Nvidia Corp and other AI accelerators — is drawing massive spending, with flash memory and low-power chips also in demand.
The record numbers and high expectations underscore how sharply the economics of the AI boom have swung in favor of Samsung, SK Hynix Inc and Micron Technology Inc.
The boom has transformed Samsung’s semiconductor business, which only a few years ago was grappling with losses after a punishing downturn in demand.
Now, the AI infrastructure buildout is absorbing vast amounts of advanced DRAM, while Samsung is gaining ground on SK Hynix in HBM.
The strength of the cycle is also showing up in South Korea’s trade data, with last month’s semiconductor export more than tripling from a year earlier.
Analysts on average estimate Samsung’s chip division will post operating profit of 110 trillion won, while its electronics unit will report a loss.
The Suwon-based company is scheduled to release a full financial statement on Oct. 29.
However, market caution persists.
Samsung’s shares remain about 25 percent below their June peak even after the company reported record-breaking results in July.
Investors retain a measure of skepticism around soaring profits in a sector prone to boom-and-bust cycles.
Samsung and SK Hynix are now expanding production capacity while also increasingly backing companies in the AI sector in a bid to drive more demand for their products.
Highlighting market dynamics, Advanced Micro Devices Inc (AMD) chief executive officer Lisa Su (蘇姿丰) emphasized long-term strategic partnerships with Samsung and SK Hynix during a visit to Seoul this week.
Su said that AMD has begun shipping its next-generation Instinct MI455X and Helios systems featuring HBM4.
“Memory is so essential to overall computing; it has been a very tight supply environment,” Su told reporters on Wednesday, adding that AMD’s HBM partnerships with Samsung and SK Hynix will span multiple product generations.
“We’re encouraging our partners to build as fast as possible,” she said.

That pushed fundraising this year above US$92 billion and within reach of the US$112.5 billion record set in 2021. Russia calls 2nd plague case false
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:46:35 UTC
01:46:35 KST

The Russian health regulator Rospotrebnadzor yesterday said that reports that a second person had fallen ill following the death of a worker at a plague research laboratory in Siberia were false.
Preventive measures have been completed for all individuals who had contact with the worker who died last week, and no dangerous pathogenic microorganisms have been detected, the watchdog said.
On Wednesday, Russia warned against “false” information as reports emerged of a second suspected, with Washington and Brussels calling for transparency and neighboring Mongolia tightening health surveillance.
Photo: AP
Russian news outlet People of Baikal on Friday last week reported that a 28-year-old woman employed at a plague research institute in Siberia’s Irkutsk region had died of the disease, possibly after contracting it from a broken test tube.
International concern has grown over the death and suspicions that a second employee at the institute fell ill.
The US, the EU and the WHO have all called on Russia to be transparent about the situation.
Mongolia’s government on Wednesday said that “health surveillance and monitoring measures [were] being implemented at the border” with Russia.
On Wednesday, WHO Epidemic and Pandemic Management Director Maria Van Kerkhove said the UN health agency did not know what caused the woman’s death, which unconfirmed reports in Russia blamed on pneumonic plague — a severe form of plague that can spread from person to person.
She urged Russia to provide more information about the case.
Russian authorities have played down the reports, determining the woman died of pneumonia and insisting there was no risk of an outbreak.
Asked about reports of a second case, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters that “the vast majority of what the media is reporting regarding this situation is false information.”
Asked if a bioweapon was involved, US President Donald Trump told reporters in the Oval Office: “We don’t think so. We’re going to find out soon enough, but we don’t think so.”
“If you listen to them, it’s under control, but you know, people have said that before about other things,” he added.
In Shelekhov, where the 28-year-old lab worker, Darya Shipilova, had been hospitalized before she was reported to have died of plague, residents spoke of stepped up health precautions in place.
“My brother’s in primary school. They’ve already made masks compulsory, so they have to wear them everywhere,” said Alina, a 22-year-old Shelekhov resident.
Oksana, a 35-year-old manager, was admitted to a maternity ward for observation, but said she could not be discharged and spent four days in quarantine.
“In the hospital, people started talking about how a woman had died and they suspected it was the plague,” she said.
“They stopped accepting lab samples and wouldn’t let anyone out. So it was very strict,” she added.
The incident has drawn criticism and comparisons with Moscow’s long history of downplaying or covering up the scale of health disasters — ranging from the Soviet response to the 1986 Chernobyl disaster to the COVID-19 pandemic.
In Shelekhov, rumors have filled the information abyss.
“I’ve read about it being some kind of unclear pneumonia or COVID, something like that. To be honest, I don’t believe in anything anymore,” said Oksana, who declined to give her surname.
“There’s so much information that I no longer know what to believe or who to listen to,” she said.
“The day it happened, my mother rang me, shouting that 10 people had already died, even though there were no official reports,” Alexandra Iskalova, a 22-year-old who works in a medical center, said.
“I’d read somewhere that it was something like Hong Kong syphilis, and that it was actually caused by bears,” she said, referring to a fictional disease from a popular Russian TV show.
“People were absolutely panicking because there were no official statements,” she added.
The Russian health agency on Wednesday said that it had determined “there are no epidemic risks for the population,” adding that extensive investigations had uncovered “no emergencies” and that the lab had complied with “proper control when working with pathogenic microorganisms.”
“More than 90 percent of contacts have completed medical observation,” it added.
The WHO on Tuesday said that its initial risk assessment, based on the information available, was moderate to low for the Irkutsk region, low for Russia as a whole and very low for Europe.

The folk artistry and architecture of dreams
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:46:34 UTC
01:46:34 KST

Known colloquially as Fuxing Township’s (福興鄉) Changhua Seashell Temple, the correctly named Sanqing Sanyuan Temple (三清三元宮) is the incredible work of just one man.
Its story began when businessman Huang Chi-Chun (黃奇春) purchased a plot of land opposite Xiuan Cemetery (修安公墓) and launched a successful tropical fish farm.
Years later, in the mid-1970s, plagued by very specific dreams, or possibly prophetic visions, Huang was instructed to erect a monumental edifice in honor of the local spirits.
Photo: Shane O’Reilly
He had full faith in his precognition, and it became his life’s calling to build what would evolve into Taiwan’s very first Seashell Temple (貝殼廟).
This was a true labor of love that would take him over 20 years to fulfill.
The dreamlike directions he received demanded an incredibly detailed, decorative aesthetic. As such, he gathered thousands of mollusk, snail and conch shells from the surrounding coastal waters and imported coral and seaweed from abroad.
Working with compliant sandstone on top of a wire and concrete foundation, he was able to easily affix and bind the precise pieces of his assemblage with little help.
As the project unfolded, many locals thought Huang was crazy. But as Huang’s artistic flair became apparent, respect grew.
The circular entrance acts as a portal to an almost carnivalesque 200-square-meter realm watched over by a crenelated arch and high boundary walls fastened with an assortment of colorful figurines.
Beyond the ubiquitous Tiangong Censer (天公爐) dedication to the Jade Emperor, a variety of deities in all shapes and sizes come into focus, ranging from the reverent to the fantastical.
A collection of idolatrous human figures, dragons, phoenixes, various mythical creatures and farm animals peer out from every ledge, grotto and wall.
In certain sections, colonies of coral are used to create decorative waves of symmetrically aligned formations with a highly defined porous texture.
Other designs, more mosaic in nature, are created in an almost pointillist manner, necessitating tiny seashells arranged by color within the weaving of marine sea fans (海樹) for added dramatic effect.
Visitors are flanked by all manner of exquisitely intricate depictions that continue around the back of the altar room along a highly ornate walkway.
Deep within this central chamber, the highly venerated Taoist deities, the Three Pure Ones (三清道祖), representing all cosmic energy and wisdom, preside over the space.
It’s here that visitors will find a stairway that leads down to a long, neon-lit and similarly adorned corridor guiding them to what remains of Huang Chi-Chun’s initial venture, the tropical fish farm.
Alternatively, a separate entrance can be found next to the temple gateway. There the beautiful grave and monument dedicated to Huang’s late wife stands.
Upon entering the farm, to the sounds of cackling chickens, you’ll find a large open grid of concrete ponds inhabited by crocodiles, enormous turtles, nests of terrapins, diverse shoals of fish and tanks of koi.
Adjacent to this is a barn-like inventory space, crystal warehouse and shop selling everything from bags of shells to semi-precious stones, handmade jewelry, figurines and trinkets.

Canadian poet Anne Carson wins Nobel in Literature
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:46:34 UTC
01:46:34 KST

Canadian poet and writer Anne Carson yesterday won the Nobel Prize in Literature “for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature,” the Swedish Academy said.
“She was very taken by surprise,” said Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary of the academy, which awards the 12 million kronor (US$1.2 million) prize.
“We didn’t have so much time to speak, and all she had time to tell me was that she is for the moment in Iceland, where she’s listening to the wind,” she said.
Photo: TT News Agency, Pontus Lundahl via Reuters
Carson’s work often blends verse, prose, dialogue and translation in a genre-defying mix. Born in Toronto, the 76-year-old has also held Icelandic citizenship since 2022 and has spent considerable time on the arctic nation in the past few years.
She is widely known for her translations of classical Greek literature, which heavily influences her work that ranges from opera libretti to literary criticism and verse novels such as Autobiography of Red from 1998.
“Almost all her literary production has centered upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning,” the academy said.
“She has herself identified the etymology of words as the starting point for all her work. Her translations from Classical Greek may be regarded as independent works in their own right,” it said.
Her style is exemplified in Norma Jeane Baker of Troy from 2019, a performance piece that mixes the stories of Helen of Troy in Euripides’ play Helen and Marilyn Monroe.
The academy also praised her ability to explore “the possibilities of writing, a process by which the literary sketch has become of particular value to her.”
“Bearing witness to this is Float, a work consisting of 22 chapbooks on different subjects, capable of being read in any order,” it said.
Often heralded as her greatest work, Autobiography of Red demonstrates Carson’s ability to “actualize the classical literary tradition,” the academy said.
In the book, she re-examines age-old questions such as “what happens when you love someone who will ultimately destroy you?”

The Rays edged the Yankees 4-3 in New York to complete a 3-0 sweep in their American League Division Series, fueled by a two-run home run from Victor Mesa Jr and aided by a spectator interference call that denied the Yankees a two-run homer.
Photo: Brett Davis / Imagn Images

Photo: AP

Photo: Matt Marton / Imagn Images

Court revokes Taichung Power Plant project review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:46:33 UTC
01:46:33 KST

The Taipei High Administrative Court yesterday revoked the conclusion of the environmental impact assessments (EIA) for Taichung Power Plant’s second-phase gas-fired generator project.
The project on Oct. 30, 2024, passed its initial EIA review with the conclusion that a second-stage EIA review was not required.
That galvanized local residents from Changhua and Nantou counties and Taichung to file an administrative lawsuit against the Ministry of Environment via lawyers of the Environmental Rights Foundation and the Wild at Heart Legal Defense Association, Taiwan.
Photo courtesy of the Taichung City Government
The lawsuit was officially filed on July 11 last year.
Critics said that the passage of the project was fast-tracked, given that it involved an additional 5,500 megawatts (MW) of gas-fired power generation capacity, but was exempted from the second-stage review.
Environmental groups yesterday urged the ministry and Taiwan Power Co (Taipower) to subject the project to a second-stage review and reduce the planned installed capacity to 2,600MW.
The project is part of the government’s “replace coal with gas” policy, but would not fully replace coal power, as six coal-fired power units would remain at the plant for backup electricity supply, the advocates said.
Combined with the 2,600MW of gas power capacity built during the project’s first phase, the plant’s total gas power capacity could reach 8,100MW, they said.
The project set annual greenhouse gas emissions at 21,160 kilotonnes for the plant, a figure that fell short of expectations given the original annual emissions of 26,548 kilotonnes in 2022, they said.
The environmental advocates also cited concerns that the newly built gas-fired generators would be allowed to operate after 2050 without a sunset provision.
The project’s air quality assessment criteria and its passage without a vote among EIA committee members were also questionable, they said.
The advocates called on the ministry and Taipower to comply with the latest air quality assessment standards, and put forward a sunset roadmap for the plant’s coal-fired and gas-fired power units.
The court yesterday unveiled the reasons for the judgement, citing two non-compliant acts.
First, the regulations and standards applied to assessing pollutants produced during the project’s construction were improper.
Second, the environmental impact of the combined use of existing coal power units and additional gas power units was not properly reviewed, it said.
The court dismissed the lawsuit applicants’ demand for enforcing the project’s second-stage EIA review.
The ministry yesterday said that it had not received the court’s written judgement and would likely file an appeal.
Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin (龔明鑫) said the project aims to improve the environment by replacing coal with gas and was passed by the EIA committee in 2024.
The Ministry of Economic Affairs would respect the EIA committee’s decision, he said, adding that Taipower would assist in providing evidence if the ministry appeals.
Taipower yesterday said that the second-phase project’s additional gas power units would be the key to decommissioning the plant’s six coal power units.
Taipower has initiated a plan to dismantle two of the six coal power units from this month, it said, adding that it seeks to fulfill the plant’s coal-free target.

Photo: AFP

S Korean banks likely hacked by China-based actor: CrowdStrike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:46:29 UTC
01:46:29 KST

The suspect behind cyberattacks at South Korean banks was likely a China-based 26-year-old who used a Chinese-developed artificial intelligence (AI) agent and Anthropic’s Claude Code, US cybersecurity company CrowdStrike said.
In a report published on Wednesday, CrowdStrike said it believed the suspect was likely based in China’s Guangdong Province after uncovering personal details linked to the suspected attacker while analyzing AI coding-tool sessions and infrastructure associated with the hacking campaign.
At least nine South Korean banks have disclosed or have been reported by local media as having been targeted by cyberattacks since late last month, prompting South Korean police to launch a probe this week and South Korean President Lee Jae-myung to call for robust response measures.
Photo: Reuters
CrowdStrike senior vice president of counter adversary operations Adam Meyers yesterday told reporters on a call that this was an example of a human adversary leveraging AI agents to conduct widespread attacks.
“And this is significant because it allows one human to target many customers in a very short period of time using the power of AI,” he said.
The case is likely to intensify security concerns over the rise of AI agents and whether organizations are prepared to defend their systems against them.
Shinhan Bank last week said that personal information of about 25,000 of its customers was compromised, while KB Kookmin Bank said that the personal information of 119 of its customers was leaked.
The attacker used ARTEX, a Chinese-developed open-source penetration testing tool, alongside large language models such as Anthropic Claude, CrowdStrike said.
“While this activity has not been attributed to a named adversary, the threat actor is likely a Chinese speaker and financially motivated,” the report said. “This assessment is made with moderate confidence based on the use of the Chinese-developed tool ARTEX and observed Chinese-language prompts.”
The individual also asked Claude where threat actors typically sell Korean data breach information and sought assistance in finding Korean Telegram data sales groups, CrowdStrike said.
In another session, the person also requested Claude to create a security researcher resume, which included details such as a Telegram account, age, educational background and a location in Maoming, China, which CrowdStrike said likely belonged to the attacker.
A man who answered a phone number published by CrowdStrike in its report said he had no knowledge of the matter.
Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokeswoman Mao Ning (毛寧) told a regular news briefing that the ministry was not familiar with the case and that China as a matter of principle has consistently opposed and combated hacking activities.
Anthropic and South Korean police did not respond to requests for comment.
ARTEX is an open-source AI agent for automated penetration testing that was published on GitHub this year by a Chinese security engineer with the handle Autumn. It is not a standalone large language model (LLM), but connects to external LLMs such as ChatGPT, Claude and DeepSeek (深度求索) to help organizations test for vulnerabilities in their networks.
The tool’s GitHub page says it is intended for personal learning, code research and local technical verification and should not be used to conduct real-world testing against online systems or Web sites.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
