Call for more defense hackathons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:45:50 UTC
01:45:50 KST

I served as a mentor and judge for last weekend’s inaugural Taiwan Defense Tech Hackathon, which was cohosted by the European Defense Tech Hub, National Taiwan University’s Unmanned Vehicles Research and Development Center, and the Institute for National Defense and Security Research, providing feedback to students, researchers, entrepreneurs and engineers who developed concepts for dual-use technology solutions to certain challenges and problems.
The value of this experience was being in the same room as the people who ordinarily sit outside Taiwan’s national security establishment, and observing them produce unconventional solutions using commercially available off-the-shelf technologies with civilian and military applications in a crisis.
Several teams proposed concepts focused on Taiwan’s coastal security gaps to help the National Police Agency (NPA), coast guard and navy address problems ranging from protecting undersea cables to alerting users to suspicious coastal activity. Before deployment, prospective end users would need to test and evaluate these concepts in realistic conditions.
To ensure that Taiwan continues to build its defense innovation and dual-use technology ecosystems while strengthening whole-of-society defense resilience, hackathons should become a regular part of the ecosystem. Taiwan’s existing competitions, research programs and accelerators could expand scenario-based experimentation to develop dual-use technologies that help sustain communications, logistics and other essential services during disasters or conflict.
Taiwan’s whole-of-society defense resilience can draw on an immense reservoir of technical expertise and ingenuity. Ukraine’s experience shows how civilian skills and networks can support national defense. Regular defense technology hackathons around Taiwan could help build those connections before a crisis, provided they lead to sustained collaboration and usable capabilities.
Hackathons could complement existing competitions, including the upcoming National Chungshan Institute of Science and Technology’s AEGIS CTF International Invitational Tournament & National Defense AI Competition and the Presidential Cup Drone Competitions, which are scheduled later this year.
Such events can expose more of the nation’s technology sectors to security problems through rapid team formation, intensive prototyping and interaction with end users. Taiwan’s civilian technology sector offers a reservoir of expertise that could bolster whole-of-society defense resilience through closer connections with end users, as Ukraine’s experience illustrates.
Following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, civilian expertise was rapidly turned toward national defense, with programmers, engineers, drone enthusiasts and volunteers from various fields contributing to its whole-of-society effort to resist Russian armed coercion.
Some of Ukraine’s civilian technical networks were established before the full-scale invasion, including Aerorozvidka, a non-governmental organization founded in 2014 that pioneered drone warfare. By February 2022, Aerorozvidka had modified commercial drones, built a team of experienced operators and contributed to the military’s response. Hackathons can help technically capable people engage with civil defense and national security problems before a crisis hits.
During this year’s Han Kuang live-fire exercise, the Ministry of National Defense’s Cyber Command mobilized more than 100 civilian cybersecurity specialists to test and assess the defenses of energy, transport and telecommunications infrastructure. Similarly, the ministry’s All-Out Defense Mobilization Agency (ADMA) mobilized civilians to help military units set up barriers and provide civilian transport capacity to move ammunition and other supplies.
Hackathons themselves would not deter “gray zone” activities, coercive behavior, compellent actions or a full-scale invasion by China. However, a robust ecosystem of these events and similar competitions could help build resilience and deterrence, and shape an adversary’s judgement of Taiwan’s ability not only to absorb a attack, but also to improvise, repair and mobilize civilian expertise. If these connections produce credible, tested capabilities that can function under an attack, they could undermine Beijing’s expectations of rapid success.
Policymakers, industry and other stakeholders should work toward creating a repeatable pathway for similar events so the hackathon’s impetus does not end on Sunday last week. Taiwan needs a pathway that lets more problem solvers address operational problems, build prototypes, test with end users, secure funding and ultimately field capabilities for civilian and, if needed, military end users.
Hackathon organizers should publish six-month results documenting continued collaboration with end users, realistic prototype testing, follow-on funding and any adoption. Holding such events alongside military exercises could connect civilian technologists with end users to explore problems exposed by unscripted scenarios.
Taiwan already has a starting point in this integration through the ministry’s Defense Innovation Office. The office offers prototype calls, research cooperation and small-quantity procurement for evaluation. A solicitation in February last year included intelligent warehouse management. Promising teams need operational sponsors and follow-up resources to navigate these mechanisms; funding and military adoption would depend on further evaluation.
It is key to do this all around Taiwan, not just in Taipei, given the unique insights that might come from Taichung’s advanced manufacturing sector, Kaohsiung’s maritime focus or rural areas, such as Taitung. Entities such as ADMA, the Industrial Technology Research Institute, the NPA and others could host hackathons.
Bryce C. Barros is a visiting fellow at the Institute for National Defense & Security Research. He previously served as a US Senate national security adviser from 2023 to 2024. The views expressed do not reflect those of the US government or other affiliations.
China prefers to win without firing a shot in its bid to strangle Taiwan’s strategic autonomy. Chinese military strategist Sun Tzu (孫子) would have approved. Its central tool at sea is the “cabbage strategy”: the Chinese People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) layers fishing boats, maritime militia, coast guard cutters and warships around Taiwan’s contested waters in overlapping rings. Each layer normalizes daily coercion, narrows Taiwan’s freedom of movement and chips away at its maritime sovereignty — all while staying below the threshold of armed conflict. This is “gray zone” warfare at its most cost-effective — one of Beijing’s most promising

It would create what Chiang called Taipei’s version of Omotesando — an upscale, tree-lined boulevard and shopping district in Tokyo — to attract young people and international tourists. 'The Nativity Scene of St. Francis': Italian and Irish traditions come together
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
18:45:23 CEST
01:45:23 KST

“The Nativity Scene: The Legacy of St. Francis of Assisi Through Italian Design and Irish Craftsmanship.” This is the title of an exhibition currently on view in Dublin that celebrates the meeting of two traditions in the name of the saint of the Canticle of the Creatures.
                                    
The initiative was inaugurated by the Italian Ambassador to Ireland, Nicola Faganello, and by the director of the Italian Cultural Institute in Dublin (IIC), Michela Linda Magrì, representing the two institutions that promoted it as part of a project organized in collaboration with designer and curator Andrea Vecera. Hosted at Rathfarnham Castle in Dublin, the exhibition is part of the commemorations honoring St. Francis of Assisi on the 800th anniversary of his death, serving as a celebration of an important element of Italy’s spiritual and cultural heritage and, at the same time, as a symbolic bridge to local culture.
                                    
The event was made possible thanks to the crucial support of partners such as the Irish government agency responsible for historical and architectural heritage (the Office of Public Works, represented at the opening by CEO John Conlon and Mary Heffernan), which provided the prestigious venue of Rathfarnham Castle; and the Design & Crafts Council Ireland (represented by CEO Mary Blanchfield), which facilitated connections with local artisans. On display are nine nativity scenes created for the occasion by some of the best-known names in Italian design, in dialogue with the sensibility and craftsmanship of Irish artisans: nine works, nine original interpretations of the Nativity that creatively convey—through natural materials and contemporary artistic languages—the delicate encounter between tradition and innovation, between Italian culture and Irish identity.

Iran rejects giving up uranium enrichment, handing over enriched stockpile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:44:38 UTC
01:44:38 KST

Sahin Demir
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
Iran will not give up its right to enrich uranium or hand over its enriched uranium stockpile, the country's nuclear chief Mohammad Eslami said Thursday.
Speaking to reporters, Eslami, head of the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran, said uranium enrichment is an inseparable part of the nuclear process, according to state broadcaster IRIB.
When asked whether Tehran could abandon uranium enrichment, he said: “Under no circumstances.”
“How can you claim to have a nuclear industry without having the starting point of the process?” he asked.
Eslami said the nuclear industry is a driving force behind scientific and technological development, stressing that Iran would not retreat from its right to technological advancement.
He also ruled out handing over Iran's enriched uranium stockpile, saying: “No, there is no such thing.”
Regarding cooperation with the International Atomic Energy Agency, Eslami said inspections of nuclear facilities damaged by US-Israeli attacks remain impossible because of continuing security threats.
“The agency itself knows that the facilities have been bombed and that the threat remains active,” he said.
Eslami said Iranian legislation restricts cooperation with the UN nuclear watchdog, particularly over concerns about the safety of nuclear facilities, personnel and researchers.
“As long as security is not established, naturally, their entry is not possible,” he added.
However, Eslami said IAEA inspectors had visited facilities that were not targeted in the attacks and carried out routine inspections under arrangements made by Tehran.
He criticized the agency for failing to acknowledge those inspections and accused it of acting under pressure from the US and Israel to gather information about damaged nuclear facilities.
The remarks came amid continuing disagreements between Tehran and the IAEA over access to nuclear sites damaged in US-Israeli strikes.
Iran's parliament approved legislation in June 2025 suspending cooperation with the IAEA following Israeli and US attacks on the country's nuclear facilities. The legislation made inspections conditional on security guarantees and approval by Iran's Supreme National Security Council.
Iran's Natanz, Fordow and Isfahan nuclear facilities were targeted during the June 2025 conflict, while Natanz was struck again during US-Israeli attacks in March 2026.
In June, the IAEA Board of Governors adopted a resolution calling on Tehran to provide information about its enriched uranium stockpiles and grant inspectors access to verify nuclear material.
The agency has said it remains unable to verify the status and whereabouts of Iran's enriched uranium stockpile because of restricted access to nuclear facilities.
Tehran maintains that its nuclear program is exclusively peaceful and insists that uranium enrichment is its legitimate right under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.

Focused on building a strong, aligned leadership team and ensuring long-term financial health for the institution, Garimella has consistently championed student access and affordability.Previously President of the University of Vermont, as well as the Goodson Distinguished Professor of mechanical engineering and executive vice president for research and partnerships at Purdue University, he earned his bachelor’s degree from the Indian Institute of Technology Madras before moving to the US. A highly cited scholar, Dr. Garimella was appointed to the newly established office of science advisory committee for the US Department of Energy earlier this year.In an exclusive interview with Ishani Duttagupta, he discusses his deep connection with the global IIT alumni network, the contribution of Indian students to his university, and more. Edited excerpts:In your role, leading the University of Arizona, what have been the most complex leadership challenges you have faced?Every leader and every university faces moments that test their resilience, but I have found that the most effective leaders remain focused on a clearly articulated mission while bringing people together around a shared vision for the future.
Public higher education is changing rapidly. Universities are being asked to prepare students for career paths that are continually and rapidly evolving, accelerate research that addresses society's most pressing challenges and demonstrate their value to the communities they serve. Meeting those expectations requires both disciplined decision-making and the ability to unite people around a common purpose. At the University of Arizona, that has meant making difficult decisions while keeping our eyes firmly on the future. We have strengthened our financial foundation, brought greater focus and discipline to our priorities and positioned the university to build on its considerable strengths. I believe leadership is ultimately about creating the conditions for talented people to succeed. When people understand where an institution is going, how their work contributes and what success looks like, remarkable things become possible.What are the current trends for international student enrolment from India at the University of Arizona? Are numbers fluctuating, and how is the university actively recruiting global talent?India continues to be one of the University of Arizona’s most important international partners, and Indian students make extraordinary contributions to our campus community through their scholarship, research and leadership. Like at many universities, international enrolment naturally fluctuates in response to global conditions, but our long-term commitment to India remains strong. We continue to explore and secure partnerships with Indian institutions and industry, especially building on areas in which we rank at the top in the world. The future of higher education will increasingly be defined by global collaboration. Whether addressing advances in artificial intelligence, health care, water resources and sustainability, or semiconductor manufacturing, universities must work together to prepare the next generation of leaders and solve challenges that no single institution or nation can address alone. That spirit of collaboration is central to our vision at the University of Arizona.A growing number of Indian Americans now lead major US universities. Did your journey as an immigrant present unique institutional or cultural hurdles, and how did you navigate them?Moving to live in another country is an exercise in learning and in adapting. Every institution has its own culture and expectations, but I quickly discovered that curiosity and integrity with a sense of purpose transcend borders. My education at IIT Madras and before, as well as at Ohio State and at the University of California Berkeley, gave me an outstanding technical foundation, and perhaps more importantly, it instilled discipline and a lifelong commitment to learning. Those lessons have stayed with me throughout my career. I have also been fortunate to work alongside exceptional mentors, colleagues and students from many different backgrounds. Those experiences have reinforced my belief that universities are strongest when they bring together people with diverse perspectives in pursuit of shared goals. Some of our greatest innovations, and our greatest opportunities, come through learning from one another.Looking back at your time at IIT Madras, what specific elements of that rigorous educational foundation gave you a competitive edge in your American academic career?IIT Madras challenged us to think critically and take on complexity with confidence. It taught us to remain curious and continue learning throughout our lives. It was a hyper-competitive atmosphere, but perhaps that helped me discover my core strengths and built resilience. My training prepared me well for graduate study in the United States, and it shaped my approach to leadership. Whether in research or university administration, progress begins with asking the right questions and listening carefully. Bringing together talented people with different perspectives is invaluable. The challenges facing higher education, and society more broadly, are increasingly complex. Solving them requires institutions that are willing to innovate, partner strategically and remain focused on uplifting society.AI is rapidly transforming higher education. Do you view it primarily as a disruptive operational challenge for universities, or a tool for academic advancement?Artificial intelligence offers a generational opportunity. As chair of the US Department of Energy’s Genesis AI Mission advisory subcommittee, I would like to emphasize the opportunity and the challenge. Like every transformative technology, AI presents challenges that must be addressed thoughtfully, but it also has tremendous potential to accelerate discovery, improve teaching and prepare students for a rapidly changing workforce. Our responsibility is to help students think critically, apply these technologies ethically and develop the creativity, judgment and leadership that remain uniquely human. Throughout history, universities have helped society navigate periods of profound change. AI is no different. Public research universities have both the opportunity and the responsibility to ensure these technologies are developed and applied with humanity at the core.How do you successfully balance your role as an active researcher and academic with the demanding administrative responsibilities of a major university president?My research and teaching career has fundamentally shaped how I approach leadership. Engineers are trained to ask questions, rely on evidence and solve complex problems collaboratively. Those same habits are invaluable in leading a university. Although I spend less time directly conducting research today, remaining engaged with our faculty, students and research enterprise keeps me connected to the university's core mission. Great public research universities create opportunity. They prepare students to lead, advance discoveries that improve lives and serve as engines of economic growth and societal progress. At the University of Arizona, success for every student is our North Star. My responsibility is to help create an environment where students, faculty and staff can thrive, where discovery translates into opportunity and where our work uplifts the people of Arizona and communities around the world.I also enjoy staying connected with cutting-edge research in my roles providing strategic research leadership through advisory committees for the National Science Foundation, US Department of Energy, and Sandia National Laboratories among others.In what ways do you stay connected to your Indian roots today, and how active are you within the global IIT alumni network?India will always be an important part of who I am. I remain connected through family, lifelong friendships, professional colleagues and the global IIT alumni community. Those relationships continue to be an important part of my personal and professional life. I also value opportunities to remain engaged with higher education leaders across India, including through my role as Chair of the Global Advisory Council for the Confederation of Indian Private Universities. I maintain a longstanding commitment to strengthening collaboration between universities in India and the United States and creating opportunities for institutions to learn from one another.As Arizona’s flagship, land-grant university, we believe our responsibility extends beyond our campus. We are committed to building partnerships that expand educational opportunity, strengthen research and create meaningful impact for the communities we serve. I believe India’s universities will play an increasingly important role in shaping the future of higher education, and I look forward to strengthening those relationships in the years ahead.What do you consider your most impactful achievement or turnaround success since taking office at the University of Arizona?I am deeply proud of what our university community has achieved together. We implemented a new enrolment management strategy that creates multiple pathways to the university while investing in the academic and well-being programs students need to graduate in four years with minimal debt and pursue strong career opportunities. That commitment includes making counselling services available to students at no cost, removing a financial barrier to care and helping ensure students have the support they need to thrive. We are equally committed to preparing students to succeed in an increasingly interconnected world. One example is the expansion of our Study Abroad program, made possible by a generous $20 million gift from the Garcia Family Foundation. This investment will provide international experiences to students who otherwise might not have had the opportunity to study abroad, broadening their perspectives and better preparing them to lead in a global economy. We continue to build momentum. Our responsibility is to serve as a force for good for Arizona and beyond. That is the work that inspires me every day.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

The KVS is a relatively new Russian strike drone developed by the Ushkuynik research and production center. The system uses a 10-inch frame and was designed for strikes at medium distances, according to data cited by ArmyInform.

The KVS belongs to a broader family of Russian drones developed by Ushkuynik. The company also produced the "Knyaz Veshchiy Oleg" reconnaissance drone and the fiber-optic "Knyaz Vandal Novgorodskiy."

Ukraine to Get Tens of Thousands of SPYS Interceptor Drones Built to Hunt Russia’s Jet Shaheds
German defense company Quantum Systems plans to supply Ukraine with tens of thousands of SPYS interceptor drones designed, among other missions, to counter Russia’s new jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 UAVs, company Vice President Matthias Lehna said during a press briefing in Berlin, according to Ukrinform on October 7.
“Over the weekend, an LOI [letter of intent] was signed to provide a package of tens of thousands of SPYS, which, as already mentioned, are capable of shooting down jet-powered drones,” Lehna said.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
SPYS was developed jointly by Quantum Systems and Ukrainian partner WIY through their joint venture, Quantum WIY Industries.
According to the company, experience gained from operating earlier systems in Ukraine—including the STRILA interceptor drone—was incorporated directly into the development of the new platform.
Quantum Systems also said Ukraine has become significantly more effective at countering Russia’s jet-powered UAVs, which are faster and more difficult to intercept than conventional propeller-driven Shahed-type drones.
“Initially, we observed an interception capability in Ukraine at a very low percentage. Then it increased to more than 30%, and recent nights have shown an increase to more than 50%,” a company representative said.
The company stressed, however, that the improvement cannot be attributed to interceptor drones alone. Ukraine has built a layered response that combines multiple air defense systems, fighter aircraft, and increasingly specialized anti-drone platforms.
“But this is a combination of different measures. Ukraine has also adapted, deployed different capabilities, makes extensive use of its F-16 fleet, which is capable of intercepting jet-powered Shaheds. And it is increasingly using developments from companies like ours, which, within this mix of capabilities for countering the new threat, are demonstrating increasingly greater effectiveness,” the Quantum Systems representative said.
The planned SPYS package could become one of the largest interceptor-drone deliveries announced for Ukraine so far. Quantum Systems said it can build on manufacturing infrastructure already established for the STRILA interceptor, allowing production to scale quickly.
“And I’m talking here about several thousand per month,” Lehna said when discussing potential output.
Asked when Ukraine could begin receiving SPYS drones under the new package, he said deliveries could start almost immediately.
“Thousands of units are ready for delivery this year,” Lehna said.
Previously, reports emerged that Russia is increasingly using jet-powered drones in attacks against Ukraine.
Such systems now account for approximately 40% of all UAVs deployed in strikes, with their share potentially rising to around 80% in the future.

Andrew Wasike 
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
Kenya has recorded 84 of its citizens as killed or missing in the Russia-Ukraine war, Foreign Minister Musalia Mudavadi told lawmakers Thursday.
Appearing before a joint Senate committee on labor and defense, Mudavadi, who also serves as prime cabinet secretary, said 354 Kenyans have been documented as involved in the conflict.
“The ministry has records of 354 Kenyan nationals involved in the Russian-Ukraine crisis and the record is as follows,” he told senators.
“On the front lines, we have indications of 77. In camp, 38. Those who are in unknown locations or unclassified, it's estimated at 52. Those killed or missing in action, 84.”
Mudavadi said 34 Kenyans had been hospitalized, 62 repatriated, five identified as prisoners of war, one detained and another had completed a military contract.
He said some families only approach authorities after losing contact with relatives in Russia, complicating efforts to establish their whereabouts.
“We therefore encourage families to engage with the department as soon as possible,” he said.
Mudavadi said the State Department for Diaspora Affairs collects identification and travel details before referring cases to Kenya's Embassy in Moscow for verification.
Kenya says Russia halted new recruitment
Mudavadi told lawmakers that his visit to Moscow in March 2026 resulted in Kenya being placed on a Russian military recruitment stop list intended to prevent further enlistment of Kenyan nationals.
“During my official visit to Moscow in March this year, 2026, we secured Kenya's inclusion on Russia's stop list,” he said.
“The Embassy of Kenya in Moscow has since confirmed that no additional Kenyan nationals have been enlisted in the special military operation following the implementation of the stop list.”
Mudavadi said Russian authorities were considering requests to terminate military contracts individually, with decisions resting with military unit commanders.
He also said Russia's Defense Ministry had declined to cover the cost of returning the remains of deceased Kenyans, leaving Nairobi to negotiate burial, cremation or repatriation arrangements with Russian authorities and affected families.
Kenya is also engaging Ukrainian authorities through its embassy in Vienna, which is accredited to Ukraine, over Kenyan nationals detained during the conflict.
The Senate committee is examining concerns surrounding the recruitment of Kenyans into Russia's military and efforts to locate and bring home those affected by the war.

Drought: groundwater levels in France remain very low
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:40:06 UTC
01:40:06 KST

France's groundwater levels remain deeply worrying at the start of October: two-thirds of monitoring sites are below normal and 81% are still falling. The autumn recharge, vital to rebuild reserves, has yet to get under way.
After a summer marked by exceptional drought, the situation beneath our feet remains highly worrying.
According to the latest bulletin from the French Geological and Mining Research Bureau (BRGM), published on Thursday 8 October, 66% of groundwater monitoring points are below seasonal norms (source in French) (source in French)as of 1 October.
More importantly, the situation is continuing to deteriorate: 81% of levels are still falling, compared with only 7% that have started to rise.
After their natural decline over spring and summer, autumn rains usually begin to seep into the ground and replenish underground reserves. This year, however, the recharge has been very slow to get under way.
Why are the current rains not enough to recharge the aquifers?
For groundwater tables to refill, rainwater has to infiltrate deep into the soil. At the moment, this process is being blocked by three factors:
The prior drying of soils: after a hot, dry summer, soils are parched. The first rains are used mainly to re-moisten the surface rather than feeding underground reserves.
Evapotranspiration: under the effect of warmth and vegetation, a large part of the rainwater evaporates or is absorbed by plants before it can reach deeper layers.
The accumulated deficit: light rainfall and high temperatures at the start of the autumn season have delayed the beginning of the recharge period, which normally starts around this time.
The situation is all the more worrying as it is already clearly less favourable than a year ago. On 1 October 2025, only 31% of monitoring points were below normal, compared with 66% today. The BRGM considers the 2026 situation to be "as worrying as in 2022", even if the aquifers concerned are not exactly the same.
According to the BRGM website, in 2022 an exceptional drought, combined with scant rainfall and heavy abstraction, led to an exceptionally severe low-water situation in aquifers, with below-normal levels across much of the country.
This year the problem is also affecting so-called "inertial" aquifers, which respond slowly to changes in rainfall. Some can take months, or even longer, to recover.
By contrast, "reactive" aquifers can rise quickly after several bouts of rain. For now, though, almost all of these are still declining.
The situation is not uniform, however. Levels are very low in Limousin, Morvan, Livradois, Forez, Vivarais, and in the east, from Champagne to Lorraine via northern Alsace and as far as the Jura. Conversely, several aquifers in the south-east of the country still show more favourable levels, as this BRGM map illustrates.
Autumn will be decisive
Aquifer recharge can still begin over the coming weeks, but it will depend on regular and substantial rainfall to infiltrate the soil. A few isolated episodes will not necessarily be enough to make up the accumulated deficit.
The BRGM believes that the slowest-responding aquifers will probably continue to fall until the end of autumn. For the others, everything will depend on the rainfall still to come.
In the most depleted areas, a wetter-than-normal winter may be needed to bring levels back close to normal.
The stakes are high: groundwater supplies nearly two-thirds of drinking water and more than one-third of the water used by agriculture in France, a sector whose activity has already suffered from the 2026 drought.
Seasonal forecasts nonetheless remain uncertain. Météo-France does not yet have a sufficiently clear scenario to say whether autumn in France will be generally dry or wet.

Brazil's tight election raises questions over fate of its climate-finance push
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:39:41 UTC
01:39:41 KST

Brazil's tight election raises questions over fate of its climate-finance push
SAO PAULO/BRASILIA, Oct 8 - Brazil's tight presidential election has some investors, executives and climate-focused businesses worried that a government led by conservative Senator Flavio Bolsonaro may not maintain the policies underpinning the country's emerging green economy.
Bolsonaro topped the first-round vote on the weekend with a stronger-than-expected performance, after a campaign in which he promised to strengthen the regulated carbon market but did not criticize the climate track record of his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, under whom deforestation soared.
In the October 25 runoff, he will face left-leaning President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who has sought to position Brazil as a hub for climate finance, launching programs to attract private capital into green projects and laying the groundwork for a regulated carbon market.
Industry has pressed Bolsonaro not to abandon that program, given the potential costs to the $2.6-trillion economy that has grown under Lula as a leading player in global climate finance.
“It would be economic stupidity to roll back this agenda," said Tereza Campello, socio-environmental director at state development bank BNDES.
PAST REMARKS
While Bolsonaro's campaign also promised to expand the bioeconomy by focusing on pharmaceutical and cosmetics products, concerns remain among investors and executives over his past remarks on climate change.
In an August interview with Brazil's Globo, he described extreme weather events as cyclical and said he did not believe they were directly linked only to human influence. He recently said the best way to address climate concerns was through investments in basic sanitation.
Bolsonaro's plan largely ignored emissions-reduction targets, said climate advocacy group Observatorio do Clima.
"Proposals such as fighting deforestation or bolstering environmental enforcement are starkly at odds with his track record in the Senate," it said.
A spokesperson for the campaign said the senator's environmental agenda would be further developed during a transition period between governments, declining to comment on whether a possible Bolsonaro administration would maintain Lula's green finance initiatives.
Bolsonaro would prioritize market-based conservation incentives, like paying for environmental services, and strengthening efforts to tackle environmental crimes to eliminate illegal deforestation by 2029, a year earlier than Lula's target, the spokesperson said.
ECONOMIC BENEFITS
During the 2019-2022 administration of Jair Bolsonaro, the government weakened environmental protections and deforestation expanded across Brazil's Amazon.
Since then, Lula's administration has encouraged the carbon-removal industry through loans and investments from BNDES. During his campaign, the president pledged to expand climate finance tools like Eco Invest, which has mobilized 190 billion reais ($37.83 billion) since 2024.
Industry experts say the economic benefits of this climate agenda are difficult to ignore.
"The climate agenda and the government's view of this industry as strategic for the country do not depend on a political party," said Gabriel Silva, chief executive of carbon-removal startup Mombak.
Regardless of who wins the election, Silva said he expects continuity in part due to Brazil's developing regulated carbon market and credit options offered by BNDES.
Brazilian carbon credits are traded by businesses with self-imposed emissions goals. Under legislation passed in 2024, the country is preparing to launch a regulated carbon market where companies can buy credits to meet official decarbonization targets, and that will allow Brazil to trade them internationally.
HARD TO REVERSE
Support for the program from businesses could also encourage Bolsonaro to stick with it.
Before the first-round vote, the Brazilian Business Council for Sustainable Development (CEBDS), whose members include oil producer Petrobras and miner Vale, told candidates it viewed the regulated carbon market as a key issue for the country's economy.
"In 2025, around $2.2 trillion was invested globally in clean-energy technologies; that capital is mobile," said Daniela Mignani, CEBDS executive director for corporate management, adding that investors could move elsewhere in the face of regulatory uncertainty.
Campello of BNDES said the economic rationale behind Lula's climate agenda could make it difficult to reverse, given the growing demand for bioeconomy products including certified timber, as well as cocoa and coffee grown in reforested areas.
The BNDES forest program has provided roughly 15 billion reais in loans and investments for projects aimed at recovering and protecting local forests. REUTERS

Kyiv • UNN
Director Pavlo Ostrikov is preparing the film "Tragedy" about a professor and a student who travel across Ukraine to the Realm of the Dead. Filming will begin in summer 2027.
Ukrainian director Pavlo Ostrikov is working on his second film, "Tragedy," following his successful feature directorial debut with the sci-fi drama "You, the Universe." Filming will begin next year. The announcement was made by ForeFilms, which also presented the film's first teaser, reports UNN.
Details
The film is set in the near future, where the war has ended. After overthrowing the Christian god, the ancient Greek gods now rule the world. Philosophy professor Yurii Voloshyn and his student Kolia embark on a journey across Ukraine to the Realm of the Dead to bring their loved ones back from the afterlife.
The teaser's animation style is symbolic in a certain sense and continues a practice begun by ForeFilms back with the film "You, the Universe": an animated teaser that not only presented the film at pitching sessions but even became part of the film itself.
As in his previous works, in "Tragedy," screenwriter and director Pavlo Ostrikov continues to work at the intersection of different genres, employs a variety of stylistic techniques, and introduces unexpected plot developments, while not forgetting to address topical issues.
In form, the story resembles an ancient Greek tragedy, in which the chorus is an integral part of the work. And it will become one of the film's key artistic devices, singing certain parts of the plot throughout the film and connecting the story into a unified whole.
The film's events unfold in the genre of magical realism, where the characters accept fantastical phenomena as everyday occurrences.
Despite the project's title, its genre is more accurately described as tragicomedy, because even in difficult times there is room for hope and humor. I believe in the power of humor as a tool for reflection, so in my future film I want to find a balance between drama and comedy. It is important for me to tell this story because, for me, it is a form of therapy that helps me come to terms with reality. I believe in the power of art; I believe that looking at events from a different angle can sometimes make it possible to see more
The film is being produced by Anna Yatsenko and Volodymyr Yatsenko, co-founders of the production company ForeFilms. They produced such Ukrainian films as "Me and Felix," "Reflection," "Luxembourg, Luxembourg," "You, the Universe," and others.
The project is currently in development, and filming is scheduled to begin in summer 2027.
The project is being implemented with the support of the Ukrainian Cultural Foundation.

Aleksander Ceferin to seek 4th and final term as UEFA president in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:39:31 UTC
01:39:31 KST

Halis Sunnetci
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
UEFA President Aleksander Ceferin announced Thursday that he will seek a fourth and final term in 2027, reversing his earlier decision not to stand for reelection.
Ceferin confirmed his decision during a meeting in Berlin with the presidents and general secretaries of UEFA's 55 national associations, which unanimously had urged him to reconsider his previous stance.
The 58-year-old Slovenian will stand for reelection at the 51st UEFA Ordinary Congress in Astana, Kazakhstan, on April 22, 2027.
“I want to thank the national associations for their trust. We have faced extraordinary challenges over the past years, and we have faced them as one team,” Ceferin said in a statement.
“There is still important work ahead, and I have therefore accepted their request. My ambition remains the same: to keep European football united, make our game stronger and leave UEFA ready for the next generation,” he added.
Ceferin, who has led UEFA since 2016, announced in February 2024 that he would not seek reelection in 2027, despite changes to the governing body's rules allowing him to serve a fourth term.
If reelected, he would remain in office until 2031.
UEFA calls for change in FIFA leadership
The Berlin meeting also addressed FIFA's future leadership, with UEFA and 54 of its 55 national associations, excluding Azerbaijan, agreeing on proposals to reform world football's governing body.
The associations said they had lost confidence in FIFA's current leadership under Gianni Infantino and called for a change at the top, arguing that institutional reforms alone would not be sufficient.
They called for a new FIFA president capable of restoring confidence across football's governing bodies and committed to reform, integrity and independence.
The criticism follows a dispute over Infantino's proposal to seek private investment in a company managing commercial rights linked to FIFA competitions, including the World Cup.

Ceferin had previously ruled out challenging Infantino in the FIFA presidential election scheduled for March 2027.

Ukraine remains priority issue for EU summit – Costa's letter to leaders
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:36:11 EEST
01:36:11 KST

European Union leaders will discuss both Ukraine's urgent needs in countering Russian aggression and its progress toward EU membership.
European Council President António Costa announced this agenda item for the European Council meeting, scheduled for October 15–16 in Brussels, in an invitation letter to EU leaders. The text of the letter was released on Thursday.
“Ukraine remains a key priority for the European Union. We will reaffirm our continued support to Ukraine in the face of Russia’s war of aggression. Considering Russia’s escalating attacks on critical infrastructure, it will be important to hear from President Zelenskyy on the country’s operational needs ahead of the coming winter,” the letter says.
Costa also announced that during the meeting, leaders would assess Ukraine's progress toward EU accession, "that hopefully new negotiating clusters will have already been opened by then."
The President of the European Council identified another issue “increasingly reckless behaviour by Russia, including its campaign of hybrid attacks across Europe.” “We stand united and determined in the face of this escalation and will continue to advance our defence readiness agenda. Building on our previous work, we will take stock of implementation to maintain momentum and accelerate progress across all work strands, including on addressing critical military capability gaps,” he emphasized.
According to Costa, another discussion will focus on enlargement and reform, based on the Commission's communication "Preparing for a wider Union." “Our debate will provide strategic guidance on the way forward. It will specifically highlight the ongoing work on the accession Treaty with Montenegro, and the aim to conclude negotiations with that candidate country hopefully by the end of this year,” he noted.
In addition, the issue of migration has been put forward for discussion. “The figures show that our comprehensive approach is working, as evidenced by a significant and sustained decrease in arrivals of irregular migrants. Adopted EU legislation is producing results. However, we must remain vigilant and prepared, act in solidarity when Member States face crisis situations and continue the work to improve our ability to deal with crises, including all cases of instrumentalization,” Costa emphasized.
The President of the European Council also announced that, at the meeting, EU leaders will “focus on the economy, and on delivering answers to challenges to European competitiveness and to affordability.” “For the short-term, we need to provide guidance to the Commission on targeted and temporary measures to alleviate the impact of high energy prices on our citizens and businesses – while continuing to pursue our strategy to reduce Europe’s dependence of fossil fuels,” he wrote.
Furthermore, Costa proposed to the leaders, together with the President of the European Parliament, that they review the implementation of the overarching competitiveness strategy for 2026–2027, known as the "One Europe, One Market" agenda. “I know this is a major priority for all the Leaders and the Irish Presidency is working hard to achieve results. We need to ensure that additional progress is made, so that the ambition at Leaders’ level – and the expectations that have been raised – are matched by concrete outcomes. These outcomes must translate into tangible opportunities for our companies, our start-ups and our citizens,” the President of the European Council said.

Drones target Eritrean troops inside Ethiopia, conflict monitor says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08

Drones target Eritrean troops inside Ethiopia, conflict monitor says
Oct 8 - Drone strikes targeted Eritrean forces deployed inside northern Ethiopia overnight, a conflict monitor said on Thursday, following an incursion that has brought the Horn of Africa neighbours closer to the brink of outright war.
The strikes, believed to have been carried out by Ethiopia's military on Wednesday and Thursday, targeted Eritrean military vehicles near the Tigrayan town of Adigrat as they withdrew from positions, the US-based conflict monitor ACLED said.
On Wednesday, witnesses said they saw Eritrean troops being transported in trucks through Adigrat, which is about 25 km (15 miles) inside Ethiopia.
That was the first confirmation of Eritrean forces’ presence in northern Ethiopia since fighting broke out last month between Ethiopia's military and a rebel alliance.
Eritrea’s information minister Yemane Gebremeskel did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Thursday. On Wednesday, he called reports of an Eritrean incursion part of an Ethiopian plan to justify a war of aggression against its smaller neighbour.
Spokespeople for Ethiopia’s government, military and prime minister’s office did not respond to requests for comment.
In a meeting with UN Deputy Secretary-General Amina J. Mohammed on Thursday, Ethiopia's foreign minister, Gedion Timothewos, "called for the immediate withdrawal of Eritrean forces from Ethiopian territory, and reaffirmed Ethiopia's right to defend its sovereignty and territorial integrity in accordance with international law", the foreign affairs ministry said on X.
The two countries severed diplomatic ties last week over Addis Ababa’s allegations that Asmara was supporting the rebels. Eritrea has repeatedly denied the accusation.
BLASTS HEARD NORTH OF ADIGRAT
ACLED said the Eritrean soldiers had crossed into Ethiopia on Wednesday and advanced dozens of kilometres into Tigray but then withdrew under heavy drone strikes.
Two sources — a diplomat and a conflict expert in contact with both sides — said they had reports of Eritreans moving back north as a result of heavy bombardment by Ethiopian drones. It was not clear if the Eritreans were leaving Ethiopia or redeploying within the country, they said.
In Adigrat, a resident said they had heard three explosions overnight to the north of the city.
A senior Ethiopian official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Eritrea had one mechanized division and three infantry divisions in Tigray consisting of about 1,500 soldiers each.
Reuters could not independently verify the information.
SOURING RELATIONS OVER ETHIOPIA'S SEA ACCESS CLAIMS
Eritrea accuses landlocked Ethiopia of plotting to invade it, pointing to repeated public declarations by Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed that sea access is vital to his country’s security and economy.
Abiy has said Ethiopia aims to gain sea access peacefully.
The fighting that broke out last month has been the biggest escalation of violence since a 2020-2022 civil war in Tigray and raised fears that unrest could spread more widely across the Horn of Africa, where a three-year civil war in Sudan is already raging.
Eritrea, a former province of Ethiopia, won its statehood in 1993 after a 30-year independence struggle. The two countries fought a border war from 1998-2000 that killed tens of thousands.
They normalised diplomatic relations in 2018, and Eritrea fought in support of Ethiopia’s federal government against the TPLF during the 2020-2022 Tigray war, but relations soured again toward the end of that conflict. REUTERS

South African anti-migrant protests turn violent, with cars torched, gunshots fired

South Africa blames disinformation as anti-migrant protests turn violent
DURBAN/JOHANNESBURG, Oct 8 - Anti-migrant protests in two South African cities including Johannesburg's Soweto township turned violent on Thursday, with the government blaming disinformation over a court ruling on asylum seekers.
In coastal Durban, the second city hit by protests, a Reuters reporter saw five torched cars in the urban centre, where foreign-owned shops were also looted.
The unrest followed a protest by a group demanding that a refugee centre stop processing asylum applications.
In Soweto, a Reuters reporter saw residents carrying groceries out of a shop that they said was owned by a person from Somalia, whom they chased away. The looters fled after police arrived and made them disperse.
Government spokesperson William Baloyi said the violence was triggered by people spreading deliberately false information about a constitutional court ruling in July.
The country's highest court ruled that asylum seekers cannot be denied access to South Africa's asylum system solely for procedural reasons such as having entered the country illegally.
Baloyi said the ruling had been widely misrepresented and did not automatically grant refugee status, permanent residence or other legal rights to undocumented migrants. "We are deeply concerned by what is going on now," he added.
Police said in a statement that they had mobilised more officers in Durban, where they said at least 14 vehicles had been set alight while a guest house and warehouse were partially burned.
A top police official, Lieutenant General Puleng Dimpane, told a press conference in Soweto: "Those responsible for acts of violence and destruction will be identified, investigated and where sufficient evidence exists, arrested and brought to book."
Dimpane said 10 vehicles had been burned in Soweto but the situation was now under control.
South Africa has seen months of anti-migrant marches this year that have drawn international criticism.
Some of the marches have descended into violence and looting, and thousands of African foreign nationals have fled the country.
Migrants are often blamed for taking jobs, fuelling crime and straining public services, claims that social scientists say are not supported by evidence.
Three decades since apartheid ended, South Africa remains deeply unequal and about a third of people are out of work. Despite this, it remains Africa's largest economy and continues to draw migrants. REUTERS

If Lula loses, BRICS could face its biggest political test yet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:34:17 UTC
01:34:17 KST

If Lula loses, BRICS could face its biggest political test yet
Flavio Bolsonaro, the right-wing senator and son of imprisoned former President Jair Bolsonaro, emerged victorious from the first round of Brazil’s presidential election, and commentators now suggest that the incumbent, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, may struggle to catch him in the second round.
If they’re correct, Brazil will become the latest country to join Latin America’s shift to the right.
The Brazilian story, adapted to local circumstances, bears a striking resemblance to the American experience with Donald Trump. After the turbulent presidency of Bolsonaro senior, a representative of the moderate left returned to power, while attempts were made to remove the former president from political life for good.
In the United States, Trump was fiercely condemned as the instigator of an attempted coup, although criminal proceedings against him ultimately failed to prevent his return to power. In Brazil, Jair Bolsonaro was convicted, but his son took up the torch and now the family may be returning to power, accompanied by promises to settle accounts with its opponents.
Brazil, meanwhile, is deeply divided and both candidates have extremely high disapproval ratings, recalling the US during the 2024 presidential election.
For Lula, age is an additional problem because however vigorously he tries to present himself, the fact remains that he is 80, and he lacks Trump’s particular brand of political brutality.
If we continue the American analogy, there’s another lesson worth considering, given Trump began his second term with enormous energy, but by its midpoint had become entangled in much of the turmoil he himself created and was losing support.
Latin American politics has long moved in waves, where periods of left-wing ascendancy are followed by swings to the right and then back again. At present, the right is advancing.
Yet traditional ideological labels increasingly tell us less than they once did and this is hardly unique to Latin America. Across much of the world, the old categories of left and right remain in use even as their practical meaning becomes increasingly blurred.
The domestic implications of Brazil’s election are best left to specialists on the country, but its international consequences are already easier to discern and most importantly, a political shift in Brazil would reverberate throughout BRICS.
There’s already no shortage of internal tension within the grouping; one need only consider the difficult relationship between Iran and the United Arab Emirates. Now the country represented by the first letter of the BRICS acronym, and one for which membership has traditionally been an important source of international status and prestige, could move towards political forces openly skeptical of the project itself.
Jair Bolsonaro didn’t withdraw Brazil from BRICS during his presidency, but he reduced his country’s involvement to a minimum and he subsequently said he regretted not leaving the organization altogether.
His Argentine ally Javier Milei went further; after becoming president at the end of 2023, he rejected Argentina’s planned accession to BRICS, despite Buenos Aires having already received an invitation to join.
Should Lula lose, Brazil is likely to adopt a strongly pro-American, Trump-style orientation, at least for the immediate future.
Trump’s hostility towards BRICS is well know and he regards it, not entirely without reason, as a prototype of a world in which the US no longer enjoys the international predominance to which it became accustomed after the Cold War.
That doesn’t necessarily mean Brazil would formally leave BRICS, given much would depend on the degree of pressure exerted by Washington and on the calculations of a new Brazilian government, but a freezing or significant downgrading of Brazil’s participation would become quite conceivable.
None of this means Latin America’s present shift to the right is permanent as another reversal will inevitably come.
Indeed, the willingness of voters to move repeatedly from one political camp to another suggests something more fundamental, that neither side has been able to provide lasting answers to the economic and social problems that concern the public.
But these domestic changes are taking place against a much larger international transformation.
The global environment is in flux as old institutions and assumptions are losing their authority, while their replacements are either still emerging or do not yet exist and political generations are also changing.
The generation currently governing many of the world’s major powers leaves a particularly strong personal imprint on international affairs and more importantly, these leaders were shaped by the aftermath of the 20th century, whose political inheritance is now steadily fading.
That doesn’t mean the underlying redistribution of global power will stop. The West will not recover the position it once enjoyed, not least because the West itself is becoming less monolithic whereas the Global East is exercising increasing influence over international affairs, while the Global South is becoming one of the principal arenas in which the emerging order will be determined.
BRICS belongs to this changing world as a relatively new community whose development reflects the broader movement towards a more diverse international system.
But history rarely proceeds in straight lines, and the underlying trend may continue even as individual institutions change direction, stagnate, or assume forms very different from those originally expected. Yesterday’s expectations of BRICS need not resemble tomorrow’s reality.
Brazil may soon provide an important test and equally significant will be the evolution of Washington’s increasingly explicit ambition to reassert American predominance throughout the Western Hemisphere. How that policy develops will tell us much about the future importance of the world’s major regions.
For Russia, however, the principal task lies closer to home and, as President Vladimir Putin again argued in his recent Valdai speech, Moscow’s priority must be Eurasia.
That is where Russia’s greatest efforts should be concentrated as the center of gravity is here, while everything beyond it will develop as circumstances permit.
This article was first published by Rossiyskaya Gazeta, and was translated and edited by the RT team

Oxford Union restores uncensored susan abulhawa Gaza speech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:32:36 UTC
01:32:36 KST

Breadcrumb
susan abulhawa celebrates after Oxford Union restores her uncensored Gaza debate genocide speech
Palestinian writer susan abulhawa said she felt "vindicated" after the Oxford Union restored an uncensored and full video of her speech on Tuesday, ending a two-year legal battle, telling The New Arab she knew she had to fight for her voice and her ideas.
A year into Israel's genocidal war, the writer was invited by the Union to deliver a speech in a debate on whether Israel is an apartheid state engaged in genocide. abulhawa's speech supported the motion, which passed by 278 votes to 59.
Despite the 28 November address attracting over 250,000 views online within a few days, Oxford Union quietly removed the full version speech a month later and replaced it with a version that cut out almost two minutes.
"When [the speech] was altered, I decided that this was a fight that I was going to wage," susan abulhawa told The New Arab. "My reaction was to work to fix the situation so that my intellectual labour and voice were restored in full as I had intended it to."
"I'm glad. I feel vindicated. I'm pleased that the Oxford Union came around, and it's in keeping with their reputation and stated values of open dialogue and free speech."
While the writer initially accepted the invitation to speak at the prominent institution on the written condition that her speech would not be edited, the Oxford Union removed five passages, including lines about Israel's actions and a reference to "finely dressed, well-spoken monsters who harboured the same supremacist ideologies as Zionism".
"I think the Oxford Union had their concerns, and whatever the motivation was for those concerns, they did come round and have those concerns assuaged," the writer said.
Wanting to make a historical contribution
Wanting to follow in the footsteps of her favourite historical figures, Malcolm X and James Baldwin, who spoke in the same forum, the writer explained she took great care when writing and preparing her speech.
"I spent two weeks going back and forth with this speech and also trimming it so that I said what I wanted to say in the allotted time and so forth," she said.
The author also wanted to make a historical contribution as Israel's genocide continues, hoping people in the future can understand the Palestinian struggle.
"I wanted to deposit my own contribution to this struggle in this extraordinary historic moment," abulhawa explains. "I wanted to deposit that in the historic record so maybe future generations will come back to listen and to unearth people who were part of the struggle in this time."
A spokesperson for the European Legal Support Centre (ELSC), who represented the writer, told The New Arab: "This case shows that resistance is worthwhile. People should not accept censorship."
"We support the Palestinian solidarity movement against the attempts by Zionism and its supporters to erase Palestine from public space and from the historical record. No erasure can conceal Israeli crimes and genocide."
"The world has seen it all, and we will keep fighting to ensure that Palestinian voices are heard and recorded."
Crackdown on Palestinian voices
While it is unclear why the Union censored parts of abulhawa's speech, it reflects a broader pattern of suppression of Palestinian voices and activism.
"In general, with colonialism, with the war makers, the colonisers, the oppressors, the enslavers, the thieves, there is a suppression of voices in public life," abulhawa explained, referring to cases like the Sedition Act during the First World War, to the crackdown on the student encampments for Gaza in the US.
"Unfortunately, people who hold the levers of power tend to be in that camp and can pass laws and can curtail civic life in support of ideologies that ultimately make racism and war and so forth profitable."
The author noted however a "public appetite" to hear from Palestinians, recognising that the mainstream narrative no longer adds up.
"[Palestinians] have been pushed to the margins for so long, and our voices have been silenced, they have been suppressed," abulhawa said.
"I think the people in power are just not reading the room, they're not understanding that the public is fed up, that people are no longer willing to put aside what they have seen with their own eyes, and to suspend reason and logic in favour of Zionist spin that just does not jibe with reality or with what people have witnessed over the past three years."
"There is a public appetite to hear directly from Palestinians, that was evident there."
Oxford Union said in a statement: "It is a matter of regret that this dispute arose, and we are pleased it has been possible to resolve this matter."

Asia rushes to boost oil reserves, renewables in response to US-Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:31:41 UTC
01:31:41 KST

Asian countries are racing to raise their oil stockpiling capacity, complete a regional power grid and speed up renewables in response to supply risks laid bare by the US-Iran war.
Southeast Asia has been worst hit by the energy impact, as 80 percent of the oil transported through the Strait of Hormuz from the Gulf flowed to the region before the Iran war began.
"The most advanced efforts are support for the development of oil stockpiling systems in each country and regional joint stockpiling on a voluntary basis," nine Southeast Asian nations said in a joint statement issued along with Japan and Australia.
Japan agreed on action plans with its Asian partners to boost crude oil reserves across the region following a meeting of the Japan-led Asia Zero Emission Community (AZEC), a Japanese state minister on trade said on Thursday.
After a separate session with Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, Japan's State Minister of Economy, Trade and Industry Takagi Kei said they had expressed a willingness to cooperate to strengthen Asia's oil stockpiling capacity.
The Philippines, which imports nearly all of its oil and fuel, will create a national reserve by the end of 2027, its energy secretary, Sharon Garin said, adding that it could subsequently be converted into a regional stockpile.
The Southeast Asian archipelago is the chair of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) this year.
Garin said countries will decide if they want to host a regional oil stockpile, and also the terms of sale that should be determined by the country itself.
"In the Philippines, what we want is if there's any country that wants to store the crude or their petroleum products here.
In case of any emergency, the country gets priority on these stocks," she said.
The ASEAN member countries also pledged to increase the share of clean energy in power generation, targeting 30 percent renewables in total primary energy supply and 45 percent in installed power capacity.
The region is among the biggest laggards in green energy.
Renewables make up 14.1 percent of primary energy, well short of a 2025 target of 25 percent, while green power has made up 33.7 percent of total capacity since 2020 against a 2025 target of 35 percent, the ninth ASEAN energy outlook showed this week.
The countries also reached an enhanced preliminary agreement on developing a long-delayed regional power grid, which Garin called a landmark accomplishment. The concept of a regional electricity network was first announced in December 1997.
"The first study was to connect by 2045, and that's too far because that's 20 years. So they're reviewing again to make it a faster implementation," Garin said.

A better way to inspect and evaluate schools | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:30:48 UTC
01:30:48 KST

The news that Ofsted inspections are to be overhauled again indicates that a fundamental rethink is required, rather than tinkering again with the grading system (England school inspections to be overhauled again after barrage of complaints, 2 October). As an educator with 30 years’ experience in international schools (21 years as head of two schools), I would suggest that when further changes are made, the first step should be to stop calling them “inspections”. The word implies an unfeeling, top-down procedure. While British curriculum international schools tend to use an Ofsted-style procedure, American international and international baccalaureate schools tend to use “evaluation” or “accreditation” procedures.
In these, the school evaluates its own performance against a set of standards. The people who work in the school, including students, plus parents and board members, spend a year discussing the school’s achievements and identifying areas for improvement. They submit their report to the agency, which then puts together a team who will visit the school. The team is made up of practising educators from other international schools. So the school is evaluated by fellow professionals, which is much less threatening than a team of inspectors. Their job is to decide whether the school has accurately evaluated its own performance.
My experience is that schools generally do an excellent job of self-evaluation, which means that the visitors can say: “Well done, you know your strengths and weaknesses, we can now offer our expertise in building on this report and helping you to move up to the next level.” The team visit is a positive, collegial experience whose aim is to validate the work that the school’s own staff has done. This contrasts with the seagull approach of an Ofsted visit – they fly in, make a lot of noise, disrupt everything and then take off, leaving a load of guano behind.
The sympathetic, supportive model of evaluation is already out there waiting to be adopted.
Gareth Jones
London
I have experienced four Ofsted inspections: as the chair of governors at a primary school, an early years group, head of a large adult learning service, and vice‑chair of governors at a further education college. Three received favourable judgments under the previous Ofsted framework; the fourth was rated “requires improvement”, severely affecting staff morale and mental wellbeing.
However courteous the inspectors, the methodology in all cases created considerable pressure and anxiety. The process sometimes resembled a police search: practices and records were scrutinised, staff questioned under suspicion and the final judgment delayed.
Educational institutions require rigorous inspection and poor practice must be addressed. But the current model appears to favour enforcement over constructive professional support. A more effective model would combine inspection with consultation. Inspectors would identify strengths and areas for improvement, followed by targeted support for a defined period. A shorter follow-up would assess progress. One has only to refer back to the more collaborative model adopted by the former Adult Learning Inspectorate to appreciate the difference.
This would retain rigour while reducing the punitive tone, and foster a more collegiate relationship between Ofsted and institutions. It would also require inspectors to offer remedies as well as judgments.
Richard Hooper
Penistone, South Yorkshire

Astronaut Sophie Adenot returns to Earth after record space mission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:30:45 UTC
01:30:45 KST

Sophie Adenot left the International Space Station on Wednesday after an eight-month stay, the longest by a European astronaut, and splashed down on Thursday at around 5.30 pm with three fellow crew members.
Sophie Adenot spent 235 days 400 kilometres above the Earth. After a day-long journey, the French astronaut splashed down on Thursday 8 October at 5:35 p.m. (French time), together with three other members of the International Space Station crew, in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of San Diego, California.
The final minutes of the flight brought intense sensations for the Frenchwoman, Russian cosmonaut Andrei Fediaiev and the two Americans Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway: a high-speed plunge through the atmosphere, then a slowdown under powerful parachutes, all while communications were cut.
After exiting the spacecraft and undergoing a brief medical check-up, the four astronauts will be flown back to dry land in the United States, first to Naval Air Station North Island in San Diego, then on to NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas.
A medical team from the European Space Agency (ESA) will then take charge of Sophie Adenot during the long return flight to Cologne, in Germany. There, the astronaut will be reunited with her loved ones and will begin a recovery programme lasting several weeks.
Thirty years after Claudie Haigneré, Sophie Adenot became in February the second Frenchwoman to cross the Karman line, the internationally recognised boundary between the atmosphere and outer space. She also became the first French woman to venture into the vacuum of space, during three spacewalks on 18 and 25 August and 1 September.
With 237 days spent in space, the eleventh French astronaut now holds the record for the longest European spaceflight. The previous record-holder, Italian astronaut Luca Parmitano, spent 201 days in orbit in 2019–2020.

Legal rights must be retained for children with special educational needs | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:30:39 UTC
01:30:39 KST

The legal rights of children and young people with special educational needs and disabilities (Send) are still under threat. The government’s proposed Send and education otherwise than at school (Eotas) reforms would significantly reduce existing legal rights to enforceable education, health and care plans (EHCPs), parental choice of educational settings and independent routes of appeal.
We support the government’s ambitions for a more inclusive education system. Better teacher training, earlier identification of need, greater specialist expertise and a properly staffed workforce are all necessary. But none of these initiatives require children and families to surrender the legal protections they currently have.
The proposals impact everything from how children and young people qualify for statutory support, what can be written into EHCPs, who decides the provision delivered, where children and young people are educated, how families can challenge poor decisions, and whether children and young people who cannot attend school can secure suitable education elsewhere. The Children and Families Act 2014 places children and families at the centre of decision-making, and the current proposals reverse this.
This is not simply a technical change to Send law. When provision is unsuitable or unavailable, legal rights are often the mechanism through which families can secure a suitable education for their child. A promise that the system will work better cannot substitute for an enforceable right when it does not.
Lucy Powell was a member of the education select committee during its 2019 Send inquiry. The committee concluded that the 2014 reforms were the right ones if problems of implementation and funding were addressed, and specifically warned the government against responding to those problems by “weakening or watering down duties”. We therefore urge ministers to work with Send families and organisations to retain existing Send legal rights, preserve individual provision, improve accountability in the system, and retain meaningful independent routes of appeal.
A genuinely inclusive education system should reduce the number of families who need to enforce their rights. It should not reduce their rights when the system fails.
Chris Packham Broadcaster and campaigner
Carrie Grant Broadcaster and Send parent

Campaigners led by Chris Packham urge prime minister to rethink Send overhaul
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:30:23 UTC
01:30:23 KST

Campaigners are calling on Andy Burnham to abandon the core elements of the government’s overhaul of special educational needs provision in England, arguing they unfairly remove children’s legal protections.
A group of children, parents and experts, led by the broadcaster Chris Packham, have written a letter calling for the prime minister to gut the plans laid out under his predecessor Keir Starmer.
Starmer and Bridget Phillipson, the former education secretary, announced the sweeping changes this year, aiming to curb the increase in legally mandated education, health and care plans (EHCPs) and save money in the long term.
Now campaigners are hoping the change of prime minister and education secretary may bring a change of heart from the government – even though officials say it is unlikely.
In the letter, published in the Guardian, the campaigners say: “The legal rights of children and young people with special educational needs and disabilities (Send) are still under threat.
“The government’s proposed … reforms would significantly reduce existing legal rights to enforceable EHCPs, parental choice of educational settings and independent routes of appeal.”
They add: “We … urge ministers to work with Send families and organisations to retain existing Send legal rights, preserve individual provision, improve accountability in the system, and retain meaningful independent routes of appeal.”
The letter is signed by 36 people, including Packham, the actor Sally Phillips, the clinical psychologist Simon Baron-Cohen and the Guardian columnist John Harris.
The changes were announced in February after lengthy consultation by ministers with experts and Labour MPs.
Under the plans, instead of legally enforceable EHCPs, millions of pupils will be given individual support plans, which will be agreed between parents and schools but will not be subject to independent legal appeal.
These support plans will be administered by schools rather than local authorities, and parents who are unhappy with them will be asked to appeal to the school rather than being given recourse to an independent tribunal.
Schools will be given more resources to help support Send children, but the overall package is designed to curb the rapid escalation in costs under the current system, which has left councils in England facing a projected £6bn financial black hole in two years’ time.
However, the Guardian revealed on Thursday that the projected savings risk being undermined by a flood of new applications for EHCPs, as parents look to secure legal protections before the new system takes force.
The campaigners say they want significant changes to the proposals, including keeping the current threshold for EHCPs, allowing parents to appeal against decisions at a tribunal and scrapping the assessment system proposed for individual support plans.
Ministers are consulting on the measures and are expected to recommend some changes to Phillipson’s proposals.
However, those close to the process say Burnham and Lucy Powell, the new education secretary, are likely to adopt more minor modifications to reinforce legal protections rather than the wholesale changes called for by the campaign group.
A spokesperson for the Department for Education said: “We inherited a Send system under immense strain. Our once-in-a-generation reforms will change that.
“Legal duties on schools to identify and support children’s needs are getting stronger, not weaker. And we will never leave parents without a route to challenge decisions about their child’s support.
“We have consulted on our proposals to make sure we get these reforms right, and in the meantime we’re investing in schools to improve inclusion.”

To reduce reoffending, prisoners need better support after release | Letter
