====================================================================================================

Bulgaria Is Dangerously Unprepared for Drone Defense
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
15:06:00 UTC
00:06:00 KST

On October 6, drones struck two commercial vessels inside Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea, roughly 70 nautical miles off the coast near Cape St. Atanas and the town of Byala. It was the first attack of its kind recorded there. The Togolese-flagged vessel suffered severe structural damage and sank within three minutes and the fate of its crew remains unknown despite a search involving two helicopters, a Su-25 and the Bulgarian ro-ro vessel Dioscuria, which spotted the explosion and reached the scene to find an overturned boat, three capsized life rafts and life jackets, but no survivors. The second ship, flying the flag of Palau, caught fire. All eighteen of its crew were rescued, though an Indian sailor remains hospitalized in Varna with serious burns and the Turkish captain was treated for injuries before being discharged. The attack came a day after a similar strike sank a grain ship off the Romanian coast, killing two.
Days on, the most basic question, who did it, remains officially unanswered, and the dispute over that question has become almost as revealing as the attack itself.
A fight over facts before a fight over blame
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukrainian and Bulgarian services had jointly established that Russia was behind the strikes. Radev disputed that account directly. "Here, at the Consultative Council, we received very clear reports from the Minister of Defense, the Chief of Defense, and the heads of the security services stating that there had been no communication with the Ukrainian side identifying the type of drone. As for what Zelensky said, that is his own responsibility," Radev said, adding that "my job is not to counter Zelensky, but to establish the truth."
Radev's own reasoning points toward Moscow without quite accusing it. "If we judge by the nature of the cargo and the ships' direction of travel, then the outcome, logically speaking, favors Russia. However, that does not mean we can claim the strike was carried out by Russia without having evidence. That is a hypothesis, and when discussing national security, we cannot operate based on hypotheses," he said. He announced that Bulgaria would seek to coordinate with Turkey and Romania, ask for American support in examining the attack site, and had already asked the European Maritime Safety Agency to carry out a free analysis of debris recovered from the sunken ship. Particular hope rests on the Able, the vessel that caught fire but did not sink, whose hull and surviving debris Radev said could help establish where the drones came from. He said Bulgaria would follow the same procedure it used after the August incident near Kardam, where officials withheld the drone's identity until technical analysis was complete, and that a diplomatic note would go to whichever country, Russia or Ukraine, is eventually confirmed responsible. Despite the attack, Radev maintained that "there is no direct threat to Bulgaria's national security" and questioned the logic of pure military responses to drone warfare, asking pointedly how many hundreds of billions have been spent on defending Ukraine against drone strikes, and whether the strikes had stopped. They had not, he noted, on either side.
The leader of the pro-Russian party, "Revival", Kostadin Kostadinov, who left the subsequent Consultative Council for National Security meeting without endorsing its conclusions, went further, accusing Zelensky of lying and suggesting Bulgarian services had requested information from Kyiv and simply not yet received an answer. "I asked a specific question. Our services have requested information. They do not yet have an answer. They will receive one, but they do not have it yet," he said. He also objected that the council's proposed statement addressed the consequences of the attack rather than its causes and that calling on Bulgaria to help broker peace sat awkwardly alongside its recent support for an EU declaration condemning Russia and its ongoing arms exports, which he said run into the hundreds of millions of euros and have not slowed. Whatever one makes of his framing, Kostadinov was blunt about what he heard in the closed session on Bulgaria's actual readiness: "Other things were said as well, things I cannot share, but they are quite alarming regarding our readiness for surveillance, defense, and so forth."
What the Council actually proposed
Unlike the question of attribution, the Consultative Council, convened by President Iliana Yotova rather than Radev, did produce a concrete set of proposals, adopted with the three-quarters majority the law requires, over the objections of three parliamentary groups. Yotova described a security environment in clear deterioration, citing a growing pattern of drone attacks on commercial shipping that has already disrupted freedom of navigation, driven up insurance costs and raised the risk of environmental pollution, and warning that the same long-range unmanned systems threatening the Black Sea now threaten critical infrastructure across the entire country.
The package calls for Bulgaria to pursue consensus among all Black Sea littoral states, Russia and Ukraine included, on a moratorium on hostilities at sea and on turning the Black Sea into what Yotova called a zone of shared security. It asks for urgent consultations with Romania and Turkey on coordinated protection of shipping, for Bulgaria to push the European Union toward a dedicated framework mechanism for free and safe Black Sea navigation, and for the matter to be raised at the EU summit on October 15 and 16 and at the United Nations, through the International Maritime Organization, to help establish the technical and legal facts of the incidents. On capability, the council recommended improving maritime surveillance through reconnaissance drones, strengthening coastal defenses, and explicitly called for faster acquisition of anti-drone systems with kinetic engagement capability, in coordination with NATO and the EU, alongside a push for greater allied contributions to Black Sea security under NATO's enhanced forward presence framework, potentially including additional air and maritime surveillance assets. The council considered and rejected invoking Article 4 consultations with NATO allies, reasoning that the matter was better raised directly in the North Atlantic Council.
It is, on paper, a serious and fairly comprehensive diplomatic and procurement agenda. What it is not is fast. A moratorium negotiated among Russia, Ukraine, Bulgaria, Romania, Georgia and Turkey, an EU navigation framework, and UN-level fact-finding are all measures whose timelines are measured in months or years, not the weeks in which Bulgarian-flagged and foreign commercial shipping is currently exposed to repeat attacks.
The procurement Bulgaria already has underway and its real timeline
That gap between diplomatic ambition and physical readiness is not new and it did not begin with the October 6 attack. Bulgaria's Defense Ministry recorded roughly 60 drone incidents on Bulgarian territory between January and the end of August 2026, including five drones that washed up on the Black Sea coast within a single 24-hour span in late August, and the Kardam incident in early August in which a Ukrainian-type decoy drone crossed the Romanian border and exploded roughly 100 meters inside Bulgarian territory, undetected by radar on either side. Bulgaria's own Chief of Defense, Admiral Emil Eftimov, has acknowledged that conventional radar struggles against small, low-flying targets, with specialized anti-drone radar picking them up only four or five kilometers out, and Radev himself admitted that "the procedure for the delivery of modern, digital three-dimensional radars has been delayed for years."
The centerpiece of Bulgaria's response has been the IRIS-T SLM system, a mobile, medium-range ground-based air defense system built by Germany's Diehl Defence with Hensoldt and Airbus, offering an effective range of up to 40 kilometers and altitude coverage up to 20 kilometers against aircraft, helicopters, cruise missiles and drones. Bulgaria joined the European Sky Shield Initiative in 2022, and the original 2024 contract for a single fire unit, comprising a launcher, radar and tactical command post, was worth just over 182 million euros, later revised down to roughly 180.6 million euros after changes to equipment and delivery schedules. Following the October 6 attack, the Council of Ministers formally proposed to parliament the acquisition of five more units, bringing the planned fleet to six, with Radev telling reporters on October 7 that "the goal is to guarantee the protection of the Bulgarian territory and the country's contribution to the general defense capabilities of NATO," and that he expects a contract "within weeks." The combined cost of both procurement stages, financed through the EU's SAFE instrument, is put at just over 1.1 billion euros, part of a 3.26 billion euro SAFE loan package covering nine Bulgarian defense projects in total, with loan terms running up to 45 years and a grace period of up to ten. Bulgaria's original 2024 plan envisaged, in the longer term, two longer-range systems alongside eight medium-range ones, with a further IRIS-T SLX variant floated as a possibility. Radev separately noted that a 2023 caretaker-government plan to acquire surveillance drones covering the entire exclusive economic zone had simply gone nowhere since. "Many governments have come and gone since then. Absolutely nothing. Zero," he said.
The system itself is not unproven. Germany delivered the first IRIS-T SLM to Ukraine in 2022, and Diehl Defence has cited Ukrainian operational data showing success rates as high as 95 to 100% against more than a dozen targets, figures that are manufacturer-reported rather than independently verified but that have nonetheless made IRIS-T, in the German military's own description, "combat-proven." Eight countries have now selected the system under the European Sky Shield framework: Germany, Estonia, Latvia, Slovenia, Bulgaria, Sweden, Denmark and Switzerland, with Estonia receiving its first units as recently as June 2026.
What combat-proven does not solve is the queue. Diehl Defence builds roughly ten IRIS-T SLM fire units a year, and the associated Hensoldt radars are capacity-constrained to around 30 a year against Germany's own domestic requirement of 40 to 60. Sweden, which ordered its own units in 2024, does not expect full delivery before 2028 to 2030. For Bulgaria, various analysts have placed a realistic delivery horizon at five years or more from signature, putting meaningful Bulgarian IRIS-T capability somewhere around 2031, and that is before the newly announced five-unit expansion adds its own delay to an already backlogged production line shared with seven other buyers. IRIS-T, moreover, is one middle layer of a multi-layer air defense system meant to work alongside radars, fighters, shorter-range systems and dedicated counter-drone capability and it is built to intercept aircraft, cruise missiles and larger drones rather than the small, low-flying drones that Admiral Eftimov says conventional radar struggles to detect.
Ivan Lalov, who chairs parliament's defense committee, was unusually candid about what that leaves exposed in the meantime. "We are behind, and I will not hide this, in the acquisition of drones, their use and the acquisition of anti-drone systems," he told bTV, adding that catching up cannot happen in days because weapons procurement involves lengthy approval, contracting and ratification procedures. He pointed to nine key projects laid out in the defense investment program running to 2032, including new 3D radars and Stryker armored vehicles, and noted Bulgaria has also joined a NATO initiative to acquire unmanned systems and train their operators. He maintained that Bulgaria's national security was not directly at risk from the October 6 attack, precisely because it occurred outside the 12-nautical-mile territorial waters the Navy's existing radar and maritime operations center can actually monitor, while acknowledging he could not guarantee detection of every type of drone used in such attacks. Security expert Professor Nikolay Radulov went further on the council process itself, telling Bulgarian media that even recovered drone debris would not conclusively settle who was responsible, that Bulgaria's core problem remains inadequate anti-drone protection and delayed acquisition of modern detection technology, and that the Consultative Council convened to address it was, in practical terms, "more of a formality."
A commitment made a year ago that still isn't ready
The most striking part of this picture is that Bulgaria already signed on, over a year before the October 6 attack, to a multilateral framework built specifically around this threat. In late September 2025, Bulgaria joined Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland and Romania in defense ministers' talks on what became known as the EU's "Drone Wall" initiative, part of the broader Eastern Flank Watch program, after nineteen Russian drones violated Polish airspace in a single incident, followed by drone incursions into Romania, Russian MiG-31 flights through Estonian airspace and unidentified drones that forced Danish airports to close. Then-Defense Minister Atanas Zapryanov explicitly tied Bulgaria's participation to the Black Sea, pledging the country would build maritime drone-defense capability "with the means we have and with new ones that we need to acquire," a framing that distinguished Bulgaria's contribution from the land-focused Baltic states.
Even at the time, Bulgarian defense experts were candid about how far that was from reality. Reserve colonel Ivan Milanov, vice president of the International Association for Combating Drones, said bluntly that "we are still at the theoretical stage" and "we are not ready yet," noting that Bulgaria's MiG-29s and F-16s are "completely insufficient" against drone threats and that a single drone incident near Varna had already required a helicopter, a boat and a ship to respond, the same resource-heavy, cost-mismatched pattern now playing out at far greater scale. European Commissioner for Defense Andrius Kubilius said at the time he expected the first stage to be ready within a year, while admitting his own skepticism about that timeline. The project has since been rebranded the European Drone Defence Initiative, with the Commission's roadmap targeting initial capability by the end of 2026 and full operation by the end of 2027. The first deadline has not yet fallen due, but the picture with less than three months to go is not encouraging. As of late July, analysts such as Ulrike Franke of the European Council on Foreign Relations described the EU's drone defenses as "largely missing in action," with no continuous detection and interception line along the eastern border and the initiative functioning mainly as a funding label over national projects already underway, such as Poland's 3.5 billion euro SAN counter-drone system, itself due to reach initial capability only by the end of this year. It is this same EU program that Defense Minister Stoyanov cited in September 2026 as the reason Bulgaria did not need to also join NATO's parallel Drone Edge initiative.
Two different problems, not one duplicated effort
Stoyanov's central justification for skipping NATO's Drone Edge, that Bulgaria already has "the same project" through the EU, has been challenged by critics who argue the two frameworks are not actually aimed at the same threat. The distinction, laid out in commentary that has circulated widely among Bulgarian security watcher, runs roughly as follows: the EU's drone efforts are built around civilian security, public order and economic disruption, the cheap hobbyist drone that shuts down an airport for hours, loiters over a power plant, or smuggles contraband across a border. Brussels funds projects that repurpose existing infrastructure, such as 5G antennas, into makeshift radar capable of spotting the small, low-flying drones conventional military radar often misses, plans an "EU Trusted Drone Label" for civilian drones, due by the end of 2026 and relying on independent third-party verification, alongside a certification scheme for counter-drone systems, with the aim of keeping insecure and high-risk equipment off the market, and channels support to border police and Frontex against smuggling and organized crime.
NATO's drone problem is a different one by design. For the alliance, a drone is not primarily a public-order nuisance but a weapon or a military-grade reconnaissance asset, and operations like Eastern Sentry along the eastern flank respond to it accordingly, scrambling fighters, activating military radar and ground-based air defense when a drone approaches or crosses allied territory. NATO's counter-drone systems are built to network directly with Patriot batteries and F-35s for a real-time air picture and its joint procurement mechanism exists specifically to let member states buy proven equipment faster and more cheaply than they could alone. On this reading, the EU functions as the building's security desk, guarding the doors, the airports, the power plants and setting the rules so a thief or a spy cannot walk in, while NATO is the army at the border, stopping armed attacks and shooting down military hardware before it reaches the cities behind it. The two efforts hand off to each other rather than duplicate one another: when a civilian drone incident escalates into a military threat, NATO is meant to take over response, with the EU providing the underlying technological and industrial base.
If that framing holds, Stoyanov's reasoning does not quite survive contact with the October 6 attack. Two commercial vessels struck by munition-carrying drones roughly 70 nautical miles offshore, with the Navy, helicopters and a Su-25 called out for the search and rescue, is a case of a threat that has moved from the EU's civilian-security remit into the military domain NATO's initiative targets. An EU-funded 5G radar retrofit or a trusted-certification scheme for commercial drones does little for a country whose problem, as Lalov and Radulov have both acknowledged in different words, is its limited ability to detect and stop military-grade drones. The EU's own initiative is not purely civilian either, since the Commission describes it as a layered system to detect, track and neutralize hostile drones, so the distinction is one of emphasis rather than a clean split. Even so, declining NATO's Drone Edge on the grounds that the EU program already covers the need describes, at best, half the problem Bulgaria is actually facing.
A cheaper, faster alternative Bulgaria has so far ignored
That mismatch, a roughly 1.1 billion euro, multi-year system aimed at a threat category different from the one actually attacking, is precisely what has drawn criticism from a different direction entirely. Former Prime Minister Kiril Petkov argued in a post on Facebook responding to the Kardam drone incident back in August, that the logic other frontline and near-frontline states have followed is simpler and far cheaper. Estonia, Denmark, Germany and Latvia have all signed so-called drone deals with Ukraine, he noted, specifically to build domestic production capacity for interceptor drones, systems costing under 5,000 euros apiece that can shoot down attacking drones directly, instead of scrambling fighter jets or firing vastly more expensive air-defense missiles at targets worth a fraction of the interceptor's cost. That, Petkov argued, is what strategic thinking on national security actually looks like: investing in capability before the next incident, not cordoning off a blast site afterward and explaining to people what happened. His pointed conclusion was that Bulgaria's political energy has gone into disputes over which sanctioned Russian oligarch gets removed from an EU list, rather than into exactly the kind of Ukrainian cooperation on drone production that countries far less exposed to Black Sea risk than Bulgaria have already pursued.
Whatever one makes of the framing, the substance of the comparison holds up. Bulgaria has spent 2026 declining several of the multilateral tracks built for this threat. On July 13, Radev declined to take part in a Coalition of the Willing meeting in Paris, saying Bulgaria "does not belong there" and does not join a coalition that "insists on continued financial and military assistance to Ukraine." The next day he distanced Bulgaria from the Ukrainian-led Freyja anti-ballistic missile initiative, saying key security decisions are made "in a different format and in a different place." On August 24, he again brushed off the coalition, saying there was "no need for speculation" about Bulgaria's absence and that the group is "not the whole of the European Union." On September 11, Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov told parliament Bulgaria would not join NATO's billion Drone Edge initiative, backed by 20 member states, arguing Bulgaria already participates in a parallel EU program, which the Commission does not expect to be fully operational until the end of 2027 and that joining both would stretch the ministry's limited resources without adding value. Democratic Bulgaria's Ivaylo Mirchev did not let the sequencing pass. "The irony is that only a month ago, Minister Stoyanov was explaining how urgently Bulgaria needs anti-drone capabilities," he wrote, adding that "the empty chair has become Rumen Radev's foreign policy. Today, this chair is also empty in NATO."
What it adds up to
None of these choices looks indefensible entirely on its own. Preferring one funding track to an overlapping one is ordinary fiscal discipline. Choosing a cheaper air-defense system over a costlier one is the kind of trade-off most mid-sized militaries make. Insisting on verified attribution before sending a diplomatic note, rather than reacting to a foreign president's public claim, is a defensible standard for a government that does not want national security policy set by headlines.
What is harder to defend is the pattern those choices form when read together, against a trend line that has been worsening for a year rather than days. Sixty drone incidents in eight months, an undetected cross-border incursion at Kardam, and now the first direct drone attack on commercial shipping inside Bulgaria's own economic zone do not describe a hypothetical risk that patience and diplomacy can be expected to outlast. Nor can this be called a surprise the government had no time to prepare for. Bulgaria's own officials said openly, more than a year before the Alfa Watan went down, that the country was "still at the theoretical stage" on exactly this threat. The Consultative Council's new package, for all its breadth, rests overwhelmingly on negotiation, coordination and procurement processes measured in months and years, the same kind of timeline the EU's own drone-defense initiative is running on, with its first milestone due by the end of this year and little visible on the ground. The one concrete capability gap exposed by this year's attacks, the inability to detect and intercept drones cheaply and quickly, is the one area where Bulgaria has so far not pursued, or has declined, the fastest and least expensive options on the table, from Ukrainian-style sub-5,000-euro interceptors to NATO's own dedicated drone-procurement track, which is aimed squarely at the military threat Bulgaria faced on October 6. Instead it has committed to a solid but slow-arriving system that, even in the best case, will not meaningfully protect Bulgarian shipping or territory for years. Whether that is a deliberate strategic bet or simply the absence of one remains an open question. The clock, however, is not: the Black Sea has been setting the pace for a year, and Bulgaria is still answering on a timeline of years.

An oil slick in the Black Sea near Russia’s resort city of Sochi has expanded following a fire aboard a tanker attacked by sea drones earlier this week, Greenpeace said Friday, a day after authorities reopened beaches and reported no oil contamination.
The slick grew from 8 to 25 square kilometers over three days, the environmental group said, citing satellite images from Planet Labs.
Greenpeace said the slick extended along the route taken by the Aframax Rio after the attack. Around midday Wednesday, the tanker was near Lazarevskoye, about 50 kilometers from the site of the fire. By Thursday, it was near Tuapse. Environmentalists believe the vessel may be under tow to Novorossiysk.
Sochi and the neighboring federal territory of Sirius closed their beaches on Tuesday after the Liberian-flagged tanker caught fire following an attack attributed to Ukrainian sea drones.
Authorities reopened the beaches Thursday, saying tests found no oil contamination.
Sochi’s administration said seawater samples taken across the city met sanitary standards, according to consumer protection watchdog Rospotrebnadzor. Satellite monitoring also found no oil slicks, it added.
Sirius administration head Dmitry Plishkin said tests found no traces of oil in seawater and air pollution levels remained within permitted limits.
The tanker was attacked on the evening of Oct. 6. The fire sent thick black smoke over Sochi. Russia’s Transportation Ministry said burning oil prevented rescue vessels from approaching the ship. The flames were extinguished on Wednesday.
All 23 crew members, who were Indian nationals, were rescued.
The amount of oil aboard the tanker has not been disclosed. The Mash Telegram news channel, citing unidentified sources, reported that the vessel was fully loaded.
The tanker continued to drift along the coast after the fire. Its operator, Executive Ship Management, said Wednesday that officials and two senior crew members had started inspecting the vessel to assess its condition.
Built in 2004, the Aframax Rio is 247 meters long and 42 meters wide, with a deadweight capacity of 107,100 metric tons.
According to the investigative outlet The Insider, the tanker has called at Russian Black Sea ports and is under Ukrainian sanctions. Kyiv has linked it to Russia’s “shadow fleet,” a network of tankers used to transport oil and circumvent sanctions.

NADI, Fiji, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- The ministerial preparatory meeting held ahead of the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, known as the Pre-COP31, concluded Thursday in Nadi, Fiji, with various commitments on practical climate action.
The Pre-COP31 brought together Pacific and international leaders, ministers and senior officials to discuss issues such as climate action, resilience, energy security and climate finance.
The meeting saw new international commitments to the Pacific Resilience Facility (PRF), a Pacific-led initiative designed to help communities prepare for climate and disaster risks before disasters strike.
Electrification emerged as a key priority for COP31, with delegates highlighting its potential to reduce emissions, strengthen energy security, lower energy costs and create economic opportunities.
Ocean-climate action is also expected to feature prominently at COP31.
Pacific countries have long emphasized the central role of oceans in regulating the global climate, and the Pre-COP31 reinforced calls for stronger integration of ocean action into global climate policy.
Türkiye, which will host the 31st COP31 next month, has said it would work toward an Antalya Ocean Declaration at the conference, aimed at strengthening recognition of the ocean-climate nexus and advancing ocean-based climate solutions.
The outcomes of the Pre-COP31 are expected to help bring Pacific priorities and frontline experiences to the global climate negotiations at COP31. ■

It took 10 billion years for this signal from the early universe to reach us
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
15:05:57 UTC
00:05:57 KST

Earliest fast radio burst from 3 billion years after big bang detected
In short:
A study has found the oldest fast radio burst yet discovered.
The mysterious, high-energy burst has been linked to a galaxy from the early universe 10 billion years ago.
What's next?
Researchers believe these far-travelled bursts may help scientists understand more about the vast cosmic web, which forms the backbone of the universe.
Long before our solar system formed, a millisecond flash of light with a huge amount of energy erupted from a galaxy far, far away.
A study published in Science today captures the moment the flash, called FRB 20240304B, arrived on Earth 10 billion years later.
Study lead author Manisha Caleb, an astrophysicist at the University of Sydney, said this time frame was "insane", even for astronomers.
"If you put this in human perspective, when the light left the source, the Sun didn't exist, the solar system didn't exist, no humans existed," Dr Caleb said.
"Civilisation formed and we built radio telescopes and then we just happened to look at the right patch of sky at the right time."
The mysterious flash of radio energy, called a fast radio burst, is the oldest yet-discovered and may help scientists better understand the universe.
What are FRBs?
Fast radio bursts, or FRBs, are extremely high-energy pulses of radio waves that almost always come from outside our galaxy.
An Australian team found the first FRB using the Parkes telescope in 2007.
Despite astronomers finding hundreds since then, Dr Caleb said we do not know what produces them.
"We know there are thousands of these events that go off in the sky every day," she said.
"And because they occur at radio wavelengths they are invisible to the human eye."
Lasting only a few milliseconds, they produce immense energy.
"In those few milliseconds, they emit as much energy as the Sun would over several days," she said.
Ryan Shannon, an astrophysicist from Swinburne University who has discovered other FRBs, said one potential source could be a magnetar, a neutron star with a powerful magnetic field.
"We found there's a magnetar in our own galaxy that emitted a pulse which looked like an FRB," Professor Shannon said.
"But I wouldn't rule out having more than one way to produce an FRB."
What is FRB 20240304B?
The newly discovered FRB was recorded in 2024 by the MeerKAT telescope in South Africa, which is reflected in its name.
"The B means it was the second FRB to be discovered that day," Dr Caleb said.
"I don't know who discovered the first one, but I like to think ours is way cooler."
The team's FRB had a very high "dispersion measure" (DM), meaning the light travelled a long way before being captured.
"Typically we find [FRBs with] a few hundred DM, or maybe even a thousand," Dr Caleb said.
"With about 2,400 units of DM we figured it had to be coming from really far away."
The team then used the James Webb Space Telescope to pinpoint where the FRB came from, homing in on a galaxy that existed just 3 billion years after the big bang.
"The galaxy itself was surprisingly small," Dr Caleb said.
"We didn't expect to find the FRB to be associated with such a puny little dwarf galaxy that's actively forming stars."
How can FRBs map the cosmic web?
Professor Shannon, who was not involved in the study, said the discovery "pushed the frontiers of FRBs".
"One of the big achievements was that this was an FRB that [they] could pinpoint its location on the sky," he said.
He also noted that dispersion from these far-flung FRBs could be useful to map the cosmic web.
This skeleton-like framework can tell us how the universe evolved.
"The majority of the normal matter in the universe, the stuff that Earth, you and I are made of … is spread out in the cosmic web," Professor Shannon said.
"We're able to use the FRBs now to study the cosmic web in ways that were impossible before."
Just even clocking this ancient flash was exciting.
"You've got this brief flash, lasting milliseconds, and here we are billions of years later lucky enough to catch it," he said.

China Focus: China's new nuclear clock to redefine ultra-precise time measurement
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
23:05:29 CST
00:05:29 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- Chinese scientists have developed a nuclear clock and achieved stable operation, shifting ultra-precise time measurement from electron transitions inside atoms to transitions within atomic nuclei, according to a research article published in the journal Nature.
Solid-state nuclear clocks have potential advantages in miniaturization and engineering, and are expected to meet the high-precision time and frequency requirements in such scenarios as satellite navigation and deep-space exploration.
The nuclear clock uses lasers to drive precise energy-level transitions within the atomic nucleus of thorium-229, a special radioactive isotope, and uses the frequency of these nuclear transitions as its time reference. Researchers built the device with a self-developed 148-nanometer continuous-wave vacuum ultraviolet laser and a thorium-229-doped calcium fluoride crystal.
The new clock is expected to set a next-generation time and frequency standard, and marks an important breakthrough in the field of quantum precision measurement, said Zhai Hui, head of the Department of Physics at Tsinghua University.
"The successful development and stable operation of the nuclear clock means that the capability of quantum manipulation has extended to the nuclear scale," said Zhai.
Atomic clocks use transitions between specific energy levels of electrons inside atoms as their frequency reference, making them the most accurate timekeeping devices available so far. The nuclear clock, however, uses transitions between different nuclear energy levels to measure time.
Since the atomic nucleus scale is far smaller than the atom and nuclear transition can be less sensitive to some external electromagnetic disturbances, nuclear clocks are expected to provide a more precise and more practical time and frequency standard than atomic clocks.
A research team led by Ding Shiqian, associate professor in the Department of Physics at Tsinghua University, developed the world's first 148-nanometer continuous-wave vacuum ultraviolet laser, solving the core light source challenge of precisely driving energy-level transitions inside the thorium-229 atomic nucleus.
In collaboration with partners, they also developed a thorium-229-doped calcium fluoride crystal using only 1.4 micrograms of thorium-229, laying a core technological foundation for the development of the nuclear clock, according to the researchers.
"We have established a complete technological system covering the key light source, nuclear clock crystal, nuclear transition spectrum and closed-loop operation," said Ding. ■

Meet the Nobel Peace Prize Contenders Who Could Beat Trump This Year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
15:03:19 UTC
00:03:19 KST

President Donald Trump on Wednesday revisited his argument that he deserves to be awarded the Nobel Peace Prize this year, telling reporters in the Oval Office that he has done “far more” than any other U.S. President.
“I don't know what their decision is going to be. They have a reputation for maybe not giving it to people like me,” Trump said, insisting that it would be a “great discredit” to the Norwegian Nobel Committee if they do not announce him as the recipient Friday morning.
“I've stopped maybe the total obliteration of the world, because Iran will never have a nuclear weapon, and that's a positive thing,” he claimed, listing the reasons why he believes he is deserving of the prestigious prize.
Trump said he was “very honored to receive it indirectly last time by the recipient, who said nobody in history deserves it more” than him. The 2025 winner, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, notably gave her medal to Trump in January as she pressed the U.S. to support democracy in Venezuela, days after the U.S. capture of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores.
Following the regifting of the medal, the Norwegian Nobel Committee emphasized that “the prize itself—the honor and recognition—remains inseparably linked to the person or organization designated as the laureate by the Norwegian Nobel Committee.”
Trump has long said he is deserving of the prize. The leaders of Israel, Cambodia, and Pakistan have all previously said they nominated Trump. However, all nominations remain private and the Norwegian Nobel Institute doesn’t release a shortlist of contenders. Still, each year, names are circulated in public discourse and bets are made as to who might come out on top.
The Norwegian Nobel Institute has registered a total of 287 candidates for this year’s prize, of which 208 are individuals and 79 are organizations.
As Trump’s war with Iran stretches into its eighth month, polls have tipped him as an unlikely contender to walk away with this year’s award. Amid mounting speculation over who may be the chosen recipient, here’s a look at some of the contenders.
Sudan’s Emergency Response Rooms
The start of Sudan’s current civil war in April 2023 escalated an already desperate humanitarian crisis. Fighting between the army and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in late 2025 pushed civilians further toward risk of famine, with even more people displaced and killed.
Sudan’s Emergency Response Rooms have provided desperately needed relief. The collapse of the state and increasingly difficult access for humanitarian groups over the past three years has led to a rise of 700 ERRs across all of Sudan’s 18 states, mobilizing over 26,000 volunteers, according to Alsanosi Adam, a journalist and ERR volunteer himself.
The community-led initiative provides healthcare, food assistance, education, civilian protection, and psychosocial support. According to Right Livelihood, volunteers have been detained and tortured while offering assistance.
The charity is a lead contender to win the Nobel Peace Prize, with Polymarket citing a 17% chance.
Mark Carney
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney arrived in Office last April amid an emerging trade rift with Trump and threats from Washington to annex Canada and make it the 51st state.
The tariff threats escalated and, following the collapse of negotiations in August, the U.S. and Canada are now engaged in a trade war.
Carney has opened up new trading and diplomatic relations with China and Europe in an effort to move away from U.S. reliance. He delivered a defiant speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, denouncing “American hegemony” and insisting there has been a “rupture in the world order.”
Carney’s efforts to unite Canada in the face of Trump’s threats have seemingly helped his popularity at home, with his approval rating back up to 66%, according to new data from Liaison Strategies.
When it comes to the Nobel Peace Prize, he’s more an outsider, with a 1% chance of receiving the honor.
Pope Leo
Pope Leo XIV, the first American pope, has made strident global outreach efforts since his ascension to the head of the Catholic Church in April 2025.
His repeated calls for peace, including his spotlight on Gaza, have made an impact, and even earned him criticism from Trump.
“Today, sadly, war has returned, even to Europe: a new senseless slaughter, claiming countless civilian lives every day,” Leo told European leaders in September, referencing the Russia-Ukraine war. “We must ask whether we are truly making creative efforts to advance world peace, or whether we are simply seeking to stem the tide of war and better prepare ourselves for wars that we assume are still to come.”
In the aftermath of the first U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February, Leo said “stability and peace are not achieved through mutual threats, nor through the use of weapons, which sow destruction, suffering, and death, but only through reasonable, sincere, and responsible dialogue.” 
Trump responded by falsely claiming that Leo would “be fine with Iran having a nuclear weapon”—Leo rejected the claim and urged critics to speak “truthfully.”
Pope Leo stands with a 1% chance of being awarded the prize.
Mykola Kuleba
Mykola Kuleba co-founded Save Ukraine in 2014 during the early days of the conflict in Eastern Ukraine. The organization’s work has become increasingly important since Russia’s full-scale invasion of its neighbor in 2022.
Missing Ukrainian children have become a focal point of humanitarian efforts amid the war, with Moscow contending that it relocated children in an effort to protect them. Save Ukraine has so far helped reunite 1,763 children with their parents, but the organization has said thousands more need to be brought home.
“[Kuleba’s] work combines direct humanitarian action with strong advocacy for children’s rights, making him a compelling candidate for international recognition,” said Haakon Gjerløw, acting director of the Peace Research Institute Oslo (PRIO), as he detailed his list of suggested candidates for the 2026 prize.
Kuleba is currently listed as having a 9% chance.
Yulia Navalnaya
Yulia Navalnaya, widow of Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny, has become an activist in her own right, challenging President Vladimir Putin’s regime and fighting for democracy.
Alexei died in an Arctic penal colony in February 2024. A few weeks later, Yulia vowed to take up his cause in an interview with TIME, where she expressed hope that Russia might one day be a “normal, democratic country”—the future Alexei “dreamed about.”
Navalnaya is listed as having a 5% chance of winning the Nobel Peace Prize.

The source suggested Washington could reach an agreement with Moscow to hold talks in the second half of October to discuss possible steps toward ending the war. That timetable has not been officially confirmed.

What were Trump operatives doing for pro-Russian politician Dodik in Bosnia?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
15:01:18 UTC
00:01:18 KST

What were Trump operatives doing for pro-Russian politician Dodik in Bosnia?
Reports of Trump aides paid to advise Bosnian Serb leader ahead of parliamentary election raise alarm.
A New York Times report has raised questions about what two key political operatives for US President Donald Trump were doing visiting pro-Russian politician Milorad Dodik in Bosnia and Herzegovina ahead of parliamentary elections there on Sunday.
According to sources cited by the US newspaper, James Blair and Chris LaCivita advised Dodik and were paid hundreds of thousands of dollars for their work.
The revelation has triggered a wave of criticism from within the Republican Party. Blair currently runs Trump’s main fundraising organisation, MAGA Inc, while LaCivita is a senior adviser to Trump.
Blair, who has previously served as Trump’s deputy chief of staff, and LaCivita have not commented on the visit.
Here is what we know so far:
Who is Milorad Dodik?
The Bosnian Serb is a pro-Russian politician in Bosnia and Herzegovina. He last met Russian President Vladimir Putin on September 29 in Moscow in a notably cordial meeting, just five days before Bosnia and Herzegovina’s general election.
Last November, the Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina – the country’s highest – upheld a ban on Dodik from formally running in this year’s October 4 elections, after a Sarajevo court convicted him of refusing to comply with decisions issued by the international envoy overseeing the country’s peace deal.
The former president of Bosnia’s autonomous Serb Republic – or Republika Srpska – was sentenced in February to one year in prison for defying Christian Schmidt, the German diplomat responsible for safeguarding the 1995 peace accords that ended Bosnia’s war in the 1990s.
He was also banned from holding political office for six years and stripped of his post as president.
Dodik nevertheless campaigned for the election. His pro-Russian, nationalist SNSD party went on to celebrate major wins on multiple levels. It won more than 55 percent of votes in regional elections, maintaining its strong grip on power in the Serb-dominated entity of Republika Srpska.
Dodik has led Republika Srpska since 1998, with brief interruptions. He advocates the secession of the entity, established in 1995 under the Dayton Peace Agreement and its eventual unification with neighbouring Serbia – a position that has raised fears of a new conflict in the country and the wider region.
Peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina was achieved in 1995 after four years of bloody conflict and genocide against Bosniak Muslims, under pressure from the administration of US President Bill Clinton, at a US military base in Dayton, Ohio. The agreement therefore became known as the Dayton Peace Agreement.
Ironically, Dodik then came to power with the backing of the US administration, as an alternative to the Serbian nationalists who dominated the political scene at the time. Madeleine Albright, then US secretary of state, famously described him as a “breath of fresh air” in the Balkans.
Dodik soon turned against US interests, however, and moved closer to Russia. After Donald Trump returned to power in 2025, he again sought to establish closer relations with Washington. During the 2024 US election campaign, he was seen wearing a MAGA hat.
He appears to have achieved at least some of his goals. Although he had been under US sanctions for years over his role in destabilising Bosnia and Herzegovina, those sanctions were lifted this year. The Trump administration said the move was pragmatic and aimed at easing tensions in the country. In return, Dodik dropped several unconstitutional laws.
How did key Trump advisers end up working for Dodik?
The New York Times reported that James Blair and Chris LaCivita were hired through a Washington law firm retained by the government of Republika Srpska.
According to sources cited by the newspaper, each received hundreds of thousands of dollars.
Documents filed with the US Department of Justice show that Republika Srpska has paid more than $4m since the beginning of 2025 to lobbyists and political operatives linked to Trump for lobbying activities.
The issue of Republika Srpska using public funds to pay lobbying firms recently also reached the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. On September 25, the court ruled that Republika Srpska’s lobbying acts and activities were not in accordance with the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina as their objectives were contrary to the constitution, decisions of the Constitutional Court or the institutions of Bosnia and Herzegovina.
Ivana Korajlic of Transparency International told Al Jazeera that Republika Srpska would likely not stop lobbying, “it will only be presented in a different way”.
LaCivita previously worked as a political campaign strategist for Sali Berisha, one of the most influential Albanian politicians of the post-socialist period, in the run up to Albanian elections last year.
Berisha is a former president of Albania (1992-1997) and prime minister (2005–2013), and is currently the leader of Albania’s opposition, centre-right Democratic Party.
The administration of former US President Joe Biden banned Berisha from entering the United States in 2021, citing corruption and the misuse of public funds as the reasons. Berisha denied the allegations.
In June this year , during Trump’s second term as US president, it was reported that the US had lifted the travel ban on him and members of his family, just as it had done with Dodik.
How have Republicans reacted to Trump advisers visiting Republika Srpska?
The news prompted reactions within the Republican Party, particularly because of the timing.
Blair and LaCivita were in Republika Srpska at a time when Trump’s political operation was focused on the final stretch of its campaign for midterm congressional elections in the US. According to polls, Republicans are not performing well among voters amid the war on Iran, which has proved deeply unpopular in the US.
Steve Bannon, Trump’s former chief strategist, called Blair and LaCivita “grifters” and demanded a detailed review of the money they had received, Politico reported.
What has Donald Trump said?
Trump initially said he was unaware of Blair and LaCivita’s other engagements and that he would ask them who else they were working for. He added that if he found a conflict of interest, he would fire them immediately.
Later, responding to questions from reporters in the Oval Office, Trump softened his rhetoric.
Trump said Blair and LaCivita did not actually have a conflict of interest because they were not currently White House employees and, as consultants, are allowed to have multiple clients.
Why would Dodik hire Trump’s political operatives?
It is unclear what Dodik gains by hiring people close to Trump.
Aleksandar Trifunovic, editor of Buka magazine in Banja Luka, said he could see no concrete result from their work advising Dodik.
“We don’t see anything that would allow us to say: ‘This is what they taught him, and that is why he won the election.’ Dodik’s rhetoric has not changed. It has been similar to MAGA rhetoric for a long time. But it was important for Dodik to be able to say that he had Trump’s people working for him. So what Dodik paid for and what he got was proximity to Trump through Trump’s people,” Trifunovic told Al Jazeera.
Trifunović said he views the answer to why Trump’s political operatives would work for Dodik through the lens of the pragmatic nature of the US political system. The American lobbying system is relatively transparent.
“The more money you give, the more support you get,” he said.
However, Trifunovic singled out the relationship between Trump’s political circle and Dodik as particularly significant, given Dodik’s ties to Russia and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“The main criticism is actually something else: how is it possible that Trump’s people are on good terms with someone who has such close relations with Russian President Vladimir Putin? You cannot be with both Trump and Putin at the same time. That certainly does not have a great future,” Trifunovic said.
What effect could this have on Trump-Dodik relations?
Dodik’s ties to Trump’s political circle have a broader context.
Miljan Kovac, an editor and political commentator from Nevesinje in southeastern Bosnia and Herzegovina, said Trump and the Republicans have given Dodik political space after years of US sanctions imposed on him, members of his family and his associates.
The lifting of sanctions against Dodik last October was justified by the US administration as a pragmatic move aimed at easing tensions in Bosnia and Herzegovina.
“Dodik was clearly bargaining with the US administration, in his own way,” Kovac told Al Jazeera.
On election night, after declaring victory for his SNSD party, Dodik himself spoke about the significance of Trump’s return to the political stage in the United States.
“If it had not been for Trump’s magnificent victory, we would probably be political corpses today. But thanks to the new environment, we are now political winners,” Dodik said.

Punjab's Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann has leveled allegations against the BJP, claiming the use of Central investigative agencies for political leverage.

French students continue protests, saying ministers’ pledges not enough
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
15:00:03 UTC
00:00:03 KST

High school students have again blockaded schools and marched through cities across France, promising to continue their campaign against the poor state of the national education system in the 10th day of protests that have left hundreds injured.
Large crowds took to the streets on Thursday for mainly peaceful demonstrations in cities including Lille, Rennes, Nantes, Lyon, Toulon and Marseille, while in Paris a large procession marched through the city centre to the Place de la Bastille.
An estimated 25,000 students thronged the square in the east of the capital, with some climbing the monument at its centre, which commemorates France’s 1830 July revolution, while waving the tricolour flag and singing the Marseillaise.
As the evening drew in, riot police fired teargas and crowd-dispersal rounds and carried out repeated baton charges to clear the protesters, some of whom hurled bottles, paving stones and other projectiles at the heavily armoured squads.
Eliane, 16, a pupil on the Paris march, said she had come to “defend and encourage high schools in an even worse state than mine”, calling the march “magnificent”. She said she planned to continue protesting until concrete progress was achieved.
The education minister, Édouard Geffray, told TF1 television on Thursday night that 3,000 substitute teachers would be deployed to about 100 high schools identified as having particularly acute teacher shortages “between tomorrow and Tuesday”.
Geffray said he would also authorise the recruitment of “several hundred” new teachers. The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said the government would propose amendments to the 2027 budget to “translate some of the students’ demands into concrete measures, particularly regarding teacher replacements”.
Students earlier said the government’s reaction was not sufficient. Ryad Rani, the president of one high school students’ union, said the protesters had heard “no concrete measures whatsoever, no response to our demands”. The movement “will continue”, he said.
Sabrine Kharbach, from another students’ association, said the protest, over teacher shortages, long school hours and dilapidated buildings, would last “for as long as €10bn hasn’t been put on the table”, the amount students and some leftwing politicians have said needs to be urgently invested in France’s schools.
According to an Elabe poll for BFM TV, 72% of French people think the students’ demands are legitimate but 55% of them think the protests should stop. Unions called for another national day of action in support of the students next Tuesday.
The education ministry said fewer high schools had been forced to close than in recent days, with 224 shut on Thursday morning and 157 by lunchtime, meaning that about 95% of the country’s high schools were at least partly open.
But more than 71,000 protesters took to the streets on Thursday, the interior ministry said. The demonstrations, backed by many teachers, parents and unions, involved further clashes with police around some school barricades in Paris. In Rennes riot officers used water cannon to disperse protesters.
A prominent complaint on student banners and placards was the heavy-handed police response to the wave of protests. “Too young to be listened to, but old enough to be teargassed,” read one banner on the Paris march.
Over the past two weeks, some demonstrators have set dustbins on fire outside their schools, destroyed bus shelters and hurled projectiles at riot police, who have responded using batons, teargas and riot-control rounds.
At least 215 teenagers, 89 school staff and 761 police officers have been injured since the start of the protests, which were triggered by chronic teacher shortages, crowded classes, dilapidated buildings and long school days.
The government on Wednesday suspended the use of stun grenades by police after a teenager’s hand was blown off, while saying it was “excessive” to speak of “police repression” and denying that officers had “orders to confront” the young protesters.
The protests have rocked a government caught between popular demands for investment in deteriorating public services and pressure from markets to reduce France’s ballooning budget deficit and debt mountain, among the highest in the EU.
The economy minister, Roland Lescure, said this week there was room to address demands for more school resources in the 2027 budget. In the current draft, schools have the second-largest funding increase after defence, with a 1.4% hike to €90.9bn.
Six months away from a crucial presidential election to replace Emmanuel Macron, politicians are jockeying to exploit the protests, with the far-right frontrunner, Marine Le Pen, highlighting the damage to schools and calling for parents to foot repair bills.
Her hard-left opponent, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, has praised the protesters as “incredible” and denounced police brutality.

Kim Yo Jong, sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, called Seoul’s request for a UN exemption to provide medical equipment to North Korea an “insult to our state,” a politically motivated provocation and a “grave encroachment” on its national law, according to a statement published by the state-run Korean Central News Agency (KCNA).

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said that Russia’s war in Ukraine has reached a dangerous stalemate, while stressing that Washington will continue efforts to secure a lasting negotiated settlement.
“We’d love to see a negotiated settlement to this war that is permanent, enduring, and fair. And that’s what we’re committed to continuing to do,” Rubio told reporters on Thursday during a visit to Portugal.
The Trump administration has sought in recent weeks to revive negotiations aimed at ending the four-year conflict, Europe’s bloodiest war since World War Two.
Ukrainian negotiators are due to visit the United States for talks on Friday and Saturday.
Rubio warns of wider regional conflict
Rubio said the conflict’s continued escalation could eventually spread beyond Ukraine and draw neighboring NATO members into a broader confrontation.
“That escalation could wind up being a sabotage campaign in neighboring countries that are members of NATO,” he said, warning that other developments “could quickly turn what is a war between two countries into a much broader and far more dangerous regional conflict.”
Drone attacks by Russia and Ukraine have increasingly extended beyond traditional military targets, hitting energy facilities, refineries, ports and vessels carrying oil and grain.
More recently, attacks have also targeted e-commerce warehouses and data centres.
Washington to keep pushing for talks
Rubio said the United States wants the war to end through negotiations but acknowledged that Washington’s diplomatic efforts depend on tangible progress.
“This war needs to end in a negotiated settlement. The sooner, the better,” he said.
“The United States stands ready to facilitate that. We have tried. We will continue to try. But we’re also not going to invest in pointless processes if we can’t make progress,” Rubio added.
The upcoming talks with Ukrainian negotiators come as Washington seeks to determine whether renewed diplomatic efforts can produce a path toward ending the fighting while avoiding further escalation.

Were Oct. 7 records altered? New allegations target Netanyahu's inner circle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:56:05 UTC
23:56:05 KST

The October Council, an organization representing former hostages, bereaved families and survivors of the October 7 massacre, has appealed to Shin Bet chief David Zini, Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara, Cabinet Secretary Yossi Fuchs and State Archivist Ruti Abramovitz, raising concerns that individuals close to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have concealed information related to the events of the massacre, ynet learned Thursday morning.
"According to people in the prime minister's inner circle, transcriptionists were threatened and pressured to alter official transcripts," the letter states.
The appeal by the October Council families follows a July 2024 report by Nadav Eyal in ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth revealing that Maj. Gen. (res.) Avi Gil, Netanyahu's military secretary at the time of the massacre, had contacted the attorney general to express concerns that attempts had been made to alter official transcripts in the Prime Minister's Office during the war.
Even before that report, officials in the Prime Minister's Office had alleged that attempts were made during the war to change some of the transcripts of security Cabinet discussions and even transcripts of security-related telephone conversations.
The former military secretary said in media interviews that he had noticed early in the war that Netanyahu associates were engaged in what he described as a "disproportionate collection of materials."
He added that a stenographer in the Prime Minister's Office had told him that Tzachi Braverman, Netanyahu's former chief of staff, who was later implicated in the "late-night meeting" affair and whose appointment as ambassador to Britain was delayed, had demanded that the stenographer change the recorded time of a conversation Gil held with Netanyahu on the morning of October 7.
Asked whether he could assess why Braverman had done so, Gil replied: "First of all, this is a pattern of criminal conduct by people who think they can do whatever they want, and the chief of staff behaved like someone who could do whatever he wanted."
According to Gil, "It's possible they were already working on the narrative we're seeing now, portraying the prime minister as the only one functioning when the chaos began, supposedly because he had issued all the necessary instructions from the very beginning. That's a serious but plausible scenario."
"There's another possibility, one that is far more serious. Eleven minutes passed between the first and second calls. During that time, I received intelligence and information I didn't have during the first call, intelligence and information that I passed on to the prime minister during the second call. And if they can prove that this intelligence and information already existed at 6:29 a.m., that would mean someone already knew at that point what was going to happen. In other words, there had been a betrayal."
Allegations against Netanyahu and Braverman
In the October Council's letter, which alleges that transcriptionists in the Prime Minister's Office were threatened and ordered to alter official transcripts, the families raised a question:
"The transcriptionists are heroes who came forward and told the military secretary what had happened. Otherwise, the alteration of the transcript would never have been discovered. Who knows how many other transcripts were changed?"
The families' letter further stated: "An associate of Avi Gil, who was serving as Netanyahu's military secretary at the time, told us what Gil had revealed to him about the alleged alteration of the transcript.
"'Braverman definitely changed the time in the transcript. The transcriptionist told Avi that she had said to him, "But Tzachi, I'm not allowed to. The time is 6:40 a.m. It's recorded in the computer.'
"'He told her, 'Don't argue with me. Change it to 6:29 a.m. I was on that call."
"'That was her testimony to Avi. She then says that Tzachi looks at the transcript [after it was altered] and enthusiastically tells her, "Look how sharp the prime minister is. As soon as he's woken up, he immediately gives instructions."
"And that, of course, was a lie. The transcriptionists felt they were being asked to do something they weren't allowed to do, so they turned to Avi. They told him that Braverman would walk around carrying stacks of transcripts. He had collected a large amount of material."
The families added in their letter: "Another senior official, who had extensive information, documents and records related to October 7 in his possession, told us: 'I have three hidden folders containing all the documents related to October 7. One will go to the State Archives and the other two will go to the state commission of inquiry. For now, everything is being kept in safes at different locations because I'm afraid the documents could fall into the wrong hands.'
In their appeal to the senior officials, the families added: "One of the most senior officials serving on October 7 told us: 'It bothers me that the prime minister of Israel is breaking the law and the system doesn't know how to deal with it. He takes transcripts from sensitive discussions, presents half-truths from them in a manipulative way and tries to turn them into the truth, even though he knows that isn't the case.
"'If he has already taken it upon himself to exercise authority he doesn't actually have to release excerpts, then why release fragments of sentences taken out of context?
"'Netanyahu publishes 55 pages, and I was there. I saw a large portion of the original documents. Who gave you the authority to publish partial quotations rather than the full discussion?
"Yet Netanyahu repeatedly chooses to present only part of the picture rather than the whole story in an attempt to manipulate the public."
The families' letter to the Shin Bet chief, the attorney general, the Cabinet secretary and the state archivist also stated: "Another senior official, who headed a security agency at the time, testified: 'As time passes and more reports emerge on the matter, it is becoming clear that we did not necessarily know everything and that some people chose to conceal things from us.'"

Germany to buy 4 more frigates to track enemy submarines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:54:07 UTC
23:54:07 KST

Ayhan Simsek
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
Germany’s parliamentary budget committee approved the purchase of four more frigates on Thursday from Thyssenkrupp Marine Systems, raising the navy’s order to eight identical warships for anti-submarine warfare.
The Defense Ministry said the Bundestag’s budget committee cleared the additional ships from Thyssenkrupp Marine Systems, or TKMS. Lawmakers already approved the first four of the same type on July 8. Industry has pledged that the first of the eight ships will join the fleet in 2029.
The vessels are MEKO A-200 DEU frigates, a design TKMS sells in adapted versions to allies and partners. The ministry said those export ships have been in service for years and have proved themselves.
“Germany is taking responsibility for conventional defense in the alliance,” said the ministry. “For that, we have pledged NATO a range of capability contributions under capability and defense planning.”
“Alongside other capabilities, the navy will make an important contribution to defense and deterrence in the North Sea and Baltic Sea region, as well as in the Atlantic and the High North, through sea-based anti-submarine warfare,” it said.
Exit from Damen contract
The ships replace a plan that assigned sea-based submarine hunting to the F-126 frigate.
That program had been led by Damen, a shipyard group based in the Netherlands, as general contractor. After major performance failures, Germany ended the contract following a full assessment, according to the ministry.
The navy then reviewed alternatives available on the market and concluded that the MEKO A-200 DEU frigates are suitable for anti-submarine warfare and for Germany’s NATO commitments, it said.
“The procurement of eight frigates of a single ship type also offers the German navy considerable advantages in operation, maintenance and repair, as well as training,” said the ministry.
Damen, the Dutch shipbuilder, disputes the German government’s account and argues that the cancellation was politically motivated. The company is seeking nearly €4.7 billion ($5.25 billion) from the German government for the scrapped F-126 frigate program.

In sickness and in health: An Israeli writer throws her lot in with the country

In Sickness and in Health: An Israeli Writer Throws Her Lot in With the Country
"Israel is neither a country, nor a nation," the writer Amos Oz once told an audience in Portland, Oregon. "Actually, it is a fiery collection of arguments." For Israeli journalist Ruth Margalit, Israel is a collection of fiery people, too – all kinds of people, from contentious political extremists like National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir to Sayed Kashua, the eminent Palestinian writer driven all the way to the United States by Israel's demoralizing treatment of its Palestinian citizens.
Margalit's nonfiction debut, "In the Belly of the Whale," which was released on September 22, draws from years of studying some of Israel's biggest personalities in granular form. The result is a searing, deeply compassionate – sometimes even comically absurd – view of Israel, "a place vigorously debated but little understood," as her introduction says.
Margalit strings together, in one efficient volume, published in the United States by Steerforth Press in collaboration with Altneuland Press internationally, a variety of characters she has covered over the last decade, a checkered pantheon of Israeli personalities and provocateurs told through close narratives, her vivid observations cutting close to her subject's bones.
Characters like Miri Regev and Ben-Gvir, easy targets for liberal contempt due to their outsized influence and media antics – to say nothing of their actual politics – come across as people who could be the eccentric aunt or uncle pressing buttons around the family dinner table. At an event hosted by Haaretz, Margalit describes Regev's spectacular persona: "Standing in front of the audience, her expression set between a smirk and a scowl, she clutched the lectern with one hand. 'I was always told to start a speech with a quote; it makes for a cultured impression,' she began. 'So here goes. As the famed Chinese philosopher Sun Tzu once put it' – she switched to accented English – 'Cut the bullshit! Cut the bullshit!'"

Details
South Korea conducted the first test launch of a hypersonic glide vehicle (HGV) on Thursday, the presidential office of Cheong Wa Dae said. It was apparently a show of force directed at North Korea amid heightened inter-Korean tensions following a recent mine explosion at the border.
The test was conducted to verify key hypersonic technologies, including flight trajectory and speed, as a strategic asset capable of delivering sudden, high-precision strikes against enemy targets, presidential spokesperson Kang Yu-jun said in a written statement to the press.
President Lee Jae-myung personally observed the launch, accompanied by Defense Minister Kang Shin-chul and other officials.
An HGV is a missile system that uses a booster to build up speed and climb into the upper layers of the atmosphere, after which it separates from the booster and glides at lower altitudes at hypersonic speeds.
Lee’s office did not disclose the location of the test, but reports said the launch took place from a barge at the Agency for Defense Development’s test center in Taean, approximately 130 kilometers south of Seoul.
According to Kang, the launch tested heat-shield materials designed to withstand extremely high temperatures, guidance and control systems, as well as the vehicle’s ability to perform irregular maneuvers at low altitudes.
Unlike traditional ballistic missiles, after separation the HGV lowered its flight altitude, made horizontal and vertical course corrections, and precisely hit the target, she said.
Update
The unannounced launch on Thursday is widely viewed as a response to the September 21 mine explosion on the South Korean side of the Military Demarcation Line (MDL), which seriously injured two South Korean servicemen. Seoul determined that the explosion was caused by mines planted by North Korean military personnel in violation of the armistice agreement.
Tensions rose after the explosion: Pyongyang categorically denied responsibility and threatened retaliation if the South took any measures in response.
The government of Lee Jae-myung, which seeks rapprochement with Pyongyang, came under criticism for its passive response to the mine explosion.
Critics accused Lee and his officials of taking an excessively soft stance in order not to provoke the North.

Byzantium recognises Damian as Bulgaria’s first patriarch in October 927
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:52:07 UTC
23:52:07 KST

Author
Ivo Ivanov
Byzantium recognises Damian as Bulgaria’s first patriarch in October 927
Thursday 8 October 2026 16:18
Thursday, 8 October 2026, 16:18
The ruins of the Patriarchal Basilica in Drastar (present-day Silistra), on the banks of the Danube.
PHOTO bulgarianhistory.org
Font size
In 927, Bulgaria and Byzantium (the Eastern Roman Empire) signed a peace treaty under which Constantinople officially recognised the autocephalous Bulgarian Church as a patriarchate for the first time, acknowledging its status as equal to that of the Eastern patriarchates and the Church of Rome. A later historical list, dating from the 12th century, names Damian as the first Bulgarian patriarch and associates him with the Danube city of Drastar.
The following historical events led to Byzantium’s recognition of the Bulgarian Orthodox Church’s independence.
On 27 May 927, the medieval Bulgarian ruler Tsar Simeon the Great died. After fighting numerous wars against Byzantium, Bulgaria’s principal rival during the Middle Ages, Simeon had sought recognition as ruler not only of the Bulgarians but also of the Romans, or Byzantines. He did not achieve this during his lifetime.
Coin bearing the image of Tsar Peter I.
PHOTO wikipedia.org
Simeon was succeeded by his son Peter I. The young tsar launched a military campaign in Thrace, forcing Byzantine Emperor Romanos Lekapenos to negotiate. In early October 927, the two sides concluded what became known as the Deep Peace.
Constantinople recognised Peter as Basileus of the Bulgarians. To seal the agreement, the Bulgarian ruler married Maria, a granddaughter of Emperor Romanos Lekapenos. At their wedding, Maria took the name Irene, meaning “peace”.
Under the same agreement, Patriarch Stephen II of Constantinople reaffirmed the Bulgarian Church’s independence and recognised its patriarchal status.
Until then, the Bulgarian Church had been an autocephalous, or self-governing, archbishopric. It had acquired this status in 870, during the reign of Prince Boris I, who established Christianity in Bulgaria after 866.
The Round Church in Veliki Preslav, built during the reign of Tsar Simeon I (893–927), is a masterpiece of early medieval European architecture.
PHOTO wikipedia.org
In 924, following the death of Patriarch Nicholas Mystikos of Constantinople, Simeon proclaimed himself Basileus of the Bulgarians and Romans. Joseph I was then consecrated as patriarch. These unilateral Bulgarian actions, however, were not recognised by Byzantium.
Little is known about Damian, the first Bulgarian patriarch recognised by Constantinople.
Apart from his name, almost nothing is known with certainty about Damian. Numerous, often contradictory theories concern his identity, the dates and location of his ministry, and the extent of his ecclesiastical authority. His name first appeared in a published historical work in 1680, in Charles du Cange’s Historia Byzantina.
Miniature from the Madrid manuscript of John Skylitzes’ Chronicle: Emperor John Tzimiskes takes the royal icon of the Virgin Mary, the captive Tsar Boris II and his family from Preslav to Constantinople.
PHOTO Archive
During his research, du Cange discovered a collection of ecclesiastical lists from the chancery of the Patriarchate of Constantinople in the Royal Library in Paris. The documents are now held by the National Library of France. Among them was a 12th-century list of the primates of the Bulgarian Church and its successor, the Archbishopric of Ohrid. The document, also known as the Du Cange List, was published in the catalogue accompanying Historia Byzantina, a collection of translations of Byzantine texts.
The source states: “Damian held ecclesiastical office in Dorostol, now called Dristra. In his time, Bulgaria too was granted autocephalous status. By order of Emperor Romanos Lekapenos, he was proclaimed patriarch by the imperial council, and was later deposed by John Tzimiskes.”
PHOTO wikipedia.org
Why does the document place Damian in Silistra rather than in the royal capital of Preslav?
One possible explanation lies with the author of the list, Archbishop John Komnenos of Ohrid. The Byzantine cleric may have wished to diminish the Bulgarian patriarch’s standing by presenting him as the Metropolitan of Drastar and emphasising his expulsion by Byzantine Emperor John Tzimiskes. Following the death of Tsar Peter, Tzimiskes invaded Bulgaria, capturing first the capital, Preslav, and then Drastar, also known as Dorostol.
Yet the Du Cange List names another church leader after Damian: “German, also called Gabriel, who served as bishop in Voden and Prespa.”
Emperor John I Tzimiskes’ campaign against Drastar – a 14th-century miniature from the Manasses Chronicle.
PHOTO Archive
These brief accounts have led Professor Plamen Pavlov and several other Bulgarian historians to argue that Damian refused to submit to Byzantine authority after the capture of Preslav and the imprisonment of Tsar Boris II. According to this interpretation, the patriarch fled Drastar and moved the seat of the Bulgarian Patriarchate westwards, to Sredets and the Bulgarian territories that remained independent under the future Tsar Samuel.
The circumstances of Patriarch Damian’s death, however, remain unknown.
