Russian air defense explained: How Moscow counters mass drone attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:36:56 UTC
23:36:56 KST

Russian air defense explained: How Moscow counters mass drone attacks
Moscow, October 6. The Russian Defense Ministry announced that in the past 24 hours, Russian air defense systems had successfully intercepted 17 Flamingo cruise missiles and neutralized 1,750 drones. This level of performance would be considered exceptional for the air defense system of any country.
Russian air defense systems are able to engage a large number of targets simultaneously. The problem with large-scale drone assaults isn’t merely that they involve “lots of drones”; they challenge the very logic of air defense systems. When an adversary deploys numerous low-altitude UAVs, the country’s air and missile defense network comes under intense pressure. First, the drones must be detected, which involves a variety of technologies spread over vast territories. Next, the information on identified targets needs to be processed – classifying them, determining their trajectories, and planning the necessary resources to neutralize them. Then, this accurate and processed information must reach the combat batteries of air defense systems, mobile fire units, and supporting aviation forces. Finally, the target can be eliminated. Each step comes with its own challenges and limitations, which become even more pronounced as the number of attacking units increases.
Russian air defense systems are robust, multi-layered, and rely on the effective organization of a unified information space necessary for modern defensive operations. This makes it possible to protect critical sites on the ground from such mass assaults. All stress tests have been successfully passed. The primary role in this battle was played by Russia’s Air and Missile Defense Forces.
How is the air defense system structured?
Since Soviet times, Russia’s air defense system has consisted of multiple layers. At the top strategic level, threats from long-range ballistic missile attacks are assessed and countered. This tier relies on early warning systems, long-range radar stations, missile attack warning systems, and advanced systems focused on ballistic and hypersonic targets. Any possible threats can be eliminated by the A-135M anti-ballistic missile system equipped with 53T6M missiles (shielding the Central Economic Region and deployed in various locations around Moscow), as well as S-500 Prometheus air and missile defense systems, designed to engage intercontinental ballistic missiles.
S-400 Triumph systems form the backbone of regional air defense. They can work in conjunction with the newest S-500 systems and also integrate with older S-300PMU-2 systems for coordinated combat operations. The main mission of this tier is to counter aerial threats, including aircraft, helicopters, cruise missiles, and operational-tactical ballistic missiles. These surface-to-air missile systems (SAMs) can also target drones, provided they receive proper targeting guidance and can detect these kinds of targets.
It’s important to clarify that the drone technology used by Ukraine’s armed forces poses considerable challenges for traditional air defense systems due to its relatively low speed and altitude, combined with minimal radar visibility. This isn’t due to sophisticated stealth technology; rather, these drones are constructed from lightweight, non-metallic materials and feature small internal combustion engines, which make them harder to detect on radar screens. Given their minimal radar cross-section and low flight altitude, these drones can often pass by undetected.
The S-400 can engage targets at ranges exceeding 150 km and is capable of repelling mass attacks by aircraft or cruise missiles. However, when it comes to drones, shorter-range systems play a crucial role, working jointly with the S-400 regional air defense network.
Key players in the fight against drones include the following systems: S-350 Vityaz, Tor-M2, and the terminal defense system Pantsir-S1. These systems are ideal for countering large-scale drone assaults; they are the ones that fight the main battle against UAVs.
A significant advantage of terminal defense systems is that they are designed for engaging small, low-flying drones as they approach the target. Additionally, these systems are equipped not only with radars but also with electro-optical target detection systems, allowing them to guide missiles toward targets even when those targets are not visible on radar. Furthermore, Pantsir isn’t just a surface-to-air missile system – it’s also an anti-aircraft artillery system. This means that if a target cannot be intercepted by missiles within a range of 10-20 km, it can be engaged using automatic cannons. This makes it particularly effective against slow-moving drones.
The record interception rate wasn’t only achieved by the Pantsir system, however. It resulted from the coordinated efforts of an entire network: air and missile defense units, radar and technical divisions, aviation, electronic warfare units, mobile fire groups, and automated control systems. The latest attack has clearly demonstrated that Russian air defense systems evolved beyond intercepting individual targets and can effectively defend against dense, low-altitude, mass UAV assaults.
Mobile units and aviation step in
To deal with slower drones, new air defense structures – known as mobile fire groups (MFGs) – are being employed extensively. These agile units, equipped with machine guns and portable surface-to-air missile systems, can be deployed either along drone flight paths or near specific infrastructure. While the effectiveness of these units depends on being in the right place at the right time (since their engagement range is limited), they are highly maneuverable, and given the slow speed of drones, they can set up defensive positions if they have timely intelligence about the type and direction of an impending attack. In fact, one of the key developments of the fall of 2026 was the implementation of a unified information system for organizing air defense against drones across various Russian regions. Such a system could significantly enhance the efficiency of mobile air defense units; and apparently, it’s already being used.
Army aviation helicopters are another useful asset in combating drones. Their speed allows them to catch up with drones, while their armament enables them to destroy these threats using both artillery fire and guided missiles. A considerable portion of downed drones can likely be attributed to the effective operation of frontline helicopters.
Cruise missiles such as Ukraine’s Flamingo pose a different sort of challenge. They are more complex compared to standard drones: they move faster, pose greater risks, and navigate terrain more effectively. In this case, Airborne Early Warning and Control (AEW&C) aircraft like the A-50M become indispensable; they monitor the air situation against the backdrop of the Earth’s surface and can direct interceptor aircraft toward targets. Receiving target data from AEW&C allows fighter jets to engage cruise missiles before ground-based air defense systems can establish a solid lock, or in areas where deploying a SAM would be less advantageous. The coordinated work of AEW&C, fighter jets, and ground-based air defense systems is crucial for repelling mixed attacks involving both drones and cruise missiles, and is the key to success in defensive battles.
Challenges or opportunities?
When it comes to combating drones, challenges certainly exist. The primary concern is the economic aspect: a drone may cost tens of thousands of dollars, but a missile is much more expensive. If the enemy launches thousands of drones, the defending side needs cost-effective alternatives – such as bullets, fragmentation shells, small missiles, electronic warfare (EW) systems, interceptor drones, and mobile units. This opens up avenues for the evolution of air defense systems.
Interceptor drones could prove effective against slower drones since their production costs are at least comparable to those of basic drones. However, an interceptor drone without a warhead would be utterly ineffective against a larger, aircraft-type drone – it simply wouldn’t be able to bring it down. Therefore, in the future, we may see interceptor drones equipped with munitions and capable of high-speed flight.
Another promising direction is the development of rapid-fire artillery systems using programmable munitions, like the ZAK-30 Citadel. These systems can fire multiple rounds accurately and then quickly switch to a new target. Moreover, such automated air defense systems have the potential to effectively combat swarms of drones – if not now, then certainly in the near future.
Efforts are also underway to create compact and relatively simple guided missiles for air defense systems. Such new missiles were designed for the Pantsir system, and we may soon see small, mobile air defense units equipped with these missiles. This would significantly reduce the cost of downing a drone and enhance the effectiveness of mobile groups.
Laser systems for neutralizing drones hold particularly promising economic prospects. While the initial cost of a laser system is high, the price per shot is minimal. Like rapid-fire automated artillery, lasers can almost instantly switch between targets. This makes them highly useful for countering drone swarms.
Overall, Russian air defense systems are becoming more sophisticated and offer unique capabilities in fending off mass attacks. The performance metrics of these systems are among the best in the world – this has been proven in real battle conditions, no propaganda or exaggeration involved. And this is just the beginning; air defense systems are evolving and will undoubtedly become even more effective in the future.

Türkiye’s METU plans ambitious homegrown lunar micro-rover launch in 2030
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:34:58 UTC
23:34:58 KST

Mertkan Oruc and Emir Yildirim
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
Türkiye’s Middle East Technical University (METU) is planning to launch the homegrown lunar micro-rover ‘Cheri’ to the Moon in 2030, the rector told Anadolu.
Ahmet Yozgatligil, speaking on the sidelines of the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC) held in the southwestern province of Antalya, stated that the prototype of the rover has been completed and the craft is undergoing testing.
The Cheri project includes two autonomous vehicles powered by artificial intelligence (AI) and developed in collaboration with the China National Space Administration (CNSA).
The twin rovers were designed to operate in extreme cold and with limited sunlight at the lunar south pole, running simultaneously to conduct topographic studies and analyze rock samples via remote sensing.
“Our two Cheri rovers will work together and even take a ‘selfie’ of the mission, while carrying out mapping activities at the sites they discover, which we’re very excited about,” he said.
The prototype of the Cheri micro-rover was presented to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan by the head of the Higher Education Council (YOK), Erol Ozvar, during the opening ceremony of the national academic year.
“Over 120 of our students are working on this project alongside faculty members, while as a part of the EU’s ‘Go Space’ program, our students are also focused on developing communications protocols for satellites in space, stations to be established on the lunar surface, and orbital stations,” he said.
Yozgatligil noted that the faculty is also contributing to the space sector through initiatives like the Aselabs Program in collaboration with the defense firm Aselsan.
He mentioned that METU recently joined the microgravity research collaboration established between leading European and US universities, after signing a deal with Axiom Space.
“The most important international project we’re carrying out is the METU Space Technology Park, which will be a hub for space sector research and commercialization activities,” he added.
The premier aerospace event IAC 2026 kicked off on Monday and will run until Friday. It is co-hosted by the Turkish Space Agency (TUA) and SAHA Istanbul defense cluster and organized by the Industry and Technology Ministry. Anadolu serves as its global communications partner.

Herzog honors 6 Israelis who thwarted flydubai terror attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:34:38 UTC
23:34:38 KST

One week after the attempted terror attack aboard a flydubai flight, President Isaac Herzog on Thursday presented civilian bravery awards to six Israelis who rushed the attacker, subdued him and helped prevent him from crashing the plane.
The awards were presented at the President’s Residence in Jerusalem to  Tali Manes, Zvika Manes, Yaniv Hayun, Asaf Rajuan, Or Pardilov and Dr. Shota Musaiev, who also provided life-saving medical treatment to the flight’s captain after he was stabbed by the attacker.
The six thanked Herzog for the recognition. “It is a great honor that the president chose to award me the bravery medal,” Hayun said. “It will be displayed proudly in our home, and my children will be able to see it every day.”
Tali Mans said: “Apparently I’m a mother with maternal intuition, and I was in the right place at the right time, with the best possible people.”
Her husband, Tzvika Mans said it was the cries of his daughters that drove him to act. “When a parent hears a scream like that, you act without thinking,” he said.
Musaiev described the chain of events as a series of extraordinary coincidences. “A lot of miracles happened that day,” he said. “We were a chain of people helping one another, and if one link had been missing, the chain would have broken. Everyone acted heroically.”
Herzog praised the six for what he called extraordinary civilian courage.
“I have the privilege and honor of hosting you here at the President’s Residence, recognizing the tremendous civilian bravery embodied in your actions and bearing witness to one of the most chilling aviation stories known to humanity in general and Israeli society in particular,” Herzog said.
“This was a story in which there was no time to think, formulate a plan, consult or prepare. A story written without orders and without a briefing, without ranks and without prior coordination. A story in which fate was decided in a single moment. A moment in which a person discovers who they really are. A moment in which we discover who Israelis are.”
Herzog said the lives of all 174 people aboard the plane, as well as potentially many more on the ground, had been at stake.
“Tali, you immediately recognized what was happening and called for help; Yaniv, Tzvika, Or and Assaf, you jumped into danger, subdued the attacker and helped bring the aircraft back under control; and you, Dr. Musaiev, helped overpower him and also provided life-saving treatment to the wounded pilot,” Herzog said.
“You are the six who prevented a major aviation disaster, a disaster that would have changed the face of the country and the Middle East.”
Herzog also praised the flight’s captain, Smit Machchhar, who continued fighting the attacker despite being badly wounded and managed, with his remaining strength, to open the cockpit door.
“From here, on behalf of all of us, I send him wishes for a full and speedy recovery,” Herzog said. “I also intend to honor him, as the committee recommended, with the President’s Civilian Bravery Award.”
Herzog thanked the replacement pilots and other passengers who assisted during the incident, saying their actions would also be examined and recognized.
At the same time, the president stressed that the passengers’ heroism could not substitute for a full investigation into how the attack was allowed to happen.
“The civilian courage and resourcefulness demonstrated by the heroes here cannot cover up the obligation to provide full answers,” Herzog said. “Everyone deserves clear and satisfactory answers.”
‘Resourcefulness is a way of life’
Herzog said the award reflected not only the lives the six had saved but also what their response revealed about Israeli society.
“Tali, Yaniv, Tzvika, Or, Assaf, Dr. Shota, the Civilian Bravery Award does not symbolize only the fact that you saved lives,” he said. “It is also being awarded because, at the moment of truth, you revealed something much deeper: you revealed the face of the Israeli spirit. A spirit of courage. A spirit of tremendous resourcefulness. A spirit that says: when there is danger, you act.”
“You did not stop to ask one another, ‘Which side are you on?’ ‘Who are you planning to vote for?’ ‘Where do you come from?’ or ‘What is your worldview?’ You did not look for what divided you, because when the plane was in the air and lives hung in the balance, all those disagreements were meaningless,” he added.
“There was only one thing left: the person beside you. Your responsibility toward them. The duty to save them. That sacred mutual responsibility.”
Herzog noted that the ceremony came one day after the third anniversary, on the Gregorian calendar, of the October 7 massacre.
“Over these three years, time and again we have seen Israeli society at its finest,” he said. “A society that, in its hardest moments, proves that resourcefulness is not just a characteristic, it is a way of life.”
“This moment is also a reminder to all of us of the society we want to live in and the Israelis we want to be: a society in which, in difficult moments, we do not ask who is standing beside us, we stand beside one another. A society that does not ask who belongs to which camp, but who needs our help right now.”

Germany's Left to start Berlin coalition talks after antisemitism deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:34:34 UTC
23:34:34 KST

Germany's Left to start Berlin coalition talks after antisemitism deal
Oct 8 - Germany's Left Party agreed measures on Thursday to address antisemitic incidents, satisfying a key condition set by potential coalition partners and allowing it to begin exploratory talks on Berlin's next state government.
The agreement revives prospects for a three-party coalition between the Left, the centre-left Social Democrats (SPD) and Greens after the Left, a hard-left party represented in Berlin by lead candidate Elif Eralp, emerged from the September 20 state election as the largest force, with 25.7% of the votes.
The three parties confirmed at a press conference that they would begin exploratory coalition talks immediately.
The breakthrough highlights how tensions over antisemitism and the Israel-Gaza conflict have become a major fault line in German politics, with the SPD and Greens insisting on binding safeguards before entering coalition talks with the Left.
A successful coalition could help rehabilitate the Left as a potential governing partner elsewhere in Germany, offering a model for centre-left cooperation at a time when traditional coalition options have become increasingly fragmented.
However, it could also deepen cracks within the struggling federal government, with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz warning his SPD coalition partners not to enter into government with a party that he argues puts the "non-negotiable principle" of Germany's commitment to Israel up for debate.
SAFEGUARDS AGAINST ANTISEMITISM
The Left's success, displacing Merz's conservative party in the mayor's office, has been overcast by allegations of antisemitism over some members' association with pro-Palestinian protests.
Eralp and other party leaders say they oppose all forms of antisemitism while defending the right to criticise the Israeli government.
"Safety means being able to go to school without fear, to wear a kippah, and to speak Hebrew without having to explain yourself," said Kerstin Wolter, co-chair of the Left Party in Berlin, during a joint press conference. "We see the fear felt by Jewish Berliners".
The issue has been particularly significant in Germany amid a rise in antisemitic incidents since the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack on Israel and the subsequent war in Gaza.
Under the proposed measures, the state legislature whips of all three parties would deliberate on any antisemitic incidents and expel the accused lawmaker if they reach a consensus; in case of disagreement, experts would be called in to review the case.
The parties have also agreed to the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance's (IHRA) definition of antisemitism, which has been rejected by some Left Party members who argue that it can conflate criticism of Israel with antisemitism.
COMPARISON WITH AFD REJECTED
The prospective coalition partners also rejected any comparison between the Left Party and the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which polls indicate as the most popular party in Germany.
"The AfD fights against democracy. The AfD talks about deporting millions of people from this country," said Steffen Krach, SPD lead candidate for Berlin. "At its core, the AfD is an anti-democratic party, whereas standing before you here are three democratic parties." REUTERS

Türkiye and France have signed a roadmap aimed at developing bilateral defence and security ties and placing existing cooperation on a more institutional footing, the Turkish National Defence Ministry has said.
The roadmap was signed "with the aim of developing relations between Türkiye and France in the fields of defence and security on the basis of mutual interests and establishing the existing cooperation on a more institutional footing," ministry spokesperson Zeki Akturk told a weekly press briefing in Kocaeli on Thursday.
Under the roadmap, the two countries plan to hold regular consultations on defence and security issues and deepen cooperation in combating hybrid threats, intelligence sharing and air defence, while improving interoperability between their systems.
It envisages increased joint training, personnel exchange programmes between military academies, port visits and joint exercises involving land, naval and air forces.
The two sides also aim to develop joint projects and business opportunities in the defence industry, encourage information and technology sharing, and increase contacts between their defence companies.
Meetings under the roadmap are expected to be held alternately in Paris and Ankara, with the first planned for the final quarter of 2026, subject to agreement between the sides.
Mecca defence agreement
The spokesperson also addressed the Strategic Political and Defence Committee meeting of the Mecca defence agreement held in Riyadh on Oct. 5, saying regional developments and collective defence measures were discussed.
The meeting, he said, determined the initial structure of the alliance's secretariat and discussed a framework for developing defence industry cooperation.
"Necessary measures for the provision and deployment to Saudi Arabia of the agreed military forces and capabilities were discussed," the spokesperson said. "The process concerning the military forces and capabilities that may be provided by our country will be carried out in accordance with our Constitution and relevant legislation."
Israel's actions in region
Akturk also criticised Israel's actions in the region, saying they were contributing to heightened tensions.
He said Israel continued raids on residential areas, arbitrary detentions, land border violations, and air and artillery attacks in southern Syria.
"Turning a blind eye to violations and provocations by illegal Israeli settlers and extremist Jews targeting holy sites is also escalating tensions in the region," Akturk said.
He called on the international community to take "concrete and determined steps" against Israeli government policies and actions that he said were obstructing peace and stability in the region.

EU faces gas shortfall of up to 15% if severe winter hits, report warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:33:36 UTC
23:33:36 KST

The EU is entering the winter season on thin ice, facing a double-edged geopolitical squeeze that threatens to expose the fragility of its post-Russian energy architecture.
Europe could face a gas shortfall of 12% to 15% of demand if a severe cold snap hits this winter, according to a report published on Thursday by the EU's gas transmission operators.
The warning comes as the bloc enters winter with gas storage facilities just 72% full as of October 1, down from 83% at the same point last year, following what the report describes as a "challenging injection season".
The winter supply outlook, published by the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas (ENTSOG), examines two scenarios that assume no Russian pipeline gas supplies. The EU has largely phased out Russian gas, although exceptions remain for landlocked countries such as Hungary and Slovakia.
The report, published on October 8, warns that a disruption to the largest offshore gas infrastructure supplying continental Europe, combined with a complete halt to pipeline imports from Algeria, would pose a serious threat to the bloc's energy security.
Brussels has urged EU countries to maximise early-winter storage injections and maintain rigid cooperative behaviour to ensure equal sharing of any eventual demand curtailments.
LNG to the rescue
The report highlights Europe's growing dependence on the volatile global market for liquefied natural gas (LNG) as it moves away from Russian pipeline supplies.
The US has emerged as the EU's top LNG supplier, replacing much of the gas previously imported from Russia.
Even under normal winter conditions, a squeeze on LNG supplies could drive European gas storage levels down to just 13% by March 2027, potentially forcing energy-intensive industries to cut production.
"Under tight LNG supply conditions, high gas prices may also lead to a response from price sensitive demand, highlighting the importance of securing sufficient LNG imports and maximising storage levels ahead of and during the early stages of the winter season," reads the report.
Shipping constraints through the Strait of Hormuz — a chokepoint controlling 20% of global LNG trade — have severely throttled exports from Qatar and the United Arab Emirates since the US-Israeli war against Iran on 28 February.
While direct European exposure to Qatari gas is modest at roughly 8%, with Italy being the country most affected, the resulting global supply crunch has triggered an aggressive bidding war between Europe and Asia, driving up price volatility and leaving Europe vulnerable.
Europe's gas vulnerabilities
Western European countries have benefited from new coastal LNG terminals and access to pipeline supplies from countries such as Norway. But landlocked countries in Central, Eastern and South-Eastern Europe remain more exposed to supply disruptions.
If major pipeline infrastructure — such as the North Sea's Europipe 2 or Algerian import lines — suffers a disruption alongside a harsh winter, infrastructure bottlenecks will physically restrict the flow of gas from West to East.
Southeastern Europe could see immediate localised supply shortfalls of up to 12% on peak demand days, testing the limits of European solidarity.
As reserves dwindle, governments could also come under growing pressure to prioritise domestic consumers over neighbouring countries.
Brussels has given member states temporary flexibility to keep storage levels at 75%-80% by 1 November rather than the usual 90% target, in an effort to avoid panic buying and prices from going even higher.
Dutch TTF, the European benchmark for gas trading, was between €79.80 and €80.22 per MWh on Thursday, almost triple since the war against Iran.

The Department of Justice Task Force to Combat Antisemitism announced that the first stop of the ‘American Tour Against Hate’ will be in Southfield, Michigan, next Wednesday.
The nationwide campaign reflects the administration’s steadfast commitment to eradicating antisemitism, with the DOJ carrying out this mission as the agency responsible for enforcing the nation’s civil rights laws. The tour is a first-of-its-kind federal initiative that brings government resources and officials directly to local communities experiencing hate and discrimination.
The inaugural event, titled “An Evening of Unity,” is scheduled for 7:00 p.m. at Shaarey Zedek synagogue in Southfield, Michigan. The gathering invites community leaders and residents to stand together against antisemitism and hate. Leo Terrell, chair of the Department of Justice Task Force to Combat Antisemitism, is featured as the keynote speaker for the evening.
Terrell stated, “I am grateful to the president for the honor of leading this Task Force and tour.”
Terrell added, “We are spearheading the fight against hate and prejudice wherever it appears across the country. Particularly on a day that was so painful for so many Jewish men and women around the world, we are proud to announce this event and look forward to gathering with many of you in Michigan.”
US A-G Todd Blanche: Trump administration will not tolerate antisemitism
Attorney-General Todd Blanche stated, “President [Donald] Trump has made clear that this administration will not tolerate antisemitism, and the Department of Justice is committed to implementing that directive.”
Blanche added, “This national tour is an important step in ensuring communities across the country know the federal government stands ready to work with them to confront antisemitic threats, protect public safety, and uphold civil rights.”
Associate Attorney-General Stanley E. Woodward Jr. stated, “No American should live in fear of unjust discrimination or violence.”
Woodward added, “The Department of Justice is working tirelessly to protect and defend all Americans’ right to freedom of speech and free exercise of religion. This event is sure to be a powerful evening.”

Flydubai passenger recounts terrifying dive as analyst warns against learning 'the wrong lesson'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:27:05 UTC
23:27:05 KST

An Israeli father who was aboard flydubai Flight 1073 when the co-pilot allegedly attacked the captain told The Jerusalem Post that passengers were convinced they were about to die as the aircraft plunged, and then spent roughly 90 minutes not knowing where they were being flown.
In this week's Deep Dive episode, Uri Pintov, who was returning from a family vacation in Thailand with his wife and three children, said to the Post Editor-in-Chief, Zvika Klein, that he was walking back from the rear of the plane when it went into a steep, banking dive that pinned him to the floor for more than a minute. "We all realized we were going to die," he said.
Pintov described how passengers bound the attacker with airline headphones, carried oxygen and water to the badly wounded Indian captain, and assigned Israelis to escort every cabin crew member because "we can't trust anybody." With the cockpit locked and almost no communication from the relief pilots, passengers feared they were being taken to Yemen or Iran, he said. Only when a crew member recognized the airport at Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, did they begin to believe they would survive.
The Israeli passenger praised the Saudi security forces who received the passengers, saying they were "very gentle with kids and women." He said a tense two hours followed after it became clear Israeli aircraft would not be allowed to land, leaving families to decide whether to board a replacement flydubai plane.
He said that apart from psychological support from the community, there had been no formal outreach from Israeli officials. He called on Israel and the airline to issue an official statement confirming the incident as an attempted terrorist hijacking, to counter claims circulating online that it was staged.
Also a guest, Seth J. Frantzman, the Post's senior Middle East analyst and correspondent, added that several of the so-called miracles were in fact protocol, including the off-duty pilots on board. He noted that because the aircraft and its flight recorders survived, investigators should be able to reconstruct events in detail. He cautioned against overreacting the way aviation security did after the shoe bomber, and said flydubai is "one of the crown jewels of the Abraham Accords."
A permanent withdrawal of the airline would push up Israeli airfares, which are already inflated by a shortage of capacity, he said. Frantzman described Riyadh's refusal to admit Israeli planes as an understandable matter of national pride but a missed opportunity. He also argued that Saudi normalization is unlikely while the current government pursues its stated policies on Gaza and the Palestinian Authority.

Second mass stabbing attack carried out, filmed in Poland in 'grim copycat phenomenon'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:26:41 UTC
23:26:41 KST

A 15-year-old former pupil killed one employee and injured two others at a Polish primary school on Thursday while wearing a helmet-mounted camera, the second school stabbing in two days, possibly in response to an internet challenge, authorities said.
A 37-year-old woman who worked as a caretaker had died in the latest attack, which took place at around 9 a.m. in Leszczydol-Nowiny, northeast of Warsaw, officials said.
On Wednesday, a 19-year-old wounded 10 people, including himself, at another school in Ostroleka, northeastern Poland, and police detained a 17-year-old in Sierpc in north-central Poland on suspicion of planning an attack.
"We fear a grim copycat phenomenon," Prime Minister Donald Tusk told an emergency meeting.
"We are facing an extraordinary situation... for the first time, we are dealing with a killer who wore a helmet-mounted camera, intending to film the knife attack." It was not clear whether the attack was actually filmed.
Teachers injured restraining attacker
He ordered police to visit schools daily in an effort to prevent further violence.
A police spokesperson said authorities had information that the incidents could be related to an internet challenge and that this was being investigated.
Tusk praised the heroism of two teachers at the school who were injured as they tried to stop the attacker.
Head teacher Krzysztof Ochmanski said he had heard a scream and ran into the corridor.
"He wounded me with the blade of a rather long knife - he had three knives on him - and hit me with the handle," he told the public broadcaster Polskie Radio RDC. "By then, I had managed to restrain him."
A Reuters reporter saw an air ambulance flying away from the school, where a small crowd had gathered. The father of one child, waiting outside the school, said pupils had not yet been allowed to leave, but were safe.
Serious offenders becoming younger across Europe
Footage on public news broadcaster TVP Info showed what appeared to be the attacker being handcuffed and put into a police van.
Inspector Katarzyna Nowak, director of communications for the national police, said serious offenders were becoming younger across Europe.
"Over the past few months in Poland, we have seen arrests of teenagers who were preparing to carry out attacks... So, this is indeed a problem we face, and one we must acknowledge," she told TVP Info.
Interior minister Marcin Kierwinski said that the 17-year-old detained in Sierpc had mentioned plans to do "something dangerous" on school grounds.
"Data recovered from electronic devices revealed online searches regarding how to orchestrate such a violent event," Kierwinski said. Police found two knives in his possession.

Italy and the Republic of the Congo Working Together to Develop Special Economic Zones (SEZs)
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:26:31 CEST
23:26:31 KST

The seminar “Regards croisés sur les Zones économiques spéciales: Italian and Congolese Experiences’ was held on October 6 and 7 in Brazzaville, the capital of the Republic of the Congo. The event focused on comparing Italian and Congolese experiences in the development of Special Economic Zones (SEZs) and, more broadly, on the prospects for economic and industrial cooperation between Italy and the Republic of the Congo, according to a press release from the Italian Embassy in Brazzaville. The initiative brought together representatives from Congolese and Italian institutions, the private sector, businesses, training organizations, and experts, with the involvement of the Italian Trade Agency (ICE). During the seminar, the Italian Ambassador to Brazzaville, Enrico Nunziata, emphasized the importance of transforming the Congolese SEZs from mere areas designated to host businesses into true productive ecosystems capable of integrating businesses, infrastructure, services, training, research, innovation, and institutions. The ambassador also highlighted the need to draw on Italy’s experience as a source of expertise and best practices, while building a model of industrial development consistent with the Congo’s resources, priorities, and territorial characteristics. The African country has four SEZs, each with distinct regional focuses: Pointe-Noire, Oyo-Ollombo, Ouesso, and Ignié. During the seminar, participants emphasized the potential to develop these zones as laboratories for territorial development, leveraging their distinct strengths and fostering the emergence of integrated production chains. The central issue that emerged from the discussions was how to transform the SEZs into hubs capable of attracting productive investments, creating jobs, developing local skills and suppliers, and fostering the Congo’s integration into regional and international value chains. Cooperation between Italy and the Republic of the Congo, as the Italian Embassy in Brazzaville further notes, is already underway in various sectors that also fall within the framework of Italian initiatives developed under the Mattei Plan for Africa. During the seminar, various examples were cited, ranging from agriculture to water management, not to mention the energy sector. Last year, Italy ranked among the Republic of Congo’s leading suppliers. Italian exports to the Congolese market totaled approximately 140 million euros. This figure was cited during the seminar to highlight the potential that still exists for the development of bilateral economic relations. The goal outlined by the ambassador is not only to increase Italian exports but also to foster a greater Italian manufacturing and industrial presence in the Congo. In the various sectors identified as particularly promising for cooperation between Italian and Congolese companies, the press release continues, Italy can provide technological expertise, industrial know-how, and entrepreneurial capabilities, while the Congolese Special Economic Zones (SEZs) can serve as platforms to foster investment and partnerships. During the proceedings, the importance of taking concrete steps to address obstacles that may limit investment was also emphasized. One of the stated objectives of the initiative was to ensure that the comparison between Italian and Congolese experiences did not remain purely theoretical, the press release further explains. The discussions therefore focused on identifying potential concrete projects to be further explored through the involvement of institutions and economic operators from both countries. At the conclusion of the seminar, the Italian Embassy in Brazzaville confirmed, together with ICE and in coordination with Congolese authorities, its willingness to support the next phase and to facilitate contacts between institutions and businesses in both countries in order to transform the dialogue initiated in the capital of the Republic of the Congo into investments, industrial partnerships, local production, the transfer of expertise, and job creation.

Germany has extended temporary protection for Ukrainians until 2028

Unknown Publisher

Germany has extended temporary protection for Ukrainians until 2028
Kyiv • UNN
Germany has extended temporary protection for Ukrainians until March 4, 2028. From October 9, 2026, an exception regarding military service obligations will apply to new applicants.
On October 8, the period of temporary protection for Ukrainian refugees in Germany was extended until March 2028. This is stated in the Federal Law Gazette of Germany, UNN reports.
Details
The regulation has already been published in the official government gazette and enters into force on the day following its publication.
At the same time, an exception is provided for Ukrainian citizens who enter Germany from October 9, 2026, and are subject to military service under Ukrainian law.
Currently, about 1.3 million refugees from Ukraine reside in Germany.

Drones reportedly strike Russia's Omsk oil refinery in Siberia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:25:58 UTC
23:25:58 KST

Ukraine's General Staff confirmed that its forces struck Russia's Omsk oil refinery in Russia's Omsk Oblast on Oct. 8.
"The destruction of such facilities is the exercise by Ukraine of its inalienable right to self-defense in accordance with Article 51 of the UN Charter and is aimed at reducing the military-economic potential of the Russian Federation," the General Staff said.
Ukrainian drone manufacturer Fire Point had previously reported an attack on the refinery, saying that the refinery was hit with its own long-range FP-1 attack drones.
Videos and images from local residents, shared by Ukrainian monitoring channels, show explosions, fire, and smoke rising from the area surrounding the oil refinery.
Omsk Oblast Governor Vitaly Khotsenko confirmed that there was a drone attack on the region. Ukrainian authorities have not yet confirm a strike on the refinery.
Omsk is located in southwestern Siberia, north of the Kazakh border. The city of more than 1 million people is some 2,500 kilometers (about 1,550 miles) east of Ukraine controlled territory.
The Omsk oil refinery is owned by Russia's state-owned energy giant Gazprom. It's the country's largest refinery by refining capacity, processing more than 21 million metric tons of crude oil per year.
The plant produces a wide range of fuels, lubricants, and petrochemical products and is involved in supplying the Russian military, Ukraine's General Staff said after Ukraine struck the refinery on July 6. According to the military, the facility has a refining depth of about 99%, one of the highest rates in Russia.
Earlier, an overnight Ukrainian strike on the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat oil refinery in Russia's Bashkortostan region caused a large blaze at the plant, Ukraine's General Staff confirmed on Oct. 8.
Several images and videos show the moment the plant was struck, as well as thick smoke and fire coming from the grounds of the refinery.
"(The facility) is one of Russia's largest oil refining and petrochemical complexes," the General Staff said in a post on social media. "The facility has a processing capacity of up to 10 million (metric) tons of hydrocarbon feedstock per year and produces automotive gasoline, diesel fuel, fuel oil, bitumen, polyethylene, and other oil refining and petrochemical products."

Iran reviews US response to seven-day plan to reopen Hormuz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:24:37 UTC
23:24:37 KST

Iran is reviewing US feedback on Tehran’s proposed seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and expects to respond within the next few days, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said.
“The negotiation process is still ongoing, and messages are being exchanged through mediators,” Araghchi said, according to Iran’s official IRNA news agency on Thursday.
“We presented our proposal, which was called the ‘seven-day plan,’ and we heard the Americans’ views in response,” he said. “We are currently reviewing them. I believe we will respond within a few days.”
Tehran links Hormuz reopening to new talks
The seven-day initiative centres on restoring normal navigation through the strategic waterway while restarting negotiations between Tehran and Washington.
Araghchi said in late September that Iran could reopen the strait within seven days if the United States accepted the proposal conveyed through Qatari mediation.
Under the plan, Washington would be expected to take agreed steps during the first four or five days. Normal navigation through the strait would then resume on the sixth day, with negotiations on a final agreement beginning on the seventh.
Iran’s stated demands include an end to hostilities, the release of frozen Iranian assets, the lifting of restrictions on Iranian oil exports and an end to the US naval blockade of Iranian ports.
The proposal was discussed through Qatari mediation during indirect Iran-US contacts on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York in September.
On September 30, Iranian government spokeswoman Fatemeh Mohajerani said Araghchi had received Washington’s response to the Qatari-mediated proposal but did not disclose its contents.
Hormuz remains at center of Iran-US tensions
Iran has kept restrictions on the Strait of Hormuz while demanding that Washington fulfill commitments under a June memorandum of understanding, saying the waterway will not fully reopen until its conditions are met and US commitments are implemented.
The United States and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28, after which Tehran responded with missile and drone attacks across the region and effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz.
Washington later imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports.
The two sides later signed a memorandum of understanding in June on freedom of navigation through the strait, but implementation stalled over disagreements on security arrangements in the strategic waterway.
The latest exchange of proposals suggests that indirect diplomatic channels remain open as both sides consider steps to ease tensions along one of the world's most important energy and shipping routes.

No new mission in Saudi Arabia, planned redeployment says Crosetto
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:23:29 CEST
23:23:29 KST

Italy has not opened a new military
mission in Saudi Arabia and an increase in Italian assets there
is part of a redeployment planned since March, Defence Minister
Guido Crosetto said Thursday.
                                    
Regarding the presence of more Italian military personnel in
Saudi Arabia, "no one ever spoke of a new mission, but rather of
a redeployment (ordered last March - Ed.). If someone made a
mistake regarding this matter..." said Crosetto during a hearing
before the Foreign Affairs and Defence Committees of the Chamber
and Senate concerning the attack on the Ta'if base and the
presence of Italian troops in Saudi Arabia.
                                    
Crosetto was responding to objections raised by opposition
members of the committee, who had pointed out that the Defence
Ministry's website referred to "new missions."
The minister said that if some defence ministry staffer had
written about new missions then they should answer for this
mistake.
                                    
The assets in Saudi Arabia, the minister explained, involve 407
Italian military personnel: 242 for the Air Task Force and 165
for Operation Cerbero. Equipment present includes SAMP/T
systems, Stinger missiles, Kronos radars, and four Eurofighter
jets redeployed to a different base.
                                    
In Bahrain, there are 28 military personnel operating Kronos
radars, and in the United Arab Emirates, there are 75 personnel
with Skynex systems.
                                    
The CAEW radar aircraft and the refueling aircraft have returned
to Italy.

One Year On, China’s K Visa Remains an Opaque Promise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:23:00 UTC
23:23:00 KST

In September 2026, a British physicist posted an update to a months-long Reddit thread, writing that he finally had a K visa and that the visa “does exist.” The process had taken roughly five months from application to passport collection, although he acknowledged that part of the delay was his own doing, since one of his degree certificates had to be reissued and an embassy email sat unnoticed in his spam folder.
The application itself, as he described it, was simple; there was no interview, no invitation letter, and no question about his plans in China, and he found the visa center staff patient and helpful. The visa he received is valid for ten years, permits multiple entries, and allows stays of 180 days.
What made his post notable was its rarity. His is one of the few first-person accounts I found of a successful K visa application online. That is why applicants from Pakistan to the United States had followed his thread for months, asking for updates on his application and comparing their own experiences in the absence of detailed official guidance.
China’s Foreign Ministry’s own online application guide shows why that guidance is needed. For São Paulo, the submission city I examined, the guide lists the K visa among the available categories and allows applicants to identify themselves as graduates of well-known universities or as employees of well-known research institutions. Although the category is therefore visible, the page neither explains how “well-known” is assessed nor displays a checklist of supporting documents specific to the K visa. As a result, applicants can find the category but cannot determine from the online guidance whether they meet its requirements or what evidence they should submit.
The K visa exists, and there are public accounts of successful applications. What applicants cannot obtain from the sources I reviewed is the information needed to assess their own prospects. There is also no public indication of scale, since China has not published how many K visas it has issued.
The K visa was announced in August 2025 through a State Council revision of China’s entry-exit regulations as a new category for young foreign professionals in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) who graduated from “well-known” universities. It requires neither employer sponsorship nor an invitation letter and there is no numerical cap on the total number of K visas. It took effect on October 1, 2025, shortly after the Trump administration announced a $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions. International media promptly described the K visa as “China’s H-1B.”
The domestic reception was far less welcoming. In the days before the launch, hashtags about the K visa drew tens of millions of views on Weibo, where the policy arrived at a difficult moment. Urban youth unemployment stood near 19 percent, and recirculated clips of Indian media celebrating the visa persuaded many commenters that foreign competitors were about to enter China’s already strained job market. On September 30, the state-run People’s Daily responded with a commentary titled “Distorting the K visa will only mislead the public,” which rebutted the criticisms one by one and promised that the new visa would come with “supporting management systems.”
Those supporting systems have not been published in the year since. In December 2025, two months after the visa was launched, The Diplomat reported that the K visa was absent from the official list of China’s visa application service centers and unmentioned on embassy websites. In January, University World News reported that four government agencies were still jointly drafting implementation guidelines, which were expected to specify university rankings, subject lists, and age limits. Applications were expected to open by April 2026 at the earliest.
April passed without an announcement. In May immigration practitioners noted that the parameters for the K visa – including the age range defining “young,” the standard for “well-known” universities, document checklists, and fees – remained unpublished. As of early October, the public guidance I have reviewed still does not resolve these questions.
A comparison with China’s other openings is instructive. China has expanded visa-free access; such entries rose 49.5 percent in 2025. More directly related to the K visa, Shanghai’s Lingang new area published new measures designed to facilitate foreign talent residence in 2026. For both visa-free access and the Lingang new area measures, the guidance clearly states who qualifies and on what terms.
The K visa, by contrast, specifies the related fields and its minimum degree requirement, while the age boundary defining “young,” the standard for “well-known” universities, and the evidence required remain unstated. Applicants cannot determine whether they meet the requirement or how to demonstrate that they do.
In the vacuum, the standards that applicants encounter depend on the office they approach. An applicant in Pakistan reported that, after a month of waiting, the embassy told him the K visa “hasn’t been rolled out yet” in his region, and that the local document portal demanded a master’s degree although official explanatory guidance specifies a bachelor’s degree. Another applicant recounted being told in Beijing that the visa was reserved for fresh 2025 graduates, a criterion that doesn’t appear in any public document. The British physicist, by contrast, was approved in London as a Ph.D. holder who had graduated several years earlier, facing no such constraints.
These accounts are self-reported and should be read with caution. The difficulty is that, one year in, such self-reports are the only available accounts of how K visa applications are handled, because no official source settles these questions. When terms such as “well-known universities” remain undefined, applicants cannot assess their eligibility in advance, while the interpretation of these requirements remains with the officials reviewing their applications.
It’s not clear why the implementation guidelines have not appeared. Practitioners and scholars have offered technical explanations. Shi Hui, a senior partner at the law firm Dacheng, attributed the delay to the need for government departments to finalize supporting operational details, update the visa application and review system, and coordinate processes across agencies. Liu Guofu of the Beijing Institute of Technology, a leading scholar of Chinese immigration law, identified system upgrades and the establishment of procedures for an “employer-independent” visa, a category new to China’s immigration framework, as the primary technical challenge.
There is precedent for such a gradual path. The R visa for high-level foreign talent was created in 2013 and was supplemented in 2017 by implementation measures that further specified its conditions and procedures. These measures were extended nationwide in 2018 after trials in nine provinces and cities. That means the R visa took five years to go from the initial announcement to national application.
There may be a political explanation for the delay as well. The backlash to the K visa’s launch plausibly raised the political cost of visible implementation. The absence of published guidelines – and especially the lack of hard counts of the number of visas being issued – is consistent with that reading as well as theories about administrative difficulty.
Chinese officials justified the K visa by pointing to global talent competition; in its editorial, People’s Daily cited a projected shortfall of nearly 30 million workers in key manufacturing fields. However, critics evaluate the K visa against domestic youth unemployment, which reached 18.9 percent again in August 2026, its highest level in a year. These are two different standards for judging what openness is for.
The reaction among the visa’s supposed beneficiaries suggests a parallel misalignment. In one thread on an Indian diaspora forum – admittedly a single discussion rather than a representative survey – the top-voted response to a question about the K visa held that “Chinese government want K Visa folks but Chinese people won’t want K Visa folks.” Another commenter wrote, “I might consider a BYD car in India sooner than I’d consider a second innings as an NRI [Non-Resident Indian, an Indian citizen living abroad] in China.” The reasons offered – including language, “996” work culture, geopolitics, and China’s own youth unemployment – mirror the anxieties voiced on the Chinese side.
Such threads suggest that both the feared influx of foreign workers and the promised talent wave may be overstated. Each public is responding to domestic concerns at least as much as to the policy itself.
The K visa thus merits continued observation. Upon its launch, the visa was widely read as China’s entry into an intensifying global competition for scientific and technological talent. Its opaque beginning shows how much administrative work it takes to go from declaring an opening to building a channel that qualified foreigners can actually use. Whether the coming year brings published criteria, issuance figures, and consistent consular practice will indicate how far China intends to pursue that competition in practice as well as in announcement. This makes the K visa a case worth following for anyone watching how the global contest over STEM talent unfolds.

Estonia–Kyrgyzstan political consultations focus on bilateral relations and regional security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:22:05 UTC
23:22:05 KST

The consultations focused on strengthening bilateral relations between Estonia and Kyrgyzstan, with a particular focus on economic, trade and education issues. Opportunities for development cooperation were also discussed.
Estonia’s projects in Kyrgyzstan to date have focused primarily on improving access to and the use of information and communications technology, while cooperation has also taken place in the fields of education, healthcare, entrepreneurship and human rights. Estonia confirmed its readiness to continue sharing its experience in e-governance and supporting Kyrgyzstan’s goals of digital development and modernising public services.
Kyrgyzstan has been elected as a non-permanent member of the United Nations Security Council for 2027–2028. During the meeting, Estonia shared its experience as a Security Council member in 2020–2021, and both sides affirmed their mutual interest in strengthening cooperation in international organisations.
Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine was a key topic of discussion. Estonia stressed that Russia has not changed its aggressive course and that international pressure must continue through both sanctions and political isolation. Estonia also reaffirmed its continued and comprehensive support for Ukraine. Russia’s actions constitute a grave violation of international law and the principles of the UN Charter and must have clear consequences.
The meeting also covered the security situation in both the Baltic Sea region and Central Asia, with the participants noting that cooperation between countries has increased in both regions. Kyrgyzstan’s possible participation in the Ukraine Recovery Conference taking place in Tallinn in January 2027 was also discussed.

Experts in Baku urge action as missing persons surge worldwide and in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:21:34 UTC
23:21:34 KST

Around 280,000 people are registered as missing in Ukraine alone, with 10,000 new cases added each month, part of a 70% global rise since 2019. Forensic experts meeting in Baku said the obstacle was not forensic capacity but governmental reluctance.
Hundreds of thousands of people worldwide remain missing in wars, as experts who met in Baku warned that political will, not technology, is the obstacle to identifying them.
The figures have continued to grow, rising 70% between 2019 and 2024, according to the ICRC.
In Ukraine alone, around 280,000 people are registered as missing as of September 2026, with an estimated 10,000 new cases added every month, according to the same data.
Government officials, forensic experts, and diplomats met at the fourth International Conference on Missing Persons in Baku, under the Baku Dialogue on Missing Persons, to discuss how countries can cooperate to identify the dead and locate those who disappeared in both historical and ongoing conflicts.
Argentinian forensic anthropologist Luis Bernardo Fondebrider, who has worked across 66 countries over 42 years, said the pattern he encounters is consistent.
"In every country, I see the same pattern. The families want justice, want reparation, want memory, and want to know what happened," he said, attributing failure to act to a "lack of political will from the states."
He was unambiguous about governmental pledges. "The speeches about the commitment of the states" were "just words," he said.
"Today, there are almost no governments with the willingness to really investigate how it's happened with the missing and to ask for justice for the perpetrators."
Lord Brady, a member of the UK House of Lords who last visited host country Azerbaijan 16 years ago during the Karabakh conflict, said much had changed since then.
"We've had so much progress in the last few years," he said, adding that technological advances had opened up possibilities that "simply couldn't have been done in the past."
Christian Rivier, head of the ICRC's Central Tracing Agency, told Euronews that technology was only part of the answer.
"We don't need to be blindsided by the fact that technology helps us," he said. Processing the information it generates remained the central challenge, he added.
According to Rivier, it required "the human capacity to understand the information, to make sense of it, to ensure that there is an investigative medical-legal process that follows processes that are efficient and that avoid misidentification."
Azerbaijan's search continues
As of 31 August, 4,010 Azerbaijani citizens remain registered as missing linked to the first and second Karabakh conflicts.
Azerbaijan's State Commission says it has collected DNA samples from more than 11,000 donors to help identify more than 3,700 missing persons.
Rizvan Nabiyev, a member of the State Commission, said cross-border information-sharing was essential for "confidence-building measures" and "trust between societies".
Iranian-French photojournalist Reza Deghati, who presented a collection at the conference documenting the human cost of the Karabakh war, said he had set out to understand who those 4,010 people were.
The state, he said, had begun systematically collecting DNA from the relatives of the missing, "a list of all the families that are missing people."
Finding Ukraine's missing 'a colossal job'
The scale of the challenge is most acute in Ukraine, where the ICRC described in September 2026 "a staggering 280,000 people registered as missing amid the Russia-Ukraine war".
An average of 10,000 new cases have been registered every month since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Former Ukrainian President Viktor Yushchenko told Euronews that recovering the bodies of Ukrainian soldiers remained an enormous undertaking, describing it as "a colossal job."
Yushchenko said he did not expect Russia to provide information on those who remain unaccounted for. "In short, I am not sure that we will get such information from Russia, because it is Russia," he said.
"Russia is a permanent member of the Security Council of the United Nations, the most peaceful organisation in the world. Russia is a criminal," Yushchenko added.

Canada’s Anne Carson wins Nobel literature prize
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:20:53 UTC
23:20:53 KST

Copies of books by Canadian author Anne Carson are on display at the Swedish Academy in Stockholm after the press conference on Oct 8. (AFP Photo)
The Nobel Prize in Literature was awarded on Oct. 8 to Canadian poet Anne Carson, an essayist and classicist who brings a modern twist to mysticism and antiquity in her writings about love, desire and despair.
The 76-year-old was honored “for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature,” the Swedish Academy said.
The permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy, Ingrid Carlberg, said she had briefly spoken to Carson.
“We didn’t have so much time to speak. All she had time to tell me was that she is for the moment in Iceland, where she’s listening to the wind.”
“She was taken by surprise, but very happy. I could hear that in her voice.”
The Academy said almost all her literary production “has centred upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning.”
It singled out her poem “Nox,” printed on one continuous sheet of paper in homage to her dead brother, as “an unforgettable work.”
Carson has been mentioned as a possible Nobel laureate for years.
Many literary critics had predicted the award would go to a woman this year, given the frequent criticism directed at the Academy over the overrepresentation of Western white men among its picks.
There have been just 19 women laureates out of 122 since the Nobel literature prize was first awarded in 1901.
A 2018 sex assault scandal left the Academy in tatters and more than half of its 18 members were replaced.
Since then, every other literature laureate has been a woman.
Last year, the award went to Hungary’s Laszlo Krasznahorkai, whose works explore themes of postmodern dystopia.
The Nobel Prize comes with a diploma, a gold medal and a $1.2 million prize sum.
Carson will receive the award from King Carl XVI Gustaf in Stockholm on Dec. 10, the anniversary of the 1896 death of scientist and prize creator Alfred Nobel.

DM Katz initiates exclusion orders against activists deemed a ‘threat to public order’ during the West Bank olive harvest, i24NEWS learns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:20:28 UTC
23:20:28 KST

- i24NEWS

- Katz seeks exclusion orders against activists ahead of West Bank olive harvest
Katz seeks exclusion orders against activists ahead of West Bank olive harvest
The move follows a Yesha Council appeal citing plans by foreign activists, including participants recruited by the Global Sumud Flotilla organization, to join harvest activities
Defense Minister Israel Katz has directed officials to take steps toward issuing administrative exclusion orders against activists whose activities are found to threaten public order and security during the West Bank olive harvest, i24NEWS learns.
The directive followed an appeal by Israel Gantz, head of the Binyamin Regional Council and chairman of the Yesha Council, on behalf of local authority leaders in the West Bank. Gantz asked Katz to prevent activists he accused of planning provocations and confrontations from reaching harvest sites.
The olive harvest season began this week. According to the statement, the Global Sumud Flotilla organization, which led the Gaza flotilla attended by Greta Thunberg, announced that it was recruiting foreign activists to travel to Israel and take part in activities in West Bank harvest areas.
The appeal also cited organizing by Go Palestine, Protect the Harvest, Faz3a and the International Solidarity Movement.
In response, Katz instructed officials to pursue exclusion orders against activists assessed as posing a threat to public order and security in the area. The statement did not specify how many people could be affected or whether any orders had already been issued.
“The residents of Judea and Samaria are not a backdrop for the campaigns of foreign activists,” Gantz said, using the Israeli designation for the West Bank.
Gantz accused Israeli and foreign activists of seeking to create confrontations and said the olive harvest should not become a means of deliberately generating friction. He thanked Katz for responding to the appeal.

Zelensky to Rubio: There is no diplomatic dead end

Asked whether the war was indeed at an impasse, as Rubio had put it, Zelensky said: “You cannot, you understand, on the one hand negotiate with the ‘Russians’ about some economic projects for the future, and on the other say that we are in some kind of political situation, a diplomatic dead end, and so on. They will be happy to help us, but they are not yet as close to the result we need – to control the skies so that we can protect ourselves. We are talking about protection. The United States has this capability,” the President said.
As reported, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that he currently sees no prospects for resolving Russia’s war against Ukraine through negotiations. He said the situation now resembles a strategic impasse, which is a dangerous development.

Defense agency launches €195M tender for arms and ammunition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:20:00 UTC
23:20:00 KST

Defense agency launches €195M tender for arms and ammunition
The Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) has launched a tender for weapons, ammunition, components and training with an estimated value of up to €195 million.
The procurement is split into five lots — three for ammunition worth €145 million and two for weapons worth €50 million — with seven-year framework agreements for each.
The sum makes it among the larger defense procurements the RKIK has issued to date.
Under the terms of the tender, the RKIK intends to conclude a framework agreement to purchase 40 mm and 23 mm weaponry plus 76 mm, 40 mm and 23 mm ammunition. The tender also covers the purchase of various types of these weapons and ammunition and their components, along with training and instruction, as well as life-cycle support services.
The ammunition types include blank rounds, training and practice ammunition, as well as a range of live ammunition with various lethal and non-lethal projectiles.
The products must be manufactured in EU or NATO member states and currently be in use as standard equipment by conventional military units or special forces in EU or NATO countries. Products currently being introduced into service in these countries are also eligible.
The RKIK will conclude framework agreements with a maximum estimated total value of €195 million.
Under the draft contract, the seller may, in justified cases, request an advance payment of up to 30 percent of the contract value, but RKIK retains the right to refuse the advance payment.
If an advance payment has been made but the seller fails to fulfill its obligations, it must immediately refund the advance payment, including VAT, to the buyer.
The RKIK is accepting tender bids until November 13 this year.
Estonia's largest defense contract so far remains the €400 million IRIS-T SLM air defense system, signed jointly with Latvia in 2023. A HIMARS deal in 2022, worth over $200 million, was described at the time as the largest weapons procurement in Estonia up to that point.

Drugs gangs adapting as customs faces cuts, chief tells MPs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:18:18 UTC
23:18:18 KST

Drugs gangs adapting as customs faces cuts, chief tells MPs
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The Dutch customs service will have to endure substantial budget cuts because it is not formally counted as part of the country’s security system, its director general has told MPs, warning of the impact cutbacks could have as criminal gangs step up pressure on the country’s ports.
Customs chief Nanette van Schelven told parliament in a position paper on Wednesday that the agency will be hit by cuts planned for government departments. It will also miss out on the extra money the cabinet has made available to strengthen the national security sector.
The agency’s role in tackling organised crime “requires continuation and intensification”, Van Schelven wrote. Customs is looking for smarter ways of working, she said, “but efficiency alone will not resolve this tension.”
Customs, which comes under the finance ministry, has a budget of almost €982 million for 2027.
New smuggling methods
Customs officers seized 19,332 kilos of cocaine in the first half of this year, up 20% on the 16,104 kilos seized in the same period of 2025, according to the paper and figures provided by customs. That is already close to last year’s total of almost 24,500 kilos.
The paper also cited more than 106 million illegal cigarettes seized in the first half of the year.
Gangs adapt quickly, Van Schelven wrote, and customs has to anticipate trends rather than rely on seizures alone. She named dropping drugs at sea for collection, soaking cocaine into other materials, chemically disguising it, and smuggling via private aircraft.
The risk of drop-offs means smaller Dutch ports need to stay alert, the paper said.
Pressure on staff
Van Schelven’s “first concern” was criminal networks’ growing willingness to use violence and the pressure they put on the organisation and individual officers.
Arrests of customs staff for corruption show how concrete that threat is, she wrote.
Measures like periodic screening take a long time to introduce, and customs needs proper resources to protect its people, the paper said.
The hearing was held by parliament’s justice committee to discuss the government’s first national threat assessment of how organised crime undermines Dutch society. MPs will debate organised crime with justice minister David van Weel later this month.

Eckert free to stay as Southampton boss after suspended ban over Spygate scandal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:18:14 UTC
23:18:14 KST

Halis Sunnetci
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
Southampton head coach Tonda Eckert will remain in charge of the English Championship club after receiving a suspended six-week ban over his involvement in the Spygate scandal.
The Football Association (FA) said Wednesday that an independent Regulatory Commission had sanctioned the 33-year-old German coach after he admitted to three breaches of its misconduct rules.
Eckert was fined £28,000 ($37,000) and reprimanded, while his six-week suspension from all football-related activities was suspended until the end of the 2027-28 season.
The ban will take effect if Eckert commits a similar offense before the end of the 2027-28 season.
The charges are related to Eckert directing or authorizing the observation of Oxford United, Ipswich Town and Middlesbrough training sessions ahead of Southampton's matches against those clubs between December 2025 and May 2026.
The scandal had already resulted in Southampton being expelled from last season's Championship promotion playoffs and handed a four-point deduction for the current campaign by the English Football League (EFL).
Southampton welcomed the FA's decision, saying it hoped the outcome would bring an end to a regrettable period in the club's history.
"We are confident the manager has learned from this matter, and a suspended sentence allows him to continue in his role," club owner Dragan Solak said in a statement.
"I firmly believe that Tonda is one of Europe’s most exciting young coaches, and with this distraction removed, I am confident he can lead the team to a successful season," he added.

Prosecutors probe 'Islamic arbitration centre' in Padua
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:17:15 CEST
23:17:15 KST

Padua Prosecutor Angelantonio
Racanelli said Thursday that his office has opened an
investigation into an 'Islamic Arbitration Centre' giving
decisions on civil and commercial disputes on the basis of
Sharia Law in the northern Italian city after a complaint was
filed by a lawyer who is a member of the far-right National
Future (FNV) party.
                                    
Racanelli said his office would "carry out the duties entrusted
to it by law, conducting the necessary investigations, as
always".
                                    
He said that there were no suspects or alleged crimes at the
moment.
                                    
Earlier on Thursday Union of Islamic Communities of Italy
(UCOII) issued a statement distancing itself from what it
described as a "so-called Italian Islamic Arbitration Chamber",
telling members not to trust it.
                                    
It said the chamber was "an initiative launched entirely
independently by individuals unknown to Italy's Islamic
communities and lacking any mandate from them.
                                    
"None of the associations, Islamic centres, or mosques
represented by UCOII nationwide have promoted, supported, or
recognized this initiative, nor were they consulted," it added
"Actions of this kind cannot be accepted by Italian Muslims.
                                    
"The UCOII reiterates that justice in Italy is administered by
the courts of the Republic, in compliance with the Constitution
and State laws.
                                    
"It is a system that fully guarantees the rights of all citizens
and residents—including Muslims—and requires no parallel
structures".
                                    
The president of the centre, however, said it was not a court
and did not mete out alternative justice.
                                    
"We want to state this clearly: the Italian Islamic Arbitration
Chamber is not a court, it does not administer a form of
'alternative justice,' and it could not be otherwise. We conduct
arbitration—a widely used mechanism that has long been provided
for by the Italian legal system—aimed at resolving commercial
and property-related disputes," said the official, Omar Vanin.
                                    
"We do this," Vanin added, "to offer a tool to businesses and
individuals—including those of the Islamic faith who, due to
their culture and religious orientation, choose to follow
certain Islamic principles in commercial matters, such as the
prohibition of interest, principles of fairness in transactions,
and the pursuit of consensual dispute resolution. All of this is
done in full compliance with Italian law."
Noting "media attention that has left us bewildered," Vanin
warned that "fortunately, we possess the legal means to protect
our honor and reputation, and, if necessary, we will take
appropriate legal action."
The right-wing League party's leader, Deputy Premier and
Transport Minister Matteo Salvini, welcomed the probe and said
the League would do all it could to stop the centre from
operating.
                                    
"That's good news! I will be in Padua in person next week. The
League will do everything possible—filing complaints, raising
alarms, submitting formal reports, and mobilizing—to stop this
madness. There is only one law in Italy: Italian law," Salvini
posted on X.
