Ukraine targets Russian industrial hub in Siberia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:16:30 UTC
23:16:30 KST

Ukraine targets Russian industrial hub in Siberia
Ukrainian drones have targeted a major industrial hub in the Siberian city of Omsk, as Kiev carried out another UAV raid inside Russia.
Omsk Region Governor Vitaly Khotsenko confirmed the attack on Thursday, saying Russian air defenses had intercepted most of the incoming UAVs.
“One drone reached the northern industrial hub. Emergency services are working at the scene,” he wrote on Telegram, without providing details regarding any casualties or damage.
The northern industrial hub is home to several major petrochemical facilities, including the Omsk Oil Refinery, Russia’s largest. The area was previously targeted by Ukrainian drones in July, when several UAVs reached the site.
Operated by Gazprom Neft, the refinery has an annual processing capacity of more than 20 million tons of crude oil and is located approximately 2,500km from the Russian-Ukrainian border.
Kiev has ramped up its long-range UAV attacks on energy facilities and civilian targets inside Russia amid continued setbacks on the battlefield in recent months. On Wednesday, a child was killed and four other civilians were wounded in a strike on Belgorod Region, according to local authorities.
Russian Ambassador-at-Large Rodion Miroshnik said that Ukrainian attacks took the lives of 29 civilians, including two children, and wounded another 206 between September 28 and October 4.
Moscow has repeatedly described Ukrainian attacks on civilian targets as acts of terrorism. The Russian Defense Ministry has vowed to intensify strikes on Ukraine’s military and military-industrial facilities and related infrastructure in response to Vladimir Zelensky’s threats to expand attacks on oil refineries.
The ministry has since reported large-scale strikes on Ukrainian facilities involved in producing and storing long-range weapons, including sites linked to the domestically developed FP-5 Flamingo missile.

Germany wants UK to raise tariffs on Chinese EVs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:15:20 UTC
23:15:20 KST

LONDON — Germany wants the U.K. to raise tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles in exchange for protection from Made in Europe rules, according to a person familiar with Berlin’s position.
Friedrich Merz’s government believes the move would show reciprocity on trade and counter accusations from other EU member states that Britain is trying to “cherry pick” the benefits of EU membership, said the person, who was granted anonymity to discuss closed-door talks.
It comes as Prime Minister Andy Burnham met with the German chancellor on his first official visit to the country this week.
Advertisement
Burnham and Merz were due to talk about possibilities for Britain’s future relationship with the EU — after the British prime minister put rejoining the bloc back on the table of U.K. politics for the first time in a decade.
Berlin’s position on EV tariffs is significant as Germany has broadly backed a tolerant policy towards the U.K. on trade matters since Brexit — in contrast to more hard-line positions taken by countries like France.
The EU is in the process of drawing up new Made in Europe rules that would favor European producers over those outside the bloc — in response to trade practices by competitors like China and the United States.
The U.K. is worried that the measures will hit British business — especially automakers — and wants assurances from Brussels that it will get an opt out. If Berlin gets its way, those assurances could be dependent on emulating EU trade policy with regard to Chinese EVs.
Predatory strategy
Germany’s vaunted car industry, arguably the jewel in the country’s economic crown, has faced stiff competition from Chinese imports in recent years.
EU countries have accused China of dumping low-cost, state-subsidized electric vehicles into the European market and in December 2024 imposed countervailing duties as high as 35.3. percent on some manufacturers.
Advertisement
Industry Commissioner Stephane Séjourné accused China of pursuing a deliberate “predatory strategy” with state subsidies to the tune of €10,000 per vehicle.
The U.K.’s Trade Secretary Jonathan Reynolds told POLITICO last month that the government was keeping tariffs “under review, to be frank, more closely than lots of other issues” and that “different parts of our own sector want different things from” the government’s policy.
Hamish Falconer, the U.K.’s minister for European relations, told POLITICO's Brussels Playbook Podcast this week that he was “surprised” at reports tariffs might be a condition of Made in Europe opt-outs, adding: “That’s not the kind of conversation that I’m having with my European counterparts.”
Going ahead with higher tariffs risks alienating Beijing, which has expressed serious concerns about the policy. It would also raise the price of electric vehicles on the market, potentially making it harder for the government to meet its decarbonization targets.

South Korea Recalls Ambassador From Ukraine as Dispute Over North Korean POWs Escalates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08

23:14:29 KST

- Category
- World
South Korea Recalls Ambassador From Ukraine as Dispute Over North Korean POWs Escalates
South Korea announced on October 8 that it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine amid a diplomatic dispute over Kyiv’s disclosure of the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to Seoul.
Reuters reported the decision, citing South Korea’s Foreign Ministry, while Yonhap provided additional details about the dispute. Seoul has demanded an official explanation and apology over Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s disclosure of the prisoners’ transfer.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“The government has decided to recall its ambassador to Ukraine to Seoul,” the South Korean Foreign Ministry stated. "We hope that various issues between the two countries will be resolved smoothly, and we will continue consultations with the Ukrainian side to that end."
South Korea has accused Ukraine of violating an agreement to keep the transfer confidential. Seoul also objected to a statement from Zelenskyy’s office denying that such a confidentiality agreement existed.
Despite the recall, the South Korean government indicated that negotiations with Kyiv would continue as the two sides seek to resolve the dispute.
The dispute intensified earlier this week after Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha sent a message to South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun that included an apology. Cho stated on October 6 that the message fell short of Seoul’s expectations and announced that South Korea intended to take “firm measures.”
The diplomatic rupture adds to scrutiny of Seoul's stance on Russia's war, after South Korea shipped more than 176,000 tons of fuel, largely diesel, to Russia in July and August.
Seven tankers made 14 voyages from South Korean ports, including three vessels under UK and EU sanctions that declared destinations in Japan or Singapore before sailing to Vladivostok.
In August alone, South Korea supplied about 112,000 tons, or 31% of Russia's seaborne petroleum imports, making it Moscow's second-largest supplier after India. The shipments do not breach South Korean law, as Seoul's export controls primarily cover industrial equipment, technology, and electronics rather than petroleum products.

Russia Seeks Combined 152 Years in Prison for Eight Crimeans Accused of Ukrainian Intelligence Ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:13:58 UTC
23:13:58 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Seeks Combined 152 Years in Prison for Eight Crimeans Accused of Ukrainian Intelligence Ties
A Russian prosecutor has requested a combined 152 years in prison for eight residents of Russian-occupied Crimea accused by Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) of belonging to an alleged Ukrainian intelligence network, Ukrainian human rights initiative Tribunal. Crimean Episode reported on October 7.
According to a statement published by the organization on Telegram, the FSB described the defendants as members of a highly clandestine Ukrainian intelligence group allegedly involved in sabotage operations and preparations for attacks against Russian-installed officials in Crimea.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russian authorities claim the group operated secret channels for supplying explosives, carried out railway sabotage, installed surveillance equipment, and planned assassination attempts against Sergei Aksyonov and Vladimir Konstantinov, two senior Russian-installed officials in occupied Crimea.
However, the human rights organization questioned the credibility of the accusations, arguing that the prosecution's account began to unravel during the first court hearing due to contradictory testimony from the defendants.
Viktor Podvalnyi, whom investigators identified as the alleged coordinator of the group, told the court that he barely knew the other defendants.
Another accused, Kyrylo Barannyk, admitted to blowing up railway tracks but maintained that he had acted independently and did not know any of the other defendants. Barannyk also alleged that he had been subjected to torture during detention, including electric shocks, suffocation, and simulated drowning.
A separate defendant suggested that his arrest may have been connected to parking his vehicle near the residence of Russian-installed Crimean official Vladimir Konstantinov.
Another accused, Voynarovska, said she had signed testimony after an FSB investigator threatened to place her child in an orphanage.
The human rights initiative argued that these accounts raised serious concerns about the reliability of the evidence presented by Russian investigators and the circumstances under which testimony had been obtained.
The proceedings are being overseen by Russian judge Igor Kostin and two other judges, according to Tribunal. Crimean Episode.
The organization criticized Kostin's previous judicial record, alleging that he had earlier sentenced an innocent Ukrainian farmer to life imprisonment despite evidence establishing an alibi.
“Kostin was not the only judge involved in the trial of the Crimean residents, and the identities of the others will also be established. All of them will undoubtedly face an international tribunal for the war crimes of denying defendants access to a fair trial and complicity in unlawful imprisonment,” the organization added.
The case follows another lengthy prison sentence imposed on a Ukrainian citizen by a Russian military court. On August 4, the Crimean Tatar Resource Center reported that 30-year-old Ukrainian national Yan Haupt had been sentenced to 24 years in prison over allegations of planning and committing a “terrorist act.”
The Southern District Military Court in Russia ordered Haupt to serve the first five years of his sentence in prison, followed by 19 years in a maximum-security penal colony. The court also imposed a fine of 700,000 rubles (approximately $8,700).

Russian Oil Gets Too Expensive for India as Imports Sink to Lowest Level Since 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:13:55 UTC
23:13:55 KST

- Category
- World
Russian Oil Gets Too Expensive for India as Imports Sink to Lowest Level Since 2022
Indian refiners are cutting purchases of Russia’s flagship Urals crude for November delivery as higher prices erase much of the discount that helped Russian oil capture a dominant share of the Indian market after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Bloomberg reported on October 8, citing people familiar with the matter.
The pullback is being driven primarily by economics rather than political pressure. Urals crude loaded at Russia’s Baltic ports is now being offered at a premium of more than $10 per barrel to Dated Brent, according to Bloomberg’s sources, making it far less attractive to Indian buyers than it was when Russian barrels were sold at steep discounts.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Cargoes that once undercut competing grades by a wide margin are now priced close to crude from the Middle East, prompting Indian refiners to reconsider suppliers in the Persian Gulf. Some Russian barrels originally aimed at India are also being offered to independent Chinese refiners as traders look for alternative buyers.
India, the world’s third-largest crude importer, had already begun reducing its exposure to Russian oil after the adoption of new US sanctions legislation raised the threat of punitive tariffs. However, Bloomberg’s sources said pricing has now become the more immediate factor shaping purchasing decisions.
Russia’s share of Indian crude imports fell to about 35% in September, according to analytics firm Kpler, down sharply from a peak of 56% in July. The drop reflects both growing sanctions risk and the narrowing price gap between Russian and competing crude grades.
The decline is also visible in tanker-tracking data. During the four weeks through October 4, Russian crude shipments averaged only about 310,000 barrels per day, according to Bloomberg data—the lowest level recorded since March 2022, shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
China and India remain the two largest buyers of Russian crude, although the final destination of many cargoes is not always fixed when tankers leave port. Traders often decide where to send individual shipments while the vessels are already underway, depending on prices, sanctions exposure, and demand.
Earlier, the US House of Representatives passed bipartisan legislation granting US President Donald Trump expanded authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top importers of Russian oil and gas in an effort to squeeze Moscow’s war revenue.

AfD and Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance in Saxony-Anhalt call for a halt to aid for Ukraine and an end to Russia sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:06:27 UTC
23:06:27 KST

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the left-wing populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) have introduced a resolution in the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament calling for an end to aid for Ukraine and the lifting of economic sanctions against Russia. Regional AfD leader Ulrich Siegmund, who is seeking to become the state’s premier, posted a video on social media outlining the proposal. Political scientists interviewed by The Insider said the resolution has no legal force because Germany’s federal states do not have authority over foreign policy.
AfD and BSW lawmakers submitted the resolution to the Saxony-Anhalt Landtag (state parliament), calling for an end to military deliveries to Ukraine and the lifting of sanctions on Russia. The document states:
“The policy of sanctions against Russia, economic embargoes, and arms deliveries and financial aid to Ukraine has failed. The West’s one-sided partisanship in the war in Ukraine has not helped to end the war; rather, it prolongs the suffering of the population and increases the risk of the war spreading to other countries. The energy and economic war directed against Russia is causing massive damage to industry, commerce, and trade in Germany, as well as to our citizens.”
In the resolution, AfD and BSW call for diplomacy to become the main focus, for sanctions against Russia to be lifted immediately, and for financial and military support for Ukraine to end at once. The authors also call for Ukraine to retain neutral-state status while urging the Saxony-Anhalt government to “use all means at its disposal…to launch a corresponding initiative in the Bundesrat,” the German federal government’s upper legislative chamber.
Local AfD leader Ulrich Siegmund wrote on X:
“Not even 24 hours have passed since the constituting session [the first meeting of the newly elected parliament], and we are already getting to work. We are applying for a peace initiative and a special session of the state parliament. End the war, end the payments to Ukraine!”
German political scientist Alex Yusupov, the head of the Russia Program at the Friedrich Ebert Foundation (FES), told The Insider that, from a legal standpoint, the resolution introduced by the far right and populist left has no force. He said the fact that AfD and BSW made foreign policy, rather than regional problems, the first initiative of the new state parliament shows that both parties “continue to pursue a public relations strategy rather than practical policymaking.”
“It is simply a resolution, meaning a public statement of the Landtag’s position, nothing more and nothing less. It is a call to action and an appeal,” Yusupov added.
Dimitri Stratievski, director of the Berlin Center for East European Studies, told The Insider that all the issues raised in the resolution fall exclusively under the authority of Germany’s federal government, meaning AfD and BSW have no ability to carry out what they are demanding. He said:
“This is a populist move. But it is notable that, for their first test initiative, they chose an issue that has nothing to do with state-level politics. I think that was deliberate, because no concrete decisions are expected here and there is no political responsibility attached. Voters cannot hold these two parties accountable for promises they fail to keep. At the same time, AfD and BSW need to send signals to their voters.
As a rule, voters for right-wing and left-wing populists are not especially familiar with how powers are divided among different levels of government. And even if some are, it is not particularly important to them. They want the sense that their representatives in government are dealing with major issues. Ending weapons deliveries to Ukraine is also important to them because they believe it would save federal budget money at a difficult time.
In addition, to form a government in Saxony-Anhalt, AfD would have to enter a coalition with the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance. And they very much do not want to do that. The far right is not enthusiastic about the prospect of partnering with people who spent a long time in the left-wing party and are supposed to be strong opponents of the right. BSW does not look like a reliable coalition partner for AfD. But a joint statement like this on Ukraine — which cannot have concrete political consequences — is a trial balloon and an attempt to demonstrate some common ground and pull the two parties closer together.”
Stratievski noted that Ulrich Siegmund is already presenting himself as the leader of Saxony-Anhalt, framing his statements as though they were being made on behalf of the state even though he has not yet become its premier:
“Siegmund is behaving like a state official without having any authority to do so, but he has repeatedly said that he will become the state premier in December. He is doing this deliberately. On the one hand, he is mobilizing supporters. On the other, he is trying to impose on his political opponents a sense that it is inevitable that he, Ulrich Siegmund, will become the next premier of Saxony-Anhalt. It is a psychological and political tactic designed to convey the idea that ’the matter is settled, and I am already behaving like the acting head of the state.’”
In early September, AfD finished first in Saxony-Anhalt’s state election with nearly 44% of the vote. The far-right party won 39 of the Landtag’s 83 seats. The left-populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance won five seats and said it was prepared to cooperate with AfD.
On Oct. 6, AfD lawmaker Tobias Rausch, 35, became the first far-right politician in postwar German history to be elected speaker of a state parliament, taking the top post in the Saxony-Anhalt Landtag by a vote of 48-34. AfD and BSW together controlled 44 votes, meaning Rausch received support from at least four lawmakers outside either party. Because the ballot was secret, it is unclear who backed him, though speculation in Germany has focused on members of the CDU, the party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz. The other parties in the Landtag had said they would not support Rausch.

Europe’s changing face: How migration is reshaping the continent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:20:35 UTC
23:20:35 KST

Europe’s changing face: How migration is reshaping the continent
The native population in several European countries could become a minority within the next two decades if current demographic trends continue, according to a new model projecting the long-term effects of migration and declining birth rates.
Meanwhile, European governments continue to portray migration as an investment in the future, even as local communities grapple with high housing costs, overstretched public services, and persistent failures in border enforcement.
Who is doing the counting?
The Demography Dashboard was published earlier this week by the Institute for Remigration (IFR), run by Austrian activist and author Martin Sellner. He campaigns for sharply reducing immigration and encouraging or enforcing migrant departures, with the aim of preserving native majorities.
The model uses official national population statistics to project how migration, births, and deaths could change Europe’s population. It generally carries forward migration levels averaged over 2015-2024 and holds birth and death rates constant.
When will Europeans become a minority in their own country? The IFR Demography Dashboard answers that question - and shows how remigration could change the course. https://t.co/alL0saMOhb
— Institute for Remigration (@remigrationinst) October 5, 2026
Its “migrant” category includes arrivals from Africa, the Middle East, and elsewhere, as well as other European countries, both inside and outside the EU. Depending on the country, it also includes locally born descendants and people who have acquired a national passport. Citizenship alone does not remove someone from the category: Germany, for example, counts people who were born without German citizenship or have at least one parent who was.
“Native” generally means people without that migration background, but the definitions vary. Britain’s calculation uses ethnicity instead – White British and White Irish people count as native, while all other ethnic groups fall into the model’s migrant category, regardless of birthplace or passport.
The IFR’s projected dates show what could happen if its assumptions about migration, fertility, and mortality hold. According to Eurostat data, the EU’s fertility rate has dropped from 1.54 children per woman in 2014 to 1.34 in 2024, below the 2.1 replacement level. Deaths have outnumbered births since 2012, with 10.7 deaths against 7.9 births per 1,000 residents in 2024.
A generation of change
Switzerland is projected to cross the dashboard’s 50% threshold first, in 2038, from a modeled migrant-background share of 41.2% in 2026. Belgians will become a minority in their own country in 2044, Germany will cross the threshold a year later, and Sweden a year after that (2046). Their modeled immigrant starting shares were respectively 36.6%, 32%, and 36.8%.
The UK is also expected to reach that threshold in 2053, starting at 27.2%, while Spain follows in 2057, from a 25.4% base. For France, the dashboard cites a separate study projecting a similar shift around 2050 under its high-migration scenario.
Sustained immigration, alongside aging populations and low birth rates, are the primary drivers of the demographic shifts, according to dashboard data. Arrivals also include workers, students, family members, and asylum seekers from Africa, the Middle East, and elsewhere. Ukrainians have added another large European component, with some 4.43 million holding temporary protection in the EU at the end of July.
More arrivals, fewer affordable homes
Across Europe, immigration has added demand for housing and public services that were already struggling to cope. Spain and Ireland are stark examples of governments admitting newcomers without ensuring there are enough homes and infrastructure.
In Spain, immigration-driven population growth has outpaced housing construction, while soaring rents have pushed residents into the streets. The eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her Madrid home of 70 years last month has become a rallying point for sprawling protests across the country. The woman died on October 7.
Immigration is the main driver of housing demand in both Ireland and Spain. It is long past time government slowed the pace of worker and student visa issuance to ease housing demand growth. It should not be controversial to say demand needs to managed, and it is certainly not anti-immigration never mind anti-immigrant.

In Ireland and Britain, taxpayer-funded accommodation for asylum seekers has fueled resentment among residents struggling to rent or buy. Ireland’s purchase of Dublin’s Citywest Hotel for asylum accommodation prompted protests over the loss of a local amenity in an area already short of facilities.
Britain’s asylum accommodation contracts, meanwhile, are projected to cost £15.3 billion ($21.2 billion) over a decade, more than triple the original estimate. Private providers have amassed substantial profits while communities face added pressure on housing and services.
Security failures
The influx of migrants to Europe over the past decade has also contributed to a major security debate, sharpened by attacks involving people who should already have been removed, or whose dangerous behavior was known to the authorities.
Deadly suspected terrorist attacks have taken place in France, Germany, and Britain involving migrants, exposing failures in screening, monitoring, and deportation enforcement.
Foreign nationals accounted for 42.9% of identified violent-crime suspects [in Germany?] in 2025, disproportionately represented even as recorded violent crime declined, according to police figures.

Crackdown on dissent
Drawing attention to the issue, however, has been effectively banned in some European countries. In Britain, the overzealous crackdown on “anti-migrant sentiment” has extended to criminally prosecuting locals for social media posts opposing uncontrolled migration, or even something as mundane as waving the British flag in public.
In Spain, a group citing police inaction over crime and irregular migration has taken matters into its own hands, launching street patrols and handing suspected thieves to police. Its activities, however, are now the subject of a “hate crimes” investigation.
Former French presidential candidate Eric Zemmour has also faced prosecution over his immigration rhetoric. In September 2025, France’s highest court upheld a €15,000 fine for racial insults and inciting hatred over a speech in which he described immigrants as “colonizers” and Muslim clothing as the “uniforms of an occupation army.”
Growing backlash
Hundreds of thousands of people across Europe voiced their opposition to migration policies during the summer. Large marches were held in London, Madrid, and Dublin that saw protesters demanding stronger border controls and an end to governments leaving local communities to absorb the consequences.
The authorities, however, have frequently responded by condemning the protests rather than addressing their complaints. Ahead of May’s London march, the British prime minister accused its organizers of “peddling hate and division.”
Meanwhile, parties promising tighter controls have continued to gain public support. In Germany, an October 3 poll put the right-wing AfD at 30%, well ahead of the governing CDU/CSU’s 18%.
Washington’s warning
Europe’s immigration policies have also drawn criticism from abroad. US President Donald Trump has repeatedly attacked the approach, accusing European leaders of “destroying your heritage” through migration policies adopted in the name of being politically correct. His administration has put border restrictions and deportations at the center of its own approach.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio delivered a similar warning at February’s Munich Security Conference, saying mass migration threatened “the cohesion of our societies, the continuity of our culture, and the future of our people.”
Speaking in Athens on Wednesday, he accused Western governments of opening borders while surrendering sovereignty to global bureaucracies. He criticized the fashion of prioritizing the “global community over one’s own people” and called for cooperation to secure Europe’s borders against mass migration.
Orders to leave, little effect
European governments have increasingly promised tougher migration controls, but enforcement continues to lag. In the second quarter of 2026, EU countries issued around 110,000 orders to leave, while fewer than 37,000 people were actually returned outside the bloc.
July’s Ceuta invasion, which saw some 72,000 people cross from Morocco into the Spanish North African exclave in a single day, further exposed the cracks in what Brussels claims is a comprehensive migration policy.
Appeals, missing documents, and countries refusing to take people back have repeatedly delayed removals, while European governments’ own asylum laws have created further bureaucratic barriers to deportations.
Moving detention abroad has offered no simple solution either. Britain abandoned its Rwanda scheme in 2024 after spending nearly a billion dollars only to ultimately relocate four volunteers. Italy’s attempts to offshore asylum processing to Albania were also blocked by the courts, which allowed Rome to use just one of the centers to hold migrants awaiting deportation.
The pressure has also exposed divisions within Europe’s supposedly border-free Schengen area. Germany, France, Austria, and several other members have reinstated checks on travelers arriving from neighboring countries, citing migration and security concerns. Following the Ceuta crisis, Italy also reinstated border checks on all air and sea routes from Spain, with Madrid responding in kind.
The EU’s Migration and Asylum Pact, applied since June, has promised faster screening, asylum decisions, and returns. However, it has so far been unable to clear backlogs, carry out removals at the necessary pace, or give communities relief, instead adding yet another layer of procedures.
